# THEOPHYLACT ON THE FOUR
# GOSPELS

<note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107) was a prominent Byzantine archbishop and scholar. His commentaries on the New Testament were highly regarded for their clarity and were frequently translated from Greek into Latin for use by Western scholars during the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.</note>

# THE TRANSLATOR GREETS THE READER

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

The famous Theophylact, dear reader—though he is among the more recent of the Greek theologians and more approachable in his style of concise speech—is in my opinion by no means to be looked down upon by scholars; and not only should he not be looked down upon, but he should be commended on many counts. For he compresses into a narrow space those things which many others have handed down at great length, not without causing boredom for the readers. And indeed, he is brief, yet in most places he explains the mind of the Evangelists <note>The authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note> quite sufficiently; through this, you may clearly see that he aimed at this one thing: to be as helpful as possible. He is so approachable that he does not cause weariness, yet so brief that you cannot complain that he is obscure—a gift granted to few. 

It is apparent that, like a little bee making honey for its hive, he has gathered the most approved opinions from many authors. Above all, he has drawn the most "golden" interpretations from <term>Chrysostom</term> <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an Early Church Father. His name literally means "golden-mouthed," which the translator puns on by calling him a "golden fountain."</note> as if from his own golden fountain. Thus, in this summary, you will find very little lacking for explaining the Gospels among those things which Chrysostom had put forth in his winding volumes. He also follows Chrysostom regarding <term>free will</term> <note>original: "libero arbitrio." The capacity of agents to choose between different possible courses of action unimpeded.</note> and faith, and certain other matters, and consequently he is somewhat more forceful in interpreting certain points. 

I say this so that you may apply your own judgment—you who know yourself to be devoted to the canonical Scriptures alone. I do not say it to call you away from reading him entirely, as is the custom of some who, as soon as one or two sayings displease them, renounce the whole book. Rather, let us not reject useful things because of small blemishes. Even in humble huts there are... <note>The sentence ends abruptly at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>In this preface, the translator introduces the 11th-century theologian Theophylact, praising his ability to summarize the complex works of earlier Church Fathers, especially John Chrysostom, into a clear and useful commentary on the Gospels.</summary>
<keywords>Theophylact of Bulgaria, John Chrysostom, Biblical Commentary, Gospels, Free Will, Renaissance Scholarship, Humanism</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded the first part of the translator’s preface, praising Theophylact’s ability to summarize the complex commentaries of John Chrysostom. This page concludes that preface and begins the alphabetical index for the four Gospels.</meta>

...venerated. We have sometimes heard even stammerers discussing certain matters wisely. Look, here the author adds frequent paraphrases that bring much light; he beautifully connects things which <gloss>because of their complexity</gloss> <note>original: "διὰ τὴν πλάνην," literally "through the wandering" or "error," likely referring to confusing or difficult passages</note> seem to differ. In his use of allegories, though he is not solid in every instance, he is nonetheless pleasant. Indeed, I do not at all regret the labor which I spent on this book over a few months, at the request of my friends. And although I have not adorned it in a rhetorical style—nor would my daily readings, sermons, the pressing printer, and our own dangerous days have permitted this even if I had most desired it—I have nevertheless taken care to faithfully render what I had undertaken to share. My goal was nothing less than to avoid mixing in anything of my own or anything foreign to the text. Therefore, if he speaks well, the praise is his; but if in some place he does not satisfy your expectation, I am not the one to be blamed—I acted as a translator, not a dogmatic teacher. I will be able to publish the trifles of my own foolishness in my own books, if they seem to me to be of use to scholars. I have always dreaded having my own clumsy sayings sold under someone else’s venerable name. However, a mutilated manuscript forced me to fill in certain parts in one location, for a leaf was missing. Regarding this, however, I have provided a warning (as you will see), lest anyone accuse my faithfulness even in this; and you will not, I think, accuse me—however harsh and clumsy the writing may be—for I did not want Theophylact, the commentator on the Gospels, to be delayed from coming forth, who was previously almost unknown to our people. For it seemed more advisable to provide those things than nothing at all, if perhaps in this way I might earn your favor through such services. Farewell. In the year 1524.

# THE EXPOSITION OF THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,
### on the Gospel of Matthew: translated by Johannes Oecolampadius.

<margin>A</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'Q' featuring floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>JUST AS THOSE GREAT and divine men who lived before the Law was given to Moses did not learn from letters and books, but being endowed with a pure mind, were enlightened by the illumination of the Spirit, and in this way—with God speaking to them face to face—they came to know what was pleasing to God. Such were Noah, Abraham, Job, and Moses. 

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Why the Gospels were written down.</margin>
But after men became worse and unworthy of being enlightened and taught by the Holy Spirit, the merciful God finally granted the Scriptures, so that through them at least they might be mindful of the divine will. In the same way, Christ spoke to the apostles face to face in his own person, and sent the grace of the Holy Spirit as their teacher. But, since heresies were destined to sprout up <note>original: "pullulaturæ erant"</note> which would devour <note>original: "depascerentur," literally "graze upon" or "consume"</note> our morals, it was seen as a worthwhile task that the Gospels be written, so that by learning the truth from them, we would not be deceived by the lies of heresies, and our morals would not be utterly ruined. 

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Why four.</margin>
He gave us four Gospels, perhaps because we learn four universal virtues from them: fortitude, prudence, justice, and temperance. <margin>Matthew 10.</margin> Fortitude indeed, when the Lord says, "Do not fear those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul." <margin>Ibid. <note>In the same place (Matthew 10)</note></margin> Prudence, when he warns, "Be prudent as serpents." <margin>Matthew 7.</margin> Justice, when he teaches, "Whatever you want men to do to you, do also to them." <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> Temperance also, when he affirms, "Everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart." 

<margin>What the Gospel is.</margin>
It is called the "Gospel" <note>original: "Euangelium"; derived from the Greek word for "Good News"</note> because it announces to us prosperous and favorable matters, which is to say, "good things": namely the forgiveness of sins, righteousness, the return to the heavens, and adoption into <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page; the catchword indicates the next page continues the definition of the Gospel.</note>

<meta>Catchword: [Euange]lium quid. (What [the Gos]pel is.)</meta>

<summary>This page serves as the introduction to Theophylact's commentary on Matthew, explaining that while early holy men received direct divine revelation, the Gospels were written as a safeguard against heresy and a guide for moral virtue. The author justifies the existence of four Gospels by linking them to the four cardinal virtues: fortitude, prudence, justice, and temperance.</summary>

<keywords>Theophylact of Bulgaria, Johannes Oecolampadius, Gospel of Matthew, divine revelation, history of scripture, heresy, four cardinal virtues, fortitude, prudence, justice, temperance, definition of Gospel</keywords>

# CHAPTER 2. THE EXPOSITION OF THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.
<sig>a ij</sig>

<margin>Note the difference between merits and grace.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
...the Son of God. He announces, however, that we have received these things easily and freely, and that we have not attained these goods by our own labor, nor by **merit** <note>The author emphasizes that salvation is a gift, contrasting human effort with divine favor.</note>: for we have not received these things as a result of our own good works, but we have obtained such blessings through the grace and mercy of God.

**According to Matthew.**] There are four Evangelists, two of whom—Matthew and John—are from the number and choir of the twelve apostles; but Mark and Luke are from the seventy <note>This refers to the seventy (or seventy-two) disciples mentioned in Luke 10.</note>. Now, Mark was a disciple and companion of Peter, and Luke was a companion of Paul. Therefore, Matthew was the first of all to write the Gospel in the **Hebrew language** <note>original: "Hebraico idiomate"</note> for those among the Hebrews who had believed, eight years after Christ was taken up into heaven. Furthermore, John (as they say) translated this from the Hebrew language into Greek. But Mark wrote ten years after the Ascension of Christ, having been instructed by the mouth of Peter; Luke wrote after fifteen years; and finally, John after thirty-two years. For they relate that after the deaths of the others, the three Gospels were brought to the survivor [John], so that he might see them and judge whether they had been truly written. John himself, having been allotted an even more abundant grace of truth, filled in whatever had been omitted by the others; and those things which the others had spoken of briefly, he handed down more extensively in his own Gospel. 

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>On the harmony of the evangelists.</margin>
Furthermore, he obtained the title of **Theologian** <note>original: "Theologi nomen"; in the Eastern tradition, John is specifically called "Theologos" for his focus on the divinity of Christ.</note> because the others made no mention that the Word of God existed before the ages; about this, he himself divinely revealed it, so that the Word of God might not be thought to be a mere man—that is, to be without divinity. For Matthew, writing for the Hebrews, discussed only the substance of Christ in the flesh; for them, it was enough to learn that Christ was born from Abraham and David. For one who has believed from among the Hebrews is satisfied if he is made certain that Christ was born from Abraham and David. Now, what do you say—was one Evangelist not enough? Listen: one was indeed enough, but so that the truth might be shown more abundantly, four were permitted to write. For when you see four writers, who did not meet in one place, nor sit together, but lived their lives in different places, and yet wrote about the same things as if from one mouth, you will not wonder at the truth of the Gospel, but you will confess that they spoke by the **Holy Spirit**. And do not tell me that they do not agree in all things; for look: in 

---

those things where they might seem to differ: did one say Christ was born, while another says he was not? Far from it! For they are in agreement in those things which are most necessary and principal. Therefore, if they are not divided in the principal things, why do you wonder if they seem to vary in the smallest details? Indeed, for this very reason—that they do not agree in every tiny detail—they speak with even greater truth. Otherwise, they might have been held under suspicion of having sat down together and, having held a council, written by mutual agreement. But as it stands, when one wrote what another omitted, this is the only reason why they seem to vary. And that is how these matters stand. Let us now approach the sequence of the text.

### C H A P T E R I.

<margin>B</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' depicting a figure, possibly an evangelist or saint, holding a book or tablet.</image-desc> **The Book**] For what reason did he not say "the vision," or "the word," as the prophets did, who titled their books in that way? "The vision which Isaiah saw," and "the word which came to Isaiah." Do you ask to learn why? The prophets spoke to those who were hard of heart and disobedient, and therefore they used to say, "This is a divine vision," and "the word is from God," so that the people might fear and not despise what was said. But Matthew was addressing the credulous, the grateful, and the obedient, and for that reason, he foretold nothing in the manner of the prophets. I could also say something else: that the prophets saw with their minds the things they saw, with the Holy Spirit creating the apparition, and therefore they called them "visions." But Matthew did not see Christ merely mentally or through an apparition; rather, he was with Him corporally, and heard Him with his own senses, seeing Him in the flesh. And for that reason, he does not say, "the vision which he saw" (that is, an apparition), but: **The book of the generation of Jesus.**
<margin>Isaiah 12.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>

**Jesus.**] The name **Jesus** is not Greek, but Hebrew, and it is interpreted as **Savior**. For *Yeshua* <note>original: "Iesua"</note> is called "salvation" among the Hebrews.

**Christ.**] Kings and priests used to be called "Christs" <note>meaning "Anointed ones," from the Greek 'Christos'.</note>. For they were anointed with holy oil from a horn, which was placed over the head and allowed to drip down. Therefore, the Lord is called **Christ** both as **King**, because He reigned against sin, and as **Priest**, for He offered Himself as a sacrifice for us. Moreover, He was Himself anointed with that oil...
<margin>Who were called 'Christs'.</margin>

It also provides the Hebrew etymology for the names Jesus and Christ.</summary>
<keywords>Evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Hebrew Gospel, Harmony of the Gospels, Theologian, Jesus, Christ, Anointing, Prophecy vs Gospel</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary of Theophylact, moving from the general introduction of the four Gospels to the specific analysis of the genealogy of Jesus Christ as recorded in the first chapter of Matthew. It picks up mid-sentence discussing the unique nature of the Holy Spirit in Christ compared to the saints.</meta>

### CHAPTER 1. THE EXPOSITION OF ARCHBISHOP THEOPHYLACT ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. PAGE 3
a iij

...indeed and primarily, namely by the Holy Spirit. For who else possessed the Spirit as the Lord did? In the saints, the grace of the Holy Spirit was effective, but in Christ, it was not merely the grace of the Spirit that worked; rather, Christ worked miracles with the consubstantial <note>Sharing the same divine essence or substance.</note> Spirit.

<margin>Christ the son of David.</margin>
<margin>Psalm 132.</margin>
**The son of David.**] Because he had said "Jesus," he added "the son of David" lest you think he was speaking of another Jesus. For there was another famous Jesus <note>original: "Iesus filius Naue." In the Latin Bible, the name Joshua is written as "Jesus," the son of Nave (Nun).</note>, who took up the leadership of the people of Israel after Moses and waged war; but he was called the son of Nun, not of David. He lived many centuries before David and was not from the tribe of Judah, from which David descended, but from another.

**The son of Abraham.**] Why did he add David and the son of Abraham? Because among the Jews, David was more celebrated, though he lived after Abraham, and he was more illustrious in his kingship. For among the kings, he was the first to please God, and he received a promise from God that Christ would arise from his seed; for that reason, everyone called Christ the "son of David." Furthermore, David maintained a true type <note>A "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality in Christian theology.</note> of Christ. For just as David reigned after Saul was rejected by God and became hateful, so also Christ—after Adam was deprived of the kingdom and dominion he held over all living things and demons—came incarnate and reigned.

<margin>Why he begins the genealogy from Abraham.</margin>
**Abraham begat Isaac.**] He begins the genealogy from Abraham because Abraham himself was the father of the Hebrews and because he was the first to receive the promises: that in his seed all nations would be blessed. It is fitting that he recounts Christ's generation from him. For Christ is the seed of Abraham, in whom all of us from the nations are blessed, we who were previously cursed. Moreover, Abraham is interpreted as "father of nations," while Isaac means "laughter" or "joy." However, the Evangelist does not mention Abraham's sons from concubines—such as Ishmael and others—because the Jews did not descend from them, but from Isaac.

**And Isaac begat Jacob, and Jacob begat Judah and his brothers.**] You see that he mentioned Judah and his brothers for this reason: that the twelve tribes descended from them.

<margin>Genesis 25, 29, 30, 38.</margin>
**And Judah begat Pharez and Zarah by Tamar.**] Judah had betrothed Tamar to one of his sons, Er; but when he died without children, he joined her to Onan,

<column-break/>

who was also his son. When this one also died because of his wickedness, Judah did not join her to anyone else. But she, desiring offspring from the seed of Abraham, set aside her garments of widowhood, took up the clothing of a prostitute, and acting as if she were a harlot, had relations with her father-in-law and conceived two twin boys by him. Furthermore, when she was giving birth, the first one put forth his hand from the womb, as if he were about to come out first; the midwife immediately stretched out a scarlet thread and marked the boy's hand so he could be recognized as the firstborn. But the boy immediately drew his hand back into the womb, and the other was born first. Then, the one who had put forth his hand first was called Pharez, which means "breach" or "division" <note>original: "dissectio"</note>; for he broke through the natural order. But the one who drew back his hand was called Zarah. Now, this history signifies a certain mystery. For just as Zarah showed his hand first and then withdrew it, so the Christian life appeared in the saints who were before the Law and under circumcision. For all of those people were not justified by the observations and mandates of the Law, but because they lived a Gospel life. Observe how Abraham left his father and home for God's sake and denied his own nature. Consider Job and Melchizedek. But when the Law came, such a life was contracted. Just as in that birth, after Pharez was born, Zarah came out again later; so when the Law had been given, that life appeared again which was marked by the scarlet bundle, namely the blood of Christ. Therefore, the Evangelist mentioned both of them as if declaring that their birth was full of mysteries. And you can say it another way: you remember Tamar, even though she might not seem worthy of praise because she slept with her father-in-law, to show that since Christ took on all things for our sake, he even accepted this—to have such ancestors. Indeed, he did this so that by the very fact of being born from them, he might sanctify them; for he did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.

<margin>The mystery of Pharez and Zarah. Genesis 12.</margin>

<margin>1 Chronicles 2. Ruth 4.</margin>
**And Pharez begat Hezron, and Hezron begat Ram, and Ram begat Amminadab, and Amminadab begat Nahshon, and Nahshon begat Salmon, and Salmon begat Boaz by Rahab.**] Some think Rahab is the harlot Rahab who received the spies of Joshua son of Nun and saved her own people, and was herself saved.

<vocab>Theophylact: A 11th-century commentator and Archbishop; Matthew: The first Evangelist; Genealogy: A line of descent; Christ: The Anointed One; David: The second King of Israel; Abraham: The patriarch of the Hebrews; Isaac: The son of promise; Judah: The son of Jacob from whom the tribe of kings came; Tamar: The woman who bore Judah's twins; Pharez: Meaning "breach," ancestor of David; Zarah: The twin brother of Pharez; Rahab: The woman of Jericho who assisted the Israelites; Law: The Mosaic code; Gospel: The "Good News" or life of grace.</vocab>

Moreover, he makes mention of her <note>Referring to Rahab, mentioned at the end of the previous page.</note> to declare that just as she was a harlot, so also was the gathering of the Gentiles. For they committed fornication in their own pursuits; but having received the spies of Jesus—I mean the apostles—all who believed in their words were saved.

<margin>Ruth as a figure of the church.</margin>
**And Boaz was the father of Obed by Ruth.**] This Ruth was a foreigner, yet joined to Boaz; so also the Church, being a foreigner from among the nations and outside the covenants, having forgotten her own people and the worship of idols and the devil to whom she was joined, married the Son of God.

<margin>2 Kings 12. <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Samuel 12.</note></margin>

And King David was the father of Solomon by her who had been the wife of Uriah.**] Here also he mentions the wife of Uriah <note>Bathsheba.</note> to teach that no one should blush on account of their ancestors, but rather should take care to make them more illustrious by one’s own virtue; and that all are acceptable to God even if born of a harlot, provided they are endowed with virtue.

**And Solomon was the father of Rehoboam, and Rehoboam the father of Abijah, and Abijah the father of Asa, and Asa the father of Jehoshaphat, and Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah, and Uzziah the father of Jotham, and Jotham the father of Ahaz, and Ahaz the father of Hezekiah, and Hezekiah the father of Manasseh, and Manasseh the father of Amon, and Amon the father of Josiah, and Josiah the father of Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the migration to Babylon.**] He calls the "migration to Babylon" the captivity which they suffered when they were led away together into Babylon. The Babylonians had also waged war at other times, but they had afflicted them only moderately; at this time, however, they made them migrate from their own fatherland.

**And after the migration to Babylon, Jeconiah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel, and Zerubbabel the father of Abiud, and Abiud the father of Eliakim, and Eliakim the father of Azor, and Azor the father of Zadok, and Zadok the father of Achim, and Achim the father of Eliud, and Eliud the father of Eleazar, and Eleazar the father of Matthan, and Matthan the father of Jacob, and Jacob the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.**] Why does he recount the genealogy of Joseph? For what connection is there between Joseph and a birth without seed? For Joseph was not truly the father of Christ, such that the genealogy of Joseph should be considered the genealogy of Christ. Listen then: truly Joseph has no share in the birth of Christ, but it was necessary on that account for the genealogy of the Mother of God <note>The Greek term used by Theophylact is *Theotokos*.</note> to be reckoned. Truly, because it was the Law not to record the genealogy of women, he did not record the genealogy of the Virgin; but having set down the genealogy of Joseph, he thereby set down her genealogy as well. For it was the Law <note>Theophylact refers to the laws in Numbers 36 regarding inheritance within tribes.</note> not to take a wife from a different tribe, nor from a different family (that is, kinship), but from one's own kinship and family. And therefore, since such was the Law, it is manifest that by setting down Joseph's genealogy, he also compiles the genealogy of the Mother of God. For the Mother of God was clearly from the same tribe and family. For if she had not been, how could she have been betrothed to him? And thus the Evangelist observed the Law which commanded that the genealogy of women should not be set down, and yet he nevertheless provided the genealogy of the Mother of God. Moreover, he called him the "husband of Mary" according to common custom. For it is the custom to call a betrothed man, while still acting as a suitor, the "husband" of the betrothed, even if the marriage has not yet taken place.

<margin>1 Chronicles 3.</margin>
**So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations; and from David to the migration to Babylon fourteen generations; and from the migration to Babylon to the Christ fourteen generations.**] He distributed the generations into three orders to show that it profited the Jews nothing, though they were subject to judges <note>Theophylact interprets the first period as the era of judges/patriarchs, the second as kings, and the third as the era of exile leading to the Savior.</note> until Christ, and that they had need of a true Judge, King, and Priest, which is Christ. For after the kings failed, Christ came according to the prophecy of Jacob. But where are the fourteen generations from the Babylonian migration until Christ, since only thirteen persons are found? If indeed a woman were recounted in the genealogy, we could count Mary and complete the number; but we have just said that a woman does not pertain to the genealogy. How then is this said? Some say that he placed the "migration" itself as occupying the place of a person. Now the birth of Christ was like this:

### CHAPTER 2. THE EXPLANATION BY ARCHBISHOP THEOPHYLACT OF BULGARIA ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

<margin>Why Mary was betrothed.</margin>
Why did God permit her to be betrothed, and even allow people to suspect that Joseph had known her? It was so that she might have a protector in times of trouble; for he cared for her and kept her safe during the flight into Egypt. There is also another reason: to hide the truth from the devil. For when the devil heard that a virgin would carry a child in her womb, he watched her closely. Therefore, so that the deceiver might be deceived, she is betrothed. Mary remains a perpetual virgin; there is the outward form of marriage, but not the reality itself.

<margin>"To come together" means to meet or have sexual union.</margin>
**Before they came together, she was found to be with child of the Holy Spirit.**] "To come together" here signifies sexual union. For she conceived before they had any such meeting. Thus, the Evangelist is struck with wonder and cries out: "She was found," as if speaking of something truly marvelous.

<margin>Whether Joseph was righteous in deciding to dismiss Mary.</margin>
**But Joseph her husband, being a righteous man, and not wanting to expose her to public disgrace, decided to dismiss her secretly.**] How was Joseph "righteous" if the Law commanded that an adulteress be exposed—that is, denounced and punished? If he intended to hide the sin and transgress the Law, how could he be called righteous for wanting to send her away? This is resolved by the fact that he was righteous because he did not wish to be cruel. Out of great kindness and mercy, he looked after her, showing himself to be superior to the Law and living already beyond the literal legal mandates. Furthermore, because he realized she had conceived by the Holy Spirit, he did not want to expose or afflict her, as she had conceived from the Spirit and not from an adulterer. For look at what the text says: "she was found with child." By whom was she "found"? By her husband; that is, it became known to him that she had conceived from the Holy Spirit. Therefore, he wanted to dismiss her secretly, for he did not dare to keep as a wife one who possessed such great grace.

**But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying,**] While the righteous man was in distress, the angel stood by him, teaching him what should be done. He appeared to him in a dream. To the shepherds, who were simple country folk, the angel spoke openly; but to Joseph, as a righteous and faithful man, he spoke through a dream. And how could he fail to believe, since the angel taught him about the very things he was pondering in his mind—things he had told to no one? For while he was thinking and not speaking, the angel appeared. Rightly, therefore, did he believe this was from God. For it belongs to God alone to know the things we do not speak aloud.

**Joseph, son of David.**] By calling him the "son of David," the angel brought to mind the prophecy that the Christ would come from David’s seed. By saying this, he warned him not to be skeptical, but to think of David, who had received the promise concerning the Christ.

**Do not fear.**] This shows that Joseph was afraid to keep her, lest he might offend God by harboring a woman he suspected of adultery. Alternatively, "Do not fear" means: you are afraid to be joined to her because she has conceived from the Spirit, but do not be afraid.

**Take her.**] This means, keep her in your home and within your heart. For in his thoughts and mind, he had already sent her away.

**Mary your wife.**] The angel says this to mean: you perhaps think she is an adulteress, but I tell you that she is your wife—that is, she has been violated by no one, but remains your betrothed.

**For that which is born in her is from the Holy Spirit.**] Not only is she free from any illicit union, but she has conceived in a more divine way; therefore, you ought all the more to rejoice.

**And she shall bring forth a son.**] Lest anyone should say, "Why should I believe you that this is from the Holy Spirit?", the angel speaks of the future: that she is to bring forth a son. For if the angel speaks the truth about this future event, it is clear that what he said about the Holy Spirit is also true. He did not say, "she shall bear *for you* a son," but simply "she shall bear." For she did not bear Him for Joseph, but for the whole world; the grace was not done for him alone, but was poured out upon all.

**And you shall call his name Jesus.**] You shall call Him, acting as his father and the caretaker of the Virgin. Do not suspect, Joseph, that because the conception is from the Spirit, you should therefore dismiss the Virgin and leave her without help; rather, you shall serve her in all things.

**For he shall save his people.**] At this point, the text interprets what "Jesus" means—namely, "Savior." For He Himself (it says) shall save His people—not only the Jewish people, but also the Gentiles who do not hesitate to believe and become His people. But how will He save? From their enemies? Not at all, but from their sins. From this it is clear that the one being born is God, for it belongs to God alone to forgive sins.

<summary>Theophylact explains the betrothal of Mary as a divine strategy to protect her and deceive the devil, while interpreting Joseph's desire to "secretly dismiss" her as an act of superior, merciful righteousness rather than Law-breaking.</summary>

### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>Isaiah 7.</margin> **D** **All this was done that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying.**] Do not think that these things only recently began to please God; they were planned in the ages above and from the beginning. For you know that Joseph, being learned in the Law, was a prophet, and you should take note of what was "spoken by the Lord." He did not say "spoken by Isaiah," but "by the Lord." For it was not a man who spoke, but God through the mouth of a man; therefore, the oracle is worthy of faith.

**Behold, a virgin shall be with child.**] The Hebrews <note>Theophylact often uses "the Hebrews" to refer to Jewish scholars or the Hebrew text of the Old Testament.</note> claim that the word in the prophet is not "virgin," but "young woman." To this, it must be said that in Scripture, "young woman" and "virgin" mean the same thing. For the text calls her a "young woman" to mean she is incorrupt. Moreover, if she had not given birth as a virgin, how would it be a "sign" and a "wonder"? For listen to Isaiah **E** saying, "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign." And he immediately adds, "Behold, a virgin," etc. Otherwise, if she did not give birth as a virgin, it would be no sign at all. Thus, the Hebrews through their own malice corrupt the Scripture and put "young woman" in place of "virgin." Therefore, whether she is called a young woman or a virgin, it must be understood entirely as a virgin, so that this may truly be a miracle.

<margin>Isaiah's testimony concerning the virgin against the Jews.</margin> **And she shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us.**] The Hebrews ask: "How is it then that he was not called Emmanuel, but Jesus Christ?" It must be answered that the text does not say "he called," but "they shall call"—that is, his works will demonstrate that he is God and that he lives among us. For Divine Scripture assigns names based on works, just as when it says: "Call his name **F** 'Swiftly Spoil'." <note>original: "Velociter prædare." This refers to the prophetic name Maher-shalal-hash-baz in Isaiah 8:3.</note> And where was he ever called by such a name? Because as soon as the Lord was born, error was plundered and led away captive; thus he is said to be named from the work performed, an appellation found in his deeds.

<margin>"Swiftly Spoil."</margin> **Then Joseph, being raised from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him.**] See his eager spirit, and how immediately he obeyed.

**And took unto him his wife.**] He continuously calls her Joseph's "wife," casting out any evil suspicion and teaching that she did not belong to another, but was indeed his wife.

**And knew her not until she had brought forth her firstborn son.**] This means he never had sexual relations with her.

<column-break/>

<header>EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. 6</header>
<page-num>6</page-num>

**A** For in this place, the word "until" <note>original: "donec"</note> does not imply that he did not know her up to the birth and then knew her afterward; rather, it means he never knew her at all. This is a common idiom of Scripture. For example, when it says "the raven returned not to the ark *until* the earth was dried," <margin>Genesis 8.</margin> it does not mean the raven returned afterward. Likewise, in another place, "I am with you *until* the end of the world"; <margin>Matthew 28.</margin> does this mean he will not be with us after the end? By no means! For then he will be with us much more. Thus, in this place, understand "until she had brought forth" to mean he knew her neither before the birth nor after the birth. For how could that holy man have touched her after she had experienced such an ineffable birth? He calls him his **B** "firstborn" son, not because another was born after him, but simply as the first and only one born. For Christ is both the firstborn, as the first to be born, and the only-begotten, as having no other brother. 

<margin>Christ as firstborn and only-begotten.</margin>

**And he called his name Jesus.**] This demonstrates Joseph's obedience, because he did everything exactly as the angel had told him.

### CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "C" depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, within a circular frame.</image-desc>

**Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea.**] Bethlehem is interpreted as "house of bread," and Judea as "confession." <note>Theophylact is using etymologies: Bethlehem from Hebrew 'Beit Lechem' (House of Bread) and Judea from 'Yehudah' (praise/confession).</note> Let it be, then, that through confession we may now become a house of spiritual bread.

**In the days of Herod.**] He mentions Herod so that you may learn that the kings and princes from the tribe of Judah had failed, and therefore Christ necessarily came. For Herod was not a Jew, but an Idumaean <note>An ethnic group from Idumea/Edom, south of Judea.</note>, the son of Antipater by an Arabian wife. Since the [Jewish] princes had failed, the "Expectation of the Nations" arrived, just as Jacob predicted.

<margin>The origin of Herod. Genesis 49.</margin>

**The King.**] For there was also another Herod who was a Tetrarch, and for this reason he specifies the title of "King."

**Behold, there came Wise Men from the east to Jerusalem.**] Why do the Wise Men [Magi] come? For the condemnation of the Jews. For when the Magi, men devoted to the worship of idols, believed, what defense can the Jews later offer? There is another reason: so that the glory of Christ might shine more brightly through the testimony of the Magi, who were previously adversaries of God and subject to demons.

### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. 7

<margin>D</margin> **From the east.**] This also serves as a condemnation of the Jews. For these men came from such a great distance, while the Hebrews persecuted Christ even though they had him right among them.

**Saying, Where is he who is born king of the Jews?**] It is said that these Magi were the descendants of Balaam the soothsayer <note>Balaam was a non-Israelite prophet in the Book of Numbers who famously predicted a "star" rising out of Jacob.</note>. For when they discovered his prophecy, <margin>Numbers 24.</margin> "A star shall rise out of Jacob," they understood the mystery of Christ, and for that reason, they wished to go to him when he was born.

<margin>The star was an angelic power.</margin> **For we have seen his star in the east.**] When you hear of a "star," do not think it was one like those we see in the sky, but rather a divine and angelic power appearing in the form of a star. Since the Magi were astrologers, <margin>Luke 2.</margin> the Lord led them by a sign they were familiar with. This is just as he hunted for Peter the fisherman by a multitude of fish and brought him to the name of Christ by making him marvel. It is manifest that the star was an angelic power from the fact that it shone during the day, moved when the Magi moved, and rested when they rested. Furthermore, it moved from the northern region, where Persia is, to the south, where Jerusalem is. A natural star never turns from the north to the south.

<margin>E</margin> **And we have come to adore him.**] These Magi appear to be endowed with great virtue. For since they were willing to adore him in a foreign land, how much more must they have preached with great freedom in Persia itself?

<margin>F</margin> **When Herod the king heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.**] Herod was indeed troubled because, as a foreigner, he feared for his kingdom; for he knew that he was unworthy of it. But why were the Jews troubled? They ought to have rejoiced instead, that their king was being adored by Persian kings. But in truth, malice is a foolish possession.

**And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ should be born.**] <margin>Scribes.</margin> The scribes were the teachers of the people, similar to those we call "grammarians" <note>Theophylact compares the biblical Scribes to the *grammatoi* of his own time—scholars of literature and law.</note>. By a singular divine arrangement, they are questioned so that they might confess the truth; thus, they are condemned for later crucifying the one whom they had previously confessed.

<margin>A</margin> **And they said to him, In Bethlehem of Judah. For so it is written by the prophet.**] By which prophet? By Micah. For he says:

**And you Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means the least among the princes of Judah.**] For it was despised because it was small; but now, because Christ came forth from it, it is famous. <margin>Micah 5.</margin> For all people come from the ends of the earth and adore holy Bethlehem.

**For out of you shall come a ruler.**] "He shall come out," he says; he will not remain in you—and rightly so. For Christ did not remain in Bethlehem, but after he was born, he departed from it, <margin>Matthew 2.</margin> and frequently lived in Nazareth. The Jews, however, say that this was predicted concerning Zerubbabel <note>A governor of the Achaemenid Empire's Judean province and a grandson of Jehoiachin.</note>, but they are clearly lying. For Zerubbabel was not <margin>B</margin> born in Bethlehem. Indeed, his name "Zoro" signifies "seed" or "birth," and "Babel" signifies "Babylon"—that is, "one born or begotten in Babylon." But the prophet also clearly refutes them, saying: "His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity." Whose "goings forth" are from the beginning and from the days of eternity other than Christ’s? He had two "goings forth," that is, two births. For his first birth was from the beginning from the Father, and his second was from the days of the age, taking its beginning from the Mother of God <note>original: *mater dei*, likely referring to the Virgin Mary</note>, which occurred in time. <margin>Micah 5.</margin> Let the Jews say, then, whether Zerubbabel existed from the beginning; they have nothing they can say.

**Who shall feed my people Israel.**] He said "shall feed," not <margin>C</margin> "shall exercise tyranny" or "shall devour." For other kings are not shepherds but wolves; Christ, however, is a shepherd, as he himself says: "I am the good shepherd." He says "the people of Israel" to refer to both those of the Jews and those of the Gentiles who believed. For "Israel" is interpreted as "one seeing God" <note>A common medieval etymology of the name Israel (Yisra-El).</note>; therefore, all <margin>Christ the shepherd.</margin> who see God are Israelites, even if they were born from the Gentiles.

**Then Herod, privately calling the Magi.**] He called them secretly because of the Jews. For he suspected that the Jews might perhaps make a great deal of the child and care for him as their liberator, and for that reason, he laid his snare in secret. <margin>John 10.</margin>

**He diligently inquired of them the time of the star which appeared.**] That is, he learned it accurately. For the star, before—

### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

<margin>D</margin> **When the Lord was born,**] he had already appeared to the Magi. Because they were going to undertake a journey of a long duration, the star appeared much earlier. They adore him while he is still in swaddling clothes. However, some say that the star appeared at the moment Christ was born, and that the Magi traveled for a two-year period, and thus did not find the child in swaddling clothes or in a manger, but in a house with his mother at two years of age. But you should hold to the former opinion, as it is the better one. <note>Theophylact is weighing two common traditions: one where the Magi arrive at the Nativity, and another where they arrive much later, which Herod used to justify killing children "two years old and under."</note>

**And sending them to Bethlehem, he said, "Go, and search diligently for this child."**] He did not say "for the king," but "for the child." He could not even bear to speak the name, demonstrating how much he raged against him in his madness.

<margin>E</margin> **"But when you have found him, report back to me, so that I too may come and adore him." But having heard the king, they departed.**] Being without deceit themselves, they thought that he also spoke without deceit.

**And behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them.**] The star was hidden for a short time by a singular divine arrangement, so that they might question the Jews, Herod might be troubled, and the truth might be made more manifest. But as they departed from Jerusalem, it appeared again leading them. From this it is clear that the star was a power <note>original: "virtus" — likely referring to an angelic or spiritual force rather than a physical celestial body.</note>.

**Until, having gone ahead, it stood over where the child was.**] This too was extraordinary. For the star descended from the heights and, having been made closer to the earth, it showed them the place. For if it had appeared from the heights, how could they have been certain of the place where Christ was? Stars encompass a vast area. For this reason, you might see the moon over your house, and I see the same moon, but it seems to be only over my house; to everyone, the moon or any other star seems to stand only over their own house. Therefore, that star would not have pointed out Christ unless it had descended and stood, as it were, over the head of the child.

<margin>F</margin> **But seeing the star, they rejoiced with very great joy.**] Because they had not gone astray, but had found what they were seeking.

**And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother.**] Indeed, as soon as he was born, the Virgin laid the child in a manger, for they had not found a house. But it is likely that they found a house afterward, where the Magi also found them. For they had gone up to Bethlehem so that

<column-break/>

<page-num>8</page-num>
**ENARRATION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW**

<margin>A</margin> they might be registered there, just as Luke says. But with a great multitude gathering for the census, they did not have a house for a time, so he was born in a cave; then, after a house was found, the Lord was seen there by the Magi.

**And falling down, they adored him.**] Behold the illumination of the soul. They saw a poor child and they adored him. For they had learned by many proofs that he was God; therefore they also offered gifts to him, as to God and as to man. Listen now:

<margin>Why gold, incense, and myrrh.</margin> **And opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.**] Indeed, they offered gold to him as to a king. For subjects pay gold to kings. Frankincense, however, as to God. For we burn frankincense to God. But myrrh as to one who would taste death. For the Jews bury the dead with myrrh so that the body may remain incorrupt. For since myrrh is dry, it parches and dries up moisture and does not allow worms to be born. You see the faith of the Magi, that they also learned from the prophet Balaam <note>A non-Israelite prophet from the Book of Numbers, whom tradition links to the Magi's wisdom.</note> that he was Lord and God and King, and would die for us. Listen to the prophet: "When he has lain down," he says, "he shall rest like a lion." <note>original: "Quum recubuerit... requiescet vt leo" — a reference to the prophecy in Numbers 24:9.</note> Behold, he signifies royal dignity through the "lion," but mortality when he says "when he has lain down." "Those who bless you shall be blessed": behold also his divinity. For only the nature of God has this power of blessing.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>Numbers 24.</margin>

**And having received an oracle in their sleep not to return to Herod, they went back to their own region by another way.**] See the sequence: first God brought them to faith through the star; then when they came to Jerusalem, he taught them through the prophet that he was born in Bethlehem; and finally through an angel. And they obeyed the oracle, that is, the divine conversation. Therefore, having received the oracle and the vision from God, they deceived Herod and did not fear that he might perhaps pursue them, but trusted in the power of him who was born, and were true witnesses.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Micah 5.</margin>

**But when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: "Rise, and take the child and his mother."**] Did you see for what reason God permitted the Virgin to be betrothed? For here it appears that it was done by God so that Joseph might carry out diligent care for her. He did not say, however, "take your wife," but "his mother,"

### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

For since the suspicion <note>referring to Joseph's earlier doubt about Mary's pregnancy</note> was resolved, and the righteous man proved through miracles at the birth that all things were from the Spirit, he no longer refers to her as "his wife."

**"And flee into Egypt."**] The Lord also flees, so that it might be believed that he is truly a man. For if he had fallen into the hands of Herod and had not been killed, people would have thought that his incarnation was only an appearance <note>original: "incarnatum eum apparenter"; this refers to the heresy of Docetism, which claimed Christ only seemed to have a physical body</note>. Moreover, he flees into Egypt so that he might sanctify it; for there are two regions that are workshops of all wickedness: namely, Babylon and Egypt. He accepted Babylon when it came to adore him through the Magi, and he sanctified Egypt by his own presence.
<margin>Babylon and Egypt as workshops of evil.</margin>

**"And be there until I tell you."**] "Be" here stands for "you shall be there" until you are commanded by God. For it is necessary for us to do nothing apart from the divine will.

**"For Herod is going to seek the child, to destroy him."**] Behold the thoughtlessness of a man who labors to overcome the divine will. For if this child is not from God, what do you fear? But if he is from God, how will you destroy the child?

**"But he took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt, and was there until the death of Herod: so that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by God through the prophet, saying: 'Out of Egypt I called my son.'"**]
<margin>Hosea 11:1</margin>
The Jews say that this was said on account of the people of Israel, who were led out of Egypt through Moses. We say, what then is new? That which was said figuratively of the people was truly fulfilled in Christ. Furthermore, who is the Son of God: the people, who adored the idol of Baal-Peor and carved images, or he who is truly the Son of God?

**"Then Herod, when he saw that he had been mocked by the Magi."**] Just as God mocked Pharaoh through Moses, so he mocked Herod through the Magi; for both Herod and Pharaoh were killers of children. Pharaoh killed the male children of the Hebrews in Egypt, while Herod killed them in Bethlehem.
<margin>Exodus 5, 2, 9, 7</margin>

**"For he was (it says) exceedingly angry, and sent and killed all the male children who were in Bethlehem and in all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the Magi."**] He showed his wrath against the Magi, who had offended in nothing. But why were the children permitted to be killed? So that Herod might demonstrate his own malice.

<column-break/>

### EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, PAGE 9

But perhaps you will say to me: "And what of this? Must an injustice be done to children just so that his malice may be demonstrated?" Listen, therefore: they were not affected by injustice, but rather earned crowns <note>original: "coronas meruerunt"; a metaphor for the reward of martyrdom</note>. For everyone who suffers some evil either suffers so that sins may be dissolved, or so that their crowns may be increased—just as those children were more greatly crowned.

**"Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah the prophet, saying."**] Lest anyone think that the slaughter of the children was done against God's will, he shows that God foreknew and foretold it.
<margin>Jeremiah 31</margin>

**"For a voice (he says) was heard in Ramah."**] Ramah was a high place in Palestine—for this name signifies "high"—and it was in the portion of the tribe of Benjamin, who was the son of Rachel. Rachel was buried in Bethlehem. The prophet therefore calls Bethlehem "Rachel," because Rachel was buried there, and says that weeping and wailing were heard in the high place. Listen, then, to the prophet.

**"Lamentation and wailing, and great weeping: Rachel weeping for her children."**] This refers to Bethlehem.

**"And she would not accept consolation, because they are not."**] They "are not" in this life, because their souls are immortal.

**"But when Herod was dead."**] Herod perished by a bitter death: from fever, dysentery, itching, gout, and a rotting of his private parts which bred worms; with difficulty breathing, tremors, and a contraction of his limbs, he released his evil soul.

**"Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying: 'Arise, and take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel.'"**] He does not say "flee," but "go," for there was no longer any fear.

**"For they are dead who sought the child’s soul."**] Where now is Apollinarius <note>a 4th-century bishop who taught that Christ had a human body but not a human soul/mind</note>, who used to say that the Lord did not possess a human soul? For he is refuted by this very passage.

**"And he awoke and took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel. But because he had heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there."**] Herod left behind three sons: Philip, Antipas, and Archelaus. He commanded Archelaus to be king, and the others to be tetrarchs <note>a governor of one-fourth of a province</note>. But Joseph was afraid...

# CHAPTER 3. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.
### PAGE 10

Joseph went to the land of Israel—that is, into the land of Judea—because Archelaus <note>the son of Herod the Great, known for his cruelty</note> was like his father.

**"But having received a warning in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee."**] Galilee was not part of the land of Israel <note>the author refers here specifically to the province of Judea</note>, but of the Gentiles; for this reason, the Jews viewed them as an abomination.

<margin>Luke 2</margin>
**"And having arrived, he lived in a city called Nazareth."**] But how is it that Luke says that after he was born, and the forty days were completed and he was carried by Simeon, the Lord went down to Nazareth—yet in this place, it says that he came to Nazareth after the return from Egypt? Learn, therefore, that Luke speaks of the things Matthew remained silent about. To give an example: After he was born, he completed the forty days, then he went down to Nazareth; this is what Luke says. But Matthew says that after these things, he fled into Egypt, and then came from Egypt to Nazareth. They are not, therefore, in disagreement with one another. For Luke speaks of the descent from Bethlehem to Nazareth, while Matthew later speaks of the return from Egypt to Nazareth.

<margin>Many books of the sacred scriptures are lost due to the negligence of the Jews.</margin>
**"That it might be fulfilled what was said through the prophets: He shall be called a Nazarene."**] And which prophet said this? It is not found now. For through the negligence of the Jews, many books have been lost, and also because of continuous captivities; perhaps this was spoken among the Jews without being written down. Moreover, "Nazarene" signifies "sanctified." Therefore, since Christ is holy, he is rightly called a Nazarene. For the Lord is called the "Holy One of Israel" by many prophets.

### CHAPTER III.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a figure amidst foliage.</image-desc>

**"In those days."**] Not when the Lord was a child and living in Nazareth, but he says it simply in this way, as in "at that time," which refers to the time before the present age.

**"John the Baptist arrived."**] John was sent by God for this purpose: to rebuke the Jews and persuade them to recognize their own evils and receive Christ. For unless one has received a sense of their sins, they do not come to repentance.

**"John was therefore sent, preaching in the desert of Judea and saying: Repent,"**] The Jews were arrogant, and for that reason, he compels them toward repentance <note>original: "resipiscite," implying a return to one's senses or a change of mind</note>.

**"For the kingdom of heaven is at hand."**] By "kingdom of heaven," he means the first and second coming of Christ, and a virtuous life. For when we walk upon the earth living as if in heaven without worldly passions, we possess the kingdom of heaven.

<margin>Isaiah 40</margin>
**"For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah, saying: 'The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.'"**] The "way" refers to the Gospel, while the "paths" refer to the legal mandates of the Old Law, as they are worn and old. He says, therefore: Be prepared for the Gospel life, and make the mandates of the Law "straight"—that is, make them spiritual, for the spirit is straight. Therefore, when you see a Jew understanding the things of the Law carnally <note>literally/physically</note>, say that he himself does not make the ways straight; that is, he does not understand the Law spiritually.

**"But John himself had his garment made of camel's hair."**] He exhorted them to repentance even by his clothing, for he wore a garment of mourning. They say, moreover, that the camel is a middle-ground between clean and unclean animals: for because it chews the cud, it is clean, but because it does not divide the hoof, it is unclean. Because John led the Jewish people (who seemed clean) and the Gentiles (who were unclean) to God, and because he was a mediator between the Old and New Testaments, he therefore wore camel's hair.

**"And a leather belt around his waist."**] All saints are introduced by the scripture as being "girded," as if they are always at work. Those who are negligent and fond of luxury do not gird themselves, such as the Saracens <note>a medieval term for Muslims</note> today. Or, it signifies that they have mortified the passions of desire. For skin <note>original: "pellis"</note> is a part of a dead animal.

**"But his food was locusts and wild honey."**] Some say that "locusts" <note>original: "locustæ"</note> are herbs, and some say they are wild fruits. Wild honey, however, is that which is made by wild bees and is found in trees and rocks.

**"Then Jerusalem went out to him, and all Judea, and all the region round about the Jordan, and they were baptized, confessing their sins."**] Although they were baptized, John's baptism did not yet have the remission of sins.

<sig>b ij</sig>

<meta>This page continues Theophylact’s commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, Chapter 3, focusing on the ministry of John the Baptist and his warnings to the Pharisees and Sadducees.</meta>

...but John was preaching repentance alone, and he directed people toward the remission of sins; that is, he led them toward the baptism of Christ, with whom the remission of sins resides.

**"But when he saw many of the Pharisees."** <note>original: "Quum vidisset autẽ multos ex Pharisæis"</note>] "Pharisee" is interpreted as "set apart" and "divided." For the Pharisees appeared to be separated from others in their way of life and knowledge, and to surpass them.

**"And the Sadducees."** <note>original: "Et Sadducæis"</note>] These believed in neither the resurrection, nor angels, nor the spirit. Their name is interpreted as "the just." For *Sedek* means justice <note>Hebrew: tzedek</note>, and they called themselves the just ones; alternatively, they are named after the leader of their sect, Sadok.

**"Coming to his baptism, he said to them."** <note>original: "Venientes ad baptismum suum, dixit illis"</note>] They had not come with a good intention like the others, and for that reason, he even rebuked them.

**"Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?"** <note>original: "Progenies viperarum, quis submonstrauit vobis fugere a futura ira?"</note>] He speaks harshly to them, knowing their perversity, even though he praises them slightly by saying, "Who warned you?" For he marvels at how it could happen that such an evil nation as theirs should come to its senses. He calls them a "brood of vipers" because, just as vipers are said to be born by devouring their mothers, so too did these men kill their fathers—that is, their teachers and prophets. By "the coming wrath," he means the punishment of Gehenna <note>Hell</note>.

**"Produce, therefore, fruits worthy of repentance."** <note>original: "Facite igitur fructus dignos pœnitentia"</note>] You see what he says: it is not enough simply to flee from evil; <margin>Psalm 33</margin> one must also produce the fruit of virtue. For it says: "Turn away from evil and do good."

**"And do not be of such a mind as to say among yourselves: We have Abraham as our father."** <note>original: "Et ne sitis hac mẽte, vt dicatis apud vosipsos, Patrẽ habemus Abraham"</note>] They perished because they placed their confidence in their noble ancestry.

**"For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones."** <note>original: "Dico enim vobis, quod potest deus ex his lapidibus suscitare filios Abrahæ"</note>] By "stones," the Gentiles are understood, among whom many have believed. Nevertheless, John was speaking simply: that God is able to make children of Abraham out of literal stones. For even Sarah's womb was like a stone because of her sterility, and yet she gave birth. Furthermore, God raised up children for Abraham from stones when many, seeing the crucified Christ and the rocks splitting, came to believe.

**"Even now the axe is laid at the root of the trees."** <note>original: "Iam vero & securis ad radicem arborũ posita est"</note>]

<column-break/>

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. 11
# PAGE 11
b iij

By "the axe," he means the judgment of the Lord, and by "the trees," he means individuals. Therefore, he who does not believe is already being cut off at the roots and sent into Gehenna.

**"Every tree, therefore."** <note>original: "Omnis igitur arbor"</note>] Even if it descends from Abraham.

**"Not producing good fruit."** <note>original: "Non faciens fructum bonum"</note>] He did not say "which *did not* produce," but "not producing" [in the present tense]; for it is necessary to always bear fruit. For even if you were merciful yesterday, but today you are a plunderer, you will not be considered good.

**"Is cut down and thrown into the fire."** <note>original: "Exsecatur, & in ignẽ mittitur"</note>] That is, the fire of Gehenna.

**"I indeed baptize you in water for repentance, but he who comes after me is stronger than I."** <note>original: "Ego quidem baptizo vos in aqua ad pœnitentiam, qui autem post me venit, fortior me est"</note>] He said to them: "Produce fruit." He shows them, therefore, what that fruit is—namely, to believe in the God who was to come after him. For Christ came after him. Just as He was six months younger than John, so too was He later in His manifestation. For the Forerunner was manifested first, and then Christ, who had received testimony from him.

**"Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry."** <note>original: "Cuius non sum idoneus calciamenta gestare"</note>] <margin>What is meant by the sandals.</margin> By "sandals," you should understand His two descents: namely, that from heaven to earth, and that from earth to the underworld. For a sandal is made of "leathern flesh" and mortality <note>Theophylact uses the metaphor of the leather sandal to represent Christ's human nature/flesh</note>. These two descents, then, the Forerunner cannot "carry," as he is unable to comprehend how they were accomplished.

**"He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit."** <note>original: "Ipse vos baptizabit in spiritu sancto"</note>] This means He will flood you abundantly with the graces of the Holy Spirit. "Because my baptism," he says, "does not give spiritual grace, nor even the remission of sins; but He will both remit your sins and give the Spirit generously."

**"Whose winnowing fan is in his hand."** <note>original: "Cuius ventilabrum in manu eius"</note>] <margin>The winnowing fan.</margin> Do not believe that if you have been baptized by Him and then later commit sins, He will simply overlook them. For He also has a winnowing fan—that is, judgment and investigation.

**"And he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor."** <note>original: "Et repurgabit aream suam"</note>] <margin>The threshing floor is the Church.</margin> This means the Church, which indeed contains many who are baptized, just as a threshing floor holds everything that was cultivated in the field. But among these, some are like "chaff"—those who are flighty and driven by spirits of malice—while others are like "wheat"—those who are useful and feed others through their teaching and their works.

Theophylact provides allegorical interpretations for the "sandals," the "axe," and the "threshing floor," identifying the latter as the Church.</summary>

**"And he will gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire."** <note>original: "Et congregabit triticum suum in horreum, paleas autem comburet igni inextinguibili."</note>] He calls that fire "unquenchable." From this, Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) who controversially suggested that all beings, including the damned, might eventually be saved.</note> talks nonsense when he suggests that there will be an end to punishments.

**"Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to be baptized by him. But John tried to prevent him, saying."** <note>original: "Tunc aduenit Iesus a Galilæa ad Iordanem, vt baptizaretur ab eo. Ioannes autem prohibebat eum, dicens."</note>] Although he was pure, he is baptized so that he may wash us and show you that if you wish to be baptized, you should first be cleansed, lest you defile the baptism by easily falling back into filth because of bad habits. Moreover, John prevents him so that those seeing him do not think he is being baptized for repentance as just one among the many.

**"I have need to be baptized by you."** <note>original: "Mihi opus est, vt a te baptizer."</note>] For the forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note> had need to be baptized by the Lord, as one descending from Adam. For he himself had contracted defilement from disobedience, but Christ purified everyone, himself being already pure.

**"And do you come to me?"** <note>original: "Et tu venis ad me?"</note>] He did not dare to say, "And are you baptized by me?" but rather, "And do you come?" He was that pious.

**"Jesus answered and said to him, 'Permit it now.'"** <note>original: "Respondit autem Iesus, & dixit, Dimitte nunc."</note>] "Now," he says, "allow it; for there will be a time when glory will be worthy of us, even though it does not appear now."

**"For so it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. Then he allowed him."** <note>original: "Sic enim decet, vt impleamus omnem iustitiam. Tunc omittit illum."</note>] He calls the Law "righteousness." Human nature, he says, is cursed because it could not fulfill the Law. I, therefore, having fulfilled the other things which are in the Law, and this one thing remains—that I be baptized—by doing this, I shall free nature from the curse. This is fitting for me.

<margin>Nature could not fulfill the Law.</margin>

**"And Jesus, being baptized, immediately went up from the water."** <note>original: "Et baptizatus Iesus, statim ascendit ab aqua."</note>] Christ was baptized when he was thirty years old, because that age takes all sins upon itself. In the first age <note>childhood</note>, there is great foolishness. In the second, which is youth, there is a great flame of lust and anger. In the mature age, however, the love of wealth reigns. He therefore waited for this age so that through all ages he might fulfill the law and sanctify us. He "immediately went up from the water." The Manichaeans <note>Followers of Mani who believed matter was evil and that Christ only *appeared* to have a physical body.</note> say that he left his body in the Jordan and showed another body according to appearance. They are refut-

<column-break/>

A -ed here, for "Jesus," it says, "went up": no one else went up, but he who had descended into the water.

**"And behold, the heavens were opened."** <note>original: "Et ecce aperti sunt cæli."</note>] Adam closed them, but through Christ they are opened: so that you may learn that when you are baptized, you open them.

**"And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and coming upon him, and behold, a voice from the heavens saying."** <note>original: "Et vidit spiritū dei descendentem quasi columbam, & venientem super eum, & ecce vox e cœlis dicens."</note>] The Spirit descends to bear witness that he who is baptized is greater than he who baptizes. For the Jews magnified John, but they did not care much for Christ. All saw the Spirit coming upon Jesus, lest they think that the voice saying,

<margin>John 5.</margin>

B **"This is my beloved Son."** <note>original: "Hic est filius meus dilectus."</note>] ...was spoken on account of John; but seeing the Spirit, they would believe that the voice was on account of Jesus. **"(Like a dove)"** because of innocence and gentleness; and because the dove is a most clean creature and does not stay where there is a stench, so also the Holy Spirit. And as it is said of Noah, that a dove announced the end of the flood by bringing an olive branch, so here the Holy Spirit reveals the release from sins. There, an olive branch; here, the mercy of God.

<margin>Genesis 8.</margin>

**"This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."** <note>original: "Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene cōplacitū est."</note>] That is, in whom I shall rest, and in whom I shall be appeased.

<margin>Genesis 3.</margin>

### CHAPTER 4.

C **Then Jesus was led into the desert by the Spirit.** <note>original: "TVnc Iesus ductus est in desertum a spiritu."</note>] Teaching us that after baptism it is more necessary to expect temptations. He is led by the Holy Spirit: for he did nothing without the Spirit. Moreover, he is led into the desert to show us that the devil tempts us when he sees us solitary and not helped by others. We ought not, therefore, to trust rashly in ourselves.

**"To be tempted by the devil."** <note>original: "Vt tentaretur a diabolo."</note>] He is called "devil" <note>from the Greek 'diabolos', meaning slanderer or accuser</note> because he accused and defamed God before Adam. For he said to him, "God hates you," and now he slanders virtue among us.

**"And when he had fasted."** <note>original: "Et quum ieiunasset."</note>] He fasted to show that fasting is a great armor against temptations: just as

### ->CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.<-
->A B C D E F<-

...the beginning of all sin is luxury. <note>original: "principium omnis peccati, delitiæ." This sentence concludes a thought from the previous page regarding the roots of temptation.</note>

<margin>Exodus 24. 3 Kings 19.</margin>
**"Forty days and forty nights."** <note>original: "Dies quadraginta, & noctes quadraginta."</note>] He fasted for as many days as Moses and Elijah did; for if he had fasted for more, his incarnation might have seemed fictitious and a mere appearance. <note>Theophylact is defending the reality of Christ's human body against Docetism, a belief that Christ only "seemed" to be human.</note>

**"Afterward he was hungry. And when the tempter had come to him, he said."** <note>original: "Postea esuriit. Et quum accessisset ad eum ille qui tentat, dixit."</note>] When He permitted His human nature to do so, then He became hungry, so that He might give the devil an opportunity to approach and engage in combat with Him on account of the hunger; thus He might overthrow and cast him down, granting the victory to us.

**"If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread."** <note>original: "Si filius dei es, dic vt lapides isti panes fiant."</note>] The thief <note>A common patristic epithet for the Devil.</note> heard the heavenly voice. Again he sees Him hungering, and he still doubts how the Son of God could be hungry, and for that reason, he tempts Him so that he may learn. Moreover, he flatters Him, thinking he might steal something away by saying, "If you are the Son of God." Now you might ask: what sin was it to make stones into bread? Hear then: to obey the devil in anything is a sin. Notice also another thing. He did not say "that this stone become bread," but "stones," wanting to incite Christ toward superfluity. For one loaf of bread is enough for a hungry man, and for this reason, Christ did not listen to him.

<margin>Deuteronomy 8.</margin>
**"But he answering, said: It is written, Not by bread alone does man live, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God."** <note>original: "At ille respondens, dixit: Scriptum est, Non in pane solo viuit homo, sed in omni verbo, quod egreditur per os dei."</note>] This is from the Old Testament; indeed, it is the speech of Moses. <margin>Manna.</margin> For the Hebrews were also fed with manna, which was not bread, but through the word of God, it fulfilled every need of the Hebrews and became whatever they desired to eat. If a Jew craved fish, or an egg, or cheese, the manna provided that taste for him. <note>This reflects a common Jewish and medieval tradition that manna was a miraculous substance that adapted its flavor to the desires of the person eating it.</note>

**"Then the devil took him into the holy city, and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple."** <note>original: "Tunc assumit eum diabolus in sanctam ciuitatem, & statuit eum supra pinnaculum templi."</note>] This was a certain part of the temple, like what are called among us <term>pterygiis</term> <note>original: "πτερύγια", meaning little wings or decorative parapets</note>; for they appear to be like wings.

<margin>Psalm 19.</margin>
**"And said to him, If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. For it is written: He has given his angels charge over you, and they will bear you up in their hands, lest perhaps you dash your foot against a stone."** <note>original: "Et dicit ei, Si filius dei es tu, mittito te deorsum. Scriptum est enim. Angelis suis mãdauit de te, & in manibus portabunt te, ne forte impingas in lapidem pedem tuũ."</note>] "If you are the Son of God"—as if he were saying: "I do not believe the voice sent from heaven; nevertheless, if you are the Son of God, show me." Even though He was the Son of God, O cursed one, ought He to throw Himself down? It belongs to your cruelty to throw down those driven by demons, but it belongs to God to save. It is not written "In their hands they shall bear you" on account of Christ, but on account of the saints, who stand in need of angelic protection. Christ, however, who is God, has no need of it.

<margin>Deuteronomy 6.</margin>
**"Jesus said to him again: It is written, You shall not tempt the Lord your God."** <note>original: "Dixit illi Iesus iterum: Scriptum est, Non tentabis dominũ deum tuum."</note>] God repels him mildly, teaching us also to conquer demons with mildness.

<margin>Love of riches and the mountain.</margin>
**"Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to him: All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me."** <note>original: "Iterum assumit eum diabolus in montem excelsum valde & monstrat ei omnia regna mundi, & gloriam eius, & dixit ei, Hæc omnia tibi dabo, si procideris & adoraueris me."</note>] Some think the "very high mountain" refers to the affection and zeal for possessing riches, into which the enemy tries to lead Jesus, but they are not thinking correctly. For the devil appeared to Him in a sensible <note>perceptible to the physical senses</note> form. For the Lord did not have such thoughts—far be it from Him. Sensibly, therefore, he showed Him all the kingdoms on a mountain, making them appear before His eyes. And "All these I will give you," he says, putting the world forward as if it were his own, out of pride. He says this even now to the greedy, so that by worshiping him, they might have all these things.

<margin>Ibidem.</margin>
**"Then Jesus said to him: Get behind me, Satan. For it is written, The Lord your God shall you worship, and him only shall you serve."** <note>original: "Tunc dicit ei Iesus, Vade post me Satana. Scriptum est enim, Dominum deum tuum adorabis, & illum solum coles."</note>] The Lord is angry with him when He sees him claiming those things which are God's for himself, and saying, "I will give these to you as my own." Learn, moreover, how the Scriptures are profitable, through which the Lord hardened the mouth of the enemy.

**"Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him."** <note>original: "Tunc omittit illum diabolus, & ecce angeli accede bant & ministrabant ei."</note>] The Lord experienced three temptations: gluttony, vainglory, and avarice. <note>These three were often cited by Church Fathers as the roots of all human sin.</note> For these are the principal passions. Therefore, he who conquers these will conquer others all the more. Hence Luke says that he "ended every temptation," since he conquered the heads of temptation. Consequently, the angels minister: by which it is demonstrated that after our victory, angels will minister to us as well; for the Lord both did and showed all things for our sake, since as God, the angels always minister to Him.

<margin>Three temptations.</margin>
<margin>Luke 4.</margin>

**"Now when Jesus had heard that John was delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee; and leaving Nazareth, he set out for Galilee,"** <note>original: "Quum audisset autem Iesus, quod Ioannes traditus esset: recessit in Galilęã, & relicta Nazareth, profectus Galilęa,"</note>

<summary>Theophylact provides a detailed commentary on the Temptation of Christ, explaining how Jesus overcame gluttony, vainglory, and avarice to secure victory for humanity. He also clarifies that the temptations were physical encounters, not merely internal thoughts.</summary>
