### ## CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

<margin>D</margin> **"He dwelt in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali."** <note>original: "Capnaũ. habitauit in Capernaũ, quę est apud mare in confiniis Zabulõ. Zabulon & Nephthalĩ."</note>] Jesus withdraws, teaching us not to throw ourselves into dangers without cause. He withdraws specifically into Galilee, which means "rolling" or "turning away." <note>Theophylact uses a traditional etymology where Galilee signifies the "turning" of the Gentiles toward sin or change.</note> For the Gentiles are "rolled" about in their sins. He dwells in Capernaum, which means "the house of consolation," for He descended so that He might make the Gentiles a house of the Consoler. Zebulun is interpreted as "nightly," and Naphtali as "breadth." <note>original: "Zabulon interpretatur nocturna, Nephthalim autem latitudo."</note> For the Gentiles possessed both the darkness of night and the "breadth" of life; they did not walk along the narrow path, but rather along that wide road which leads to destruction.

<margin>Isaiah 10.</margin> **"That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, saying: The land of Zebulun, and the land of Naphtali, by the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles—"** <margin>E</margin> **"the people who sat in darkness saw a great light, and upon those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, a light has dawned."**] The "way of the sea" refers to the land situated along the sea-path. The "great light" is the Gospel. For the Law was also a light itself, but only a small one. The "shadow of death" is sin, for sin is the likeness and outward form of death. For just as death seizes the body, so does sin seize the soul. <margin>Gospel light.</margin> This light "has dawned" upon us; for we did not seek it ourselves, but it was sent to us, appearing as if it were pursuing us.

**"From that time Jesus began to preach and to say."**] From the time that John was held in chains, Jesus began to preach. For Jesus waited for John to first bear witness about Him and prepare the way for His coming, <margin>F</margin> just as servants prepare the way before their masters. For the Lord, being equal to the Father, also had His own prophet, John, just as His Father, God, had prophets before John—indeed, those prophets belong both to the Father and the Son.

**"Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."**] <margin>Kingdom of heaven</margin> The Kingdom of Heaven is both Christ Himself and a life distinguished by virtues. When someone lives on earth like the angels, are they not "heavenly"? Thus, the Kingdom of Heaven is within each of us if we lead an angelic life.

**"And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen."**] These men had been disciples of John. While John was still 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> living, they had approached Christ. However, when they saw John was imprisoned, they returned to their fishing business. Thus, Christ comes and "fishes" for them, saying:

**"Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. And they immediately left their nets and followed him."**] See how obedient these men were; they followed Him immediately. From this, it is clear that this was a second calling. For they had been taught by Christ previously, but then they left Him; now, seeing Him again, they followed Him at once.

**"And going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a boat with Zebedee their father."**] It is a supreme virtue to support an elderly father, and to do so with honestly earned means.

<margin>B</margin> **"Mending their nets; and he called them."**] They were poor, and because they could not afford to buy new nets, they repaired their old ones.

**"And they immediately left the boat and their father, and followed him."**] It appears that Zebedee did not believe the ancient promises, and for that reason, they left him. You see that it is necessary to leave one's father specifically when he stands in the way of virtue and piety. Moreover, these men saw the others who had preceded them in following Christ, and they followed with good reason, imitating them.

**"And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the Gospel of the kingdom."**] To show that He was not opposed to the Law, He entered the synagogues of the Hebrews.

**"And he healed every sickness and every infirmity among the people."**] He begins with signs <note>miracles</note> so that the things He teaches might be believed. <margin>Sickness. Infirmity.</margin> <margin>C</margin> Now, a "sickness" is a long-term state of ill health. An "infirmity," however, is a temporary disorder or imbalance in the body.

**"And his fame went throughout all Syria; and they brought to him all who were sick, taken with various diseases and torments, and those who were possessed by demons, and lunatics, and paralytics, and he healed them."**] Christ did not demand faith from those who were brought to Him; for the very act of bringing them from such a distance was a sign of faith. He calls those "possessed by demons" "lunatics." For the demon, wishing to persuade men that the stars are the cause of evil, observes the moon when it is full and then sets his traps. He does this so that the moon might be blamed as the cause of suffering and disease, and so that God's handiwork might be slandered—just as the Manichaeans are in error regarding this. <note>The Manichaeans were a dualistic sect that viewed the physical world as inherently evil; Theophylact is defending the goodness of the created moon against their views.</note>

<margin>E</margin> **"And great multitudes followed him from Galilee, and Decapolis, and Jerusalem, and Judea, and from the regions beyond the Jordan."**

<summary>This page describes Jesus beginning his ministry in Galilee after John the Baptist's arrest, the calling of the first four disciples (Peter, Andrew, James, and John), and his initial miracles of healing. Theophylact provides etymological and symbolic interpretations of the locations and explains the distinction between chronic illness and temporary infirmity.</summary>

# CHAPTER 5. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>D</margin> **"And when He had seen the crowds, He went up into a mountain."** <note>original: "ET quū vidisset turbas, ascendit in montem."</note>] He teaches us to do nothing for the sake of outward show. **"He went up into a mountain"** because He was about to teach; He taught us to withdraw from the midst of the crowd when it is time to teach. 

**"And when He had sat down, His disciples came to Him."**] Other crowds come because of the miracles, but the disciples come because of the teaching. Therefore, after He healed bodies and performed miracles, He now heals the soul, so that we may learn that He is the Maker of both souls and bodies. 

**"And opening His mouth."**] Why is it added, "opening His mouth"? It seems to be superfluous. Not at all: for He also taught <margin>E</margin> without opening His mouth. How? Through His life and miracles; but now, opening His mouth, He teaches. 

**"He taught them, saying."**] Not only the disciples, but also the crowd. He begins with the Beatitudes, just as David began the Psalms with a blessing. <note>Refers to Psalm 1:1, "Blessed is the man..."</note>

**"Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."**] First, He lays down modesty and humility of mind as the foundation. For since Adam fell through pride—seeing as Adam hoped to become a god—Christ raises us up through humility. Those who are contrite in soul are the "poor in spirit." 

**"Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall receive consolation."**] Those who mourn on account of sins, not on account of worldly matters. He spoke of "mourners" <margin>F</margin> as a continuous state, not just a one-time occurrence; and not only for our own sins, but also for the sins of our neighbors. They will receive consolation even here. For one who mourns for sins rejoices spiritually, and much more so in the life to come. 

<margin>The meek.</margin> **"Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth."**] Some say this refers to a spiritual earth, namely heaven; but you should also understand it as this earth. For since the meek are thought to be despised and helpless, He says that they, in fact, possess everything more fully. The meek are not those who never get angry at all—for such people are foolish and senseless—but those who possess the capacity for anger but restrain it, and only get angry when it is necessary. <margin>A</margin>

**"Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied."**] Since He is about to speak of mercy, He shows first that righteousness must be preserved, and that alms should not be given from stolen goods. Furthermore, righteousness must be practiced with all eagerness, which is what He means when He says, "hungering and thirsting." Because some greedy people seem to be overflowing and satisfied, He says that the righteous are satisfied even more so here, because they possess what is their own in security. 

**"Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy."**] Mercy is not found in wealth alone, but also in speech; and if you have nothing, even in tears. They will obtain mercy even here from men. For he who was merciful yesterday, even if he is poor today <margin>B</margin>, obtains mercy from everyone, and in the hereafter, much greater mercy from God. 

**"Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."**] <margin>Hebrews 12. Note.</margin> Many do not steal and are even merciful, yet they commit fornication and are otherwise unclean. But Christ commands that along with other virtues we must also be pure, that is, chaste—not only in body, but also in heart. For without sanctification, that is, chastity, no one will see God. Just as a mirror, if it is clean, catches reflections, so the pure soul receives the face of God and the knowledge of the Scriptures. 

**"Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God."**] <margin>C</margin> Not only those who have peace with others, but also those who reconcile others who are in conflict. Peacemakers are also those who, through teaching, convert the enemies of God. Such people become sons of God. Indeed, the Only-Begotten Son reconciled us to God. 

**"Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."**] Not only martyrs, but many suffer persecution because they help those afflicted by injustice and, in short, foster every virtue. For "righteousness" refers to all virtue. Thieves and murderers, even though they may also suffer persecution, are not for that reason blessed. 

**"Blessed are you when they shall revile you and persecute you."**] He turns Himself toward the apostles themselves, showing...

<summary>Theophylact provides a line-by-line commentary on the Beatitudes from Matthew 5, defining spiritual virtues like humility, meekness, and purity of heart. He emphasizes that Christ’s teachings aim to heal the soul just as His miracles healed the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Matthew 5, specifically the Beatitudes and the metaphors of salt and light. The catchword "maxime" on the previous page leads into the first sentence here, which discusses the specific nature of reproaches faced by teachers of the faith.</meta>

# CHAPTER 5. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>It is especially characteristic of teachers to hear reproaches.</margin>
**"And they have spoken every evil word against you, lying because of me."** <note>original: "Et dixerunt omne malū verbum cōtra vos, mentientes propter me."</note>] It is not simply he who is reproached who is blessed, but only when it is for Christ’s sake and when the accusation is false. If these two conditions are not met, that person is wretched, as they serve as a stumbling block <note>term: stumbling block (offendiculo) — a common biblical metaphor for something that causes others to sin or lose faith</note> to many.

**"Rejoice and be glad, because your reward is great in heaven."**] When He spoke of the other beatitudes, He did not say the reward was "great"; but here He shows that enduring reproach is a great and most heavy burden. Indeed, many have hanged themselves <note>Theophylact implies that the psychological weight of social shame and verbal abuse can be more unbearable than physical pain.</note> due to it. Even Job, although he endured many other trials, was most disturbed when his friends reproached him, as if he were suffering specifically because of his own sins.

<margin>Job 4, 6, 9, 10.</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
**"For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you."**] Lest the apostles suspect they are suffering persecution because they taught things contrary to Christ, He consoles them by saying: this also happened to the prophets before you on account of their virtue. Therefore, the sufferings of those who came before should be a source of comfort to you.

**"You are the salt of the earth."**] The prophets were sent to only one nation, but you are the salt of the whole earth. You sting and season the dissolute <note>term: dissolute — those living without moral restraint or discipline</note> through your doctrine and rebukes, so that they do not breed "perpetual worms" <note>A metaphor for the corruption of the soul; just as salt prevents meat from rotting and breeding maggots, Christian teaching prevents moral decay.</note>. Therefore, do not cast away the sharp sting of your rebukes, even if you suffer persecution or if men reproach you. This is why He says:

**"But if the salt has lost its flavor, with what shall it be salted?"**] That is to say, how shall it be corrected?

<margin>F</margin>
**"Then it shall be cast out."**] Cast out from the dignity of being teachers.

**"And it shall be trampled."**] That is, it will be despised.

**"You are the light of the world."**] First He calls them salt, and then light. For he who rebukes things done in secret is a light. For everything that makes things manifest is light. They did not illuminate just one nation, but the whole world.

**"A city situated on a mountain cannot be hidden."**] He teaches them to endure in the struggle and to keep a careful account of their lives, as they are those upon whom everyone’s eyes are fixed. Do not think, He says, that you will be hidden away in a corner; you will be visible to all. Therefore, see to it that you lead a life without stain, so that you do not become a stumbling block to others.

<column-break/>

# ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. 16
<page-num>16</page-num>

<margin>A</margin>
**"Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house."**] I indeed have lit the lamp, but now it will be your duty to ensure the grace is not extinguished, so that the brilliance of your life may shine for others. For He says:

**"So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven."**] He did not say "show off your virtue," for that would not be good; rather, let the virtue itself shine so that even your enemies may wonder at it and glorify—not you—but your Father. If we perform virtuous works, we must do so for the glory of God, not for our own.

<margin>B</margin>
**"Do not think that I have come to destroy the law or the prophets: I have not come to destroy, but to fulfill."**] Since He was about to introduce new laws, He spoke first to counter the wicked suspicion of some who might think He was an adversary to God. He says He does not destroy the law, but rather fulfills it. How did He fulfill it? First, because He completed all things that the prophets predicted concerning Him. (This is why the Evangelist frequently says, "That it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophets"). Second, did He not fulfill all the commandments of the law? For He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth.

<margin>1 Peter 2.</margin>
<margin>Below in the same place. How he fulfills the law. Isaiah 53.</margin>
Furthermore, He fulfilled the law in another way, which is to say He "filled it in" or completed the picture. For whatever the old law foreshadowed in outline, He here depicted perfectly. The old law said, "Do not kill"; but He says, "Do not be angry without cause." Just as a painter does not destroy the original sketch, but rather illustrates and fills it in with color.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Truly.</margin>
**"Truly I say to you."** <note>original: "Amen dico vobis."</note>] "Amen" is an affirmative particle meaning "indeed" or "truly." It is as if He said, "For I say to you."

**"Until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota nor one stroke shall pass from the law, until all things have been done."**] He shows here that the world passes away and is transfigured. He says that as long as the universe exists, not even the smallest letter of the law will pass away. Others, however, say that the "iota and stroke" <note>term: iota and stroke (iota et apex) — The 'iota' is the smallest Greek letter; the 'apex' refers to a tiny serif or mark used to distinguish letters. Christ uses them to mean the smallest details of God's law.</note> refer to the Ten Commandments, while others say they refer to the Cross. In this interpretation, the "iota" is the upright beam and the "stroke" is the crossbeam; in this sense, He says that all things spoken concerning the Cross will be fulfilled.

<margin>Iota and stroke.</margin>

<meta>catchword: will be fulfilled (plebuntur)</meta>

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus’s teaching on the role of the Apostles as "salt" and "light," emphasizing that they must endure social reproach. He also clarifies how Jesus fulfills the Old Testament Law—not by abolishing it, but by completing its "outline" with deeper moral requirements.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Theophylact's commentary on the Sermon on the Mount from Matthew 5. Having discussed the apostles as the "salt of the earth" and the "light of the world," he now transitions into Christ’s interpretation of the Law, specifically focusing on the commandments and the internal state of the believer regarding anger and reconciliation.</meta>

### CHAPTER 5. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

<margin>D</margin>
**"Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven."** <note>original: "Quifquis igitur foluerit vnũ ex mandatis his minimis..."</note>] He calls the commandments "least," not meaning the laws of the Old Testament, but those which He himself was about to hand down. He refers to them as "least" out of humility, so that He might instruct you to speak with modesty when teaching. 
<margin>Least in the kingdom.</margin>
However, "he shall be called the least in the kingdom" means that in the resurrection, he will be last and cast into Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna — a place of fiery torment; the author clarifies that "kingdom" here refers to the time of the Resurrection, not necessarily the state of being saved.</note>. For such a one shall not enter the kingdom of heaven—far be it!—but you should understand "kingdom" here to mean the time of the general resurrection.

**"But whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven."**] He places "doing" first, and "teaching" second. For how can I lead another onto a path upon which I have never walked? Furthermore, if I "do" but do not "teach," I will not have as great a reward; indeed, I may even face condemnation if I fail to teach out of envy or negligence.

<margin>Righteousness.</margin>
**"For I say unto you, That except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven."**] By "righteousness" <note>original: "Iuftitiam"</note>, He means all virtue, just as it is said that "Job was a righteous man, pious and blameless." Tremble, O man, realizing how much is demanded of us! He then teaches us how we may abound in virtue and begins to list them.

<margin>Exodus 20.</margin>
**"Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment."**] He does not explicitly state who said this. For if He had said, "What my Father said to the ancients, I now say to you," He might have appeared to be setting down a law contrary to His Father's. Conversely, if He had said, "I said to the ancients," His speech would have been poorly received by the audience. Therefore, He spoke indefinitely, "It was said to the ancients," because since the old things are now antiquated and nearly abolished, it is necessary to leave them behind and run toward the new.

<margin>F</margin>
**"But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment."**] When the prophets were about to speak of future things, they would say, "Thus says the Lord." But Christ says, "I say," demonstrating His divine substance. For the prophets were servants, but He is the Son, possessing in Himself all that belongs to the Father. He who is angry with his brother "rashly" <note>original: "temere" — meaning without a just cause or purpose</note> is condemned. 
<margin>Just anger.</margin>
But if someone is moved to anger for a just reason, and in order to

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
instruct another, or out of spiritual zeal, he shall not be condemned. This is why Paul spoke words of anger to Elymas the sorcerer and to the high priest; he did so not rashly, but out of zeal. We are angry "rashly" when we do so for the sake of wealth or personal glory.

<margin>Rhaca.</margin>
**"And whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council."**] "Raca" <note>term: Rhaca (Raca) — an Aramaic term of contempt, likely implying "empty-headed" or "worthless."</note> signifies something similar to the word "You!"; it is like when we say "You there!" to someone we hold in contempt. Because He wants us to be careful even in small matters and to respect one another, He gives this warning. Some say that "Raca" is Syriac, signifying an expression of indignation or spitting. Whosoever, therefore, treats his brother with such an insult, attacking him with contempt, shall be liable to the council of the holy apostles when they sit to judge the twelve 
<margin>B</margin>
tribes of Israel.

**"But whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire."**] Many think this is a heavy and harsh judgment, but it is not. For he who deprives his brother of reason and prudence, making him out to be no different from a beast, how is he not worthy of Gehenna? Indeed, he who pursues another with mockery and insults destroys charity; and when charity is destroyed, all virtues are removed at once, just as they are all preserved when charity is safe. Therefore, he who treats his neighbor with contempt dissolves all virtues by tearing charity apart, and thus he is worthy of the fire of hell.

<margin>C</margin>
**"Therefore if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift."**] God disregards His own honor so long as we love one another. If your brother has something against you, the text adds no other condition: whether he holds it against you justly or unjustly, seek reconciliation. He did not say, "if you have something against him," but "if he has something against you," strive to bring him back to friendship. He commands you to leave the gift so that He may impose upon you the necessity of reconciling; if you wish to offer your gift, you are forced to reconcile first. He also teaches, in the meantime, that charity itself is a sacrifice.
<margin>Charity is a sacrifice</margin>

**"Agree with thine adversary quickly, whiles thou art in the way with him; lest at any time the adversary deliver thee to the judge..."**

<summary>Theophylact explains Christ's intensification of the Law, moving from physical acts like murder to the internal sins of rash anger and verbal insults. He emphasizes that maintaining charity with one's brother is more important to God than the formal performance of religious sacrifices.</summary>

<meta>catchword: A of their</meta>

...the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison. **D** Truly I say to you, you shall by no means come out from there, until you have paid the last penny <note>original: "quadrantem," a small Roman coin</note>. ] Some think that the "adversary" refers to the devil, and the "way" refers to this life; they believe the Lord is warning you that as long as you are in this life, you should separate yourself from the devil so that he cannot later accuse you of sin—as if you still held something belonging to him—and then you be handed over to punishment until the "last penny" is paid for the correction of your sins. A penny consists of two mites <note>original: "minuta"</note>. But you should understand that he is speaking of the adversaries who are here on earth: by this, he warns you not to struggle in legal disputes, lest you be torn away from divine works. Even if you have been treated unjustly, he says, do not go to the tribunal: but settle the dispute while on the way, lest you suffer worse things due to the power of your adversary.

<margin>One should not contend in court.</margin>
<margin>Exodus 20.</margin>
**E** You have heard that it was said, You shall not commit adultery. ] <term>Adultery</term> <note>original: "mœchia"</note> is one thing, and <term>fornication</term> <note>original: "scortatio"</note> is another. For adultery is committed with a married woman, whereas fornication is with one who is unattached.

But I say to you, that whoever looks at another’s wife to lust after her, has already committed adultery with her in his heart. ] This refers to the man who stops and stares with curiosity, who touches, and who inflames his own lust by looking: and looks again, so that he may lust after her even more. Such a man has already perfected the evil in his heart. If he did not add the outward act, what of it? He simply was not able to; for if he had been able, he would have committed the evil immediately. Truly, recognize that even if we lust, but are then prohibited from doing the deed, it is a sign that we have been clearly protected by grace. Likewise, women who adorn themselves to please men—even if they do not actually please anyone—nevertheless have mixed a poisonous potion <note>original: "pharmacum"</note>, even if no one drinks it.

**F** And if your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you. For it is profitable for you that one of your members should perish, and not that your whole body should be cast into Gehenna. ] Hearing "eye" and "hand," do not think he is speaking of these physical members: for he did not merely say "eye," but "the right one." Rather, he speaks of those who seem to be our friends but cause us harm. For example, if there is a young man who has friends who lack self-control and from whom he receives harm: cut these off, he says. For perhaps you will save even them when they realize this, or if not them, certainly yourself; but if you continue to love 

<margin>Evil company to be avoided.</margin>

A of their friendship, you will both perish.

It has been said, whoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce <note>original: "repudiarium"</note>. ] Moses commanded that if any man hated his wife, he should be separated from her, so that nothing more grievous might happen. For when she is held in hatred, she might perhaps be killed. However, he commands the man to give the woman he dismisses a legal scroll of release, which he calls a "repudiarium," so that she may no longer return to him, and so that no confusion arises from her living with another man.

<margin>Deuteronomy 24.</margin>

But I say to you, that whoever shall put away his wife, except for the cause of fornication, causes her to commit adultery: and whoever shall marry her that is put away commits adultery. ] He does not abolish the Mosaic law, but corrects it, terrifying the husband so that he does not hate his wife without cause. For if he dismisses her for a just cause—namely, if she is a fornicator—he is not subject to any condemnation. But if she is condemned without the cause of fornication, he forces her to commit adultery, and he who takes her is also an adulterer. For if that man had not taken her, she surely would have returned and remained subject to her husband. A Christian, however, ought to be peaceful, even toward others, and much more so to have peace with his wife.

**B** Again you have heard that it was said to them of old, You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform your oaths to the Lord. ] This means: when you swear, speak the truth.

<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>

But I say, do not swear at all; neither by heaven, for it is God's throne; nor by the earth, for it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great king. ] Because the Jews had heard God saying, "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool," they used to swear by the elements. Therefore the Lord, prohibiting them, does not say they should not swear by them because heaven is beautiful and great or because the earth is useful; rather, he says it is because heaven is the throne of God and the earth is his footstool, so that there may be no place for idolatry. For perhaps the elements would have been counted among the number of the gods by those swearing by them, a thing which had happened in the past.

<margin>Isaiah 66 <note>original: "Esa. vlti." referring to the last chapter of Isaiah</note></margin>
**C** Neither shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. ] God alone swears by Himself, as He is subject to no one; but we, since we are not in control of our own power, how shall we swear by our own heads?

### CHAPTER 5. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

sig: c iij
<meta>catchword: For</meta>

...for it belongs to another’s declaration <note>original: "professio"</note>. For if your head were truly yours, change a single hair if you can.

<margin>No one is trusted less than he who swears frequently.</margin>
[But let your speech be "yes, yes" and "no, no."] Lest you say: "And how will they have faith in me?" he says: If you have always spoken truthfully and never sworn an oath. For no one is trusted less than he who swears frequently.

[Whatever is more than these is from the evil one.] Swearing (he says) and adding more than "yes" or "no" is from the devil. Furthermore, if you say that the Law of Moses must also be evil because it commands one to swear, learn that then it was not evil to swear; but after Christ it is evil, just as being circumcised is, and in short, whatever is Jewish. For it is appropriate for a boy to stand up <note>original: "surgere," likely an analogy for the basic rules suitable for a child compared to the maturity expected of a man</note>, but not at all for a grown man.

<margin>Exodus 21. Deuteronomy 19.</margin>
[You have heard that it was said: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.] The Law, condescending <note>stooping down to human weakness to prevent worse violence</note>, allows one to suffer the same things he inflicted, so that they might not harm one another—or at least be deterred by the fear that they might suffer the same.

[But I say to you, do not resist the evil person; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn the other to him also.] Here he calls the devil "evil," for he works through man. Should we therefore not resist the devil? Yes. But he is not to be struck back; he must be endured. For fire is not extinguished by fire, but by water. Do not think, however, that he speaks only of a strike to the cheek, but of every other evil that is inflicted.

[And to him who wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.] Even if he drags you before a judge and disturbs you, then let go of the cloak. This is not if he simply asks for it <note>but specifically in the context of a legal dispute</note>. A <term>tunic</term> <note>original: "tunica"</note> is properly what we call an <term>undershirt</term> <note>original: "subucula" or "indusium"</note>; a <term>cloak</term> <note>original: "pallium"</note> is what we use to cover it, although often these terms are used interchangeably.

<margin>Tunic.</margin>
[And whoever forces you to go one mile, go with him two.] Why do I speak (he asks) of a tunic and a cloak? Give even your body to him who drags you unjustly, and even more than he wants.

[Give to the one who asks of you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.] Whether friend or enemy, whether an unbeliever, whether he asks for money or some other help. By "borrowing" <note>original: "mutuum"</note> he does not mean with interest, but simply for use. For even in the Law they used to lend without interest.

<margin>Leviticus 19.</margin>
[You have heard that it was said: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies.] He has reached the summit of virtues. What could be greater? Yet it is not impossible. For Moses and Paul loved the Jews who were raging against them more than themselves, and so did all the saints love their enemies.

[Bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who hurt and persecute you.] It is necessary to count those people among your benefactors. For everyone who tests and persecutes us makes the punishment we ought to bear for our sins lighter. Also for another reason: namely, the reward that God gives us for such a thing. For listen:

[That you may be children of your Father who is in heaven; for he makes his sun to rise on the good and the bad, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.] See how much good he gives who hates and hurts you, if only you are willing to endure it. By "rain" and "sun," understand also doctrine and knowledge. For He enlightens and teaches everyone.

[For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?] Let us tremble, for we are not even equal to the tax collectors if we do not love even those who love us.

[And if you love your friends, what more are you doing? Do not even the tax collectors do so? Therefore you shall be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect.] For to love some and hate others is the way of the imperfect; but to love everyone is the way of the perfect.

<margin>Love everyone.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Theophylact’s commentary on the Sermon on the Mount, transitioning from the end of Matthew Chapter 5 (regarding oaths and retaliation) into Chapter 6, which deals with the three pillars of Jewish and Christian piety: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting.</meta>

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

sig: e iiii
<meta>catchword: do,</meta>

...you may perform almsgiving before men, but if you do it for the purpose of being seen by men, you are not condemned <note>that is, if the goal is to set a good example rather than seek praise</note>; but if you aim for the goal of vainglory, even if you do it in the inner rooms of your storehouse, you are condemned. For God either crowns or punishes the will.

Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be glorified by men. The hypocrites did not actually have trumpets, but He mocks their state of mind here, because they wanted their almsgiving to be celebrated. <margin>Who the hypocrites are.</margin> Hypocrites are those who are one thing but appear to be another; they seem to be merciful, but in reality, they are something else.

Truly I say to you, they have their reward. Since they are praised, they have already received everything from men <note>meaning they should expect no further reward from God</note>.

But when you give alms, let not your left hand <margin>Hyperbole.</margin> know what your right hand is doing. He says this through hyperbole <note>an intentional exaggeration for emphasis</note>, as if to say: if it were possible, you should even be unaware of your own good deeds. Or, to put it another way: the "left hand" represents vainglory, while the "right hand" represents the act of almsgiving; therefore, let vainglory remain ignorant of your charity.

So that your almsgiving may be in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly. When? Then, when all things shall be naked and manifest <note>at the Last Judgment</note>, and then you shall be more greatly glorified.

And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, because they love to pray standing in the corners of the streets, so that they may be visible to men. Truly I say to you, they have their reward. He names them hypocrites as well, as they are people who seem to attend to God, but in truth they attend more to men, from whom they "have"—that is, they receive—their reward.

But you, when you pray, enter into your chamber, and having shut your door, pray to your Father in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you in <margin>Praying in church.</margin> the open. What then, shall I not pray in church? By all means, pray there, but with a right mind and without ostentation. For the place itself does not cause harm, but rather the manner and the intention. For many, even when praying in secret, do so only to please men.

<column-break/>

And when you pray, do not be <term>battalogi</term> <note>original: "battalogi"; meaning those who use empty, repetitive babbling</note> in your prayers like the heathens. <margin>Babbling.</margin> Babbling is trifling talk; for example, asking for something earthly, such as glory, riches, or victory. For <term>battarismus</term> <note>stammering</note> is an inarticulate sound, like that of children; therefore, do not be trifling or wordy.

For they think they will be heard for their many words; <margin>Short and frequent prayers.</margin> therefore do not be like them. Long prayers are not to be made, but rather short and frequent ones; for it is necessary to persevere in prayer while speaking few words.

For your Father knows what you need before you ask. <margin>Why one must pray.</margin> We do not pray in order to teach God what we need, but so that we may withdraw ourselves from temporal and worldly cares, and talk with Him at leisure and with great benefit.

Thus therefore pray: Our Father, who art in heaven. A <term>vow</term> <note>original: "votum"</note> is one thing, a <term>prayer</term> <note>original: "oratio"</note> another. A vow is a promise made before God, as when someone promises to abstain from wine or some other thing; but a prayer is a petition for good things. By saying "Father," He shows you how many good things you have received, having been made a son of God. And when He says "in heaven," He shows you your homeland and your paternal home. For if you wish to have God as Father, look to the heavens and not to the earth. He does not say "my Father," but "our Father," so that you may regard all as brothers of one Father.

Hallowed be thy name. That is, make us holy, so that you also may be glorified through us. For just as God is blasphemed because of me, so also is He "sanctified"—that is, glorified as holy—because of me.

Thy kingdom come. This refers to the second coming; for one who relies on a good conscience prays for the resurrection and the judgment to come.

Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Just as the angels do your will in heaven, He says, so grant that we may do it on earth.

Give us our <term>supersubstantial bread</term> <note>original: "panem superfubftantialem"; traditionally interpreted as both daily sustenance and the bread of the Eucharist</note>. He means the bread which is sufficient for our substance and our physical constitution.

Today. This word removes our worry for tomorrow. Furthermore, the Body of Christ is the supersubstantial bread, of which we pray to be participants without condemnation.

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>A</margin>
**And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.**] Because we continue to sin even after baptism, we pray that He might forgive us. However, He will forgive us in the same manner as we forgive: if we are greedy for revenge and mindful of wrongs, He will not forgive us. God holds me as a model <note>original: "exemplar"</note>; whatever I do to another, He does to me as well.

**And lead us not into temptation.**] We are weak human beings, and therefore we ought not to throw ourselves into temptations. But if we should fall into them, we must pray that we are not swallowed up by the temptation. For the person who is swallowed up and conquered is the one who has been "led" into the depths of temptation; it is not the same for the one who falls in but conquers it.

<margin>B</margin>
**But deliver us from evil.**] He did not say, "from evil men," for it is not they who truly do us wrong, but the "Evil One"—that is, the demon.

**For yours is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory forever, Amen.**] Here He encourages us. For if our Father is a King, powerful and glorious, we will certainly conquer the Evil One and be glorified hereafter.

**For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.**] He teaches us once again to be strangers to the desire for revenge. He emphasizes the memory of the "Father" so that we might revere Him; since we are His children, we should not be embittered.

**But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.**] For the kind God hates nothing so much as cruelty.

<margin>C</margin>
**Moreover, when you fast, do not be like the hypocrites, with a sad countenance. For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to be fasting. Truly I say to you, they have their reward.**] The "disfiguring of the face" refers to paleness; it is when a person does not appear as they truly are, but fakes a look of sadness.

**But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you do not appear to men to be fasting, but to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you openly.**] The ancients practiced anointing themselves after washing as a sign of joy; you also should rejoice and be glad in this way. Furthermore, "oil" can be understood to mean almsgiving <note>The Greek word for oil (elaion) sounds similar to the word for mercy/alms (eleos)</note>. Moreover, our "Head"—which is Christ—

<column-break/>

### EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. 21

<margin>D</margin>
ought to be anointed with almsgiving; and our "face"—that is, our senses—ought to be washed with tears.

**Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth consume, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth consumes, and where thieves do not break in nor steal.**] After He has cast out the disease of vainglory, He consequently speaks about poverty. For men often possess many things for the sake of empty glory. He shows how useless it is to have treasures on earth: because rust and moths consume food and clothing, while thieves take gold and silver. Then, lest someone should say to Him, "But not all things are lost to theft," He says:

<margin>E</margin>
Even if none of these things should happen, is it not still a miserable thing to be so addicted to the anxiety of riches? For God says:

**For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The lamp of the body is the eye; if therefore your eye is simple, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!**] He says this because if you apply your mind to the anxiety of wealth, you have extinguished the lamp and darkened your soul. For just as the eye, if it is "simple"—that is, healthy—illuminates the body, but if it is "evil"—that is, diseased—it brings darkness; so also the mind is blinded by anxiety. If the mind is darkened, the soul becomes dark, and much more so the body.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>The mind is blinded by anxiety.</margin>
**No one can serve two masters.**] He speaks of two masters who give contrary commands. For example: God and <term>Mammon</term> <note>a Syriac word for riches or worldly gain</note>. We, however, make the devil our master, just as some make the belly their god. By nature, God is truly the Master; but "Mammon" is unrighteousness.

**For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon.**] You see that the wealthy and the unrighteous cannot serve God. For the love of riches casts one away from God.

**Therefore I say to you, do not be anxious for your life...**

<meta>This page continues Theophylact’s commentary on the Sermon on the Mount, moving from the discussion of almsgiving and prayer in Matthew 6 into the famous exhortations against anxiety and the warning against hypocritical judgment in Matthew 7. The previous page concluded with a warning that God will not forgive those who do not forgive others.</meta>

# CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW
## PAGE 22

<margin>D</margin> **...what you will eat or what you will drink, nor for your body, what clothing you will wear.**] Why is it that one is cast out by God on account of wealth? The soul does not eat, for it is incorporeal, but He spoke according to common custom. However, it seems the soul cannot remain in the body unless the flesh is fed. He does not forbid work, but rather giving oneself over entirely to anxieties and neglecting God; this is what He prohibits, for it is necessary both to cultivate the fields and to have a care for life.

**Is not the soul worth more than food, and the body more than clothing?**] This means: will He who gave the greater thing—namely, the soul—and who formed the body, not also give nourishment and clothing?

<margin>E</margin> **Look at the birds of the heaven, for they do not sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them; are you not worth far more than they?**] He could have brought forward Elijah and John <note>John the Baptist and the prophet Elijah were both famous for living in the wilderness and being provided for by God.</note> as examples, but He mentions birds to warn us that we might be even more senseless <note>original: "brutiores," meaning more like irrational animals</note> than they. God feeds them, having instilled in them a natural knowledge for gathering food.

**And which of you by being anxious can add one cubit to his height?**] This means (He says) that although you are anxious, you can do nothing without God’s will; why then do you torture yourself in vain?

**And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not labor, nor do they spin. But I say to you, that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.**] He warns us not only through birds, which lack reason, but also through the lilies that bloom. For if God has adorned those, even though no necessity demands it, how much more will He supply our lack of clothes? He shows that even if you are very anxious, you still cannot be adorned like the lilies; for not even Solomon, the wisest and most refined <note>original: "delicatissimus," implying great luxury or elegance</note>, in all his kingdom could be adorned like one of them.

**But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will He not much more do so for you, O you of little faith?**] We say in this place that no one ought to care for finery <note>original: "ornatum"</note>. For this belongs to fading flowers, and that which is adorned is mere hay. But He calls you "rational beings," for whom God formed both soul and body. All those who are anxious have little faith. For if they had perfect faith in God, they would not be so waveringly anxious.

**Therefore do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For the Gentiles seek all these things.**] He does not forbid eating and drinking, but He forbids saying, "What shall we eat?"—just as the rich say in the evening, "What shall we eat in the morning?" You see that He prohibits luxury and indulgence.

**For your heavenly Father knows that you have need of all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.**] The kingdom of God is the enjoyment of good things, and that comes about through righteousness. Therefore, to everyone seeking spiritual things, physical things are also added by the generosity of God.

**Therefore do not be anxious for tomorrow. For tomorrow will have its own care. For the day's own trouble is sufficient for it.**] He calls the "evil" <note>original: "malitiam," here used in the biblical sense of trouble or affliction</note> of the day "affliction" and "calamity"; for it is enough for you that you are overwhelmed by today's affliction. If you are also anxious for tomorrow, when will you have time for God, while always torturing yourself for physical things?

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>C</margin> ->**N**<- <note>Decorative initial 'N' begins the Latin "Ne iudicetis" (Judge not).</note> **Judge not, that you be not judged.**] He does not forbid rebuking, but rather condemning; for rebuking is useful, but condemnation is shameful and full of contempt. Or otherwise, understand it to refer to one who, being more liable to sins himself, reproaches others and condemns those who are less guilty, and in those matters which God is to judge.

**For with what judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with what measure you measure, it will be measured to you. And why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not see the beam that is in your own eye? Or how will you say to your brother, "Let me cast out the speck from your eye," and behold, a beam is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first cast out the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to cast out the speck from your brother's eye.**] It is necessary for one who is about to criticize others...

...to be immaculate. For he who has a beam in his eye <margin>D</margin>—that is, a large piece of wood, signifying a great sin—and yet rebukes another who has a speck, makes that person even more shameless. Moreover, the Lord shows that a great sinner cannot see the sin of a brother well. For how can he who has a beam in his eye see another who is only moderately bad?

<margin>Who are the dogs and pigs.</margin> **Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.**] Dogs are the unfaithful, while pigs are those living a swinish life. Therefore, the mysteries <note>In this context, "mysteries" refers to the deep doctrines of the faith or the sacraments, which were often kept hidden from the uninitiated in the early Church.</note> are not to be betrayed to the unbelieving, nor should the clear and pearl-like discourses on theology be shared with the unclean. For pigs trample what is said, while dogs turn and tear you; this is what the philosophers <margin>E</margin> did when they heard of the crucified Christ. They tear you apart through their reasoning, making false accusations <note>original: "cavillantes," meaning to use deceptive or trivial objections</note> that such a thing is impossible.

**Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened.**] He previously commanded great and difficult things of you. Therefore, in this passage, He shows how these things may be accomplished once obtained, namely through continuous prayer. For He said "Ask," which means "always." He did not say "ask once." Then He confirms the saying with a human example.

**Is there any man among you, who, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, <margin>F</margin> will he give him a serpent?**] He teaches here that one must ask vehemently and ask for useful things. For just as you (He says), seeing your children ask for useful things like bread and fish, give them everything they ask for, so also you should seek spiritual things, not carnal ones.

**If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him.**] He calls men "evil" when compared to God; for though our nature is good, having been created by God, we are evil by our own will.

**Therefore, all things whatever you would have men do to you, do you also to them. For this is the law and the prophets.**] He shows a short path to virtue. From our own selves, we know what needs to be done. For if you wish to receive benefits, do good; if you wish to be loved by your enemies, love even your enemies. Indeed, the law of God and the prophets say these things; even natural law almost always commands it. <margin>Tobit 2</margin> <note>The marginal reference to Tobit refers to the "Golden Rule" in its negative form found in Tobit 4:15: "What you hate, do to no one."</note>

**Enter through the narrow gate, for wide is the gate and broad is the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it.**] He calls voluntary trials "the narrow gate," such as fasting and other disciplines; as well as those things that happen against our will, like chains and persecutions. Just as a heavy person or one burdened with baggage cannot enter through a narrow space, neither can one who is soft or wealthy; such people go through the wide gate. Furthermore, showing that the distress is temporary while the width is a shortcut, He called them a "gate" and a "road." For he who is afflicted passes through affliction as if through a gate, while the soft person enters as if on a road. And because both are temporary, let the better one be chosen. <margin>B</margin> <margin>See below, 2.</margin>

**How narrow is the gate and strict the road that leads to life, and few are those who find it.**] This is an expression of wonder. **"How..."** For He marvels, saying, "Oh, how narrow!" How is it then that He says elsewhere, "My burden is light"? It is because of the future rewards.

**Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. By their fruits you will know them.**] These are crafty and deceptive heretics; therefore He says, "Beware," that is, be on your guard. For they put forward a pretext of smooth speech and feign a holy life, but inwardly the sting is hidden. The sheep's clothing is the gentleness they use while they flatter and deceive. They are known by their fruit, which is to say, by their works and their lives. For even though they might feign it for a time, they are betrayed by the passage of time. <margin>C</margin> <margin>The crafty and smooth-talking.</margin>

**Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Even so, every good tree produces good fruit, but a rotten tree produces bad fruit.**] The thorns and thistles are the hypocrites. Thorns, as those who prick in secret; thistles, as those who are crafty and versatile. A rotten tree is anyone who...

# CHAPTER 7. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW
## PAGE 24
### D
<note>catchword: lam (referring to "illam" on the next column)</note>

...and a dissolute life rots.

<margin>D</margin>
**A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a rotten tree bear good fruit.**] As long as it is rotten, it cannot; however, when it is converted <note>original: "convertitur," suggesting a spiritual transformation or turning around</note>, it can. For notice that He did not say, "it *will not* be able," but rather that as long as it is rotten, it does not produce good things.

<margin>Previously in Luke 3:3</margin>
**Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Therefore, by their fruits you will know them.**] With these words He rebukes the Jews, for John the Baptist used to say similar things to them. He compares a person to a tree because a human can be grafted <note>The image of grafting implies that a person's nature can be changed through divine grace, moving from "sterile sin" into "virtue."</note> from sterile sin into virtue.

<margin>E</margin>
**Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.**] In this passage He reveals Himself as the Lord, since He says, "Lord, Lord"—for in this way He speaks of both Himself and of God. He teaches us that if we have faith without works, it will benefit us nothing. For by saying, "he who *does* the will," He does not mean someone who did it once, but someone who does it until death. Furthermore, He did not say "my will," so as not to offend His listeners, but "the will of my Father." In truth, however, the will of the Father and the Son is one and the same, unless the Son were to be of a different nature.

**Many will say to me in that day, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform miracles in your name?" And then I will declare to them: I never knew you;** <margin>F</margin> **depart from me, you workers of iniquity.**] Many, when they began to preach, cast out demons; although they were unworthy, they drove out demons through the name of Jesus. For grace is effective even through the unworthy, just as we are sanctified through unworthy priests. Even Judas performed signs, as did the sons of Sceva. As for His saying, "I never knew you," He means: "I did not love you even then, when you were performing miracles." For in this context, "knowledge" refers to "love" or "charity."

**Therefore, everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house upon a rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and they beat against that house,**

<column-break/>

**and it did not fall; for it was founded upon a rock.**] Without God, virtue cannot be perfected; therefore He says: "I will liken him to a wise man." Now, the Rock is Christ. The House is the soul. Therefore, whoever builds his soul by practicing the commandments of Christ, neither the rain—that is, the devil who fell from heaven—nor the floods—namely, harmful men who are multiplied by this rain—nor the winds—that is, evil spirits—nor, in short, any temptations, will be able to cast him down, if he be such a man.

<margin>B</margin>
**And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them, will be like a foolish man who built his house upon the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and they beat against that house, and it fell, and great was its ruin.**] He did not say, "I will liken him," but rather that by his own nature he "will be like" a fool—the one who believes but does not act. This is the one who builds on sand, working sluggishly. For this reason he is cast down by temptations; they "beat against" him, meaning the temptation strikes him, and he falls. None of the unfaithful "fall," for they all already lie on the ground; but the faithful man stands. And the ruin is "great" precisely because he is a Christian.

**And it happened, when Jesus had finished these words, the crowds were astonished at His teaching. For He was** <margin>C</margin> **teaching them as one having authority, and not like the scribes.**] It was not the leaders who were astonished—for how could they be, since they hated Him?—but the innocent multitude of the people. They did not marvel at the eloquence of His words, but at His authority and freedom. For He displayed a greater freedom than the prophets. They used to say, "Thus says the Lord," but Christ, as God, says, "I say to you."

### d

...therefore when He had come down, he [the leper] worshipped Him, displaying great faith. He did not say, "if you pray to God, you will heal me," but "if you will," <note>original: "si vis"</note> acknowledging Him as the Christ.

**And stretching out His hand, He touched him, saying: "I am willing; be made clean." And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him:** <margin>Luke 5</margin> <note>The marginal note in the source cites Luke 14, but this is a likely printer's error for Luke 5, which contains the parallel account of the leper.</note> **"See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded as a testimony to them."**] He touched the leper to show that He is not subject to the Law—which commanded that a leper not be touched—but rather that He is its Lord. He showed that nothing is unclean to the clean, and that His holy flesh communicates sanctification. Shunning worldly glory, He commands the man to tell no one, but to show himself to the priest. For unless the priest pronounced him clean, the man would have had to remain outside the city. He also commanded him to offer a gift as a testimony to the Jews: that is to say, "When they accuse me of being a destroyer of the Law, you shall be my witness, for you were just now commanded by me to fulfill those things required by the Law."

<margin>Luke 7</margin> <note>Source reads Luke 2, but the Centurion story is in Luke 7.</note> **And when He had entered Capernaum, a Centurion approached Him, pleading with Him and saying:**] He did not approach Him here on the mountain, so as not to interrupt the teaching. This man is the same one mentioned in Luke; although Luke says that he sent other messengers to Jesus, this does not contradict Matthew’s account that he came himself. It is likely that he first sent others, and then, as the danger grew, he came in person and spoke.

**"Lord, my servant lies at home paralyzed, and is in terrible suffering." And Jesus said to him, "I will come and heal him."**] He did not bring the boy on a bed, believing that Christ could heal him even while absent. For this reason:

**The Centurion answered and said: "Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed. For I also am a man under authority, having soldiers under me, and I say to this one, 'Go,' and he goes; and to another, 'Come,' and he comes; and to my servant, 'Do this,' and he does it." When Jesus heard this, He marveled and said to those who followed: "Truly, truly I say to you, I have not found such great faith even in Israel."**] "If I, who am a servant of the king," he says, "command the soldiers 

<column-break/>

subject to me, how much more can you command death and diseases, so that they depart from one and come to another like soldiers?" For bodily diseases are God’s soldiers and His avengers. Therefore Christ marvels and says that He has not found such great faith among the Israelites as in this Gentile.

**"I tell you that many will come from the east and the west, and will sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth."**] He did not say explicitly that "many Gentiles" would sit down, so as not to provoke the Jews; instead, He spoke in figures, saying, "Many from the east and the west." He mentioned Abraham to show that He is not contrary to the Old Law. Furthermore, by mentioning "outer darkness," He showed that there are certain punishments that are more tolerable and lighter than others. For there are degrees even in punishments. He calls the Jews "sons of the kingdom," as they were the ones to whom the promises were made. For He says: "Israel is my firstborn son."

**And Jesus said to the Centurion: "Go, and as you have believed, so let it be done for you." And his servant was healed in that hour.**] It is made clear from these events that if that man was healed by a word, it was also truly said that the Jews were to be cast out.

**And entering Peter’s house, He saw his mother-in-law lying down with a fever; and He touched her hand and the fever left her. And she rose and began to serve them.**] He entered Peter’s house to eat, and touching the hand of Peter’s mother-in-law, He not only extinguished the fever but also restored her to full health, so that with her strength returned, she was even able to serve them. We know that otherwise, those recovering usually take a long time to grow strong. While other Evangelists say that they pleaded with Him and thus she was healed, Matthew (for the sake of brevity) omitted this. <margin>Luke 4. Marriage does not hinder virtue. Isaiah 53.</margin> For I told you at the beginning: one says what another leaves out. Furthermore, learn here that marriage is not prohibited by virtue; for the Prince of the Apostles <note>A traditional title for Saint Peter.</note> had a mother-in-law.

**When evening had come, they brought to Him many who were possessed by demons, and He cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were sick...**

He also uses the healing of Peter's mother-in-law to note that marriage is compatible with a life of high virtue.</summary>

### d ij

**...he healed, so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: "He himself took our infirmities and bore our diseases."**] In the evening and at an unseasonable hour, they brought the sick to Him. He, however, being merciful, healed them all. Then, lest you should disbelieve how He healed so many diseases in such a short time, he brings forward Isaiah as a witness. Although the prophet says this regarding sins, Matthew applied it to physical diseases, because most of these happen as a result of sins.

**When Jesus saw great crowds around Him, He gave orders to go to the other side of the shore.**] He was not a seeker of glory, and by this act He also avoided the envy of the Jews.

<margin>E</margin>
**And when a certain scribe had heard, he said to Him: "Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go." Jesus said to him: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head."**] He calls him a "scribe," meaning one who is learned in the letter of the Law. This man, therefore, when he saw many miracles, thought that Jesus was making a profit from them, and for that reason he strove to follow Him, so that he too might collect something. Christ, however, meeting his inner thoughts, spoke to him in this manner: "You seem to want to follow me to gather riches; do you not see that I do not even have a house? Such must he be who follows me." He said these things as if He were reluctant for the man to accompany Him, and so the man withdrew. Some say that the "foxes" and "birds" refer to devils <note>original: "diabolos"</note>; as if He were saying: "Demons dwell in you, and therefore I find no rest in your soul."

<margin>F</margin>
**Another of His disciples said to Him: "Lord, permit me first to go and bury my father." But Jesus said to him: "Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead."**] After someone has handed himself over to God, he ought not to turn back again to the cares of this life. It is certainly necessary to honor one's parents, but it is more necessary to honor God. Furthermore, this man's father was an unbeliever, which is clear from what He says: "Let the dead bury their own dead," that is, the unfaithful. If it was not even permitted for those men to bury a father, woe to those who, having professed the monastic life <note>original: "monasticen"</note>, return to worldly business.
<margin>Note.</margin>

---

<margin>A</margin>
**And when He had entered the boat, His disciples followed Him. And behold, a great earthquake arose in the sea, so that the boat was covered by the waves; but He was sleeping.**] He kept only the disciples with Him so that they might see the miracle. He allowed the storm to arise so that they might be exercised against temptations, and so that they might believe through the miracle. He slept so that, being struck with fear, they might acknowledge their own weakness and plead with Him, as follows:

**And the disciples approaching, woke Him, saying: "Lord, save us, we are perishing." And He said to them: "Why are you afraid, O men of little faith?"**] He does not call them unbelieving, but of little faith. For by saying "Lord, save us," they demonstrate faith; but because they say "we are perishing," that is not of faith. For while He was sailing with them, there was nothing to be dreaded. See how, by reproaching them as fearful, He shows that fear brings about dangers. Therefore, He first calms the disturbance of their souls, and then He also settles the storm of the sea.
<margin>B</margin>

**Then (he says) having risen, He rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. But the men wondered, saying: "What kind of man is this, for the winds and the sea obey Him?"**] What was seen was that of a man, but the works were those of God.

**And when He had come to the other side into the region of the Gergesenes, two demon-possessed men met Him.**] While those in the boat were doubting what kind of man He was, the demons came as heralds. Although both Mark and Luke mention only one man who had a "legion," you should understand that one of these two was perhaps more notable. They came to Him of their own accord; for no one dared to lead them, so cruel were they.
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Mark 5. Luke 8.</margin>

**Coming out from the tombs; they were exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass by that way.**] They dwelt in the tombs. The demons wanted to establish a certain false teaching <note>original: "dogma"</note>, namely that the souls of the dead become demons—which no one ought to believe. For the soul, once departed, does not wander in the world. For the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God; but those of sinners are themselves [driven] from here... <margin>False appearances of souls. Where is purgatory?</margin>

<margin>D</margin>...[by publi]shing his own life <note>The Latin text begins with "do vitam suam," likely completing the word "publicando" from the previous page, referring to Matthew's former life as a tax collector.</note>, which others hid by calling him Levi. <note>The other Evangelists, Mark and Luke, refer to Matthew as "Levi" to spare his reputation, but Matthew identifies himself by his profession and common name.</note> Moreover, it was a work of God that he was converted by a single word.

For the Pharisees, wanting to pull the disciples away from Him, accused Him regarding the feast with the tax collectors.

<margin>E</margin>**When Jesus heard that, what did He say? "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. But go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance."**] He said: I have not come now as a judge, but as a physician; therefore, I even endure the stench <note>original: "fœtorem" — a metaphor for the spiritual "odor" of sin.</note>. He rebukes them as being ignorant, saying, "Go and learn," which means, "Because you have not learned it until now, at least go and learn it now: that God values mercy toward sinners more than sacrifice." Furthermore, when He says, "I did not come to call the righteous," He speaks with irony; that is, "You who justify yourselves." For no one among men was truly righteous (all were sinners); He calls them not so they may remain sinners, but to lead them to repentance.

<margin>Hosea 6.</margin>

<margin>F</margin>**Then the disciples of John came to Him, saying, "Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but Your disciples do not fast?"**] John’s disciples were envious of Christ’s glory and criticized Him for not fasting. For they were in doubt as to how they could conquer the passions without the punishment of the body—something that John himself could not do. They were ignorant of the fact that John was a man who was pure and righteous through virtue, while Christ was Virtue itself, inasmuch as He is God.

**So Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast."**]

<margin>A</margin>He says: The present time is a time of joy as long as I am with the disciples. For He calls Himself the "bridegroom" because He is joining to Himself a new congregation, which is the Church; the old one, the Synagogue, having died. He calls the apostles the "wedding guests" <note>original: "filios thalami," literally "sons of the bridal chamber."</note>. The "time of fasting" refers to when I shall have suffered and been taken up into heaven. They will fast with hunger and thirst, suffering persecution. He also shows that the disciples are still imperfect, and says:

<margin>B</margin>**"No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; for the patch pulls away from the garment, and the tear is made worse. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins, or else the wineskins break, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved."**] He says: The disciples have not yet been made strong, but they have need of understanding, and the heavy weight of the commandments should not be placed upon them. He said these things to teach His disciples that when they themselves are to teach the world, they should be indulgent and gentle. For the "unshrunk cloth" and the "new wine" represent fasting; the "old garment" and "old wineskins" represent the weakness of the disciples.

<margin>Harsh things are not to be enjoined upon disciples.</margin>

**While He spoke these things to them, behold, a ruler came and worshiped Him, saying, "My daughter has just died; but come and lay Your hand on her, and she will live." So Jesus arose and followed him, and so did His disciples.**] This man seems to have faith, though not a great deal. For he begs Jesus not merely to speak a word, but to come and lay His hand on her. He says his daughter has died, although in Luke she is said to be not yet dead; but he says this either as a guess, because he had left her as she was breathing her last breath, or to increase the sense of calamity so that he might provoke Christ to mercy.

<margin>C</margin>**And behold, a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years came from behind and touched the hem of His garment. For she said within herself, "If I only touch His garment, I shall be made well." But Jesus turned around, and when He saw her, He said, "Be of good cheer, daughter; your faith has made you well." And the woman was made well from that hour.**] This woman, because she was "unclean" <note>According to Jewish Law (Leviticus 15), a woman with a discharge of blood was ritually impure and could not touch others.</note>, did not approach Him openly out of piety, fearing she might be forbidden. Although she thought she could remain hidden...
