# THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW
## d iiij
<meta>catchword: coming;</meta>

<margin>D</margin> [Neve]rtheless, she hoped she would obtain health if she only touched the edge of His garment, which is signified by the fringe. But the Savior reveals her, not as one seeking glory, but to declare her faith for our benefit, and so that the ruler of the synagogue <term>archisynagogus; the leader of a Jewish congregation</term> might also be strengthened in faith. "Have courage," He says to her, because she was afraid since she had received the gift secretly. And He calls her "daughter" as one who is faithful. He also shows that if she had not had faith, she would by no means have received the benefit, even if she had touched His holy garments. They say, moreover, that she made a statue of the Lord, at whose feet grew an herb that could heal those suffering from a flow of blood, which the impious destroyed in the time of Julian <note>original: "Iuliani temporibus"; referring to Emperor Julian the Apostate, r. 361–363 AD, who attempted to suppress Christianity and restore paganism</note>.

<margin>E</margin> **And when Jesus had come into the house of the ruler, and had seen the flute-players and the crowd making a noise, He said to them, "Depart, for the girl is not dead, but sleeps," and they laughed at Him.**] Since she was not yet married, they were mourning her with wedding flutes, doing this according to the law <note>it was custom to play flutes even at the funerals of the poor, but here the "nuptial flutes" emphasize her youth and the tragedy of her dying before marriage</note>. But He says she is sleeping because to Him, death was merely sleep; for He was able to wake her easily. Moreover, do not wonder that they laughed at Him, for they give further testimony to the miracle: that He truly raised one who was dead. For lest anyone should say that she was merely in a trance, her death was acknowledged by everyone.

<margin>F</margin> **But when the crowd was put out, He entered and took her hand, and the girl arose. And that report spread into all that land.**] Where there is a crowd and a tumult, Jesus does not work miracles. But He holds her hand, giving her power. And you, if you have been dead in sins, you will then rise when He takes hold of your hand, so that you may act, once the crowd has been cast out and the tumult stilled.

**And when Jesus departed from there, two blind men followed Him, crying out and saying, "Have mercy on us, Son of David."**] As if to God, the blind men said, "Have mercy"; but as if to a man, they said, "Son of David." For it was well known among the Jews that the Messiah would come from the seed of David.

**But when He had come into the house, the blind men came to Him. And Jesus said to them, "Do you believe that I can do this?" They said to Him, "Yes, Lord."**] He leads the blind men with Him all the way into the house

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> to show their solid faith and to condemn the Jews. He asks them whether they believe, showing that faith accomplishes all things.

**Then He touched their eyes, saying, "According to your faith let it be to you." And their eyes were opened.**] He heals them privately in the house to avoid empty glory. For in all things He teaches modesty and humility of mind.

**And Jesus strictly charged them, saying, "See that no one knows it." But when they departed, they spread His fame in all that land.**] You see how He fled from pride. Yet they made it known, not as if they were disobedient, but as those who were grateful. Although in another place He is seen to say, "Go and tell the glory of God," this is not contrary to that; for He wants those remaining with Him to say nothing, but to tell the glory of God among others.

<margin>B</margin> **But as they were going out, they brought to Him a man who was mute and demon-possessed, and once the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke.**] This was not a natural disease, but one sent by a demon; therefore others also bring him. For he could not pray for himself, because the demon had bound his tongue; hence He does not demand faith, but immediately heals him by casting out the demon that prevented the mute man from speaking.

**And the crowds marveled, saying, "Nothing like this has ever appeared in Israel."**] The marvelling crowds placed Christ above both the prophets and the patriarchs; for He healed by His own power, not like those who prayed. But we see also what the Pharisees say.

<margin>C</margin> **But the Pharisees said, "He casts out demons by the prince of demons."**] Those are the words of the utmost stupidity; for no demon casts out a demon. But even granted that He might cast out demons as if serving the prince of demons, how then did He release people from diseases and sins and preach the kingdom of God? For a demon, in the opposite way, increases diseases and separates people from God.

**And Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and every disease.**] Since He is merciful, He does not wait for them to come to Him; but He Himself looks out for them so they might have no excuse...

<summary>Theophylact interprets several of Jesus's miracles in Matthew 9, emphasizing that faith is the prerequisite for healing and that Christ performed these acts with humility rather than a desire for fame.</summary>

because no one had taught them; but by work and word He draws them, teaching them and performing miracles.

<margin>D</margin> **But when He saw the crowds, He was moved with compassion for them, because they were weary and scattered like sheep having no shepherd.**] They had no shepherd because their leaders <term>principes; referring here to the Jewish religious authorities</term> not only failed to correct them, but actually caused them harm. For it is the mark of a true shepherd to be moved with mercy toward the flock.

**Then He said to His disciples, "The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few: pray therefore the Lord of the harvest, that He may send out laborers into His harvest."**] He calls the great number of people needing ministry the "harvest." The "laborers" are those who ought to teach, the likes of whom were not then found <margin>E</margin> in Israel. The "Lord of the harvest" is the Lord of the apostles and the prophets. This is manifest from the fact that He Himself appointed the apostles, without asking God <note>Theophylact is emphasizing Jesus’s divine authority; Jesus tells them to pray to the "Lord of the harvest," and then He immediately acts as that Lord by appointing the twelve</note>. Hear now:

### CHAPTER X.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a figure in profile wearing a hat, possibly a scholar or cleric.</image-desc>**And when He had called His twelve disciples to Him, He gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every sickness.**] He chooses twelve disciples according to the number of the twelve tribes of Israel. He handed over power to them and sent them out, though they were few. Indeed, few pass through the narrow gate. He gave them the power of performing miracles so that they might lead people to wonder and have listeners who were more obedient to their teaching. <margin>F</margin>

**Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother.**] He lists the names of the disciples because of "false apostles" <note>original: "pseudo apostolos"; a warning against unauthorized or heretical teachers in the early church</note>. He places Peter and Andrew first since they were the first to be called. Then, listing the sons of Zebedee, he puts James before John, not because of rank, but because that is how it happened. Thus he says:

**James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, Philip and Bartholomew, Thomas and Matthew the tax collector, James the son of Alphaeus and Lebbaeus whose surname was Thaddaeus, [Simon the Canaanite] and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed Him.**

<margin>A</margin> Observe the humility of Matthew, how he places Thomas before himself. When he comes to Judas, he does not say "that filthy one" or "the enemy of God," but identifies him as "Iscariot" from his hometown. For there was also another Judas, who was called Lebbaeus and Thaddaeus. There are therefore two named James: one the son of Zebedee, the other the son of Alphaeus. There are also two named Judas: one being Thaddaeus, the other the traitor. Furthermore, there are three named Simon: Simon Peter, Simon the Canaanite, and the traitor. For Simon was also said to be the father of Judas Iscariot <note>original: "Simon enim Iudas Iscariotes dicebatur"; Theophylact follows the tradition, often found in the Gospel of John, that Judas was the "son of Simon Iscariot"</note>.

**These twelve Jesus sent out and commanded them, saying, "Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter into any city of the Samaritans: but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of <margin>B</margin> Israel. And as you go, preach, saying, 'The kingdom of heaven is at hand.'"**] These twelve—what kind of men were they? Fishermen, commoners, and tax collectors. He sent them first to the Jews so that they could not later claim, "Since they were sent to the Gentiles, we Jews had a right not to believe." Thus He stripped the Jews of every excuse. He groups the Samaritans with the Gentiles because they were Babylonians who lived in Samaria within Judea and did not accept the prophets. Furthermore, by "the kingdom of heaven," He means the enjoyment of future blessings. He arms them with miracles, saying:

**Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received, freely give.**] Nothing so becomes a teacher as humility and a contempt for riches. Therefore, He teaches two things in this place. By saying "Freely you have received," He warns them <margin>C</margin> not to be proud because they possessed and gave such gifts. For you received such things freely and by grace; therefore, remain humble and be despisers of wealth. For "freely," He says, "give." And so that the root of all evils might be more perfectly extirpated:

**Provide neither gold nor silver nor copper in your money belts, nor a bag for your journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff: for the worker is worthy of his food.**] He trains them with great zeal, and for this reason, He removes all superfluous things from them and takes away their cares. For He does not even allow them to have a staff, which is a sign of extreme poverty; He makes those who teach through poverty worthy of faith. Then, lest they should say, "how [shall we live?]"...

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus's compassion for the leaderless Jewish people and the subsequent commissioning of the twelve Apostles. He emphasizes the need for humility and voluntary poverty among teachers of the Gospel.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Theophylact, Archbishop of Bulgaria, on the Gospel of Matthew. The previous page introduced the commissioning of the twelve Apostles. Here, Theophylact explains Jesus’s instructions on how the Apostles should sustain themselves, choose where to stay, and how to handle rejection and impending persecution.</meta>

-># CHAPTER 10. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA<-

"How shall we be fed?" He says: **"The laborer is worthy of his food,"** <margin>D</margin> meaning you will be fed by the disciples. For they will owe this to you as laborers. Note that He said "food," not "luxury." For it is not fitting for a teacher to live in luxury.

**"Whatever city or village you enter, find out who is worthy in it; and stay there until you leave."** He did not command them to go to everyone, lest by being mixed with the unworthy, they might be criticized. If they go only to the worthy, they will surely be fed. He commands them to remain and not go from house to house, so they are not spoken of poorly as gluttons <note>original: "gulosi"</note>, and so they do not seem to insult those who first received them.

**"As you enter the house, greet it: and if the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you."** By "greeting" and "peace," understand a blessing <margin>E</margin> which remains only with the worthy. Learn here, then, that it is primarily our own works that bring us blessing.

**"And whoever does not receive you or hear your words, as you leave that house or city, shake the dust off your feet. Truly I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city."** He wants them to shake off the dust to show they have received nothing from there, due to the hardness of those who could not be persuaded; or to testify that they traveled a great distance on their behalf, yet it profited them nothing. It will be more tolerable for Sodom than for the unbelievers, because the people of Sodom, having been punished here <note>Referring to the biblical destruction of Sodom in Genesis</note>, will be punished more mildly elsewhere. <margin>F</margin>

**"Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves."** He had armed them with miracles and given them confidence regarding food by opening the doors of the worthy. Now He speaks of the hardships to come, revealing His foreknowledge. He consoles them by saying, "I" (He says)—the one who is powerful—"send you," and therefore trust that you will be invincible. He is preparing them for suffering. For just as it is impossible for sheep in the midst of wolves to suffer nothing, so it is for you among the Judeans. But though you suffer, do not be angry. For I want you to be gentle, like sheep, and in that way to conquer more effectively.

<column-break/>

->## EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 31<-

<margin>A</margin> **"Be therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves."** He wants the disciples to be wise as well; therefore, when you hear Christians called sheep, do not think they should be stupid, for they must also be wise and know how to conduct themselves in the midst of enemies. For just as a serpent sometimes exposes its whole body to be struck but protects its head, so also the Christian (He says) allows everything to be taken, even by those who strike his body, but let him keep his head—which is Christ—and his faith in Him. And just as a serpent coils itself into a narrow hole and, passing through, sheds its old skin, so let us walk the narrow path to strip off the "old man" <term>old man; refers to the "vetus homo," a biblical concept of the former sinful self before spiritual renewal</term>. Nevertheless, <margin>B</margin> because the serpent is also harmful, He commands us to be simple—that is, sincere and without malice, offending no one—like doves. For when their young are taken and they suffer persecution, they still return to their masters. Be wise, therefore, like the serpent, so that you are not mocked by others for your way of life, but accomplish all your tasks without fault. Toward those who harm you, however, be like a dove—that is, not at all malicious.

**"But beware of men: for they will hand you over to councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues; and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles."** You see that this is the part of the wise: to be cautious and not give opportunity to those wanting to persecute, but to conduct our affairs prudently. If the persecutor wants money, give it; if honor, allow it, so that he <margin>C</margin> has no occasion against you. But if he takes away your faith, guard your "head" <note>Returning to the earlier analogy where the head represents faith in Christ</note>. He was not only going to send the disciples to the Judeans, but also to the Gentiles; therefore He says, **"As a testimony to them and to the Gentiles,"** that is, as a mark and a rebuke to those who do not believe.

**"But when they hand you over, do not be anxious about what or how you should speak: for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you."** Lest they say, "How can we, unlearned men <note>original: "idiotæ"; here meaning simple folk or those without formal rhetorical training</note>, persuade those endowed with wisdom?" He commands them to hope for the best and to lay aside anxiety.

<summary>This page details Theophylact’s commentary on Christ’s commissioning of the Apostles, emphasizing the balance between sheep-like gentleness and serpent-like wisdom in the face of persecution. It explains that the Apostles' needs will be met by those they serve and provides allegorical interpretations for the serpent and the dove.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Theophylact’s commentary on Matthew 10. The previous page discussed the Apostles’ instructions on where to stay and how to handle those who reject their message. This page shifts to the trials and persecutions they will face, and the divine comfort they should rely on when testifying before authorities.</meta>

-># CHAPTER 10. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW<-

<margin>D</margin> For when we must speak among the faithful, it is right that we should prepare beforehand and be ready to give a defense, as Peter admonishes <note>See 1 Peter 3:15.</note>. However, when among the crowds and threatening kings, He promises His own strength so that we do not fear. For it is our part to confess the faith, but to respond wisely is the part of God. And lest you suspect that this fitness in defending yourself is a natural talent, He says: **"It is not you who speak, but the Spirit."**

**"For brother will deliver brother to death, and a father his son, and children will rise up against parents and put them to death."** He foretells these things that are to come so they are not troubled when they occur. He also shows the power of the preaching—how it makes one disregard nature itself. This <margin>E</margin> is the nature of Christianity, and it reveals the madness of those others who do not even spare their own kin.

**"And you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But he who perseveres to the end, he will be saved."** "By all" here means "by many." For not everyone pursued them with hatred; indeed, quite a few received the faith. But the one who perseveres until the very end, and does not merely start the race, he shall be a partaker of eternal life.

**"But when they persecute you in this city, flee into another. Amen I say to you, you will not have gone through all the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes."** The things said above were terrifying—that they would be betrayed and hated—and these were <margin>F</margin> to happen after His ascension. However, what is said now concerns those things happening before the Cross. He says: "You will not finish your work in the cities of Israel amidst your persecutions before I come to you." For He commands the one suffering persecution to flee. Truly, to throw oneself into danger recklessly, making oneself the cause of a murderer's condemnation and depriving those whom one could have helped through preaching, is diabolic. **(Until the Son of Man comes)**: you should not understand this as the Second Coming, but as the meeting and consolation they had before the Cross. For having been sent to preach, they returned to Him again and lived with Him.

**"A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master; for it is enough for the disciple to be <margin>A</margin> like his teacher, and for the servant to be like his master."** He teaches in this passage that injuries must be endured. For if I, the teacher and master, have sustained them, much more should you, the disciples and servants. But you may ask, how can He say "a disciple is not above his teacher" when we see many disciples excel beyond their teachers? Understand, therefore, that as long as they are disciples, they will be lesser than their teachers; if they should become more excellent, they are no longer disciples. Likewise, a servant, as long as he is a servant, will not be above his master.

**"If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more those of his household? Therefore do not fear <margin>B</margin> them: for there is nothing covered that will not be uncovered, and nothing hidden that will not be known."** Take consolation from my own experiences. For if they called me the prince of demons <note>original: "Beelzebub"</note>, what is so heavy if they also attack you, my household, with insults? He called them "those of his household" to declare His intimacy with them. But have confidence; the truth will not be hidden, but time will reveal both your virtue and the malice of your slanderers. For nothing is hidden that will not be known. Therefore, although they may disparage you now, later you will be made famous.

**"What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach on the rooftops."** That which I said to you privately and in one place (for this is what <margin>C</margin> "in the ear" and "in the darkness" means), teach confidently and with a loud voice, so that everyone may hear you. Because dangers follow freedom of speech, He adds:

**"And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna."** He teaches that even death should be despised. For He says the punishment of Gehenna is more terrible. For those who kill only destroy the body, and perhaps they even benefit the soul <note>as in the case of a martyr’s soul being freed from the flesh</note>. But God, by casting one into Gehenna, punishes both soul and body. When He said "Gehenna," He signifies perpetual punishment. For Gehenna is said to come from "always being produced" <note>Theophylact is using a creative Greek etymology here, linking the word to the idea of unending or ever-recurrent suffering</note>.

**"Are not two sparrows sold for a small penny? And one of..."** <note>The catchword "Nonne" indicates the start of the next verse: "Are not two sparrows sold for a copper coin?"</note>

<summary>Theophylact discusses Jesus's warnings to the Apostles about coming persecutions and family betrayals, encouraging them to trust the Holy Spirit's guidance and to value the soul's safety over the body's.</summary>

-># CHAPTER 8 <note>The header indicates Chapter 8, though the text continues the commentary on Matthew Chapter 10.</note>. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW<-

->33<-

<margin>D</margin> [one of] them does not fall to the ground without your Father. Indeed, even the hairs of your head are all numbered: therefore, do not fear, for you are worth more than many sparrows.] He says this so they would not be troubled as if they were abandoned. If not even a sparrow is caught without my knowledge, how could I abandon you whom I love? Furthermore, to indicate His manifest knowledge and providence, He says that your hairs have been numbered. Therefore, do not think that an action of God is required for sparrows to be snared; rather, it means that even the catching of them is not unknown to God.

**"Everyone, therefore, who confesses in me before men, I also will confess him before my Father, who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, I also will deny him before my Father, who is in heaven."**] He exhorts them to martyrdom and bearing witness; for it is not enough to believe in the soul alone, but God also wants us to confess through the mouth. He did not say "whoever confesses me," but **"in me"** <note>original: "in me"</note>, that is, by my power. For he who confesses does so helped by heavenly power. Afterward, concerning the one who denies, He did not say "in me," but "me"; showing that one denies because they do not have heavenly help. For everyone who confesses that Christ is God finds Christ confessing about him to the Father that he is a faithful servant. But those who deny will hear: "I do not know you."

**"Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth: I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household."**] Concord is not good in every instance; rather, discord is sometimes a good thing. The **"sword"** <note>original: "gladius"</note>, therefore, is the word of faith, which pulls us away from the habits of our relatives and kindred when they hinder us from piety. For He does not simply say that we should separate and disagree with them, but only when they are not helpful and hinder our salvation.

**"He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me."**] You see that it is necessary for us to hate parents and children at the time when they wish to pull us away from Christ. And why do I speak of father, mother, and children? Hear what is even greater.

<margin>A</margin> **"He who,"** (He says), **"does not take up his cross and follow me, is not worthy of me."**] Whoever (He says) has not renounced this present life and surrendered himself to a contemptible death (for this is what the ancients called the "cross") <margin>The Cross.</margin> is not worthy of me. Since many are crucified like thieves and robbers, He added: **"and follows after me,"** that is, lives according to my laws.

**"He who finds his soul will lose it, and he who loses his soul for my sake will find it."**] He seems to "find his soul" who guards the life that is in the flesh; but he loses it, because he sends it into eternal punishment. However, he who loses his soul and dies—not as a robber or one who strangles himself, but <margin>B</margin> for Christ’s sake—he is the one who saves it.

**"He who receives you, receives me: and he who receives me, receives him who sent me. He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward. And he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward."**] He rouses us to welcome those sent by Christ. For he who welcomes the disciples honors Him, and because of Him, also the Father. It is necessary, however, to welcome the righteous and the prophets "in the name of a prophet or righteous man," that is, because they are righteous and prophets, and not because of political rank or support from kings. But if someone happens to bear the likeness of a prophet, yet in their deeds does not provide the same, and you have welcomed him as a prophet, <margin>C</margin> God will repay you as if you had welcomed a righteous man; for this is what is meant by "he will receive a righteous man’s reward." Or you might understand it another way: that the one who receives them is also considered righteous and receives the reward that the righteous receive.

**"And whoever gives even one of these little ones a cup of cold water to drink, only in the name of a disciple, Amen I say to you, he will not lose his reward."**] Lest anyone should plead poverty as an excuse, He says that even if you give a cup of cold water because that person is my disciple, you will receive a reward for this. Moreover, he also gives a "cup of cold water" who teaches someone who is burning with the fire of God <note>Theophylact here interprets "cold water" spiritually as a cooling or refreshing teaching for those on fire with zeal or desire.</note> or with passions. And he makes him to be called a disciple of Christ; nor will such a person lose their reward.

### CHAPTER 11.

<margin>D</margin>
**And it happened that when Jesus had finished giving instructions to his twelve disciples, he moved on from there to teach and preach in their cities.**] After sending the disciples out, he himself stopped performing miracles and only taught in the synagogues. For if he himself had been present healing people, no one would have approached the disciples; therefore, so that they too might have the opportunity to heal, he himself moved on.

**Now when John had heard in prison of the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples and said to him: "Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?"**] John does not ask as if he were ignorant of who Christ was. For how could he be ignorant, since he himself testified, **"Behold the Lamb of God"**? <note>original: "Ecce agnus dei"</note> But because his disciples were jealous of Christ, he sends them so that he might make them more certain through many proofs, so that by seeing the miracles they might believe that Christ is greater than John. For this reason, he pretends to ask: **"Are you the one who is to come?"** <note>original: "Tu es qui venturus es?"</note> that is, the one expected in the Scriptures to come in the flesh. However, some say that since John had said Christ was to come, he was asking about the descent into the underworld <note>original: "descensu ad inferos," often translated as Hades or Hell</note>, as if John were ignorant and asking: "Are you also the one who is to come to the underworld, or should we expect another?" But it would be frivolous to say this. Since John was more excellent than the other prophets, how could he have been ignorant of Christ's crucifixion and his descent into the underworld? Especially since he called Christ "the Lamb," because he was to be sacrificed for us. John knew, therefore, that the Lord was to come into the underworld with his soul to save those there—just as Gregory the Theologian <note>A title for St. Gregory of Nazianzus, one of the most important theologians of the early Church.</note> says—all who were willing to believe that he had been incarnated for our sake. He does not ask as one who is ignorant, but as one wishing to teach his disciples about Christ through the abundant testimony of the performance of miracles. See, indeed, what Christ says to this question.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>Gregory the Theologian.</margin>
**And Jesus answered and said to them: "Go and report to John what you hear and see: The blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have the Gospel preached to them. And blessed is he who is not offended by me."**] He did not say, "Tell John: I am the one who is to come," but as one who knew that John had sent the disciples for this very reason—to see the miracles—he said, **"Tell John what you see."** And certainly, having taken this opportunity, John will provide even more testimony about me to you. By **"the poor who have the Gospel preached to them,"** <note>original: "pauperes euangelizantur"</note> understand either the apostles preaching the Gospel (for they were poor fishermen, and as private citizens they were considered contemptible) or the listeners of the Gospel, who are hearing about heavenly treasures. Showing John’s disciples that their private thoughts were not hidden from him, he says: **"Blessed is he who is not offended in me,"** for they were doubting him greatly.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
**As they were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: "What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?"**] Perhaps the crowds, when they heard John's question, were offended, fearing that perhaps John himself had doubted Christ and had thus easily changed his mind, even though he had previously testified about Christ. Therefore, Christ, removing this suspicion from their midst, says: John is not a "reed," that is, someone inconstant and fickle. For if he were such a person, why did you go out to him in the desert? You did not go out to see a reed—that is, a man easily changed—but you went out as if to a great and steadfast man. Therefore, he remains exactly as you judged him to be.

<margin>C</margin>
**"But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft things are in the houses of kings. But what did you go out to see? A prophet?"**] Lest they be able to say that he had first served luxury and then became relaxed, he says: No. For his clothing was made of hair, which showed he was a stranger to luxury. For if he had worn soft things, he would have lived in the houses of kings, and not in prison, if he had pursued luxuries. Learn, therefore, that a virtuous Christian ought not to wear soft clothing. **"Indeed I tell you, he is even more than a prophet."** This...

Jesus defends John's steadfast character to the crowds, contrasting his ascetic life with the fickleness of a reed or the luxury of kings.</summary>

<margin>
Why John is called an messenger <note>original: "angelus"</note>.
Malachi 3.
</margin>
**For he is the one of whom it is written: "Behold, I send my messenger <note>The Latin 'angelum' translates the Greek 'angelos,' meaning messenger.</note> before your face, who will prepare your way before you."**] He is called a "messenger" or "angel" both because of his angelic lifestyle—living almost as if he were free of material needs—and because he announced and preached Christ. He prepared the way of Christ by testifying about him and by baptizing people into repentance. For after repentance comes the forgiveness of sins, which is the gift that Christ gives. Christ said these things after John's disciples had departed so that he would not seem to be flattering them in their presence. This prophecy was spoken by Malachi.

**"Truly <note>original: "Amen"</note> I say to you, among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist."**] He asserts this with a solemn affirmation. By saying "born of women," he excludes himself. For Christ was born of a Virgin, not a "woman" in the sense of one who has known a man.

**"Yet he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he."**] Since he had spoken many praises of John, he said this more clearly so they would not think John was greater than himself. He says: "I, who am 'lesser'—being younger in age and, in your opinion, inferior—am greater than him in the kingdom of heaven," which refers to spiritual and heavenly blessings. For in this earthly life I am "less" than him in the sense that he was born before me, and he seems great to you, but in the spiritual realm, I am greater.

**"From the days of John the Baptist until this day, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force."**] These words might seem disconnected from what came before, but that is not the case. Consider this: Christ had spoken of himself as being greater than John, and he urges them to believe in him, showing that many "seize" the kingdom of heaven—that is, faith in him. However, this requires great virtue. To leave behind father and mother and to disregard one's own life—how much "force" does that take?

**"For all the prophets and the law itself prophesied until John."**] From this, the following follows naturally, for he says: "I am the one who is to come." For all the prophets have been fulfilled. They would not have been fulfilled if I had not come. Therefore, you should expect nothing further.

<margin>
Malachi 3.
</margin>
**"And if you are willing to receive it, he is the Elijah who was to come."**] "If you are willing to receive it" (he says)—that is, if you judge with a healthy mind and not an envious one—he is the Elijah whom the prophet Malachi said would come. For the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note> and Elijah were assigned the same ministry: John was the forerunner of the first coming, and Elijah will be the forerunner of the second. Then, showing that it is a mystery <note>original: "ænigma"</note> that John is Elijah, and that one needs understanding to perceive it, he says:

**"He who has ears to hear, let him hear."**] In this way, he leads them to ask questions and to learn.

**"To what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplace and calling out to their companions, saying: 'We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.'"**] Here he points out the stubbornness <note>original: "morositatem"</note> of the Jews. For they were difficult in their ways; they could be invited neither by the austerity of John nor by the simplicity of Christ. Instead, they were like rebellious children whom no one can please, neither through easy-goingness nor through sorrow.

**"For John came," (he says) "neither eating nor drinking, and they say, 'He has a demon.' The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, 'Look at this glutton and wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!'"**] He likens the life of John to a dirge or lamentation, for it was a life of great severity in both words and deeds. But Jesus, marvelously arranging all things, condescended to everyone so that he might win everyone over and preach the kingdom. Therefore, he did not practice the same austerity that John did.

**"And wisdom is justified by her children."**] He means this: "Neither John’s life nor mine pleases you; rather, you reject every path of salvation. I, who am Wisdom, will appear just. For after this, you will have no excuse, but will be judged entirely. For I indeed fulfilled all things, and you, having become unbelieving, prove me just, insofar as I left nothing undone."

**Then he began to reproach the cities in which most of his miracles had been performed, because they had not repented.**

From these cities were Andrew, Peter, Philip, and the sons of Zebedee; thus, their failure was not a defect of nature, but a malice of the will. For if they had been evil by nature, those disciples would have been evil as well.
**For if the miracles <note>The Latin 'virtutes' here refers to 'mighty works' or miracles performed by Christ.</note> that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Nevertheless, I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.** He says the Jews are worse than the people of Tyre and Sidon, for the Tyrians only transgressed the natural law, but the Jews transgressed both the natural and the Mo-

<margin>E</margin>saic law. Furthermore, the Tyrians did not see miracles, whereas the Jews even accused the miracles they saw. Sackcloth is a symbol of penance. We see those in mourning sprinkle ash and dust over their heads.
> **And you, Capernaum, who are exalted to the heavens, you shall be brought down to hell: for if the miracles done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. Nevertheless, I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.** ]

Capernaum was "exalted" because it was the city of Jesus; it was glorified as his home, yet it received no benefit from this because it did not believe. Therefore, it was judged in the opposite manner—down to hell—because despite hosting such a marvelous 

<margin>F</margin>guest <note>original: "inquilinum"</note>, it was not made any better. Since anyone can interpret "Capernaum" as a "field of consolation," see this: if someone deserves to become a "field" for the Holy Spirit <note>original: "spiritus paracleti"</note> and then thinks highly of himself and is exalted toward heaven, he too shall fall through pride. Therefore, O man, stand in awe.
**At that time Jesus answered and said, "I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent, and have revealed them to little ones."** ] What he says has this meaning: "I confess," that is, "I give thanks to you," because the Jews, who seem to themselves to be wise and skilled in the scriptures, did not believe. But the unlearned and the "little ones" <note>Referring to the humble or child-like in spirit.</note> believed and 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>known the mysteries. God hid the mysteries from those who appear to be wise—not because he was envious or the author of their ignorance, but because they were not worthy, precisely because they seemed wise to themselves. For he who seems wise to himself and trusts in his own wisdom does not call upon God. Therefore, God does not call him, nor help him, nor reveal things to him. Put another way: God, out of his great mercy, does not reveal more mysteries to them so that they might not be punished more severely for despising the things they had learned.
> **Yes, Father, for such was your good pleasure before you.** ]

In this place, he manifests the kindness of the Father: that he reveals things to the "little ones" not because he was provoked by another, but because it pleased him from the beginning.

<margin>B</margin>For "good pleasure" <note>original: "complacitum" and "beneplacitum"</note> is the same as his will.
> **All things have been handed over to me by my Father.** ]

He said above that the Father had hidden things; lest you should suspect, therefore, that Christ himself does nothing and all things belong only to the Father, he says, "All things have been handed over to me," meaning my power and his are one. When you hear "handed over," do not suspect they were handed over as if to a servant or an inferior, but as to a Son. For according to the fact that he was born from the Father, all things were handed over to him. For if he were not born of him and of the same substance, they would not have been handed over to him. He does not say "by the Lord," but "by my Father": as, for example, if a beautiful boy is born to a handsome father, and says, "Beauty was given to me by my father."

<margin>C</margin>> **And no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.** ]

He says something even greater. Let it be no wonder to anyone that I am Lord of all, since I am capable of something even greater—namely, knowing the Father—and so knowing him that I can reveal him to others. Consider, however, that earlier he said the Father reveals mysteries to the little ones; here, the Son reveals the Father. You see, therefore, the one power of the Father and the Son, since both the Father and the Son reveal.
> **Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.** ]

He calls everyone—not only Jews, but Gentiles. By those who "labor," understand the Jews, as they were following the traditions of the law and were exhausted in the performance of the law's commandments. By those who are "burdened,"

...however <note>This continues the thought from the previous page regarding those who labor.</note> [he means] the Gentiles, who are oppressed by the burden of sins. These, therefore, Christ causes to rest. For to believe, to confess, and to be baptized—what labor is that? And how is it not also a rest, since here one need no longer be anxious about the things done before baptism, and elsewhere <note>Meaning in the afterlife.</note> a rest is waiting to receive you?

<margin>Jeremiah 8.</margin>
**Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.** ] The yoke of Christ is humility and gentleness. Therefore, he who humbles himself before every man finds rest, remaining undisturbed. Just as a man who is arrogant and greedy for empty glory is always full of cares, never wishing to be considered inferior to anyone, but always thinking how he might be more glorified and how he might conquer his enemies. Therefore, the yoke of Christ (I mean humility) is light. For it is easier for our nature to be humbled than to be exalted <note>Theophylact suggests that pride requires a constant, exhausting effort to maintain, while humility is a natural state of peace.</note>. Likewise, all the commandments of Christ are called a light yoke, because they are light in view of the future reward, even if they seem heavy for a short time.

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>1 Kings 22 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 21, where David eats the consecrated bread at Nob.</note></margin>
**At that time, Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath; and his disciples were hungry and began to pluck the heads of grain and eat them. But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him: Behold, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath. But he said to them: Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him? How he entered the house of God and ate the Bread of Presence, which was not lawful for him to eat, nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests.** ] Once again, the Pharisees criticize a natural passion <note>Meaning the physical sensation of hunger.</note> while they themselves commit more grievous sins. The Lord admonishes them through the history of David. For David (he says), on account of hunger, dared to do something quite significant. Now, there were twelve loaves of the Bread of Presence <note>Original: 'panes propositionis', also known as showbread.</note> which were set out daily on the table: six on the right side and six on the left. Although David was a prophet, it was still not lawful for him to eat from them, but only for the priests; how much more was it not lawful for those who were with him? Nevertheless, because of hunger, he was worthy of forgiveness; and so it is for the disciples.

<margin>Numbers 28. Exodus 20. Deuteronomy 5.</margin>
**Or have you not read in the law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath, and yet are without guilt? But I tell you that something greater than the temple is in this place.** ] The law forbade working on the Sabbath; yet the priests on the Sabbath both cut wood and lit fires, and thus they "profaned" the Sabbath—that is, they defiled it, as it seems to you. But you say to me: "That was certainly permitted for the priests, but the disciples were not priests?" I say, therefore, that something greater than the temple is in this place; that is, because I am greater than the temple, and the Lord and his disciples have a greater power to loosen the Sabbath than the priests do.

<margin>Above, Chapter 9. Hosea 6.</margin>
**But if you had known what this means, "I desire mercy and not sacrifice," you would never have condemned the innocent; for the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.** ] He shows that they are both unskilled and ignorant of the prophetic word. For it was necessary (he says) to have mercy on the hungry. And otherwise: I, the Son of Man, am Lord of the Sabbath and the maker of days, and I, as Lord, loosen the Sabbath. Understand this also according to <term>anagoge</term> <note>A method of spiritual interpretation that finds a higher, mystical meaning in the text.</note>. Since the apostles were workers, the harvest and the ears of grain are the believers. Furthermore, the apostles plucked and ate them—that is, they took the salvation of men as their food. And they did this on the Sabbath, which is to say, during the rest from evils. The Pharisees, however, were indignant; so also in the Church, when teachers are teaching and desiring to be of benefit, "Pharisees" often feel envy and take it badly.

<margin>Mark 3. Luke 6.</margin>
**And departing from there, he came into their synagogue. And behold, there was a man having a withered hand, and they questioned him, saying: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? so that they might accuse him.** ] Other Evangelists say that Jesus questioned the Pharisees. It can be said, therefore, that since they were envious, they anticipated him and asked the question, as Matthew says. Then Christ, in turn, questioned them, as if laughing at their blindness—which is what is said by the other Evangelists. They question him, therefore, so that they might have an occasion for slander.

<margin>D</margin> **But he said to them: "What man shall there be among you, that shall have one sheep, and if it shall fall into a pit on the sabbath, will he not take hold of it and lift it out? How much better then is a man than a sheep? But when they are taught by the word of the Gospel, let them stretch them out and share. The Pharisees are like proud demons who have "amputated" our hands through their own lack of mercy toward us, and they do not wish for the hand to be extended toward acts of mercy.

**The Pharisees, however, went out and took counsel against him, how they might destroy him. But when Jesus knew it, he withdrew from there.** ] They were envious; for when they are faced with good deeds, they go mad. Jesus withdraws because the time for his Passion was not yet at hand, meanwhile sparing them <note>original: "parcens interim illis"</note> so that they would not become guilty of the crime of murder. For to recklessly throw oneself into danger is not pleasing to God.

<margin>Isaiah 42:1</margin> In order to soothe their envy, he does not wish to be made known. For he omitted nothing that pertained to their care.

For "judgment" <term>iudicium: Theophylact defines this as divine doctrine or the ability to discern good from evil</term> is doctrine and knowledge, and the discernment of good; or, he will announce the future judgment to the heathens, who have never heard of a judgment to come.

**"Neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets."** ] For he did not teach in the middle of the marketplace like those seeking glory, but in the temple, in synagogues, on the mountain, and by the shores.

**"A bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench."** ] He was able (it says) to break the Jews like a crushed reed, and to quench their anger like smoking (that is, burning) flax; but he was unwilling to do so until the divine plan <term>dispensatio: the 'oikonomia' or God's planned management of human salvation</term> was fulfilled, and he overcomes them through all things. For this is what the following words signify:

**"Until he sends forth judgment unto victory. And in his name shall the Gentiles hope."** ] For lest they should have any excuse, he endured all things, so that he might later condemn them and overcome them while they could say nothing in contradiction. And what is there that he did not do to win them over? But they were unwilling. Therefore the Gentiles will hope in him, because the Jews were unwilling.

**Then was brought unto him one possessed with a devil, blind and dumb: and he healed him, insomuch that the blind and dumb both spoke and saw. And all the people were amazed, and said: "Is not this the son of David?"** ] The demon had blocked the paths to faith: the eyes, the ears, and the tongue. Jesus heals him, and he is named "Son of David" <note>The "Son of David" was a common Messianic title based on the promise that a descendant of King David would rule forever.</note> by the crowds. For the Christ was expected from the seed of David. Now, if you see someone who neither understands what is good by himself nor receives the words of another, consider him to be blind and dumb, whom God might heal by touching his heart.

**But when the Pharisees heard it, they said: "This fellow does not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub the prince of the devils."** ] Although the Lord had withdrawn because of them, they nonetheless criticized him even while hearing from afar. These men, who were being treated with many benefits, were as hostile as the devils themselves.

<summary>Theophylact comments on Jesus healing the man with the withered hand and a demoniac, contrasting the Pharisees' legalistic greed and envy with Christ's gentleness and mercy. He explains Matthew's use of Isaiah's prophecy to illustrate Jesus's humble nature and his eventual turn toward the Gentiles.</summary>

### CHAPTER 12. THE EXPLANATION OF THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.
### PAGE 39

<margin>D</margin>
**But when Jesus knew their thoughts, he said to them: "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand. And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then shall his kingdom stand?"** ] By making public their private thoughts, he proved himself to be God <note>Knowing the secret thoughts of others was considered a sign of divinity.</note>. He defends himself before them using common examples and points out their foolishness. For how could demons cast themselves out, when they are generally in agreement with one another? Satan, moreover, is defined as "the adversary."

<margin>E</margin>
**"And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges."** ] "Let it be," he says, "that I am such a person as you say: but your sons—that is, my disciples—by whose power do they cast them out? Surely they do not do it by Beelzebub?" But if they do so by divine power, then how much more do I? For they perform miracles in my name; therefore, they will be the ones to condemn you, because you see them performing miracles in my name, and yet you still accuse me.

**"But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you."** ] He is saying this: if I cast out demons by divine power, then I am the Son of God, and I have come for your sake so that you may receive these benefits; thus, my arrival has reached you. For this is the kingdom of God. Why then do you accuse my arrival, which is for your own benefit?

<margin>F</margin>
**"Or how can anyone enter into a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man, and then he will plunder his house?"** ] So far is it, he says, from me being friends with demons, that I actually have them as enemies; I bind those who were strong before my arrival. By "entering the house"—that is, coming into the world—Jesus took away the "spoils" of the demons, which are the souls of human beings.

**"He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters."** ] How, he asks, could Beelzebub be a co-worker with me, when he works for the exact opposite? I indeed teach the truth, but he teaches malice; how then is he with me? And I indeed gather people together for their salvation, but he scatters—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
—them. He is noting the Pharisees here because, while he was teaching and desiring to benefit many, they themselves were scattering the people so that they would not come to him. Thus he shows them to be truly full of demonic influence.

**"Therefore I say to you: Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven men, but blasphemy against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven men. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come."** ] He says in this passage that every other sin, however inexcusable it may be—such as sexual immorality, theft, and similar things—is of such a nature that one may appeal to human weakness, and there is a place for pardon. However, when someone has seen

<margin>B</margin>
the miracles of the Holy Spirit being performed and has accused them of being the work of the devil: what kind of excuse will that person have? For it is manifest that he knows they are done by the Holy Spirit, yet by his own will he chooses to work evil; how then will such a person be worthy of pardon? Thus, when the Jews saw Christ eating and drinking, and associating with tax collectors and harlots, and doing all other things in the manner of a human being <note>original: "more filij hominis" — in the manner of the Son of Man.</note>, and then reproached him as a glutton and a wine-drinker: in this they were worthy of pardon, and no repentance was required of them for this, because they seemed to have a "reasonable" reason to be offended. But when they saw him performing miracles,

<margin>Above, Luke 11:7 <note>This likely refers to the similar passage in Luke 11:15-20.</note></margin>

<margin>C</margin>
and yet reproached him and blasphemed the Holy Spirit, saying that this was the work of a demon, how shall this sin be forgiven unless they had performed penance? Therefore, learn that he who blasphemes against the Son of Man—seeing him living in a human way and saying "This man is a lecherous glutton and a wine-drinker" while Christ is acting thus—such a person, even if he does not repent, will not be held to account for this. For he received pardon as one who did not understand that he was God, because his divinity was so hidden. But he who blasphemes the Holy Spirit—that is, the spiritual works of Christ—and says they are diabolical: unless he performs penance, he will not obtain pardon. For he had no reasonable cause for his slander. It shall not be forgiven, therefore—

<margin>Luke 16.</margin>
...punished <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a thought on divine justice.</note> either here or in the world to come. For there are many who are indeed punished here, but are free from punishment elsewhere, such as the poor man Lazarus. Others, however, are punished both here and there, like the Sodomites and those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit. Still others are punished neither here nor elsewhere, such as the apostles and the Precursor <note>John the Baptist.</note>. For although they seem to suffer persecution, they do not suffer those things because of sins; rather, these are trials and crowns of glory.

<margin>D</margin>
**"Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree rotten and its fruit rotten; for the tree is known by its fruit."**] Since the Jews could not prove that Christ’s works were evil, they blasphemed Christ himself, claiming he performed them by demonic power. He says: "Either say that I am a good tree and my miracles—whatever they may be—are good fruit; or, if you say I am a rotten tree, it is manifest that the fruit (the miracles) will also be rotten. But you admit the miracles are good fruit; therefore, I too am a good tree. For just as a tree is known by its fruit, so I am known by my miracles."

<margin>E</margin>
**"Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?"**] "Look," he says, "since you are evil trees, you bear bad fruit when you speak ill of me. Likewise, if I were evil, I would bring forth evil fruit, and not such miracles as these." He calls them a "brood of vipers" because they boasted of being descended from Abraham; he shows, however, that they are not truly from Abraham, but from ancestors worthy of themselves.

<margin>John 8.</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
**"Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. A good man out of the good treasure brings forth good things, and an evil man out of the evil treasure brings forth evil things."**] Whenever you see someone speaking obscenities, know that they have much more of the same in their heart than what they actually say. For it is from an "abundance" <note>original: *abundantia*</note> that the heart pours itself out into external words, possessing a hidden treasury. The mouth only declares a small part. Similarly, one who speaks good things has even more stored in the heart.

<margin>Job 9.</margin>

**—words you will be condemned."**] Here he terrifies us, for we are to give an account even for an "idle word"—that is, for lies, slander, or disordered and ridiculous talk. Then he provides a testimony from Scripture so that he does not seem to be speaking only from himself: "By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned."

<margin>Prov. 12:18, Ecclus. 20</margin>
**Then certain of the scribes and Pharisees answered, saying: "Master, we wish to see a sign from you."**] Marveling at this, the Evangelist added the word "Then." For precisely when they ought to have obeyed because of the preceding signs, *then* they asked for another sign. They wanted to see a sign "from heaven," as another Evangelist says; for they thought that he performed signs on earth by the power of the devil. For the devil is the "ruler of this world." How, then, does the Savior respond to this?

<margin>B</margin>
**He answered and said to them: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. He says the "sign" is his own miraculous resurrection. After he descended into the heart of the earth—the lowest place—he rose again. You should understand "three days and three nights" as parts of days, not full twenty-four-hour periods. For he died on the Preparation Day <note>Friday</note>, which is one day; he remained dead on the Sabbath; and the night of the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note> found him still dead. Therefore, three days and nights are counted by their parts, as we are often accustomed to count in this way.

<margin>Deut. 30:2, Jonah 2.</margin>

Therefore you will be condemned by the Ninevites, who believed my servant without miracles, even though they were barbarians; whereas you, who are accustomed to the prophets..."

...prophets, yet having seen the signs you do not believe me, the Lord; which the letter D <note>Refers to a section marker in the text.</note> signifies, saying, **"And behold, something greater than Jonah is here."**

<margin>3 Kings 10; 2 Chronicles 9. <note>In the Latin Bible, 1 Kings is titled 3 Kings.</note></margin>
**"The Queen of the South will rise up in judgment with this generation, and will condemn it: because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon. And behold, something greater than Solomon is here."** "The Queen," he says, "came from far away, even though she was a weak woman, to hear about trees, timber, and certain natural matters; but you, though I have come to you and spoken of secret mysteries, have not received me."

**"But when the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it walks through dry places, seeking rest and finding none. Then it says, 'I will return to my house from which I came.' And when it arrives, it finds it empty, swept clean by brooms, and decorated. Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first. So shall it also be for this wicked generation."** He shows that they have come to the very edge of destruction because they did not receive him. And just as those who are freed from demons, if they become lazy, end up in a worse state, so also your generation was once held by a demon when it worshipped idols, but that demon was cast out by the prophets. But I have come, wishing to cleanse you even more; yet because you have rejected me and wish to kill me, as you sin more gravely, you will also be punished more severely. And your final captivity <note>Referring to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> will be more grievous than the first. Moreover, you should understand this also <margin>F</margin>: that through baptism the spirit is cast out; it goes to "waterless places," meaning unbaptized souls, but it finds no rest in them. For the demon's "rest" is to trouble the baptized through evil deeds; since it already possesses the unbaptized, it turns instead toward the baptized person with seven spirits. For just as there are seven gifts of the Spirit <margin>Isaiah 11.</margin>, so, by contrast, there are seven spirits of malice. When it has entered a baptized person, the calamity becomes worse. For previously there was hope of being cleansed through baptism, but afterward there is no hope of a second baptism, except through repentance, which is very laborious.

**"While he was still speaking to the crowds, behold, his mother** <column-break/> <margin>A</margin> **and his brothers were standing outside, seeking to speak to him."** The mother wished to show something human—that she had power over her son. For she did not yet understand anything great about him; because of this, while he was still speaking, she wanted to draw him to herself, as she was a bit status-seeking <note>original: "ambitiosula"</note> because her son was so influential. What then did Christ do, since he knew her intention? Hear what he says.

<margin>Read carefully; see the end of the book.</margin>
**"Someone said to him, 'Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you.' But answering, he said to the one who had told him, 'Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?' And extending his hand toward his disciples, he said, 'Behold my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.'"**

<margin>B</margin>
He said these things not to cause injury to his mother, but to correct her mind, which was greedy for glory and focused on human things. For he did not say, "She is not my mother," but rather that if she does not do the will of God, it will be of no benefit to her that she gave birth to me. He does not deny the natural kinship, but he adds to it the kinship that comes through virtue. For no one who is unworthy gains any benefit from a family connection. Therefore, having corrected the disease of vain glory, he again obeys his mother when she calls. For the Evangelist says:

### CHAPTER 13

**"On that day, Jesus went out of the house and sat by the sea. Truly, he fishes from the sea for those who are on the land.

**"And he spoke to them many things in parables,"** He spoke to the simple crowds without a parable on the mountain; <margin>Above, chapters 5, 6, and 7.</margin> but to these people, he speaks in a parable—as if to deceitful Pharisees—so that if they do not understand, they might seek and learn. Furthermore, it was not appropriate to set forth his doctrines nakedly <note>That is, plainly or without concealment.</note> to those who were unworthy. ### CHAPTER 13. THE EXPLANATION OF THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

f ij <note>This is a signature mark used by early printers to keep the pages in the correct order.</note>

Now he presents the first parable, which makes the listener more attentive.

<margin>D</margin> **[Behold, the sower went out to sow.]** He calls himself the sower, and the word is the seed. He "went out," however, not in a physical sense—for he was already everywhere—but rather in the sense that he became closer to us through the flesh <note>original: "per carnem"; a reference to the Incarnation, where God took on human form.</note>; thus he is said to "go out" from the Father's borders. He came out to us because we were unable to enter into him. And for what purpose did he go out? Was it to burn the earth because of the thorns? Was it to punish? Not at all, but rather to perform the sowing. He calls it "his seed" because even though the prophets also sowed, it was not their own seed they planted, but God's. He himself, as God, sowed his own seed—that is, his very own—for he was not merely someone enlightened by divine grace, but was himself the Wisdom of God.

<margin>E</margin> **And as he sowed, some seeds fell by the wayside, and the birds came and devoured them; other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and they sprang up immediately because they had no depth of earth; but when the sun rose, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.** Those who are "by the wayside" are the lazy and idle who never truly receive the word. For their mind is like a path that is trampled and hard, not plowed at all; therefore, the birds of the heaven—which are the spirits of the air, namely the demons—snatch the word from them. Those "on rocky ground" are those who hear, certainly, but do not struggle during temptations and afflictions, and so lose their salvation. By the "rising sun," you should understand "temptation"; for just as the sun reveals what is hidden, temptation shows what people are truly like and declares their character.

<margin>Temptation is the sun.</margin>
<margin>F</margin> **And other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them.** These are the people who choke the word with worldly cares. For a rich man, even if he seems to perform some good work, his work does not grow or make progress because his anxieties prevent it.

**But other seeds fell on good soil and brought forth fruit: some a hundredfold, some sixty, and some thirty.** Three parts of the seed perished, and only the fourth was saved. For those who are saved are few. Later, he speaks of the "good soil," giving us the hope of repentance <note>original: "poenitentiae spe"</note>. For it is possible, even if someone is currently "rocky" or "thorny" ground, for them to become good soil. Not everyone who receives the seed bears equal fruit: some bear a hundredfold, perhaps those who possess perfect poverty and the highest level of spiritual practice. Others bear sixtyfold, such as perhaps a <term>cenobite</term> <note>A monk who lives in a communal monastery under a rule, rather than as a solitary hermit.</note> who is still working toward perfection. Others bear thirtyfold, such as those who have chosen an honorable marriage and embrace virtue to the best of their ability. See the goodness of God: how he accepts everyone—those who cultivate great, moderate, and small things.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Given in Luke 13.</margin>

<margin>B</margin> **[He who has ears to hear, let him hear.]** This makes it clear that these things are to be understood spiritually by those who have the "spiritual ears" of the soul. Many people have ears but not for the purpose of hearing; therefore he adds, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."

**And when the disciples approached, they said to him, "Why do you speak to them in parables?" He answered and said to them, "To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. For whoever has, to him more will be given, and he will have an abundance; but whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him."** Seeing the great obscurity in the things said by Christ, the disciples approach like public representatives for the multitude to ask questions. But he says, "To you it is given to know the mysteries"—that is, because you have eagerness and zeal, it is given to you; but to those who do not apply themselves with zeal, it is not given. For he who seeks, receives. "Seek," he says, "and it shall be given to you." See also how in this place Jesus spoke a parable, and only the disciples who had questioned him received the explanation. Therefore, we have rightly said that to the one who applies zeal, knowledge is given in greater abundance—to the one who brings zeal and a worthy mind. But from the one who lacks zeal, even what he has is taken away; that is, even if he has some small spark of good, if he does not stir it up and kindle it through the Spirit and spiritual works, it is extinguished.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>See above, Luke 7 and 11.</margin>

<summary>Theophylact provides a spiritual commentary on the Parable of the Sower, explaining the four types of soil as different human responses to the Word of God. He emphasizes that the "mysteries of the kingdom" are granted to those who show spiritual zeal and eagerness.</summary>

### CHAPTER 13. THE EXPLANATION OF ARCHBISHOP THEOPHYLACT ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

f iij <note>A signature mark indicating the third leaf of the 'f' gathering in the printed book.</note>

**"Therefore I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand."** Pay attention here. For in this place, he solves the question of those who say that some people are evil by nature and because of God. For Christ said, "To you it has been given to know the secrets, but to the Jews it has not been given." We say to those people, alongside God, that God makes everyone able to understand by nature as much as is necessary. For "he enlightens every man coming into this world" <note>A reference to John 1:9.</note>; however, our own **will** darkens us. This is therefore manifested in this very place. For he says that although they see by nature—that is, they were made by God so that they are naturally able to understand—they "do not see" by their own choice. And though they hear—that is, they were naturally made by God so that they are able to hear and understand—they "do not hear nor understand" because of their own will. For tell me, I ask you, did they not see the miracles of Christ? Indeed they did, but they made themselves blind and found fault with him. This, therefore, is what is meant by "seeing they do not see." Thus, he also brings forward the prophet as a witness.

<margin>The evil are not so by nature, nor because of God. John 1.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>

<margin>Isaiah 6.</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
**"And in them is fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah, which says: 'You shall indeed hear with your ears, and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them.'"** You see what the prophet says: "for this reason you shall not understand." He does not say, "because I created your heart thick," but because it "has grown fat" <note>original: "incrassatum"; in the medical and philosophical language of the time, a "fat" or "thickened" heart was one that had become dull, sluggish, and unresponsive to spiritual truth.</note>, which clearly shows it was previously "thin" or receptive. For that which grows fat was previously thin. Moreover, since it had grown fat in this way, they "closed their eyes." He did not say that God closed them, but that they closed them by their own will. For they did these things, he says, "lest they be converted and I should heal them." For by their own malice they took care to become incurable and unfit for conversion.

<margin>F</margin>
**"But blessed are your eyes, because they see; and your ears, because they hear. For Amen I say to you, that many prophets and righteous men have desired to see what you see, and to hear what you hear, and have not heard it."** Indeed, the physical eyes and ears of the apostles were worthy of blessing because they recognized Christ. Moreover, he places them above the prophets, because the prophets saw Christ only mentally, but the apostles saw him bodily; and also because the prophets did not attain such great mysteries and such knowledge as these men did. For the apostles excelled the prophets in two ways: by seeing him physically and by understanding divine matters spiritually. Thus, he explains the parable to the disciples, saying:

<column-break/>

<margin>The Apostles excel the prophets.</margin>
**"Hear then the parable of the sower. When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart; this is the one who was sown beside the path."** He exhorts us to understand the things said by those who teach, lest we also become like those beside the path; may it not be so! Because the "path" is Christ; those who are outside of Christ are not on the path, but outside the path.

<margin>B</margin>
**"But he who had received the seed cast on rocky ground, this is he who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself, but is temporary. Furthermore, when persecution or affliction arises because of the word, he is immediately offended."** He mentions "affliction," for many who are troubled by parents or other hardships immediately begin to blaspheme. But he speaks of "persecution" on account of those who are harassed by tyrants.

<margin>Affliction and persecution.</margin>
**"But he who had received the seed among the thorns, this is he who hears the word, and the care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and he becomes unfruitful."** He did not say "this world" chokes it, but the "care of the world"; nor "riches," but the "deceit of riches." For when riches are dispersed <note>That is, given away as charity or used for good works.</note>, they do not choke the word, but rather make it grow. The "thorns" are cares and luxuries, because they kindle the fire of lust and of Gehenna <note>original: "gehennę"; the Greek/Latin term for the place of punishment or hell.</note>. And just as a sharp thorn penetrates the body and is hardly rooted out, so too do luxuries, as they grow strong, enter the soul and are hardly rooted out.

<margin>C</margin>
**"But he who received the seed on good ground, this is he who hears the word and understands it, who then yields fruit and produces, some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold."** There are various types of virtue, and various types of people who make progress.

<meta>The catchword "Varię" (Various) at the bottom of the page links to the start of the next section discussing the different degrees of spiritual fruitfulness.</meta>
