### CHAPTER 13. THE EXPLANATION OF ARCHBISHOP THEOPHYLACT OF BULGARIA ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

44

<margin>D</margin>Observe the order in the parable. For it is necessary for us first to hear the word and understand it, lest we be like those along the path. Then, we must firmly retain what has been heard; furthermore, we must not be lovers of wealth. For what will it profit if I hear and retain it, yet I am choked by the love of riches?

**He put another parable before them, saying: "The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field; but while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat and went his way. But when the grain had sprouted and produced fruit, then the tares also appeared. So the servants of the head of the household came and said to him, 'Sir, did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, does it have tares?' He said to them, 'An enemy man has done this.' The servants said to him, 'Do you want us then to go and gather them up?' But he said, 'No, lest while you gather up the tares, you also uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest, and at the time of harvest I will say to the reapers: Gather the tares first and bind them in bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my barn.'"** ] In the previous parable, he said that a fourth part of the seed falls on good ground; in this one, however, he shows that the enemy does not leave even those seeds which fell on good ground uncorrupted while we are sleeping and idle. For the field is the world, or the soul of any individual. Furthermore, it is Christ who sowed the good seed. The seed represents good people, or good thoughts. The tares <note>original: "zizania"; a type of weed, likely darnel, which looks very similar to wheat in its early stages.</note> represent heresies, or evil thoughts. Who sows these? The devil. And the sleeping men are those who, because of their own laziness, gave a place to heretics or to evil thoughts. The servants are the angels, who are indignant that there are heresies or malice in the soul, and they wish to uproot and cut off the heretics and those thinking evil things from this life. But God does not permit heretics to be consumed by wars, lest the righteous suffer and be consumed at the same time. Similarly, God does not want a person to be cut off because of evil thoughts, lest the

<column-break/>

wheat be corrupted at the same time. As an example: if Matthew <note>Referring to the Apostle Matthew, who was a tax collector before his conversion.</note> had been cut off from this life while he was a weed, the grain that was later to arise from him would surely have been cut off at the same time. Similarly with Paul, and the thief <note>The "Good Thief" crucified with Jesus.</note>. For these, while they were tares, were not uprooted, but were permitted to live so that their virtue might grow later. Therefore, it is said to the angels that at the final consummation <note>The end of the world.</note> they shall then gather the tares—that is, the heretics. But how? In bundles, which means their hands and feet will be bound; for then no one will be able to work anymore, but all power of working will be bound. The grain—that is, the saints—will be gathered by the reaper-angels into the heavenly barns. Therefore, in a similar way, the evil thoughts which Paul had when he was a persecutor were burned up by the fire of Christ, which he came to send upon the earth; but the grain—that is, the good thoughts—are gathered into the barns of the Church.

**He put another parable before them, saying: "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field; which indeed is the least of all seeds, but when it has grown, it is the greatest among herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches."** ] The grain of mustard seed is the preaching and the apostles; for they seem few, yet they have occupied the whole world, so that the birds of the air—that is, those who have a light and winged mind toward heavenly things—may rest in them. You also, be a grain of mustard seed, which may indeed seem small. For it is not necessary to show oneself as spectacular in virtue, but rather fervent, provocative, and sternly reproving. For thus you will be the greatest among herbs—that is, perfect among the weak—so that even the birds of the air—that is, the angels—may dwell in you, as you lead an angelic life. For they rejoice in the righteous.

**He spoke another parable to them: "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened."** ] He calls the apostles the "leaven," just as

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Theophylact of Bulgaria on Matthew chapter 13. ### CHAPTER 13. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin>...and a grain of mustard seed. For just as leaven, although it is small, transforms the whole batch of dough into itself, so shall you also transform the whole world, even though you are few in number. Now, a "satum" <note>original: "satum"; a Hebrew dry measure roughly equivalent to a seah or a third of an ephah</note> was a measure used by the Hebrews, just as among us there is the *modius* <note>a Roman bushel</note> or the ten-liter measure. Some, however, understand the leaven to mean the preaching of the Gospel; the "three measures" <note>three sata</note> to mean the three powers of the soul—the rational, the desiring, and the spirited; and the woman to mean the soul, which hides the preaching within all its powers, mixing it, leavening it, and sanctifying the whole through it. For it is necessary for us to be entirely leavened and transformed into divine things. For He says: "until the whole was leavened."

Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without a parable He spoke nothing to them, so that what was spoken through the prophet might be <margin>Psalm 77</margin> fulfilled, who said: <margin>E</margin> "I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world." <note>This refers to Psalm 78:2, which Theophylact identifies as Psalm 77 following the Septuagint numbering.</note> He brings forward the prophet who foretold how Jesus was to teach in parables, so that you do not think Christ invented some new method of teaching. 

<margin>As the word "that" [ut] is not always signifying a cause, but an outcome.</margin> 

The particle "that" <note>original: "Ut"</note> does not indicate the cause, but the outcome. For Jesus did not teach in this way *in order that* the prophecy might be fulfilled, but because He taught this way, the prophecy *was* fulfilled. Moreover, He did not speak without a parable to them only at that time; for He did not always speak in parables. The Lord "uttered" those things which were hidden from the foundation of the world. For He Himself has revealed to us the mysteries which are in the heavens.

<margin>F</margin> **Then Jesus sent the crowds away and went into the house.** ] Then He left the crowds, since His teaching was of no benefit to them. For He spoke in parables so that they might ask Him for the meaning, yet they did not care, nor did they seek to learn; therefore, they were deservedly left by Him.

**And His disciples came to Him, saying, "Explain to us the parable of the tares of the field."** ] They ask about this one alone because the others seemed more obvious. 

<margin>Tares</margin> 

"Tares" <note>original: "Zizania"</note> refers to those things that spring up among the crops, which are even harmful, such as darnel, vetch, wild oats, and so on.

**But He answered and said to them, "He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man; the field is the world."** Furthermore,

<column-break/>

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. 45

<margin>A</margin> the good seed are the sons of the kingdom; the tares are the sons of the evil one; the enemy who sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the age; and the reapers are the angels. As therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire, so it will be at the end of this age. The Son of Man will send His angels, and they will gather out of His kingdom all stumbling blocks, and those who practice iniquity, and will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be wailing and gnashing of teeth. ] The things which needed to be said here were mentioned above. For we said that this should be understood regarding heresies, which are permitted to exist until the end of the age. For if we were to cut them out and kill them, rebellions would occur, and perhaps many of the faithful would also perish in those rebellions. 

<margin>B</margin> Since both Paul and the thief were once tares <note>meaning "weeds" or sinners</note> before they believed; yet they were not cut off then, for the sake of the future fruit. Later, however, when they had brought forth fruit for God, the "tares" in them were burned by fire and by the fervor of the Holy Spirit.

**Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.** <margin>Malachi 4</margin> **He who has ears to hear, let him hear.** ] Since the sun appears to us brighter than all the stars, He compares the clarity of the righteous to the sun. But will they shine *only* as much as the sun? Far from it; because Christ is the Sun of Righteousness, then the righteous will shine as Christ does. For they themselves shall be gods <note>A reference to "theosis" or "deification," the Eastern Christian concept of humans participating in the divine nature.</note>.

**Again, the kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and hid; and for joy over it he goes** <margin>C</margin> **and sells all that he has and buys that field.** ] The "field" is the world; the "treasure" is the preaching and the knowledge of Christ. It is hidden in the world. For (says Paul) we preach the hidden wisdom. <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> He who seeks the knowledge of God finds it; and everything he has—whether pagan doctrines, or evil habits, or riches—he immediately throws away and buys the field, that is, the world. For he who has the knowledge of Christ possesses the world as his own property; the elements serve him, and he commands them, just as Jesus and Moses did.

**Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking beautiful pearls, who, when he had found...**

### CHAPTER 13. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA | ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

<margin>How a pearl is born</margin>
<margin>D</margin> > [...one precious pearl, he went and sold all and bought it.]
The sea is this present life. The merchants are those who travel through it seeking to find a certain knowledge. For the "many pearls" are the diverse opinions of many wise men. But the "one precious pearl" is the single truth, which is surely Christ. Therefore, just as it is handed down concerning the pearl that it is born in a shell <note>original: "concha"; referring to the oyster or mollusk</note> which opens at the time of lightning and then closes again—conceiving from the lightning and the dew, which is why it is white—so also was Christ conceived in the Virgin from the lightning from above, namely the Holy Spirit. And just as one who holds a pearl in his hand often knows how much wealth he possesses while others remain ignorant of it, so too the preaching of the Gospel is hidden <margin>E</margin> from those in darkness and is only revealed to the perfect. He teaches us, therefore, that we should give up everything else to possess this pearl.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet <note>original: "sagena"; a large weighted fishing net</note> cast into the sea, which gathered every kind of thing; when it was full, they drew it to the shore and, sitting down, gathered the good things into vessels, but threw out the bad. > So it will be at the end of the age: the angels will come forth and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.]
This parable is terrifying, for it shows that even if we believe, if we do not have a good life, we shall be cast into the fire. The dragnet is the teaching of the fisher-apostles, which is woven together from miracles and the <margin>F</margin> testimonies of the prophets. For what the Apostles taught, they confirmed by miracles and the voices of the Prophets. This net gathered every kind of people: Barbarians, Greeks, Jews, harlots, tax collectors, and thieves. When the world is fulfilled and comes to an end, those who were in the net will be discerned. For even if we have believed, if we are found to be wicked, we shall be cast out. But those who are not such will be placed into "vessels," by which I mean the eternal tabernacles. Every work, whether good or evil, is said to be the food of the soul. For the soul has "spiritual teeth." At that time, the soul will gnash them—that is, it will grind its own operative virtues in remorse because of the things it has done.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> > Jesus said to them: Have you understood all these things? They said to him: Yes, Lord. And he said to them: Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house, who brings forth from his treasure things new and old.]
Notice how the parables made them more attentive. Behold, those who were otherwise unlearned and unskilled now understand things spoken in riddles. Therefore, the Savior, praising them, says: "Every scribe, etc." He calls them "scribes" <note>original: "scribas"; technically experts in the Jewish Law, here used to mean those learned in divine things</note> because they were learned in the Law; and though they were learned in the Law, they did not remain only in the Law, but were instructed in the Kingdom—that is, in the knowledge of Christ—and they are able to bring forth things from the New and from the Old Testaments. A householder is therefore rich. <margin>B</margin> For in that very treasure-house are the sciences; He who taught new things <margin>Matthew 12.</margin> <margin>Job 9.</margin> added testimonies from the old, for the sake of example. <margin>Proverbs 18.</margin> He had said: "For an idle word you shall be justified," for this was <margin>1 Corinthians 4.</margin> new; then he added the testimony: "For by your words you will be justified and by your words you will be condemned," which is old. In this the Apostles are similar, such as Paul saying: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ."

> And it happened that when Jesus had finished these parables, he departed from there. And when he had come into his own country, he taught them in their synagogue.]
He spoke these parables because he was about to teach shortly after. He travels so that his presence might benefit others. Understand "his country" to mean Nazareth, for he was brought up there. <margin>C</margin> Furthermore, he teaches in the synagogue publicly and freely, so that they could not say later that he taught things contrary to the Law.

> So that they were astonished and said: From where does this man get this wisdom and these miracles? Is this not the son of the carpenter? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joses, Simon, and Judas? And his sisters, are they not all with us? From where then does he have all these things? And they were offended by him.]
The Nazarenes were foolish; for they thought that low birth and obscurity were reasons why a person could not please God. For even if Jesus was a humble man, was he not also God? What would prevent him from being great in miracles? Thus, they are proven to be both envious and foolish.

<margin>Joseph had six children from the wife of his brother Clopas.</margin>
Indeed, they ought to have felt greater pride that their own country had produced such a great good. However, the Lord had brothers and sisters—the children of Joseph, whom he fathered by the wife of his brother Clopas. For when Clopas died without children, Joseph took his wife according to the law <note>original: "iuxta legem"; referring to the Levirate law in Deuteronomy 25:5-6, where a man was required to marry his deceased brother's widow to carry on the lineage</note>, and fathered six children: four males and two females. These were Mary, who according to the law was called the daughter of Clopas, and Salome. "They are among us," that is, they live with us. Therefore, they too were offended by Jesus. For perhaps they themselves were saying that he cast out demons by the power of Beelzebub <note>A Philistine god, often used in the New Testament as a name for the prince of demons or Satan</note>.

But Jesus said to them, **"A prophet is not without honor, except in his own country and in his own house."** And he did not perform many miracles there because of their unbelief. See how Christ does not treat them with insult <margin>E</margin>, but bears it mildly. For we humans are accustomed to look down on those we are familiar with, while holding strangers in high admiration. As for why he mentions "in his own house": he did this because even his own household brothers hated him. Furthermore, he did not perform many miracles there because of their unbelief, sparing them so that they would not remain unbelievers even after seeing signs <note>Theophylact suggests Jesus withheld miracles as a form of mercy, so they wouldn't incur more guilt by rejecting even greater proof</note>. Therefore, he did not do many, but he did perform a few, so they could not say, "If he had done any, we would have believed." But you should understand that even today Jesus is without honor in his own country, that is, among the Jews; whereas we, who are outsiders, venerate him.

### CHAPTER 14.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial I featuring a foliage and vine motif inside a square border.</image-desc>
**At that time, Herod the tetrarch heard the fame of Jesus, and he said to his servants <margin>F</margin>, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore these powers are at work in him."** This Herod was the son of the one who killed the infants in Bethlehem. Consider here the pride of a tyrannical life. Look at how much time passed before the fame of Jesus reached Herod; it reached him late because he did not care for those who were distinguished by virtue. It appears, however, that he feared the Baptist, and for that reason, he dared to speak of these things to no one else but his "boys," that is, his servants. Since John had not performed any sign while living, Herod thought that through

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> the resurrection he had received this gift from God to perform miracles.

For Herod had arrested John, bound him, and put him in prison because of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip. For John had said to him, **"It is not lawful for you to have her."** And though he wanted to kill him, he feared the crowd because they regarded him as a prophet. Matthew did not mention this narrative about John in the preceding sections because his goal was only to write those things that pertained to Christ. Indeed, he would not have mentioned it now unless he had related it back to Christ. John rebuked Herod for holding his brother’s wife unlawfully. For the law commanded a man <margin>Deuteronomy 7</margin> to take his brother’s wife after the brother had died, if he had died without children <margin>B</margin>. But this Philip had not died without children, for there was the girl who danced. There are some who say that while Philip was still alive, Herod took both his wife and his tetrarchy <note>original: "tetrarchiam"; a province or district ruled by a tetrarch</note> from him. Whether it was the former or the latter, it was an illicit act. He did not fear God, but he did fear the crowd, which is why he delayed the murder; but the devil found a favorable time for himself.

When Herod’s birthday was being celebrated, the daughter of Herodias danced in the midst of them and pleased Herod, whereupon he promised with an oath that he would give her whatever she asked <margin>C</margin>. But she, having been instructed beforehand by her mother, said, **"Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist."** See the luxury: a Queen dances, and the more beautifully she danced, the worse it was. For it is a disgrace for a king to do something indecorous. Consider also the other folly of Herod. He swore he would give whatever she asked. If she had asked for your own head, would you have given it? "Give me here," she said, "the head of John." Why did she add "here"? She feared that perhaps Herod might change his mind and be led by repentance later; therefore she urged him, saying, "Give it to me here."

**And the king was saddened; nevertheless, because of the oath and those who sat at the table with him, he ordered it to be given.** And having sent executioners, he beheaded John in the prison, and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she took it...

<margin>D</margin>...given to her mother. And his disciples came, and took up the body, and buried it.] He <note>Herod Antipas</note> grieved because of virtue; for even an enemy admires virtue. Nevertheless, on account of his oath, he granted that inhumane gift. We should learn in this passage that <margin>It is often better to break an oath than to perform an impious vow.</margin> it is sometimes better to commit perjury <note>original: "peierare"; here meaning to break a sworn oath</note> than to do something impious because of an unholy oath. Now, the body of the Baptist was buried in Sebaste of Caesarea <note>The ancient city of Samaria, rebuilt by Herod the Great and renamed in honor of Augustus Caesar</note>. His venerable head, however, was first laid to rest in Emesa <note>Modern-day Homs in Syria</note>.

**And they went and told Jesus.**] What did they tell Jesus? Not simply that John was dead, for rumor had already brought that news, but that Herod was saying of Jesus that he was John <note>referring to Herod's fear that Jesus was John the Baptist risen from the dead</note>.

**When Jesus heard of it, he withdrew from there in a boat to a deserted place apart.**] <margin>E</margin> Jesus withdrew on account of Herod’s act of murder, teaching us not to throw ourselves recklessly into dangers. Moreover, he withdrew so that he would not appear to be incarnate <note>having a physical human body</note> only in appearance. For if Herod had seized him, he would have attempted to kill him. And if, while Herod was attempting this, Jesus had snatched himself away from the midst of the dangers because the time for his death had not yet arrived, he would have been considered a phantom <note>original: "phantasma"; an apparition without real flesh</note>. For this reason, he withdrew. He went into a deserted place apart so that he might perform the miracle of the loaves.

**And when the crowds heard of it, they followed him on foot, leaving the cities. And Jesus, going out, saw a great crowd, and had compassion on them, and healed their sick.**] <margin>F</margin> The crowds demonstrated their faith, which is why they ran to him even as he was withdrawing; therefore, they carried away health as the reward for their faith. But the fact that they traveled on foot and came without food are also signs of their faith.

**When evening had come, his disciples came to him, saying, "This is a deserted place, and the hour is already late; send the crowds away, that they may go into the villages and buy food for themselves." But Jesus said to them, "They do not need to go away; you give them something to eat."**] The disciples are compassionate <note>original: "misericordes"</note>. For they took care of the crowd and therefore did not want them to be hungry. What then did the Savior do? "You give them something to eat." He says this not as if he were ignorant of the great poverty the apostles were in, but so that

<column-break/>

<page-num>48</page-num>
->ON THE EXPOSITION OF MATTHEW'S GOSPEL<-
<meta>catchword: Et hoc (And this)</meta>

<margin>A</margin> when they said they had nothing to eat, it would be clear that he proceeded to perform the miracle not out of a desire for vainglory <note>excessive vanity or seeking worldly praise</note>, but out of necessity.

**But they said to him, "We have nothing here but five loaves and two fish." He said, "Bring them here to me." And he commanded the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed them.**] For although it is evening, I, the creator of time, am present. Although it is a deserted place, I am the one who gives food to all flesh. Let us learn in this place that we ought to spend even the little we have on hospitality. For the <margin>B</margin> apostles, having only a little, gave it to the crowds; and just as he multiplied these few things, so too will your few things be multiplied. Moreover, he made the crowds sit on the grass so that you would not lie down on precious beds and coverings. Furthermore, he looks up to heaven and blesses the loaves, perhaps so that greater faith might be placed in him—that he is not opposed to God, but came from heaven and from the Father. He also teaches that when we approach the table, we should first give thanks and then eat.

**And when he had broken them, he gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples to the crowds. And they all ate and were filled, and they took up what was left over of the fragments, twelve baskets full. Now those who had eaten were about five thousand men, besides women and children.**] <margin>C</margin> He gives the loaves to the disciples so that they might always keep the miracle in their memory and so it would not slip from their thoughts, even though they were always forgetful. But lest you should think that he performed the miracles only in appearance, the loaves were multiplied until twelve baskets were filled, so that even Judas might carry one, and might not be stubborn in his betrayal when reflecting on the miracle he carried. He multiplied both loaves and fish to show that he is the one who created the land and the sea, and that all our food is given to us by him and multiplied through him. Furthermore, the miracle takes place in the desert, lest anyone should think the bread was bought from a nearby city and distributed to the multitude; for it was a desert. And this...

### CHAPTER 14. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...at least according to the historical account. Now, learn according to the **anagoge** <note>a method of spiritual or mystical interpretation of scripture</note>. <margin>D</margin> After Herod—that is, the carnal and skin-like mind of the Jews (for that is what the name "Herod" signifies <note>Theophylact follows a traditional etymology connecting Herod with skin or fleshiness</note>)—beheaded John, the head of the prophets, which is to say he did not believe those preaching of Christ, Jesus withdrew into a deserted place to the nations <note>the Gentiles</note> who were abandoned by God. He healed their infirm souls and then fed them. For unless he forgives us our sins and heals our diseases through baptism, he will not feed us with the communion of the unpolluted mysteries <note>the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>. Indeed, no one who is not baptized may communicate. Now, the **five thousand** signify those whose five senses were poorly affected, who are cured through the **five loaves**. Indeed, because the five senses were sick, there were as many poultices as there were wounds. <margin>E</margin> The **two fish**, truly, are the sermons of the fishers <note>the Apostles</note>. One fish is the Gospel, the other fish is the Apostle <note>referring to the Apostolic Epistles</note>. Some have understood the five loaves as the five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. The **twelve baskets**, however, were taken up and carried by the Apostles. For whatever the crowds were unable to eat and understand, the Apostles, being capable, carried those things. But he excluded the women and the children. For it is required of a Christian that he display nothing childish or womanly <note>in this context, meaning spiritual instability or weakness</note>.

**And immediately Jesus compelled his disciples to enter into a boat, and to go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds.**] To signify how inseparable the disciples were from the Lord, the text says "he compelled" <margin>F</margin> <note>original Latin: "coegit"</note>; for they always wished to be present with him. He dismissed the crowds, however, wishing them to follow after, lest he should seem to be a seeker of arrogance.

**And after dismissing the crowds, he went up onto a mountain to pray alone. And when evening had come, he was there alone. But the boat was now in the middle of the sea, and was distressed by the waves: for the wind was against them.**] Showing us that it is necessary to pray without distraction of mind, he ascended the mountain. For he does all things for our sake. He himself has no need of prayers. He prays in the evening, however, teaching us that we should not immediately depart from our prayers, but that we—

### ENARRATIONS ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

<margin>A</margin> —ought to devote ourselves to them especially at night: for then there is greater quiet. He permits the disciples to be in the storm so that they might learn to bear temptations bravely and recognize his power. The boat being in the middle of the sea signifies that their fear was greater.

**And in the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went to them, walking upon the sea. And when the disciples saw him walking upon the sea, they were troubled, saying, "It is a specter," and they cried out for fear: but immediately he spoke to them, saying, "Have faith, it is I, be not afraid."**] He did not immediately stand by them to calm the storm, teaching that a solution to adversities should not be sought instantly, but they must be borne bravely. <margin>The watches of the night divided according to military discipline.</margin> But it was about the **fourth watch**. For the guards divide the night <margin>B</margin> into four parts according to military discipline, with individuals keeping their own watch for three hours each. The Lord, however, walking upon the water after the ninth hour of the night <note>the fourth watch, roughly 3:00 AM to 6:00 AM</note>, stood by them as God. But they, seeing such a rare and unusual thing, thought it was a specter <note>a ghost or phantom</note>. For they did not recognize him by his appearance, partly because of the night and partly because of fear. He, however, encouraging them, first said to them, "It is I, who can do all things; have faith."

**And Peter answering him, said, "Lord, if it be thou, bid me come to thee upon the waters."**] Peter’s love toward Christ was most fervent; for he desired to be near him immediately, and ahead of the others. He believed <margin>C</margin> that Jesus not only walked upon the waters himself, but would also give this power to him. He did not say, "Bid me walk," but "Bid me come to thee." For the former would be for ostentation, but the latter is out of love for Christ.

**And Jesus said, "Come." And when Peter had descended from the boat, he walked upon the waters to go to Jesus. But when he saw the wind was strong, he was afraid, and when he began to sink, he cried out, saying, "Lord, save me."**] The Lord withdrew the sea from Peter <note>let the natural properties of the water return</note>, declaring his own power. Note that while he was in the greater danger—the sea being troubled by winds—he feared: so weak is human nature. And as soon as he feared, he began to be submerged; for when faith is weak, then one descends into the depths. This happened to Peter so that he would not become proud, and— <sig>g</sig>

### CHAPTER 14. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...he might comfort the disciples; for perhaps they were envious, but <margin>D</margin> Christ shows how much he loves Peter himself.

**Immediately Jesus, stretching out his hand, caught him and said to him: "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?" And when they had entered the boat, the wind ceased. Then those who were in the boat came and worshiped him, saying, "Truly you are the Son of God."** ] By showing that it was not the wind, but faint-heartedness <note>original: *pusillanimitatem*, meaning a smallness of soul or lack of courage</note> that caused the sinking, Christ does not rebuke the wind, but the faint-hearted Peter. Therefore, having caught him, he stood him upon the water while the wind was still allowed to blow. Peter did not doubt entirely, but only in a certain way—that is, in part. <margin>E</margin> For in the respect that he doubted, he was unfaithful; but in the respect that he cried out, "Lord, save me," he cured that lack of faith. Thus he is called "one of little faith," not "one without faith." Then those in the boat were also released from their fear, for the wind ceased. And from these signs, having recognized Jesus, they confessed his divinity. For it is not the nature of a man to walk upon the sea, <margin>Psalm 77 <note>The marginal note says Psalm 70, but this quote is from Psalm 77:19 in modern numbering</note></margin> but the nature of God. As David says: *Your way was through the sea, and your paths through the great waters.*

According to the **anagoge** <note>a spiritual or mystical interpretation</note>, however, the boat is the earth, the waves are this life troubled by evil spirits, and the night is ignorance. Therefore, in the **fourth watch**, at the end of the ages, Christ appeared. The first watch was the covenant with Abraham; the second was the Law of Moses; the third was the Prophets; and the fourth was the coming of the Lord. For he himself saved <margin>F</margin> us when we were tossed by the waves, coming to us so that we might know him and worship him as God. Note this as well: that the events on the sea <margin>Mark 14</margin> prefigured Peter’s denial and his subsequent conversion and repentance. For just as he spoke then with confidence, saying, "I will not deny you," so here he says, "Command me to come to you upon the waters." Just as the Lord allowed him to deny him then, so here he allows him to sink. Here the Lord reached out his hand and did not let him drown; so then, through repentance, he pulled him out from the depth of his denial.

**And when they had crossed over, they came to the land of Gennesaret. And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent messengers into all the surrounding region and brought to him all who were sick, and they begged**

<margin>A</margin> **him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment; and as many as touched it were made well.** ] The Gennesarenes, recognizing Christ from the long time he had spent among them, showed a prompt faith based on both his appearance and his miracles—so much so that they desired to touch even the fringe <margin>The fringe of Christ’s garment</margin> of his garment, and thus they were healed. So you, too, should touch the edge of Christ’s clothing—that is, the end of his dwelling in the flesh. ### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>B</margin> **Then the scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem came to Jesus, saying: "Why do your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread."** ] Although scribes and Pharisees were in all places, those from Jerusalem were considered more venerable; therefore, they were more envious, being more greedy for empty glory. The Jews had a custom not to eat with unwashed hands, and this was based on the tradition of the fathers. When they saw that these traditions were not observed by the disciples, they thought the disciples were despising the elders. Jesus does not yet answer them directly, but rebukes them in turn.

**But he answered and said to them: "Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition? For God commanded, saying: 'Honor your father and mother,' and 'He who speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death.' <margin>Exodus 20 / Deuteronomy 5</margin> <margin>C</margin> But you say: 'Whoever says to his father or mother, "Whatever gift you might have received from me is now dedicated to God,"' he need not honor his father or mother. Thus you have made the commandment of God of no effect because of your tradition."** ] The Pharisees accused the disciples as if they were violating the mandate of the elders; Christ, however, shows that they themselves were violating the law of God. For they taught children not to give anything to their parents, but instead to offer whatever they had to the **gazophylacium** <note>the temple treasury or offering box</note> of the temple. There was a treasury in the temple into which anyone who wished could put a contribution.

# CHAPTER 15. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>
...and it was called *Gaza* <note>original: *Gaza*, a word of Persian origin used in the Bible to refer to a royal treasury or storehouse</note>. This treasure was distributed among the poor. The Pharisees, therefore, persuaded children not to give anything to their parents, but instead to offer it to the treasury. They taught them to say: "It is a gift to God" <note>original: *Donum dei est*</note>, which means: "O father, that which you wish me to provide for your use has already been offered to God." And in this way, they shared the wealth with the poor <note>likely referring to the Temple funds managed by the religious leaders</note>, while parents were abandoned and despised, receiving no support in their old age. Moneylenders also did this. For if someone had given money at interest to another, and then that debtor was unable to pay, the moneylender would say to that ungrateful debtor: "It is *Corban* <note>a Hebrew/Aramaic term meaning a sacrifice or an offering consecrated to God</note> what you owe me," meaning it is a gift offered to God. The debtor, therefore, as if owing it to God himself, would pay it out even against his will. This is what the Pharisees <margin>E</margin> taught the children to do.

<margin>Isaiah 29</margin>
> **[Hypocrites, Isaiah prophesied well of you, saying: This people approaches me with their mouth, and honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. But in vain do they worship me, teaching the precepts and doctrines of men.]**

He shows by the voice of Isaiah that they act toward their own fathers in the same way they are found to act toward God. For since they were wicked because of their evil works, they became far removed from God, and spoke the divine word with their mouth alone. For they worship in vain, and only imagine they worship God, while they dishonor him through their deeds.

And having called the crowds to him, he said to them:
> **[Hear and understand: Not that which enters the mouth makes a person unclean; but that which <margin>F</margin> comes out of the mouth, this renders a person unclean.]**

He no longer speaks to the Pharisees, seeing as they are incurable; instead, he speaks to the crowd. By calling the people to him, he seems to show them honor so that they might receive his word, saying, "Hear and understand," thereby stirring them up and making them attentive. Furthermore, because the Pharisees had accused the disciples of eating with unwashed hands, the Lord speaks concerning food, stating that no food pollutes or defiles a person. And if food does not defile, much less does eating with unwashed hands. For it is the speaking of things that ought not be said that defiles a person from within. He secretly notes the Pharisees through these words, who, by speaking envious

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
words, were themselves being defiled. Observe his wisdom: how he neither clearly approves of eating with unwashed hands, nor does he reject the practice; instead, he teaches something else entirely—that they should cast out evil speech from their hearts.

> **[Then the disciples, approaching him, said: Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this word? But he, answering, said:]**

The disciples speak on behalf of the Pharisees, saying they were offended, although the disciples themselves were also troubled. This is evident from the fact that Peter approached and asked about this specifically. Therefore, when Jesus heard that the Pharisees were offended, he said:

> **[Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up. Leave them; they are blind leaders of <margin>B</margin> the blind. Furthermore, if the blind leads the blind, both shall fall into the pit.]**

He said that the traditions of the elders and the precepts of the Jews were to be rooted up, not the things of the Law, as the Manichaeans <note>a dualistic religious sect that rejected the Old Testament as the work of an evil god</note> believe. For the Law is the planting of God; therefore, <margin>The Law of God is a planting of God which is not rooted up.</margin> it has not been rooted up. Its root remains—that is, the spirit which is hidden. The leaves, however—the outward letter—fall away. For we understand the Law no longer according to the letter, but according to the spirit. Because the Pharisees were desperate and incurable, he said, "Leave them." From this we learn that the offense of those who are offended by their own choice and are incurable is of no harm to us. He calls those teachers "blind leaders of the blind" to draw the crowds away from them.

<margin>C</margin>
> **[But Peter, answering, said to him: Explain this parable to us.]**

Because Peter knew the Law prohibited the eating of certain things, and he was afraid to say to Jesus, "We are offended by these things you have said"—as they appeared to be contrary to the Law—he feigns ignorance and asks for an explanation.

Jesus, however, said:
> **[Are you also still without understanding? Do you not yet understand that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is cast out into the latrine? But those things which proceed from the mouth come out from the heart itself, and those make a person unclean. For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, slanders. These are the things that defile a person. But to take food with unwashed hands...]**

# CHAPTER 15. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
## EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW
<sig>g iij / g iiij</sig>

<margin>D</margin>
**[...does not defile a person.]** The Savior rebukes the disciples and reproaches their foolishness, either because they were offended by His words or because they were clearly ignorant of the obvious. He says, therefore: "Do you not understand what everyone else understands and knows? For food does not stay inside, but passes out through the bowels, and it defiles no one in their soul because it does not remain within. But thoughts are born from within and stay there; and they 'go out'—that is, proceeding into deeds and actions—and these are what defile a person." For the thought of sexual immorality <note>original: *scortationis*</note> defiles while it stays inside, and it defiles when it goes out into an actual deed.

**[And Jesus went away from there and withdrew into the regions of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman who had come from those borders cried out to Him, saying: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is miserably tormented by a demon. But He did not answer her a word.]**
<margin>E</margin>
Why did He forbid the disciples from going the way of the Gentiles, yet He Himself went to Tyre and Sidon, which are Gentile cities? Learn, then, that He did not go there to preach (for as Mark says, He even tried to hide Himself). Or, to put it another way: because He saw the Pharisees were unwilling to accept His teaching regarding food, He transitioned to the Gentiles. She says "Have mercy on *me*," not "on my daughter" (for the daughter is out of her senses), but "on me" who suffers and feels such heavy grief. Nor does she say "Come and heal her," but simply "Have mercy." But He did not answer her a word—not because He held her in contempt, but to show that He had come for the sake of the Jews first. By teaching them first, He blocked their slanders, so they could not later say that He had favored the Gentiles while despising His own people. Furthermore, by this delay, He made the woman’s firm faith manifest to everyone.
<margin>See above, Chapter 10; Mark 7.</margin>

<margin>F</margin>
**[And His disciples came and begged Him, saying: Send her away, for she cries out after us. But He answered and said: I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.]** The disciples, find it burdensome to hear the woman’s shouting, begged Him, "Send her away"—that is, they pleaded with Him to grant her request so she would leave. They did this not because they were heartless, but rather because they wanted to persuade the Lord to have mercy on her. But He said, "I was not sent except to the Jews," who are the "sheep" that had lost the heritage entrusted to them. By saying this, He makes the woman’s faith even more widely known.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
**[But she came and worshipped Him, saying: Lord, help me. But He answered and said: It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs. But she said: Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.]** After the woman saw that even her "advocates" (the disciples) had been refused, she approached the Lord again with fervor and called upon Him as Lord. Because Christ had called her a "dog"—since the Gentiles lived impure lives and were involved in the blood of sacrifices offered to idols—and called the Jews "children," she responded with great wisdom and insight. It is as if she said: "Even if I am a dog and unworthy to receive the 'bread' <note>meaning the fullness of His power and great miracles</note>, yet give me that which is small; for while it is a small thing compared to Your great power, it would be a great thing for me. Just as those who eat the bread do not think much of giving away the crumbs, yet the dogs are well fed by them."
<margin>B</margin>

**[Then Jesus answered and said to her: O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish. And her daughter was healed from that hour.]** Now Jesus reveals the reason why He initially delayed the healing: namely, so that the faith and prudence of the woman might shine forth. This is why Christ did not agree immediately at the start, but rather pushed her away; now, so that her faith and wisdom are made manifest, He praises her: "Great is your faith." By saying, "Let it be done for you as you wish," He shows that if she had not possessed faith, she would have attained nothing. And so, if we also desire it, nothing prevents us from attaining what we wish.
<margin>C</margin>

<margin>On the intercession of the Saints</margin>
**Observe** here that although the saints pray for us—just as the apostles did for her—we are heard even more effectively when we petition for ourselves. Moreover, the Canaanite woman is a symbol of the Church gathered from the Gentiles. For the Gentiles were first rejected and later invited into the rank of "children," obtaining the bread of the Lord's body. The Jews, however, have become the "dogs," appearing to feed only on "crumbs"—that is, the small and literal meaning of the scripture. For "Tyre" signifies "restriction," "Sidon" signifies "one who hunts," and "Canaanite" signifies "prepared for humility." Thus, the Gentiles, who were once restricted by malice...

**[And Jesus moved on from there and came near the Sea of Galilee; and having climbed the mountain, He sat there. And great crowds came to Him, having with them the lame, the blind, the deaf, the mutilated, and many others, and they laid them down at Jesus' feet, and He healed them, so that the crowds wondered when they saw the mute speaking, the mutilated made whole, the lame walking, and the blind seeing; and they glorified the God of Israel.]** He does not stay continuously in Judea, but in Galilee, because of the great disbelief of the Jews. For the Galileans were more faithful than they were. Observe, then, their faith: how they even climb the mountain, <margin>E</margin> though they were lame and blind. They are not idle, but cast themselves at His feet, thinking of Him as something more than a man; and for this reason, they obtained healing. You also, therefore, should climb the "mountain of the commandments" <note>Theophylact uses the mountain as a metaphor for the high moral ground of living according to God’s laws.</note> where Jesus sits. Even if you are blind, not able to see by yourself what is good; or if you are lame, seeing what is good but unable to reach it; or if you are deaf, neither hearing another’s advice nor able to advise others; or if you are mutilated, unable to stretch out your hand for almsgiving; or if you are held by some other disease—go to the feet of Jesus, touch the tracks of His life, and you will find a cure.

<margin>F</margin> **[But Jesus, having called His disciples to Him, said: "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have already stayed with me three days and have nothing to eat; and I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way."]** The crowds did not dare to ask for bread, as they had come to receive healing. But He, being merciful, takes care of them, so that no one could say they had other supplies <note>original: *viatica* - provisions for a journey</note>; if they had any, He says, they would have been consumed, for it has already been three days. He shows that they came from a long distance by saying, "lest they faint on the way." He says these things to the disciples, wanting to stir them up so they might learn that He is able to nourish them, just as He did for the five thousand; but <margin>Above: Ch. 14, John 6.</margin> they still lacked wisdom.

## EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW
<page-num>53</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> **[And His disciples said to Him: "Where can we get so many loaves in a remote place to satisfy such a great crowd?"]** Although they should not have forgotten that He had previously fed many in the wilderness, they were dull of understanding. Yet, when you later see these same men endowed with such great wisdom, you will marvel at the grace of God.

**[And Jesus said to them: "How many loaves do you have?" And they said: "Seven, and a few small fish." And He commanded the crowds to sit down on the ground, and He took the seven loaves and the fish, and after giving thanks, He broke them and gave them to His disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven large baskets full of the fragments that remained. Now those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and <margin>B</margin> children.]** Teaching frugality, He commands them to lie back upon the ground; and teaching them to give thanks before eating, He Himself gives thanks. You may ask, however: why is it that in the previous miracle, when there were five loaves and five thousand were fed, twelve baskets <note>original: *cophini* - typically smaller, sturdy hand-baskets</note> remained, but here, when there were fewer people to be fed and more loaves, there are only seven hampers <note>original: *sportæ* - typically larger, flexible grain baskets or hampers</note>? <margin>Christ teaches by example to give thanks to God before food.</margin> It could be said that these hampers were larger than the hand-baskets, or perhaps He did this so that the exact similarity of the miracle would not make them forget it. For if twelve had remained this time as well, they might have forgotten that He had performed the miracle of the loaves a second time due to the identical outcome. ¶ You should also know this: that the "four thousand"—that is, those who rightly possess the four virtues—are fed by seven loaves, which represent more spiritual and perfect discourses. For the number seven is a symbol of the seven spiritual gifts. They sit upon the ground because they are superior to all earthly things and trample upon them, just as the five thousand sat upon the grass—meaning they subjected the flesh and its glory. For "all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of the field." <margin>Ecclesiasticus 14, Isaiah 40, 1 Corinthians 2.</margin> The seven hampers remaining in this place signify the spiritual and more perfect things which they were unable to eat. Therefore, those things remained which seven hampers could hold—that is, the things which only the Holy Spirit knows. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.

**[And having dismissed the crowds, he boarded a ship and came to the <margin>John 6.</margin> borders of Magdala.]** Jesus withdraws because he had performed no other sign quite like this one in the multiplying of the loaves; many were following him and (as John says) were intending to take him by force to make him a king. Therefore, he withdraws to escape any suspicion of <term>tyranny</term> <note>original: "tyrannis"; in this context, it refers to a secular or political uprising against the Roman authorities, which Jesus sought to avoid.</note>.

### CHAPTER XVI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'E' containing a profile portrait of a man's head facing left.</image-desc>**AND the Pharisees approached along with the Sadducees, testing him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven.]** Although the <term>Sadducees</term> <note>A Jewish sect that denied the resurrection and the existence of angels.</note> and the <term>Pharisees</term> <note>A Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional and written law.</note> differ in their doctrines, they nevertheless conspire together against Christ. They ask for a sign from heaven <margin>Exod. 7. 8. 9. 10.</margin>, such as making the sun or moon stand still. For they believed that the signs performed on earth were done by demonic power and through Beelzebub. For these foolish men were ignorant <margin>Job 1.</margin> that Moses also performed many signs on earth in Egypt, and that the fire that descended from heaven upon the cattle of Job was from the devil; thus, not everything from heaven is from God, nor is everything on earth from demons.

**[But answering, he said to them: When evening comes, you say: It will be clear, for the sky is red. And in the morning: Today a storm, for the sky is red. Hypocrites, you know how to judge the face of the sky, but you cannot judge the signs of the times.]** He rebukes their provocative question by calling them hypocrites, and says: Just as among the signs appearing in the sky, one is an indicator of rain and another of clear weather—and no one seeing the sign of rain seeks clear weather, nor does one seeing the sign of clear weather fear rain—so also you ought to think regarding me, that the time of this first coming is one thing, and the time of the future coming is another. Now there is a need for miracles on earth; but those which shall happen in heaven are reserved <margin>Below 24, Mark 13, Jonah 2.</margin> for that time when the sun shall be extinguished, the moon hidden, and the heaven changed.

**[An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it, except the sign of Jonah the prophet. And leaving them, he went away.]** A "evil" nation, because it tests him; and "adulterous," as it is falling away from God and clinging to the devil.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> To those seeking a sign from heaven, he gives none except the sign of Jonah the prophet—that is, just as Jonah was in the belly of the great sea-monster, so Christ, having entered the belly of death for three days, shall rise again. You might also call this a sign "from heaven." For at his death the sun was darkened, and all creation was transformed. Note the phrase, *no sign shall be given to it*; for signs were indeed given to them—that is, performed for their sake—even though they did not believe. Consequently, having left them as incurable, he departed.

**[And when his disciples had come to the other side, through forgetfulness they did not take bread. But Jesus said to them: See, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and <margin>B</margin> Sadducees.]** Just as old <term>leaven</term> <note>Yeast or a fermented starter. Here used as a metaphor for a corrupting influence that spreads through a whole batch of dough.</note> is bitter, so the doctrine of the Sadducees bites into souls, being bitter and introducing the old traditions of the elders. And just as leaven is a mixture of water and flour, so the doctrine of the Pharisees is a mixture of eloquent speech and a corrupt life. He did not say to them plainly, "Beware of the doctrine of the Pharisees," so that he might make them remember the miracle of the loaves.

**[But they reasoned among themselves, saying: We have taken no bread. Which when Jesus knew, he said to them: Why do you think among yourselves, O you of little faith, that you have not taken <margin>Above 14 & 15.</margin> bread? Do you not yet understand, nor remember those five loaves, when there were <margin>C</margin> five thousand men, and how many baskets you took up? Nor those seven loaves, when there were four thousand, and how many hampers you received? How is it that you do not understand that I did not speak to you about bread, but to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.]** They believed he said this to them so they would guard themselves from being defiled by Jewish foods, since they were talking among themselves about having forgotten the bread. He therefore reproaches them for being so dull and of such little faith. For they were "imprudent" and dull because they did not consider how he had previously fed many with a few loaves. And they were of "little faith" because, since they had not bought any, they doubted he could acquire bread from elsewhere. And thus he rebuked them more sharply.

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus' refusal to provide a 'sign from heaven' to the Pharisees and Sadducees, interpreting the 'Sign of Jonah' as the Resurrection and warning the disciples against the spiritual 'leaven' or corrupting doctrines of the religious leaders.</summary>

(For gentleness is not good in every instance; a reasonable rebuke is effective <margin>D</margin> only where it is warranted.) "Then," he says, "they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees and Sadducees."

**[When Jesus had come into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, he questioned his disciples, saying: Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am? And they said...]** He mentions the one who founded the city because there is another Caesarea, called Stratonis <note>original: "Stratonis"; Caesarea Maritima was originally called Strato's Tower</note>, and he questions them not in that city, but in this one. He leads the disciples far away from the Jews so that, fearing no one, they might learn freely and confidently. First, however, he asks about the opinion of the multitude so that the disciples might be brought to a greater degree of devotion, and so they do not fall into the same lowly opinion held by most people. <margin>E</margin> He does not ask, "Who do the Pharisees say I am?" but "Who do *men* say," speaking of the simple common people.

<margin>See above chapter 14; Mark 6.</margin> **[Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.]** Those who called him John were among those associated with Herod, who thought that John, after his resurrection, had also received the gift of performing miracles. Those who said Elijah were moved by the fact that he [Jesus] rebuked people sharply and they were expecting Elijah to come. Those who said Jeremiah said so because he [Jesus] was endowed with a similar wisdom <margin>Jeremiah 1.</margin> which he had learned from no one. For Jeremiah, while he was yet a boy, was taken as a prophet. <margin>F</margin>

**[He says to them: But who do you say that I am? And Simon Peter said: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.]** Again, Peter, being more fervent, leaps forward and truly confesses him to be the Son of God. For he did not say, "You are Christ, a son of God," without the definite article; but with the article: "*the* Christ, *the* Son"—that is, the very one who is the sole and only Son; not a son by grace, but one born from the very substance of the Father. For there were many "christs" <note>original: "Christi"; meaning 'anointed ones'</note>, as all priests and kings were, but with the definite article, "the Christ" is only one.

**[And Jesus answering said to him: Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.]** He calls Peter "blessed" because he had received knowledge from divine grace; but in approving

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Peter, he consequently shows the opinions of other men to be false. He called him "Bar-Jonah," which is to say "Son of Jonah," as if to say: "Just as you are the son of Jonah, so I am the Son of my Father, existing as <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "consubstantialis"; of the same essence or substance, a key term in Nicene theology</note> with him." He calls this knowledge a "revelation" because things hidden and unknown to Peter were revealed to him by the Father.

**[And I say to you, that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.]** The Lord rewards <margin>How the church is built upon Peter.</margin> Peter, giving him a great prize: that he built the church upon him. For because Peter confessed him as the Son of God, Jesus said that this confession, which Peter made, would be the future foundation for believers; so that <margin>B</margin> every person intending to build a house of faith would lay this foundation. For even if we practice countless virtues but do not have the correct confession as a foundation, we build in vain. When he said "my church," he showed himself to be the Lord of the universe; for all things serve God. "The gates of hell" are temporal persecutors, who <margin>Psalm 118 [119].</margin> attempt to send Christians to the underworld. Heretics also are "gates" leading to hell. Therefore, the church has prevailed over many persecutors and many heretics. Furthermore, each one of us is a "church" which becomes a house of God. If, therefore, we are confirmed in the confession of Christ, the gates of hell—that is, sins—will not prevail against us. Concerning these <margin>C</margin> gates, the exalted David said: "He who lifts me up from the gates of death." <margin>Psalm 9.</margin> What kind of gates, O David? Two: namely, murder and adultery.

**[And I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.]** As God, he says with great power: "I will give to you." For just as the Father gave you the revelation, so I give you the keys. You should understand the "keys" as those things which bind and loose—that is, the sins, or the pardons, or the punishments. For those who, like Peter, have attained the grace of the <term>episcopacy</term> <note>The office or rank of a bishop</note>, have the power of forgiving and binding. Although it was said to Peter alone, "I will give to you," nevertheless [it applies] to all <margin>John 21.</margin>

<margin>D</margin>
...were granted to the apostles. When? When he said, "Whosever sins you forgive, they are forgiven." <note>original: "Quoruncunque remiferitis peccata, remittuntur"; citing John 20:23</note> For when he said, "I will give," it signifies a future time—that is, after the resurrection. Moreover, the "heavens" are said to be the virtues, the keys of which are good works. For by working we enter, as if through certain keys opening each of the virtues. But if I do not work, but only know what is good, I possess only the key of knowledge but I remain outside. He is "bound in the heavens"—that is, in the virtues—who does not walk in them; for the virtuous man is "loosed" in them. Let us not have sins, therefore, so that we are not bound by the chains of our own sins.

<margin>E</margin>
*Then he commanded the disciples that they should tell no one that he was Jesus the Christ.* Christ wanted his glory to be obscured before the cross. For if people had heard before the passion that he was God, and then saw him suffer, how would they not have been offended? For this reason, he hides himself from many so that after the resurrection he might be known by many without a stumbling block; the Holy Spirit makes all things equal through the working of miracles.

*And from that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised on the third day.* He predicts his passion to them so that when it arrives unexpectedly, they are not offended, <margin>F</margin> thinking that he suffered against his will and without foreknowledge. For after they heard through Peter's confession that he was the Son of God, then he revealed the passion to them as well. After the sad things, however, he adds joy: namely, that he would rise on the third day.

*And when Peter had taken him aside, he began to rebuke him, saying: "Be it far from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you."* <note>original: "Propitius eſto tibi domine"; literally "Be merciful to yourself, Lord"</note> That which was revealed, Peter <margin>Peter is blessed when speaking correctly</margin> confessed rightly; but in that which was not revealed, he slipped—so that we might know that without God, even he did not speak of anything great. Peter, not wanting Christ to suffer and being ignorant of the mystery of the resurrection, said, "Be it far from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you."

<column-break/>

->EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW<-
->56<-

<margin>A</margin>
*But he turned and said to Peter: "Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me: for you do not savor the things of God, but the things of men."* Christ proclaims Peter blessed when he speaks correctly; but when he is irrationally afraid and does not want him to suffer, he rebukes him, saying, "Go behind me, Satan." Now, "Satan" is translated as *adversary*. <note>original: "Satanas autē aduerſari⁹ dicitur"; Theophylact explains the Hebrew etymology of the name Satan</note> Go behind me, therefore—that is, do not stand in my way, but follow my will. He calls Peter this because it also displeased Satan that Christ should suffer. He says, therefore: "To you, indeed, according to human reasoning, my passion seems indecent; but you do not understand that God works salvation through this, and that this most becomes me."

<margin>B</margin>
*Then Jesus said to his disciples, "If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross, and follow me."* "Then"—When? After he had rebuked Peter. For wanting to show that Peter was in error for forbidding him to suffer, he says: "You indeed forbid me, but I tell you that not only is it not harmful for me to suffer, but you yourself cannot be saved unless you also die, and anyone else, whether man or woman, poor or rich." He says, "Wants," so that Christ may show <term>free will</term> <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"; the power to choose good or evil</note> and not a coerced virtue. He follows after Christ not only who confesses him as the Son of God, but also who passes through all hardships and endures them. He said "let him deny himself," signifying <margin>C</margin> a perfect denial through the prefix "ab" <note>original: "abneget"; the Latin prefix 'ab-' suggests a complete or away-from negation</note>. For example: let him have no communion with the body, but let him despise himself. Just as we are accustomed to say that someone "denied" another—that is, he did not hold him as a friend or acquaintance—so he teaches all to have no communion, that is, friendship, with the body, so that they even take up the cross—that is, choose death, and with zeal seek out even the most shameful death, such as the cross was among the ancients. "But also let him follow me," he says. For many follow robbers and thieves, but they are not my disciples. Let him follow, therefore—that is, let him display every other virtue. "Let him deny himself..."

The text explains that true discipleship requires "denying the self," which involves valuing spiritual virtue over the physical body and being willing to face even a shameful death.</summary>

<margin>Galatians 2. He takes up the cross who mortifies himself to the world.</margin>
...and he who was yesterday intemperate, but today is **D** chaste and sober. Such a one was Paul, who denied himself when he said: *I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me.* <note>original: "viuo autem non iam ego, viuit autem in me Christus"; citing Galatians 2:20</note> Moreover, he takes up the cross who has mortified and crucified himself to the world.

*For whoever desires to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it.*] He exhorts us to martyrdom; for one "finds" the soul for the present—that is, he saves it by denying Christ—but later he loses it. Yet, he loses the soul for Christ’s sake who bears witness to him, and such a one will find it in incorruption and eternal life.

<margin>Romans 2. Ecclesiasticus 16.</margin>
*For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what **E** will a man give in exchange to redeem his soul? For the Son of Man is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will reward each according to his deeds.*] Suppose then, and let us imagine, that you gain the whole world; but what use is it if the body fares well while the soul is in a wretched state? It is as if the mistress of a house went about in torn rags while her maidservants walked in shining ornaments. Nor in the future age will anyone be able to give an exchange for his soul; here, indeed, one can give tears, alms, and fasting, but there one cannot. For the Judge will then receive us, rejecting gifts; for according to one's works, he will justify each person. He is also to be feared. For he will come in his glory and with **F** angels, and not in a state to be despised.

*Truly I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.*] He had said that the Son of Man would come in his glory; therefore, lest you become unbelieving, he says that there are some here who, according to what they are able to grasp, will see the glory of his second coming in the Transfiguration. Meanwhile, he shows in what glory they shall be who are to suffer for his sake. For just as his flesh then flashed like lightning, so shall the saints shine according to their own portion. Moreover, in this place, he refers obscurely to Peter, James, and John, whom he took up onto the mountain and showed

<column-break/>

<page-num>57</page-num>
->EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW<-

**A** to them the kingdom of God—that is, the future state in which he himself was to come and the righteous were to shine. He says, therefore, that some who are here shall not die until they see me transfigured. See, however, that those standing in the good and the firm are those who see Jesus more clearly transformed; and they always make progress in faith and the commandments.

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>B Luke 9. John 21. Acts 12.</margin>
<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'E' featuring a classical or biblical scene within a square frame.</image-desc>
**A**ND after six days, Jesus took Peter, James, and his brother John.] This is not different from what Luke said: *that after those sayings it was about eight days,* etc. <note>Luke 9:28</note> For Luke includes both the first and the last day on which they ascended the mountain. Matthew, however, sets down only the intervening days. He took Peter, as the one by whom he was loved; John, as the one whom he loved; and James, because he also was a zealot. <note>Theophylact uses "aemulator" to mean one full of holy zeal or a "son of thunder."</note> And it is manifest that James was of great zeal, both from the fact that he promised he would drink the cup, and from the fact that Herod, to please the Jews, killed him with the sword. <note>Acts 12:2</note>

<margin>C Transfiguration</margin>
*And he led them up into a high mountain apart, and was transformed before them. And his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as light.*] He leads them up into a high mountain, showing that unless one is exalted <note>meaning spiritually elevated above earthly concerns</note>, he is not worthy of divine contemplations. Moreover, he took them "apart," for Christ was accustomed to perform his more brilliant miracles in secret, so that he might not be seen as God by the many, but be held as a man, as he appeared. Hearing of the "transformation," do not think that he then cast aside his body; rather, the body remained in its own form. For you hear of his "face" and his "garment." He appeared more radiant, with his deity declaring its own small rays—and these only as much as they were able to see. For this reason, he called the Transfiguration "the kingdom of God" above, because his ineffable power shone forth there, and because he was shown to be the true-born <term>germanus</term> <note>Latin "germanus" here emphasizes Jesus as the natural, legitimate Son of the same substance as the Father</note> Son of the Father, and because the dignity of the second coming shone in the ineffable brilliance of Christ’s face.

->CHAPTER 17. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA<-

<margin>Chapter 17</margin>
**D** *And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him.*] What were they talking about? About the glory (he says) which he was to fulfill in Jerusalem. But why did Moses and Elijah appear? To show that he is the Lord of both the prophets and of the living and the dead. For Elijah is a prophet and still lives; but Moses was the lawgiver and is dead. Furthermore, it was to show 
<margin>2 Kings 2</margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 23</margin>
that he is not an adversary of the Law. For Moses would not have stood by his adversary, nor would Elijah, such a great zealot <note>Elijah was famous for his "zeal" or passionate defense of the Lord's honor</note>, have tolerated him. Moreover, it was to remove the suspicion of those who said he was Elijah or one of the prophets. How did the disciples know they were Moses and Elijah? Certainly not from the features of their faces, for 
**E** making images of men was seen as impious at that time. It seems, therefore, that they recognized them from the words they were exchanging with one another. For perhaps one, namely Moses, was saying: "You are the one whose passion I prefigured by the killing of the lamb and the celebration of the Passover." And the other, Elijah: "You are the one whose resurrection I prefigured in the son of the widow." 
<margin>Numbers 7</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 17</margin>
And other things of this sort. By showing them to the disciples, he teaches them to imitate such men: to be gentle and well-liked by the people, as Moses was, but also zealous and constant, like Elijah, and when the time calls for it, to risk everything for the truth, just as they did.
*Then Peter answered and said to Jesus: Lord, it is good for us to be here; if you wish, let us make three 
**F** tabernacles <note>A "tabernacle" is a temporary shelter or tent, often associated with the Jewish Feast of Booths</note> here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.*] Out of great love, Peter did not want Christ to suffer, so he said: "It is good to stay in this place and not go down to be killed." For if anyone comes here, we have 
<margin>Exodus 17</margin>
<margin>1 Kings 18</margin>
Moses and Elijah to help us. Moses indeed conquered the Egyptians, and Elijah brought down fire from heaven; they will act against our enemies if any come here against us. But he spoke these things out of excessive grief, as Luke says, "not knowing what he said." For the unusual vision had stunned him, or he truly did not know what he was saying in his desire for Jesus to remain on the mountain and not go down to suffer for us. Yet, fearing he might seem stubborn, he said: "If you wish."

<column-break/>

->COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW<-
<page-num>58</page-num>
**A** *While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them; and behold, a voice from the cloud said: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.*] You, O Peter, seek man-made tabernacles to be built; but the Father has established another tabernacle not made by hands—a cloud—and he showed that just as he appeared to the ancients in the clouds as God, so too does his Son. In this place, the cloud is bright, not dark as it was in the Old Testament, because he did not wish to terrify, but to teach. The voice came from the cloud to show that it was from God. *In whom I am well pleased*: that is, upon whom I rest, and who pleases me. 
**B** He also teaches that he must be heard, even if he wishes 
<margin>Exodus 19</margin>
to be crucified; do not struggle against it.
*And when the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were greatly afraid. But Jesus came and touched them and said: Arise, and do not be afraid. When they had lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only.*] The disciples, unable to bear the brilliance of the light or the voice, fell to the ground, and their eyes were heavy as if with sleep. He calls "sleep" the heavy burden on their vision. Lest fear sitting too long within them should cast out the memory of what they had seen, he rouses them, encourages them, and he alone appears. Do not think that the voice was spoken of Moses or Elijah, but of him; for *He* is my Son.
**C** *And as they came down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them, saying: Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.*] Out of humility, he orders that it be told to no one, lest those who hear such things be offended when they later see him being crucified. For they would have thought him an impostor who had done these things only in appearance. But you, learn that after six days—that is, after the world, which was created in six days—the contemplation of God will come. For unless you pass beyond the world and are exalted on the mountain, you will by no means see the bright things, nor the face of Jesus—by which I mean his deity—nor his clothing, that is, his flesh. But see now both Moses and Elijah talking with Jesus: for the Law, the Prophets, and Jesus speak as one.
