### CHAPTER 17. EXPLANATION BY ARCHBISHOP THEOPHYLACT

<margin>D</margin>
...and in harmony. Indeed, when you find someone clearly interpreting a sense of scripture, know that he clearly sees the face of Jesus; and if he also explains the words and makes them visible, he sees the white garments of Jesus as well. For the "garments" are the literal expressions <note>original: "dictiones"</note> of the senses. But do not say with Peter, "It is good for us to be here"; for it is necessary to always make progress, and not to remain in one degree of virtue and contemplation, but to pass on to others.

*And his disciples asked him, saying, "Why then do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?"*] The scribes, deceiving the people, used to say that Jesus was not the Christ; for if he were, Elijah would have come first. They were ignorant of the fact that there are two advents of Christ: for the first, John was the precursor; for the second, Elijah will be.
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Malachi 4</margin>
For this is how Christ interprets it for his disciples. Listen:

*Jesus answered and said to them, "Elijah indeed comes first, and will restore all things. But I say to you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they wished. So also the Son of Man is about to suffer at their hands." Then the disciples understood that he had spoken to them about John the Baptist.*] By saying that "Elijah indeed will come," he shows that he has not yet come; but coming in the second advent, he will restore all Hebrews to the faith of Christ—those whom he finds persuasive—leading them back as if to a paternal inheritance, those who had fallen away. When he says "Elijah has come," he refers to that precursor John, to whom they did whatever they wished. For by allowing Herod to kill John when they could have prevented it, they themselves killed him. Then, therefore, the disciples, having become more perceptive, understood that he called John "Elijah" because John was the precursor of the first advent, just as Elijah is to be the precursor of the second.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>E</margin>
**At that hour the disciples came to Jesus, saying, "Who then is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?"**] Because they had seen Christ honor Peter (for he was honored by giving the <term>stater</term> for Christ and for himself), and because they suffered a certain human frailty, envy crept in. They approached indirectly, asking the Lord who was the greatest.

**And calling a child to himself, he stood him in their midst and said: "Unless you are converted and become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever, therefore, humbles himself like this child, he is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven."**] When Jesus saw that the disciples were held by the vice of vain glory, he restrained them, showing them the way of humility through a child who is free from pride. For it is necessary for us to be children in humility of mind, not childish in our thinking; and children in innocence, not in foolishness. By saying **"unless you are converted,"** he indicates that we have moved from humility into pride; it is necessary, therefore, to be converted back to that place—that is, into the humility from which you departed.

<margin>Note.</margin> That is, if you have forgiven, it will also be pardoned in heaven. For <margin>D</margin> it is not only those things which priests "loose" <note>In a religious context, "loosing" refers to the ritual or spiritual release from the guilt of sin (absolution), while "binding" refers to withholding that release.</note> that are loosed; but whatever we, who have been treated unjustly, either bind or loose, those things will also be bound or loosed.

**Again I say to you, that if two of you agree on earth concerning any matter for which they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.**] He gathers us together toward charity by these words. For since he forbade us from offending one another, he now speaks of mutual concord. However, "those in concord" refers not to those who join together for evil, but for good. For look at what he says: *If two of you*—that is, of those who are believers and "breathe together" <note>Theophylact plays on the word "conspiring," which literally means "breathing together," usually in harmony, though it can mean a plot.</note>. Annas and Caiaphas <margin>E</margin> "breathed together" as well, but for evil. And for this reason, we often do not receive what we pray for, because we lack mutual concord. He did not say "I will be," for he does not delay or belong only to the future; rather, he says "I am," which means "I am already found there." Understand likewise that when the spirit and the flesh agree, and the flesh does not lust against the spirit, then the Lord will be in their midst. The three powers of the soul also "agree": the rational, the irascible, and the desiderative <note>Theophylact is using ancient Greek psychology, which divided the soul into the parts that think (rational), get angry or feel courage (irascible), and desire things (desiderative).</note>. Furthermore, if the Old and New Laws agree, Christ is found in their midst, having been preached by both.

**Then Peter came to him and said, "Lord, how many times shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?" Jesus said to him, "I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven."**] <margin>F</margin> This is what Peter is asking: How many times, if he sins and then approaches and seeks pardon led by repentance, shall I grant it to him? He added, *if he sins against me*. For if he sins against God, I, who am a layperson and a private citizen <note>original: "idiotes ac privatus sum"</note>, cannot forgive him, unless perhaps I am a priest holding God's office. But if he sins against me, and then I forgive him, he will be released, even if I am a private citizen and not a priest. However, by saying *seventy times seven*, he does not limit forgiveness to a specific number. For it would be absurd to sit and count until you have four hundred and ninety <note>70 multiplied by 7 equals 490.</note>; rather, he signifies an infinite number.

### PAGE 63

<margin>A</margin> It signifies, as if to say: "As many times as one who has fallen performs repentance, grant him pardon." He says this because we ought to be compassionate (which he also explains through the following parable).

**Therefore, the kingdom of heaven is compared to a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants.**] The meaning of the parable is that we should give pardon to our fellow servants who trespass against us, especially if they seek pardon by falling down before us. It is for the diligent to examine every single detail, but let us also approach it. The "Kingdom" is the Word of God; but not some small kingdom, but that of the heavens. Therefore, it is compared to a human king. For he was incarnated for our sake and made in the likeness of men. Moreover, he "settles accounts" as a good judge. <margin>B</margin> For he does not punish without a trial, as that would be a sign of cruelty. And—

<margin>Indeed the flesh and the wife, and the works the children.</margin> **And when he had begun to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents. But as he was not able to pay, his lord commanded that he be sold, along with his wife, and his children, and everything that he had, and that payment be made.**] We are the debtors of ten thousand talents, we who are daily affected by many blessings and yet repay nothing good to God. Those who have undertaken the leadership of the people are also debtors of ten thousand talents (for every single person is a "great talent") and then do not perform their leadership well. To be "sold with his wife and family" signifies alienation from God; <margin>C</margin> for whoever is sold becomes the property of another master. But what if the "wife" is sold? That is the flesh, which is the spouse of the soul; and the "children" are the works which are done badly by the body and soul. He commands, therefore, that the flesh be given to Satan for destruction—that is, to habits or to the suffering of a demon. Similarly, the "sons"—I mean the active powers of evil—are to be bound, just as if someone's hand is devoted to theft, God makes it withered or binds it through some demon. Behold, the woman is the flesh, and the children are evil deeds; they are handed over to affliction so that the spirit may be saved. For that man cannot cooperate in theft at that time.

**But that servant, falling down, worshipped him, saying: "Lord, have patience with me, and I will [pay] everything to you..."**

# CHAPTER 18. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
## AN EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

**I will pay. But the lord, having pitied that servant, released him and <margin>D</margin> forgave him the debt.**] See the strength of repentance and the mercy of the lord. For repentance caused the servant to fall away from the malice in which he had been standing firmly, and of which he was not worthy of pardon. Mercy, however, entirely dismissed the debt, even though the servant did not ask for everything to be forgiven, but only for the time to be extended <note>The servant asked for patience and promised to pay back the debt; the king exceeded this request by cancelling the massive debt entirely.</note>. Learn, therefore, that God gives more than we ask, because the mercy of the lord is so great that even what seemed quite harsh—namely, that he ordered him to be sold—he did not say out of cruelty, but so that he might make the servant reflect and persuade him to turn to prayers and entreaty.

<margin>E</margin> **But that servant, having gone out, found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii, and laying a hand on him, he was dragging him by the neck, saying: "Pay what you owe." And his fellow servant, falling down, begged him saying: "Be patient with me, and I will pay you everything." But he was unwilling, but went and threw him into prison until he should pay the debt.**] He who had obtained pardon "went out" and now strangles and oppresses his fellow servant. For no one who remains in God is void of compassion; but this man had "gone out" <note>original: "egressus erat"; Theophylact interprets "going out" as leaving the presence and the spirit of God’s mercy.</note> and was now a stranger to God. His cruelty was great. Ten thousand talents had been forgiven to him, yet he was completely unwilling to either forgive or extend the time for the payment of far fewer—namely, a hundred denarii <note>A "talent" was a massive unit of currency (roughly 20 years of labor), while a "denarius" was a single day's wage. The contrast emphasizes the disproportion between God's forgiveness and human grudges.</note>—even though the fellow servant used the exact same words as he had used toward the lord, bringing the mercy of the lord to his memory.

<margin>F</margin> **Furthermore, when his fellow servants saw what was being done, they were greatly grieved; and they came and revealed to their lord all that had been done.**] These fellow servants seem to be angels, who hate evil and love good. This is not because they tell these things to an ignorant lord, but so that you may learn that there are angels, and that they are indignant at those who are inhuman and unmerciful.

**Then his lord summoned him and said to him: "Wicked servant, I forgave you all that debt because you entreated me; ought you not also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?" And the lord, being angry,**

<column-break/>

<page-num>64</page-num>
**ENARATIONS ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW**

<margin>A</margin> **handed him over to the torturers until he should pay all that was owed to him.**] The lord enters into judgment with the servant because of his mercy: to show that it is not the lord himself, but the servant's own cruelty and ingratitude that voids the gift of forgiveness. To which "torturers" did he deliver him? Perhaps to the punishing powers <note>Refers to the "punitive powers" or angelic/demonic executioners of divine justice.</note>, so that he might be punished perpetually. "Until he pays what was owed" signifies that he is punished for as long as it takes to pay; but he will never pay what he owed—namely, the punishment he deserved; therefore, he will always be punished.

**So also my heavenly Father will do to you if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts their offenses.**] <margin>B</margin> He did not say "your Father" but "my Father." For such people are unworthy to have God as a father. He wants the forgiveness to come "from the heart," not just from the lips. Think, then, how great an evil the desire for revenge is: since it even revokes and voids God's gift. Although the gifts of God are those of which He does not repent, they are nevertheless revoked in this manner and voided.

<margin>C</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a human figure holding a staff within a square frame with foliage.</image-desc> **And it happened when Jesus had finished these sayings, he departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan, and great crowds followed him, and he healed them there.**] Again he is active in Judea, so that those who did not believe in Judea might have no excuse—claiming he did not spend much time with them, but only with the Galileans. Therefore, again after the teaching and the speeches were finished, miracles follow. # CHAPTER 19. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> **to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh. So they are no longer <margin>Deuteronomy 24</margin> two, but one flesh. Therefore, what God has joined, let no man put asunder.**] Oh, what foolishness! They thought they would refute Christ with their questions. For if he had said it is permitted to dismiss a wife for any cause, they could have said to him: "How then did you say, let no one dismiss his wife except for adultery alone?" If, however, he had said it is not permitted to dismiss a wife at all, they would have accused him of being an adversary to Moses. For Moses commanded that a wife who was hated be dismissed <note>Theophylact refers here to the Mosaic provision in Deuteronomy 24:1, which allowed a "bill of divorce" if a husband found something "indecent" or "shameful" about his wife.</note>, even without a difficult and rational cause. What then does Christ do? He shows that the work and legislation of Him who formed us from the beginning was intended to be monogamy. For from the beginning, God joined one man to one woman: and thus it is not fitting for one man to be joined to many women, nor one woman to many men: but as they were joined from the beginning, they should remain, and not tear apart their life together without cause. He did not say, "I made them male and female," <margin>E</margin> so as not to exasperate them further <note>Jesus avoids using the first-person "I" to minimize the Pharisees' immediate hostility, instead referring to the Creator's original design in the third person.</note>, but said "He who made them" indefinitely. And thus he says it was of the greatest care to God that this good be joined. Hence He even permitted parents to be left behind so that men might adhere to their wives. How is it that in Genesis it is written that Adam said, "Therefore a man leaves his father," while here Christ says, "God said, <margin>Genesis 2</margin> 'therefore he leaves,'" and so forth? We say, therefore, that what Adam said, he said from God; and thus the speech of Adam is the speech of God. Therefore, because they are made one flesh, clinging together through both physical union and natural love: just as it is <margin>F</margin> impious to divide one's own flesh, so it is to tear apart spouses. He did not say, "Let not Moses separate them," so as not to disturb them, but simply "man": showing how great a difference there is between God who joins and man who looses.

They say to him, "Why then did Moses command to give a bill <margin>Deuteronomy 24</margin> of divorce and to dismiss her?" He said to them, "Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. But I say to you, that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery. And he who marries her who is divorced, commits

<page-num>65</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> **adultery.**] When the Pharisees had seen that the Lord had refuted them, they were forced afterward to bring Moses forward as if he were contradicting Christ: and they say, "How then did Moses command to give a bill of divorce <note>original: "librum repudij"; a formal legal document ending a marriage</note> and to dismiss her?" Therefore, the Lord, turning the entire accusation back onto their own heads, responds on behalf of Moses and says: Moses did not establish laws contrary to God, but he pronounced this because of your "hardness of heart" <note>term: "hardness of heart" (duritia cordis); a stubbornness or spiritual insensitivity that prevents people from following God's highest standards.</note>: lest, because of your lack of self-control and your desire to be joined to others, you might kill your first wives. For since they were cruel, they would have killed their wives if they had been forced to keep them; but now he commanded a bill of divorce to be given to those who were hated by their husbands. But I say to you, he says, that <margin>B</margin> it is good to cast out a wife who has committed fornication. If anyone, however, casts out a woman who has not committed fornication, he becomes the cause of her adultery. Understand, however, that he who adheres to the Lord is one spirit, and the marriage <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin> of the faithful is with Christ. For we have all been made one body with Him, and we are members of Christ in part. Therefore, no one can rightly be separated from such a marriage, according to the word of Paul, who says, "Who shall separate us <margin>Romans 8</margin> from the love of Christ?" Therefore, what God has joined, neither man nor any other creature, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers (as Paul says) will be able to separate.

His disciples say to him, "If such is the case <margin>C</margin> of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry."] The disciples are troubled, and they say: "If they are joined for this purpose—that they might be one and remain undivided through their whole life, so that even if the woman is otherwise regrettable, it is not permitted to cast her out—it is not expedient to marry." It would be lighter not to marry at all, but to fight and struggle with natural desires, than to endure a bad woman. For he calls the "case of a man with a woman" a perpetual and inseparable union. Some, however, also understand it this way: If this is the case of the man—that is, if the husband is to bear the blame and the fault for unlawfully casting out a wife—it is not expedient to marry.

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus's teaching on the indissolubility of marriage, arguing that Moses's permission for divorce was a temporary measure to prevent uxoricide (wife-killing) among the "hard-hearted" Israelites. He emphasizes that marriage creates a "one flesh" union rooted in the original creation, paralleling the inseparable union between Christ and the Church.</summary>

> **But he said to them: Not all are capable of this word, but those to whom it is given.**]

After the apostles said that it is better not to enter into marriage, the Lord says that the possession of virginity is a great thing, but it is not rightly preserved by everyone, but only by those with whom God cooperates. For in this place, "it is given" means "those with whom God cooperates." Moreover, it is given to those <margin>Above: Luke 7, John 11, 16.</margin> who ask. For he says, "Ask and it shall be given to you." For everyone, he says, who asks, receives.

> **For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother's womb; and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. He who can take it, let him take it.**]

The virtue of virginity, he says, belongs to the few. <margin>B</margin> For there are eunuchs from the mother's womb—that is, there are some who, due to their natural constitution <note>Theophylact refers here to biological conditions or lack of desire present from birth.</note>, are not fit for sexual union; these are chaste without any spiritual merit. There are also those who are made eunuchs by men. But those who "castrate themselves" for the sake of the kingdom of heaven are not those who amputate their own private parts (for that is a cursed act), but those who practice <term>continence</term> <note>From the Latin *continentes*, referring to self-restraint and the choice to remain celibate through willpower rather than physical alteration.</note>. Understand it also this way: there is a eunuch by nature who, due to his natural <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of bodily humors that determines one's temperament and physical drives.</note>, is not moved toward lust. One becomes a eunuch by men when he has extinguished the fire of carnal desire through human instruction. <margin>F</margin> But he who castrates himself is taught not by another, but by himself, and is inclined toward continence of his own accord. This person, therefore, is the best, who has been his own guide to the kingdom of heaven. Wishing to put virtue into action, he says: "He who can take it, let him take it." For he does not compel one to be a virgin, nor does he destroy marriage, but he prefers virginity.

> **Then children were offered to him, so that he might lay his hands on them and pray. But the disciples rebuked them. Jesus, however, said to them: Let the children alone, and do not forbid them to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.**]

Mothers were bringing their children so they might be blessed by the touch of his hands. However, they were approaching him in a disorganized and rowdy manner; therefore, the disciples forbade them because they thought this would detract from the authority of his teaching

Even today, if some approach a teacher asking "childish" questions, he should not forbid them, but receive them.

That man did not come as one testing him, but as one desiring to speak and thirsting for eternal life. This means: if you call me good as if I were merely one of the teachers, you speak wrongly. <margin>D</margin>You have acted in the Jewish manner: but if you wish to be perfect, that is, to be my disciple and a Christian: go, sell all that you have, and give everything at once, reserving nothing for yourself, so that you may perform a continuous act of charity. For he did not say, "give to the poor little by little," but he said, "give it all at once and be left with nothing." Then, because there are many who are merciful yet still lead a life full of all kinds of wickedness, he says, **And come, follow me**, which means, possess every other virtue as well. The young man therefore became sorrowful; for he truly desired [eternal life], and the soil of his heart was indeed thirsty, but the thorns of riches choked the seed. For he was (it says) one having <margin>E</margin> many possessions. For he who has few is not held back by them in the same way; for in great wealth, the bond is more violent. Furthermore, because Christ was speaking to a rich man, he said, **You will have treasure in heaven**; for the young man was a lover of riches.

**But Jesus said to his disciples: Amen I say to you, a rich man shall hardly enter into the kingdom of heaven. And again I say to you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.**] As long as a man is rich, and he himself has superfluities while others do not even have necessities, he does not enter the kingdom. But after all things have been cast off, then he is no longer rich, and afterwards he shall enter. For it is impossible for one possessing many things to enter, just as it is impossible for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. Note, however, how what he previously <margin>F</margin> called **difficult**, he here calls **impossible**. Some say that the "camel" here refers to the animal, but it is actually a thick rope <note>original: "crassus funis". Theophylact is referencing a common linguistic debate: the Greek word *kamelos* means camel, while *kamilos* means a thick sailor's rope or cable.</note> which sailors use to cast anchors.

**When the disciples heard these things, they were greatly astonished, saying: Who then can be saved? But Jesus, looking at them, said to them: With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.**] The disciples, out of their mercy for others, do not ask for themselves (for they were already poor) but for all mankind. The Lord therefore teaches that salvation is not to be measured by human weakness, but by divine power. For if someone begins to cease being greedy, he will make such progress that he will receive even greater things, and eventually he will come to the point where he even lacks necessities, and thus he will [be-]

**Then Peter, answering, said to him: Behold, we have left all things, and have followed you; what then shall we have?**] Although it may seem that Peter did not give up anything great, being a poor man, learn that in reality he left a great deal. For we are held by a great affection even for small things; but Peter also left all pleasures, along with the love of the flesh for his parents. For those affections wage war not only against the rich, but also against the poor. What then did the Lord say?

**Jesus, answering, said to them: Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of man shall sit on the seat of his glory: you also shall sit upon <margin>B</margin> twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.**] Will they literally sit? Not at all; rather, he indicated an excellent honor by the word "seat." And will Judas also sit? No: for he says, **Those who have followed me**, meaning, those who did so until the end. But Judas did not remain until the end. Or put another way, God often promises good things to certain worthy people, but when they fall away and become unworthy, he takes those promises away. He does similarly with harsh things; he often threatens and does not bring the punishment if we are converted. By "regeneration," <note>original: "regenerationem"</note> you should understand the Resurrection.

**And everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name's sake: shall receive a hundredfold, <margin>C</margin> and shall possess the inheritance of life everlasting.**] Lest anyone should suspect that what was said applied only to the disciples, he expands the promise to all who do similar things. For they shall have, in place of carnal relatives, intimacy and brotherhood with God; in place of lands, paradise; in place of stone buildings, the heavenly Jerusalem; in place of a mother, the elder women <note>original: "presbyteras"</note> of the church; in place of a father, the elders <note>original: "presbyteros"</note>; in place of a wife, all faithful women—not for marriage? Far from it! But with spiritual affection and merciful care for one another. Christ does not command us to simply separate from our families, but only when they stand in the way of piety. Sell these things, therefore, and give them to the "poor" demons—those who are deprived of every good—by turning your passions back upon the authors of those passions <note>Theophylact suggests redirecting the energy of vices back to the demons who inspire them, effectively "unloading" the sin</note>. **For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house [paterfamilias], who went out early in the morning to hire laborers into his vineyard. And when he had agreed with the laborers for a penny [denarius] a day, he sent them into his vineyard. And going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: Go you also into my vineyard, and whatsoever shall be right, I will give you. And they went their way. Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour, and did likewise. But about the eleventh hour he went out, and found others standing idle, and said to them: Why stand you here all the day idle? They say to him: Because no man has hired us. He said to them: Go you also into my vineyard, and whatsoever shall be right, you shall receive.**] Christ is the King of heaven, who is compared to a man according to the human form He assumed. He is a "master of a house" <note>original: "paterfamilias," the head of a Roman household</note> because He is the Lord of the house, which is the Church. This Christ, therefore, went out from His Father's borders and hires laborers into the vineyard—either the Scriptures or the commandments. He hires each person to work the vineyard, which is their own soul. He hires one at early dawn, which 

<margin>F</margin>

<margin>A</margin>
is in childhood; another at the third hour <note>about 9:00 AM</note>, which is youth; again another at the sixth and ninth hours <note>Noon and 3:00 PM</note>, when someone is twenty-five or thirty years old—simply put, in the prime of life. Finally, around the eleventh hour <note>5:00 PM, just before sunset</note>, he hires the elderly; for many who are old have come to believe. Alternatively, the "Day" refers to the present age, for in it we labor as if in the daytime. Thus, the Lord called Enoch and Noah at the first hour; Abraham at the third; Moses at the sixth; the prophets at the ninth; and at the eleventh hour—that is, at the consummation of the age—the Gentiles. These had been idle from every good work, for no one had "hired" them, nor had any prophet been sent to the Gentiles.

<meta>This page continues Theophylact’s commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 20. The previous page discussed the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard, specifically the "eleventh hour" as a metaphor for those called to the faith late in life or at the end of history.</meta>

### CHAPTER 20. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> ...at that time death was not yet destroyed, nor the devil crushed, but sin still lived. But we, justified by the grace of Christ through baptism, receive power to conquer our adversary, who has now been cast down and slain by Christ. And according to the previous interpretation, those who believed as youths have a greater labor than those who came to the faith in old age. For a young person carries the weight of anger and the heat of concupiscence <note>original: "concupiscentiæ"; a technical term for strong, often disordered, desire or lust</note>, struggling with their passions. An old person, however, is at rest; yet we all attain the gift of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the parable teaches us that even in old age it is possible to repent and attain the kingdom of heaven. For this is the eleventh hour. The saints do not envy those who receive grace <note>original: "charitatem"</note> at the very end; rather, the text shows here that the goods given to the righteous are so great and of such a kind that they could even excite envy.

**Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, worshipping and asking something of him. But Jesus said to her, "What do you want?" She said, "Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand, and the other at your left in your kingdom."**] The sons of Zebedee <note>James and John, the Apostles</note> thought that, by going to Jerusalem, the Lord was about to reign in a temporal, earthly kingdom. For they had often heard him saying, "We are going up to Jerusalem." They suffered a human weakness, and approaching their mother, they persuaded her to ask on their behalf, being themselves afraid to approach him openly. For they themselves were approaching secretly, as Mark says <note>Theophylact is harmonizing Matthew's account with Mark 10:35</note>: "For (he says) James and John came to him," that is, they came to him privately and separately.

**But Jesus answering, said, "You do not know what you ask. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink? or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" They said to him, "We are able."**] Passing over the mother, he speaks to the sons to show that he was not unaware that the mother had been sent by them, and says to them, "You do not know what you ask." It is a great thing, shaking even the angelic powers. Then, leading them away from such thoughts, he encourages them toward dangers instead. But he asks not because he is ignorant—

<margin>We do not become sharers of the kingdom unless we are made sharers of Christ’s suffering.</margin> <margin>A</margin> —but so that he might force them to reveal the wound <note>original: "vlcus"; here referring to their hidden ambition or spiritual ailment</note> through their answer, and so they might strive to fulfill the promise. For he says this: "Because one cannot become a sharer of my kingdom, unless he also becomes a sharer of my sufferings." Tell me, can you suffer similar things? For by "the cup" he means martyrdom and his own death; at the same time showing that it is light and that we ought to approach it as easily as if a cup were to be drunk: and declaring that he himself approaches death sweetly. For just as one who drinks a cup immediately falls into a heavy sleep, so also he who drinks the cup of martyrdom is carried into the sleep of death. He also calls his death a "baptism," because it purifies us all. These men, however, not knowing what they were promising, but only looking at what they desired, easily promised everything.

<margin>B</margin> **He said to them, "You shall indeed drink my cup, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized: but to sit at my right hand and my left is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father."**] <margin>Acts 12</margin> I know indeed that you will bear witness <note>meaning to die for the faith</note>, and these things will certainly come to pass. For Herod killed James. But Trajan condemned John while he was preaching the word of truth <note>Theophylact cites the martyrdom of James by Herod Agrippa I and the exile/persecution of John under the Emperor Trajan</note>. Furthermore, "to sit is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared": understand it this way: If anyone is found with the testimony of truth and endowed with every other virtue, he shall receive the gift. For it is prepared for him who has labored, just as crowns are prepared for those who compete; as if he were to say to them, "It is not mine to give the crown as a favor <note>original: "ad gratiam"</note>, but to those for whom it has been prepared, that is, to those who have run and conquered." So also in this place Christ says, "I cannot give you a seat at the right hand as a favor; for it belongs to others who have labored and for whom it has been prepared." You will ask then: Who will be seated? You should learn that no one will sit there, for this belongs only to the divine nature. <margin>Psalm 109</margin> For to which of the angels did he say, "Sit at my right hand"? But the Lord said this according to their opinion: for they were seeking this seat, not understanding that "to sit upon twelve seats" means to be glorified on account of virtue.

They believed that Jesus (who is from the seed of David according to the flesh) could heal them, and they were clearly fervent in faith. Even when ordered to be silent, they did not hold their peace, but cried out even louder. Therefore, he did not ask them if they had faith, but what they wanted; lest anyone think he gives something other than what they desire. He showed that they cried out not for money, but to be cured. <margin>B</margin> He heals them by touch so that we may learn that all the <margin>Luke 18, Mark 10</margin> members of his holy flesh are life-giving and are the members of God. The fact that Luke and Mark say there was only one blind man does not contradict this; they simply mentioned the more notable one. Or alternatively, Luke says he healed a blind man before coming into Jericho, while Mark says after he left Jericho; Matthew, however, being a lover of brevity, encompassed both in one account. Understand the blind to be those from among the Gentiles, who were healed by the side of the road. For Christ did not come primarily for the Gentiles, but for the Israelites. Just as the blind learned of Jesus by hearing, so did the Gentiles by the "hearing of faith." Those who command the blind to be silent, <margin>C</margin> lest they call upon the name of Jesus, are the persecutors and tyrants who attempt to stop the mouth of the Church. But she confesses the name of Christ all the more; therefore she is healed and sees the light of truth more clearly, and follows Christ by imitating his life.

### CHAPTER 21. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

->Kij<-

"Which of the two did what the father wanted? They said to him, **D** 'The first.' Jesus said to them, 'Truly I say to you, that tax collectors <note>original: "publicani"</note> and harlots precede you into the kingdom of God. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and harlots believed him. But you, when you had seen him, were not moved by repentance afterward so as to believe him.'" ] He introduces two ranks: one of those who promised at the beginning, such as the Jews who said, <margin>Exodus 24</margin> "God, we will do and we will listen." The other rank consists of those who were not immediately persuaded, such as the harlots and tax collectors, and those from the Gentile people, who did not believe the divine will from the start, but were afterward <margin>E</margin> led by repentance and obeyed. Observe, therefore, the wisdom of Christ. He did not say to them immediately from the beginning, "The tax collectors and harlots are better than you," but first he caught them <note>Theophylact suggests Jesus "trapped" them in their own logic.</note> and they confessed that of the two sons, the obedient one was he who did the will of the father. Afterward, once they had confessed this, he added that John had come through the way of righteousness—that is, in a blameless life. For you cannot say that John's life was blameworthy, yet the harlots obeyed him while you did not. Therefore, they shall precede you, entering the kingdom of heaven before you: so that if you also labor, you may enter even after them; but if you remain unbelieving, you shall never enter. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, many even today promise God the Father that they will be monks, or perhaps priests; but after the promise, they are negligent. Others, however, did not promise the monastic or priestly life, yet they live worthily just as monks or priests do, and thus they are the obedient children who act, even if they promised nothing.

"Listen to another parable. There was a certain man, a householder, who planted a vineyard, and surrounded it with a fence, and dug a winepress in it, and built a tower, <margin>Isaiah 5; Jeremiah 2</margin> and leased it to farmers, and went on a journey abroad." ] <margin>Psalm 77</margin> He brings another parable to them, showing that although the greatest diligence was shown to them, they were not made better.

<margin>A</margin> For the "householder" is the Lord, who is called a "man" because of His mercy. The "vineyard" is the people of the Jews, planted by God in the land of promise. For He said, "Leading them in, you will plant them on your holy mountain." <note>Exodus 15:17</note> The "fence" is the Law, which did not allow them to be mixed with the Gentiles, or perhaps the angels guarding Israel. The "winepress" is the altar. The "tower" is the Temple. The "farmers" are the teachers of the people, the Pharisees and scribes. The householder, God, "went on a journey" when He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud. Or, the "journeying" of God is His long-suffering <note>original: "longanimitas," God's patience and delay in punishment</note>. For God seems to sleep or to be far away while He is long-suffering and does not immediately demand punishment for sins.

Another they killed, like Zechariah <note>The priest Zechariah, son of Jehoiada</note> between the temple and the altar. Another they stoned, like Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the high priest. Afterward the Son of God was sent, appearing in the flesh. As for His saying, "They will respect my son," He does not say this in ignorance that they were going to kill him, but wishing to signify what they *ought* to have done. For it was necessary, He means, that even if they killed the servants, they should at least respect the Son. But the farmers, seeing Him, said: "This <margin>The Lord killed outside the vineyard</margin> is the heir, come let us kill him." ### CHAPTER 21. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

[...outside the] city the Lord was killed. Because we said <margin>D</margin> the vineyard was the people, the Pharisees and the wicked farmers killed him "outside the vineyard," which means they acted against the consensus of the simple people.

[ **When therefore the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those farmers? They said to him, "He will bring those wretches to a wretched end and will lease his vineyard to other farmers, who will give him the fruit in its season."** ] When he comes. When will that be? Could it mean at the second coming? While it seems to suggest that, it is better understood this way: The "Lord of the vineyard" is God the Father, who sent his Son to be killed by them. Therefore, "when he comes"—that is, when he looks upon the iniquity the Jews committed—he will then bring those "wretches to a wretched end" by sending the Roman army. <margin>E</margin> He will lease his vineyard (meaning the people) to other farmers, namely the Apostles and the teachers of the Church. Understand also that the "vineyard" represents the Divine Scriptures. In this metaphor, the "hedge" is the letter <note>The "letter" refers to the literal, surface-level reading of the text.</note> of the law; the "dug-out winepress" is the deep spirit of the word; and the "tower" is **theology** <note>Theophylact uses "theologia" here in its original sense: the highest study of the nature of God.</note>, which is the summit and divine height. The wicked farmers—the Pharisees—formerly held these Scriptures, but God has now leased them to us who cultivate them well. For they killed the Lord "outside the vineyard," which means they acted against the commands of what the Scriptures actually said.

<margin>Psalm 117</margin>
[ **Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the Scriptures: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes? Therefore I tell you, the kingdom <margin>F</margin> <margin>John 8. Acts 4. Ephesians 2.</margin> will be taken from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And he who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; but on whomever it falls, it will crush him."** ] He calls himself the "stone" and the "builders" are the teachers of the Jews, who rejected him as useless, saying: "You are a Samaritan and have a demon." But after he rose from the dead, he was placed as the "head of the corner." This means he became the head of the Church, joining both Jews and Gentiles into one faith. Just as a cornerstone in a house supports the walls on both sides, so Christ has bound us all together in one faith. That "corner" is marvelous and was made by the

It is also marvelous for another reason: the word of the Lord was strengthened and confirmed by miracles; thus, the very foundation of the Church is marvelous. Therefore, the "kingdom of God" was taken from the Jews—that is, their special status as God's own people—and given to those who believed. For those who trip over the stone and are offended by Christ Jesus will indeed be "broken" at the second coming; however, even here in this life they are crushed by him, meaning they have been scattered across all the earth. They will, however, "grasp" the Antichrist and worship him; but Christ is not "taken" by them—that is, he is not understood.

### CHAPTER 22. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> [**...those murderers, and set fire to their city.**] This parable hints at the disobedience of the Jews, just like the previous one regarding the vineyard. However, just as that one declared the death of Christ, this one declares the wedding joy—that is, the resurrection. Furthermore, this shows that they committed much more atrocious acts than in the previous parable. For in that one, when the fruits were demanded, they killed those who were collecting them; but in this one, when they were called to a wedding, they committed murder. Therefore, God is like a royal man. For he does not appear exactly as he is, but in a way that is fitting, so that he may show himself to be seen by us. For when we die like men, subject to human sins, God appears to us as a man; but when we walk as gods, then "God stands in the assembly of the gods" <margin>Psalm 81</margin> <note>Modern Psalm 82:1. Theophylact suggests that God’s manifestation to us changes based on our own spiritual state.</note>. Just as when we take on the natures of wild beasts, he also becomes to us <margin>E</margin> a panther, a bear, and a lion. Moreover, he makes a wedding for his son, joining him to every beautiful soul; for the bridegroom is Christ, and the bride is the Church and the soul. The servants first sent were Moses and others, whom the Hebrews did not believe; instead, they provoked God in the desert for forty years and refused to receive the word of God and spiritual love <margin>Revelation 19</margin>. Then other servants were sent—the prophets—but some of those they killed, such as Isaiah; others they treated with insults <margin>Jeremiah 38</margin>, like Jeremiah, whom they threw into a pit of mud. However, some who were less wicked refrained from such violence, but one went away to his own <margin>F</margin> farm—that is, he indulged in the delights and pleasures of life. For each person's "farm" is their own body. Another went to his business—that is, he was devoted to greed. For the class of merchants is greedy and most desirous of profit. Therefore, the parable shows that those who are deprived of the spiritual wedding, the banquet, and the fellowship of Christ are excluded primarily for these two reasons: either because of bodily pleasures or the disease of greed. Now, he calls it a "luncheon" <margin>Luke 14</margin> in this place, although in another place he called it a "supper." It is not absurd to call it a supper, for in the final times, that wedding will appear perfectly in the evening and at the end of the ages. It is a "luncheon" because in the earlier ages the mystery was re-

-vealed, though more obscurely. <margin>A</margin> As for the bulls and fattened cattle, they represent the Old and New Testaments. For the Old is signified by the bulls, as it involved the slaughter of animals. The New, however, is signified by the fattened cattle. For we now offer loaves on the altar, which are properly called <margin>The loaves offered are so-called.</margin> "fattened" <note>The Latin 'altilia' usually refers to fattened birds or cattle; Theophylact creates a spiritual metaphor linking this to the abundance of the Eucharist.</note>, since they are made from the fruits of the earth. God therefore calls us to the altar so that we may eat the good things of both the Old and New Testaments. And when you see someone clearly interpreting the divine words, know that they are giving "fattened cattle" and food made from grain—nourishing as if with the harvest and stuffing with food by clearly teaching the simpler people. But you may ask here: <margin>B</margin> if they were already invited, how can they be called again? Know, then, that everyone is called by nature to what is good through the natural gift of reason; yet God also sends those external teachers so that those who have been called from within may also be called from without. Moreover, the king sends his armies—that is, the Romans—who destroyed the disobedient Jews and set fire to their city, Jerusalem, as Josephus says <note>Referencing the historian Flavius Josephus and the Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note>. Then he says to his servants: "The wedding indeed is prepared, but those who were invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the ends of the roads and invite as many as you find to the wedding." And his servants went out into the roads and gathered everyone they found, both bad and good, <margin>C</margin> and the wedding was filled with guests. Since the first servants—Moses and the prophets—did not persuade them, he sends other servants, the Apostles, who called the Gentiles who were not walking in the true way, but were scattered in different directions, discordant in many ways and doctrines—indeed, existing near the "ends of the roads," which is to say, in error and in great inequality. For they themselves were in disagreement and turmoil, and they were not on the paths, but outside the paths; and those are the evil doctrines which they taught. Not all loved equally, but some in this way, others in that. What if it is better understood this way? The "road" is each person's life; the "exit from the road" is a doctrine. The Gentiles, therefore, had bad roads—that is, a reprehensible life—and they exited from that bad road...

<summary>Theophylact provides a spiritual and historical interpretation of the Parable of the Wedding Banquet, identifying the servants as Moses, the prophets, and the Apostles, and the "king's armies" as the Romans who destroyed Jerusalem. He explains that humanity is excluded from Christ's fellowship primarily through the distractions of physical pleasure or greed.</summary>

The entry to the wedding happens without discernment. For by grace alone we are all called, both the good and the bad; but the life of those who have entered will not be unexamined thereafter. It is he who is not clothed in "bowels of mercy" <note>An idiom for deep compassion</note>, brotherhood, and kindness. They invent a scenario that never actually happened. # CHAPTER 22. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> and the great [commandment]. And the second is like it: *You shall love your neighbor as yourself. For on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.* <note>Matthew 22:37-40</note> The tempter approaches out of excessive envy; for because they had seen the Sadducees silenced and the Lord praised, they approach to test Him, wondering if He might add something to the first commandment—as if correcting the Law—so that they might find a handle against Him. The Lord, however, exposing his malice—that he had not come to learn, but being void of charity, acted out of envy and rivalry—shows that charity <note>The Latin *charitas* is used here for "love."</note> excels among the commandments. He shows that it is not fitting to love God only in part, but to give our whole selves to God. 

<margin>There are three powers in the soul by which one must love God.</margin> For we learn that there are three such powers planted in the soul: the **plant-like**, the **animal**, and the **rational**. <margin>E</margin> Insofar as the soul grows, is nourished, and generates its own kind, it is likened to **plants**; insofar as it feels anger and desire, it is compared to **brutes** <note>Meaning non-rational animals.</note>; and insofar as it understands, it is called **rational**. See then in this place what those three things signify: *You shall love your God with all your heart*—this is the "brute" or animal part of the soul; *and with all your soul*—this is the "plant-like" or vegetative power, for plants are said to be "animated"; *and with all your mind*—this is the rational power. And so it is necessary to love God with the whole soul; that is, to adhere to Him with all parts and powers of the soul. This is the first and great commandment, exercising us in piety. 

[And the second is like it, which stirs us to do what is just toward man. For two things lead us to destruction: evil doctrine and a corrupt life. <margin>F</margin> Therefore, so that we do not fall into impious dogmas, God must be loved; but so that our life is not perverse, our neighbor must be loved. For he who loves his neighbor fulfills all the commandments, and he who fulfills the commandments loves God. Thus those two commandments are joined and coupled together, and they contain all other commandments. For who that loves God and his neighbor would either steal, or be greedy for revenge, or commit adultery, or fornicate, or kill? <margin>Mark 12</margin> Now this lawyer <note>original: *legisperitus*, a man skilled in the Mosaic Law.</note> came at first testing Him, but then, having been made better by the response of God, he was praised, just as Mark says: "seeing this, He embraced him and said to him:

<margin>A</margin> *You are not far from the kingdom of God.*

While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus questioned them, saying: *What do you think of the Christ? Whose son is He?* <margin>Psalm 109</margin> They say to Him: *David's.* He said to them: *How then does David in the spirit call Him Lord, saying: The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet? If David then calls Him Lord, how is He his son? And no one was able to answer Him a word, nor did anyone dare from that day to question Him further.*] Since they thought Christ was a mere man, He subverts their opinion and teaches the truth through the prophet David, proclaiming His own divinity. <margin>B</margin> For when the Pharisees say that Christ is the son of David—that is, a pure man—He says: "How then does David name Him Lord?" And he does not simply name Him Lord, but "in the spirit," that is, he revealed Him through the grace of the Spirit. By saying this, He is not denying that He is the son of David, but He shows that He is not a *mere* man descending solely from the Davidic seed. The Lord asks these things so that if they say they do not know, they might ask and learn; or if they say the truth, they might believe; or, if they can say nothing, they might be confounded and withdraw, not daring to question Him further.

# CHAPTER 23. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> [all] things which they say, even if they are evil? We say first, that one who teaches never dares to exhort anyone toward evil. Then, even if we grant that someone might exhort toward an evil life, he does not then speak from the seat of Moses, nor does he speak from the law. For the Lord speaks of those who sit in the seat of Moses—that is, those who teach the things contained in the law. Therefore, it is necessary to listen to those who teach the divine law, even if they themselves do not act upon it.

*But they bind heavy burdens, hard to carry, and lay them on the shoulders of men; but they themselves will not move them with their own finger. But all their works they do to be seen by men. They make broad their phylacteries and the fringes of their cloaks.* ] The Pharisees impose <margin>E</margin> heavy burdens, forcing men to fulfill the mandates of the law, even though they are thin and difficult to observe. Or they even weighed down many mandates of the law by handing down certain traditions beyond the laws, which they themselves do not move with their finger, performing nothing. For when a teacher not only teaches but also acts, he seems to labor and work alongside those who are being taught. But when he burdens me while he himself lives in idleness, he burdens me even more. Therefore, the Lord rebukes the Pharisees because they are unwilling to carry the burdens of the commandments together [with the people] and to cooperate. Not only do they do nothing good, but they also pretend as if they do: and if ever they do anything so that they may be seen, they have already received their reward. But now, of how much condemnation are they worthy, when they neither <margin>F</margin> act, and yet wish to be seen as if they do? And what do they do?

They broaden their <term>phylacteries</term> <note>original: "phylacteria." These were small leather boxes containing scrolls of parchment inscribed with passages from the Torah, worn by Jewish men on the forehead and arm during morning prayers.</note> and magnify the fringes of their garments. This came about in this way: in the law <margin>Deut. 6.</margin> it is held: *You shall bind them on your hand, and they shall be unmoved before your eyes.* <note>Deuteronomy 6:8</note> They therefore wrote the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> of the law on two small scrolls of parchment, and placed one upon the forehead, and suspended the other upon the right hand. Moreover, they made <margin>Phylactery</margin> fringes on the edges of their garments with violet and scarlet threads. And they had found this in the law so that, seeing those things, they might never forget the commandments of God. But God did not want this; rather, by commanding them to carry the phylactery on the hand, he wished to signify that they ought to put the commandments into practice. By the scarlet

<margin>D</margin> [to do anything] unjust and absurd, but to do all things with judgment and reason. For immediately mercy follows judgment. For whoever acts with discernment in all things knows also upon whom he ought to have mercy. Furthermore, faith follows mercy. For he who shows mercy believes entirely that he loses nothing, but rather receives everything. Or put another way, it is necessary to show mercy and to believe in the true God. For many of the pagans were indeed merciful, but because they did not believe in the living God, they did not have faith as a companion to their mercy. Moreover, it is necessary for every teacher to "tithe" from his people; that is, to seek from the ten senses—the five bodily senses and the five of the soul <note>original: "animalibus"; referring to the internal faculties or the "animating" part of the human spirit</note>—judgment, mercy, and faith. These things
<margin>E</margin> "it was necessary to do," says Christ; He is not encouraging the tithing of herbs, but He says this so that He would not seem at that time to be contrary to Moses. He calls them "blind guides" because they boasted that they knew and taught all things, yet they were useful to no one; instead, they corrupted everyone, casting them into the pit. He calls them those who "strain out a gnat" because they strictly observe small sins, but "swallow a camel"—that is, they devour and despise great ones.
<margin>F</margin> **Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside they are full of plunder and lack of self-control. Blind Pharisee, first clean what is inside the cup and the dish, so that the outside of these parts may also be made clean.** ] Those who observed the traditions of the elders would wash the drinking cups and the platters—that is, the dishes in which the second courses are placed—but they drank wine and ate food obtained through plunder, which defiles much more. Therefore He says: do not possess wine gained unjustly, and then even the cup will be clean. Or perhaps He is not speaking of cups and dishes, but of the external bodily condition and the internal spiritual one. For you (He says) scrub the outer parts of the cup—that is, your outward behavior—so that it appears more elegant; but inside you fill yourself with filth, that is, with plunder, and you treat others with injustice. But it is necessary for you to be washed inside—that is, in your soul—so that the external dignity may also be graced by the purity of the soul.

# CHAPTER 23. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> [He convicts] them of lying, when they say, "If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have killed the prophets." For "behold," He says, "I will send prophets, and wise men, and scribes, yet you will kill them." He says this concerning the Apostles, whom the Holy Spirit made into scribes—that is, teachers of the people—and adorned with all wisdom and prophecy. By saying "I send," He declares the power of His own divinity.

<margin>Genesis 4. 2 Chronicles 24 <note>The source text cites 2 Par. 23, but the account of Zechariah's death is in 2 Chronicles 24.</note></margin>
"So that all the righteous blood shed upon the earth may come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed <margin>E</margin> between the temple and the altar. Truly I say to you, all these things shall come upon this generation." He says that all the blood unjustly shed will come upon those Jews who were then alive; for they will be punished more severely than their fathers. For even after such great examples, they were not corrected. <margin>Genesis 4.</margin> For just as Lamech was punished more than Cain—even though Lamech had not killed his own brother—because he had not been corrected by the example of Cain, so too shall this generation be punished. Therefore, He says, the blood from Abel to Zechariah shall come upon them. He mentions Abel quite appropriately: for just as Abel was murdered because of envy, so also was Christ slain.

But which Zechariah does He mention in this place? <margin>F</margin> Some say he was one of the twelve prophets <note>The "Minor Prophets" of the Old Testament</note>; others say he was the father of the Lord’s Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note>. For the tradition handed down to us holds that there was a specific place in the temple where the virgins stood. Therefore, while he was high priest, after the Mother of God <note>original: "Deipara"; literally "God-bearer" or "Theotokos"</note> had given birth to Christ, he placed her in that spot. The Jews were indignant against him and killed him because he had stationed a woman who had given birth among the virgins. It is not surprising that the father of the Forerunner might also have had a father named Barachiah, just as the prophet among the twelve is called the son of Barachiah. It is likely that just as the sons shared a name, so did their fathers.

"Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing? Behold, your house is left to

<margin>A</margin> you desolate. For I say to you, you shall not see me from now on until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.'" He repeats the name "Jerusalem" twice, pitying her and calling her back with great compassion. For expostulating with her as if with a beloved who despises the one who loves her, He responds that He will bring punishment. He convicts her of being bloodthirsty and notes that although He often wished to show her mercy, she was unwilling; instead, she listened to the devil, by whom she was scattered and led away from the truth, and she would not receive the Lord who was gathering her. In this place, let us learn that for our sake God dwells in temples; but if we become regrettable <note>original: "poenitendi"; those in need of repentance or whose actions lead to loss</note>, the temples are also abandoned. "Therefore, you will not see me until the second coming"; for then, even if they are unwilling, they will worship Him and say, "Blessed is He who comes." By "from now on," understand this to mean "after I have been crucified." For He is not speaking of the literal hour in which He was saying these things—since they saw Him often afterward—but after the crucifixion, they did not see Him at all until His second coming draws near.

<margin>C</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring the profile of a man wearing a scholar's cap, surrounded by floral and architectural scrollwork.</image-desc>And Jesus went out and departed from the temple. <meta>This page continues Theophylact’s commentary on the Gospel of Matthew. The previous page concluded the woes against the Pharisees and the lament over Jerusalem. We now move into Chapter 24, where Jesus describes the destruction of the Temple and the signs of the end of the age.</meta>

# CHAPTER 24. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> <note>original: "Nequaquam"</note> In no way will a stone remain here upon a stone. By using this hyperbolic language, He means that it will be utterly destroyed.

**While He sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples came to Him privately, saying, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what is the sign of Your coming and of the end of the age?"** They approach Him privately, as people about to ask about great matters. For they ask about two things: when these things will happen—namely, the destruction of the temple and the conquest of Jerusalem—and what is the sign of His own coming.

**And Jesus answered and said to them, "See that no one deceives you. For many will come in My name, saying, 'I am the Christ,' and they will deceive many."** He says many will come preaching that they themselves are "Christs." For <margin>E</margin> Dositheus the Samaritan <note>A leader of a Samaritan sect who claimed to be the Messiah or the prophet promised by Moses.</note> claimed he was the prophet predicted by Moses, and Simon <note>Simon Magus, the sorcerer mentioned in the Book of Acts.</note> called himself the "great power of God."

<margin>Acts 8</margin> **"You will hear of wars and rumors of wars; see that you are not troubled, for all things must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be pestilences, famines, and earthquakes in various places. All these are the beginnings of sorrows."** By "wars," He refers to the Roman campaigns in Jerusalem. He speaks not only of future wars but also of famines and plagues, since the wrath of God will rage against the Jews. For one might say wars are the results of human incursions, but famine and plague never come from anywhere <margin>F</margin> except from God. Then, lest they think the world would end before they had preached the Gospel, He says, "Do not be troubled." For the end is not yet, nor will the general end of the world occur at the same time as the subversion of Jerusalem. He says nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom because of the evils looming over the Jews, which are the "beginnings of sorrows." Just as a woman in labor suffers and then gives birth, so the present age "gives birth" to the next after these confusions and wars.

**"Then they will hand you over to affliction and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations for My name's sake. And then many will experience a stumbling block, and they will betray one another and hate one another; and many false prophets will rise and deceive many..."**

<meta>catchword: many, and</meta>

<column-break/>

# COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW
<page-num>84</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> **"...and because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold. But he who perseveres to the end shall be saved."** He predicts the coming evils, encouraging the disciples by forewarning them. For unexpected things usually terrify and disturb the mind. Therefore, He softens their fear by foretelling future heavy hatreds, enmities, stumbling blocks, and false prophets—who are the precursors of the Antichrist—who will deceive many so that they become hardened in all iniquity. Because iniquity will multiply through the deceptions of the Antichrist, men will become embittered and fierce, so that they will not maintain any bond of love even with their closest associates, but will betray each other. <margin>B</margin> But he who perseveres and bears it bravely, and does not yield to the trials inflicted then, will be saved and proven a vigorous soldier.

**"And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come."** There will be no obstacle to your preaching. Have confidence, for the Gospel will be preached among all nations "as a testimony"—that is, as a rebuke and condemnation of those who did not believe. And then the end will come: not yet the end of the world, but the end of Jerusalem. For before Jerusalem was captured, the Gospel was preached, as Paul also says: "The Gospel which was preached in <margin>Colossians 1</margin> all that is under the sun." For it is manifest from what follows that He is speaking of the end of Jerusalem. <margin>C</margin>

**"Therefore, when you see the 'abomination of desolation,' which was spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand)..."** He calls the "abomination of desolation" the statue of the ruler who conquered the city, which he erected in the inner sanctuary of the temple. It is called "of desolation" because the city was to be laid waste. It is called an "abomination" because the Hebrews used that term for statues and images of men, out of their hatred for idolatry.

**"Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; let him who is on the roof not go down to take anything from his house, and let him who is in the field not return to take his clothes."** Suggesting the extreme dangers that cannot be escaped, He says that one must flee without looking back, nor with...

Some, however, think that the "abomination of desolation" is the Antichrist, because he will lay waste to the world, subvert the Churches, and sit in the temple. And this is interpreted as follows: that he who is "on the roof"—that is, endowed with the highest virtues—should not descend from those heights of virtue to take up things belonging to the body. For the body is the house of the soul. One must also withdraw from the "field"—that is, from earthly things—and not take up the "garment" of malice, which is the old garment we have cast off.

> **But woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days.**

Those who are pregnant will not be able to flee because they are weighed down by the burden of the womb; those nursing because of their compassion for their children. For they can neither leave them behind nor carry them with them and save them both at the same time.
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Josephus</margin>
Perhaps **CHRIST** is hinting that they would even eat their children. For Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the Jewish-Roman historian who recorded the Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> says that when there was a famine because of the siege, a woman cooked her own son and ate him.

> **And pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath.**

He says these things to the Jews in the person of the apostles. For the apostles had already departed from Jerusalem. Therefore, He tells the Jews to pray that their flight may not happen in winter, because it is inconvenient to flee during those times, nor on the Sabbath; for then, according to the Law, they are at rest and do not dare to flee. But you should also understand it this way: that we must pray that our flight from this life—that is, death—does not happen on the "Sabbath," while we are idle in regard to good works,
<margin>F</margin>
nor in the "winter" of the barrenness of good deeds, but rather in the serenity of a soul that is not troubled.

The tribulation will be intolerable then. For the Roman soldiers were ordered to spare no one, but God, for the sake of those among them who would believe and those who already believed, did not allow everyone to be killed at once. <margin>D</margin> [Where the corpse is,] there all the saints will come, to wherever Christ may be. For these fly in the heights and are carried into the clouds like eagles. <margin>Zechariah 24, Luke 2, Joel 2</margin> be undone, He declared this by saying: "immediately the sun will be obscured," that is, it will be darkened—not by disappearing, but by being overcome by the light of Christ’s arrival, when
<margin>E</margin> there will be no night, but the "Sun of Justice" <note>A common title for Christ, derived from Malachi 4:2.</note> shall appear. Furthermore, the "powers of the heavens will be shaken," meaning they will be struck with amazement and awe, seeing the creation being transformed and all people, from Adam until that time, about to give an account of their lives.

**And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.** ] The Cross will then appear in heaven, shining brighter than the sun, to convict the Jews. For Christ will come against the Jews bearing the Cross as a great proof and testimony of His right to judge: just as if someone who was struck by a stone were to display that stone. He calls the Cross "the sign" as if it were a trophy or a royal standard.
<margin>F</margin> Then, therefore, all the tribes of the Jewish land will wail, mourning their own disobedience and unbelief, as will all those who "savor earthly things" <note>A phrase meaning those focused on worldly rather than spiritual matters.</note> even if they are Christians; for the "tribes of the earth" refers to those who focus on the earthly. Although the Lord comes with the Cross, He will nevertheless come with glory and power.

<margin>Daniel 12, 1 Thessalonians 4</margin> **heavens to their furthest bounds.** ] He will send His angels with a great trumpet blast to gather the saints and those who have risen from the dead, so that they may meet Him in the clouds. He shows them honor, therefore, even through the summons of the angels. Although Paul says—
