### CHAPTER 24. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA / EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 87

<margin>D</margin> ...that neither the Son knows, except the Father alone. <note>original: "quod neque filius nouit, nisi pater solus" (Matthew 24:36). This was a difficult verse for early theologians who wanted to defend Christ's divinity; if he is God, how can he not know something?</note> Just as fathers often hold something in their hands, but when their children seek it and the fathers do not wish to give it, they hide it and say, "We do not have what you are looking for," and thus they quiet their weeping children. So also the Lord, in order to restrain the Apostles from learning about that day and hour, said: "Neither <margin>John 13 & 17</margin> do I know, except the Father alone." For He Himself knows both the hour and that day, which is manifest from many other things. For all things whatsoever the Father has belong to the Son; since the Father has knowledge of this day, the Son likewise has it. This is even more manifest from this: how is it possible for the Son to be ignorant of the day, when He knows the things that come before the day? For he who leads one to the vestibule clearly <margin>E</margin> knows the door as well. But He did not open this knowledge for our benefit; for it is not profitable for us to know when the consummation <note>The "consummation of the age" refers to the end of the world.</note> will be, lest we become lazy. For ignorance makes us alert.

<margin>Genesis 6, 7</margin> **But as the days of Noah were, so also will the coming of the Son of Man be. For as they were in the days before the flood, eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and took them all away; so also will the coming of the Son of Man be.** ] To confirm the absolute truth of His words, He uses the events that occurred in the time of Noah. In those days, some mocked the <margin>F</margin> preparation of the ark, until the affliction came and enveloped them all. So too now, some mock the talk of the consummation of the age, but suddenly (He says) destruction will arrive. He shows, moreover, that when the Antichrist comes, men will be given over to pleasures, and more inclined toward marriage and luxuries, just like the giants in the time of Noah.

**Then two will be in the field; one is taken, and the other is left. Two women will be grinding at the mill; one is taken, and the other is left.** ] Then (He says), when all are without worry and performing their own tasks, one indeed is taken—that is, to meet Christ in the air—but the other, namely a sinner, is left behind.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> But even if some are servants and are grinding at the mill: even among these, those who are worthy are taken, while those who are unworthy are left. And so we learn from this passage that neither servitude nor being a woman are obstacles to virtue.

**Watch therefore, for you do not know what hour your Lord is coming. But know this, that if the master of the house had known what hour the thief was coming, he would have watched and not allowed his house to be broken into. Therefore you also be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.** ] He commands us to watch and be prepared—that is, to possess works of virtue as if stored in a certain treasury, so that when the Lord comes seeking what He wants, we can give it. Notice, however, how He did not say, "I do <margin>B</margin> not know at what hour the thief is coming," but rather, "You do not know." He calls the consummation of the world a "thief," as well as the death of each individual person. Furthermore, He suggests in this passage that His arrival will occur at night. Just as the thief comes secretly, so also is my arrival, so that you are not negligent, but sober and watchful. For if we knew when our death was to be, on that day alone would we strive to please God. But now, since we are ignorant, let us always be sober for the works of virtue.

**Who then is a faithful and wise servant, whom his master made ruler over his household, to give them food in due season? Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, will find so doing. Assuredly, I say to you that <margin>C</margin> he will make him ruler over all his goods.** ] He <margin>Faithfulness and prudence.</margin> asks whether such a faithful and wise man will exist, in order to show that such a person is rare and difficult to find. For two things are required of every steward: faith and prudence. For if he is faithful and steals nothing, but is not prudent and wastes resources in vain; or if he is prudent but steals, he will be of no profit. Therefore, he who is then found faithful and wise, he shall also obtain much more—I mean the kingdom of heaven. For the saints will be heirs of all things that are God's. Every man is also a faithful and <margin>1 Timothy 2, 3</margin> wise servant who has given food to the disciples in <margin>1 Timothy 1</margin> due season; just as Paul, sometimes giving them milk to drink <note>original: "lacte potans" (1 Corinthians 3:2). In the early church, "milk" referred to basic Christian teachings for beginners, while "meat" was for the mature.</note>, <margin>2 Corinthians 2</margin> and at other times speaking wisely, was a faithful minister...

### CHAPTER 25. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> "...then, gathering where you did not scatter; and being afraid, I went away and hid your talent in the earth: look, you have what is yours." But his lord answering, said to him: "You wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow, and gather there where I did not scatter. You ought, therefore, to have entrusted my money to the bankers, and when I came, I would certainly have received what is mine with interest. Therefore, take the talent away from him, and give it to him who has ten talents. For to everyone who has, shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who has not, even that which he has shall be taken away. And cast the useless servant into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth." <margin>E</margin> Both of these who work with what was entrusted to them are praised by the lord; in the same way, both heard: "Well done, good and faithful servant." <note>original: "Euge serve bone & fidelis"</note> By "good," we understand here one who is entirely merciful and generous, who imparts his own goodness to his neighbors. Moreover, those who appear faithful over a few things are set over many; for although we receive gifts here, they are not to be compared with those in the future. <margin>Psalm 103</margin> The "joy of the lord" <note>Theophylact interprets the "joy of the lord" not just as a place, but as a state of divine happiness.</note> is unceasing gladness, which God has, rejoicing in His works, as David says. In such joy, therefore, the saints rejoice, being glad in their own works; just as, conversely, sinners grieve in their own works, the saints rejoice because they have such a wealthy lord. <margin>F</margin> Note, however, that both he who had received five and he who had received two talents obtain the same goods. For whenever someone has received even a few things, and has well administered the gift given to him—even if it be small—he is destined to obtain equal honor with him who had and did great things. For each person will be seen as exalted according to how he received, if he has acted well. Furthermore, the grateful servants behave in this way: but the idle and lazy one responds differently, and as befits himself. For he calls his lord "hard," just as many of the learned <note>likely referring to the scholars or Pharisees of the time</note> say now. "Hard" indeed, to require obedience from men into whom God did not instill obedience and persuasiveness; for this is what he implies by: "Reaping where you did not sow." That is: from him to whom you did not give the power to obey, you demand that he obey. By calling the lord "hard," the servant condemns himself. For since the lord was hard, he ought to have been more diligent, seeing as he had been allotted a hard and cruel master. For

### ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. 90

<margin>A</margin> if he demands what belongs to others, much more will he demand his own, and thus it was necessary for you also to multiply what you had received, and to make disciples from whom you could reclaim the debt. He calls the disciples "bankers," <term>menſariis (bankers): from the Latin 'mensa' (table), referring to money-changers who traded at tables; here allegorically referring to those who receive spiritual teaching.</term> as they are those who test and either approve or reject words. Truly, he demands "interest" from the disciples, namely, the exhibition of works. For a disciple receiving the word from a teacher indeed holds it and returns it whole, but loses the interest—which is the performance of good works. For the gift is taken away from the evil and sluggish servant. For he who received a gift, received it to benefit others; even if he does not use it, but lets it waste away, yet he who strives to multiply it will win greater grace for himself. For to the one who applies diligence, greater grace will be given so that he may abound. <margin>B</margin> But the one who does not apply effort will be deprived even of the gift he seems to have. For the negligent person, and he who does not work through those things which he received, does not truly possess the gift, but only *seems* to have it; he has lost it through his own negligence.

"When however the Son of Man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then he shall sit upon the throne of his glory, and all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats; and he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on his left." <margin>C</margin> Since the first coming of the Lord was in ignominy and reproaches, he says, "when he shall come in his glory." For in the second coming, he will be present with the glory of the surrounding angels. First, however, he separates the saints from the sinners, freeing them from labor, and positions them, and then he speaks to them. Thus, he calls the saints "sheep" because they are mild, and give us fruit and utility, just as sheep supply wool for divine and spiritual clothing, and milk—that is, suitable food. But he calls the sinners "goats," for they go toward the precipice, and are disorderly and sterile, like goats.

"Then the king shall say to those who shall be at his right hand: 'Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you as an inheritance from the beginning of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked...'"

For that reason, they come to the high priest of that year to enter into a counsel concerning murder, in a place where it was more fitting for murderers to be punished. Now the high priest speaks to those who were already supposed to perform the annual ministry, but they were about to perpetrate a wicked slaughter, and they feared men rather than God. For they feared <margin>B</margin> lest a riot be stirred up if they killed him on the feast day; or perhaps because all the sacrifices decreed in the law were then to be offered, they feared the people might withdraw from the sacrifices on account of the murder, and they themselves would lose the profit they gained from the sacrifices. But perhaps they also feared this: lest by being killed on the feast day, his death might become more noble and famous; for they desired to abolish his memory. They, therefore, took counsel before the feast so that they might perhaps kill him after the feast day. <margin>John 10</margin> But he did not permit them to do it when they wished, but when he himself wished to suffer; namely, at the time of the Passover, so that when the typological <note>Original: "typicum pascha." The "type" refers to the Old Testament shadow or foreshadowing of a New Testament reality.</note> Passover occurred, then the true Passover would also take place. Moreover, we can learn that they were greedy for slaughter. For they who did not wish to kill him during the feast, when <margin>C</margin> they found a traitor, killed him anyway, even disregarding the crowd, provided that their will was done.

He, however, rebuked the disciples, because they had rebuked the woman unseasonably. For one ought not to demand <margin>The Highest Degree</margin> the highest degree <note>original: "summa"</note> from those who have recently been led to the faith, especially regarding the weaknesses of a woman, but rather it is necessary to accept their moderate faith. Therefore, when someone offers a gift to God, do not take it away from him, nor shatter his eagerness by leading him away to give to the poor, but let him fulfill his offering. But if someone should stand in need of your counsel as to whether he ought <meta>catchword: to</meta>

<column-break/>

<header>ON THE COMMENTARY OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW</header>
<page-num>93</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> to give to the poor or offer to God, advise him to give to the poor: but when he is already offering, it is unworthy to turn him away. For it is fitting that we should prefer the honor we owe to God simply above all things, even above mercy. For do not think (just because Christ, for the sake of mercy, took mercy upon himself as if it were done to him) that it is necessary to despise God and care only for almsgiving: because in that way even sacrilege would be permitted, and alms would be given out of sacrilegious thefts. But it is not so, because it is not the same thing to have mercy on the poor and to worship and honor Christ himself. Listen: "For the poor," he says, "you always have with you, but me you have not always." You see therefore <margin>B</margin> how it is one thing to bestow care upon Christ, and another to have mercy on the poor, even though Christ accepts what is bestowed on the poor just as if it were placed upon himself. 

"For in that she has poured this ointment upon my body, she did it for my burial. Amen I say to you, wherever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she has done shall be told for a memory of her." ] He teaches us that this woman did this according to a divine dispensation, foreshadowing his death and the burial of his body. <margin>The mystery of the anointing by Mary Magdalene.</margin> For Christ would not have endured being anointed with ointment unless some mystery <note>Theophylact uses "mystery" here in the sense of a hidden spiritual reality or sacrament.</note> were involved. Whence it would come to pass, as God foretold, that the thing the woman did would be preached everywhere to his glory. But see the mercy of God, how he rewards the woman with great gifts. For he makes her memorable everywhere, as long as his gospel shall endure. But how is his burial foreshadowed by the ointment? It was the custom for the Jews to bury the bodies of the dead with ointment, just as the Egyptians also did, so that they might remain incorrupt and not stink. He shows therefore, he says, by this, that the ointment she poured out signifies my body is soon to be buried. But he says all these things, soothing and discouraging Judas, by whom he was to be delivered to burial. Understand likewise <margin>C</margin> through anagoge <note>Anagoge is a method of spiritual interpretation that sees earthly events as symbols of heavenly or future realities.</note> that the leper is indeed the Gentile people: but the sinful woman is the assembly <note>original: "congregationem"; referring to the Church gathered from the nations.</note> of the Gentiles.

<summary>Theophylact interprets the anointing of Jesus at Bethany as a symbolic act foreshadowing His burial and an expression of faith in His divinity. He balances the duty of almsgiving with the priority of honoring God directly, using the woman's devotion as a model for spiritual growth.</summary>

<margin>D</margin> He rebukes the traitor <note>original: "proditorem reprehendit"</note>; for since he was being rebuked secretly, he was not correcting himself. Therefore, He makes him manifest, saying, *He who dipped with me*, so that even in this way he might be corrected. Truly, the shameless Judas was dipping into the dish. Then He says, *The Son of Man indeed goes as it is written*, that is, even if it was pre-ordained for Christ to suffer for our salvation, Judas should not be honored for this, but rather "woe to him." For he did not do this as a cooperator with the divine will, but to fulfill his own malice. For if you consider it diligently, Christ did not "will" to be crucified as a primary desire. He hints at this through the fact that He prays for the cup to pass. However, since He knew before all ages that it was not otherwise possible for man to be saved, because of the malice of the enemy, that which was not previously willed became voluntary. By saying, however, that it would be *good for that man if he had not been born*, He shows that the substance of sin is distinct from human nature <note>Theophylact is arguing that sin is a choice or a corruption, not an essential part of how God created human beings</note>. Observe also the word *Goes*; for it signifies a journey <note>original: "peregrinationem"</note> rather than death, or his own killing.

<margin>E</margin> **And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, "Take, eat; this is My body."** ] He added "as they were eating" to show the cruelty of Judas: because at the table and in the sharing of food, even a wild beast would have shown himself more gentle. At that time, neither when he was being rebuked did he understand, but even while tasting His body, he did not repent. Some, however, say that <margin>F</margin> after Judas had gone out, He delivered the sacrament to the other disciples. Therefore, we also ought to do the same, and bar the wicked from the sacraments. He also gives thanks as He is about to break the bread so that He might instruct us to offer the bread with thanksgiving, and to show that He Himself undergoes the breaking of His own body—that is, His killing—with gratitude, and does not take it poorly as if it were a thing displeasing to Him, so that we too may approach martyrdom with gratitude. Furthermore, by saying, *This is my body*, He shows that the very body of the Lord is the bread which is sanctified on the altar, and not <margin>The bread which is sanctified on the altar is the body and flesh of the Lord; it is bread, not a figure.</margin> merely a <gloss>it is a bare sign</gloss> figure. But why did He not say above, "Take, eat, all of you," but in <margin>B</margin> this place, *Drink from it, all of you*? <margin>Hebrews 5</margin> There are those who say this was said because of Judas. Therefore, in this place He said, *Drink, all*. According to the <term>anagoge</term> <note>A spiritual or "upward" interpretation of scripture beyond the literal meaning</note>, however, they say that while it is not for everyone to approach solid food, but rather the more perfect, yet "drinking" belongs to everyone. Therefore, in this place He said, *Drink, all*. For it belongs to everyone to receive the simpler dogmas.

**But I say to you, that I will not drink from henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom.** ] Having taken the <margin>C</margin> cup, He renounces physical drinking. But He promises something "new," that is, a certain new manner of partaking <margin>Luke 24, John 21, Acts 10</margin> in the kingdom, which is to say, in the resurrection. For when He had risen, He ate and drank in a certain new way; for He did not take physical food as if He were in need of food, but so that the true nature of His body might be believed <note>This was a common argument against those who believed Jesus rose as a ghost or phantom without a physical body</note>. Moreover, He rightly calls His resurrection "the kingdom"; for then He bound death, and proved Himself a king in actual reality. Or you may also understand it this way: the "new cup" is the revelation of the mysteries <note>original: "sacramentorum"</note> of God: that is, at the second coming, those things which are truly new will be revealed, such as we have not heard anywhere. **And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.** ] After He had dined, they sang a hymn so that we might learn to do the same. He came to the Mount of Olives, and not to some other place, so that He would not be thought to be fleeing. For He did not withdraw to an unknown spot, but to one well known to the Jews. However, He withdrew from the bloodthirsty city—leaving it so they might pursue Him—to prove that they were the ones who hunted Him even as He stepped away.

<margin>Zechariah 13. John 21.</margin> **Then Jesus said to them, "All of you will be made to stumble because of Me this night. For it is written: 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.' But after I have been raised, I will go before you into Galilee."** ] <margin>B</margin> He predicts the future as God. And so they would not be offended, as if they were being sharply accused by Him, He said it was written: *I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered* <note>original: "Percutiam pastorem, & dispergentur oues gregis"</note>. By this He was suggesting: "I will hold you together, but my departure will scatter you." Moreover, the Father is said to "strike" the Son because by His will—that is, by His permission—the Jews crucified the Lord. Because He was able to prevent them and did not, He is said to "strike" them on account of that permission. Then, relieving their sadness, He brings them good news: *I will rise and go before you*, that is, "I will meet you in Galilee." He indicates here that He would leave Jerusalem and grant Himself to the Gentiles, for Galilee was inhabited by Gentiles.

<margin>F</margin> **But Peter answered and said to Him, "Even if all are made to stumble because of You, I will never be made to stumble." Therefore, Christ permitted him to fall, to teach us that no one should trust in himself, but in God, and that the words of Christ are to be considered more worthy of faith than our own conscience. It was also full of pride to say, *Even if all are made to stumble*. This shows him to be arrogant and ignorant of his own weakness. Therefore, the Lord predicts to him the hour (that very night), the timing (before the rooster crows), and the number of denials (namely, that three times

<margin>C</margin> when they saw Him praying and suffering. Furthermore, He left even them behind, went into a most private place, and prayed. Moreover, that He is sorrowful and distressed happened by <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: "dispensationem" — This refers to the "divine arrangement" where Christ allowed His human nature to feel real human emotions to prove He was truly man</note>, so that it might be believed He was a true human. For it is the nature of humanity to fear death, because death entered "against nature" <note>In traditional theology, death was not part of God's original design but entered the world through sin; thus, it is naturally repulsive to the soul</note>, and for that reason, nature flees from it. Likewise, this was so the Devil would be ignorant of His divinity and attack Him as a mere man, through which the Devil himself would be finished off by death and thus crushed. Or alternatively: if the Lord had not feared death, He would have given the Jews an excuse that they had not sinned, since He would have leaped toward death without fear. <margin>We ought by no means to throw ourselves into temptations.</margin> From this we also learn not to throw ourselves into temptation, but to pray that we be delivered from it. And for that reason, He does not move a long distance away from the disciples, but stays nearby.

He also interprets Peter's overconfidence as a lesson in humility and the unreliability of human willpower compared to divine word.</summary>

<margin>D</margin> He remains with three disciples so that, by hearing Him, they might be mindful of His words and pray in a similar fashion when they themselves face temptations. He calls His passion a "cup" <note>original: "Calicem"</note>, either because of the "sleep" <note>This likely refers to the "sleep" of death.</note> it induces, or because it is the cause of joy and our salvation. He desires for the cup to be taken away, either to demonstrate that a human being naturally prays against death—as has been said before—or because He did not wish the Jews to commit such a grave sin, on account of which the Temple would be destroyed and the people would perish. Nevertheless, He desires the Father’s will to be done, so that we too may learn that even if our nature recoils, we must obey God rather than seek to fulfill our own will.

<margin>E</margin> **And He came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, "Could you not watch one hour with me? Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."** ] Since Peter and the other disciples had been bold <note>Theophylact refers here to their earlier boasts that they would never abandon Jesus.</note>, He rebukes their weakness for having spoken so rashly. He speaks to Peter specifically: "You could not watch for one hour, so how will you lay down your lives for Me?" But after He has stung them with this rebuke, He heals the wound by saying, "The spirit indeed is willing, but the weakness of the flesh struggles against it." That is to say: "I grant you pardon, for you did not fall asleep out of contempt, but because of infirmity." Therefore, since you are weak, do not be so bold from now on, but pray that you do not enter into any temptation. Others, however, understand "Lest you enter into temptation" as "Lest you be overcome by my temptation." 

<margin>F</margin> For He does not command us to be without temptation—for temptations crown us with glory—but rather that we should not be swallowed up by temptation, entering into its belly as if into the gut of some wild beast. This is what He commands us to pray for. For one who is conquered by temptation "enters" into it—that is, he is swallowed by it.

**Again, a second time, He went away and prayed, saying, "My Father, if this cup cannot pass from me unless I drink it, Your will be done." <column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> all things, hearing how the Lord also prayed often. Moreover, when He found them sleeping again, He did not rebuke them, so as not to cause them further sorrow. Instead, He left them and went away to pray a third time, confirming that He was truly human. For the number three is demonstrative and confirmatory of truth <note>In medieval theology, doing something three times often signified the absolute reality or completion of an act.</note>.

**Then He came to His disciples and said to them, "Sleep on now and take your rest; behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is being betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going. See, My betrayer is at hand."** ] Showing that He has no need of their assistance when He is betrayed, He says to them, "Sleep now and rest." Or perhaps He said this with irony, as if to say: "Behold, the betrayer has approached; if it pleases you and if time permits, go ahead and sleep." He then rouses them from the place where He was praying and approaches those who were about to seize Him; He meets them as if they were coming to offer Him something joyful. And those things for which He prayed, He prayed so that His dispensation <term>dispensatio: the "divine plan" or "economy" of God becoming human</term> might be more credible, and to show that He had wished not to suffer so that the Hebrews might be saved from the destruction that loomed over them because of their sin.

**And while He was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs,** <margin>John 17.</margin> **sent by the chief priests and elders of the people. Such were these "peaceful" men, supposedly possessing a spirit of gentleness. The Evangelist says "one of the twelve," marvelling that he was from the first and the elect, yet had handed himself over to the devil. Therefore, O man, you too should be afraid: even if you are among the most intimate companions, never allow yourself leisure for sloth, lest you fall away. <margin>Judas [betrays] Christ</margin> Judas gave a sign because it was night and they could not distinguish Him. Alternatively, those who came to seize Him were not the general crowd, but servants of the high priests who would have known Jesus well; yet Judas made Him known to them more clearly [by the kiss].

Therefore, since Jesus knew their judgment was unjust, He remained silent; for how would words have persuaded those whom miracles had not convinced? Furthermore, the high priest, wishing to declare Him a blasphemer, asked the question so that if He said "I am the Son of God," He might be condemned as a blasphemer. He repents, indeed, but not in a godly way <note>original: "non autem diabolicum," likely implying his repentance was despairing or influenced by the devil rather than leading to life</note>. Therefore, unable to bear the coming ignominy, he withdrew himself from life. The betrayer ought to have wept and sought a way to make amends. Some say, however, that because Judas was greedy, he hoped to make a great profit from the betrayal of Christ and thought that Christ would not be killed but would escape, just as He had done many times before. But when he saw Him condemned to die, he was struck by repentance for the deed because the matter had reached an outcome different from what he expected. ### CHAPTER 27. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> ...let it be asked whether he invaded, conspired, and attempted to reign over the Jews? But Jesus said to them, **"You say so,"** a most wise answer having been given. For he did not say, "I am not," but spoke in a middle way, saying, **"You say so."** For this can be understood in this way: "It is as you say." And also: "I myself do not say this, but you say it." But he gave no other answer. For he knew that the judgment would be unjust. Consequently, Pilate admired the Lord, both because he held death in contempt, and because, though he was so eloquent and had many things he might answer, he answered nothing, but rather held his accusers in contempt. Let us also learn in this place how we ought to conduct ourselves in an unjust trial: that we should not say anything, lest a greater tumult arise, or lest we make ourselves worthy of greater condemnation by those <margin>E</margin> who refuse to hear our defenses.

**Now at the festival, the governor was accustomed to release to the crowd one prisoner whom they wanted.** But he had at that time a notorious prisoner, who was called Barabbas. Therefore, when they were gathered together, Pilate said, **"Which of the two do you want me to release to you, Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?"** For he knew that they had delivered him because of envy. Pilate was striving to acquit him, although more slowly than was proper; for he ought to have set himself in the way for the sake of the truth. First, indeed, he asked the Lord, **"Do you not hear what things they testify against you?"** Moreover, he asked this so that if Christ excused himself, he would have an occasion for acquitting him. But when Christ did not defend himself, <margin>F</margin> knowing that he would not be released no matter how much he excused himself, Pilate found another way, and now fled to the custom, as if he were saying, "If you do not release Jesus as an innocent man, even if he is condemned, nevertheless grant this for the festival." How could Pilate have suspected that they would seek an innocent man to be crucified, and release a guilty one? Knowing therefore that he was not guilty, but delivered through envy, he for that reason questioned them. Whereby he shows himself to be more soft than was just; for it was necessary to face danger for the sake of the truth. Therefore, he is worthy of condemnation as <margin>Barabbas.</margin> a suppressor of the truth. Now, one can interpret **Barabbas** as "son of the father." For *Bar* <note>Aramaic: "son"</note> is son, and *Ab-

<column-break/>

### ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW, EXPOSITION 101
<page-num>101</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> bas* <note>Aramaic: "father"</note> is father. The Jews, therefore, asked for the son of their father the devil, but they crucified Jesus; and even unto this day they cling to the son of their father, the Antichrist, but they deny Christ.

**But while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying, "Have nothing to do with that just man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him."** But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds that they should ask for Barabbas, but destroy Jesus. But the governor, answering, said to them, **"Which of the two do you want me to release to you?"** But they said, **"Barabbas."** Pilate said to them, **"What then shall I do with Jesus, who is called Christ?"** They all say to him, **"Let him be crucified."** But the governor said, **"Why, what evil has he done?"** But they cried out all the more, <margin>B</margin> saying, **"Let him be crucified."** But Pilate, seeing that he was accomplishing nothing, but rather that a riot was beginning, took water and washed his hands before the people, saying, **"I am innocent of the blood of this just man; you shall see to it."** And the whole people, answering, said, **"His blood be upon us and upon our children."** Then he released Barabbas to them, but having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified. O miracle! He who is judged by Pilate strikes terror into Pilate's wife. He himself does not see the dream, but his wife does—either because he himself was unworthy, or because it would not have been believed and would have been considered as speaking out of favor; perhaps he would even have kept silent about such things since he was the judge. <margin>C</margin> Moreover, the dream was made as a work of providence, not so that Christ might be acquitted, but so that the wife might be saved. Why, therefore, did he not acquit him? Because it was not within his integrity <note>original: "non erat integrum," suggesting he lacked the moral wholeness or legal freedom</note> to release him who was accused of tyranny <note>original: "tyrannide," referring to the charge of treason/rebellion against Caesar</note>. Truly, he ought to have investigated the causes—whether he was enlisting soldiers, whether he was manufacturing weapons—but now, as if soft and mute, he yields, and for that reason he does not lack blame. For when they asked for that notorious evildoer, he gave him. But concerning Christ, he asks, "What then <margin>Acts 21 & 22</margin> shall I do with Jesus?" Since he was the judge, he could have rescued him by force, just as the commander of the soldiers did for Paul. But they were saying, **"Let him be crucified."** Not only wanting to kill him, but they were also imputing an evil cause <note>i.e., making the death as shameful as possible</note>.

### CHAPTER 27. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> For the cross was the punishment for the worst of men. Furthermore, he [Pilate] washes his hands to show himself pure, as he was not unaware of their hatred. For while calling Jesus "just," he handed him over to murderers. But they took upon themselves a vengeance worthy of this murder, by which they were burdened when the Romans destroyed them and their children. Even to this day, the Jews and their children experience his blood being required of them; for because of their unbelief, they suffer persecution from everyone. Moreover, Pilate scourged Jesus—that is, he beat him—either to gratify them, or to show that he himself also condemned him, so that they would not be crucifying an innocent man but one marked with ignominy. Thus, that saying was also fulfilled: <margin>E</margin> *They gave my back to the scourges.* <note>original: "Dorsum meum dederunt ad flagella." A reference to Isaiah 50:6.</note>

**Then the soldiers of the governor, taking Jesus into the Praetorium, gathered the whole cohort around him. And stripping him, they put a scarlet cloak around him, and twisting a crown of thorns, they placed it on his head, and a reed in his right hand. And kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And when they had spat on him, they took the reed and struck his head.**]
<margin>Psalm 38</margin> In this place the saying of David is fulfilled: *You have made me a reproach to the foolish.* <note>original: "Opprobrium insipienti dedisti me." Psalm 39:8 in modern numbering.</note> For the soldiers, being foolish, did things worthy of themselves. Instead of purple, they dressed him in a cloak as a king; they gave him a reed instead of a scepter, and a crown instead of a diadem. Moreover, they adored him in mockery; <margin>F</margin> for this is what it means to kneel—that is, to adore. See how they practiced every form of insult, inflicting injury: his face with spit, his head with the crown, his hand with the reed, the rest of his body with the cloak, and his ears with mocking words. Nevertheless, understand those things which are of a greater mystery. For the **scarlet cloak** <term>chlamys; a short military cloak</term> signifies our nature; since it was bloody and guilty of slaughter, he took it up, and by wearing it, he sanctified it. The **crown made of thorns** represents the sins arising from the cares of this life, which Christ consumes by his divinity; for his divinity is prefigured by the head. The **reed** is a symbol of our weak flesh, which the Lord took up, just as

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> David says: *The right hand of the Lord has exalted me.* <margin>Psalm 117</margin> <note>Psalm 118:16 in modern numbering.</note> Moreover, by receiving insults in his ears, he healed the hissing of the serpent that entered through the ears of Eve.

**And after they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak and put his own clothes on him, and led him away to crucify him. As they were going out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon; this man they compelled to carry his cross.**] Three [Evangelists] say that Simon carried the cross of Jesus, but John says the Lord himself carried it; it is likely that both occurred. Do not be disturbed that some Evangelists say vinegar with gall was brought to the Lord, and Mark says wine mixed with myrrh, <margin>Mark 15, John 19</margin> while John says vinegar, and gall with hyssop. There were many modes of death, yet Christ died on the cross so that he might sanctify the wood through which we were cursed, and bless all things: both the heavenly things, through the top part of the cross; the earthly things, through the base; and the ends of the earth—the east and the west—which are signaled by the transverse arms of the cross. He also stretched out his hands to receive us into his arms.

### CHAPTER 27. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> ...and gather the dispersed children of God. Moreover, the soldiers divided his garments, seeing him as a man of simple means who possessed nothing else. Regarding the title, which another Evangelist mentioned, Matthew stated the "cause" or the charge. For they wrote down the reason for which he was crucified: namely, as "King of the Jews" and a revolutionary <note>original: "rerum nouator" — literally "an innovator of things," which in a Roman legal context implied a political rebel or agitator.</note>. They, therefore, ascribed kingship to him as an accusation. Yet, that testimony was faithful, even though it was brought forward by his enemies. For the Lord is indeed the King, who came for this purpose: to save the Jews. But because the carnal Jews did not want him to reign over them, let him be the King of the spiritual Jews—that is, of those who confess him. For a "Jew" <margin>Jew.</margin> is so called from "confessing" or "praising" <note>A reference to the Hebrew etymology of Judah (Yehudah), which means "praise" or "confession."</note>.

<margin>E</margin> **Then two thieves were crucified with him, one on the right and the other on the left. However, they were symbols of two peoples: <margin>The thieves with the Lord foreshadowed the Jews and the Gentiles.</margin> the Jewish and the Gentile. Both were transgressors, <margin>F</margin> crucified and villainous, and both reproached Christ at first, just as both thieves originally taunted him. But one of them—the latter—later came to his senses and confessed the King; therefore he said, *Remember me in your kingdom.* Likewise, the Gentile people also used to blaspheme. But the devil was prompting those who said, "If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross," so that he might be incited to descend, and thus the salvation of all—which is achieved through the cross—might perish. But Christ, because he is the Son of God, did not obey the enemy. This was so that you might learn that one must not yield to the devil’s schemes, but must continue in good works, even if men think ill of us.

From this, others say: "Wait, let us see if Elijah comes," that is, "Leave him alone, do not let him die yet, so that we may know if he is helped by Elijah."

Jesus cries out with a loud voice so that we may know that what he said is true: "I have the power to lay down my life." For he lays down his soul by his own power. And what was that voice? He also hints that he would take it up again: for a deposit or a loan <note>original: "depositum & commodatum" — legal terms for items entrusted to another to be returned later.</note> is taken back again. Thanks be to the Lord, because by his dying and commending his spirit into the hands of the Father, from that time forward the souls of the saints are also placed in the hand of God, and not, as before, in the depths of hell; and thus the death of Christ became our sanctification. This is torn, God demonstrating that the temple—previously inaccessible and never seen, whose inner sanctum the veil secluded—is now dissolved and profaned, so that it might be visible to all. The centurion, a Gentile man, believes because of the signs, along with those who were with him; but the Jews, who had heard the law and the prophets, remain unbelieving. Such a great evil is malice.

### CHAPTER 27. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA | EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

And here the Centurion bears witness to Christ. Indeed, the women watching what was happening, since they are most compassionate and a condemned gender <note>original: "genus damnatum" — Theophylact refers to the traditional view of womanhood inheriting the legacy of Eve, though he immediately praises their courage compared to the men.</note>, are the first to enjoy the contemplation of these good things. While the disciples flee, the women remain strong. When he speaks of Mary the mother of James and Joseph, he means the Mother of God <term>Deiparam: literally "God-bearer" or Mother of God</term>. For James and Joseph were the sons of Joseph from his former wife. Truly, because the Mother of God was called the wife of Joseph, she was rightly called the mother of his sons—that is, their stepmother. Now the mother of the sons of Zebedee was called Salome, whom they say was also a daughter of Joseph.

<margin>Theophylact shows that Joseph had a wife with children.</margin> When evening had come, a rich man from Arimathea came, named Joseph, who himself had been a disciple of Jesus. He went to Pilate and requested the body of Jesus. Then Pilate ordered the body to be given over. And when Joseph had received the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen shroud and placed it in his own new tomb which he had hewn in the rock; and after rolling a great stone to the door of the tomb, he departed. Now Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, sitting opposite the sepulcher. Joseph used to hide in the past, but now he dares a great thing, risking his own life for the body of the teacher and taking upon himself such great enmity from the Jews. Furthermore, the body of Jesus was given to him as a great gift; for since he had been killed as a rebel, it was expected that he would be cast away unburied. Truly, since Joseph was rich, it is likely that he gave gold to Pilate. Accordingly, treating the body he had received with honor, he laid it in a new tomb in which no one had ever been placed. This was done by divine providence so that when the Lord rose, no one could say that someone else buried there before him had died and risen; for this reason, it was a new monument. <margin>F</margin> Now Mary Magdalene and the other Mary—that is, the Mother of God, whom he had previously called the mother of Joseph and James—both sat by the burial site, so that when the fury of the Jews ceased, they might go and wash and anoint the body. Isaiah spoke of these women: "Women coming from the spectacle, come; for it is not a people having understanding." <note>A reference to Isaiah 27:11.</note>

<column-break/>

A It clearly speaks of the Jewish people who had crucified the Lord, saying they lack understanding. He calls the women, therefore, to leave behind the people lacking understanding and go to the apostles to preach the Gospel of the resurrection to them.

On the next day, which follows the Day of Preparation <term>Parasceue: The Day of Preparation before the Sabbath</term>, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered before Pilate, saying: "Lord, we remember that this impostor said while still alive, 'After three days I will rise.' Therefore, order the tomb to be secured until the third day, lest his disciples come and steal him away and say to the people, 'He has risen from the dead,' and the last error will be <margin>B</margin> worse than the first." Pilate said to them: "You have a guard; go, secure it as you know how." So they went and secured the tomb, sealing the stone and posting guards. <margin>Deut. 7</margin> He does not call the Sabbath "the Sabbath," because it was not a Sabbath as far as the madness of the Jews was concerned. <margin>Mark 8, Luke 11, Jonah 2, John 2</margin> For although the law forbids anyone from moving from their place on the Sabbath day, the law-breaking Jews went to the foreigner Pilate, and not to the congregation where the law permitted. And they are indeed driven by their own malice to go to the tomb and secure the tomb; but by God's providence this happened so that the resurrection might be proven by the testimony of enemies while the tomb was being secured and guarded. It is worth asking: <margin>C</margin> how did the Jews know Christ would rise on the third day? For the Lord had not yet spoken of this to them openly and clearly. It can be said they knew from the sign of Jonah, especially since Christ said: "As Jonah was three days in the belly of the whale, so will I be in the heart of the earth." Or from what he said: "Destroy this temple," which they first misunderstood, thinking he meant the Jewish temple, and therefore they brought this testimony against him. But now, when they realized he had called his own body a "tomb," they were afraid, and they called him an impostor; even after his death, they did not cease from their malice. Furthermore, "guard" <note>original: "custodia"</note> is a Roman name; for so he names the soldiers assigned to keep watch.

**B**ut on the evening of the Sabbaths, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the sepulcher. And behold, there was a great earthquake. For an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and approaching, rolled back the stone from the door, and sat upon it. Now his appearance was like lightning, and his clothing white as snow. And for fear of him the guards were struck with terror and became like dead men. But the angel, answering, said to the women: "Do not be afraid; for I know that you seek JESUS who was crucified."

<margin>E</margin>
"He is not here, for he has risen just as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord was laid. And going quickly, tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead; and behold, he precedes you into Galilee; there you shall see him. Behold, I have told you." And departing quickly from the monument with fear and great joy, they ran to report it to his disciples.

<margin>The same. The evening of the Sabbaths. The deep twilight of the dawn. Very early.</margin>
The "evening of the Sabbaths" is the same as the "deep twilight of the dawn" in Luke, and "very early as the sun was rising" in Mark. For we ought to understand "the sun" in that place as the morning rays of the sun. Indeed, from the eighth hour of the night, the beginning of the coming day occurs, and the morning appears to draw near. It was, therefore, the evening of the Sabbath, but the beginning of the Lord’s

<margin>F</margin>
day, which he calls "the first of the Sabbaths" <note>original: "vnam sabbatorum" — a literal translation of the Greek phrase for the first day of the week</note>. For they called the days of the week "Sabbaths." And "one," that is, "the first," so that the Lord's day is the first of the Sabbaths—that is, the first of the days of the week. For immediately after the first, the second is named, then the third, and the others in succession. The Lord, therefore, rose while the stone was still placed upon the sepulcher. But after the Lord had risen, the angel also came, so that by rolling back the stone, the women might have access to the sepulcher. Moreover, an earthquake occurred so that the guards might be awakened and might learn of the new thing that was happening. Thus the Lord rose as one "three days dead" <term>triduanus: a term referring to the three-day period Christ spent in the tomb</term>.

<margin>How Christ was "three days dead."</margin>
But how were there three days? He was crucified at the sixth hour of the Preparation <term>parafceue: the Day of Preparation, or Friday</term>; from that hour until the ninth there was darkness; through

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
these, you may understand a "night" for me. Then from the ninth hour, light returned, which is a "day." Behold, one day and night. Again, the night of the Preparation and the day of the Sabbath; behold, a second day and night. Also the night of the Sabbath and the dawn of the Lord's day, according to Matthew, because it was dawning toward the first day of the week—for from the dawn the whole day is counted. Behold, a third day and night. One can also count the three days in another way: He gave up His spirit on the Preparation; behold, one day. He was in the sepulcher on the Sabbath; behold, the second day. He rose on the night of the Lord's day, and it is counted openly as the Lord's day into another day, and thus there are three days. For we also say of the deceased, if one dies around the tenth hour of the night and another around the first hour of that day, that both died on the same day. I can also tell you another reason

<margin>B</margin>
how three days and three nights are counted. Pay attention, then: On Thursday evening the Lord held the supper, and giving it to the disciples, He said: "Take and eat, for this is my body." And thus, because He had the power to lay down His life, it is manifest that He sacrificed Himself from the moment He handed over His body to His disciples. That night He sacrificed, and on the day of the Preparation until the sixth hour; behold, one day and night. Again, from the sixth hour there was darkness until the ninth, and from the ninth hour light until the evening; behold, a second day and night. Again, the night of the Preparation and the day of the Sabbath; behold, a third day and night. Moreover, on the Sabbath evening He rose; behold, three full days and nights. Now, as for Matthew saying that the angels sat upon the stone, while Mark says that with the stone rolled away he sat on the right side inside the sepulcher,

<margin>C</margin>
do they disagree with each other? Not at all. But it is likely that the first angel appeared sitting upon the stone, and then as the women entered, he went before them and appeared again inside the sepulcher on the right. Moreover, he said to the women, "Do not be terrified"; that is to say, the guards indeed are worthy to be terrified, but you, disciples of the Lord, should not be afraid. And after he freed them from fear, he announced the Good News of the resurrection to them. For it was necessary first to cast out fear and then to evangelize. He is not ashamed, moreover, to name the Lord as "the crucified." For he glories in the cross as a trophy <note>Theophylact uses the imagery of a military trophy—a monument to victory—to describe the cross</note> through which all good things have been reconciled to us.

### CHAPTER 28. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> They worshiped him in Galilee; first they had doubted in Jerusalem, as Luke says. Jesus spoke to them, saying: "All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth." This indeed carries the following meaning: as God and Creator <note>original: "opifex" – a term for God as the master craftsman of the universe.</note>, I certainly held power over all things. <margin>Psalm 118.</margin> As David said to him: "For all things serve you." However, I did not have that voluntary subjection which I am now about to have. <margin>Two kinds of obedience.</margin> For obedience and subjection are of two kinds: Involuntary—according to which we are all servants of God, even the demons themselves—and voluntary, in the way that Paul was a servant of Christ. While previously all things displayed an involuntary obedience, and the Savior of all held a power that was, as it were, only half-realized, after the cross, as the knowledge of God was to become known to everyone, he was also to have all those who were subjected to him as voluntarily obedient. Rightly, therefore, does Christ say: "Now I have received all power." For previously my power was partial, because they served me like a creator against their will; but now, since men serve me willingly and knowingly, all and complete power has been given to me. But by whom was it given to him? He had it entirely from himself, through his own humility. For unless he had been humbled and had engaged the adversary through the cross, he would not have saved us. And understand it thus: "All power has been given to me." <margin>F</margin> By my own struggles and labors I have saved men, and they have become my heritage and a special people. For the Lord has power over the earth because the whole earth has recognized him; and in heaven, because the reward and citizenship of those who believe is in heaven. Or perhaps in another way: because human nature, previously condemned, now sits in heaven united personally to the Word of God <note>The "Word" or "Logos" refers to the second person of the Trinity.</note> and is worshiped by the angels, he rightly says, "Power has been given to me in heaven." For indeed human nature previously served, but now in Christ it commands all things. In short, then, understand it thus: "All power has been given to me" because those who previously served me in the manner of involuntary obedience, now recognize me as God, whether they want to or not.

<column-break/>

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

<margin>A</margin> Regarding what is said about human nature, understand it this way: "I, who exist as a nature previously condemned but now God according to the union with the Son of God without confusion of natures <note>A reference to the orthodox doctrine that Christ is one person in two distinct natures—human and divine—without them being mixed together.</note>, have received power over all things, so that I may be worshiped by the angels in heaven and glorified by all the ends of the earth." Furthermore, he no longer sends the Apostles to the Jews alone; but because he has received all power and has sanctified all human nature in himself, he rightly sends them to all nations, commanding them to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Let Arius and Sabellius be confounded. <margin>Arius and Sabellius.</margin> Arius <note>Arius (c. 256–336) taught that the Son was a created being, not equal to the Father.</note> indeed is refuted because Christ did not command them to be baptized in the *names* (plural), but in the *name* (singular). Now, the "name" of the three is one Godhead. Therefore, there is one God in three. Sabellius <note>Sabellius (fl. c. 215) taught "Modalism," the idea that Father, Son, and Spirit are just different roles or "masks" of a single person.</note> is refuted because Christ mentions three persons, not just one; for Sabellius trifles with the idea that the same one has three names, being called now Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit. On the contrary, three persons have one name: namely, "God." Next, because it is not enough just to be baptized, but one must also perform good works after <margin>It is not enough to be baptized; one must work well afterward.</margin> baptism, he says: "Teaching them to observe," not just one or two, but "all my commandments." Let us tremble and fear, brothers, because if we fail in even one, we will not be perfect servants of Christ. For all things are required to be kept. See also the Lord’s discourse, how it embraces both heads of Christianity: the contemplative and the practical. <margin>Two heads of Christianity.</margin> By saying that it is necessary to be baptized in the name of the Trinity, he handed down the contemplative part to us; but by saying that it is necessary to teach and keep the commandments, he introduced the practical part. He also confirms and encourages them—since he is sending them to the nations and into death and dangers—saying, "For behold, I am with you even unto the end of the age." See here also how he was mindful of the "end," so that he might further rouse them to despise hardships. Do not be burdened by your troubles, for all worldly things shall have an end, whether they be <margin>All things, whether prosperous or bitter, will have an end.</margin> harsh or prosperous; and therefore, do not succumb to adversity, for it passes away; nor be deceived by prosperity, for it too will have an end. Nor did he promise this only to the apostles...

He uses the baptismal formula to refute the heresies of Arianism and Sabellianism while emphasizing that faith must be paired with the keeping of all commandments.</summary>

# CHAPTER 28. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>
The words "Until" and "Even to" in the Holy Scriptures do not exclude what follows.
</margin>

<margin>D</margin>

...but simply to all his disciples. For the apostles were not going to live until the end of the world. Therefore, he promised this to us, and to those who will come after us: not that he will be absent after the end of the world—far be it! For then he will be with us even more, and more clearly, and more purely. For whenever "Until" or "Even to" <note>original: "Donec vel Vsque"</note> is found in scripture, it does not take away what comes after. <note>Theophylact is explaining a common linguistic rule in biblical interpretation: saying something lasts "until" a certain point does not mean it stops afterward. For example, if Christ is with us *until* the end of the world, he is certainly with us in eternity as well.</note> Therefore, let us give thanks to the Lord, who is with us now and provides every good thing, and will be with us again more perfectly after the end. And so, let us also conclude our explanation in this place. For all thanksgiving, glory, and honor befits Him forever and ever. 
Amen.

# CHAPTER 1. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> Reason <note>The original Latin "Ratiocõ" likely refers to the "Logos" or Reason of John’s Gospel.</note> says, "In the beginning was the word, and the word was with God." However, the Gospel of Matthew bears the likeness of a man, because that Evangelist began from the incarnation and birth of the flesh. Furthermore, <margin>Mark,</margin> we liken Mark to an eagle, for he began with the prophets and John. And prophetic grace, because it sees things situated far off with a sharp eye, is like an eagle. They say the eagle has such extremely sharp eyes that it alone among other birds can gaze at the sun without its vision blurring. Finally, <margin>Luke.</margin> the Gospel of Luke would be like a calf, since he started from the priesthood of Zechariah, who offered incense and sacrificed for the sins of the people. A calf was the sacrifice used then. Thus, Mark begins his Gospel from the life and revelation of the forerunner <note>The "forerunner" is a traditional title for John the Baptist, who "ran before" Christ to announce his coming.</note>. Hear, then, what he says:

->CHAPTER I.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting a bearded man (Saint John the Baptist or a prophet) in a robe, holding a staff in his left hand and gesturing with his right hand, set against a landscape with a tree.</image-desc>

> <margin>Malachi 3.</margin> <margin>Isaiah 40.</margin> <margin>Matthew 3, 11.</margin> <margin>Luke 3, 7.</margin> The beginning of the Gospel of JESUS CHRIST the Son of God; as it is written in the prophets: Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who shall prepare your way before you. The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

<margin>E</margin> He says that John, the last of the prophets, is the beginning of the Gospel of the Son of God. For the end of the Old Testament is the beginning of the New. This testimony concerning the forerunner is taken from two prophets. That of Malachi is: "Behold, I send my messenger <note>original: "angelum meum"</note> before your face, who shall prepare the way before you." That of Isaiah is: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness." This is the word of God the Father to the Son, saying that the messenger is the forerunner, because he lived an angelic life free from material concerns, and he announced and pointed out the coming Christ.

<margin>F</margin> He prepared the way of the Lord—that is, the souls of the Jews—so that through baptism they might receive Christ. Furthermore, "before your face" means that your messenger will be near to you. This shows the familiarity of the forerunner toward Christ. For those who walk closest to kings are those who are most intimate with them. Moreover, "the voice of one crying in the wilderness" refers perhaps to the wilderness of the Jordan, or perhaps to the synagogue of the Jews, which

<margin>A</margin> was deserted of all good. <margin>The Way.</margin> The "Way" is the New Testament; <margin>The Paths.</margin> the "Paths" are the Old Testament, as if they were worn down. Therefore, they had to be prepared for the Way—that is, for the New Testament. As for the paths of the Old, they were once straight, but they were later found to be perverted and limping from their own tracks.

John was in the wilderness baptizing and preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. and all the region of Judea and those of Jerusalem went out to him, and they were all baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <margin>B</margin> <margin>What kind of baptism John’s was</margin> John’s baptism did not have the power to remit sins; rather, it brought only repentance to men. In what way, then, does Mark say in this place, "unto the remission of sins"? We say that he preached the baptism of repentance—that is, he preached where the baptism of repentance would lead: namely, toward the remission of sins. <margin>A beautiful comparison.</margin> It is like when we say: "A certain guard of the king has come, preaching the preparation of food so that it may go well for those who prepare the royal meals." We do not mean by this that the guard himself will reward those who prepare the royal food, but that he preached the preparation of the food so that those who prepared it and received the king might obtain benefits. Thus, in this place, the forerunner preached repentance so that those who performed repentance might receive CHRIST and consequently obtain the remission of sins.

<margin>C</margin> John was clothed with camel's hair, and a leather belt was around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. We have spoken of these things in the commentary on Matthew, and now we will also mention what was omitted there: his clothing was a symbol of mourning, the prophet showing that a penitent person ought to mourn. <margin>Sackcloth.</margin> For sackcloth pertains to mourning. <margin>The leather belt.</margin> The leather belt <note>original: "Pellicea zona"</note> signifies the mortification <note>In a theological sense, "mortification" means the "killing" or subduing of worldly desires and the flesh.</note> of the Jewish people. That his robe indicated mourning is confirmed by the Lord when he says: "We have wailed for you, and you have not mourned," referring to the life of the forerunner through "wailing." <margin>Matthew 2.</margin> For he says: "John came neither eating nor drinking, and you said: he has a demon." But entirely, here too, the food of John signifies self-control...

# CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>The nature of locusts.</margin> ...reveals: but perhaps it was also a sign of the spiritual nourishment of the people of that time. They did not eat certain "clean" birds of heaven <note>A reference to the dietary laws in Leviticus; Theophylact is suggesting the people's spiritual understanding was limited</note>: they understood something sublime, yet they were fed by a word that seemed to leap upward toward the heights, only to fall back down immediately. For it is the nature of locusts to hop up and then fall back down again. In a certain way, therefore, the people also ate honey which was made by "bees"—that is, the prophets—but it was not produced by agriculture, nor was it domestic. By this he means it was not something easily understood, sought after, or fully grasped through human effort. They held the scriptures like a kind of honey, but they did not cultivate the fields themselves <note>original: "non ipsi colebant agros"; meaning they did not do the spiritual work to produce the "crops" of understanding</note>, nor did they search deeply into them.

**And he preached, saying, "One mightier than I comes after me, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. I indeed baptized you in water; but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit."** ] <margin>E</margin> I am not worthy to be even the least of his servants, so as to untie the strap—that is, the binding—made from the leather of his sandal. This is also understood in another way: All who came and were baptized by John were released through repentance from the bond of their sins while they believed in CHRIST. John, therefore, untied the "sandals" and bonds of sins for everyone else. But he could not untie the strap of Jesus, because he found no strap—that is, no sin—within him.

**And it happened in those days, JESUS came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized by John in the Jordan. And immediately as he came up out of the water, he saw the heavens split open, and the Spirit like a dove descending upon him. And a voice came from the heavens: "You are my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased."** ] <margin>F</margin> Jesus did not come to baptism so that his own sins might be forgiven, for he committed no sin. Nor did he come so that he might become a partaker of the Spirit; for John’s baptism (as I have said) did not cleanse sins—so how could it have given the Spirit? <margin>Why Christ came to baptism.</margin> Nor did he come to be baptized for the sake of repentance, for he was far more excellent than the Baptist. Why then did he come? Primarily so that he might be revealed by John to the people. For because the people were flocking together,

<margin>A</margin> it appears that he came for this reason: to receive testimony before many people as to who he was. Or, to "fulfill all righteousness," which means to fulfill all the commands of the law. Since this also appears to be a command—to believe in a prophet who is baptizing and sent by God—Jesus fulfills that as well. But the Spirit descends, not because CHRIST has any need of it (for how would that be possible, since the Spirit remains in him substantially?), but so that you may learn that when you are baptized, the Holy Spirit comes upon you as well. <margin>The Spirit is given to those baptized.</margin> Meanwhile, the descent of the Holy Spirit also performs this task: lest, when the Father spoke from above, "This is my son," those who heard might think he spoke of John. The Spirit descended upon Jesus to show that the words were spoken about him. Furthermore, the heavens are split open so that we may learn that when we are baptized, they are opened for us too.

<margin>B</margin> **And immediately the Spirit drove him into the wilderness, and he was there in the wilderness forty days, and was tempted by Satan, and was with the wild beasts, and angels ministered to him.** ] The Lord, teaching us not to take it poorly if we fall into temptations after baptism, ascended the mountain to be tempted for the sake of his grace. Indeed, he did not just "ascend," but was "led up" by the Holy Spirit: demonstrating to us that we should not rashly throw ourselves into temptations, but rather endure them if we are attacked. <margin>Do not throw yourself into temptations.</margin> Moreover, he ascended the mountain so that the devil might become more bold due to the solitude of the place, and thus approach him. For the devil is accustomed to lie in wait immediately when he sees us alone. <margin>C</margin> Indeed, the place was so inaccessible that many wild beasts were there. But the angels ministered to him when, having been tempted, he had conquered; you will learn of this more extensively in the Gospel of Matthew. <margin>Matthew 4.</margin>

**After John was arrested, JESUS came into Galilee, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God, and saying, "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand. Repent, and believe the Gospel."** ] He withdraws into Galilee after he heard that John was arrested and thrown into prison, to show us also that we should withdraw from temptations and not rashly rush into them; but where we have fallen into them, we should bear them. The Lord appears preaching the same things as John, namely, "Repent, and the kingdom of God has approached." But it is not quite the same, for John...

<margin>Why Mark added, "when the sun had set"</margin>
Not without cause did he add, *when the sun had set*, but because they thought it was not lawful for anyone to heal on the Sabbath day, and for that reason they waited until sunset. And then they brought those to be cured. Moreover, He healed many—that is, all—or perhaps He did not heal all because some were unbelieving, and those who were not healed remained so because of their unbelief; but that He healed many of those presented was a sign that they had believed. Furthermore, He did not permit the demons to speak, as I have said, teaching us not to believe them even if they speak the truth. For since they find some who believe them completely even while they are lying, what might happen if they were to mix falsehoods with truths? ### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>Healing the soul is more difficult than healing the body</margin>
...He knew. Therefore, He provides proof and confirmation by healing the body, <margin>D</margin> showing that He is also able to heal the soul. Thus, He confirms what was hidden through what was visible, and the more difficult thing through the easier, even if it did not seem so to those men. For the Pharisees thought it was more difficult for the body to be healed, which they could see, but easier for the soul because that healing was hidden. And perhaps they were thinking such things: "Behold, this impostor, in order to escape the need to heal the body, claims in plain sight to heal the soul which is hidden, saying, 'Your sins are forgiven you.' Surely, if he could heal the body, he would not take refuge in what we cannot know." Therefore, the Savior, showing that He is able to do both, asks: "Which is easier? <margin>E</margin> (He says) to heal the body or the soul? Truly, it is easier to heal the body, but to you it seems the opposite. Therefore, by healing the body—which is indeed easy—I will make the more difficult thing credible to you, namely the healing of the soul, which is truly difficult; but because it happens in secret and cannot be detected, it seems easy." Then He says to the paralytic, "Rise and take up your mat," for a greater confirmation of the miracle—to show that you have not been healed merely in appearance, and to declare that "I have not only granted health but also infused strength." This is also how He acts in diseases of the soul. He not only frees us from infirmities but also infuses virtue so that we may perform the commandments. I also, therefore, since I am paralyzed, can be healed. 

<margin>The Lord, in healing the soul, also infuses virtue</margin>
For even now Christ is in Capernaum, the "house of consolation" <note>Theophylact interprets the Hebrew name Capernaum as 'Village of Comfort'</note>, which is the Church. For the Church is called the house of the Paraclete <note>original: "paraclæti" — referring to the Holy Spirit as the Comforter</note>. <margin>The Church is the house of the Paraclete</margin> <margin>F</margin> However, I am paralyzed because the powers of my soul are not working and are immobile toward what is good. But if I am carried by the four Evangelists <note>The four Gospel writers: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John</note> and brought to the Lord, then I shall hear, "Son." For a person becomes a son of God through the performance of the commandments, and my sins are forgiven me. But how shall I be brought to Jesus? If I dig through the roof. What is the roof? The mind, which is the highest part of us. This roof has much earth and mud—that is, earthly business. But when this is set aside and the power of the mind within us is dug through and unburdened, then I must be let down—that is, humbled. Then I shall be healed, and I shall take up my mat—that is, the body—
