### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW. 116
<note>original: "IN EVANGE. MATTH. ENAR." Although the header says Matthew, the chapter number and sequence align with the Gospel of Mark, chapter 2.</note>

P iiij

...he would follow Him and joyfully call many others to a banquet. <margin>D</margin> The Pharisees, however, reproach Him for this, striving to make themselves appear pure by comparison. But the Lord said: "I did not come to call the righteous," that is, you who justify yourselves (for He says this <term>ironically</term><note>Theophylact suggests Jesus is being sarcastic: calling them "righteous" because they think they are, not because they actually are.</note>), "but sinners," who are called not so that they might remain sinners, but to repentance, which is to say, a conversion. He adds this so that you do not think sinners are called without the requirement of mending their ways.

"And the disciples of John and of the Pharisees were fasting; and they come and say to Him, 'Why do the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?' And Jesus said to them, 'Can the sons of the bridal chamber fast while the bridegroom <margin>E</margin> is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. But the days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.'" The disciples of John, being still imperfect, were devoted to Jewish customs. For this reason, some approached Christ to report that His disciples were acting differently, and they criticized why His disciples did not fast as they did. But here He now says, "I am the bridegroom," and it is necessary for them to be of good cheer and not to fast; "but when I have been taken away from this life, then temptations will rush in, <margin>Why Christ is the bridegroom. John 3. Revelation 21.</margin> and they will fast and be afflicted." Accordingly, He calls Himself the bridegroom not only because He betrothes virginal souls to Himself, but also because the time of His first coming is not a time of mourning <margin>F</margin> or of severity for those who believe in Him. It is not a time of heavy labors, but a time of refreshing us through baptism, which is easy and apart from the works of the Law. For what labor is it to be baptized? Yet through these easy things, we attain salvation. <margin>Sons of the chamber.</margin> The "sons of the bridal chamber" are the Apostles, seeing that they themselves have attained the Lord's joy and are participants in every heavenly good and all delight. Understand also here that every person, when they perform virtue, is a "son of the bridal chamber." As long as they have Christ the bridegroom with them, they do not fast—that is, they do not perform works of penance—for they have not fallen. But when Christ has been taken away from them and they slip into sin, then they must fast and perform penance

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> so that they may be healed from sin.

"And no one sews a piece of raw cloth onto an old garment; otherwise the new patch pulls away from the old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the new wine bursts the old wineskins, and the wine is spilled, and the wineskins are ruined; but new wine must be put into new wineskins."] What He is saying is this: just as raw cloth—that is, new cloth—if it is sewn onto an old garment, tears it by its own strength, and new wine by its fermentation bursts old wineskins; so also my disciples have not yet been made strong, and therefore if I burden them <margin>B</margin> I will cause them to stumble. For He compares the Old Law to old garments because of the "thick" or heavy understanding of the Jews. It is not appropriate, therefore, to weigh them down with the heavy precept of fasting. Or understand it this way: the disciples of Christ, since they are "new," cannot serve ancient customs.

"And it happened that He was passing through the grainfields on the Sabbath, and His disciples began to pluck the ears of grain as they went. And the Pharisees said to Him, 'Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?' And He said to them, 'Have you never read what David did when he had need and was hungry, he and those who were with him? How he entered the house of God under <margin>1 Samuel 21.</margin> Abiathar the high priest and ate the <term>showbread</term><note>original: "panes propositionis." Twelve loaves of bread set out in the Temple as an offering, usually reserved for priests.</note> <margin>C</margin> which it is not lawful to eat except for the priests, and gave also to those who were with him?' And He said to them, 'The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.'"] The disciples of the Lord pluck the ears of grain, as they were no longer accustomed to living strictly according to the Law. The Pharisees were indignant, but were silenced by Christ, who brought forward the example of David, who had broken the law because of necessity under Abiathar the high priest. For the prophet David, fleeing from the face of Saul, came to that high priest and deceived him, acting as if he had been sent by the king for a military matter, and then he ate the showbread and offered to the Lord the sword of Goliath which he had taken. Now, there were twelve loaves which were set out daily...

It must be said, therefore, that perhaps he had two names, and that Abiathar and Abimelech are the same person. Learn also according to the <term>anagoge</term><note>A method of spiritual or mystical interpretation that finds a higher meaning in the text.</note>, that the disciples of Christ are in the Sabbath, which is to say, in the rest of their souls. For we interpret "Sabbath" as "rest." Therefore, when they have rest from all passions and are not <margin>E</margin> infested by demons, then they make their journey—that is, they become guides to virtue for others, plucking away all things that sprout from the earth and from humble imagination. For unless someone first rests from their passions and withdraws themselves into solitude, they will by no means be a leader toward the good for others.

<margin>F</margin>
thorns, but to sow the seed. But what kind of seed? Was it that of Moses? Was it that of the prophets? No, but his own—that is, he came to preach his own Gospel. From that source, then, he sowed. Now, some seed fell into a soul that was trampled down by many, and the birds of the air—I mean the demons who inhabit the air—ate the seed. These are the people who seek to please everyone.

<margin>The trampled soul</margin>
The soul is "trampled" when someone seeks to please this person and that person, and thus is walked over by many. Notice, however, that he did not say he *threw* the seed into the road, but that it *fell* there. For he who sows throws it as if into good ground;

<meta>catchword: throws (proij-)</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
but if that ground is found to be bad, it corrupts the word. Some have beautifully understood the seed that fell by the wayside as falling into an unfaithful heart. For Christ is the Way. Others "by the wayside" are the unfaithful who are outside the way, which is Christ. Other seed falls into a stony soul—I mean those who easily receive it and then cast it away. Those who are "stony" are made like the Rock <note>The Latin word for "stony" (petrosa) shares a root with Peter/Rock (Petrus/Petra).</note>—which is Christ—for a short time in that they received the word, but they become unlike him because they received it for only a brief time and then threw it away. And other seed fell into a soul subject to many cares, for cares are "thorns." Finally, the fourth part fell onto good ground.

<margin>B</margin>
Observe, therefore, how rare good things are and how few are those who are saved; for only a fourth of the seed is found to be preserved. Furthermore, when the disciples asked him privately, he said: "To you it is given to know the mysteries." Is it then through segregation or some natural fate that it is given to some and not to others? Far from it! Rather, it is given to those who seek. For he says, "Seek and it shall be given to you." <note>Matthew 7:7</note> But God blinded the others so that it might not result in a greater condemnation for them if they were to understand and yet not act. In another way, do you wish to know that God makes all people see? Listen: "That seeing"—which is of God—"they may not see"—that is from their own malice. For God formed them seeing (that is, understanding what is good), but they themselves do not see of their own will, lest they should be converted and reformed, as if

<margin>Matthew 7. Luke 8, 11. Isaiah 6.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
they begrudged their own salvation. This very thing can also be understood in this way: "I speak to others in parables so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand, and that they may never be converted or reformed because of this."

**And he said to them, "Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The sower sows the word. And these are the ones by the wayside where the word is sown; when they hear, Satan comes immediately and takes away the word that was sown in their hearts. These likewise are the ones sown on stony ground; who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with gladness; and they have no root in themselves, but endure only for a time. Afterward, when tribulation arises..."**

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

...nor [do they reach] perfection, but because of the word they are immediately offended. <margin>D</margin> And there are others who receive the seed among thorns; these are those who hear the word, but the worries of this world and the deceitfulness of riches, and the desires for other things entering in, choke the word, and it is rendered unfruitful. And there are others who have received the seed upon good ground; those who hear the word and welcome it and bring forth fruit, so that one grain brings forth thirty, another sixty, and another a hundred.] <margin>E</margin> In this passage, there are three ranks of those in whom the word is lost. For those who are by the wayside are insufficiently attentive; those compared to the rock are faint-hearted; and those compared to the thorns are lovers of luxury. Likewise, there are three ranks of those who welcome and preserve the word. <margin>Three ranks of those who welcome and preserve the word of God, [including] the married.</margin> For those who bring forth a hundredfold fruit are those who lead a perfect and supreme life; those who bring forth sixtyfold are those of a moderate life; and those who bring forth thirtyfold are those who are indeed small, yet they themselves bring forth according to their own strength. For example, [the hundredfold are] the young, the virgins, and the solitary hermits; likewise others [the sixtyfold] who live with us in communities and congregations; and still others [the thirtyfold] who are married laypeople. Nevertheless, the Lord welcomes them all. Thanks be to His mercy.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>Matthew 5. Luke 8, 11.</margin> **And he said to them: "Is a lamp brought in so that it may be put under a bushel or under a bed? Is it not so that it may be put upon a lampstand? For there is nothing hidden that will not be revealed, nor was anything made secret but that it should come into the open. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear."**] In this place, he warns the Apostles that they should lead clear and honest lives. For he says: "Just as a lamp is placed so that it may shine, so also your life shall be visible to all, and all shall look toward it; therefore, take care that your life is good." For you shall not sit in a corner, but you are lamps. A lamp is not hidden under a bed, but is placed upon a lampstand. <margin>The bushel and the bed represent hidden lamps and gluttony.</margin> Each of you shall be a lamp, which ought to be placed upon the lampstand—that is, upon the height of a divine life—so that it can shine for others. It should not be under a bushel—that is, under *gastrimargia* <term>original: "gastrimargia," a Greek term for gluttony or "belly-madness"</term> and the worry over food—nor under a bed, which signifies [slothful] rest. For no one who is concerned with food and who

If any of you does anything, whether good or evil, in secret, it shall be made manifest even here, and much more so in the world to come. For what is more hidden than God? Yet even He was revealed in the flesh.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>Matthew 4</margin> <note>The text likely intends to reference the parallel in Mark 4 or Matthew 13.</note> **And he said to them, "See what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and more will be added to you who hear. For to him who has, more will be given; and from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away."**] He exhorts the disciples to vigilance. For he says, "See what you hear," meaning let none of my words escape you. In the measure you have measured, others will measure back to you; that is, whatever measure of attention you bring, such a degree of benefit will be given to you. For if a listener attends as much as he can, God will give him a great advantage; but if he is remiss, his gain will be diminished according to his remissness. For it shall be given to him who is eager and diligent; but from him who is sluggish and idle, even what he seems to have will be taken. For because of idleness, even the small spark he possesses is extinguished, just as it is relit through eagerness.

<margin>C</margin> **And he said, "The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should sprout and grow, though he knows not how. For the earth produces fruit of itself: first the blade, then the head, then the full grain in the head. But when the fruit is produced, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come."**] By the "kingdom of God," understand the incarnation of God for our sake. For the "man" is God Himself, who became man for us. He cast the "seed" of the preaching of the Gospel upon the earth; and having cast it, he "sleeps"—that is, he ascended into the heavens. Yet he "rises night and day." <margin>God awakens [us] day and night.</margin> For although God may seem to sleep, he nevertheless awakens us: and indeed by "night" when he rouses us to the knowledge of Himself through temptations; and by "day" when he directs our life through sweet and pleasant things. <margin>D</margin>...theless, the man himself knows not <note>original: "tamen ipso nescio"</note>: for we are endowed with free will. And it must be by your choice that the seed either grows or does not. For we do not bring forth fruit by compulsion or necessity, but of our own accord, that is, from ourselves: first showing the flowering blade and the beginning of good when we are small children, and have not yet reached the full measure of Jesus Christ. Then we bring forth the ear, when we are also able to stand firm against temptations. For the ear is both girded with joints <note>Referring to the nodes on a stalk of grain.</note> and stands upright, and is more perfect and swelling. When, <margin>What should be understood by the harvest.</margin> however, someone has brought forth perfect fruit, and the harvest is at hand, then the sickle, which is the word of God, gathers the fruit. By the harvest, understand the end of the age <note>original: "consummationem seculi," a common term for the Last Judgment or the end of the world</note>.

<margin>Matt. 13. Luke 11.</margin>
<margin>E</margin> And he said, To what shall I liken the kingdom of heaven? Or by what comparison shall we compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when it is sown in the earth, is smaller than all the seeds that are on the earth: and when it is sown, it grows up, and becomes greater than all garden plants, and makes great branches, so that the birds of the air can nest under its shadow. And with many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear. But without a parable he did not speak to them, but privately he explained everything to his disciples. ] The word of faith is indeed small. For if you believe in CHRIST, you will be saved. See what kind of word it is; such also is the grain of mustard. For the preaching sent upon the earth was spread abroad and <margin>F</margin> grew, so that the birds of heaven, that is, all those high in knowledge and understanding, might dwell in it. For how many wise men, having left behind the wisdom of the gentiles <note>The secular or "pagan" philosophy of the Greeks and Romans.</note>, have found rest in the preaching? Therefore the preaching was very great, and it produced great branches. For one of the Apostles was sent to India, another to Rome, and another to another part of the earth, divided like branches. Moreover, he spoke to the crowds in many parables composed according to the capacity of the listeners. For since the crowd was unskilled and untaught, he therefore mentions the grain of mustard, and the herb, and the seed, so that by familiar and accustomed names he might teach them something useful, or stir them up to approach and ask questions, and by asking, learn what they do not know. For he explained everything to the disciples because they approached him privately and questioned—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>—him. But he resolved everything: whatever they asked in their ignorance; for he did not simply explain everything, including the things that were manifest. For they asked about those things he had said to them, while the rest were manifest to them, and in this way he explained everything to them.

And he said to them on that day, when evening had come, Let us cross over to the other side. And having dismissed the crowd, they took him just as he was in the boat, but other small boats were also with him. And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves were rushing into the boat, so that it was already filling. And he himself was in the stern, sleeping upon a pillow, and they woke him and said to him: Teacher, is it no care to you that we are perishing? And having been awakened, he rebuked the wind, and said to the sea: Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great <margin>B</margin> calm, and he said to them: Why are you so fearful? How is it that you have no confidence? And they feared with a great fear, and said among themselves: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? ] Matthew narrated these things one way, and Mark another: for what the former said more diffusely, the latter has contracted into a summary: and conversely, what the former said more briefly, the latter says more diffusely. He takes <margin>Matt. 8. Luke 8.</margin> therefore only the disciples, that they might be spectators of the future miracle. Furthermore, lest they be puffed up because he had taken them while dismissing the others, and to teach that temptations must be endured, he leaves them to be endangered by the storms. But he sleeps, so that the miracle might appear greater once they had first been troubled. For if CHRIST had been awake and the storm had happened, they either would not have feared, or would not <margin>C</margin> have prayed: therefore he permitted them to fall into the fear of danger, so that they might feel his power more clearly. For because they saw benefits being given to others while they themselves enjoyed no such thing, there was a danger that they might become negligent. Therefore he permits the storm to arise. Moreover, he sleeps upon a pillow <note>original: "ceruical," specifically a headrest or cushion.</note> which was in the boat, which was surely made of wood. Having been awakened, he first rebuked the wind (for it is this which had made the sea fierce) and then the sea. But he rebuked the disciples because they did not have faith. For if they had possessed faith, they would surely have believed that even while sleeping he could keep them unharmed. For they said among themselves, Who then is this? For they still had doubts concerning him.

general sense, the Lord says that all prophets are held in contempt in their own country, in their own house, and among their own kin. He was not able, therefore, to perform miracles there—not because he himself was weak, but because they were unbelieving. He spared them, therefore, by not performing signs, lest the signs lead to their greater condemnation for not believing even then; and for that reason, he performed few miracles there.

Others, however, say that Philip had indeed died, but had left behind a young daughter; and since he had left a daughter, Herod ought not <margin>Deuteronomy 25</margin> <margin>What the madness of love does.</margin> to have married his brother’s wife even after his death. See, then, what the madness of love does and how much power it has. For behold, Herod disregards John—whom he used to observe with such great honor and reverence—simply so that his lust might be satisfied.

### CHAPTER 7. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
<meta>catchword: likeness.</meta>

<margin>Isaiah 29</margin> ...concerning you hypocrites, as it is written: *This people honors me with their <margin>D</margin> lips, but their heart is far from me; but in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men.* For setting aside the commandment of God, you hold to the traditions of men: the washing of pitchers and cups, and you do many other such similar things. And he said to them: *Well do you reject the commandment of God so that you may keep your own tradition.* <margin>Exodus 20, Deuteronomy 5, Leviticus 20</margin> For Moses said: *Honor your father and your mother,* and so on. *He who curses father or mother, let him die the death.* But you say: *If a man says to father or mother, "Corban" <note>A Hebrew term meaning a gift or offering dedicated to God.</note> (which is a gift) whatever of mine might benefit you,* and thereafter you do not permit him to do anything for his father or mother. <margin>E</margin> And you make the word of God void through your tradition which you have handed down. For they were rebuking the disciples because they had transgressed the traditions of the elders; but the Lord charges them with a far more serious crime: that they transgress the Law of Moses. For the Law says: *Honor father and mother.* But you teach children <margin>Corban.</margin> to say to their parents, "Corban"—that is, a gift and offering to God—whatever you seek from me. For the Pharisees, wishing to devour those things belonging to the common people, taught children that if they had anything as their own property <note>original: 'peculium' - referring to private savings or property.</note> and their parents asked for it, they should say: "I have already consecrated this to God," so that they would no <margin>F</margin> longer seek what has already been offered to the Lord. Thus they deceived the children, and simultaneously persuaded them to consecrate to the Lord what they had; by which they caused parents to be despised, while they themselves devoured the things sacred to God. Therefore the Lord rebukes them, because they transgress the law of God for the sake of profit.

All these affections defile the soul, and they spring up from it <margin>C</margin> and go out. Furthermore, God spoke more obscurely to the crowds; for that reason he also said: *He who has ears to hear, let him hear,* that is, let him understand. But the Apostles thought the Lord was saying something deeper. And they approach and ask about the *parable*—that is, about the <margin>Parable.</margin> darkened and obscure speech. For a parable is a shadowy speech. And first he rebuked them, saying: "Are you also thus without intellect?" Then he resolved what was troubling them.

### ENARRATION <note>A detailed explanation or commentary</note> ON THE GOSPEL OF MARK

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Toward the unteachable, it is not fitting to be austere.</margin>
Notice also the disciples, how foolishly they behave, not yet believing in his powers despite the previous signs. However, he does not rebuke them, teaching us as well not to be too moody or austere toward those who are slow to learn; rather, there are things that must be forgiven them as though they were foolish. Consider also this: that CHRIST wants to send no one away from him hungry, for he wants to nourish all people with the delights of his own goods, and especially those who remain with him for three days—that is, the baptized. For <term>Baptism</term> <note>original: "baptifma"</note> is called "illumination" <note>original: "Illuminatio"</note>; and because baptism is performed in three immersions, those who are illuminated through baptism are said to remain for three days. He took seven loaves—by which I mean spiritual discourses. 

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>The number seven.</margin>
For the number seven is a symbol of the Holy Spirit, who perfects all things. For this life and this world are completed in the number seven <note>This refers to the seven days of creation and the idea of seven ages of the world</note>. Moreover, the illuminated eat and are satisfied, and there are remains left over. Not everyone is able to consume all the divine meanings. Truly, just as in that miracle of the five loaves there were twelve baskets and more remains—for there were five thousand, that is, they served the five senses, and therefore they could not eat much but were content with little, and so there were more remains—likewise, for these seven loaves there are seven hampers and fewer leftovers. This is because there were four thousand people—that is, those exercised in the <term>four virtues</term> <note>The cardinal virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance</note>—and therefore, being more powerful, they ate more and left less behind. 

<margin>C</margin>
For they alone could not eat those things which were more spiritual and deeper, which is why they are designated by the seven hampers. Learn this also from the history: that we ought to be content with those things we need and seek nothing more. For behold, the crowds who ate and were satisfied did not take the remains of the bread with them, but the disciples carried these. Thus, it is fitting for us to be content with what is suitable for our use.

### CHAPTER 8. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA / ENARRATION ON THE GOSPEL OF MARK

[...to you, if a sign shall be given to this generation.] After this sign <margin>D</margin> of the seven loaves, he immediately withdraws to another place, fearing lest the crowd, excited by such a great miracle, might attempt some revolution and try to make him king. The Pharisees seek a sign from heaven—such as stopping the sun or the light, leading down rivers, or changing the air. For they believed that he could not perform signs <margin>Matthew 24. Below, 13.</margin> from heaven, but that he only performed signs on earth through Beelzebub <note>The name used in the Gospels for the prince of demons; the Pharisees were accusing Jesus of using dark magic rather than divine power.</note>. However, he does not comply with them. For there is another time for signs from heaven—namely, the time of the second coming, when the powers of heaven will be moved and the moon will not give its brightness. But the time of the first coming <margin>E</margin> has no such thing; instead, all things are full of gentleness. And so, no such sign—that is, from heaven—will be given to this generation.

And leaving them, he entered the ship again and crossed the lake. And they had forgotten to take bread, and had only one loaf with them in the boat. And he commanded them, saying, "See, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod." And they argued among themselves, saying, "We have no bread." And Jesus, knowing this, said to them, "Why do you argue that you have no bread? Do you <margin>John 6.</margin> not yet notice or understand? Do you still have your hearts blinded? Having eyes, do you not see? Having ears, do you not hear? And do you not remember? When I broke five loaves for five thousand men, how many baskets full of fragments did you take up?" <margin>F</margin> They said to him, "Twelve." "And when seven for four thousand, how many hampers of leftover fragments did you carry away?" They said, "Seven." And he said to them, "How is it that you do not understand?" 

The Lord left the Pharisees as uncorrectable. For where there is hope of correction, one should stay; but where that is lacking, one must move on. By a singular divine arrangement <note>original: "dispensatione"; refers to the way God manages or orders events for a specific purpose.</note>, it happened that the disciples forgot the bread so that they might become better after being rebuked and understand the Lord's power. For when he said they must beware of the leaven of the Pharisees—that is, their doctrine—they thought he was speaking about the leaven used in bread. Hence, they are rightly criticized as being dull

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and not understanding the power of Christ, who can make bread from nothing. He calls the doctrine of the Pharisees and Herodians "leaven" because it is bitter and full of ancient malice. For whoever is hardened in malice and can say nothing spiritual that is sweet to the listener’s throat has "leaven" and a biting doctrine of ancient malice, which leads the one who obeys it to repentance at last. The Herodians, however, were certain teachers who had recently arisen, saying that Herod was the Christ and that he should be believed.

And he came to Bethsaida, and they brought a blind man to him and <margin>B</margin> begged him to touch him. And taking the blind man's hand, he led him outside the village; and when he had spat into his eyes and laid his hands on him, he asked him if he saw anything. And having received his sight, he said, "I see people, for I see them walking like trees." Then he laid his hands on his eyes again, and made him receive his sight, and he was restored, and saw everyone clearly again. And he sent him to his house, saying, "Neither enter the village nor tell anyone in the village." 

It appears that Bethsaida suffered from great unbelief; therefore Christ calls it miserable, as Matthew says: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, <margin>Matthew 11</margin> <note>original: "Matt. 12," likely a citation error for Matthew 11:21.</note> Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago." Therefore, when Jesus had come here, they <margin>C</margin> brought a blind man from the village to him. But the faith of those who brought him was not pure; thus the Lord leads the blind man out of the village and heals him there. He spat in the eyes of the blind man and laid hands on him so that we might learn that the divine word is effective. For the hand is a symbol of action, while spit <margin>Hand. Spit.</margin> is a symbol of the word, because it comes from the mouth. And because that blind man did not have perfect faith, he does not make him see all at once, but gradually, as one lacking complete faith. For health is given according to the magnitude of faith. He forbids him, however, from entering his village, because, as I said, the people were unbelievers and would have harmed his soul. But neither does Christ want this told about him for long, lest they persist in their unbelief...

### CHAPTER 8. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA 134

...should die, but whoever wills it. For I force no one. I call you to good things, not to evil, so that I might not have to compel you; and thus, if someone does not will it, he is not worthy of these things. What it means, however,

<margin>To deny oneself.</margin>
to deny oneself, we shall learn if we learn what it means to deny another. For he who denies another—perhaps a brother, or a close friend, or a father—even if he sees him being whipped or killed, does not take notice, does not grieve, and feels no compassion, once he has become alienated from him. In this same way, He wants us to look down upon our own body, so that whether it suffers whippings or anything else, we do not spare it. Let him "take up his cross," which means a shameful death. For at that time, the cross was seen as shameful. Furthermore, because many robbers were being put to the cross, He adds that along with crucifixion, one must also possess every other virtue;

<margin>E</margin>
for this is what is meant by "and let him follow me." But because this seemed heavy and cruel—that He commands us to expose ourselves to death—He says that this way possesses more mercy. For "whoever loses his soul for my sake"—not like a robber who is killed, or like one who is hanged (for this is not for my sake)—such a person "will find his soul." Conversely, if anyone seems to "gain" it, he will lose it if he does not stand firm in a time of martyrdom. Do not tell me that he has gained his life; for since it must be laid down later anyway, even if he has gained the whole world, there will be no benefit. For salvation cannot be bought back with riches; for if that were possible, a man who gains the whole world but loses his soul

<margin>F</margin>
would simply pay it back. Even the rich man who was tortured in the flame <note>A reference to the parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16.</note> would have paid and been made innocent. But there is no such "exchange" in that place. Accordingly, in this passage, we shall also refute

<margin>The Origenists are refuted.</margin>
the Origenists, <note>Followers of Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD). Theophylact is refuting the doctrine of *apokatastasis*, the belief that all souls, even those in Hell, will eventually be restored to God.</note> who say that there will be a certain restoration of souls after they have been punished according to the measure of their sins. For we hear here that nothing can be given in exchange for the soul in that place. Therefore, the punishment is not a finite thing that can be paid off like a debt for sin.

# AN EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MARK.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Matthew 18.</margin>
<margin>Luke 9.</margin>
<margin>The sanctification of body and soul.</margin>

**AND he said to them: "Amen I say to you, there are some among those standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God come with power."** ] Mental faith is not enough, but the confession of the mouth is also required. For because man is a dual being <note>Consisting of both physical body and spiritual soul.</note>, let there be a dual sanctification. The soul is indeed sanctified through faith, but the body through confession. Therefore, whoever is ashamed to confess his God as the "Crucified One," of him will God Himself be ashamed. He will judge him as an unworthy servant when He comes—not humble then, nor appearing despised as He did here (such that one might be ashamed of Him), but in glory and with a company of angels.

<margin>B</margin>

<margin>D</margin> [In a form] such as it was before, there occurred an increase of ineffable light.
And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus. <margin>Reasons why Moses and Elijah were on the mountain and what they spoke about with Jesus. John 9 <note>The marginal reference to John 9 likely refers to a parallel or related thematic discussion, though the primary text here is Mark 9.</note></margin>
<margin>E</margin> Elijah and Moses are seen talking with Him for many reasons. For because the disciples had said the people were saying that Christ was either Elijah or another from the number of the prophets, He showed them the chief of the prophets, so that from this they might learn how great the difference is between the servant and the Lord. This is indeed one reason. Another is because many thought Him an adversary to God, and that He was breaking the Sabbath and transgressing the Law; therefore He showed on the mountain the prophets, of whom one was the Lawgiver <note>Moses</note> and the other had been a zealot <note>Elijah</note>. For the prophets would not have held a conversation with one who was seen to be breaking the Law. 

But Peter was afraid to descend from the mountain; he feared, namely, lest the Lord should be crucified, and he said, "It is good for us to be here," and not to descend there into the midst of the Jews. For if those who pursue you should come here, we would have Moses, who triumphed over the Egyptians; we would also have Elijah, who brought down fire 
<margin>F</margin> from heaven consuming the captains of fifty. <margin>Exodus 14; 2 Kings 1; Genesis 1. <note>Original margin cites 4. Reg. 1, which is 2 Kings in modern Bibles.</note></margin> But what were the prophets talking about with Him? About His cross and death. Furthermore, concerning Peter, it says that he did not know what he was saying. For they were struck with terror because of the ineffable light and glory. For it was not fully right in his mind that Jesus should never want to descend to be crucified for our salvation, but rather to remain always on the mountain. 

Now let us also lift up the discourse to an <term>anagogy</term> <note>Anagogy is a method of spiritual interpretation that looks forward to the afterlife or the end of the world.</note>. After the completion of the world, which was established in six days, the Lord will also cause us to ascend—if indeed we have been His disciples—into the high mountain (by which I mean heaven), and He will show Himself to us more radiant. Now indeed, as if 

<column-break/>

136
### EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MARK

<margin>A</margin> in lowliness, He appeared crucified, and the son of a carpenter; but then we shall see the glory of that Only-begotten One; we shall also see the Law and the prophets talking with Him—that is, the things which were said of Him both by Moses and by the rest of the prophets—and then we shall discover and see that they harmonize with His works. And then we shall truly hear the Father's voice, which reveals to us the Son of the Father and teaches, "This is my Son." How will He teach us? By the overshadowing cloud, which is the Holy Spirit, who is the fountain of wisdom.

Furthermore, as they were descending from the mountain, He commanded them not to tell anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man 
<margin>B</margin> had risen from the dead. And they kept this word among themselves, questioning one another what this meant, "to rise from the dead." 

For what reason does the Lord forbid the disciples from saying anything to anyone regarding the transfiguration? So that men might not be scandalized <note>In this context, "scandalized" means to be led into doubt or a loss of faith.</note> if, after they had heard such honorable things about Christ, they later saw Him being crucified. Therefore, after He rose from the dead, it was the proper time to speak of the glorious things of Christ that were done before the cross. Thus the apostles kept the discourse to themselves, debating among themselves what it meant to rise from the dead; for they did not yet know (it says) that it was necessary to rise from the dead.

And they questioned Him, saying, "Why do the 
<margin>C</margin> scribes say that Elijah must come first?" But He, answering, said to them, "Elijah indeed, when he has arrived, will first restore all things; and just as it is written of the Son of Man, that He should suffer many things and be despised. But I say to you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they wished, just as it was written of him." 

There was a certain rumor among the Hebrews regarding Elijah, that he would come before <margin>Isaiah 53; Malachi 4</margin> Christ. Nevertheless, the Pharisees did not interpret the truth about Elijah as they ought, but out of spontaneous malice, they hid the truth. For there are two advents of Christ: that one which has passed, and that one which is to come. The precursor of the first was John; but of the second, it will be Elijah. Therefore, Christ calls John "Elijah" because he was a precursor and because he sharply rebuked others and emulated Elijah's character.

Indeed, Elijah, when he comes, will restore all things: and just as it is written of the Son of Man, that he must suffer many things. <margin>What is the meaning of these words?</margin> The meaning of the words is this: When Elijah the Tishbite <note>original: "Thesbitas"; a traditional title for the prophet Elijah referring to his hometown, Tishbe</note> comes, he will make peace with the Jews who do not believe, and will lead them to faith, and so he will be the precursor of the second coming. <margin>1 Corinthians 3</margin> For "everyone will be seasoned with fire"; that is, they will be tested, just as <margin>Leviticus 2</margin> **Paul** says that all things will be tested in fire. <margin>A comparison.</margin> For just as salt preserves meat and does not allow worms to grow in it, so also the word of the teacher—if it is fresh and sharp <note>original: "mordax"; biting or pungent</note> and restrains carnal men—does not allow the "restless worm" to be generated within them. Therefore, have salt within yourselves—that is, the grace of the Spirit—which restrains you so that you may be peaceful. For he who is bound by charity toward his neighbor possesses this salt and is at peace with his brother.

The Lord frequently left the Jews because of their envy, but now he passes into their region again. For the people of **Jerusalem** were a "workshop of all malice" <margin>Pretext <note>original Greek: "ἀφορμῆ"</note> in the name of the Pharisees</margin> because of the wickedness of the **Pharisees**. 

Observe their malice: how they test the Lord, not leaving him alone, fearing that the crowds might believe in him. They always approach him hoping they might make him confused by their questions and refute him. <margin>B</margin> For they were asking a question that had "cliffs on both sides" <note>A "captious" or trap question where any answer seems dangerous.</note>. <margin>The Pharisees' trap question.</margin> "Is it lawful for a man to send away his wife?" For if he had said it was lawful to release her, they would have thrown it back at him that he had previously said it was not lawful to release her except in the case of fornication. But if he said it was not lawful, they would label him an adversary to the teachings of **Moses**.

The chains of those who possess much are loosened with greater difficulty. Truly, if someone is a "youth"—I mean a youth and a little child in their understanding, with an ill-composed heart—let them sell their faculties, namely their anger and lust, and whatever evils sprout from these, and let them give and cast these things to the "poor," that is, to the demons. For the demons are truly poor, deprived of every good, and have fallen from the riches of God's goodness; and only then let them follow CHRIST. For he who casts the riches of sins to the demons will be able to follow CHRIST.

<margin>A</margin> "Children, how difficult it is for those who have confidence in money to enter the kingdom of God. It is easier for a <gloss>camel <note>original Greek: "χάμηλος"</note></gloss> camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God." For they are called <term>wealth <note>original Greek: "χρήματα" (chrēmata), derived from the word for "use"</note></term>, that is, resources, because they are for the use of humans and bring help and aid; they are not <term>possessions <note>original Greek: "κτήματα" (ktēmata), derived from the word for "to acquire" or "hold onto"</note></term> to be hoarded. Therefore, those who have them and lock them up <margin>B</margin> enter the kingdom of God with difficulty. 

Understand "difficult" in this place as "impossible." For it is impossible for a rich man to be saved. This is manifest from the example the Lord provides, saying it is easier for a <gloss>camel <note>original Greek: "χάμηλος"</note></gloss> to go through the eye of a needle than a rich man into the kingdom. By "camel," <term>kamilos <note>original Greek: "καμῖλον"</note></term>, understand either the animal or the thick rope used by sailors. For it is impossible for a man, insofar as he is rich, to be saved. However, with God this is possible. For Christ said, "Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity." Do you see how it becomes possible if we listen to God? With men it is impossible—that is, when human perspectives are favored, it is impossible. 

Now, why were the disciples stunned by his words? For they themselves were not rich. It seems to me they were anxious on behalf of all humanity. For they had already begun to become merciful. Some doubt this passage, asking how he could say, "All things are possible for God," since God cannot sin. We say, therefore, that when he says "all things," we understand those things that have existence; but sin is nothing. For sin is a thing without essence and without substance. Or to put it another way: sin is not a matter of power, but of weakness. Just as the Apostle says, "Christ died when we were weak." And again David says, "Their weaknesses were multiplied," and thus sin is not possible for God because it is a weakness. And would they say God can make what has been done into something that never happened? We say God is truthful; but to make what was done undone is a lie.

It is likely, however, that both things happened: the apostles, out of a certain sense of shame, sent their mother first, and then they approached him separately themselves. This is why the Evangelist <note>Mark</note> specifies this, saying, *They approached*, that is, they went to him privately, apart from the others. Let us learn, then, what it was they were asking. They thought that he was going up to Jerusalem to reign in a kind of temporal, earthly kingdom, and that after he had reigned, he would suffer the things he had spoken of. Thinking such things <margin>E</margin> to themselves, they asked for a seat at both his right and his left. Therefore, the Lord rebukes them as people asking for something foolish: *For you do not know*, he says, *what you are asking.* For you believe my kingdom is something sensible to the touch <note>original: "sensibile," meaning perceptible by the senses or physical</note> and you ask for a temporal seat. <margin>Sitting at the right hand of Christ.</margin>
And to sit at my right hand is a great thing, something that excels even the angelic orders. You indeed hurry toward glory, but I call you to a mountain <note>Theophylact likely means the "mountain" of the Cross or a difficult ascent.</note>. 

<margin>The Cross as cup and baptism.</margin>
For he calls the cross the "cup" and "baptism." He calls it a **cup** because it quickly brings on sleep <note>A metaphor for the "sleep" of death.</note>, and because it was taken by him with great sweetness. He calls it **baptism**, <margin>F</margin> however, because it was to be the purification of sins. But they, not understanding what he was saying, made their promise. For they thought he was speaking of a physical cup and the baptism with which the Jews were baptized when they washed themselves before eating.

**But Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink, you shall drink; and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you shall be baptized; but to sit at my right or left is not mine to give, but it will happen for those for whom it has been prepared."**] You will indeed come to martyrdom, he says, and you will die for the truth; but to sit at the right and left is not mine to give. In this place, two questions are usually asked: 

<margin>Two questions.</margin>

<margin>And what is understood by "throne" in the scriptures.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> We say, therefore, that no one will sit at the right or left in a physical sense. Whenever you hear of a "throne" <note>original: "cathedram," a seat of authority or chair</note> in the scriptures, do not think of a literal chair, but of an excellent dignity or rank. As for the statement *it is not mine to give*, it has this meaning: It is not mine—that is, as a just judge—to give this dignity to you as a personal favor; for then I would not be just. Instead, that dignity is prepared for those who have labored for it. It is just as if a righteous king presided over a contest, and some of his friends came to him and said, "Give us the crowns." He would surely say, "It is not mine <margin>Luke 22</margin> to give; but if anyone has competed and won, the crown is prepared for him." And so it is for you, O sons of Zebedee: you will indeed be <margin>B</margin> martyrs for my sake; but if someone is found who, along with martyrdom, possesses all other virtues to a greater degree than you, he shall precede you.

interpretation: Jericho is that "lower place." The blind man who sits in this place represents human nature, which was once a child of God and possessed every dignity. Therefore, this nature cried out to Jesus as he passed through Jericho—that is, through this life. Moved by mercy toward it, and because of its faith, he saved it when it cast off the old garment of sin. Once saved, it followed him by performing his commandments on the "way," which is to say, in this life. ### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>B</margin><image-desc>Large decorative drop-cap 'E' inside a square frame. The illustration shows a man in classical robes walking through a landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc> And when they approached Jerusalem, at Bethphage and Bethany, near the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the village opposite you, and immediately as you enter it, you will find a colt tied, upon which no man has ever sat; untie it and bring it here. And they went and found a colt tied outside a door at a crossroads, and they untied it. And some of those standing there said to them, "What are you doing, untying the colt?" But they told them just as Jesus had commanded, and they let them go. <margin>Matthew 21. Luke 19.</margin> He had often come to Jerusalem at other times, but never with such majesty as now. Previously he would hide himself because of their envy, but now, because the time of his Passion was at hand—which he himself had preordained—he comes more openly <margin>C</margin> so that, if they wish, they may understand his glory and recognize from the prophecies concerning him that he is the true God. If they refuse, it results in their greater condemnation, because they did not believe even such clear miracles. For see what signs he gave them in this place. He told them, "You will find a colt"; he spoke of the owners' prohibition and then their release of the animal when told "The Lord has need of it." For it would have been no small thing for the apostles to be permitted to lead away a colt unless some divine power had compelled the owners—especially since they were likely poor men and farmers.

But the man himself should never be separated from God by saying: "I have nothing from God, nor do I need his help."

Approaching indirectly, like deceitful men, they devise a certain narrative to subvert the idea of resurrection, weaving an argument based on something that 
<margin>F</margin>
never happened, and perhaps never would. They imagine seven men who marry one wife, the better to tear apart the concept of the resurrection. Therefore, because they used the law of Moses as a pretext, he showed them to be ignorant of the scriptures. He says: You do not understand of what kind of resurrection the scripture speaks. For you imagine that the resurrection to come will be of a more physical nature, but it will not be so. Thus you are ignorant of the mind of scripture, and you also ignore the power of scripture. Indeed, you perhaps look at the difficulty of the matter, and for that reason you doubt how dissolved bodies can return to the soul. But to divine power, this will be as nothing. Therefore, there will be a resurrection, and it will not be physical, but a certain more divine state of life, namely an angelic one. For we shall be incorruptible; and though remaining the same individuals we are,

<margin>A</margin>
marriage will therefore be abolished. For now, marriage exists because of corruption <note>Theophylact uses "corruption" here to mean mortality; marriage is necessary for the continuation of the species because individuals die.</note>, so that through the succession of the race, humanity does not perish; but then, like the angels, they will exist as themselves without the need for marital succession and will never fail. So too, those who rise remain without marriage, never to be diminished. And they are rebuked in another way as those who do not know the scripture. For if they had understood them, they would also understand how it is written: "I am the God of Abraham," clearly implying the God 
<margin>Exodus 3</margin>
of the living. For he did not say, "I was," but "I am" <note>Theophylact emphasizes the present tense of the Latin *sum* and the Hebrew context to prove that the Patriarchs must still exist in some form.</note>; indicating they are present and not lost. Now perhaps someone will say that the Lord said this only regarding the soul of Abraham, 
<margin>B</margin>
and not likewise regarding the body, and thus bodies do not rise. I say, therefore, first of all, that "Abraham" refers to both soul and body, so God is also the God of the body, which itself lives before God and is not reduced entirely to nothing. 
<margin>Resurrection</margin>
Furthermore, because the Sadducees doubted the resurrection of the body, it is certain that the Lord spoke of bodies—that they live before God—not just of the soul; for that was already admitted even among the carnal Jews. Observe this also: "Resurrection" <term>resurrectio: a rising again</term> is the "rising up" of that which had fallen. The immortal soul, however, did not fall; but this body did. Therefore, it is the body that shall rise again, joined once more to the soul.

**A** "—of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory." ] Because he has completed the matters pertaining to Jerusalem, he begins now to speak of the coming of the Antichrist. As for his saying "Then," do not understand it as meaning *at the time* when those things mentioned above regarding Jerusalem occur—as in "then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ,' do not believe it"—but know that this is a stylistic trait of Scripture. Just as Matthew says after the genealogy of Christ, "In those days John arrived." In which days? Surely not immediately following Christ's birth? No, but in an indefinite sense. Thus, in this place also, he says "then": not when Jerusalem was desolated, but regarding the time of the coming of the Antichrist, so that you might not be led astray. For many will use the name of **B** Christ as a pretext, so much so that they might even be able to seduce the elect. But after the coming of the Antichrist, every creature will be changed, when the stars are darkened because of the immense light of Christ. Moreover, the angelic powers will be moved—that is, they will be struck with awe—seeing such a great change of things happening and seeing their fellow-servants being judged. And then they will see the Lord as the "Son of Man," that is, in a body. For that which is seen must necessarily be a body. Although he will come as a man, he will nevertheless be present with power and great glory.

<meta>This page continues Theophylact’s commentary on the 13th chapter of the Gospel of Mark, specifically focusing on Christ’s prophecy regarding the end of the age and the destruction of Jerusalem. # CHAPTER 13. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> Just as summer follows winter, so for sinners, winter <note>In this context, "winter" represents the time of judgment and tribulation.</note> follows the "summer" of Christ. Truly I say to you, this generation—that is, the generation of Christians—shall not pass away until all these things concerning Jerusalem and the coming of the Antichrist take place. For he does not mean the generation of the Apostles, since many of them did not live until the destruction of Jerusalem; how then could they be said to reach the end of the world? Therefore, he speaks of the generation of Christians, consoling the Apostles so they do not suspect that faith might fail when such great evils occur. It is as if he said: "Have confidence and be of good heart; the generation of the faithful shall not pass away, nor shall it fail." For these immovable elements, I mean heaven and earth, shall sooner pass away than 
<margin>E</margin> my words should fail in any part. Everything I have said shall be fulfilled.

->But of that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels who are in heaven, nor the Son himself, but only the Father. Take heed, watch, and pray, for you do not know when the time is. It is like a man going on a journey, who left his house and gave his substance to his servants, and to each his work, and commanded the gatekeeper to watch. Watch therefore, for you do not know when the master of the house is coming—in the evening, or at midnight, or at the cock-crowing, or in the morning—lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. But what I say to you, I say to all: Watch.<- 

<margin>F</margin> The Lord, wishing to restrain the disciples from questioning him about that day and hour, says that neither the angels nor the Son knows. For if he had said, "I know, but I do not wish to reveal it to you," he would have filled them with sorrow. But now he acts prudently, and entirely prohibits them from learning it, persuading them by saying, "Neither the angels know, nor do I." You may understand what is said through an example. 
<margin>An example of the hiding of the day of his coming.</margin> Little children often see their fathers holding something in their hands and they ask for it; when the fathers are unwilling to give it, the children cry because they do not receive it. Finally, the fathers hide what they are holding and, showing their empty hands to the children, they stop their weeping. So too the Lord, addressing the Apostles as if they were children, hid the day. For if he had said, "I know, but I will not tell," they would have grieved that 

**Right Page**

# IN THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF MARK
<page-num>155</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> they were not deemed worthy by him. However, that the Lord knew both the certain day and the hour is manifest, because he is the Creator of the world. And in what way could he not know it? In truth, God usefully hid the end of life—whether the end of all things in common, or of each individual person—so that while the end is uncertain, we might always be solicitous and anxious, expecting it and fearing lest it come upon us unprepared. Let us consider the words. "Late" <note>original: "Sero"</note> signifies the end when one dies in a good old age. 
<margin>B</margin> "At midnight," when one has completed the middle of their life. "At the cock-crowing," when reason has been perfected in us. For the "cock" is reason, which awakens us from sleep and drives away stupor. Therefore, when a child begins to live and grow wise according to reason, then the cock crows for him. Before the cock-crowing is the purely childish age. Everyone, therefore, ought to keep the end in memory; even if one is a child, care must be taken lest perhaps they die unbaptized. The Lord commands these things to all—both to those living in the world then and to those who have succeeded them. We ought, therefore, to watch and pray. Both of these are necessary. For many "watch" <note>In the sense of staying awake at night.</note> but spend the night badly. Note, however, how he did not say, "For *I* do not know when the time is," but "for *you* do not know." He hid it for our benefit. For if even now, when the end of the world is uncertain, we are mad with mutual hatreds, what would we not do if we knew the end? We would surely spend our lives in extreme malice, 
<margin>C</margin> and then on the last day, perform penance with the greatest loss <note>i.e., a last-minute repentance that lacks the merit of a lifelong conversion.</note>.

<margin>D</margin> **"But there were some who were indignant within themselves, and said: Why was this waste of ointment made? For it might have been sold for more than three hundred denarii <note>A denarius was a standard day's wage for a laborer; three hundred denarii represented nearly a year's salary.</note> and given to the poor. And they grumbled against her."** ] On the fourth day of the week <note>original: "Feria quarta"; Wednesday</note> the council assembled, and for this reason we also fast on Wednesdays.
<margin>Why we fast on Wednesdays.</margin>
They indeed consulted to skip the time of the festival, but it was not permitted to them; instead, Christ himself, establishing the time of his own passion, willed to be crucified at the Passover, for he himself was the true Passover.
<margin>Christ the true Passover.</margin>
From this, one may admire his power. For when they wished to seize him, they were unable; yet when they did not wish to do so because of the feast day, then he voluntarily gave himself up. But while he was in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came. All four Evangelists make mention of the ointment. To some, it seems there was only one pouring out, or that it happened just once, but there are actually two. One is the account in John, where the woman is the sister of Lazarus. The other is mentioned by the remaining three Evangelists.
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>John 12.</margin>
<margin>Concerning the three [women].</margin>
However, pay attention and you will find that there are actually three. In John there is one; in Luke there is another; and in those other two [Matthew and Mark] there is yet another.
<margin>Magdalenes <note>The author is distinguishing between the different women often conflated with Mary Magdalene.</note></margin>
<margin>Luke 7.</margin>
<margin>Matt. 26.</margin>
For the woman in Luke was a prostitute and came to Christ in the middle of his preaching. The one in Matthew came at the time of the Passion and is not called a prostitute. Christ approves of her will, because she spent so much on the nard. Concerning "pure nard," <note>original: "nardum pistica"</note> know that there is a certain species of nard called <term>pistica (pure)</term>, either because it is sincere and unadulterated, or because it was prepared with "faith" <note>The Greek word "pistikos" can mean both "genuine/liquid" and "faithful."</note>.
<margin>What is pure nard.</margin>
But there were some who took it ill. John says that Judas was the one who was annoyed. It is likely, therefore, that the other Apostles also rebuked the woman, as they had always heard Christ teaching many things about almsgiving. Judas, however, was not indignant against the woman for the same purpose, but because of his greed and shameful desire for gain. Because of this, John mentions only him, as if he had criticized the woman with a deceitful bite. **"And they grumbled at her,"** that is, they were indignant, they reviled her, and they spoke harshly to her. 

**"But JESUS said: Let her alone; why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish you can..."**

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> **"...do them good: but you do not always have me. She has done what she could; she has come beforehand to anoint my body for burial. Amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel shall be preached throughout the whole world, what she has done shall also be told in memory of her."** ] The Lord rebukes the disciples because they are opposing the woman’s eagerness at an inappropriate time. "For why," he says, "do you give her trouble and bother her? Is it because she brought a gift that you oppose her with shame?" Again, he stings the betrayer by saying, "She did this for my burial," and clearly convicts his conscience, as if he were saying to him: "You indeed have betrayed me to death, and you do not rebuke yourself; but she, bringing ointment for my burial, moved by God—is she worthy to be rebuked by you?"
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Christ as prophet.</margin>
The Lord acts as a prophet in this place and predicts two things: both that the Gospel is to be preached in the whole world, and that the woman’s work is to be preached at the same time. Let those who prefer the poor over CHRIST be put to shame in this place. For I have heard goldsmiths saying, "If I give a cut-up sacred vessel to the poor, I will not be condemned in life." Let them hear, therefore, how CHRIST prefers the care of himself over the care of the poor.
<margin>Care for Christ is to be preferred over care for the poor.</margin>
Christ's body is specifically present both in the golden dish <note>original: "disco aureo"; the paten used for the bread</note> and his blood is in the cup. Therefore, he who takes away a precious vessel and forces the body of Christ to be placed in a cheaper one—under the pretext of the poor—let him know who his father is <note>An allusion to Judas or the Devil.</note>.
<margin>C</margin>

**"And Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went to the chief priests to betray him to them. When they heard it, they were glad, and promised to give him money. And he sought how he might conveniently betray him."** ] While the woman was declaring her generosity, one disciple—one of the twelve—was acting out of madness. It is not added without reason that he was **"one of the twelve,"** but to show that he was one of the chosen twelve. What does he mean when he says, **"that he might betray him"**? This means he would signal to them when Jesus was alone; for they feared to attack him while he was teaching because of the crowd. He, therefore, promised them that he would tell them when he was alone.

**[And on the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the passover, his disciples said to him, "Where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the passover?" And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, 'The Teacher says, where is my guest room, where I may eat the passover with my disciples?' And he will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready; there prepare for us."]** He calls the "first day of unleavened bread" the fifth day of the week <note>Thursday</note>, which was the day before the feast of unleavened bread began. For they ate the unleavened and unfermented bread on the day of preparation <note>original: "parascenes"; Friday</note>. And so the disciples approach and ask where they should eat the passover. From this, moreover, it is manifest
<margin>Neither Christ nor the disciples had their own houses.</margin>
that **CHRIST** did not have his own lodging, nor did the disciples have a house of their own. <margin>E</margin> For if they had possessed one, they would have received him there. But he sends two of his disciples, Peter and John, as Luke also says, to an unknown man; this was to show them that he had the power to avoid suffering if he chose. For if he could sway the mind of an unknown man to receive him, what could he not have done to others? Furthermore, he gives them a sign of how to find the house: namely, that they should follow a man carrying an earthenware vessel of water. These things can also be understood in a more sublime sense. The one carrying the water jar represents the one who baptizes; he goes into a house that is worthy of its rational order. For he who possesses baptism goes toward rest, living according to reason, and lives in an orderly way, as if in
<margin>F</margin>
a certain house. The "master of the house" is the mind, which reveals a "large upper room"—that is, lofty spiritual perceptions. Indeed, this upper room is "furnished" <note>original: "stratum"; literally "spread with carpets" or "laid out"</note>; this means that although it is sublime, it contains nothing harsh or proud, but is smoothed over and leveled by humility. There, in such a mind, the passover is prepared for **CHRIST** by two disciples, Peter and John—whom I call "Action" and "Contemplation." For Peter, because of his fervor, represents the practical or active life; John, as the "Theologian," represents the contemplative life.

It is likely, therefore, that they first completed the requirements of the Law, and then reclined to receive the delivery of his own passover <note>the Eucharist</note>. <margin>B</margin> The disciples began to be sad because of the word the Lord had spoken, that one of them would betray him. For although they were conscious of no such thing in themselves, they were nevertheless anxious, trusting more in him who knows hearts than in themselves. Note also the word "goes" <note>original: "vadit"</note>. The death of **CHRIST** was like a journey or a pilgrimage, not a permanent death. As for the saying, "it would be better for that man if he had never been born," this was said because of the punishment with which Judas was to be tormented. For it is better not to be born at all than to be born for such a punishment. Therefore, as far as faith is concerned, it seems it would have been better if Judas had never existed. **GOD** indeed made him for good works; but because he fell into such wickedness, as is evident, it would have been better if he had never been brought into existence.

# CHAPTER 14. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>The bread is not a figure; it is changed into the body of Christ. John 6.</margin>
**[And as they were eating, Jesus took bread...]** He did not give it before he had sanctified it. When he had blessed it—that is, when he had given thanks—he
<margin>D</margin>
broke the bread: which is exactly what we also do, adding prayers. **"This is my body,"** he said; this very thing, I say, which you are receiving. For the bread is not merely a figure or a symbol <note>original: "figura & exemplar"</note> of the Lord’s body, but it is changed into the very body of Christ. For the Lord says: "The bread that I will give is my flesh." He did not say, "it is a figure of my flesh," but "it is my flesh." And again: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man." And how, you ask, is it that the flesh is not visible? O man, this happens because of our own weakness. Because bread and wine are among those things to which we are accustomed, we do not shrink from them; however, if we saw actual blood and flesh set before us, we would not be able to bear it, but would be repulsed. Therefore, the merciful God, stooping down to our weakness,
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Exodus 24.</margin>
preserves the appearance of bread and wine, but changes the elements <term>transelementat: a term used in Eastern theology to describe the change of the bread and wine into Christ's body and blood, similar to the Western "transubstantiation"</term> into the power of flesh and blood. He spoke of the "blood of the new testament" to contrast it with the old. For the old testament also had blood, with which the people and the book of the law were sprinkled. "But I will not drink of this wine," he says, "until the resurrection." For he calls the resurrection the "Kingdom," as a king
<margin>John 21.</margin>
who has fought against death and now reigns. Indeed, after the resurrection, he ate and drank with his disciples to show that he was the same one who had suffered. But he drank it "new," that is, in a new and unusual way, for he no longer had a physical body that was subject to suffering or in need of food, but one
<margin>F</margin>
immortal and incorruptible. Understand it also in this way: the Lord himself is the Vine, and the fruits of the vine are the mysteries and hidden knowledge which he himself brings forth, 
<margin>John 15.</margin>
teaching man knowledge. Therefore, in the Kingdom of God—that is, in the eighth age <note>The "eighth age" refers to eternity or the world to come, following the seven "days" of worldly history.</note>—he drinks with his disciples, teaching us and revealing new mysteries and wisdom that had been hidden.

**[And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. And Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away because of me this night, for it is written:]**
<margin>Zechariah 13</margin>
**[‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee." But Peter said to him, "Even if everyone else...]**

<page-num>158</page-num>

# EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF MARK.

<margin>A</margin>
**[...falls away, I will not." And Jesus said to him, "Truly I say to you, that today, even in this night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." But he spoke all the more vehemently, "Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you." And they all said the same.]**

**"They gave thanks."** Both before and after they had drunk, they gave thanks, so that we too might learn that it is necessary to give thanks to **CHRIST**, and to praise him both before and after a meal. Furthermore, this indicates that his death for us was pleasing to him; since he was going out to be betrayed, he praises the Lord. Above all, he teaches us that if we should ever
<margin>B</margin>
fall into adversity for the sake of the salvation of many, we should not be sad, but should give thanks to God, who works our affliction into the salvation of many. He goes out to the Mount of Olives so that they might attack and seize him in a solitary place, lest they cause a great riot. For if they had attacked him in the city, a crowd might have gathered, and his enemies might have appeared to be justly killing him as a rebel if they had seized him on some seemingly legal occasion. He predicts to them that they would fall away. Then, lest these words seem like a direct accusation against them all, he brings forth testimony from the prophet
<margin>How Peter's denial occurred: The Lord permitted Peter and the others to fall so that human nature might reveal its own frailty.</margin>
Zechariah, that they were to be scattered. Finally, he offers them consolation, saying, "I will go before you into Galilee," that is, I will arrive there before you. But Peter insists, and so he is told that before the rooster crows twice, he will deny him three times. This happened in this way: Peter denied him once, then the rooster crowed; after he had made two other denials, the rooster crowed again.
<margin>C</margin>
And this is what is said in this place: "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." Similarly, all the others, showing a cold sort of eagerness and making the truth itself out to be a lie, made their promises. Therefore, the Lord permits it, so that human nature may reveal its own weakness. For the Lord could certainly have kept them safe, and Peter especially; but he permitted it so that we might not trust in ourselves. Furthermore, "I will strike the shepherd" is the voice of the Father. He calls the apostles "sheep" because they were innocent.

# CHAPTER 14. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

And they come to a place, whose name is Gethsemane, and he says to his disciples, "Sit here, while I go and pray." And he takes Peter, and James, and John with him: and he began to be struck with fear and distress. And he says to them, "My soul is sorrowful even unto death. Stay here and watch." And having gone forward a little, he fell prostrate on the ground, and prayed that if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, "Abba <note>Aramaic for 'Father,' expressing an intimate, familial relationship.</note> Father, all things are possible to you; take away this cup from me: nevertheless not what I will but what you will." And he comes and finds them sleeping: and he says to Peter, "Simon, are you sleeping? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."

<margin>E</margin> He was always accustomed to pray in private, giving us a model so that we might seek quiet for our own prayers. But he takes only those three who had been spectators of his glory on Mount Tabor <note>The Mount of Transfiguration, where these three disciples saw Jesus in his divine glory.</note>, so that those very men who had seen the glorious things might also see the sorrowful ones; and so they might learn that he is truly human, and that he grieves and is distressed just as we are. For he who took upon himself the whole man along with all our natural conditions, certainly possessed both natural sadness and distress.

<margin>F</margin> All of us are by our nature unusually affected by the prospect of death. Furthermore, by saying, "Let the cup pass," he demonstrated his humanity. By saying, however, "not as I will, but as you," he teaches us that if we ask God for something that goes against the natural impulses that struggle within us, we are acting wisely. After he returned from his prayers, he found the three sleeping, and he rebuked Peter alone, as if saying to him: "Are you not the one who promised you would die with me? If you could not watch for one hour, how will you despise death?" But watch and pray, so that you do not fall into the temptation of denying me. The spirit is indeed willing, so that—

<margin>A</margin> —it might not deny me, and for that reason you also make this promise to me; but the flesh is weak, and so if God does not grant strength to the flesh through prayer, you will be in danger. And when he had found them sleeping again, he did not rebuke them harshly: for their eyes were heavy with sleep. From this, learn of human fickleness and weakness; since we cannot even resist sleep, we often promise things that are impossible for us. Therefore he prays now a third time for those same reasons we mentioned above.

<margin>B</margin> And he comes again, and speaks to them, no longer rebuking them so harshly, although they deserved it because they had not become better after the first rebuke but had instead indulged in sleep. And what does he say? "Sleep now, and rest."

<margin>The Disciples <gloss>katheudete</gloss> <note>original: "καθεύδετε"</note> sleep.</margin> He says these things to them with irony, because he knew the traitor was coming. He says to them, "Now is the time for sleeping; sleep now, behold the enemy comes." He said this mocking their sleepiness. And to hear that he spoke in irony, listen to what he adds immediately: "Rise, let us go." He says this not so that they might flee, but rather so that they might go to meet their enemies. Some, however, have understood his words, "My soul is sorrowful even unto death," in this way: "I am sad, not because I am about to die, but because the Israelites, my own household, are going to crucify me, and for that reason they will be cast out of the kingdom."
