However, God permitted this to happen by a singular dispensation, so that he would not be puffed up; and furthermore, so that he might have compassion for those who fall, having been taught by his own experience how great human <margin>B</margin> weakness and fragility are. It does not matter whether it was one or <margin>The Evangelists do not disagree in essential matters.</margin> two servant girls who accused Peter. Matthew indeed says it was not the same one, but Mark says it was the same one. However, there is no obstacle for us in this regarding the truth of the Gospel. For do they disagree on anything great or anything involving our salvation? Did one say he was crucified and another say he was not? Far from it. Therefore Peter, troubled by fear and forgetting the speech the Lord had said—that "whoever denies me, I also will deny before my Father"—denied him; but repentance and tears led him back to Christ. Now, as for what Matthew said obscurely—that "before the cock crows"—Mark interpreted it: "before it crows twice." For cocks are accustomed to crow many times in one period, then sleep, and after a certain time begin their song again. Therefore, what Matthew said—"before the cock crows"—means "before it completes the cry of the first crowing, you will deny me three times." <margin>A</margin> the Lord gave a doubtful answer. For, "You say so" can be understood as "You have spoken truly" or "You have said what I am." Again, however, when he was questioned and answered nothing, he caused Pilate to wonder. He wondered that one who was learned in the law and eloquent, and who could have wiped away the slanders through a defense, said nothing, but bravely endured the false accusations. Note, however, the bloodthirsty minds of the Jews and the restraint of Pilate, although he himself also deserves condemnation because he did not vigorously defend the just man. For while they were indeed shouting for him to be crucified, Pilate, more gently, tried to rescue Jesus from condemnation; for that reason, <margin>B</margin> he asks again, "What shall I do with Jesus?" Everywhere <margin>Pilate seeks an opportunity</margin> Pilate offers opportunities so that the innocent Jesus might be released. Finally, succumbing to their will, he flogged the Lord—that is, he beat him with lashes—so that they might think he had been condemned by the tribunal, and he handed him over to them to be crucified. For he wished to satisfy the common people—that is, to gratify them as much as possible—rather than doing what was pleasing to the just man and to God.

**And the soldiers led him away into the courtyard, which is the Praetorium, and they called together the whole cohort. For when the Jews—who had heard so many teachings and upon whom many benefits had been bestowed—were so inclined toward such behavior, what can we say of the Gentiles? And so they called together the whole cohort—that is, the entire army—and they clothed him in purple to mock him as a king, and they crown him. Perhaps the wine was also vinegary and the myrrh bitter, and thus they agree: one calls it "myrrhed wine," while the other "vinegar with gall." For wine can be called vinegar because it is sour, and myrrh can be called gall because it is bitter. Nor do they disagree in this: that one says "He was giving him to drink, but he did not take it," and the other, "And when he had tasted it, he would not drink." By saying he "did not receive it," it is made entirely clear that he did not drink. They also cast lots upon his clothes, doing this to mock him, as if they were dividing the clothes of a king, even though they were not of great value. But here, the Gentile <note>Represented by the "good thief" who repents.</note> becomes grateful and recovers his senses; the Jew, however, blasphemes until the end. Furthermore, the Lord is fixed between the two peoples, for He himself is the "cornerstone" joining us together.

Those passing by, that is, those who were traveling along the road, blasphemed the Lord, taunting him as a fraud. Similarly, the high priests said: "He saved others, himself he cannot save." They said this to mock his miracles and to nitpick at them, as if they had been mere illusions. For by performing miracles, he had made many into "false" followers <note>The author implies the priests viewed the miracles as deceptive magic rather than divine acts.</note>. However, the Devil incited them to say, "Let him now descend from the cross." Because the author of evil recognized that salvation would be achieved through the cross, he tempted the LORD again to descend from the cross; for if he had, it would be certain he was not the Son of God, and thus the salvation which comes through the cross would perish. But he truly was the Son of God, and for that very reason, he did not descend. For if he had wished to descend, he would not have ascended in the first place. Knowing that men were to be saved through this, he endured being crucified and suffered many other things to complete his work. And those who were crucified with him also insulted him at first; <margin>E</margin> but afterward, one of the two recognized him as innocent, as Luke <margin>Luke 23.</margin> says, and rebuked the other who was blaspheming.

When the sixth hour had come <note>This corresponds to noon.</note>, darkness fell over the whole earth until the ninth hour <note>3:00 PM.</note>. and at the ninth hour, JESUS cried out with a loud voice, saying, "Eloi, eloi lamasabacthani," which is, if anyone should translate it, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" <margin>Psalm 21.</margin> And some of those standing by, when they heard it, said, "Behold, he calls for Elijah." But someone ran and, having filled <margin>F</margin> a sponge with vinegar and placed it on a reed, offered him a drink, saying, "Let him be, let us see if Elijah will come to take him down." But JESUS, having let out a loud cry, breathed his last. ] The darkness occurred not just in one place, but over the whole earth. If it had been the time of an eclipse, one might say the failing of light was natural; but it was the fourteenth day of the moon <note>The time of Passover, which always occurs during a full moon.</note>, when a natural eclipse is impossible. <margin>Christ held Hebrew things in honor.</margin> Indeed, JESUS cried out the prophetic words in the Hebrew language, showing that even unto death he held Hebrew things in honor. Furthermore, regarding his saying, "Why have you forsaken me," he speaks from the perspective of human nature; as if he were saying, "Why have you forsaken me, a man, O God?" so that he might pray to God

<margin>A</margin>
as one crucified for me? For we humans were the ones deserted, but he was never forsaken by the Father. Listen to what he says: "I am not alone, but the Father is with me." <margin>John 16 <note>The text mistakenly cites John 18.</note></margin> Or perhaps he says this on behalf of the Hebrews; for he himself was a Hebrew according to the flesh. "Why have you forsaken me?"—that is, why have you deserted the Hebrew people, so that they would crucify your Son? For just as we are accustomed to saying, "God raised me up," meaning human nature, so also in this place, "you have forsaken me" means either "my human nature" or "my people." Someone ran to offer him vinegar to drink so that the bitterness of the vinegar might finish him off more quickly. But when <margin>B</margin> JESUS had cried out with a loud voice, he breathed his last, as if provoking death like a Master, and dying by his own power. For this is also a benefit from Christ: that now the spirits of the saints ascend into the hands of the Father, whereas formerly they were held by the underworld, until he came who preached release to the captives.

And the veil of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. When the Centurion <note>A Roman officer in command of 100 men.</note> who stood opposite him saw that he had died after crying out in this way, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God." There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the Less and <margin>C</margin> Joses, and Salome; who, when he was in Galilee, had followed him and ministered to him, and many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem. ] The veil was torn, and by this God manifested that the grace of the Spirit was flying out of the temple, and that the "Holy of Holies" would become visible and accessible to everyone—which indeed happened when the Romans entered. And also, let the temple mourn; that which people usually do in times of calamity, when garments are torn, the temple also did as if it were alive, feeling compassion for its suffering Creator and tearing its own garments. And something else is manifested in this: the flesh itself is the "veil" of our temple, that is, of the mind. Therefore, the power which the flesh held against the spirit was dissolved by the passions of CHRIST.

<margin>D</margin> [The veil was torn] from top to bottom, that is, from Adam until the last of humanity. For Adam is sanctified by the sufferings of Christ; his flesh shall no longer be cursed, nor <margin>The Centurion.</margin> subject to corruption, but we are all honored with incorruptibility. Furthermore, the Centurion (that is, the one who was in charge of a hundred men), seeing that he had died so powerfully and as the master of death, marveled and confessed. Notice, however, the reversal of the order of things: the Jews die <note>Theophylact implies a spiritual death or loss of faith.</note>, the Gentile confesses, the disciples flee, and the women remain. For there were (it says) women there, among whom were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Mary the mother of Joseph. And this was the Mother of God; <margin>The mother of Jesus is called the stepmother of Joseph’s sons.</margin> insofar as she was betrothed to Joseph, she was the <note>original: "noverca"</note> stepmother of Joseph's sons, whose sons were James and Joses. She is called their mother—that is, their stepmother—just as Joseph was called her husband—that is, her betrothed. <margin>E</margin> Salome was the mother of the sons of Zebedee. And there were many other women also, for the author recorded only the names of the more famous ones.

And when evening had already come, because it was the day of preparation <note>original: "parasceue," referring to the Friday before the Sabbath</note>, Joseph came, who was from the city of Arimathea. He was an honorable senator who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God; taking courage, he went in to Pilate and asked for the body of JESUS. Pilate, however, marveled that he was already dead. And having summoned the Centurion to him, he asked him if he had been dead for some time. And when he learned the truth from the Centurion, he granted the body to Joseph. And Joseph, having bought a linen shroud, took him down and wrapped him in the shroud, and laid him in a tomb <margin>F</margin> which had been cut out of the rock; and he rolled a stone to the entrance of the tomb. But MARY Magdalene and MARY the mother of Joses watched where he was laid. Blessed Joseph, while still serving the Law, recognized CHRIST as God; therefore, he dared this praiseworthy deed. He did not think to himself, "I am rich, I might lose my wealth; if I ask for the body of one who was condemned for attempting to seize power, I will be accused by the Jews." He said no such thing to himself, but setting all such thoughts aside, he asked to bury the body of the condemned man. Pilate, indeed, wondered that he was already dead. For he thought that he would struggle in the agony of death for a long time, just as the thieves did.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> He also asked the Centurion if he had died a while ago, that is, before the hour Joseph arrived. Therefore, having received the body, Joseph bought a linen shroud in which he wrapped the one he had taken down; and that which was worthy of honor, he buried with honor. For he himself was a disciple of JESUS, knowing the Lord was worthy of honor. He was "honorable," that is, pious and blameless. He was a "Senator," which was a certain rank <margin>Senator.</margin> that forced those endowed with it to focus on external affairs, and many dangers often arose from it because of the malice of the public forum. Let the wealthy and those performing public duties hear how senatorial dignity was no obstacle to virtue for Joseph. We can interpret "Joseph" as <term>increase</term>; <margin>Joseph of Arimathea.</margin> and "Arimathea" as <term>taking this</term>. <margin>B</margin> May God grant that we also, like that Joseph, may always be increased and added to in the race of virtue, and "taking this"—that is, the good—may receive the body of JESUS through communion, and place it in a tomb cut from rock; that is, in a mindful soul that does not forget God. For that soul is cut from the rock, that is, from CHRIST, who is the rock upon which we can stand firm. Let it be wrapped in a linen shroud, that is, let it be received in a clean body. For the shroud of the soul is the body, like a garment. It is necessary, therefore, not only to receive the divine body of the Lord in a <margin>The soul and the body of the Lord. One should not receive the body of the Lord with things that are not pure.</margin> pure soul, but also in a pure body. Moreover, that other thing must be restrained <margin>C</margin> and explained: for the Mystery is in what is compressed and hidden, and not to be opened to just anyone.

<margin>D</margin> [clothed] in a white robe, and they were terrified. But he said to them: "Do not be terrified; you seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. Behold the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he goes before you into Galilee; there you will see him, just as he told you." And going out quickly, they fled from the tomb. For trembling and amazement had seized them, nor did they say anything to anyone <note>The Latin text here adds "dignum deitate," suggesting they said nothing worthy of His divinity, though the Vulgate simply says they said nothing to anyone.</note>; for they were afraid. ] These wise women were thinking of nothing great or worthy of Jesus's divinity as they sat by the tomb and bought ointments, so that they might anoint the body according to custom, that it might remain fragrant and that nothing foul might arise from corruption. They intended the ointments and other substances, which have the power of drying and absorbing the body's moisture, to keep it uncorrupted. These were the thoughts of the women. And <margin>E</margin> <margin>Matthew 18 <note>Likely a misprint for Matthew 28.</note>, Luke 23 <note>Likely a misprint for Luke 24.</note></margin> **very early in the morning**, which Matthew calls the **evening of the Sabbath**, and Luke calls **deep dawn**. On **one of the Sabbaths**, that is, the first of the days of the week. For they used to call the days of the week "Sabbaths," and the first day "One." They rose and came to the tomb, and they were debating: **who will roll away the stone for us?** While they were wondering, the angel rolled back the stone, without the women noticing. This is also what Matthew says: that as the women were going, the angel rolled back the stone. Mark remained silent on this point, because Matthew had already said by whom the stone was rolled away. However, as to what Matthew says—that the angel was **atop the stone**—whereas Mark says that after they entered the tomb, the women saw <margin>F</margin> him sitting inside, there is no contradiction. For it is possible that the one they saw sitting outside on the stone, as Matthew says, they saw again inside the tomb, having preceded the women and entered before them. Some say, however, that the women in Matthew’s account were different from those in Mark’s. But Mary Magdalene was a companion to them all, doubtless because she was eager, fervent, and diligent in her service. Therefore, the one who had appeared said to the women, **"Do not be terrified."** First, he frees them from fear, then he brings the good news of the resurrection. He specifically calls him **"the Crucified."** For he is not ashamed of the cross, which is the salvation of mankind and the source <note>original: "caput"</note> of all good things. **"He has risen."** From where

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> is this manifest? **"He is not here."** And do you wish to be confirmed in faith? **"Behold the place where they laid him."** For he had also rolled back the stone for this reason: to show them the place. **"But go, tell the disciples and Peter."** He singles out Peter from the other disciples as the leader <note>original: "praecipuum"</note>, and names him specifically because of his excellence. Or perhaps it was because Peter had denied him: if the women had come and said that they were commanded to announce this to the disciples, Peter might have said, "I denied Him, I am no longer His disciple, He has cast me off and detests me." Therefore, for his sake, the angel adds **"and Peter,"** so that Peter would not be offended or feel he did not deserve the message because he had denied Him, or that he was unworthy to be numbered among the other disciples. Furthermore, he sends them into Galilee, snatching them away from <margin>B</margin> the tumult and fear of the Jews. Moreover, trembling and ecstasy—that is, stupor—had seized the women, both at the sight of the angel and in the awe of the resurrection. And for that reason, they said nothing to anyone. For they were afraid, and had forgotten everything they had heard. 

**"But when Jesus had risen early on the first day of the Sabbath, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, out of whom he had cast seven demons. She went and reported it to those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe. And they went and reported it <margin>C</margin> to the rest, but they did not believe them either."** ] Place a period at this point: **"When Jesus had risen."** <note>Theophylact is providing a lesson in punctuation to clarify the Greek grammar: Jesus didn't necessarily rise "early," but he *appeared* early.</note> Then: **"Early on the first day of the Sabbath, he appeared to Mary Magdalene."** For he did not necessarily rise in the morning. Indeed, who saw when he rose? But he appeared in the morning on the Lord's day, which is the "first day of the Sabbath," that is, of the week, which he called "one of the Sabbaths" above. To Mary Magdalene, out of whom he had cast **seven demons**, which means "many." For Scripture is accustomed to use the number seven to represent a multitude; for example, "the barren woman has borne seven." Or, **seven demons** <margin>The number seven in the Scripture of Isaiah 11.</margin> which are contrary to the seven spirits of virtue <note>The "Sevenfold Spirit" or Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit.</note>, such as the spirit of presumption (which is the opposite of humble fear), the spirit of folly (without intellect), the spirit of ignorance, or the spirit of lying—however many there are that are contrary to the gifts of the Spirit. After these things, he appeared to two of them as they were walking.

<margin>D</margin> [Jesus appeared] in another form, about which Luke also speaks, and those disciples announced it to the others. And they did not believe them either. How, then, does Luke say that upon returning they found the eleven gathered together saying, "The Lord has risen"? We say, therefore, that when Mark says they announced it to "the rest," he is not speaking of the eleven apostles, but of certain others. For he who believes and is baptized—though if he is still a catechumen <note>A "catechumen" (Greek: *katekhoumenos*) is a person receiving basic instruction in Christianity before full initiation. It can also be understood this way: "They will pick up serpents," just as Paul held a viper in his hand and was not harmed by it. "Even if they drink anything deadly, it will not hurt them." Often these things have happened, as we find in historical accounts. For many, even...

### ARGUMENT FOR THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO LUKE.

<margin>
When Luke wrote the Gospel.
To whom the title "Most Excellent" was attributed in antiquity.
Acts 26.
</margin>

Saint Luke was a native of Antioch by birth, skilled in the art of medicine, and highly accomplished in secular philosophy. He was also thoroughly educated in the Hebrew disciplines in Jerusalem. Indeed, while our LORD was teaching (as some report), he became one of the seventy disciples. And when Christ had risen from the dead, he encountered Him along with Cleopas <note>This refers to the appearance on the road to Emmaus described in Luke 24.</note>. After the LORD was taken up into heaven, and Paul was converted to the faith, Luke became his companion in travel—Paul's, I mean—and he wrote the Gospel with all diligence, as his own prologue declares, fifteen years after Christ’s assumption into heaven. He writes, moreover, to Theophilus, a man of senatorial rank and perhaps a governor. For the title "Most Excellent" <note>original: "Strenui nomen"; a translation of the Greek 'kratiste', a formal address for high-ranking officials</note> was attributed to princes and governors, just as Paul says to the governor Festus, "Most Excellent Festus" <note>Acts 26:25</note>. ### PROLOGUE OF THE BLESSED LUKE to his Gospel.

Inasmuch as many have attempted to weave together a narrative of those things which have been proven among us by many arguments, just as they were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, it seemed good to me also, having investigated everything carefully from the beginning, to write to you in order, Most Excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the certainty <note>original: "communionem" here used in the sense of the established truth or common understanding</note> of those words in which you have been instructed. ] Who were those "many" who attempted this? The false apostles. For many at that time wrote Gospels, such as what they call <margin>The Gospel of the Egyptians; The Gospel of the Twelve.</margin> the Gospel according to the Egyptians, and that which is titled the Gospel according to the Twelve. These people merely attempted, but did not finish. Because they began without divine grace, they did not complete the work. Luke rightly said "many have tried." But a few, like Matthew and Mark, did not just attempt it, but finished it. For they were gifted with the Spirit, who brings works to perfection. He spoke of things "proven by many arguments." For the things of CHRIST were not handed down simply or nakedly, but with true and solid faith, and the certainty of many proofs. And how, tell us Luke, are they proven by many arguments? "Just as they were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word." From this it is clear that Luke was not a disciple from the beginning, but joined in later times. For others had learned from the beginning, such as Peter and the sons of Zebedee, who handed down to him the things he himself had not seen or heard. But what does he mean when he says, "so that you may know the certainty of the words in which you have been instructed"? I have two interpretations for this. One is this: "Earlier, I instructed you without writings, O Theophilus; now I deliver the written Gospel to you, and thus fortify your mind so that it does not forget those words..."

CHAPTER 1. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...those things which were handed down without being written. For the second point: we humans are often accustomed, when someone speaks to us without writing, to suspect that perhaps some lie has been mixed in. However, when a person also writes down what they speak, then we believe them, because they would not have written it unless they were confident they were speaking the truth. Therefore, the Evangelist says: "For this reason I have written the Gospel for you, so that you may preserve with greater security those things in which you were instructed without writing, having greater faith in me now, as I am so confident in these things I taught orally that I did not fear to commit them even to writing." Note also that he says "that you might recognize" <note>original: "agnoscas"</note> and not simply "know" <note>original: "scias"</note>; that is, that you may receive a second time a greater knowledge, trust, and security that I am not lying.

## CHAPTER I.

<margin>How the prophets are accustomed to begin their narratives.</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial letter E containing a seated figure, possibly an evangelist or saint, writing at a desk with a book on a lectern.</image-desc>**There was in the days of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.**] 
He makes mention of the reign of Herod, partly to preserve the style of the prophets—for they begin in this way: "In the days of Joachaz and Hezekiah," or some other king, "these things took place"—and partly because he is about to speak of Christ. He mentions Herod to show that Christ truly came under Herod's reign. For this Herod was in power when the native princes among the Jews had failed, according to the prophecy of Jacob. <margin>F</margin> <margin>Genesis 49.</margin> Thus it is demonstrated that <term>CHRIST</term> <note>The text uses the prophecy in Genesis 49:10, "The scepter shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh comes," to argue that the arrival of a foreign king like Herod signaled the time for the Messiah.</note> had indeed come. But he also does rightly in this: by showing the time, he shows the Gospel to be more certain. He provides the opportunity for any who wish to search and learn the truth of the Gospel based on the date. He begins with Zacharias, the father of John, and rightly so; since he is about to speak of Christ’s birth, and John was the forerunner of Christ, he narrates that even John's birth was not without a miracle. And because a virgin was to give birth, God pre-ordained that an old woman should give birth—not according to the law of nature, although by a husband. What, then, does **Of the course of Abijah** <note>original: "Ex vice Abia"</note> mean? Some understand it to mean that there were two priests who performed the ministry in succession, one of whom was 

<column-break/>

EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE.
169

<margin>A</margin> Abijah, and the other Zacharias. Therefore, because Abijah had performed the priestly office, Zacharias ministered after his service. However, it seems this is not the case. For when Solomon had finished the temple, he established <term>courses</term> <note>original: "vices"; these refers to the twenty-four priestly divisions or "shifts" that served in the Temple for a week at a time.</note>, that is, weeks of service. In one he appointed the sons of Korah, in another Asaph, in another Abijah, and in another someone else. Therefore, when it says he was "of the course of Abijah," it must be understood that he was of the "week" of Abijah. It does not mean that he performed his ministry *after* the week of Abijah; for then it would have said "after the week of Abijah." But when it says "of the course of Abijah," it shows that he was from the order and the week belonging to Abijah. Furthermore, wishing to show that John was legitimately from a priestly line through both parents, <margin>Numbers 36.</margin> he says: <margin>B</margin> **And his wife was of the daughters of Aaron.** For it was not permitted to take a wife from another tribe, but only from the same one. **Elizabeth** is interpreted as "God’s rest," while **Zacharias** means "the memory of the Lord."

**And they were both righteous before God.**] Some are righteous, but not before God; they are so in appearance only and before men. But these two were righteous even before God.

**Walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.** **Commandments** <margin>Commandments.</margin> indeed are such as "thou shalt not kill," "thou shalt not commit adultery"; <margin>Exodus 20.</margin> but **ordinances** <note>original: "iustificationes," often translated as "justifications" or "statutes."</note> <margin>Ordinances.</margin> are such as "he who curses father or mother, let him die the death." <margin>Exodus 21.</margin> For this is just <note>original: "iustum," implying the legal penalty or "justification" of the law.</note>. Know also that a **commandment** <margin>C</margin> <margin>Leviticus 20.</margin> can be called an "ordinance" insofar as it makes a person just—indeed, even being God's own ordinance. <margin>John 15.</margin> For on that day, he condemns us as if a certain written ordinance exists within us. "If I had not come," He says, "and spoken to you, they would not have had sin." And again: "The word that I have spoken to them, that shall condemn them." But why, when he said "walking in all the commandments," did he add **blameless**? Many walk in the law of God, but they do everything so that they may be seen by men. Such people are not blameless. But Zacharias both performed the commandments and did so without cause for reproach, not doing such things to please men.

**And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren...**

# CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin>
**[...to the] Apostles.** For the Jews were the "fathers," but the Apostles were their "sons." He [John] therefore turns the hearts of the Jews toward the Apostles by teaching and testifying about Christ. For whoever testifies about Christ makes all people faithful and his own disciples. John did not convert everyone, but he did convert many; Christ, however, enlightened all. And he [John] went before Him "in the spirit of Elijah." <note>John the Baptist is often compared to the prophet Elijah because of his fiery preaching and ascetic lifestyle.</note> For just as grace was effective in Elijah, so it was in John. And just as Elijah is the forerunner of the [Christ's] second coming, so John was the forerunner of the first. He came "in the power of Elijah" because both had the same goal for their coming: both gather people toward Christ. In another sense, John came in the power and spirit of Elijah because he too was a dweller of the wilderness, lived a simple life, and rebuked others just as Elijah did. He also converts the unbelieving <margin>E</margin> Jews to the "prudence of the just," which is the doctrine of the Apostles. 

<margin>The prudence of the apostles.</margin> 
The prudence of the Apostles is the grace of the Spirit within them. He also prepared for the Lord (that is, Christ) a "prepared people," which means a people capable of receiving the preaching. For example: when any prophet came preaching, not everyone believed, but only those who were prepared and who disposed themselves toward it. For just as if someone arrives at a house at night, not everyone receives him, but only those who are awake, waiting, and ready to welcome him; so too John prepared a people for the Lord—not an unbelieving people, but one worked upon and made ready to receive the Lord.

And Zacharias said to the angel, "By what sign shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife <margin>F</margin> is advanced in years." And the angel, answering, said to him, "I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you these glad tidings. And behold, it shall come to pass that you will be silent and unable to speak until the day these things happen, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their own time."] Although Zacharias was righteous and holy, yet looking at the miraculous nature of conceiving a son, he did not easily believe. For this reason, the Angel declares his own dignity: "I am the Angel who stands in the presence of God; I am not a deceiving demon, but an Angel of God." Therefore, because you are hesitant, I will make you deaf and you will not be able to speak. Rightly, however, he suffered these two

<margin>D</margin> [David] conquered through gentleness and reigned, and the Lord reigned through the gentleness of the cross he took up. Do you see how he is said to sit "on the throne of David"? For just as David received a sensible <note>Meaning a physical or earthly kingdom that can be perceived by the senses.</note> kingdom, so the Lord received a spiritual one. Of this kingdom there will be no end. For there is no end to the kingdom of Christ—that is, the knowledge of God and of Christianity. For even when we suffer persecution, we flourish by the grace of Christ.

**And Mary said to the Angel, "How will this be, since I do not know a man?" And the Angel answering, said to her, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you, therefore also that which is born holy will be called the Son of God."** ] <margin>E</margin> The Virgin did not say "How will this be for me?" as if she lacked faith; rather, as a prudent and intelligent woman, she sought to understand the *manner* in which it would happen. For such a thing had never happened before, nor would it ever happen again. Therefore, the Angel forgives her and does not condemn her as he did Zechariah, but instead teaches her the method. Zechariah was rightly condemned because he had many examples to look to—for many sterile women had previously conceived—but for a virgin, there was no prior example. "The Holy Spirit," the Angel says, "will come upon you and the power of the Most High will overshadow you," making your womb fruitful and creating the flesh for the Word <note>The Logos or Second Person of the Trinity.</note> who is of the same substance. The "power of the Most High" is the Son of God, for Christ is the power of God.

<margin>To overshadow.</margin><margin>F</margin> "He will overshadow you," that is, he will cover you and surround you on all sides. Just as a bird overshadows its chicks with its wings, so the divine power takes hold of the whole Virgin; this is what it means to "overshadow." Perhaps someone else might say that just as a painter first sketches the outlines and adds the shadows, and then adds the perfect color, so the Lord himself, creating his own flesh and forming the image of a man, first sketched it in the womb of the Virgin—compacted from the blood of the ever-virgin flesh—which he then gradually shaped. But this is a point of debate. For there are those who say that as soon as the Lord overshadowed the womb of the Virgin, the infant was immediately perfect. Others do not accept this. For listen to what he says: "Therefore

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and that which is born holy," which means that which grows little by little in the womb and does not exist as a perfect being immediately. Furthermore, let Nestorius <note>A 5th-century bishop whose views on the nature of Christ were declared heretical; he was accused of separating the humanity and divinity of Jesus into two distinct persons.</note> be confounded in this place. For he said that it was not the Son of God resting in the womb of the Virgin, but that a <margin>The Nestorian heresy.</margin> "naked man" was born of the Virgin, who afterwards had God as a companion. Let him hear, therefore, that what was being born in the womb *was* the Son of God. The offspring of the womb is not one thing and the Son of God another; rather, the Son of the Virgin and the Son of God are one and the same. See also how he declared the Holy Trinity, by naming the Holy Spirit, the Son as "the Power," and the Father as "the Most High."

**"And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman, she also has conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called sterile, because no word will be impossible with God." And Mary said, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord, let it be to me according to your word." And the Angel departed from her.** ] <margin>B</margin> Someone might perhaps doubt how the Virgin was a kinswoman to Elizabeth. For the Virgin was from the tribe of Judah, but Elizabeth was from the daughters of Aaron <note>The priestly line of the tribe of Levi.</note>. The Law commanded that spouses be from the same tribe, so that kinships remained within a single tribe. It must be said, therefore, that since the Babylonian Captivity, the lineages have become mixed. It is better said that Aaron took as his wife Elizabeth <note>In the Old Testament, Aaron's wife is Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab.</note>, who was the daughter of Amminadab, who was from the tribe of Judah. Do you see how Elizabeth was related to the Mother of God <note>original: "Dei genitrix" — the Latin equivalent of the Greek title *Theotokos*.</note> from the beginning and from Aaron? Because the wife of Aaron descended from Judah—the tribe from which the Mother of God came—and Elizabeth was of the daughters of Aaron, the Mother of God is rightly called the kinswoman of Elizabeth, for her great-grandmother (that is, the wife of Aaron) was from the tribe of Judah. <margin>C</margin> Consider the logic of this kinship. But let us see what the Virgin says: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord, let it be to me according to your word." She is saying, "I am a painter's tablet; let the painter paint what he wishes, let God do what he wills." And thus, even what she had said before—"How will this be?"—was not a sign of unbelief, but of a desire to learn the manner of it. For if she had disbelieved, she would by no means have said, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord, let it be to me according to your word." "He departed," for Gabriel (if anyone interprets the name) remains Gabriel. <note>The name Gabriel means "God is my strength" or "Man of God."</note>

...attributing nothing to herself. For He said—<margin>D</margin> "He looked upon my lowliness," not "I looked toward Him." His mercy followed me; I did not seek Him. And from this time all generations shall call me blessed: not only Elizabeth, but the generation of those who have believed. But why do they call me blessed? Not because of my own virtue, but because "He who is mighty has done great things for me." She calls God "Mighty" so that no one might doubt the things she says, considering that God is powerful enough to do them. Furthermore, she calls His name "Holy," declaring that that most pure conception in her womb is not defiled, but remains holy. Nor is His mercy upon me alone, but upon all who fear Him. <margin>E</margin> Indeed, those who are entirely unworthy do not attain mercy. By saying that the mercy of God is "from generation to generation," she shows that they attain mercy both in this present age and in the eternal one. For here they receive a hundredfold, and there far more. Notice, however, that first she says, "My soul magnifies the Lord," and then, "my spirit exults," to say something similar. You "magnify" God when you walk worthily according to God as a called <term>Christian (one who follows Christ)</term>, not thinning out the name and dignity of Christ by doing what is not <margin>The distinction between soul and spirit. 1 Corinthians 2. Galatians 6. Ephesians 1. Colossians 1.</margin> appropriate, but magnifying Him by performing great and heavenly works. And then your spirit will also exult—that is, the spiritual gift you received through your excellent works will rejoice and make progress, and it will not be shriveled or (so to speak) put to death. You should know, moreover, that while Scripture appears to <margin>F</margin> use "spirit" and "soul" simply as the same thing, they actually differ in a proper sense. For he calls a <term>natural man (literally 'soulish man')</term> one who lives according to nature and is governed by human reasons—for instance, if he eats when hungry, hates an enemy, and in short, if nothing beyond human nature appears in him. But he calls a "spiritual man" one who transcends the laws of nature and does not think in a human way. This is the difference between soul and spirit in Scripture. Physicians perhaps distinguish these things differently, but we hold Scripture to our heart; let the physicians be well. <margin>Genesis 22.</margin> The Lord has shown strength with His arm; He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. Therefore, God performed strength and virtue and power against nature in His Son. For when the Son became incarnate, nature was conquered—a virgin giving birth, God becoming true man. And the Lord scattered the proud demons, casting them out from human souls; some were sent into the abyss, and others into swine. This can also be understood regarding the Jews, whom He scattered into every region, <margin>B</margin> and now they are scattered. There are also the Pharisees, <margin>The Pharisees are the powerful ones who snatch away the things of the poor.</margin> who were certainly powerful in snatching away the things of the poor, and who held "chairs" as teachers, from which they were deposed. And He exalted the humble and hungry—humanity whom sin had humbled, or the Gentiles. He exalted them by adopting them as sons. Therefore, just as we may call the Gentiles "the hungry" (since they did not have the scriptures, the law, or the commandments), whom He filled with the good things of the scriptures, so too the Jews were "rich" in the law and the commandments, whom He sent out empty from the earthly and heavenly Jerusalem. For the Jews have nothing, even if they seem to have something. <margin>C</margin> "He helped Israel His servant"—either he is speaking of the fleshly Israelites (for many thousands of them believed) and the promise made to Abraham was fulfilled, to whom God had said: "In your seed shall all the tribes <margin>Genesis 22. The double Israel. Mary while she returns to Elizabeth.</margin> of the earth be blessed," or he is speaking of the spiritual Israel. For everyone who "sees God" is called Israel, according to the interpretation of the name <note>original: "iuxta nominis interpretationem". Theophylact uses the common medieval etymology of Israel as "the man who sees God."</note>. Therefore, He helped those who see God, leading them into the heavenly inheritance. Now, Mary remained with Elizabeth for about three months, and then returned. Because Elizabeth was about to give birth, the virgin departed on account of the multitude of people who would gather for the birth; it would be unbecoming for a virgin to be involved in such matters.

### CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,
### ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 176

<margin>D</margin> That the Virgin returned home just as Elizabeth was about to give birth is clear from this: the Angel came to Mary in the sixth month of the <term>precursor's (John the Baptist, who "runs before" Christ)</term> conception, and she stayed with Elizabeth for about three months. Look, that makes almost nine months.

[Now the time was fulfilled for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown His great mercy toward her, and they congratulated her. And it happened on the eighth day, they came to circumcise the boy, and they were calling him by the name of his father, Zacharias. And responding, his mother said, "Not so, but he shall be called 
<margin>B</margin> John." And they said to her, "There is no one in your family who is called by that name." They made signs to his father as to what he would want him called. And having asked for writing tablets, he wrote, saying, "John is his name." And they all marveled. And immediately his mouth was opened, and his tongue [loosed], and he spoke, praising God.] 

The Virgin indeed stayed with Elizabeth for about three months, perhaps astonished by such a great miracle and needing a kind of consolation, which she received from her regular company with Elizabeth. But when the birth drew near, she departed. Now, when "the time was fulfilled" for Elizabeth to give birth, it should be noted that this is not said of sinners. "The time of giving birth was fulfilled" is found only where the birth of the righteous is mentioned. For (as it appears) the births of sinners are imperfect and unfulfilled, and it would be better for them if they had not been born. Why, however, 
<margin>F</margin> is the name given after circumcision? Because the seal of God must be received first, and then the human
<margin>What the name and circumcision represent.</margin> name. Or otherwise, circumcision signifies the casting off of fleshly things. No one, therefore, unless he first casts off and cuts away fleshly things, is worthy to be called a soldier of God or to have his name written in the book of the heavens. Elizabeth, truly like a prophetess, indicated the name: "JOHN shall be his name." But perhaps John himself bestowed the name upon himself and shared the prophetic gift with his mother. Furthermore, Zacharias, since he could not indicate the name by a nod <note>original: "nutu" - Zacharias was mute and likely deaf as well, as they had to "make signs" to him</note>, asked for tablets. And because he 

---

<margin>A</margin> agreed with his wife's opinion regarding the boy's name, they were all amazed, for there was no one in their family of that name, so that one might say they had both discussed this beforehand. JOHN, according to its interpretation <note>The Hebrew name Yochanan means "The Lord is Gracious"</note>, is THE GRACE OF GOD: consequently, his father immediately obtained grace, and prophesies first concerning CHRIST, and then concerning the boy.

### CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,
### ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 177

<margin>Horn.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Now the **horn of salvation** refers to power and a saving kingdom. For a **horn** signifies either power—since horned animals have their strength in their horns—or a kingdom, for kings used to be anointed from a horn <note>In biblical times, kings were often anointed with oil poured from a ram's horn, symbolizing both strength and divine selection</note>. Therefore, Christ is both the power and the kingdom of the Father. Thus, the horn of salvation, **CHRIST**, was "raised up." For He seemed to be sleeping, disregarding the sins of many, showing patience during the insane worship of idols; but incarnated in the last times, He was raised up, and He crushed all the demons who hated us, no longer patient and sleeping. Furthermore, He was raised up in the house of David, that is, in Bethlehem, for He was born there.

<margin>Bethlehem, the homeland of David. Micah 5.</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
Bethlehem was the homeland of David. **As the prophets have spoken**, for they all spoke of the incarnation. Micah also mentions the house of David—I mean Bethlehem—saying: *And you, Bethlehem, are by no means the least, for from you shall come a leader.* <note>original: "Et tu Bethlehem neutiquam minima es, ex te enim egredietur dux"</note> Moreover, He **showed mercy**, not only to the living, but also to 

<margin>His mercy reaches even to those who died long ago. The mercy of Christ benefited them.</margin>
our fathers. For the grace of Christ reaches even those who died long ago. He gave to us who are living the hope of the resurrection before it happened, and we have risen; but we were not the only ones to obtain this grace, but also those who had died before us. For all nature partook of the good. Or otherwise: He **showed mercy to the fathers** because He fulfilled their hope. For they saw fulfilled whatever they had expected concerning Christ. But also when the fathers see 

<margin>Genesis 22. Hebrews 9.</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
their children enjoying such good things, they rejoice and share in the joy, just as if it had been bestowed upon themselves. And of which **covenant**, and of which **oath**, does he remember that was made to Abraham? Certainly this one: *Blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.* <note>Genesis 22:17</note> Now Abraham is truly multiplied, since children from all the nations have been adopted for him through faith. For just as he believed, so they have claimed him as their own through faith. Moreover, He **delivered us** 

<margin>Why Christ delivered us.</margin>
**from our enemies without fear**. Often certain people deliver others, but not without our own fear, struggle, and contest; but Christ, when we had not labored, was crucified for us and delivered us without fear—that is, without danger to us. Why then did He deliver us? Was it for food and 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
drink? No, but **so that we might serve Him**: not once, nor for two days, but all our days. And let us serve not with bodily adoration and ministry alone, but in **holiness and justice**. Now, **holiness** is justice toward God; whereas **justice** is fairness toward men. For example, if someone abstains from sacred things and does not approach divine matters impiously but shows all honor to venerable things, he is **holy**.

<margin>Holy. Just.</margin>
Similarly, he who honors his parents is holy; for they are also "domestic gods" <note>The author uses this term to emphasize that the honor due to parents is a form of religious piety second only to God</note>. But if someone is not greedy, not a robber, not a thief, not an adulterer, he is called **just**. Therefore, it is necessary to serve God in **holiness**—that is, reverence toward divine things—and in **justice**—that is, a life praised in human affairs. Finally, we must serve **before Him**, not before men, like those who want to please men, as the hypocrites do.

<margin>B</margin>
[**And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare His ways, to give knowledge of salvation to His people, through the remission of their sins. Through the tender mercy of our God, by which the rising sun from on high has visited us. To give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace. But the child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and he was in the desert until the day he was to be revealed to the Israelites.**]

It seems rare that Zacharias speaks to a child who is as yet without sense; how could he speak to him?

<margin>C</margin>
It must be said, therefore, that just as the child had a rare and admirable birth—who leaped and prophesied in the womb at the arrival of Mary—so it is no wonder if he understood those things which were said by his father after his birth. "**You shall go before the Lord**," he says, "leaving me behind," though not immediately. For Zacharias knew that not much later he would be deprived of him, when the boy would flee into the desert. But why "**shall you go before**"? So that the 

<margin>The ways of the Lord.</margin>
**ways of the Lord might be prepared**. The **ways** are the souls in which the Lord walks, which the <term>precursor (John the Baptist, who prepares the way)</term> prepared, so that **CHRIST** might walk in them. But how did he prepare them? By giving knowledge of salvation to the people. Indeed, the Lord **JESUS** was the salvation...

### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>To whom it belongs to forgive sins. Malachi 4.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Therefore, this is the **knowledge of salvation** <note>original: "scientia salutis"</note> given to Christ’s people by **JOHN**. For John bears witness to Jesus. This knowledge, however, consisted in the **remission of sins**. Indeed, Christ would not have been recognized as God unless He had forgiven sins, for it belongs to God alone to forgive sins. It was not because of our works—for we have done nothing good—but He visited us from on high, He who is called the **Rising Sun** <note>original: "Oriens"; a reference to the 'Dayspring' or 'Dawn' mentioned in Luke 1:78</note>. For He is the **Sun of Justice** and has shone upon 

<margin>Sin</margin>
us who were in darkness—that is, in ignorance—and in the **shadow of death** <note>original: "umbra mortis"</note>—that is, sitting in sins. Two evils invaded the human race: ignorance of God, which the **Gentiles** <note>Non-Jewish peoples who at the time were considered to be without the knowledge of the one God</note> had, and sin, which the **Hebrews** had, 

<margin>E</margin>
even though they knew God. Thus He appeared to human nature so that He might enlighten both those sitting in darkness (the ignorance of God) and those in the **shadow of death**. (He calls sin the shadow of death, for sin is indeed the shadow cast by death). I believe sin is called the shadow of death because just as a shadow follows a body, so where there is death, there is sin. Hence, because Adam died, it follows that sin was also there. You will not even find Christ’s death without sin; for Christ died, but He died **because of our sins**. Thus, sin is deservedly called the shadow of death, because death always accompanies it. Other things could be said on this, and I believe we discussed it in our commentary on Matthew. Is it enough, then, for the sun to have shone upon those in darkness? Not at all. 

<margin>F</margin>
There is also a need for our feet to be directed into the **way of peace**, which is the way of justice. For just as sin is a state of enmity with God, so justice is peace. The way of peace, therefore, is the way of justice, toward which **CHRIST**, who rose from the highest, has directed the feet of our souls. Furthermore, the child grew in physical stature and was **strengthened in spirit**. For the spiritual gift grew along with his body. The more the child grew, the more the power of the spirit manifested in him, as his physical "instrument" became capable of holding it. But why was he in the deserts? So that he would not become a partaker in the malice of the crowds, and so that, fearing no man, he might rebuke them freely. For if he had been in the world, he might perhaps have been defiled by the habits of friends and social company; but he lived there so that he might be held worthy of trust 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
as one who would preach **CHRIST**, being a hermit whose life excelled all others. He remained hidden in the deserts until it seemed right to God that he should be shown to the people of Israel.

<margin>D</margin> [And he was] afterwards the second. He is laid in a manger, however, so that from the very beginning he might teach us frugality. In this passage, however, "words" seem to mean "matters" or "deeds," <margin>D</margin> and the meaning is this: Mary was preserving all these things which I am now speaking of, and she made them into deeds. For when deeds are narrated, they are called "words" <note>original: "verba" — in Biblical Hebrew and Greek, the word for "word" often also signifies an "event" or "thing."</note>. Furthermore, the shepherds returned, giving thanks to God for everything; for they were not hated by the Jews.

And after eight days were completed, so that the child might be circumcised, his name was called **JESUS**, which had been called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. <margin>Gen. 17.</margin> And after the days of their purification were completed <margin>Lev. 12.</margin> according to the law of Moses, they <margin>Exo. 34.</margin> brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the **LORD**, <margin>Exo. 13.</margin> just as it is written in the law of the Lord: "Every <margin>Deut. 15. <br/> E</margin> male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord"; and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord, "a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons."] Those who transgressed the mandates of the law were under a curse. Therefore, the Lord is circumcised so that, by fulfilling the law even in this, and omitting nothing that it commanded, he might rescue us from the curse. <margin>Curious questions should be avoided.</margin> Let those feel a sense of shame here who say that **CHRIST** was incarnate in appearance only <note>Theophylact is arguing against Docetism, an early belief that Jesus only "seemed" to have a physical body.</note>. It is useless, however, to ask where that cut-off piece <note>original: "particula" — referring to the foreskin removed during circumcision.</note> might be. For one ought not to seek out those things which scripture has kept silent, especially where there is no benefit. However, it could be said that when the cut-off portion touched the ground, it sanctified it, just as did the blood and water which flowed from his side. <margin>F</margin> And it seems likely that he preserved that portion unharmed, and took it up again in the resurrection, so that even this piece would not be found missing. Indeed, we too shall take up a perfect body in the resurrection. Observe, moreover, that the Angel did not say "you are conceiving a son" and immediately the Lord was conceived; rather, he was conceived later, when he willed it. For see what is said in this place: that he was "called by the Angel, before he was conceived in the womb." This phrase demonstrates what we have said. For he did not say, "Behold, you [now] conceive," but "Behold, you *shall* conceive." From this we may notice that the Lord was indeed conceived on that day,

<margin>A</margin> but not at the very moment the angel spoke, but perhaps after he had finished his speech. However, we do not say these things definitively. "And the days of their purification were fulfilled according to the law of Moses." He said "according to the law of Moses" rightly, for according to the truth, he was bound by no necessity to wait for the days of purification—which are forty days for a male child. For it is said in the law, "A woman who has conceived by seed <note>original: "femine" / "semine"</note> and given birth to a male." But the Virgin did not conceive by seed, but gave birth from the Holy Spirit; thus no necessity urged her, but wishing to fulfill the law, she came into the temple. Moreover, what it says, "Every [male] opening the womb," applies properly to Christ alone. <margin>B</margin> For he himself opened the virgin's womb, whereas for others, a man opens the womb. Furthermore, the law ordered a pair of turtledoves to be offered, showing that he was procreated from a chaste marriage. <margin>The nature of turtledoves.</margin> For they say that the turtledove is a chaste animal; when it loses its mate, it does not mate a second time. However, when they did not have turtledoves, they offered two young pigeons, so that the multiplication of offspring might be signified. For the pigeon is a fruitful animal.

And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon, and this man was just and pious, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. A light for the revelation of the gentians, and the glory of your people Israel."] Simeon was not a priest, but a man who loved God, <margin>That Simeon was not a priest.</margin> and was waiting for when Christ would come to console the Hebrews and liberate them from the slavery of sin—and perhaps also from the slavery they served under the Romans and Herod. For he who believes in Christ is truly free, and more worthy than all kings and enemies. See the apostles: they were not slaves of the Romans.

Put a full stop after you have said "for the fall"; then begin "for the resurrection of many." 

As for the "sign," it is the cross, <margin>The Cross.</margin> which even to this time is spoken against—that is, it is not accepted by the unbelieving. The incarnation is also called a sign, and a miraculous sign. <margin>B</margin> For God was man, and a virgin was a mother; yet this sign—the incarnation, I mean—is spoken against. For some say his flesh was from man, others that it was only in appearance <note>referring to Docetism, the belief that Christ only appeared to be human</note>, and others babble various other things. 

"And a sword," I say, "shall pierce your own soul, O Virgin." Perhaps this refers to the pain she bore during the Passion. Perhaps he calls the "stumbling block" a *rhomphæa* <note>original: "rhomphæam" — a large, double-edged sword or polearm, emphasizing the intensity of the grief or doubt.</note>, by which she was offended; for seeing him crucified, she perhaps thought: "How is it that he who was born without seed, who performed miracles, who raised the dead, is now crucified, spat upon, and dead?" When he says, "so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed," this signifies that the thoughts of many who are offended will be revealed and made manifest, and having been rebuked, they will find a sudden <margin>C</margin> remedy. Just as you, O Virgin, will be revealed and it will be manifest what you think about Christ, and then you will be confirmed in faith in him. Similarly, Peter will be revealed when he denies him, but the power of God will be clearly shown, which received him back through repentance. And another way: "thoughts were revealed from hearts" when the traitor appeared, <margin>Matt. 25.</margin> and those who loved him appeared—such as Joseph <margin>John 16.</margin> who went to Pilate, and the women who remained with Christ.

### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> [ ...she was a widow of about eighty-four years, who did not depart from the temple, serving night and day with fastings and prayers. And coming up at that very hour, she in turn gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke of him to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem. And when they had performed all things according to the law of Moses, they returned into Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and was filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him. ] The Evangelist provides the genealogy of Anna, listing her father and tribe, so that we may know he speaks the truth by summoning so many witnesses who knew her father and her tribe.

<margin>E</margin> She, therefore, in turn "confessed to God" <note>original: "confitebatur" — in this context, the Latin carries the sense of public acknowledgement or thanksgiving.</note>, that is, she gave thanks, and she taught everyone about the Lord: that he himself was the Savior and the consolation for us who await redemption. Moreover, after they had performed all these things, they returned to Galilee, to their own city, Nazareth. Bethlehem was indeed their city, but as a place of birth; Nazareth, however, was their city as a place of residence. Now, Jesus grew in regard to his body, for although he could have come forth from his mother’s womb in the stature of a perfect man, he would have then seemed like a phantom <note>original: "phantasma" — a reference to the Docetic heresy which claimed Christ only appeared to be human but had no physical substance.</note>; for this reason, he grew little by little. As he grew, the wisdom of the Word of God shone forth. For he did not become wise by making progress—far from it!—but rather he revealed his innate wisdom little by little. Thus, he is said to "progress" and be "strengthened in spirit" in accordance with the physical stature of his body.

<margin>F</margin> For if he had displayed all his wisdom while his stature was still small, he would have appeared miraculous and strange; but now, according to the proportions of his stature and how much it could contain within itself, he revealed himself to be fulfilling the divine plan <term>dispensationem: the Greek term 'oikonomia', referring to the way God manages the salvation of humanity through the Incarnation</term>, not by "acquiring" wisdom. For what could be more perfect than He who was perfect from the beginning? Rather, he uncovers that wisdom gradually.

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

...years old the Lord was when he was baptized, because that age is the most perfect; it is then that a man is recognized as either upright or wicked. Luke, however, recounts the lineage in a reverse order from Matthew, to show that he who is now born in the flesh is from God. For see how, by recounting the catalog of names, he returns to God, so that we may learn that he brings all the intervening fathers back to God and makes them sons, which is the reason he became incarnate. I can also state it another way: the Birth of Christ is difficult to believe because it happened without seed. Therefore, the Evangelist, wishing to show that man was made without seed in another instance, ascends from the lower names to Adam and God. It is as if he is saying: "If you do not believe that the second Adam <note>The "Second Adam" is a common theological title for Jesus, contrasting him with the first man, Adam.</note> was made without seed, I pray you, ascend in your memory to the first <margin>E</margin> Adam, and you will find that he too was made without seed by God; and from now on, do not be unbelieving."

<margin>How Joseph is the son of Jacob in Matthew, but the son of Eli in Luke. Deuteronomy 20 <note>The text cites Deuteronomy 20, though the law of the Levirate marriage is found in Deuteronomy 25.</note></margin>
Some, however, ask how Matthew can say Joseph is the son of Jacob, while Luke says he is the son of Eli. It is impossible for one man to have had two fathers. They say, regarding this, that Jacob and Eli were uterine brothers <note>Brothers born of the same mother but different fathers.</note> from different fathers. When Eli died without children, Jacob married his wife to procreate children for him. Thus, Joseph is said to be the son of Jacob by nature, but the son of Eli by the law. For Jacob begot him by nature, and he is truly and naturally his son. But he is the legal son of Eli. For the law commanded that if anyone died without children, his wife should be joined to his brother, and the child born from that union should be considered the child of the deceased, <margin>F</margin> even though he is living by nature. Thus, the Evangelists speak correctly and are not contrary to one another. Matthew described the natural father of Joseph, while Luke described the legal and supposed father—that is, Eli. Both show that the Lord was born for this purpose: to sanctify both nature and the law.

And the devil said to him: "I will give you all this power and their glory, because they have been delivered to me, and I give them to whomever I wish. Therefore, if you fall down and worship before me, they shall all be yours." And Jesus, answering, said to him: "Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve." <margin>Deuteronomy 6.</margin> And he led him to Jerusalem and set him upon a pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: "If <margin>B</margin> you are the Son of God, cast yourself down from here. For it is written, <margin>Psalm 90.</margin> He has given his angels charge over you, to keep you, and they shall bear you up in their hands, lest you dash your foot against a stone." And Jesus, answering, said to him: "It is said, You shall not tempt the Lord your God." <margin>Deuteronomy 6.</margin>] The Lord was baptized for our sake, so that he might sanctify the waters for us who had obtained grace. But after he was baptized, he was carried by the Spirit into the desert mountain. For the Holy Spirit led him to a contest with the devil. For this reason, he also departed into the desert to give the devil opportunities for plotting against him; for the devil is most accustomed to lie in wait when we are alone. By fasting for forty days, he did not exceed the measure of the fast of Moses and Elijah, lest he give Satan cause for suspicion in this place that he was greater than them; rather, he allowed the devil to think he was merely a man. Furthermore, this was so he would not appear to have become incarnate only in outward appearance <note>A reference to Docetism, a heresy claiming Jesus only "seemed" to have a physical body.</note>. Moreover, he is tempted after baptism to show us that temptations are destined to follow us after baptism. They fast because, in temptations, fasts serve as weapons; at such times, we should not be occupied with luxuries, but with fasting. <margin>C Genesis 3.</margin> The enemy, therefore, approaches him first and tempts him with gluttony—the same way he tempted Adam. Then, he tempts through greed by showing him all the kingdoms. How did he show them? Indeed, some say that he presented them to his imagination; but I do not think he offered them only to his imagination, but in a way perceptible to the senses...

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.
### COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE.

<margin>D</margin> ...having shown those things, he made them clear to him. Thirdly, however, he approaches tempting him with vainglory <note>Latin: *vana gloria*</note>, for he says, "If you are the son of God, cast yourself down." Flattering him, he spoke such nonsense, hoping perhaps that Jesus, deceived by flattery, would wish to show himself as the Son of God by throwing himself down, so that the devil might know who he was. But the Lord repels him with the scriptures. "You shall not tempt," he said, "the Lord your God." For no one should cast themselves into obvious dangers to test whether God will help them. Note, in the meantime, how great <margin>The utility of the knowledge of the scriptures.</margin> is the utility of knowing the scriptures. For with the scriptures the Lord repelled Satan. This phrase, "Man does not live by bread alone," is a Mosaic saying spoken concerning manna; for although manna was not bread, the people were nevertheless nourished by it. Similarly, <margin>B</margin> those other words are taken from Moses: "You shall worship the Lord your God," and "You shall not tempt."

And when every temptation was finished, the devil departed from him for a time. And Jesus returned in the power of the spirit into Galilee, and his fame went out through the whole region concerning him. And he taught in their synagogues, and was glorified by all. Luke says the Lord "finished every temptation," although he was only tempted by three; this is because <margin>The three heads of temptations.</margin> these three are the "heads" or main categories of all temptations: greed <note>Latin: *avaritia*</note>, gluttony <note>Latin: *gula*</note>, and vainglory. Furthermore, he repelled the temptation of gluttony, saying, "Man shall not live by bread alone." For with this the devil first attacked him, just as he did Adam. For he could not trip Adam up through greed <margin>F</margin>, since Adam, being alone, could not desire more than others (which is the nature of greed). Nor could he through anger—for at whom would he have been angry? Nor through envy. Therefore, he tripped him up through gluttony. On the other hand, the Lord repelled the temptation of greed by not falling down before the devil nor worshipping him. For when he had shown all the kingdoms to his imagination in a way that could be perceived, he did not look at them; although some have understood this not as physical kingdoms, but as mental ones—that he showed him the kingdom of envy, the kingdom of gluttony, and in short, the kingdoms of all sins. It was as if he said to him, "If you wish to reign over those passions, and if you have come for this reason—to snatch away those who are under me—fall down and worship me, and receive...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...receive all those who are governed by me." The Lord, however, does wish to reign, and came for this purpose, but to reign without sin and not without a struggle, but rather by struggling and conquering. Thus indeed have they understood it; which sense, if it pleases anyone, let him receive it. Furthermore, he repelled vainglory by the word of scripture. Therefore, deliver us also, Lord, from those three heads of the dragon. And Jesus returned in the power of the spirit; it seems to me that he returned by a certain divine inspiration <note>Latin: *afflatu*</note>, which some call "fury" <note>The word *furorem* here likely refers to a state of divine possession or prophetic zeal rather than anger.</note>. Observe also the scripture, that after he conquered the tempter and showed his power, it is written: "in the power of the spirit." The phrase "he departed from him for a time" has this meaning: the devil attacked the Lord with two passions <margin>B</margin>, namely pleasure and sorrow. He approached the Lord with pleasure when tempting him on the mountain, but he departed until the time of the cross, when he would tempt him through adversity and hardships.

And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and entered according to his custom on the day of the Sabbath into the synagogue, and he stood up to read. And the book <margin>Isaiah 61.</margin> of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him; and as he unrolled the book, he found the <margin>The book of Isaiah offered to Christ about to read.</margin> place where it was written: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives and sight to the blind, and to set at liberty <margin>Isaiah.</margin> those who are bruised through forgiveness, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord." <margin>C</margin> And having folded the book, he gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, "Today this scripture is fulfilled in your ears." Jesus indeed wished to make himself manifest to the Israelites, and to show that he was anointed by God the Father to save those who are under heaven. He does this with great wonder. He manifests himself especially to the Nazarenes, with whom he lived, so that he might teach us to first do good to our own and teach them, and afterward to pour out kindness upon others as well. Furthermore, he opened the book offered to him and found not what happened by chance, but what he himself willed. For do not think that he happened upon that passage by opening the book at random...

He then transitions to Christ's public reading in the Nazareth synagogue, identifying Jesus as the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy.</summary>

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> ...in which these things were written about him: for this happened by his own will. But what was written? "The Spirit of the Lord has anointed me," <note>original Latin: *Spiritu domini unxit me*</note> that is, he has consecrated me and appointed me to preach the gospel to the poor—that is, the Gentiles, who had neither the Law nor the Prophets and were truly very poor. As for the "brokenhearted," these were perhaps the Israelites, whose heart was formerly a great and sublime house of God. But later, when they began to give themselves over to idols and sinned in various ways, their heart was broken and destroyed—meaning the house of God was turned into a "den of thieves." Therefore, the Lord came to heal them, and to give release to captives and sight to the blind, meaning both the Gentiles and the Jews. <margin>E</margin> For both of those peoples were captives under Satan and were blind. These things can also be understood in terms of the dead. For they too were captives and wounded, and they were freed from the power of hell through the resurrection. He also preached the "acceptable year." But what was that acceptable year? Perhaps it refers to the future age, about which the Lord preached, saying, "On that day you will not ask me anything." And again, "The hour is coming when the dead shall rise." That year is "acceptable," meaning it is desirable, just, and lovely—a reward received by all who have labored here on earth. It is also the time of the Lord’s coming in the flesh, of which Paul says: "Now is the acceptable time, now is the day of salvation." <margin>2 Corinthians 6</margin> Furthermore, when he read these things and said, "Today this scripture is fulfilled in your ears," <margin>F</margin> he was clearly commending himself to those listening, showing that he is the one about whom these things were written.

And all bore witness to him and wondered at the grace of the words that proceeded from his mouth, and they said: "Is this not Joseph's son?" And he said to them: "Surely you will say this proverb to me: 'Physician, heal yourself.' <note>A common ancient proverb used to suggest that one should fix their own local problems before helping others.</note> Whatever we heard was done in Capernaum, do here also in your own country." But he said: "Truly I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own country." But in truth I say to you, there were many widows in the days of Elijah in Israel, when the heaven was shut for three years and six months, when there was a great famine throughout all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them except to Sarephtha...

This was a proverb among the Jews usually said to sick physicians. "But I say to you that I would have performed many signs even among you, my fellow countrymen, but I know the common proverb: that even the greatest things are held in contempt unless they are rare, <margin>C</margin> whereas if they are common and daily, and everyone enjoys them in abundance, they are ignored." For men are always inclined to value rare and wonderful things, but to despise those that are common and familiar. And for that reason, no prophet is held precious in his own country; but if he comes from elsewhere, people will admire him. Thus the widows of the Jews did not receive Elijah, but the woman of Sarephtha <note>A Phoenician woman living outside the Jewish borders.</note> received him. And Elisha purified a foreign leper because of the faith he showed, for his own relatives who were of the same country did not believe him, and therefore they were not purified. Similarly, I do not seem wonderful to you, my countrymen, but rather contemptible, and therefore I perform no signs. To those indeed who are in Capernaum, I seem wonderful, and I perform signs, and I am accepted by them. But hearing these things, those who were in the synagogue were filled with fury.
