<margin>D</margin> And they attempted to cast him down headlong. But he himself passed through the midst of them, not indeed fleeing from suffering, but awaiting the proper time. For he came in order to suffer for us; but now, at the very beginning of his preaching, he ought not to have exposed himself to death. Rather, he was to die only after he had taught us with sufficient doctrines. And thus, from this it is clear that when he was <margin>What is the homeland of the prophets?</margin> crucified, he was not crucified against his will, but underwent death voluntarily. Know, however, that the homeland of the prophets is the synagogue of the Jews, in which the prophets are despised and not looked up to; we, however, who were foreigners, receive them. For the Church is a widow, gathered from among the nations, who received Elijah—that is, the prophetic word—when there was a famine in Judea, a famine (I say) of hearing the word of God. Of this widow, the prophecy surely says, <margin>Isaiah 54</margin> "Many more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband," because <margin>1 Samuel 2</margin> <note>The text cites 1 Kings 2, but refers to the Song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2.</note> the sterile woman has given birth to seven, and she who had many children has become weak.

After neither reason nor doctrine could seize the unbelieving for the faith, the Lord turned himself to the performance of miracles, as if to a most effective medicine. Therefore, he performs miracles in Capernaum. For they were greatly unbelieving and needed many things to come to faith; for this reason, after he had taught sufficiently—and that as one endowed with power—for he did not say, "Thus says the Lord," but "I say to you," because he was not merely one of the prophets, but truly

<margin>A</margin> the Son of God—he also adds a miracle and heals one agitated by a demon. But the demon first confesses his enmity so that his testimony might be more worthy of belief; then he adds his testimony: "I know who you are, the Holy One of God." First, therefore, he rebukes him: "Why have you come here to destroy us?" Afterward, he flatters him, thinking that the Lord, softened by flattery, might permit him to stay—so foolish a thing is malice. But the Lord, teaching us not to use the testimonies or opinions of demons, says: "Be silent and go out of him." Moreover, he permits the demon to throw the man down, so that those standing around might learn that he truly had a demon whose words these were, even if it used the tongue of a man as its servant. Therefore, they spoke among themselves, all wondering at such deeds: <margin>B</margin> "What word is this?"—that is, what is this command by which he rules?

"Come out of him and be silent?" Know, however, that even now many have "demons"—those who fulfill the desires of a demon, such as an angry man who has a "demon of rage." But if **JESUS** comes into the synagogue—that is, when the mind has been gathered together and does not wander—then he will say to the demon of rage, which could not be restrained: "Be silent," and immediately it throws the man into the midst and goes out of him. Now, learn what it means to "throw into the midst." A man ought not to be entirely wrathful and bitter, for this would be the trait of a cruel and savage beast; nor should he be entirely lacking in anger, for this would be the trait of a senseless person. Rather, he should walk the middle path <note>The "middle path" or Golden Mean is a classical virtue where one uses anger only against evil, rather than against people.</note> and preserve his fury only against <margin>C</margin> malice. When, therefore, someone is "thrown into the midst" by an evil spirit, he is left by it.

And when **JESUS** had risen from the synagogue, he entered into the house of Simon. Now, Simon’s mother-in-law was gripped by a great fever, and they petitioned him for <margin>Matthew 8</margin> her. And standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and the fever left her; and immediately rising, she ministered to them. And when the sun was setting, all who had those sick with various diseases brought them to God. And he, laying hands on each one, healed them. And demons also went out from many, crying out and saying: "You are **CHRIST** the Son of God." And rebuking them, he did not permit them to speak, because they knew that he was the **CHRIST**.

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE.

When day had come, he departed and went into a deserted place, and the crowds sought him, and came to him, and they restrained him so that he would not depart from them. To whom he said: I must also preach the kingdom of God to other cities, for I was sent for this purpose. And he preached in the synagogues of Galilee.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Christ is received with hospitality at Peter's house.</margin>
The **LORD** of all was received and fed by his disciples, just as now he is also received with hospitality at Peter's house and heals his mother-in-law, so that he might instruct you not to reject the modesty and zeal of the poor. He does not simply cure her from the disease, but provides her with both good health and the strength to serve him. And if we also receive him, he will extinguish our <margin>E</margin> fever of anger and desire, and he will lift us up and strengthen us so that we may be able to serve him—that is, to do the things that please him. See, I pray, the faith of the crowd, <margin>Ecclesiasticus 15</margin> <note>The margin likely refers to Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 15:9: "Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner."</note> how even as the sun was setting, they brought the sick to him, and were not hindered by the time. He does not allow the demons to speak, both because he did not need the testimony of the unclean—for "praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner"—and because he wanted the envy of the Hebrews to be ignited when they saw him celebrated by everyone. Likewise, the crowds seek him even as he goes to a deserted place, and they hold him back. But he is not confined to one place, but says: "I must also preach the kingdom of God to other cities." From this, it is necessary for us not to be lazy, <margin>F</margin> nor content with one place, but to go around everywhere and be of benefit to some.

And he saw two boats standing by the lake; but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. And when they had done this, they enclosed a great multitude of fish. But their net was breaking. And they signaled to their partners, who were in the other boat, that they should come and help them. And they came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink. When Simon Peter saw this, he fell down at the knees of **JESUS**, saying: Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man. For amazement had surrounded <margin>B</margin> him, and all who were with him, at the catch of fish they had taken; and similarly also **JAMES** and **JOHN**, the sons of Zebedee, who were partners of Simon. And **JESUS** said to Simon: Do not fear; from now on you will be catching men. And when they had brought their boats to land, leaving everything, they followed him.

The Lord flees from glory, which followed him all the more for this reason. Therefore, as the crowd presses him, he enters the boat, so that he may teach even from the boat those standing on the shore, with everyone appearing directly in front of him and no one coming from behind. After he taught the crowd from the boat, he did not leave the master of the boat unrewarded, but benefited him in two ways: because he both gave him a multitude of fish and made him his disciple. <margin>C</margin> Marvel, therefore, at the Lord’s <term>dispensation<gloss>The divine arrangement or management of affairs (from the Greek 'oikonomia') by which God leads people to salvation.</gloss></term>, how he attracts each person through things that are their own and familiar—just as he led the Magi by a star, so he leads fishermen by fish. Furthermore, see the gentleness of **CHRIST**, how he entreats Peter to draw back from the land. For "he asked" is the same as "he entreated." But see also how obedient Peter was, so that he received into his boat a man he had not seen, and obeyed him in all things. For when he told him to go out into the deep, he did not refuse, nor did he say: "I have worked through the whole night and achieved nothing; should I now obey you and sink into more exhausting labors?" Instead, he said: "At your word I will let down the net." belongs to heal this kind of disease. But JESUS touches him, and not
without cause; since according to the Law, anyone who touched a leper was
considered unclean, he wished to show that he was not bound to observe
such a minor decree of the Law, and that he himself is the Lord of the
Law. He shows that a clean person is not defiled by that **B** which is seen as
unclean, but rather it is the leprosy of the soul that defiles. Therefore,
he touches him, also indicating this: that his holy flesh possesses divine
power and both purifies and gives life, since it is the flesh of the Word
of God. "But go," he said, "and present yourself to the priest and offer a
gift as a testimony to them." The Law required that lepers be examined by
a priest to determine if they had been purified. If someone was purified
within seven days, he remained within the city; if not, he was cast out.
And this is what the Lord says: "Go show yourself to the <margin>Leviticus 13, 14</margin>
priest and offer a gift." But what was the gift? Two <margin>How "Go, show yourself to the priest" is to be understood.</margin> birds. But what
does "as a testimony to them" mean? It means as a rebuke and condemnation
of them; so that when they condemn me as a transgressor of the Law, they
**C** may be argued against by this very act—that I did not transgress what was
commanded, namely that a gift be offered to them just as Moses prescribed.
Now, it would not be out of place to explain how those two birds were
offered to the Lord. One bird was killed, and they caught its blood in a
new earthen vessel; then both wings of the other bird were dipped in the
blood, and thus the live bird was released. These things prefigured
Christ. For the two birds are the two natures of CHRIST, the divine and the
human. One of these was killed—namely the human nature—but the other, the
divine, was released. For the divine nature remained <term>impassible</term> <note>Incapable of suffering or injury; a standard theological term for the divine nature of God.</note>,
though joined to the blood of the suffering nature and taking the passion
upon itself. Moreover, the blood...

### CHAPTER 5. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.
#### ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, COMMENTARY 192

The Lord received a new clay vessel, which is to say, a new people from the Gentiles <note>The "Gentiles" refers to non-Jewish nations who joined the early Christian church.</note>, capable of receiving the New Testament. Observe, however, that when someone has been purified, only then is he worthy to offer this gift to the Lord—that is, to sacrifice and offer Christ. For one who is a leper and unclean in soul would hardly be worthy to offer such gifts—that is, to offer the body and blood of the Lord, which is united to the divine nature. 
<margin>Num. 12.</margin> Observe also how the Lord excels Moses with an ineffable excellence. For Moses was not able to heal his own sister <note>referring to Miriam, who was struck with leprosy in Numbers 12</note>, even though he prayed much. But the Lord cleansed the leper by his word alone. Note also the humility of the Lord: how, while the 
<margin>E</margin> crowd was desiring for him to touch them, he instead spent his time quietly in solitary places and prayed. He did this to provide us an example in all things, both of praying in private and of shunning worldly glory.

"And it happened on a certain day, as he was teaching, there were Pharisees and teachers of the law sitting there, who had come from
<margin>Matt. 9. Mark 2.</margin> every village of Galilee, and Judea, and Jerusalem; and the power of the Lord was present to heal them. And behold, men were carrying on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they sought to bring him in and place him before him. And finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up onto the roof and lowered him with his stretcher through the tiles into the midst before Jesus." 
<margin>F</margin> When he saw their faith, he said to him, "Friend, your sins are forgiven you." And the scribes and Pharisees began to reason, saying, "Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?" But when Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered and said to them, "What are you thinking in your hearts? Which is easier: to say, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say, 'Rise and walk'? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins," he said to the paralyzed man, "I say to you, rise, take up your stretcher, and go to your house." And immediately he rose up before them, took up what he had been lying on, and went to his own house, glorifying God. And amazement seized

<column-break/>

them all, and they glorified God and were filled with fear, saying, "We have seen incredible things today." It was necessary for the Lord to perform a rarer miracle in the presence of his enemies; therefore, he heals a man of a most difficult disease, so that by healing such a sickness he might also heal the remarkable insanity of the Pharisees. First, therefore, he heals the soul, saying, "Your sins are forgiven," so that we might learn that many infirmities are born from sins. Then he also heals the body, having seen the faith of those who brought him. For often he saves some on account of the faith of others. Furthermore, the Pharisees say, "Why does this man 
<margin>Levit. 24.</margin> speak blasphemies? Who can forgive sins
<margin>B</margin> but God alone?" They say these things because they are condemning him as one guilty of death. For it was established in the Law that anyone blaspheming God should be punished by death. Therefore, the Lord 
<margin>2 Chron. 6.</margin> demonstrates to them that he is the true God, and that his words were not spoken out of arrogance; he persuades them by another sign. For he knew what they were thinking. From this it is entirely clear that he is God. For it belongs to God alone to see into the heart. Therefore he said, "How does it seem to you? Is it easier to forgive sin or to heal the body?" Entirely according to your opinion, it seems easier to forgive sins, as it is an invisible thing and not subject to physical proof, even though in reality it is more difficult. But to heal a disease of the body seems more difficult (as it is visible), even though by nature it is easier. "Nevertheless, I will do both this and that, and I will therefore heal the body—which seems more difficult to you—
<margin>C</margin> so that I may make the healing of the soul credible to you, which is truly more difficult, though it seems easy to you because it cannot be seen." Note also that sins are forgiven "upon the earth." For as long as we are upon the earth, we are able to blot out our sins; but after we have departed from the earth, we will no longer be able to do so through confession, for the door is closed. We have spoken more abundantly regarding this closing of the door in the other Evangelists.

Jesus saw Matthew the tax collector sitting at the tax office. But Luke and Mark, out of respect for the Evangelist, put forward his other name, Levi. Observe, however, the mercy of God <margin>Chapter 2.</margin> and how he plunders the vessels of the wicked one. For a tax collector was a vessel of the wicked one, and an evil vessel at that. Those who have experienced it know how persistent and troublesome debt collectors are. For tax collectors <term>Publicani: individuals who purchased the right to collect public taxes, often enriching themselves through extortion.</term> are those who buy the public revenues so that they may gain something for themselves, though it be to the ruin of their <margin>E</margin> souls. But the Lord did not only win over Matthew at that time, but he also won over other tax collectors with whom he was dining. For this reason, he became their dinner guest: so that he might draw them to him. See, however, what he says to the Pharisees who were rebuking him: "I have not come," he said, "to call the righteous," that is, you who justify yourselves, "but I have come to call sinners." Moreover, every person is a "tax collector" who serves the master of this world and pays tribute to the flesh. The glutton pays tribute to the belly in the form of food; the fornicator in foul encounters; and others in other ways. Therefore, when the Lord—that is, the <margin>F</margin> Word of the Gospel—sees such a person sitting at the tax office, which is to say, not making progress, nor moving forward, nor even moving toward greater malice, but as if idle, he will then raise him up from evil. And that man will follow Jesus and receive the Lord into the house of his soul. He calls the Apostles <margin>Chapter 9.</margin> the "sons of the bridechamber." For the coming of the Lord is likened to a wedding because he has taken the Church as his bride. Therefore, it was not fitting for the Apostles to fast. However, the disciples <margin>B</margin> of John were required to fast, surely because their master was preparing their virtue through labor. Below.</margin> and they themselves have been sent out to preach, then they will both fast and pray, as if preparing themselves for great struggles. Or even in another way: for now, while they are weak and not yet made new by the Holy Spirit, they are compared to old wineskins; it is not right for them to be burdened and weighed down by a more severe way of life, just as a new patch should not be added to an old garment. You can certainly (as I said) understand the "old wineskins" <margin>C</margin> to be the Apostles in their weakness; you can also understand them to be the Pharisees, to whom the Lord was saying, as it were: "My doctrine is indeed new wine; but you, since you are old wineskins, cannot contain it, but you say, 'The old wine (that is, the Old Testament) is better.'"

<margin>The Jews called their feasts Sabbaths.</margin>
The Jews used to call every feast a "Sabbath." For the word "Sabbath" means "rest." Often, therefore, a feast would occur on the day of preparation <term>parasceue: the day before the Sabbath, used for preparing meals and tasks forbidden on the holy day</term>, and they called that preparation day a "Sabbath" because of the feast; then, that which is properly the Sabbath, they called "second-first," because it followed both a feast and the Sabbath that had preceded it. <note>Theophylact is explaining a difficult chronological term in the Greek text, "sabbato deuteroprotō."</note> And as for the fact that the Pharisees were criticizing the disciples because they were plucking grain on the Sabbath <margin>E</margin> and eating it, plucking it—that is, pulling off the ears—and rubbing them—that is, grinding them in their hands—the Lord brings up the example of David, who was hungry and ate the bread of the presence <term>panes propositionis: the twelve loaves of "showbread" set out in the Temple as a perpetual offering</term>, which they set out daily. For while fleeing from Saul, David came to Abiathar the high priest and deceived him, as if he had been sent by the king for some <margin>Bread of the presence. Leviticus 24.</margin> necessary task. And being hungry, he also received from the high priest the bread of the presence, twelve of which they placed daily upon the sacred table, six on the right and six on the left. He also received the sword of Goliath. The Lord told them this history and admonished them by David’s action. "For if you honor David," he says, "how can you condemn my disciples?" Or otherwise: "The Son of Man," <margin>Son of Man</margin> <margin>F</margin> that is, I am the Lord of the Sabbath as its founder, maker, and legislator, having the power to loosen the Sabbath. For the "Son of Man" refers to none other than CHRIST, who, although he was the Son of God, miraculously deigned to both become and be called the Son of Man. And though you and I are called a "son of man," there is nothing new in that. But he is worthy to be called *the* Son of Man, who was made man in a truly miraculous way.

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 196

<margin>D</margin> [...they should] bear bravely whatever comes upon them, even though some may treat them with injury and religiously <term>religiose: here meaning with a pretense of piety or strictness</term> lay snares for them, just as He Himself did on the cross, saying: *Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.* <note>original: "Pater dimitte eis nesciunt enim quid faciunt."</note> Then, lest the apostles might say that the commandment to love one's enemies is impossible, he says: *What you wish to be done to you, do this also to others.* <note>The Golden Rule, found in Luke 6:31.</note> Be such toward others as you wish others to be toward you. If you do not want your enemies to be harsh, impatient, and angry toward you, then you also be like that. But if you want them to be good, compassionate, and forgetful of injuries, do not believe it is impossible for you to become such a person yourself. You see the natural law written in our hearts. So the Lord also said in those days: *giving my laws into their minds, and I will write them in their hearts.* <margin>The law of nature written on the hearts of men.</margin> Afterward, he urges us by another necessity: <margin>E</margin> *If you love those who do good to you, you are like sinners and the heathens. But if you love those who do evil to you, you are like God, who is good to the ungrateful and the wicked.* Do you wish, therefore, to become like God or like a sinner? Do you see the divine teaching? First, he taught you from the natural law: for what you want to be done to you, do that also to another. Then, he teaches from the goal and the reward, for he promises a reward to you: that you may become like God. *Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and it will be forgiven you. Give, and it will be given to you.* <margin>Matthew 7.</margin> *A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, they will give into your lap.* <margin>F</margin> For with the same measure by which you measure, others will measure back to you. Moreover, he told them a parable: *Can the blind lead the blind? Do they not both fall into the pit? The disciple is not above his master; but everyone will be perfect if he is like his master.* ] The Lord removes every difficult disease from our souls; I speak of the root <margin>Suspicion of evils wears away [the soul].</margin> of suspicion. For he who does not consider himself and only attends to the affairs of his neighbor, and wishes to criticize them, is certainly seized by suspicion and forgets himself. For he feels entirely about himself that he does not sin, and because of this, he sharply rebukes others who are sinning. Therefore, if you wish to always remain uncondemned, do not condemn others.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> For tell me, I ask, why do you condemn another as a transgressor <margin>Romans 2.</margin> of the divine laws? Do you not also transgress the divine law? To say nothing of other sins, you certainly sin in this very thing: that you judge others. For the divine law commands you not to judge your brother. And so, you too are a transgressor of the law. And since you are a transgressor, you ought not to judge another as a transgressor. For the judge ought to be superior to the one whose nature is sinning. Therefore, forgive, and it will be forgiven you; give, and it will be given to you. For a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, they will give into your lap. For the Lord will not measure back sparingly, but abundantly. Just as when <margin>B</margin> measuring flour, you pile it up, shake it, and make it overflow, if indeed you wish to measure without stinginess, so also the Lord will give a great and overflowing measure to you. Here, perhaps, someone more acute might ask: "How is it that after he said, 'by what measure you measure, they will measure back to you,' he says again that the measure overflows? How is this measure the same?" We say, therefore, it was not said that *so much* a measure will be measured back to you, but the *same* kind. If he had said "so much," then there would be no lack of difficulty and contradiction in the speech. The Lord says, therefore, that if you do good, good will also be done to you. Just as he said regarding condemnation: for he who condemns and is afterward condemned, receives the same measure. <margin>C</margin> But he who is condemned more than he condemned, <margin>John 3. <note>The marginal note "Ioan. 3" is likely an error or a specific cross-reference to Christ as the Light/Judge in the original text's apparatus.</note></margin> possesses an overflowing measure according to that saying. Moreover, the Lord said these things to prohibit us from condemnation. He also tells us a parable, which is an example. For tell me, I ask, he says: is not the one judging another while sinning in the same way compared to a blind man leading the blind? For if you condemn another, and you yourself fall into the same sins, you are both blind; and you seem indeed to be a leader to the good for him because you condemn, but you are not a leader. For how will he be led to the good by you when you yourself are slipping? For the disciple is not above the master. If, therefore, you appear to be the leader and you slip, in every way he who is being taught and led will also fall. For the fully trained disciple—that is, the perfect one—will be like his master. ### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 197

<margin>D</margin>...so that those who are inferior to us are not condemned if they seem to sin. He also adds another point on the same subject.

Why do you see the **speck** <term>festuca: a small straw, splinter, or mote</term> in your brother's eye, but do not notice the **beam** <term>trabs: a large wooden structural beam or log</term> which is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother: "Brother, let me cast out the speck that is in your eye," when you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? **Hypocrite**, first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to cast out the speck which is in your brother's eye. For a **good tree** is not one that produces bad fruit, nor is a **bad tree** one that produces good fruit. For every tree is known by its own <margin>Matt. 7</margin> fruit. For they do not gather figs from thorns, <margin>E</margin> nor do they harvest grapes from a bramble bush. A good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and a bad man brings forth evil from the evil treasure of his heart. For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. ] Why then, He asks, do you see the speck—that is, the small sin of your brother—but do not notice the beam, which is your own great sin? This can be said to all people, and especially to teachers and leaders, who punish the sins of those under them, however small, while they leave their own sins, even the greatest, unpunished. Therefore the Lord calls them **hypocrites**. Just as some people appear to be one thing while they punish the sins of others—for in this they appear righteous—they are actually something else, because they themselves sin more gravely. <margin>F</margin> Afterward, He also confirms His discourse with an example. Just as, He says, there is no good tree that produces rotten fruit, nor a rotten tree that produces good fruit, so also he who attempts to chastise and correct others, and lead them to the good, should not himself be evil; for if he is evil, he will not make others better. For the heart of each person is a treasure; if it holds good things, the man is good and speaks good things; but if the heart is full of evil, the man is evil and speaks evil things. You can also understand these things as referring to the **Pharisees** <note>The Pharisees were a Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional and written law, often criticized in the Gospels for legalism.</note>. Directing His speech to them, He said: "First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then the speck that is in your brother's eye," just as He says elsewhere, **swallowing a camel**

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and **straining out a gnat**. <note>original: "Camelum glutientes, & culicem excolantes." See Matthew 23:24.</note> <margin>Matt. 23</margin> How then, you Pharisees, who are rotten trees, will you be able to bring forth good fruit? For your speech is always rotten, just as your life is. For He says: "out of the abundance of the heart." How then will you correct others and punish the sins of others, when you yourselves sin more gravely?

But why do you call me "Lord, Lord," and do not do what I say? Whoever comes to me, and hears my words, and does them, I will show you whom he is like: He is like a man building a house, who **dug deep** and laid the **foundation upon the rock**. When a flood came, the river rushed against that house, but could not move it, for it was founded upon the rock. But he who <margin>B</margin> heard and did not act accordingly, is like a man who built his house upon the rock without a foundation, against which the river rushed, and immediately it fell, and the <margin>1 Tim. 1</margin> ruin of that house was great. ] This is necessarily said to us, who indeed confess Christ with our mouth, but deny Him by our works. If I am the Lord, He says, it is entirely your duty to do those things which belong to servants. For it is the work of a servant to do rightly what the Lord commands. Then He tells us what he gains who hears Him—and not only hears, but <margin>1 Cor. 10</margin> also acts: for he is like a man building, as the Apostle <note>Likely referring to St. Paul's imagery of building on a foundation in 1 Corinthians 3:10-11.</note> testifies. Moreover, he "digs into the deep" who does not accept the words of Scripture superficially, but searches their <margin>C</margin> depths in the spirit. Such a person, therefore, also builds upon the rock; and then when a storm arises—that is, persecution or temptation—the river rushes against that house. The "river" is the tempter, whether a demon or a man, and he has no power to move the house. Indeed, that tempting man is compared to a river, and very deservedly. For just as a river is made to overflow by water falling from above, so also **Satan**, who fell from the heavens, causes that tempting man to grow [in malice]. But the house of those who do not do the word of the Lord falls, and the ruin of that house is great. For the ruin of those who do not hear and do not act is great. For he who does not hear and does not act does not fall as heavily [as a believer might]; but he who hears and does not act sins more gravely.

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 199

<margin>A</margin> Among those born of women, there is no greater prophet than **John the Baptist**; yet he who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he. And all the people who heard, including the tax collectors, justified God, having been baptized with John’s baptism; but the **Pharisees** and lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves, not having been baptized by him. The miracle that took place in Nain became well known throughout all Judea and was even heard by John's disciples, who were burdened by the praises of Christ, as they were still imperfect in their understanding. Therefore, John, wishing to show them the greatness of Christ and how much he excelled him, devised this plan. He said nothing definitive to the disciples about Christ but, pretending to be ignorant, he sent them so that, having seen the miracles, <margin>B</margin> they might be confirmed in the faith by the works themselves—that the Lord is the **Christ** and John is but a servant. Do not believe, then, that <margin>Why John sent them to ask, "Are you the one who is to come?" etc. See above, John 1.</margin> John sent his disciples to ask Jesus out of true ignorance. For how could he be ignorant, since even before his birth he leaped in his mother’s womb, recognizing him, and later testified in the Jordan that he was the Son of God? He therefore sent his disciples to ask him, telling them to inquire of Jesus: "Are you the one who is to come?" You see how he leads the disciples to believe that Jesus is **God**. For prophets are said to be "sent" <note>original: *missi*</note>—and John himself, as the Evangelist testifies, "was a man sent from God"—but the Lord is "the one to come" <note>original: *venturus*</note>. For he came by his own power, not by compulsion. "Are you then," he says, "the one who was expected to come into the world?" Some, however, understand "to come" as referring to his descent into hell <note>original: *infernum*</note>, and that <margin>C</margin> what is said has this meaning: "Are you the one who is to come to hell?" What then did the Lord do? Knowing John’s purpose and mind—why he had sent them: so they might see what he did and be confirmed by those things—he therefore said to those sent to him: "Report what you see." Then he lists the works of miracles, which had also been announced through the prophets. For that the blind see, the lame walk, and the Gospel is preached to the poor, is written in **Isaiah**. <margin>Isaiah 35.</margin> Then he says, "And blessed is he who is not offended in me," as if saying to them: "And you are blessed, if you are not offended in me." For it was likely that many were offended by John, who offered such great testimony...

Therefore, you are not able to pay back even a minor debt, for you lack the spirit of confession, being puffed up with pride—nor can the woman pay. Therefore, he will forgive both. And which one will love more? Surely the one to whom many things were forgiven. And when he had said these things, he silenced the arrogant man.

And turning to the woman, he said to **SIMON**: <margin>B</margin> ["Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet; but she has wet my feet with tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss; but she, from the time I entered, has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil; but she has anointed my feet with ointment. Because of this, I say to you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much. But he to whom less is forgiven, loves less." And he said to her: "Your sins are forgiven." And those who sat at the table with him began to say within themselves: "Who is this, who even forgives sins?" And he said to the woman: "Your faith has made you whole; go in peace."]

The Lord showed that Simon was both arro- <margin>C</margin> gant and foolish. Arrogant and insulting indeed, because even though he himself was only a man, he condemned another person because of her sins. Foolish indeed, because he did not consider what great signs of faith and love she displayed. He ought to have welcomed her, not rejected her. Therefore, the Lord rebukes him for condemning her who did such great things—things that Simon himself did not do; indeed, Simon did far less. It is as if he said: "You did not even provide water to wash the dust from my feet, but she wet them with tears. You did not kiss my face, but she kissed my feet. Likewise, you provided no oil, but she poured out ointment." Therefore, because you said, "If he were not a prophet," from this...

### CHAPTER 8. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, 
### ON THE COMMENTARY OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Psalm 77</margin>
<margin>Why does the Lord speak in parables?</margin>
[...of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.] Now at last that has come to pass which David once said in the person of Christ: "For I will open," he said, "my mouth in parables." <note>original: *Aperiam enim... in parabolis os meum*. A reference to Psalm 78:2, though the margin notes Psalm 77 following the Vulgate numbering.</note> The Lord, therefore, speaks in parables for many reasons: namely, to make his listeners more attentive and to stir their minds to inquire about those things which are spoken more obscurely—to investigate more curiously those things which are hidden, rather than neglecting what is plain—and so that the unworthy might not understand what is said more deeply, and for many other reasons he speaks in parables. "Therefore a sower went out," which is to say the Son of God went out from the bosom and secret place of his Father and was made visible.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>The Son of God is always sowing.</margin>
But who went out? He who always sows; for the Son of God does not cease to always sow in our souls. For he sows good seeds in our souls not only when he is seen to be teaching, but also through this world and through those things which he does daily for us. He went out, however, not to kill the farmers or to burn the field, but to sow. For a farmer often goes out for other reasons as well, not only to sow; but he "went out to sow his seed." For the word of doctrine is his own, and not another's. For whatever the prophets said, they spoke from the Spirit and not as their own; hence they said, "Thus says the Lord." But CHRIST has his own seed, and therefore he did not say while teaching, "Thus says the Lord," but "I say to you."

<margin>F</margin>
While he was sowing—that is, teaching—some fell by the wayside; he did not say the sower threw it, but that it fell. For he who sows, sows and teaches, but the word falls upon the listeners. These listeners are found to be either the way, the rock, the thorns, or the good soil. Furthermore, when the disciples asked about the parable, the Lord said: "To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God," that is, to you who seek so that you may learn.

<margin>Matthew 7</margin>
For everyone who asks, receives. But to the rest, who are unworthy of the sacraments, things are spoken obscurely; they think they see, but they do not see; they hear, but they do not understand. And this is for their own good, so they are not more heavily condemned

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
for having despised the mysteries they had known; for this reason, Christ hides these things from them. For he who knows and yet shows contempt deserves more severe punishments.

This then is the parable: The seed is the word of GOD. Those by the wayside are those who hear; then the devil comes and takes the word from their hearts, lest by believing they might be saved. For those upon the rock are those who, when they have heard, receive the word with joy, but these have no roots; they believe for a time, and in the time of temptation they fall away. As for what fell among thorns, these are those who have heard, and as they go, they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and they bear no fruit. But that which fell on good ground,

<margin>B</margin>
these are they who, hearing the word with a generous and good heart, retain it and bring forth fruit through patience.] Here there are three orders of those who are not saved: for those by the wayside do not receive the word at all. For just as a path that is trampled and muddy does not receive the seed, because <term>it</term> <note>original abbreviation: *q̇* for *quod*</note> becomes hard, so also those hardened in heart do not receive the word; even when hearing, they do not pay attention. But those understood as the rock receive it indeed, but they wither away because of human weakness. The third are those who, when they have heard and received it, are choked by the cares of this life. Therefore, there are three parts of those who perish, and only one of those who are saved. Thus, there are a few who are saved, but many who perish.

<margin>C</margin>
See also when he speaks of those who are choked, how he does not say they are choked by riches, but by the cares and anxieties of riches. For it is not riches that harm, but the worry over them. For many perceive great benefits from riches when they apply them to the bellies of the poor. Consider also the diligence of the Evangelist, how he said of those who are saved that they "retain" the word they have heard. He said this because of those understood by the way, from whom the devil takes the word; and he said they "bring forth fruit" because of those who are choked and those who do not endure until the end. For those who do not persevere until the end do not bring forth fruit. Furthermore...

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, when he says, **in patience**, <note>original: *in patientia*; in this context, it refers to "steadfast endurance" or "perseverance."</note> he said this on account of those who fall upon the rock; they indeed receive the word, but they do not withstand the snares of temptation and are proven to be reprobate. You see how he spoke of those who are saved: that they "retain" it and "produce fruit," and that they do so "in patience." He distinguishes them by three traits from those who do not retain it (who are those by the wayside), from those who do not endure (who are those among the thorns), and from those who do not withstand the snares of <margin>Matthew 5</margin> temptation (who are those upon the rock).

**No one, when they have lit a lamp, covers it with a vessel or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a lampstand, so that those entering may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come into the open. Therefore, take care how you hear. For to whoever has, more will be given; and from whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away.** ] At this point, there is the beginning of another teaching. For directing his speech to the disciples, he says these things to lead them toward a diligent guarding of a holy life. He is instructing them to always be in the "agony" <note>original: *agone*; referring to a spiritual struggle or athletic contest.</note> and the struggle, since they are to be scrutinized by everyone. For he who teaches and preaches is observed by all and judged by all to see if he is honorable; nothing that he does is hidden. Therefore, O disciples, attend well to yourselves and be studious, for <margin>F</margin> greater grace will be given to you by God. But he who does not apply study and attention—even if he has some grace from God—loses it and it is extinguished.

**Then his mother and brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And it was told to him, saying, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wanting to see you." But answering, he said to them, "My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it."** ] In this passage, it is shown how Christ dealt <margin>Matthew 21, Mark 2</margin> with his fleshly relatives. Leaving them behind, he was occupied with spiritual teaching, which is why they came to him. So also it is necessary that all to whom the ministry of God has been entrusted should hold nothing more ancient <note>original: *antiquius*; meaning more important or of higher priority.</note> or prefer anything else above it. Even parents are to be turned away if, 

---

<margin>A</margin> indeed, they are going to hinder us in the work of God uselessly and in vain, just as the Lord does now. For because certain people had spoken to him about his relatives, he himself does not confine "brotherhood" to a small number. Nor does he give this honor to the sons of Joseph alone, as if they were his only brothers; but because he came to save the whole world and to make everyone his brothers, he says, "My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God." Furthermore, because simply hearing the word does not save if it is not also kept in the soul, but rather condemns, he says, "And they do it." It is necessary, therefore, both to hear and to do. Moreover, he calls his own teaching "the word of God." For whatever he himself spoke belonged to his <margin>B</margin> Father; he was not an adversary to him, such that he would say things that were not of God. 

Yet many understand this passage to mean that certain people were mocking Christ while he was teaching, and out of envy for the wonderful way his teaching was received, they said, "Behold, your mother and brothers are outside, desiring to see you." This was because his mother appeared to be lowly and his brothers obscure—since they were the sons of a carpenter <note>original: *fabri filii*</note>—and therefore, as if he were of ignoble birth, they mockingly brought up his mother and brothers. Therefore, knowing their thoughts, he said, in effect: "Since an ignoble lineage does me no harm, how much more so if anyone is of 'ignoble' birth but hears me? I make that person my own relative."

**And it happened on a certain day that he went up into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, "Let us cross over to the other side of the lake." And they set sail. But as they sailed, he fell asleep. And a storm of wind came down upon the lake, and they were being filled with water and were in danger. And coming to him, they woke him, saying, "Master, Master, we are perishing!" But he, having been awakened, rebuked the wind and the raging of the water; and they ceased, and there was a calm. And he said to them, "Where is your faith?" But being afraid, they wondered among themselves, saying, "Who do you think this is, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?"** ] By exercising the disciples and examining their faith so that they might be undaunted in their own temptations, the Lord, by a certain singular dispensation, <note>original: *dispensatione*; a theological term for God's structured plan or management of human history.</note> sleeps. He reproves their weakness, for they did not have perfect faith, but rather faith mixed with unbelief.

...they were displaying. <margin>D</margin> For they believe that he is able to save, yet as people of little heart, they say, "Save us, we are perishing!" <note>original: *Salua, perimus*</note> For if they had possessed perfect faith, they would have been certain enough that it was impossible for them to perish while he was present who has power over all things. Therefore, he saved them by being awakened not at the beginning, but at the very moment of danger. <note>Theophylact suggests that divine intervention is often delayed until the moment of greatest need to strengthen human recognition of God's power.</note>

And see also the **anagogy** <note>Anagogy is a method of spiritual interpretation that sees historical events in the Bible as symbols of higher spiritual truths or future realities.</note>, because it is a figure of what happened later to the disciples. For the lake is Judea, in which a storm arose on account of the infamy of the Jews who had crucified the Lord. Indeed, the disciples were troubled, <margin>E</margin> for they fled after he had been abandoned; but the Lord was awakened from the highest, that is, he rose again. From which tranquility was restored to the disciples. <margin>John 20</margin> He came to them and said, "Peace be with you." And these things are indeed through anagogy. But as for their saying, "Who then is this?" they do not say it as those who doubt, but as those who marvel—as if they were saying, "Who is this?"—that is, how great and of what kind, and with what great power does he do these things?

<margin>A</margin> from the man and entered into the swine; and the herd went with a rush down a steep place into the lake and was drowned. ] See how the demon is held by two evil dispositions: audacity and fear. ...of **Jesus**, that is, they implored Him to depart from them. <margin>D</margin> For they feared lest they might suffer some other loss, seeing that the pigs had perished. But the man who had been healed displayed an unspeakable sign of health. For he was so healed in his heart that he recognized Jesus, praying that he might be permitted to be with Him. Indeed, as it appears, he feared that if he were far from Jesus, he might perhaps be invaded by demons again. But the Lord indicated to him that even if he were not with Him physically, he would still be protected by His grace and become superior to the assaults of demons. "Return," He said, "to your house, and tell what great things God has done for you." He did not say, "what great things **I** have done for you," <note>original: *quęcunque ego tibi fecerim*</note> giving us a pattern of humility so that we might attribute all our good works to God. <margin>E</margin> Moreover, that man was so grateful that he told everyone what Jesus had done for him. For while the Lord had commanded him to tell what *God* had done, he went and told what *Jesus* had done. Therefore, we also, when we do good to anyone, should not wish for it to be proclaimed; yet it is fitting for the one who has received the benefit to proclaim it to everyone, even if we are unwilling. <margin>Matthew 9. Mark 5.</margin>

And it happened that when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed Him, for they were all waiting for Him. And behold, a man came named **Jairus**, and he was a ruler of the synagogue. He fell at Jesus' feet, begging Him to enter his house because he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying. But as He went, the crowds pressed against Him. <margin>F</margin> And a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, who had spent all her substance on physicians and could not be cured by anyone, approached from behind and touched the hem of His garment, and immediately the flow of her blood stopped. Jesus indeed returned from the region of the **Gadarenes**, and the crowd was waiting for Him, both because of His teaching and because of His miracles. Likewise, a certain ruler of the synagogue approached—not a common or lowly man, but one of the chief men. <note>original: *exprimis*</note> The Evangelist records his name so that the miracle might be better known as having truly happened. He fell at the feet of Jesus out of urgent necessity, although even without that, it was right to prostrate oneself and recognize that Jesus is God.

<column-break/>

<margin>Psalm 30</margin> <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 32:9.</note> Yet affliction also compels men to seek better things; whence David said, "With bit and bridle bind their jaws, those who do not draw near to you." Furthermore, the woman approached Him in passing, bringing a greater faith. For approaching, she touched the hem of His garment with good hope and certain faith, believing that if she only touched it, she would be saved. And immediately the flow of her blood stood still. Just as if someone were to bring an eye toward a shining light, or straw toward a fire, they would immediately experience their operation; so she, bringing her faith to Him who was able to heal, immediately obtained health. Nor did she think of the long duration of the disease, or the desperation of the physicians, or anything else; she only believed, and was saved. <margin>B</margin> And, as it seems, she first touched Christ with her mind, and then with her body.

And **JESUS** said, "Who is it that touched me?" When everyone denied it, Peter and those with him said, "Master, the crowds hem you in and press against you, and you say, 'Who touched me?'" But **JESUS** said, "Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me." The woman, seeing that she was not hidden, came trembling and fell down before His feet, and she declared before all the people the reason why she had touched Him, and how she had been immediately healed. But He said to her, "Take heart, daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace." <margin>C</margin> The Lord, wishing to make the woman's faith manifest to everyone so that they might become imitators of her, and so that Jairus might take greater hope for the safety of his little daughter, made manifest what had been done secretly. He asked who had touched Him. But Peter, boldly rebuking Him for this question, said, "So many crowd you, and you say, 'Who touched me?'" He did not understand why Jesus was asking. For Jesus asked, "Who touched me *with faith*?" and not merely in a simple way. For just as one person has ears for hearing, and another has ears but does not hear; so one person touches with faith, while another approaches with his feet but is far away in his heart. Therefore, the Lord asked, not being ignorant of what the woman had done, but for the reason I said: to bring her faith to light.

# CHAPTER 8. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
### ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 207

<margin>D</margin> ...show her to others, and to give good hope to the ruler of the synagogue. He asks [who touched Him], and makes the woman visible. "For I know," He says, "that power has gone out from me." <note>original: *virtutem exiisse a me*</note> And rightly so. For the prophets did not have power proceeding from themselves, but worked miracles by the grace of God. Jesus, however, since He was the fountain of all good and all power, has power proceeding from Himself. For the Lord heals the woman in two ways: first by healing her disease, and then by taking away the fear of her soul, through what He said: "Take heart, daughter." <note>This "double healing" refers to the physical cure and the spiritual peace Jesus grants her.</note>

<margin>E</margin> While He was still speaking, someone came from the house of the ruler of the synagogue, saying to him, "Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the teacher." But Jesus, hearing this word, answered the girl’s father, "Do not fear, only believe, and she will be saved." And when He had come into the house, He did not allow anyone to enter with Him except Peter, James, and John, and the girl’s father and mother. Now all were weeping and mourning for her. But He said, "Do not weep; she is not dead, but sleeping." And they ridiculed Him, knowing that she was dead. But He, having put them all outside and taking her by the hand, cried out, saying, "Child, arise." <note>original: *Puella surge*</note> And her spirit returned, and she rose immediately; and He commanded that food be given to her. And her parents were amazed. But He charged them to tell no one what had happened. ] When Jesus heard what the messenger said to the leader of the synagogue—"Do not trouble the teacher," <note>original: *archisynagogum*</note> that is, do not cause him business or bring him here—He did not wait for the ruler of the synagogue to speak to Him, but anticipated him, <margin>F</margin> lest perhaps the ruler might say, "I have no need of you, for the evil is already done; she whom we hoped you would heal is dead." Therefore, so that he would not say such a thing—for he was an unbeliever and a Jew—Christ anticipated him and said, "Do not fear, only believe: look at this woman who suffered from a flow of blood; if you imitate her, you will not go wrong." Furthermore, He permitted only John, James, and Peter from among the disciples to enter with Him, as they were the foremost and the most silent of the disciples. For He did not want this miracle to be revealed to many before the proper time, lest, inflamed by envy, they might become guilty of judgment. In this same manner also

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> it is necessary for us to act when someone envies us: we should not reveal our good works to them, but take care that they remain unknown. Moreover, when the Lord said, "she is not dead, but sleeping," and called death "sleep," it was because He was about to wake her from death as if from a dream. They ridiculed Him when they heard this, so that the miracle might be further confirmed. For, so that they could not later say that she had not been dead but merely sleeping, He permitted Himself to be ridiculed first by those saying she was dead, so that the mouths of those wishing to slander Him might be stopped. For her death was so certain that they laughed at Him for saying she was not dead. He cast everyone outside, perhaps teaching <margin>B</margin> us to be free from the pursuit of empty glory and to do nothing for ostentation; but perhaps also teaching that one who is to perform miracles should not do them in the midst of many, but should be alone and undisturbed. Therefore, the girl’s spirit returned; He did not bring in another soul, but made the one that had flown from the body return to it again. He commanded them to give her food so that faith and the truth that she had truly risen might be confirmed. This can also be understood spiritually: every soul gushing with bloody sin and bloodguilt is like the woman with the flow of blood. For every sin is a murderer and a killer of the soul. But if the soul touches the garment—that is, the incarnation of **JESUS**—and believes that the Son of God was made flesh, it will be sanctified. And if anyone is a ruler of the synagogue—that is, a mind that presides over many things <margin>C</margin> gathered through greed and the pursuit of gain—and his daughter (meaning his thought) falls ill, let him only invoke Jesus and believe, and he shall be saved.

# CHAPTER 9. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
### ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 207

<margin>D</margin> ...since you do not even have two tunics. And into whatever house you enter, stay there, and leave from there. And whoever does not receive you, as you leave that city, shake off even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them. And so they went out and traveled through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

In this passage, the excellence of the divinity of Jesus is shown, for He not only performs miracles Himself but also grants this power to His disciples. Surely, it would not belong to a mere man, but to God, to provide such great and such kinds of gifts to His friends. While giving <margin>Some miracles are performed through demons</margin> them some power against evil spirits, He was not content with that alone, but also commanded them to preach the Gospel. For He teaches that the one to whom doctrine is entrusted ought both to preach and to perform miracles. For then <margin>B</margin> the preaching is confirmed through miracles, and the miracles through the preaching: for many have performed many miracles through demons, whose preaching was not sound, and their miracles were not from God. 

Furthermore, He strips them of every superfluous thing, so that He does not even want them to carry bread, nor anything else which most people take with them. Moreover, He commands them this: that they should not hop from place to place, but in whatever house they enter, they should remain in it, so that they do not appear inconsistent or fickle. <margin>Mark 6</margin> Indeed, He says the dust must be shaken off if they do not receive you: "for a testimony to them," that is, for their own rebuke and condemnation, showing them that the disciples completed a great journey for their sake, and yet received no <margin>F</margin> gain from it. Some, however, understand the apostles not carrying a staff or a pouch, and not having two tunics, in this way: "Do not store up treasures," of which the pouch is a symbol, as it collects many things; nor should you carry a staff, that is, do not be troublesome or prone to striking others; nor should you have two tunics, that is, do not be double-minded or inconsistent in your character.

...absurdities. <margin>D</margin> As the day was drawing to a close, the disciples, beginning to become more humane and attentive to their duty, took pity on the crowds and said, "Dismiss them," that is: heal their infirmities more quickly, and fulfill their petitions. But the Lord said to the disciples, "You give them something to eat." He says this not because He is ignorant of the disciples' lack of resources, but because He wishes to prompt them to state how many loaves of bread they have, so that the miracle might be demonstrated as even greater when they themselves report the number of loaves. As for His saying, "Make them sit down in groups of fifty," it shows that we too, when we receive someone with hospitality, ought to have them recline and be attentive to their needs. 

<margin>B</margin> Furthermore, by looking up to heaven, He demonstrates that those who are about to eat ought to give thanks to God. He gives the bread to the disciples, and then to the crowds, so that they might not forget the miracle, but remain mindful of it, reflecting on how many loaves they took into their hands. Twelve baskets remained, so that we might learn how much hospitality can accomplish, and that our own resources are multiplied when we provide for those in need. These matters have been discussed more extensively in the commentary on <margin>Matthew 14</margin> Matthew.

In this passage, He calls the "cross" the most contemptible form of death; for no death was considered so shameful as that of the cross. Thus He shows that if anyone <margin>C</margin> wishes to be His disciple, he must die not a glorious death, but a contemptible one, and be killed like a condemned man. However, since many are killed by a shameful death, such as thieves and evildoers, He adds this: "and follow me," which means he should practice every virtue. For whoever wishes to preserve his life will lose it, that is, whoever wishes to live according to this world here kills his soul. He is ashamed of Christ who says, "How can I believe in a crucified and mocked God?" And he is ashamed of His words <margin>Those who are ashamed of Christ's name</margin> who mocks the simplicity of the Gospel; such a person the Lord will be ashamed of at His second coming. What He says carries this meaning: just as if a master of a house has a wicked servant, he is ashamed to have him called his own servant; so too (He says) I will be ashamed...

# CHAPTER 9. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>Fear increases reverence</margin>
...and their reverence; how because of their reverence they did not <margin>Matthew 18</margin> dare to ask him—rather, it was because of fear. For reverence is an immediate increase of piety and respect, just as reverence or piety is a form of restrained fear.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**An argument arose among them as to which of them would be the greatest. But Jesus, seeing the thought of their hearts, took a child and stood him next to himself, and said to them: "Whoever receives this child in my name, receives me; and whoever receives me, receives him who sent me. For he who is the least among all of you, this one will be great." John, answering, said: "Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name and we forbade him, because he does not follow with us." And Jesus said to him: "Do not forbid him. For he who is not against us is for us."** 
] The disease of vainglory <note>original: "inanis gloriæ" — excessive pride in one's own accomplishments or appearance; vanity.</note> invaded the Apostles. It seems to me it arose among them because they had not healed the demoniac <note>Referring to the boy with the spirit whom the disciples could not heal earlier in the chapter.</note>. For it is likely that they argued over this, each saying that it was not because of his own weakness but someone else's that the boy was not healed, and from this, a quarrel flared up over who among them was the greatest. 
<margin>The beginning of a disease is easily cured.</margin>
But the Lord, having seen the hearts of each, intervened; and before the disease could grow worse, he cared for it so it might be pulled out by the roots. For diseases are easily conquered at the beginning, but when they have worsened, they are difficult to cure. Therefore, <margin>E</margin> how does he correct this evil? Taking a child, he shows him to the disciples, manifesting to them by this that we ought to prepare such a mind in ourselves as is in children. For they are free from malice and most simple; they are not tormented by thoughts of vainglory or ambition. "Whoever, therefore," he says, "receives such a child in my name, receives me." For what he says has this meaning: You indeed think that if you are pompous and glorious, you will please many, and more people will receive you. But I say to you that I rejoice so greatly in simplicity, and it distinguishes my disciples so much that whoever receives a most simple and innocent man as my disciple (for this is what it means to say, "in my name"), receives me. 

<column-break/>

# EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
<page-num>212</page-num>

<margin>A</margin>
But he who receives an arrogant man receives neither my disciple nor me. John, answering, said: "Lord, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him." What is the logical connection of that speech which John spoke to the things the Lord said? Truly a great one. For because the Lord had said that "he who is the least among you will be great," John began to fear that perhaps he had done something evil by forbidding the man through arrogance and pride. For to forbid someone from something does not prove that the one who forbids is the lesser, but rather that he feels something greater about himself than about the one he is forbidding. 
<margin>B</margin>
Therefore John was afraid that perhaps he had acted too proudly by forbidding the man. For what reason, then, did they forbid the man? Not because they were envious, but because they judged him unworthy to work a miracle; for he was not with them when the grace of performing miracles was given, nor had he been sent for this by the Lord like the others, nor did he follow Christ anywhere. What then does the Lord say? "Allow him," he says, "to do this." For he also crushes the head of Satan, and because he does not stand in our way regarding the preaching, he does not cooperate with the devil; therefore he is for us. For he who is not against God is for God; just as he who does not gather with God is with the devil. But I beg you, admire the power <margin>C</margin> <margin>The power of the name of Christ works even through the unworthy.</margin> of the name of Christ, how grace works even through the unworthy and those who were not disciples, just by being named; so also grace works through priests, even if they are unworthy, and all are sanctified, even if the priest is unworthy.

...did he do? **But Jesus, having turned, rebuked them, saying: <margin>D</margin> "You do not know of what spirit you are. That is, the time was approaching when, after he had endured the saving passion for us, it was necessary for him to be taken up into heaven, and to sit with God the Father. Therefore, when the time of his passion and assumption from this world drew near, he decided not to wander here and there any longer, but to go up to Jerusalem. Furthermore, he sends messengers before his face to prepare a lodging for him. Knowing that they would not be received by the Samaritans, he nonetheless sends them, so that he might take away every excuse from the Samaritans <margin>E</margin>, lest they should be able to say, "We would have received him if he had sent some ahead of him." Meanwhile, this was also useful for his disciples, so that seeing him later insulted on the cross, they might be less scandalized; instead, they might learn more from this act, that just as he now patiently bore being despised by the Samaritans and rebuked the disciples who were exasperated against the insulting ones, so also then, when he was being crucified, he might bear it not as one powerless, but as one long-suffering. It also benefits the disciples in this, that he teaches them by his own example to be patient. They, looking back to Elijah, who had burned twice fifty men with their captains <note>Referring to the story in 2 Kings 1, where Elijah calls down fire on the soldiers of Ahaziah.</note>, were exasperating the Lord against those who had committed the injury. For they were <margin>F</margin> <margin>The law of Christ is more sublime than the life of Elijah</margin> still imperfect. But Christ, teaching that his law is more sublime than the life of Elijah, rebukes them, and leads them away from such a sentiment, having taught that those who commit injury must be borne with gentleness. But what is it that he says, "they did not receive him because his face was that of one going to Jerusalem"? Does he mean they did not receive him because he had determined to go to Jerusalem? And if we understand it this way—that they did not receive him for the reason that he had determined to go to Jerusalem—then they might be found excused for not receiving him. Therefore, it must be said that the Evangelist says this: they did not receive him, nor did he enter Samaria. Then, as if someone had asked:

-># CHAPTER 9. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,<-

...we understand that he only buried him, and did nothing else good for him, but that he took diligent care of him until death and burial. Therefore, let those who are indeed dead—that is, the unbelieving—bury their own dead; I mean your father. But you, because you have believed: announce, as my disciple, the Gospel of God.

<margin>Piety to be shown even to unfaithful parents.</margin>
The Lord said this, however, not to prohibit us from providing for our parents, but to teach us that piety toward God is to be preferred over unbelieving parents. This is because nothing should be an obstacle to virtue, and one must even disregard one's own natural inclinations. For this reason, when a man asked to follow Him, but requested first to say goodbye to those at his home, the Lord did not allow it—that is, to go to his house and give notice to his <margin>E</margin> household; or to put it more accurately, to bid them farewell. That man was hinting that he still held a certain familiarity with the world, and was not of the same disposition as the apostles, who, as soon as they heard the call, followed Christ, seeking nothing else with curiosity and not even saying farewell to their kinsmen. For it often happens that when someone says farewell to his friends, some are found who might lead him away from a holy life and hinder him. Therefore, it is good that when someone wishes to do a good thing, he should not delay, but complete it immediately. For **no one who puts his hand to the** spiritual **plow** <note>original: "aratrum spirituale" — Theophylact interprets the plow as the labor of the Gospel.</note> **and looks back again to the world is fit for the kingdom of heaven.** Furthermore, understand "foxes" to mean the <margin>F</margin> malicious demons, who are also called "the birds of the heaven," that is, of the air. For it says, "according to the prince of the power of the air." <margin>Ephesians 2</margin> Therefore, the Lord says to the man:

<margin>What the head of Christ is.</margin>
<margin>The dead man is he who does not confess evil thoughts.</margin>
"Because the demons have dens within you, for that reason I, the Son of Man, have no place in you where I may lay my head—that is, faith. I see no place in your heart that is not filled with demons." For the "head" of Christ is faith in Him. For when someone believes that Christ is God, then he holds the "head" of Christ. The "dead man," moreover, is the sinner, who also buries his own dead—that is, the evil thoughts which he does not confess. Likewise, the Lord forbids his follower to bury or hide evil <column-break/> <margin>A</margin> thoughts; for He wants them to be made manifest through confession.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Exodus 15. Elim.</margin>
It is written in Exodus that the children of Israel came into Elim, and there were twelve springs of water there and seventy palm trees. Therefore, what was done then as a historical event and as a figure <note>A "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament event seen as a symbolic prophecy of a New Testament reality.</note> has now truly come to pass. "Elim" is interpreted as "ascent," which signifies nothing other than this: do not remain with the Jews in the "letter" of the law, but ascend into Christianity toward a more perfect understanding and spiritual growth. We find twelve springs, and we find twelve primary Apostles, who are the sweetest springs of all doctrine. The palm trees are those who were to be brought up and taught by the Apostles. For although Christ chose them, they were nevertheless inferior to those twelve, and were later their disciples and companions. <margin>C</margin> <margin>The Palms.</margin> Those palms, therefore, were nourished by the springs—I mean the Apostles. For us, however, they have supplied fruit that is sweet and, in a certain way, austere. For such is the doctrine of the saints: it is not entirely sweet and flattering, nor is it entirely austere and punishing, but it participates in both; it is truly "seasoned with salt" and possesses grace. <margin>Colossians 4</margin> Hence Paul also says: "Let our speech be seasoned with the salt of grace." <margin>Work for many laborers. Matthew 11, John 1.</margin> Moreover, the Lord shows, through the seventy disciples, the multitude of disciples that is needed. For just as fruitful fields require many reapers, so when there were many and innumerable people about to believe, they required many teachers. Furthermore, He sends them two by two, as if they were less perfect, so that one might help the other. They went...

<margin>D</margin> **And before his face,** <note>original: "ante faciem eius" — Luke 10:1</note> because they were teaching, just like John the Baptist: "Prepare the way of the Lord." Consider, however, how he said, **Pray the Lord of the harvest to thrust out laborers,** and then he himself sends them out by his own authority. For he himself is truly the Lord of the harvest—that is, the true God of all believers. He also foretells persecutions to them, saying that they would be **like lambs in the midst of wolves**, so that if they suddenly encountered such adversity, they would not be overly disturbed by the surprise.

**Carry no purse, nor bag, nor sandals; and greet no one on the road. Whatever house you enter, first say, "Peace to this house." And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him;** <margin>E</margin> **if not, it will return to you. Remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they give. For the laborer is worthy of his wages. Do not move from house to house. And whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you, and heal the sick who are there; and say to them, "The kingdom of God has come near to you."** 

Because he was about to send out preachers of the Gospel, he says: "Do not carry a purse, nor this or 그that"; for it is sufficient for you to have care only for the Word. For if <margin>Why Christ commanded the disciples to greet no one on the road.</margin> you carry a purse, it is clear that your care is for your belongings, and you despise the Word. Or otherwise interpreted: since you are to be fed by those you teach, what need have you of purses, or bags, or sandals? For those who are taught by you will supply everything you need. Furthermore, he commands them to **greet no one on the road** for this reason: so that they would not be occupied with human greetings and social curiosities, which would hinder them from their preaching. For it is likely that when someone greets another, they must be greeted in return, and the conversation is interrupted by further familiarities, as usually happens among those traveling together. For as soon as they become friends, they begin to inquire into matters even more extensively and curiously; and thus, little by little, the apostles would fall into human affairs and neglect the Word. Therefore, he prohibits greeting anyone on the journey for that reason. But having entered a house, he says: "Say, peace to this house"—that is, greet those who are in the house. And then,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> showing that this is not merely a greeting, but also a blessing, he says: "If indeed the head of the household is worthy, he shall be blessed; but if he is insolent and not capable of receiving peace—being combative and an adversary to your speech and teaching—the blessing will not come upon him, but will return to you." He also commands them not to move from house to house, so that they do not appear gluttonous, or become a scandal to many, or grieve those by whom they were first received. Furthermore, he says: **Eat those things which are among them**, that is, whatever they set before you, even if the food is cheap or small, seeking nothing more. Consider the food as your reward. Do not seek both to be fed and to receive a separate payment besides; rather, let the food be your reward. <margin>B</margin> See, therefore, how he instructs the disciples in a state of poverty and makes them secure. He commands them to heal the sick in the cities so that, through the working of miracles, they may draw men toward the Word they preach. And look at what he says: **And say to them, "The kingdom of God has come near to you."** <margin>When preaching runs successfully.</margin> For if you first heal them, and then teach the message, your speech will run successfully, and men will believe that the kingdom of God has reached them. For they would not have been healed unless some divine power were performing the work. Moreover, when someone is healed in their soul, then the kingdom of God comes into them. For the kingdom is far from the sick soul, since sin reigns and dominates within it.

**In whatever city you enter and they do not receive you, going out into its streets, say: "Even the dust that clings to us from your city, we wipe off against you; nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near to you."** <margin>C</margin> **I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Sodom on that day than for that city.** When, he says, they do not receive you, go out and bear witness to them that we have nothing in common with you, nor do we keep anything from your city. Instead, even the dust that clings to us, we wipe off—that is, we shake it off, clean it away as if with a sponge, and cast it back at you. <margin>How the kingdom of heaven approaches both those receiving and those not receiving the apostles.</margin> Nevertheless, know that the kingdom of God has come near to you. At this point, someone might ask: How does the Lord say that the kingdom of heaven has approached [both groups]?
