<margin>D</margin> **The kingdom of God** <note>original: "regnum Dei"</note> is for both those who received and those who did not receive the Apostles. He says that the kingdom of heaven "draws near" to those who received the Apostles because of the benefits bestowed upon them; but it draws near to those who did not receive them as a sign of their condemnation. Imagine a spectacle where many are condemned and others are not—let us say, indebted soldiers and noblemen. Then suppose a herald says to all of them, both the condemned and the honored, "Your king has approached." Does the king not approach the former for punishment, but the latter for glory and kindness? Understand this passage in the same way. It will be more tolerable for Sodom, he says, than for the city that did not receive you. Why? Because the Apostles were not sent to Sodom. Therefore, those who did not receive the Apostles are worse than the inhabitants of Sodom. <margin>Matthew 7</margin> Note that a city that does not receive the Apostles is said to have "streets." For wide is the road that leads to destruction, and whoever enters it does not receive the apostolic and divine word.

<margin>Why all things were handed over to Christ rather than to an angel or archangel.</margin> Lest anyone should doubt for whose sake all things were handed over to you <margin>D</margin> and not to another—perhaps to an angel or archangel—he says that He handed all things to me for this reason: because I am of the same nature and substance <note>original: "substantię"</note> as He is. And just as no one knows Him, so no one knows me, except the Father alone. Thus, He rightly handed all things over to me, as I am of the same nature as He, surpassing all understanding, just as He Himself is above every power of knowledge. For the Father says that He is known only by the Son, and by whomever the Son wishes to reveal Him. Observe, however, that the Son does not know the Father through revelation, but the creatures know Him through revelation; for they receive knowledge by grace, <margin>E</margin> therefore the Son is not a created being. Turning then to the disciples, he calls them blessed, as well as all those who with faith see Him walking in the flesh and performing miracles. For the ancient prophets and kings desired to see the Lord in the flesh and to hear Him, but it did not happen for them. And in another sense, because he said above, "to whom the Son reveals Him, he knows the Father," he now calls the disciples blessed because this revelation happened to them. For He revealed the Father to them through Himself. Indeed, seeing Him, one sees the Father; this is a good that none of the saints who lived before the incarnation obtained, because they did not see the LORD in the flesh, through whom the Father <margin>F</margin> would be known; thus they did not see the Father in the way the apostles did.

<margin>Matthew 22.</margin> And behold, a certain lawyer <note>original: "legisperitus," an expert in the Mosaic Law</note> stood up, tempting him and saying: Teacher, what must I do to possess eternal life? But he said to him: What is written in the law? How do you read it? He answering, said:

> You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.

<margin>Deuteronomy 6. Romans 13.</margin> And he said to him: You have answered correctly; do this and you shall live.
This lawyer was arrogant, or rather proud, as is manifest from what follows, and moreover, he was deceitful. So he approaches to tempt the Lord. For he thought that he could trip up the Lord with his answers. But the Lord leads him to the Law, in which he took such great pride.

<column-break/>

<header>EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 218</header>

<margin>A</margin> Observe with what great zeal the law commands us to love God. Man is the most perfect of all living beings, sharing in the nature of all things, and besides this, possessing something divine and more sublime. To give an example of what I mean: Man shares in the nature of a stone, for he has hair and nails, which are without feeling, just like a stone. He shares in the nature of plants, because he grows and is nourished and generates his own kind, just as plants do. He shares in the nature of the beasts, in that he has senses, feels anger, and has desires. But he also shares in the nature of God, according to the rational soul <note>Theophylact is describing the "Great Chain of Being" where humans sit at the intersection of the physical and divine worlds.</note> which is above all other living creatures. Therefore, the law, wishing to show that man ought to give his <margin>B</margin> whole self to God and use all his living powers for the love of God, by saying "with all your heart," declared the coarser power, the one common to plants <note>This refers to the "vegetative soul" responsible for basic biological life.</note>. By saying "with all your soul," he showed the middle power, congruent with things that have senses <note>The "sensitive soul" shared with animals.</note>. By saying "with all your mind," he signified the power most proper to man, the rational soul. Furthermore, what he says about "all your strength" is to be applied to all of these. For it is necessary for us to subject our natural and growth-producing <note>original: "vegetatiuum"</note> power to the love of Christ. But how? Strongly, and not loosely. And the sensory power, that too strongly. Finally, the rational power, and that with all one's strength. And so we ought to give our whole selves to God and subject our nutritive, sensory, and rational powers to the <margin>C</margin> love of God. "And your neighbor as yourself." The law, not yet being able to teach perfection because of the childishness of its hearers, urges one to love his neighbor as himself. CHRIST, however, taught us to love our neighbor even more than ourselves. For he said, "Greater love than this no one can show, than that a man lay down his life for his friend." He says therefore to the lawyer: "You have answered correctly." Because (he means to say), since you are still subject to the law, you have answered according to the wisdom of the law.

But he, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: And who is my neighbor? Jesus answering, said:

> A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers, who also stripped him...

...and spoken, not in appearance only, but in truth. Accordingly, he immediately **D** binds the wounds, and does not permit the malice to spread further, but binds it up. He pours in oil and wine: oil, which is the word of doctrine that encourages us through gentle means; and wine, the word that leads us to virtue through more austere means. For example, when you hear <margin>Matthew 11</margin> the Lord saying, "Come to me, and I will refresh you," this oil shows cheerfulness and rest. And <margin>Matthew 25</margin> again, "Come, inherit the kingdom prepared for you." But when He says, "Go into the darkness," this is wine—that is, a more austere teaching. You can also understand this another way: oil signifies His human conduct, and wine the divine. To put it this way, the Lord performed some things in a human manner and others in a divine manner. It was human to eat **E** and drink, and to follow a less rigid life, not displaying such austerity as John the Baptist did; and this would be the oil. But the miraculous fasting, the walking on the sea, and other divine powers are the wine. For the divinity is likened to wine, which no one could endure or carry undiluted <note>The original Latin *meracam* refers to wine that has not been watered down, a common metaphor for the overwhelming nature of pure divinity</note> unless the oil were also present—that is, His more human conduct. And therefore, because He saved us through both—I mean through His divinity and His humanity—He is said to have poured in wine and oil. And daily, those who are baptized are delivered from the wounds of the soul, being anointed with the oil of chrism; and immediately afterward, they become communicants and partakers of the divine blood <note>A reference to the Eucharist following Baptism</note>. Furthermore, the Lord placed our wounded **F** nature upon His own beast of burden—that is, upon His own body. For He made us His members and partakers of His body; and though we were situated in the lowest place, He set us in that dignity so that we might be seen to belong to that same body. The inn, moreover, is the Church, which receives everyone; for the Law did not <margin>Deuteronomy 23. Acts 10.</margin> receive everyone. For it says that the Moabite and the Ammonite shall not enter into the assembly of God. But now, in every nation, he who fears God is accepted by Him, provided he is willing to believe and become part of the Church, which receives all sinners and tax collectors. See also the diligence: how "leading him," it says, "into the inn, he took care of him." For before he led him into this place, he only bound his wounds. What then is it that I am saying? Because when the

<column-break/>

**A** Church was established and the inn was created—that is, increased from nearly all nations—then there were also the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the grace of God was expanded. You will learn this from the Acts of the Apostles. Moreover, every apostle, teacher, and pastor holds the figure of the innkeeper. To these the Lord gave two denarii: the two Testaments, the Old and the New. For both hold the image of the one King, and both are the utterances of God. Therefore, the Lord, ascending into heaven, left those denarii to the apostles, and to other bishops and teachers. He said, "Whatever you spend of your own, I will give to you." For indeed, the Apostles spent much of their own, laboring greatly and sowing all the <margin>B</margin> doctrine. And the teachers who explain the Old and New Testaments also spend much of their own, for which they will receive a reward when the Lord returns in His second coming <margin>Matthew 25. Luke 19.</margin>. For then each one will say to Him, "Lord, you gave me two denarii; behold, I have spent another two besides." To whom He Himself will say, "Well done, good servant," and so forth.

Now it happened as they went, that He entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received Him into her house. And she had a sister named Mary, who also sitting at His feet, heard His word. But Martha was distracted about much serving; and standing there, she said, "Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? <margin>C</margin> Tell her therefore to help me." And Jesus answering, said to her, "Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things: but one thing is necessary; Mary has chosen the good part, which shall not be taken away from her." Great indeed is the virtue of hospitality, which Martha showed, and it is not to be rejected; but it is greater to attend to more spiritual words. For by the former the body is fed, but by the latter the soul is given life. "For we are not present for this purpose," He says, "to fill the mind <note>The Latin *mentem* (mind) here is likely a printer's error for *ventrem* (stomach), as the context refers to filling up on various foods</note> with various foods, but to be useful to souls." See also the Lord's judgment. He said nothing to Martha until He took the opportunity of being rebuked by her. For after she attempted to pull her sister away from the hearing, only then did the Lord, seizing the opportunity, correct her. Thus far...

For hospitality is indeed worthy of respect, provided it is not the kind of over-eagerness that pulls us away and leads us from more necessary things. <margin>Martha signifies the practical virtue; Mary, the contemplative.</margin>
Understand also that Martha represents practical virtue, while Mary represents contemplation. For the practical life bears distractions and turmoils, but contemplation becomes the mistress of the passions. For Mary is interpreted as "Mistress" <note>The name Mary was traditionally interpreted in the Middle Ages as meaning "Lady" or "Mistress," from the Aramaic *marta*.</note>, and she is occupied solely in the contemplation of divine words and judgments. Observe also this: that she sits at the feet of Jesus and hears His words. Indeed, by the "feet" they understand practical virtue, for they show movement and walking. Furthermore, "sitting" is a symbol of stability. Therefore, whoever sits at the feet of Jesus and is established in practice, and imitates the life and conduct of Jesus, that person afterwards 
<margin>F</margin>
comes to the hearing of divine words, namely to contemplation; for Mary first sits, then hears the words. You, therefore, if you are able, ascend to the order of Mary: become the mistress of your passions, and you will come to contemplation. But if this is not possible for you, be Martha, devoted to the practical part, and through this, receive Christ. But see this: *which shall not be taken away from her*. For the practitioner has something that may be taken away from them—that is, distraction and busy occupation—for by advancing, one comes to contemplation and is freed from turmoil and distraction, and so something is "taken away" from them. But the contemplator is not deprived of this good

...as it is done in heaven by the angels, so let it be done by us humans upon the earth. For the angels act entirely according to the will of God. He also teaches that only "daily bread" should be sought—that is, that which is suitable for our substance and the preservation of our life: not what is superfluous, but what is necessary. Furthermore, "not to enter into temptations" <note>This refers to the line "lead us not into temptation" from the Lord's Prayer.</note> signifies that one should not rashly leap into trials. For we ought not to pray to God to send us into temptation; rather, they are to be prayed against, and if they happen to us, they must be borne bravely. However, we can say that there are two kinds of temptations. Some are voluntary, such as drunkenness, murder, adultery, and other passions.
<margin>Two types of temptations</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
For we submit ourselves to these temptations of our own accord. Involuntary ones, however, are those to which tyrants and those more powerful than us subject us. Therefore, we must flee from voluntary temptations—that is, the passions—and pray against them, saying, "lead us not," which means, "do not permit us to fall into temptation," specifically voluntary temptation. "But deliver us from evil." For he <note>The "Evil One" or the Devil.</note> is the one who brings both voluntary and involuntary temptations. Therefore, you who are tempted by a person and suffer violence, do not think that a human is the author of your temptation, but rather the Evil One. For it is he who persuades a brother to rage and act insanely against you.

**And he said to them, "Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go to him at midnight, and say to him, 'Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him,' and he from within answering, should say: 'Do not trouble me, the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give to you.' I say to you, even if he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence** <note>original: "improbitatem" — in this context, it refers to a relentless, almost shameless persistence in asking.</note> **he will rise and give him as many as he needs."** The Lord tells this parable and example to instruct us not to pray sluggishly. ...that is, seek continually. For "everyone who asks, receives." Does this mean that even one who asks for things that are not expedient receives them? No. For first of all, a request for harmful things is not called a "petition" in the eyes of God; for he who prays to God ought to ask for what God gives. When someone asks for harmful things, he does not truly make a petition, for God does not give harmful things. Furthermore, hear the Lord himself as he teaches us how we ought to ask. <margin>Bread, fish, and an egg are to be asked from God</margin> A son, he says, asks for bread, a fish, and an egg. <margin>A</margin> But it is different if someone’s hearing is damaged by accident. For nothing prevents such a person from speaking. Let us listen, therefore, we who have diabolical works within us and yet think we can teach others, and who desire to be greeted by men as "Rabbi." To whom the Lord said: "How," he asks, "can a demon cast out another demon? For this would be the destruction of his own kingdom." For they consider it a "kingdom" and a state of rest to dwell in humans. And if their prince casts them out, it is manifest that he destroys himself. For every kingdom divided and seditious is destroyed, as is a house divided. Whether you understand "house" as a physical building, it works well. For a building stands as long as it holds itself together and preserves its continuity; but after the walls are scattered, it falls. Or if you understand <margin>C</margin> those who inhabit the house; for these are preserved as long as they are at peace, but when they disagree among themselves, they fall. Therefore, they themselves shall condemn you." For it is manifest that they cast out demons in my name, and I have no need of another’s power. "In the finger of God, therefore—that is, in the Holy Spirit—I cast them out, and not in an evil spirit."

### CHAPTER II. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE.

<margin>D</margin>
He calls the Spirit the "finger" so that you may know that just as the finger is of the same <term>substance</term> <note>Original: "substantiae." This refers to the theological concept of "consubstantiality," meaning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share the same divine essence.</note> with the rest of the body, so also the Spirit is of the same substance with the Father and the Son. And perhaps for this reason—because the Son is called the "hand of God," and the seven operations of the Spirit rested upon Him—it is not because He is acted upon by the Spirit, but because He is <margin>And by what manner, Isaiah 11</margin> of the same substance as the Spirit.

<margin>E</margin>
One of the gifts and workings of the Holy Spirit is to heal; therefore, it is said "in the Spirit of God," that is, He casts out demons in a spiritual gift. For just as the finger is part of the hand, so the spirit of gifts was part of the "spirits" which <term>CHRIST</term> possessed—that is, the operations of the Spirit. Therefore, if I (He says) cast out demons, the efficacy of divine power has surely come upon you: <margin>B</margin> the kingdom of God. This has such a meaning: the kingdom of the devil is now destroyed, and God, who puts demons to flight, reigns. For hear what He says next:

[When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are in peace. But when one stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils. He who is not with me is against me: and he who does not gather with me, scatters. When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it walks through dry places, seeking rest, and finding none, it says, "I will return to my house, from which I came." And when it comes, it finds it swept clean and decorated; then it goes and takes seven other spirits, more wicked than itself, and entering they dwell there, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.] <margin>F</margin> Satan (He says) was indeed "the strong one" before my coming, and he guarded his courtyard—that is, he prevailed and ruled over human nature forcefully and securely. But after I came, being stronger than he, and conquered the world, I took all his armor in which he trusted, <margin>What are the weapons of the devil?</note> namely all kinds of sins. For those are the weapons of the devil, in which he trusted and prevailed. I, therefore, who was found without sin, have plundered those weapons of his. Whence his spoils were weakened—that is, the men whom he held; I snatched them from him like spoils and I hand them over, one to another, to a faithful guardian angel, so that instead of a demon, whose tyranny he had endured, he may have an angel. Or otherwise, do I have

<column-break/>

A communion with Beelzebub? My work is to gather the scattered children of God, but his is to scatter those who are gathered. How then do you think of me, that I have communion with Satan? And certainly, this thought arises from the fact that the demons now oppress you more than they once did. For you also had an unclean spirit once, which dwelt in you when you worshipped idols and killed the prophets; and it seemed afterward to go out from you. But now it has returned to its house, that is, your souls, with seven spirits—that is, many; for <margin>p</margin> scripture uses "seven" for "many"—and it has made your last state worse than the first. For when you worshipped idols <margin>B</margin> and killed the prophets, you had not yet committed an injury against the Son of God, who has now appeared in the flesh for your sake. But now, what hope of salvation is there, when you have broken out into such ingratitude and insult even against the incarnate Son of God, who has performed miracles for your sake?

Furthermore, the "waterless places" are the souls of those who have nothing watery or dissolved <note>In this context, "watery" or "dissolved" refers to being spiritually weak, fluid, or lacking in moral discipline.</note> about them, but are dry and diligent, in whom the spirit of uncleanness finds no rest. And since the wicked one finds no place of dwelling in such souls, he returns to the Jews, and their latter state becomes worse than the first. They no longer have prophets, for they killed the Word; <margin>C</margin> nor do they have the anointing, for they crucified **CHRIST**. For these things once appeared among them, even though they worshipped idols; but now, because they have sinned against the Son of God, they are deprived of all those things.

But as the crowds were gathering, he began to say: "This generation is evil; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. <margin>Jonah 2</margin> For just as Jonah was a sign to the Ninevites, so also the Son of Man will be to this generation. <margin>3 Kings 30, 2 Chronicles 9</margin> The Queen of the South will rise in judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn them; because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here."

**The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this nation and will condemn it, because they were led to repentance by the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.** While the Pharisees and scribes were criticizing his miracles, a simple woman, free from deceit, celebrated him. Where now are those who say the Lord only appeared to be human in outward form? Let this woman be a witness that he even had breasts that nursed <note>original: "vbera lactent"; Theophylact is arguing against Docetism, a belief that Jesus's physical body was an illusion.</note>. Yet he calls those blessed who keep the word of God, not depriving his own mother of blessedness—far from it—but showing that there would be no benefit to her from having given birth to him and nursing him unless she also possessed all other virtues. Furthermore, he says these things opportunely. Because the envious and disobedient were rebuking others who heard his words, Christ, on the contrary, calls them blessed. Perhaps he also says these things because of the man who was healed of deafness: so that he himself, when he has heard, might act upon the word, and that the power of hearing he received might not become a cause for his condemnation. 

As the crowds were gathering, Jesus began to rebuke the ungrateful. For there were some among them who were seeking a sign from heaven to be performed by Jesus. For both because of my dignity and the nature of my preaching, a greater excellence is shown. ### CHAPTER XI. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>
One who is wise has already entered; however, one who is still learning is currently entering. But you Pharisees do not wish to do this; instead, you have made the eye of your mind—which was meant to be simple <note>In this context, "simple" implies single-mindedness or sincerity, as opposed to being "double-minded" or deceptive.</note>—crooked and dark. Indeed, just as the eye of the physical body, if it possesses anything, causes the whole body to have it as well—if it has light and is bright, the body will also be in the light; but if it is dark, the body will also be in darkness—in the same way, the soul has the same disposition as the mind. And if the soul finds the eye which it received from God to be darkened, either by envy or by greed, or to put it briefly, if it is darkened by carnality, then the soul itself is darkened.

<margin>E</margin>
**And as he was speaking, a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him. And Jesus went in and sat down at the table. But when the Pharisee saw this, he wondered why he had not first washed before the meal.** 

<margin>Matthew 23</margin>
**And the Lord said to him: Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but what is inside you is full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside also make the inside? Nevertheless, give what remains as alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.** 

<margin>Why the Lord eats with Pharisees and wicked men.</margin>
The Lord certainly knew the spite of the Pharisees, yet he ate with them nonetheless, for the very reason that they were wicked and had need of correction. For this purpose he ate with them: so that he might take the opportunity to amend their character. Accordingly, he now rebukes their foolish custom—namely, 

<margin>F</margin>
the washing before they eat—teaching that it is necessary to purify the soul through good works. For washing with water does not purify the soul, but only the body. But those fools thought that when the body was baptized <note>original: "baptizabatur"; here referring to ritual immersion or washing.</note> and washed, the soul was purged at the same time. The Lord therefore used the beautiful example of the cup. Because it was mealtime, he mentioned the cup and the dish, bringing forth testimony from the things set before their eyes. He persuaded the Pharisees that just as there is no benefit to a cup being clean on the outside if the inside is filled with filth, so it is of no use if the body is washed but the soul is full of every impurity, such as greed and wickedness. Moreover, he hinted at two conditions from which the Jews suffered: 

<column-break/>

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 226
<page-num>226</page-num>

<margin>A</margin>
greed, expressed through theft; and envy, along with those things that arise from envy, expressed through wickedness. Therefore, there is no benefit when the soul of a fool is in such a state. Did not he who made the body, which you deem worthy of much care, also make the soul? You ought, therefore, to purify that as well. Next, he teaches them how it must be purified: namely, that the internal part is purified through <term>almsgiving</term> <note>original: "eleemosynam"; from the Greek 'eleemosyne', meaning works of mercy or charity.</note>. Observe how he heals their two conditions—I mean envy and greed—by what he adds regarding alms. For he who truly shows mercy does not envy the one who receives that mercy. And because he rebuked them for two diseases, he heals both with the single remedy of alms, which is the primary daughter of deifying <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charitatis"; Christian love or 'agape'. Theophylact calls it "deifying" because it makes the believer more like God.</note>. 

<margin>Almsgiving is the daughter of deification.</margin>
For if love is present, where will greed and envy remain? 

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, "the things that are within" refers to your resources. He spoke well in saying "the things that are within," rather than just "the things that exist," because riches are within the heart of the greedy man and reside there. For this reason David also says that the heart must not be set upon riches, so that the heart is neither glued to them nor gathered into them.

<summary>In this passage, Theophylact explains Jesus's rebuke of the Pharisees' obsession with ritual purity, arguing that true cleanliness comes from internal virtue and acts of charity rather than external washing. He characterizes almsgiving as a remedy for the "diseases" of envy and greed, and concludes with Christ's "woes" against the hypocrisy of the religious leaders.</summary>

Therefore, the Lord says: Just as you do not neglect those things, so it is necessary for you to practice both judgment and the love of God. Since they were unjust and were crushing <note>The Latin 'pessundabant' implies trampling or ruining.</note> widows and orphans, He says that it is necessary for them to have judgment, which is to say, just judgment. <margin>B</margin>

two kinds of love—one toward God, the other toward one's neighbor—He is alluding to those two. For by saying "judgment," He indicates love toward one's neighbor. For to judge a neighbor justly and not to trample him happens out of love. By saying "the love of God," He certainly signifies a general affection toward God. And when one loves a neighbor, it should not be because of a certain widowhood or some shameful affection, but according to God. Therefore, that love is also called the "love of God" because God commanded it. Furthermore, the Pharisees wanted to be honored and greeted by all men as "Teachers" in the marketplace. You are like monuments (He says), which are indeed full of all rot, but on the outside men see them shining with marble, not knowing what they are stepping on; otherwise, they would recoil from the abomination that is within. Then a lawyer <note>The 'legisperitus' was a scholar specialized in the interpretation of Mosaic Law.</note> foolishly proceeds to offer a rebuke. Truly, some were lawyers and others were Pharisees. For the 
<margin>Pharisees</margin>

Pharisees appeared like monks <note>Theophylact uses 'monachi' (monks) to explain the Pharisees' name, which means "separated ones."</note> and those who separated themselves from others. Therefore, they burdened men with heavy and intolerable things, commanding those things which are difficult to observe in the law, while they themselves did not touch them with a finger; that is, they themselves did nothing of what they commanded others to do.

that is, to question Him frequently and make Him perplexed. This is what usually happens when many people question one person on various arguments; for then he who is unable to answer everyone gives the appearance of a fool, because he has been made perplexed. For many questioning one man seemed to stop His mouth and make Him perplexed, so that He could not answer them, which likely would have happened [to any other man]. They were questioning Him about the law to prove Him a blasphemer who had criticized Moses—for this is what they suspected. At other times they questioned Him about things pertaining to Caesar, so they might denounce Him as seditious and a seeker of tyranny—altogether such things as the worst and most malignant souls, full of all iniquity, might devise.

You could also understand those words in this way: that the "light" is the Gospel, and the "high house" represents the lofty souls of the Apostles. For not all sinners who die are sent into Gehenna, but they are in the power of God, so that they might even be released. I say this on account of the offerings and distributions <note>Refers to liturgical offerings (Eucharist) and alms given on behalf of the deceased.</note> which are made for the departed, which are of no small benefit even to those who have died in grave sins. Therefore, He does not entirely send them to Gehenna after they have died, but He has the power...

### CHAPTER 12. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>
...has the power to cast. Therefore, let us not cease, through almsgiving and intercessions, to make Him favorable who has the power to cast [into hell]; yet He does not always use this power, but is also able to grant forgiveness. Since many think that those who die for the sake of the truth are abandoned by God, He says: "Do not think this, for they do not die as if abandoned by me." For if not one of the sparrows sold for a small price is forgotten, how much more significant will your death be, you who are my friends? As if I would not provide for you? Indeed, I care so much for you that all your affairs are precisely observed, and even your hairs are numbered. Therefore, although I permit you to fall into temptation, I will nevertheless <margin>E</margin> supply the strength to endure in abundance. Often, if I see someone who is weaker, I do not permit him to fall into temptations. For I am the caretaker, and I know all things well; I even have the smallest things numbered, and I distribute to each what <margin>Exodus 38. Numbers 26, 32.</margin> suits his own measure. Furthermore, if you look in the Scripture, you will find Him numbering all those who reach the measure of manhood <note>original: 'mensuram virilis aetatis', referring to the census of fighting men in the Old Testament</note> and are worthy of divine counting. By the "head" of each of the faithful in Christ, we should understand a life pleasing to Christ; and by his "hairs," the particular works and the means by which the body is mortified, which are numbered and reckoned by God. For such works of ours deserve divine visitation. Now, some understand the "five sparrows" to be the five senses <margin>F</margin>, which are sold for two small pennies <note>original: 'assibus', a low-value Roman coin</note>, that is, the New and Old Testaments, and they are not forgotten by God. For those whose senses are rightly ordered, and are sober, and are subject to reason—so that they are not useless but very useful for spiritual food—these are not forgotten by the Lord.

### CHAPTER 12. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, 
### EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE.

<meta>Catchword: temporal</meta>

...attributing [miracles to a demon], he blasphemes and speaks an insult against the <margin>D</margin> Holy Spirit. By saying that miracles are performed by an evil spirit and not a divine one, he will not obtain forgiveness, and he will not be innocent unless he repents. For to the one who blasphemes the Son of Man, the sin is not imputed; therefore, even if he does not perform penance, he may obtain forgiveness. But for the one who sees the works of the Divine Spirit and yet blasphemes, the sin will not be forgiven without repentance: for it is considered the greatest sin. <note>Theophylact is explaining that rejecting Jesus's humanity is understandable, but rejecting the obvious power of the Holy Spirit working through Him is a deeper rejection of God.</note> "When they lead you away to the priests, magistrates, and others." Because <margin>Human weakness is twofold.</margin> our weakness is twofold—either we flee martyrdom because of the fear of punishment, or because of our simplicity, because we cannot give an account of our <margin>E</margin> faith—He has indeed healed the fear arising from punishment when He said: "Do not fear those by whom the body is killed." He also now heals the sickness arising from simplicity <note>Here, "simplicity" refers to being unlearned or lacking formal education in rhetoric.</note>: for since not many "wise according to the flesh" believed, but mostly common people. "Do not fear," He says, "you who are simple, unrefined, and an unlearned man <note>original: 'idiota'</note>, nor be anxious how or what you should answer the tyrant when you are questioned, or what you should say." There will be another manner of speaking. For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what it is necessary to say; and so, what need was there for anxiety, if indeed in that hour you are to be taught by the Holy Spirit? Thus, in both ways He prepares us for martyrdom: He heals the fear which is from physical weakness, and that which is from simplicity.

Someone from the crowd said to Him, "Master, tell my <margin>F</margin> brother to divide the inheritance with me." But He said to him, "Man, who appointed me a judge or a divider over you?" And He said to them, "See and beware of greed, because a person's life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses." The Lord, teaching us how it is necessary to despise temporal things, and that there is no need to be greatly occupied with earthly matters, dismisses from Himself the one who had called upon Him to divide a paternal inheritance. Therefore He also says, "Who appointed me a judge or a divider over you?" For since that man had neglected to ask for things that are useful and conducive to the soul's salvation, he sought to make Him a divider in earthly and tempo-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ral affairs. For this reason, as if the man were common and unable to learn anything useful, He dismisses him, doing so gently and not harshly. He teaches, however, through this to all who heard Him then and who hear Him now, that all earthly things are indeed to be neglected, and <margin>We should not strive with brothers for temporal things.</margin> one should not contend with brothers for the sake of temporal affairs, but rather yield to them, even if they wish to be greedy. For from the one who takes away your things, do not demand them back. Therefore, whatever is useful and necessary for the salvation of the soul must be sought. For this reason He added: "See and guard yourselves against greed," warning us to flee it as if from a certain demonic pit. To whom, then, did He say, "See and guard yourselves against greed"? To those <margin>B</margin> two brothers, since they were contending over an inheritance. It was likely that one of those two had wronged the other, and for that reason He speaks to them about greed. For this is a great evil; therefore Paul also <margin>Colossians 3</margin> calls it "idolatry" itself. Perhaps because it belongs only to those who are ignorant of God; or, what is even truer, because the idols of the Gentiles are silver and gold: therefore he who worships silver and gold is like the worshippers of idols. For both adore and embrace the same material. Thus, superfluous things are to be fled. Why? Because their life is not in a certain abundance; the measure of life is not contained in plenty. For neither does he who possesses much live longer, nor does longevity of life accompany a multitude of riches. <margin>Longevity of life does not accompany riches.</margin> <margin>C</margin> The Lord says this, refuting the thoughts of those who love riches. Since lovers of riches think that they will possess their wealth for a long time, and they collect resources from every side as if they were going to live long, He says: "Wretched and miserable man, will your life be made longer by the possession of many things? Why then do you afflict yourself?" It is clearly for an uncertain rest. For it is uncertain whether you will reach old age, for the sake of which you store up treasure. It is clear, however, that you are now exhausted in acquiring resources.

And He told them a parable, saying: "The field of a certain rich man brought forth a bountiful harvest, and he..."

<margin>Ecclesiastes 11.</margin>
...[The rich man] thought within himself, saying: "What shall I do, because I have nowhere to gather my fruits?" And he said: "This I will do: I will pull down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will gather all my goods that have grown for me. And I will say to my soul: 'Soul, you have many goods stored up for many years; rest, eat, drink, and be merry.'" But God said to him: "Fool, this night they will demand <note>original: 'repetent'</note> your soul from you; and the things you prepared, whose will they be?" So it is for the one who stores up for himself and is not rich toward God.

<margin>B</margin>
After He said that a man’s life is not extended by an abundance of riches, He brings forth a parable to confirm this. See how He describes for us the insatiable thoughts of the foolish rich man. For God was doing His part, showing His accustomed mercy, so that not just one small field, but the whole region brought forth abundant fruit for him. Yet this man was so merciless that, even before he had received the harvest, he sought to shut it away. Look also at the pleasures of the rich. "What shall I do?" A poor man would never speak this way, saying "What shall I do?" except perhaps to say, "I have no way to clothe myself, or no way to feed myself." But observe the words of the rich man: "What shall I do, because I have nowhere to gather my fruits?" Truly, rest is a good thing. Yet if the poor man says, "What shall I do, because I have nothing?" and the rich man says, "What shall I do, because I have everything?" then what do we gain from gathering more? We do not gain rest—as is clear from these anxieties—but we only accumulate a multitude of sins for ourselves.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>Let the bellies of the poor be the storehouses of our riches.</margin>
"I will pull down my barns and build larger ones." If the region brings forth more fruit in the future, will we pull those down again and build others? What is the use of pulling down and building up? You have barns already: the bellies of the poor, which can hold much and are incorruptible, for they are heavenly and divine. Since whoever feeds the poor, feeds God. See also his other folly: "my produce," he calls it—that is, "the things grown for me"—and "my goods." For he did not think that he held these things from God; otherwise, as a steward of God, he would have distributed them differently. Instead, he thought they were produced by his own labors; therefore, attributing them to himself, he called them his "goods" and things "born for him." As if say-

-ing: "I have no partner, I share with no one; they are not God’s, but mine. Therefore, I alone shall enjoy them, and I will not include God in the enjoyment of them." Because these thoughts are foolish, let us look at the rest. "Soul, you have many goods stored up for many years." He promised himself a long life, as if he had also cultivated the earth to produce that life—for that was not born for you there, nor is life your "good" to control. "Eat, drink, and be merry." Oh, what wretched conditions for your soul! For eating and drinking are the "goods" of an irrational soul <note>In medieval philosophy, the "irrational soul" refers to the part of the human psyche shared with animals, governed by physical instincts rather than reason.</note>. Since you have chosen such a soul for yourself, you rightly offer it these things.

<margin>What are the goods of the rational soul?</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
The good of the rational soul, however, is to understand, to reason, and to rejoice in the law of God and in good thoughts. Is it not enough for you to eat and drink, O fool, but must you also command the soul to pursue the abominable and most shameful pleasure that follows these? For the Lord clearly says this through the word "merry," declaring the lustful and intemperate affections that accompany the satiation of food and drink.

But God said to him: "Fool, this night they will demand your soul." This is not said as if God held a familiar conversation with the rich man, for this is a parable. Observe also the word "demand" <note>original: 'repetent' - literally 'they will demand back'.</note>. For the angels, like cruel and terrible tax collectors, will demand your soul back even against your will, because you struggle against them due to an excessive love for this present life. For the soul is not "demanded" from a righteous man; rather, he, rejoicing and exulting, commends his soul to God, the Father of spirits, and does not take death hard. For he is clothed with the body as if with a burden, which he lays down lightly. But the sinner, who has subjected his soul to the flesh and has become too attached to the body, has made the soul itself into "flesh." He wishes to keep it inseparable from the body; therefore, it is said to be "demanded" from him, just as from...

...could be clothed in all his delights as even one of these lilies is, and this despite there being no absolute necessity for the beauty of lilies. How much more, then, will He clothe you, who are such worthy creatures—especially since the necessity of the body requires clothing? What then will someone say: "Are you commanding us not to cultivate the fields?" He did not say, "do not cultivate the fields," but rather, "**do not be anxious**." For I do not forbid you to work, but I do forbid you to be anxious; that is, I forbid you to place your hope in those works. Thus, he who works but keeps his hope in God lives without anxiety. For God cuts away anxiety as something that leads us away from Him. Therefore He says: "Do not seek what you should eat or what you should drink, and do not
<margin>To be lifted up on high: what it is.</margin> <margin>E</margin>
**be lifted up on high.** To be "lifted up on high" is nothing other than distraction and an unstable turning of the mind, thinking now of this and now of that, leaping from one thing to another, and always imagining something "higher" for oneself. Is this not what it means to be "lifted up"? Therefore, the Lord forbids this anxiety—this being lifted up—because it leads away from God, saying that "the Gentiles seek after all these things." For anxiety is not content with only what is necessary, but as I said, it always requires something more
<margin>Why anxiety is called <term>suspense</term> <note>original: μετεωρισμός (meteorismos)</note>.</margin>
and greater, and for this reason it is called <term>suspense</term> <note>A state of being "up in the air" or mentally unsettled</note>, an elation toward the high. To give an example: we do not have bread, and so we are anxious about where to get it; but we do not stop there. Instead, we seek to obtain fine wheat, then wine (and the most fragrant kind at that!), then roasted meats, and then even francolins and pheasants. You see the anxiety, that "lifting up" toward more and more, which He calls <term>suspense</term>. <margin>F</margin> For this reason, the Lord cuts all these things away, for the Gentiles seek these things. Furthermore, He brings another reason: "for your Father knows that you have need of these things." Indeed, He does not use just one reason, but many. He is "Father" (He says), and if He is Father, how would He not give? But He also "knows"—for how could He be ignorant? And He knows "what things you have need of." For these are not superfluities, but things necessary for us. Therefore, since He is the Father, and you have the need, and He knows it, how could He not give? Seek therefore the Kingdom of God before all things, and cast away the anxiety for temporal things, which leads away from Him.

For when He sees you occupied with the Kingdom of God, He will necessarily provide for all your needs. Do we not do the same in our own affairs? Therefore, the Lord rejects care for all temporal things so that we may seek His Kingdom, which those who are anxious about temporal things fail to do.

# CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>
...the moth corrupts, but in heaven it is not so. Would it not, therefore, be the mark of a foolish man to gather treasures in a place where they are destroyed? Later, because gold is not destroyed by the moth, he said, *and where no thief approaches.* The moth indeed does not destroy gold, but the thief snatches it away. Finally, because not all things perish by theft, he adds a greater reason, superior to any counter-argument. **For where your treasure is,** he says, **there also will your heart be.** For suppose, he says, that neither the moth destroys nor the thief approaches; yet to have one’s heart enslaved to a corruptible treasure, and to cast the soul—which is a divine possession—into the earth, how much punishment would that in itself be worthy of? Indeed, let one observe how one might be in the highest state. For where your treasure is, there also is your heart; if that treasure is on earth, then the heart is on earth; but if that is in heaven, then this too is above. Who, therefore, would not prefer to be above, rather than under the earth? Who would not choose to be an angel, rather than a mole always acting in subterranean hiding places?

**Let your loins be girded, and your lamps burning, and you yourselves like men waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding: so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him immediately. Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, finds watching. Amen I say to you, that he will gird himself and make them sit down at table, and passing by he will serve them. And if he comes in the second watch, or if he comes in the third watch and finds them so, blessed are those servants. But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would have watched and not allowed his house to be broken into. And you therefore, be ready, because at an hour you do not expect, the Son of Man will come.** After the Lord made his disciple free from superfluous things, and stripped him of all anxiety and desire for temporal goods, and thus rendered him clearly light, now he also makes him his minister. For he who wishes to be a minister must be light and unencumbered; therefore he says, **Let your loins be girded**, that is, be prepared in every way for the works of your lord. And **burning lamps in your hands**, that is,

<margin>A</margin>

Furthermore, those with "girded loins" are those who lead an <term>active life</term> <note>The "active life" (vita activa) refers to the practice of virtues and physical works of mercy, as opposed to the "contemplative life" of prayer and study.</note>, for workers use such garments, and they also have need of burning candles. For the active life also requires the gift of judgment, so that he who leads an active life may not only know what he ought to do, but also how. For many have indeed done a "good thing," but not *well*; and such people were indeed girded at the loins and did the works, but not well; nor did they have burning lamps in their hands—that is, they did not have right judgment, but either fell into pride or into some other precipice of arrogance. Consider also this, 
<margin>B</margin>

<margin>First action, then contemplation.</margin>
For first comes <term>action</term>, and then <term>contemplation</term> <note>original: operatio ... contemplatio</note>, which is the illumination of the mind. For our mind is a lamp, which is said to "burn" when it has the light of God shining in the law. Let us therefore strive to be endowed with virtue, having two burning lamps: both the internal word in our affections, and the one which we pronounce. The internal one is so that it may illuminate the soul through all things; the one we bring forth is so that it may shine brightly upon the tongue. Let the internal one enlighten us, while the word of teachers—that which is pronounced—enlightens others. **And let us be like men waiting for their Lord, when he returns from the wedding.** Who is this lord 
<margin>C</margin>
but Christ Jesus? He assumed human nature and joined it to himself like a bridegroom, and made a wedding by joining it into "one flesh"; or rather, he did not make just one wedding, but many. For every day weddings of holy souls take place in heaven, 
<margin>2 Corinthians 11</margin>
whom Paul (or anyone like Paul) commends to him as a chaste virgin. But he returns from the heavenly wedding, perhaps in the universal consummation of the world when he shall come from heaven in the glory of the Father; but perhaps also he comes unexpectedly in each person’s own death. # CHAPTER 12 THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...not only doing what is good, but doing it well, and receiving the lamp of contemplation; for by acting well and rightly we also acquire the lamp of contemplation: indeed, we acquire two lamps—one which is in the heart and the other which is in speech. To such ministers, the Lord Himself will also be a minister. For He girds Himself (it says) and makes them sit at table, and passing by He will serve them.

<margin>1 Corinthians 15</margin>
He girds Himself in the sense that He does not supply us with the outpouring of all His goods at once, but reserves that for Himself. For who can grasp how great God is? This is manifest from the Seraphim, who cover themselves because of the excellence of the divine light <note>A reference to Isaiah 6, where the Seraphim use their wings to veil themselves from God’s overwhelming glory</note>. Furthermore, He makes the good servants sit at table: for He makes them rest entirely in all things. 
<margin>E</margin>
For just as one who reclines rests with the whole body, so in the second coming all the saints will rest in every way. For in this life they do not find rest for the body. But elsewhere, along with their souls, their spiritual and divine bodies will inherit incorruption and enjoy every rest. And God will be "all in all" for them. Indeed, He serves the worthy by repaying them in kind: and just as they served Him, so He also serves them in turn, and provides a <term>sumptuous banquet</term> <note>original: *dapfilem mensam*</note> for them, exhibiting the delicacies of spiritual gifts. 

<margin>What is to be understood by the second and third watches.</margin>
But by the second and third watch, you should understand the various stages of our life: to give an example, just as one who keeps watch in the second or third watch seems most vigilant (for in those hours, men are held by the greatest and heaviest sleep), so I pray you also understand that in the different states of our life there are hours that make us blessed if we are found watching. Suppose someone has snatched your riches, your children have died, or you have suffered slander; if in such times you have not fallen, but were found watching by God and the Lord, and did nothing other than the commands of the Lord—certainly He will have found you watching in the second and third watch. 
<margin>F</margin>
That is, in a dangerous and grave time, which offers a deadly sleep and a fall to lax souls. Therefore, vigilance is necessary. For we are likened to a householder who, if he watches, can have nothing taken from his possessions...

<margin>A</margin>
...by thieves; but if he is <note>original: *forniculosus*, likely a typesetter's error for *dormitulosus*, meaning sleepy or sluggish</note> sleepy, the thief escapes after taking everything. Some understand the "thief" in this place to mean the devil, just as the "house" is the soul and the "householder" is the man; but this explanation does not seem sufficiently suited to the text. For in this passage, the Lord’s coming is compared to a thief because it will come suddenly and unexpectedly: just as one of the apostles says, *The day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night.* And in this place, see how the Lord interprets who the thief is. For He says: **And you therefore watch, because at the hour you do not think, the Son of Man will come.** 

<margin>B</margin>
Some say that by the first watch are understood those who are more diligent than others; by the second, those who have progressed somewhat; and by the third, those who are even inferior to them. But others have explained them as the different ages of life: the first when we are adolescents, the second when we are men, and the third when we are old. Blessed, therefore, is whoever is found watching at whatever age, and not conducting himself negligently in doing good.

Peter asked this as if having the care of all, being solicitous for the listeners as a lover of his brothers—and as one to whom the church was already entrusted—asking whether He says the parable to all. The Lord, however, does not answer the question explicitly, but indicates in a certain hidden way that the said parable is common and indeed pertains to all the faithful: to you apostles, and especially those who preside either by teaching or by dignity. But listen to who is the "faithful and wise steward." For the aforementioned parable (He says) fits many. But now, concerning those who are set over others, I wonder who is found having these two things: I mean faith and prudence. For this is rare.

# CHAPTER 12. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>
...is both unique and difficult to find. For just as in the management of <term>riches</term> <note>original: *divitiarum*</note>, if anyone is faithful to his Lord but not 
<margin>Faith and prudence are needed no less in divine matters than in secular ones.</margin>
prudent, he wastes the Lord's property, not knowing how to distribute those things as is fitting, and giving when he ought not, he causes a greater loss to the Lord. On the other hand, if someone is prudent and manages the spending, but is unfaithful and a thief, he is all the more intolerable the more prudent he is. Thus, in divine matters, there is a need for both faith and prudence. For I know many who seem to be endowed with virtue, piety, and faith, yet are harmful to the Church and lose not only resources but even souls. For example: suppose someone has committed a sin that offends the soul; unless the one who presides is prudent—even if he has faith, which is to say, virtue without judgment—then either through immoderate rebuke or through untimely 
<margin>E</margin>
gentleness, the one who has fallen is corrupted and is not healed, but is crushed. Therefore, whoever is found faithful and prudent shall be appointed to the Lord’s ministry—that is, over all the servants—to give to each one their <term>measure of wheat</term> <note>original: *mensuram frumenti*</note> in its proper time. This may be the word of doctrine by which souls are nourished, or the example of deeds and the commandment of how one ought to live. Blessed is the one found to be such, for the Lord will set him over all His possessions. He will not only be among the servants, but being promoted to a more sublime rank, the Lord will set him over all things, so that both earthly and 
<margin>Joshua 10. 1 Kings 17. Acts 4.</margin>
heavenly things are subject to him. Such a man was <term>Joshua son of Nun</term> <note>original: *Iesus Naue*</note>, and such was Elijah; for the former commanded the heavens, and the latter commanded the clouds of heaven. And, quite simply, all the saints, as friends of God, use those things which belong to God. 
<margin>F</margin>
For all things are common among friends. And everyone who leads an active life in the solitary life governs the servant-like affections of anger and desire, and distributes to each its own measure of wheat in due time: to anger, indeed, so that he may hold in hatred those who hate the Lord and abolish his own enmities; but to desire, so that he may take the necessary care of the flesh while directing his whole self toward God. Every such person is therefore blessed; he attains piety and will be set over all things that belong to his Lord. He will be worthy to perceive with a contemplative eye both those things which are not strictly called "resources" and those eternal things which I call resources in the proper sense.

# COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

<margin>A</margin>
**But if that servant says in his heart: "My Lord delays his coming," and begins to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat and drink, and to be drunk: the lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not hope and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces, and appoint his portion with the unfaithful.** ] Woe to such servants, who have received the gift of spiritual leadership but carry out the stewardship committed to them unfaithfully, and who drink and become intoxicated. You may choose to understand "drunkenness" in a physical sense (for this also signifies bad leaders of the churches who live luxuriously off the goods of the poor), or it may please you to understand drunkenness as the perversion of the state of the mind through false doctrines or the love of riches. For 
<margin>B</margin>
such leaders "beat" the menservants and maidservants—that is, they are a stumbling block to the weaker members of the Church, whose consciences they strike. Indeed, when a weak and faint-hearted person sees me, a bishop, living a bad life, his conscience is struck by the offense; he receives a blow in his heart and becomes even weaker. All these things happen to the unfaithful servant because he says, "My Lord delays His coming." He does this out of laziness, not thinking of the hour of death. For if we kept in mind that the Lord is coming, and that the end and consummation of our life is at the very doors, we would certainly sin less. But look also at the punishment: "He will cut him in pieces," it says. That is, He will deprive him of the grace of teaching, 
<margin>C</margin>
lest anyone think the gift will not result in a greater punishment for him. "How," you ask, "will the gift result in something good for him when he is to be stripped of it?" Truly, he is then found to be miserable, since he is flesh and not spirit. 
<margin>When we are in the spirit.</margin>
For we are "in the spirit" when the Spirit of God dwells in us. But he who does not walk by the spirit, but is in the flesh and is found to be devoid of spiritual life, is ranked with the unbelievers, inasmuch as he is condemned with the unbelieving world; for he perceives no benefit from the faith he possesses. For true faith was not in him; for if true faith had been in him, he would have been a faithful steward. But now, because he was drinking and making himself drunk, and ruining the Lord's affairs, he did not have the true faith which is required of stewards. Rightly, therefore, is his portion placed with the unfaithful, for he is deprived...

# CHAPTER 12. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...to the Lord, he is found naked and useless, and not whole. <margin>D</margin>
**But that servant, who knew the will of his lord, and did not prepare himself, nor did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes: but he who did not know, and did things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few. For to whomsoever much is given, much will be required of him, and to whom they have committed much, of him they will ask more.** ] In this passage, the Lord demonstrates something even more significant and terrible to us. For He says that such a person will not only be stripped of grace—and it will benefit him nothing in terms of being freed from punishment—but the very greatness of his dignity will be the cause of a greater condemnation. For the more a sinner knows, the more severe a punishment he brings upon himself.

<margin>E</margin>
And in the following verses, this becomes more manifest. For to whom much is given, from him also much will be required; and to whom they have entrusted much, they will ask more from him. By this, it is signaled that the punishment which the <term>teachers</term> <note>original: *doctores*—referring to bishops, priests, and theologians</note> deserve will be greater. Therefore, things are "given" and "entrusted" to teachers. That which is "given" is like the grace of healing diseases and performing miracles; but that which is "entrusted" to them is the gift of the word and doctrine. And when He said "is given," He did not add "they will demand more," but He did so when He said "is entrusted." And indeed, the gift of the word requires labor, and more is demanded from the teachers. For it is necessary for a teacher not to be lazy or sluggish, but to multiply the <term>talent</term> <note>original: *talentum*—referring to the biblical unit of value and the parable of the talents</note> of the word. Therefore, where it says "to whom they have committed," you should understand this as one to whom a loan is given for 

<margin>Interest. F</margin>
interest. For here, "interest" <note>original: *usura*—in this context, spiritual growth or "return" on God's investment</note> signifies that which is entrusted and deposited. But there are those who ask: "Granted, this is well: let him who knows the will of the Lord and does it not be punished; but why is he who does not know it punished?" Because he himself could have learned, yet would not, but was lazy; he himself was the cause of why he did not learn. Wherefore he is to be punished, because he did not learn of his own free will. Let us fear, brothers! For if he who knows nothing at all is worthy of stripes, what excuse will free those who sin knowingly, especially if they are teachers? For this condemnation is more severe.

> **I have come to send fire upon the earth, and what will I, if it be already kindled? But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how am I constrained until it be accomplished?** ] By "fire"

<margin>A</margin>
indeed, preaching is understood. For the Word is a fire that consumes every material and imperfect thought, and abolishes idols of whatever material they may be. It is also understood as the zeal for virtue kindled in each of us; and perhaps this is that which happens because of the word of God, nor is it different from the former: for by this fire, God wants our hearts to be kindled. We ought to have a burning zeal for virtue. Whence, **what will I?**

<margin>Romans 12. 2 Corinthians 11.</margin>
that is, "how much I desire," if it be already kindled! For He urges that this fire be lit. Just as Paul says: *Be fervent in spirit* and *I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy.*

<margin>B</margin>
Moreover, He calls His death a **baptism**. For since that fire was not to be kindled in any other way than after His death (since from that time preaching and zeal increased), He therefore adds the mention of His death, calling it a baptism. Desiring this greatly, He says: **And how am I constrained**, that is, how solicitous and anxious I am, and I am pressed until it be finished. For I thirst for death for the salvation of all. He came to send fire not only upon all the earth—in which preaching and faith have been spread—but into the soul of each person, which is indeed a "thorny and sterile earth," but by the word of God, as if kindled by fire, it is made capable of divine seeds and fertile in spiritual fruits. For wherever divine grace has invisibly touched 

<margin>C Luke 24</margin>
someone's soul, that soul is seen to blaze with a desire for God beyond what can be described, just as <term>Cleophas</term> <note>one of the disciples on the road to Emmaus</note> blazed with divine fire when he said: *Was not our heart burning within us?* Whoever, therefore, has experienced this affection will know what we are saying. And many experience it even when the divine scriptures are read, or the lives of the holy fathers, or if they are admonished or taught; their souls are kindled to do good, and some indeed blaze until the end, while others immediately grow cold.

# CHAPTER 12. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
## AN EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 239

<margin>D</margin>
**...against the mother: mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.** <note>Luke 12:53</note> Christ indeed is our peace, but he did not come to send peace: wherefore this was spoken enigmatically. We say, therefore, that <margin>Not all peace is good.</margin> not all peace is free from blame and good; indeed, it is often dangerous and casts us far from divine charity, such as when we have peace and conspire in the destruction of the truth. For Christ did not come to give this kind of peace, but wants the opposite: namely, that we should disagree for the sake of the good, which even happened during the times of persecution. For in one house a pagan father differed from a faithful son, and a mother from a daughter, and vice-versa. But how, by saying "five in one house will be divided," did he list six persons in the enumeration? We say, therefore, that one person is counted twice. The "daughter" and the "daughter-in-law" are the same person. For she is called a daughter if referred to her mother, but a daughter-in-law if referred to her mother-in-law. There will be three divided—father, mother, and mother-in-law—against two—son and daughter. For the daughter, though she is one person, takes on two relationships, and according to this, she appears as a double person when compared to the mother and mother-in-law. Understand, however, in a simple sense: by the father, mother, and mother-in-law, understand all *old* things; by the son and daughter, understand all *new* things. Thus the Lord wants his new and divine precepts and doctrines to fight with our ancient, wicked customs and doctrines. Understand it also in this way: the Father is the mind, the son is reason; let the division of these be in every "house"—of a man, I mean—to speak more clearly.

<margin>Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
The mind of Dionysius the Areopagite was enlightened and he received the preaching; but his pagan reason—which was trying to show through <term>dialectic snares</term> <note>original: *dialecticis tendiculis* — logical traps or tricky philosophical arguments</note> that he should follow those old ways—resisted his mind, which had so eagerly received the faith. <margin>Acts 17</margin> Do you see the division of "father" and "son" fighting against each other because of Christ and the preaching? You will also call the mind the "mother" and "mother-in-law," and the senses the "son" and "daughter-in-law"; and between these there is a fight because of Christ, with the mind rising up against the senses, since the mind persuades us that eternal things are to be preferred over fleeting ones, and invisible things over visible ones, and it has many supporting demonstrations for this. But a war of the senses against the mind is also joined. For the senses,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
having been led to faith through the miracles and signs which are seen, do not believe the logical thoughts of the mind; for they do not wish to follow the demonstrations of the pagans, which compel those who listen to them not to believe that God became man, or that a virgin gave birth. Such are the ravings of the pagans, which are enslaved to the laws of nature. But the senses, through the miracles that are seen, are more excellent than any logical demonstration, leading one by the hand to the knowledge of God. Therefore, not all peace and concord is good, but there is a time when even conflict and discord is seen as a certain divine possession. Therefore, let no one love the wicked; even if a father or mother oppose the law of Christ, they must be resisted just like enemies of the truth.

<margin>Matt. 16.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
**And he said also to the crowds: When you see a cloud rising from the west, immediately you say, A shower is coming, and so it happens; and when the south wind blows, you say that there will be heat, and it happens. <margin>Mark 8.</margin> Hypocrites, you know how to judge the face of the sky and of the earth, but how is it that you do not judge this time? <margin>Matt. 5.</margin> And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? For when you go with your adversary to the magistrate on the way, take pains to be delivered from him, lest perhaps he drag you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and the officer cast you into prison. I tell you, you will not go out from there until you pay the very last penny.** ] <note>Luke 12:54-59</note> After he discussed the preaching and named the fire and the sword, because it was likely that those hearing him would be troubled—not understanding what was being said—he said: Just as you recognize the qualities of the air from certain signs, so it was necessary to recognize my coming from these things which are said, and from these things which are done by me. <margin>C</margin> For my words show me to be contrary to you, and likewise my works; for you indeed are <term>tax collectors</term> <note>original: *publicani* — used here to imply greed and worldly corruption</note> and <margin>Earlier, chapter 9</margin> plunderers, but I have nowhere to lay my head. It was necessary for you, therefore, just as you conjecture a shower from the clouds and heat from the south wind, so also to judge and conjecture the time of this my coming—that I have not come to send peace, but a shower and disturbance. For I myself am a cloud, and I come from the "west" of human nature, which was previously humble and had a great darkness from sin. But I have also come to send fire and to create heat. For I am the South Wind, a fervent spirit...

It concludes with an exhortation to recognize Christ's mission through his miracles, just as one reads weather patterns in the clouds and wind.</summary>

# CHAPTER 13. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
## AN EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 239

<margin>Bethlehem is situated to the South.</margin>
...contrary to the North wind. Since he also appeared in Bethlehem, which is situated to the south. <margin>D</margin> And when he said these things, he also teaches them about laudable peace. For since he had shown a laudable discord <note>Referring to the earlier passage where Christ says he came to bring division rather than peace</note>, he also shows an irreproachable peace, and says: **When your adversary drags you to the tribunal, on the way give effort, hasten and labor,** <note>Luke 12:58</note> that is, think of every way how you might be freed from him. Or otherwise: **Give effort,** that is, even if you have nothing, so that you might gain something. **Give effort,** that is, interest <note>original: "usuram," meaning the growth or payment of one's debt</note>, so that you may be freed from him, lest he ever drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison until you pay back the last mite. <note>original: "minutum," the smallest denomination of coin</note> Now the Lord says these things, terrifying the more dull-minded <note>original: "crassiores," those who are more focused on the physical world than the spiritual</note> through these words and compelling them to make peace, knowing that for those who are more earthly, the fear of loss and punishments corrects them more; and therefore he says these things. <margin>E</margin> These things are also understood concerning the devil, who is our adversary. Therefore, while we are on the way of this life, let us give effort by devoting ourselves to virtues, so that we may be freed from him and have nothing in common with him, lest at any time in the future judgment he hand us over to the judge. For his works, which we do in this life, those things hand us over to the judge; and the judge hands us over to the officer—a demon—a certain demon tormenting and afflicting us; and afterward he punishes us until we pay the penalty even for small sins and fulfill the measure of the punishment. But the measure of punishment is never fulfilled; therefore we will be punished forever. <margin>F</margin> For if we remain in prison until we pay back the last mite, and we are never going to pay it back, it is manifest that the punishment will be eternal.

<margin>A</margin> **whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were debtors beyond all men living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.** <note>Luke 13:1-5</note> Judas the Galilean, whom our Evangelist himself mentions in the Acts <note>Acts 5:37. Judas of Galilee led a tax revolt against the Romans</note>, since he was somewhat learned in the law, also taught other Galileans to adhere to his dogma. For he taught that it was not to be endured that any man at all should be called "lord," neither for the sake of honor nor modesty, nor even the king himself. Wherefore many of them were severely struck, as were those who taught that the sacrifices ordained by Moses should not be offered, on the grounds that sacrifices were being made for Caesar and the Roman people. <margin>B</margin> It is likely, therefore, that [Pilate] being indignant because of this sin, ordered those Galileans to be killed over the sacrifices which were being prohibited by them from being made for the Roman people, and so their blood was mixed with the blood of the sacrifices. Therefore, certain people announced these things to the Savior as if they were deeds done somewhat piously, wishing through this to learn what in it would please him. For some thought those men had suffered most justly, as being sinners and seditious, and provoking Pilate to a hatred of the Jews because they urged that Caesar should not be called [lord]: a thing which resulted in a disadvantage for the whole Jewish nation. Therefore, the Savior, not denying that they were sinners, says that they did not suffer because they were greater sinners <margin>C</margin> than those who suffered nothing. For unless you too repent, and cease from kindling internal wars with seditions, and hasten to please God with your works, you will suffer heavier things. For one ought not, under the pretext of piety, seek one’s own glory and stir up internal seditions. <margin>One ought not under the pretext of piety...</margin> Furthermore, the tower which had fallen in Siloam was a foretelling of those things which would later happen to the people. <margin>...those eighteen</margin> For the tower is a figure of the whole city: but those eighteen are a figure of the whole people. For when the city fell under Titus <note>The Roman general who besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in 70 AD</note>, the whole people, remaining in unbelief, perished together. Let this also be an admonition to us in those things which happen daily: some fall into temptations while we are placed outside of temptation, lest we cast away anxiety and fear as if we were just—as if we were not [sinners].
