...liable: but on the contrary let us be taught, that in this life those people are punished so that we may be made better; but if we should be negligent, we will suffer most grievous things.

And he was also telling this parable: **A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it, and did not find any. Moreover, he said to the dresser of the vineyard: "Behold, there are three years since I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none: cut it down: why does it even occupy the ground?" But he answering, said to him: "Lord, let it alone this year also, until I shall dig around it, and put manure, and if indeed it should bear fruit: but if not, hereafter you shall cut it down."** <note>Luke 13:6–9</note> By a good sequence he joins this parable; after he said, "unless you repent, you will perish," he rightly adds this parable as well. Therefore, the fig tree is the generation of the Jews, making only bitter leaves and bringing forth no fruit. Moreover, the Jewish life stood in the vineyard of God. But the Master of the house, Christ, came and sought the fruit of faith and of good works in it, and did not find any. Moreover, he came for three years: through Moses, through the prophets, and through himself; and because they did not repent, he cut them off from the love of God: for no longer is it called the nation of the Lord and a holy people. 

<margin>B</margin> In its place, however, the Gentiles were introduced, who are able to produce fruit. The fig tree is also understood as the whole human race: by the Master of the house, the Father and God; by the dresser of the vineyard, the Son of God, who journeyed with us so that he might cultivate and cleanse the vineyard. Christ, however, does not allow that fig tree to be cut down as barren, saying, **"Let it alone this year also."** For although they were not made better through the law and the prophets, nor did they produce the fruit of repentance; nevertheless, with me watering them by my teachings and passions, perhaps they will produce the fruit of obedience: **"But if not, hereafter you shall cut it down,"** they being cut off from the region of the righteous. 

<margin>C</margin> Moreover, after the third year, our nature <margin>Genesis 3. Exodus 32. Psalm 105. John.</margin> did not give the fruit sought in itself. For first, in paradise, we transgressed the commandment; second, when the law was given, a calf having been made, the glory of God was changed into the likeness of a calf eating hay; <note>A reference to the idolatry of the Golden Calf at Sinai.</note> third, the Lord and Savior was denied by those saying, "We have no king but Caesar." <note>John 19:15</note>

## AN EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

<margin>A</margin> And each one of us is a fig tree in the Lord's vineyard, namely in the Church, or simply speaking, planted in this world. God comes therefore seeking fruit, and if he finds you without fruit, he commands that you be cut off from this life; but the dresser of the vineyard supplicates that you be spared. But who is that dresser of the vineyard? Either one's own guardian angel, or even the man himself, for each is the dresser of his own vineyard. Often, therefore, when we fall into lethal diseases or other dangers, we say: "Let it be, O Lord, even this year, and we will do penance." For this is what it means to **"dig and put manure around it."** For the soul is "dug" when the dust of temporal cares is shaken off and she herself is lightened. Truly, the manure being placed around signifies fervor and severity in the humbler path <note>original: "via viliori," referring to the ascetic or lowlier path of the penitent</note>—namely, of repentance, which is despised by all. 

<margin>B</margin> For when someone lowers himself from glory into an inglorious life for the sake of the soul's salvation, he is said to "put manure around the soul," to the end that it might bear fruit. If indeed we shall have produced fruit: but if not, he no longer leaves us in that vineyard, but cuts us off from the world, so that we do not occupy the place in vain. For if anyone sees a sinner delaying for a long time, he is offended and becomes worse; and thus the sinner is found neither producing fruit himself, nor allowing another to produce fruit. But if he is cut off from this life, perhaps those who have seen him cut off, weighing this in their minds, will be changed and will produce fruit. 

<margin>C</margin> Moreover, the Master of the house is said to come to the fig tree for **"three years,"** perhaps because of the three laws which the Lord gave us: which are the <term>natural law</term> <note>The innate sense of right and wrong implanted in all humans.</note>, the <term>legal law</term> <note>The Mosaic Law of the Old Testament.</note>, and the <term>spiritual law</term> <note>The Gospel or Grace of Christ.</note>. It was certainly fitting for us, having been warned by the natural law, to produce fruit; for nature teaches what ought to be done: but because he found the natural law useless in us, he also gave the Mosaic law as an aid to nature, which, since it also was found unfruitful because of our laziness, he added the spiritual law. Therefore, where those three have not rendered someone's soul better, nor does it become more amended by the long-suffering and mercy of God, then afterwards he ceases to warn: for God is not often mocked by procrastinations. But what if you understand this through the three stages of age? Boyhood—that is, the youth of eighteen years; manhood; and thirdly, those who are already...

<summary>Theophylact provides a multi-layered commentary on the Parable of the Barren Fig Tree, interpreting it as a metaphor for the history of the Jewish people, the three stages of divine law (Natural, Mosaic, and Spiritual), and the individual soul's opportunity for repentance.</summary>

<margin>D</margin> ...begin to become old men. Therefore, when in the third year—that is, in old age—we do not give fruit, and yet we are permitted to live so that we may add manure <note>Representing the "filth" or humility of repentance.</note>, receiving a humble life of repentance for the sake of CHRIST, and then if even then we prove false, the Lord will no longer spare us, so that we do not occupy the ground in vain and offend others. And this exposition seems to many to be consistent with the proposed text.

<margin>E</margin> **Moreover, he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbaths: and behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was bent over: nor was she able to look up at all. And when Jesus saw her, he called her to him, and said to her: "Woman, you are released from your infirmity." And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God. But the ruler of the synagogue, being indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, answering, said to the crowd: "There are six days in which it is necessary to work; in these, therefore, come to be healed, and not on the Sabbath day." But the Lord, answering him, said: "Hypocrite, does not each one of you on the Sabbath loose his ox or his donkey from the stall and lead it to water? And this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound, behold, for eighteen years, ought she not to be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?" And when he said these things, all his adversaries were ashamed: and all the people rejoiced over all the glorious things that were done by him.** <note>Luke 13:10–17</note> 

<margin>F</margin> That disease <margin>All infirmities are from the demon</margin> had happened to the woman because the devil was afflicting her: just as the Lord also says, "whom Satan has bound for eighteen years." For perhaps Satan punished her because she had been abandoned by God on account of her sins. For Satan brings all evils upon human bodies when it is permitted to him by the Lord. Indeed, from the beginning he was the author of our fall, so that we fell from the incorruption in which we were created and were bound to a body that is weak and capable of suffering. For this is what we understand by the "garments of skins" <note>original: "pelliceas tunicas"; a reference to Genesis 3:21, often interpreted by Church Fathers as the mortal, physical state humans took on after the Fall.</note>. But the Lord, with a voice most worthy of God and full of power, puts to flight the disease of this woman. Moreover, he also lays his hands on her, so that we may learn that his holy flesh possessed the word, power, and operation of God. For through his own 

<column-break/>

# AN EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 242
<page-num>242</page-num>

<margin>Genesis 3</margin> property of person they are not separate, as it seems to the impious Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century bishop whose views led to the belief that Christ existed as two separate persons (one divine, one human), a view condemned as heresy by the Council of Ephesus.</note>. Therefore, so great indeed was the kindness of the Lord, that he was merciful toward his own handiwork. But Satan, who had previously bound the woman, grieving at the release of the disease and desiring to afflict her further, binds the ruler of the synagogue with envy, and through his mouth he slanders the miracle: for according to his custom, he imposes himself everywhere upon good things. 

He is indignant, therefore, because she is healed on the Sabbath; the Lord refutes him with the most beautiful examples of brute animals. Wherefore not only he himself was confounded by such speeches, but also all the others who opposed Jesus. For it was a matter of great folly to forbid a person to be healed on the <margin>B</margin> Sabbath because of the rest which the law had commanded in some part for the Sabbath. Therefore, those who opposed Jesus were confounded. But the crowds rejoiced in his works, just as those leaders did not rejoice in the works, but were driven mad while Christ was performing miracles. But the crowds, perceiving the benefit from the miracles, rejoiced, especially because they enjoyed the healings. 

But you should also understand (I pray) this miracle regarding the internal man. The soul is bent over when it turns only toward earthly cares, and conceives nothing heavenly or divine within itself. Therefore, it is said to be sick for eighteen years. For when someone has been weak in the observation of the commands of the divine law (which are ten) and in the hope <margin>Another understanding of the present miracle</margin> of the eighth age <note>The "eighth age" or "eighth day" signifies eternity or the world to come, following the seven days of temporal creation.</note>, he is said to be bent over for eighteen years. Is not he who is addicted to earthly things, and <margin>C</margin> always sins, one who rejects the commandments and does not expect the future age? But the Lord heals such a soul on the Sabbath and in the synagogue. For when someone collects the thoughts of confession within himself—for "Judas" <margin>Judas</margin> is said to mean "confession" <note>A common medieval etymology: the Hebrew name Yehudah (Judah) is derived from the root "to praise" or "to confess."</note>—and keeps the Sabbath, that is, rests from evils: then Jesus heals him, not only saying to him by his word, "Be released from your infirmity," but also laying on his hands. For it is necessary for us, in order to undertake the performance of works of virtue, to also have the cooperation of the divine hands, and not to think that we have obtained health while being content to be instructed only through the word and teachings.

<summary>Theophylact interprets the healing of the crippled woman both as a historical miracle proving Christ's divinity against Nestorianism and as an allegory for the soul "bent over" by earthly cares. He argues that true healing requires both divine instruction and the active "work" of virtue, symbolized by Jesus's touch.</summary>

<margin>Matt. 13.</margin> **He said therefore, “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his garden; and it grew, and became a great tree; and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.” And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.” And he went through the cities and villages, teaching, and making his way toward Jerusalem.**] <margin>The Kingdom of God.</margin> He compares the kingdom of God to a grain of mustard seed. Now, the "kingdom of God" is the preaching and the word of God. For through preaching, He has reigned in the souls of men. Indeed, just as mustard appears to be small, yet possesses great power, so also the word of the Gospel is despised by many and appears to be foolishness; but when a man has received it and sowed it in the "garden" of his soul, it becomes a great tree, so that it spreads its branches, and the birds of the air—that is, men who strive to fly toward the heights—have their nests in its branches. For those who have transcended earthly things find rest in the branches of preaching, which is to say, in the expanded meanings of the text. To give an example of what I mean: Paul took a "grain," which was the small instruction he received from Ananias <note>original: "Ananiæ instructionem"; referring to the disciple who baptized Paul in Acts 9.</note>, but when this <margin>Acts 9.</margin> grain was planted in the rich garden of his soul, it produced branches—I mean many good doctrines and epistles—in which those who were then high-minded and wise, such as the Corinthians, Dionysius, Hierotheus, and many others, made their nests. In every age, certain individuals can also be understood through the grain of mustard, as can the Lord himself. For He appeared lowly; <margin>John 12.</margin> indeed, He was the son of a carpenter and very poor. But when He fell into the heart of the earth, having died and been buried in a garden, He produced the beautiful branches of the apostles, in whom all those who were previously driven and tormented by the spirit of error—namely the Gentiles—find rest. These Gentiles were compared to birds because of their easily changeable minds, subject to illusion and great levity. For all who wander are like the birds of the sky (or the air). Again, the divine word is likened to leaven, which a woman—that is, human nature—took and hid in three measures of flour—that is, in the body, spirit, and soul—so

<column-break/>

that they might be sanctified; just as the blessed Paul says, that it might become one blend through communion with the Holy Spirit. You may also understand the woman to be the soul, and the three measures to be its three parts: the <term>rational</term> <note>original: "rationalē"; the part of the soul responsible for logic and reasoning.</note>, the <term>concupiscible</term> <note>original: "concupiscibilem"; the part associated with desires and appetites.</note>, and the <term>irascible</term> <note>original: "irascibilem"; the part associated with anger, courage, and vigor.</note>. If, therefore, anyone hides the word of God in those three parts <margin>1 Tim. 4</margin>, it will make the whole soul spiritual, so that the rational part does not slip into false doctrines, and the irascible and concupiscible parts are not carried away without reason, but are leavened and made like the word of God. Now, Jesus traveled through villages and cities teaching. He did not go to small towns and villages in such a way as to neglect the great cities—which is what those do who wish to deceive simpler people—nor did he come to the cities like a show-off or someone seeking glory while neglecting the small ones. Rather, like the common Lord, or indeed like a father who cares for everyone, He went everywhere. Did He travel through the outlying cities because there were fewer experts in the law there, while fleeing Jerusalem because He feared being rebuked by the lawyers, or suspecting He might be killed by them? That is not to be said; instead, the text says He was **making his way toward Jerusalem.** For where there are more who are sick, the doctor hastens there all the more.

And someone said to him, **“Lord, are there few who follow the path to salvation?” And he said to them, “Strive to enter through the narrow gate, for many (I tell you) will seek to enter and will not be able. When the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us,’ he will answer and say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ And he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you who work iniquity.’ There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves are cast out. And people will come from the east and west, and from the north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, there are those who are last who will be first, and there are those who are first who will be last.”**] There are few who are saved because the narrow way does not accommodate many. <margin>D</margin> The word "that" <note>original: "illa," referring to the phrase "that fox"</note> is a demonstrative pronoun; he signaled that those very men were those deceitful ones. And indeed, the Pharisees displayed the wicked and shifty character of foxes. Observe, I pray, how he responds to their malice. Because they envied him for his healings, they tried to strike fear into him through Herod; therefore, he says to them exactly what he believed would grieve them most: "Behold," he says, "I perform healings and cast out demons." For (as was said before) they were hounding him for this reason: so that he would not attract many to believe in him by showing miracles. "Today and tomorrow" signifies a period of several days, just as we are accustomed to say in familiar speech, "Today and tomorrow this will be done," not strictly limiting the matter to such a short interval of time, but signifying that it will happen soon. In the same way, **C H R I S T**, by saying, "I perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am finished," did not mean that he must necessarily be finished on the literal third day, but declares that his death would be in a short while. "Nevertheless, I must remain in this place today and tomorrow, and work miracles, and on the following day set out for Jerusalem": for it was there that I chose death. For they said to him, "Leave, because Herod is going to kill you." He said these things in Galilee, which Herod ruled, showing them that even if Herod wished it very much, he could not be killed by him. For it was not in Galilee, but in Jerusalem that it was foreordained for Christ to suffer.

<margin>F
A clearer explanation of "today and tomorrow."</margin>
And to explain the Gospel’s saying more clearly to you: when you have read "today and tomorrow," make a pause <note>original: "punctum," a punctuation mark or stop</note>, and then say, "on the next day set out." This is how we often count: "I am going out on Sunday, the second, and the third day," not meaning I will go out on both Sunday and the second day, but we list those two days to make the third day clear. In this same way, the Lord, counting first in this place, says: "I must be here today and tomorrow, then on the third day set out for Jerusalem": for there is my end. As we said above, he was not limiting his life to three days, but to a number of days; nevertheless, he signifies that he will not remain for a very long time, as if he were saying these

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> things to those who envied him: "Why do you meditate on my death? Behold, in a little while it will be upon me." But when you hear that it is impossible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem, do not think the Jews are driven to do this by some kind of necessity; rather, know that they commit this murder by their own will. It is like someone seeing a most cruel and bloodthirsty robber haunting the roads who might say, "It is impossible for this road, where a robber lies in wait for passersby, to be clean of blood." For in this place, he speaks of what follows naturally from the works of robbers. So, in Jerusalem, which is occupied by "robbers" and scribes, it is impossible for the Lord of the prophets to perish <margin>B</margin> in any other place than that in which the robbers are. For, being accustomed to shedding the blood of servants <note>referring to the previously sent prophets</note>, they will also kill the Master himself.

<margin>Matthew 23</margin>
> Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her: how often I wanted to gather your children together just as a bird gathers her nest under her wings, and you were unwilling? By the duplication of the name, the Lord shows the love he has for them. For like a lover rejected by his beloved, he calls back the adulterous synagogue. He shows his mercy in that he frequently wished to gather them. And he signifies their arrogance by saying <margin>C</margin> "because you were unwilling." Afterward, he says, "I leave you." For as long as you conducted your lives well, it was also my temple; but because you contaminated it, and made it a house of trade and a den of thieves, <margin>Trade is called robbery.</margin> and you serve various trades and your greedy pursuits in turn. (For trade is robbery, tripping up brothers and seizing what is theirs; which is what robbers do, for they attack travelers to seize their goods). ### CHAPTER XIV.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap initial letter "E" at the beginning of Chapter 14, featuring a seated scholar or evangelist writing at a lectern, surrounded by foliage.</image-desc>
<margin>F</margin> And it happened, when he entered the house of a certain leader of the Pharisees on the Sabbath to eat bread, they were watching him. And behold, a certain man with dropsy <term>dropsy: an archaic medical term (hydrops) for edema, or the swelling of the body due to excess fluid</term> was before him. And responding, **J E S U S** spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" But they kept silent. But he took him, healed him, and let him go. And responding to them, he said, "Which of you shall have a donkey or an ox fall into a pit, and will not immediately pull it out on the Sabbath day?" And they could not answer him. 

The Lord, knowing well the fault-finding nature of the Pharisees, enters their houses. For the benefit of souls was his concern; therefore he entered. For they could have received benefit either from his teaching and speech, or from the demonstration of miracles, if indeed they had been willing. Furthermore, when the man with dropsy came into their midst, the Lord did not

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> consider how he might avoid offending the many, but how he might heal those who needed his care. For where a great benefit is expected, we ought not to worry about those who watch to take offense. 
<margin>Great benefit is hoped for among the wise</margin> <note>The marginal note is partially corrupted in the original printing but points to the wisdom of seeking spiritual benefit over social approval.</note> Moreover, he argues against the foolishness of those who were about to rebuke him, and therefore he asks: "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" Does he not clearly mock them as fools? Since God blessed the Sabbath, they themselves forbid doing good on it, and by this they make it entirely cursed. For a day is not "blessed" in which no good is customarily done. But when these men, knowing where his questioning was leading, remained silent, **J E S U S** does what is his own to do: he heals the man by touch, despite the scandal. 
<margin>B</margin> Then he also admonishes the Pharisees, as if he were saying to them: "If the law had forbidden showing mercy on the Sabbath, would it not have been a concern to you if your own son was in danger on the Sabbath? And why do I say 'son'? You would not even have left an ox without help if you saw it in danger." How then is it not foolish that you watch for a healing of a man with dropsy on the Sabbath? 

A "dropsical" person is anyone who is gravely ill in their soul through a dissolute and slippery life, and who stands in need of **C H R I S T**. Such a person will be clearly healed if they are "before **C H R I S T**." For he who stands before **C H R I S T**, always thinking of how he is seen by Him, will sin very little.

<margin>C</margin> He also spoke a parable to the guests, noticing how they chose the first seats <note>original: "primos accubitus," the most honorable places at a reclining dining table</note> at the table, saying to them: "When you are invited by someone to a wedding, do not sit down in the first place, lest perhaps someone more honorable than you has been invited by him, and he who invited both you and him comes and says to you, 'Give this man your place,' and then you begin with shame to take the lowest place. Rather, when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place so that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you, 'Friend, move up higher'; then you will have glory in the presence of those who sit at meat with you. For everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted." 

You see what kind of dinners **C H R I S T**’s are: they are turned toward the benefit of the soul, and not the filling of the belly. Behold, for he healed the man with dropsy and taught...

<margin>D</margin> ...to the Pharisees, that it is good to do good on the Sabbath. And afterward, seeing them quarreling over the first place at the table, he heals this affection as well—a sickness that begins not from a small cause, but from a great and hardly escapable one: vainglory <note>original: "inanis gloria" - empty pride or the desire for worldly recognition.</note>. And let no one think it beneath the dignity of the Word of God to speak of such things; indeed, it is most fitting. For a physician who promises to heal gout <note>original: "podagram" - a painful joint disease often associated in antiquity with luxury and excess.</note> and all diseases but refuses to heal the pain of the mind is no physician at all. Furthermore, consider how small the disease of vainglory seems, yet it entirely disturbs those who seek the first seats. It was therefore necessary for Christ—the teacher, prince, and finisher of humility—to prune all the branches of vainglory. <margin>E</margin> Consider this also: if it had not been the time for a meal, and the Lord had set aside other matters to discourse on this, there might be room for criticism. But now, because it was the hour of the feast and the disease of ambition was playing out right before the Savior’s eyes, it was the proper time for an admonition. See also, from another perspective, how he frees a person from fault and makes them civil. For what great shame you feel when you have sought a place unworthy of you, and then when someone more honorable arrives, the one who invited you says, "Give this man your place," and this happens often: for as you move down, others will occupy the place. On the contrary, what great praise is deserved by the one who, though worthy of the first seat, sits in a humble place from the start, and is later found to be seated above others. Does this admonition of the Lord seem small to you, which teaches humility—the greatest of virtues—and plants it in the <margin>F</margin> souls of the listeners, leading them to an honorable way of life? This is what Christ’s beloved disciple Paul later <margin>1 Cor. 14</margin> said: "Let all things be done honestly and according to order." <note>original: "Omnia honeste, & secundum ordinem."</note> How then shall this be done? Let no one seek what is his own, but each what belongs to the other. Do you see the disciple speaking the same things as his master? "Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled." How should I understand this? For <margin>What it is to be humbled.</margin> many in this life who exalt themselves enjoy great honor. Therefore, this "being humbled" occurs when someone enjoys great honor in the world but is wretched and humble in the sight of God. Moreover, such honor does not last until the end, nor is it held among all people.

# CHAPTER 14. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> There is one type of person who wishes to rejoice and be glad when he has done evil to others; such is the nature of all greedy people. Then there is the "natural" person <note>original: "animalis" — referring to the *soul-led* or *unspiritual* man (from the Latin 'anima' or Greek 'psychikos'), who lives according to basic human reason rather than divine revelation.</note>, who wishes neither to steal nor to do harm; for this is to live according to nature, since nature has implanted this sense within us. But the spiritual person is one who is willing to suffer both affliction and loss for the sake of virtue. Therefore, the first is against nature, the second is according to nature, and the third is above nature.

<margin>2 Cor. 5</margin> Everyone, therefore, who tastes only of human things and is not strong enough to understand those things which are above nature is called "natural," as one who is governed only by the soul and the breath of life. But when someone is moved by the Spirit, and it is no longer he himself who lives, but Christ who lives in him, this person is spiritual, having stepped beyond nature. This man was also "natural" who thought that the rewards <margin>E</margin> of the saints would be sensory <note>original: "sensibiles" — things that can be perceived by the five senses, like physical food or gold, rather than spiritual joys.</note>, because he could understand nothing above the level of nature.

<margin>Mat. 22</margin> But He said to him: A certain man had prepared a great supper, and he invited many, and he sent that servant of his at the hour of the supper to say to those invited, "Come, for everything is now ready." <margin>The names of God as punisher and God as merciful in Scripture.</margin> For when Scripture signifies the vindictive power of God, it calls Him a panther, a bear, or a leopard; but when it wishes to suggest His mercy, it introduces Him as a "man." <margin>A</margin> by all accounts the mystery of our salvation is great. And He sent His servant at the hour of the supper. Who is 그at servant? He who, having assumed the form of a servant, though He is the Son of God, became man and is said to have been "sent" as a man. Notice how He did not simply say "a servant," but used the definite article: "that servant of His" <note>original: "cum articulo seruum illum suum" — Theophylact points out that the Greek text specifies *the* particular servant, referring to Christ.</note>. He specifically called "that one" the one who, according to His human form, pleased Him and served. For <margin>Philip. 2</margin> He is well-pleasing to the Father not only as Son and God, but also as a man, being alone without sin; He ministered to and prepared all the Father’s counsels and commands, and by fulfilling all righteousness, He pleased the Father and God. Therefore, He alone is properly called the "servant" of God. <margin>B</margin> He was sent at the "hour of the supper," which is to say, at the defined and opportune time. For no other time was more suitable for our salvation than when Caesar Augustus was reigning, when wickedness was at its height and needed to be destroyed. Just as doctors allow the fluid to collect in the ulcers of a cruel disease and then apply remedies, so too it was necessary for sin to show all its forms, and then for the Great Physician to apply the medicines. And for this reason, Christ waited until the devil had filled the measure of his malice, and only then was He incarnated, healing every kind of malice through His holy life. <margin>Psal. 44</margin> He was sent, therefore, in time—that is, at the opportune and fitting time—just as David says: <margin>C</margin> "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one, in your timeliness" <note>original: "tempestiuitate tua" — often translated in modern Bibles as "in your glory and majesty," but here interpreted as "at the right time."</note>. For the sword is entirely the Word of God, and the "thigh" signifies the birth in the flesh. It was in "timeliness," which means the opportune time. He was sent to speak to those invited. Who are these who were called? Perhaps all people. For God called everyone to the knowledge of Himself, partly through the orderly arrangement of invisible things <note>referring to the creation of the universe</note>, and partly through the natural law. But perhaps, more specifically, it refers to the Israelites, who were called through the Law and the Prophets. To them, therefore, the Lord was sent first, as if to the sheep of the house of Israel. ### CHAPTER 14. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>One who observes nature does not receive what is above nature.</margin>
...to excuse themselves. For all the leaders of the Jews rejected having Jesus as their king, and thus they did not deserve the supper. One refused because of a desire for riches, another because of pleasure. For the first man had bought a farm, and the other five yoke of oxen; these signify those who are greedy for wealth. But the one who had married a wife was a seeker of pleasure. Furthermore, he who prepares a farm is like one who, because of worldly wisdom, does not accept the mystery <note>The "mystery" here refers to the divine truths of the Gospel which require faith beyond human logic.</note>. For this "farm" is this world, and nature in its simplest form. He who observes only nature does not receive that which is above nature. Therefore, the Pharisee who perhaps had "bought a farm"—that is, one who looked only to the laws of nature—does not accept that a virgin could give birth to God, because that is above nature. Indeed, all those who glory in external wisdom, because of this "farm" (which is nature), have ignored Jesus, the one who established and renewed the order of nature. Furthermore, the man who bought five yoke of oxen to test them signifies the carnal man, who has joined the five senses of the soul to bodily things, and has made the soul itself into flesh. Because of this, as one occupied with earthly things, he does not wish to be a partaker of the spiritual supper.

<margin>Proverbs 14. A higher sense according to the letter.</margin>
For the Wise Man says: *Who is he that slanders one who prevails over another?* <note>original: "Qui calumniatur qui alteri prævalet?" — This is a Latin rendering of a Proverbial sentiment about social and moral standing.</note> But he who falls away because of a wife is certainly a lover of pleasure, who is bound to the flesh as if it were the soul's spouse. While he is in the flesh, adhering to it, he cannot please God. You should understand all these things also according to the letter <note>The "literal" or "historical" sense, as opposed to the allegorical one.</note>. For we fall away from God because of our estates, because of our business (the oxen), and because of our marriages. For by clinging to these things, and spending our whole lives upon them, being vexed and worn down even unto blood, we neither think upon nor attempt any divine perception or word.

The Gentiles, however, were alienated from the covenants and the law of God; they were not made citizens of the saints. They lived not in just one, but in many iniquities and great rudeness, dwelling "by the hedges"—by which I mean sins.

<margin>What sin is. Why the Lord said, "compel them to enter."</margin>
For sin is a great hedge and a gap, dividing us from God. By "the highways," he means the passable life of the Gentiles, which is cut into many different opinions. By "the hedges," he understands their life spent in sins. He does not simply command the servant to call them, but says, "**compel them**." Although believing is a voluntary act for everyone, he said "compel" so that we might know it is a work of God's great power that the Gentiles believed while living in such deep ignorance. If a great power were not preached, and if the truth of the Word were not great, how could men who were raving in the worship of idols and doing filthy works be persuaded to suddenly acknowledge the true God and love a spiritual life? Therefore, wishing to signify a miraculous transformation, he used the word "necessity," as if to say: even though the Gentiles did not want to leave their idols and delights, they were "forced" to leave them by the preaching of the truth. Or, to put it another way: the power of the signs <note>The "signs" refer to miracles performed by the Apostles.</note> brought a great necessity upon them to be transferred to the faith of Christ. And that supper is prepared daily, and we are all called to the kingdom, which...

# CHAPTER 15. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
## COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
II iiii

...ministers, but I also require that the laity themselves be of good fruit and useful to their neighbors. Now, if one who is meant to benefit others becomes reprobate and is cast out from the order of Christians, he will be able neither to provide benefit nor to receive any utility. "It is useful," he says, "neither for the soil nor for the manure pile" <note>original: "Neque in terram, inquit, neqȝ in sterquilinium vtile est"; Luke 14:35</note>. By "the soil," it is suggested that one might receive utility; by "the manure pile," that one might provide it. Therefore, such a person is rejected, and is to be rejected, as one who neither provides nor perceives any utility. And since that discourse was obscure and parabolic, the Lord—rousing his listeners so that they would not take the saying about salt in a simple or literal way—says: "He who has ears to <margin>Ears.</margin>hear, let him hear." This means: he who has understanding, let him understand. For "ears" in this place signify the sensory power of the soul and its aptitude for understanding. 
<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Colossians 4</margin>Thus all the faithful are salt, receiving their quality from the divine words and supernal grace. And that grace is salt, hear Paul saying: "Let your speech be in grace, seasoned with salt" <note>Colossians 4:6</note>. And so, if the speech is <term>ἄχαρις</term> <note>original Greek: "acharis," meaning "ungracious" or "unpleasant"</note>—that is, without grace—it is called tasteless. Therefore, if we despise the quality of the divine oracles and do not receive them into ourselves, we are made foolish and lacking in understanding; and indeed your salt is made unsavory if it does not possess the quality of heavenly grace.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>F</margin> **A**ll the tax collectors <note>original: "publicani"</note> and sinners were drawing near to Him to hear Him, and the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, "This man receives sinners and eats with them." But He spoke this parable to them, saying, "What man among you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one which was lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing; and coming home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost.' Or what woman, having ten drachmas <note>A drachma was a silver coin roughly equivalent to a day's wage</note>, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her female friends and neighbors, saying, 'Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma which I had lost.' So I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner repenting." 

The Lord indeed did that for which He was incarnated: approaching tax collectors and sinners like a physician approaching the sick. But those who were truly sinners repaid such great humanity with grumbling. For they considered <margin>B</margin> tax collectors abominable, while they themselves devoured the houses of widows and orphans. What then did the Lord do? Just as He was merciful toward the tax collectors, so also was He toward those who slandered His mercy. For He does not turn away from them as though they were foolish and grumbling, but gently heals them, telling this parable of the sheep; and by things manifest and certain, He persuades and refutes them, so that they might not take offense at such a great outpouring of goodness. For if there is such joy over one irrational sheep—which was not made in the image of God—when it is found after wandering, how much more likely is it to occur for a rational man, created in the image of God? Clearly, therefore, <margin>C</margin> in this parable He calls the ninety-nine sheep the righteous, and the one sheep the sinner. 

However, some say that the hundred sheep represent the whole of rational creation, and the one sheep represents the human race of rational nature, which the Good Shepherd sought when it went astray, leaving the ninety-nine in the solitude—that is, in the supernal heavenly place. For heaven is <margin>Solitude</margin> a "solitude" <note>The Latin "solitudo" implies a wilderness or a place set apart</note>, sequestered from worldly tumult and full of all tranquility and peace. But when the Lord found the one who had strayed, He placed it on His shoulders. For He Himself <margin>The Lord [in] heaven</margin> bore our infirmities and our sins, and He Himself took up all our burdens without being weighed down, having paid all that we owed; and He bore us willingly and gladly all the way to our home—that is, into heaven—and He calls together His friends and neighbors...

# CHAPTER 15. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
## COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

<margin>D</margin> ...perhaps the angels, whom we also called sheep according to another account. For insofar as every created thing is compared to God, it is like a small coin <note>original: "pecunia"</note> or a brute animal; and in this sense, the celestial powers are called sheep. But if they are compared to other creatures, these choirs of angelic powers are called "friends and neighbors" because they are rational beings. And by "the woman," you should understand the Wisdom and Power of God the Father—Jesus himself—who lost the one drachma <note>A silver coin representing a day's wage; here symbolizing the human soul.</note>, that is, the creature made from rational beings and formed in His image: I mean humanity. And He lights His "lamp," which is His flesh. For just as a lamp, although it is made of earth, illuminates dark places through the light it receives, so also the flesh of the Lord, though it was earthly and similar to ours, appeared with the light of His divinity which it received within itself when He became incarnate. <margin>E</margin> And the "house"—that is, the whole world—was cleansed of sin. For Christ took away the sin of the world. And clearly, when the drachma was found, there was joy both for Christ and for the celestial powers, who are His friends and neighbors. They are "friends" because they do His will, and "neighbors" because they are incorporeal <note>Being spirits without physical bodies, they are "nearer" in nature to God than humans are.</note>. What if all the celestial powers are friends, but those who are closer to Him, like the Thrones and Cherubim, are the neighbors? By saying "friends and neighbors," He revealed two types, though this may seem a point for the overly curious.

> But He said, "A certain man had two sons, and the younger of them said to his father: 'Father, give me the portion of substance that comes to me.' And he divided the substance between them. <margin>F</margin> And not many days later, when the younger son had gathered everything together, he set out for a far country, and there he squandered his substance by living luxuriously. And after he had consumed everything, a great famine arose in that region, <margin><unclear>obinitu(?) lb multo(?)</unclear></margin> and he began to be in want. And he went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that region, and he sent him to his farm to feed the pigs. And he desired to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything."

And this parable is similar to the one above. For it also introduces a "man"—namely, God, who is truly merciful—and "two sons," meaning the two orders of men: the righteous

<column-break/>

**COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 253**
<page-num>253</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> and the sinners. Now the younger one said, "Give me the portion of substance that belongs to me." Of old, the possession of human nature was righteousness; therefore, the older son does not become insolent. Sin was born later, which is why the younger son becomes insolent—he who grew along with the sin that was introduced afterward. Or otherwise, the sinner is called "younger" because he is an insolent innovator of things, failing in his father's will. "Father, give me the portion of substance that belongs to me." The "substance" of man is his rational nature, from which follows free will. For every <margin>Free will.</margin> rational being possesses free will. Therefore, the Lord gives us reason so that we may use it freely, as if it were our own substance. And He gives to all equally. For all <margin>B</margin> are equally rational and have equally free will. But some of us use this liberty according to reason, while others squander the divine gift. And simply put, everything that the Lord has given us can be considered our "substance": for example, the heaven and the earth, and in short, all creatures, the Law, and the Prophets. Yet the younger son looked at the heaven and made the heaven a god; he looked at the earth and worshipped it. He did not wish to walk in the Law of God, and he committed fornications against the Prophets. But the older son used all these things for the glory of God. Therefore, He who gave all these things equally permitted man to enter into them freely. For He forces no one to serve Him against their will. For if <margin>Psalm 67.</margin> He had wished us to be forced, He would not have made us rational and possessed of free <margin>C</margin> will. Furthermore, the younger son "boiled down" <note>meaning: squandered or wasted</note> all these things at once. And what was the cause? He set out for a far country. For whenever a man departs from God and distances himself from the fear of God, he spends all his divine gifts. For those who remain near to God do nothing worthy of destruction, <margin>Psalm 15.</margin> according to that which is said: "I set the Lord always in my sight, for He is at my right hand, that I be not moved" <note>Psalm 16:8 (Vulgate 15:8)</note>. But when He is far from us, we become <margin>Psalm 62.</margin> apostates, doing and suffering all the worst things, according to that saying: "Behold, those who distance themselves shall perish" <note>Psalm 73:27 (Vulgate 72:27)</note>. Therefore, he squandered his substance. Justly so, for Virtue has one limit and is a single thing, but malice is divided in many ways, and of those many...

<margin>D</margin> ...the cause of virtues, for example: there is one limit for fortitude—to use anger when it is necessary, in the manner it is necessary, and toward whom it is necessary. But there are two types of its vice: fear and audacity. Do you see how reason is scattered and the unity of virtue perishes? Once that substance <note>original: "substantia"; here meaning the soul's natural reason and spiritual inheritance.</note> is consumed—by which I mean a man following natural reason but not walking according to the written law, nor listening to the prophets—a great famine arose. Not a famine of bread, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord <note>A reference to the prophecy in Amos 8:11.</note>. The beginning of poverty occurs when one does not fear the Lord but departs far from Him; for to those who fear the Lord, there is no poverty. 

<margin>E</margin> How is it that there is no want for those who fear the Lord? Because he who fears the Lord will greatly desire His commandments, and therefore glory and riches shall be in his house. He has dispersed and given to the poor; he is so far from being in want. But he who has gone far from the Lord, and does not have His terrible face before his eyes, will certainly labor in poverty, with the divine word working nothing within him. "And he went"—that is, he proceeded and advanced in malice. "He joined himself to one of the citizens of that region." For he who joins himself to the Lord becomes one spirit with Him <margin>1 Corinthians 6</margin>; but he who joins himself to a harlot becomes one body with the nature of demons, and becomes entirely flesh, incapable of the spirit, like those who lived in the time of the Flood. 

<margin>F</margin> The citizens of that region had revolted from God; they are entirely demons. But he progresses and becomes powerful in sins. <margin>Who the pigs are.</margin> "He feeds pigs"—that is, he teaches others malice, and they wallow in the mud of vile and material affections. <margin>How shepherds make grunting pigs silent.</margin> For the eyes of pigs can never look upward, having received a different physical formation. For this reason, when a pig is squealing, if they flip it onto its back, they make it squeal less. For they come as if to a spectacle, looking at things they never saw before, and looking upward, they are stunned into silence. Such are the eyes of those who are poorly educated; they never see the things that are above. Such people are fed by the one who leads many in malice, such as a master of harlots,

<column-break/>

<page-num>254</page-num>
## COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

<margin>A</margin> or a chief of tax collectors, or a leader of thieves: for it must be said of all these that they "feed pigs." That miserable man desires to be satisfied with sin, but no one lets him be satisfied. For to one accustomed to evil, no one gives satiety. For pleasure does not last, but hungers and perishes, and that miserable man becomes empty again. For sin is likened to husks <note>original: "siliquis"; the pods of the carob tree, which were sweet on the outside but hard to digest.</note>, having both sweetness and harshness. For it delights for a time, but truly tortures forever. For this reason, no one gives satiety of evils to the one who is accustomed to them. For who can satisfy and bring rest? God—but He is not present; for he who eats such things is far from God. Or the demons? But they are much more concerned that we never rest and that we be filled with malice.

<margin>B</margin> "But returning to himself, he said: How many of my father’s hired servants have bread in abundance, while I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants. And arising, he came to his father. But while he was yet a great way off, his father saw him and was moved with mercy, and running, he fell on his neck and kissed him." The intemperate man finally returned to himself. As long as he was doing evil, he was outside himself. For he had consumed (as it says) his substance, and for this reason, he was deservedly outside himself. For he who is not governed by reason, but lives contrary to reason and begins other absurdities, is outside himself and does not remain in his own substance—that is, in reason. 

<margin>C</margin> But when someone considers into what great misery he has come, then he "returns to himself," reflecting and coming to repentance from his external wandering. Furthermore, he calls the catechumens <note>Individuals receiving basic instruction in Christianity before baptism.</note> "hired servants," because they have not yet reached the point where they are called sons, because they have not yet been rightly enlightened. However, the catechumens certainly have an abundance of rational bread, hearing the readings every day. And so that you may learn the difference between a hired servant and a son, listen: there are three orders of those who are saved. For some do good as slaves, fearing judgment; which David also suggests, saying: <margin>Psalm 118</margin> "Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have been afraid of your judgments." But those who seem to be "hired servants" are those who desire to please God out of a longing for rewards.

<summary>Theophylact provides an allegorical reading of the Prodigal Son, identifying the "pigs" as earthly passions and the "hired servants" as catechumens. He emphasizes that sin is a state of being "outside oneself" or divorced from reason.</summary>

In the same place, just as David himself says: *Incline my heart, O God, to perform your justifications forever because of the reward.* <note>Theophylact is contrasting those who serve God for a reward with "children" who serve for love.</note> But those who fulfill the commandments out of love for God are children, as David again testifies:

Thus, he who puts earthly things before them sins against heaven. He is entirely absent from the path that leads to heaven. Know also that when he sinned, he sinned as if he were not acting in the presence of God. But when he confesses, he realizes that he has sinned *before* God. Furthermore, "rising up," he goes to his father. For one must not only deliberate on what pleases God, but there is a need for the deed itself. Now, just as you have seen his fervent repentance, see also the swift mercy of the father. For he did not wait until the son came to him, but he anticipated him and embraced him. For by nature and kindness God is a father, and he embraces the whole person so that he might bind the son to himself on all sides, and as it is said, the glory of God surrounds him. Once, when the son moved far away, it was a time for the father to keep himself from the embrace; but now, when he returns and draws near through conversion, it is a time for embracing. He falls upon his neck, showing that he who once rebelled has now been made obedient. And he kisses him, indicating 
<margin>E</margin>
reconciliation, and as it were, sanctifying the polluted mouth as a kind of vestibule, and through this, admitting him to internal sanctification.

<margin>D</margin> Although perhaps no one would find fault with us, nevertheless, wishing to show the greatness of his benevolence, we describe it thus. Let us look at the parable both specifically and briefly. The elder son was in the field, that is, in this world, and he was working his land—by which I mean the flesh—so that he might be filled with bread, and he was sowing in tears so that he might reap in joy. Furthermore, when he learned what had been done, he was unwilling to enter into the common joy; but the merciful father goes out and entreats him, and teaches him that the cause for joy is the restoration to life of one who was dead. This was because the man, being ignorant, had been offended, and had rebuked the father for not having given him even a kid <note>original: "hædum" — a young goat, contrasted here with the more valuable fatted calf.</note>, yet for the intemperate son, he had killed the fatted calf. But what is signified by the kid?

<margin>E</margin> Learn at this point: Every sinner is assigned to the left side <note>A reference to Matthew 25, where the "goats" (sinners) are placed on the left hand of God.</note>. Therefore, the son of good fruit says, <margin>Matthew 25</margin> "I have spent my life in all labors, having suffered persecution and affliction, and having suffered at the hands of sinners, yet you never killed a kid for me"—that is, you never humbled a sinner so that I might find even a small amount of rest. <margin>3 Kings 17</margin> Such a "kid" for Elijah was Ahab. For he persecuted the prophet, and the Lord did not immediately give the kid over to be killed so that the prophet might be refreshed for a little while and rest with his fellow prophets. Hence he says to God: <margin>3 Kings 19</margin> "Lord, they have killed your prophets and overturned your altars." <margin>1 Kings 22 & 25</margin> For David, the kid was Saul and all those who slandered him, whom the Lord permitted to test him, and did not kill so that David might rejoice; therefore he also said, <margin>Psalm 93</margin> "How long, O Lord, shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked glory?" <note>original: "Vsquequo peccatores Domine: vsquequo peccatores gloriabuntur?"</note> <margin>F</margin> The son also says these things in the Gospel, since he was in many labors and had attained no consolation. "He has delivered none of my persecutors to death, yet now he saves the prodigal so easily." This, then, is the whole aim of the parable, on account of the Pharisees who were grumbling because he received sinners: by which he teaches that even if we are righteous, sinners are not to be rejected, nor should we grumble when God awaits them. Therefore, the younger son represents the harlots and tax collectors; but the elder son represents the Pharisees and scribes, who according to the subject matter of the parable are understood as the righteous—as if God were saying: "Granted, you

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> are truly righteous and have transgressed no commandment; is it not therefore necessary to welcome those who are converted from sins?" Such, then, are those who grumble in the parable. However, I am not unaware that some interpret the elder son as the angels, and the younger son as human nature which was in turmoil and, having been given a commandment, abandoned itself to luxuries. Others see them as the Israelites and the Gentiles. But this which we have said must be held as true: that the elder son carries the person of the righteous, and the younger of the sinners and those converting themselves. The entire context of the parable was set forth on account of the Pharisees, so that the Lord might teach them not to take offense at the reception of sinners, even if they themselves were righteous. Therefore, let no one bear the judgments of God with grievance, but let it be pleasing to him if sinners act happily and are saved. <margin>B</margin> For how do you know if he whom you consider a sinner, through performing penance, might become more pleasing? Or what if he has hidden virtues, and for that reason is looked upon kindly by God?

<margin>C</margin> He said also to his disciples, "There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and he was accused to him of wasting his goods. And he called him and said to him, 'What is this I hear of you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward.' Then the steward said within himself, 'What shall I do, since my lord is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig, to beg I am ashamed. I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.' So, having called every one of his lord's debtors, he said to the first, 'How much do you owe my lord?' And he said, 'A hundred baths of oil' <note>original: "batos" — a Hebrew liquid measure roughly equal to 8-9 gallons.</note>. And he said to him, 'Take your bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty.' Then he said to another, 'And how much do you owe?' Who said, 'A hundred cors of wheat' <note>original: "choros" — a 'cor' or 'homer,' a dry measure roughly equal to 10-12 bushels.</note>. He said to him, 'Take your bill, and write eighty.' And the lord praised the unjust steward because he had acted prudently. For the children of this world are more prudent in their generation than the children of light."

<margin>The nature of parables and their parts, and how far they should be investigated.</margin>
Every parable manifests the nature of certain things in an indirect and figurative way, and is not similar in every single detail to the things for which it was adopted. For this reason, one ought not to investigate every part of a parable too curiously, but only as far as the parts appear useful to the proposed theme; the remaining parts are to be left aside, as they merely weave the story together and contribute nothing to the purpose at hand—which is exactly what must be done in this present parable. For if I were to try to explain every tiny detail—who the steward is, who the steward’s master is, by whom he was accused, who the debtors are, and for what reason one owed oil and another wheat, and why they are said to owe a hundred, and if we searched out all other such things—we would make the discourse obscure and troublesome, and perhaps, if we hesitated too much, we would even be **E** ridiculous. Therefore, one ought to take as much utility from the present parable as possible. To say something briefly: the Lord, in this place, wishes to teach us that the riches entrusted to us should be well-administered. And first we learn this: that we are not the masters of our riches. For we have nothing of our own, but we are stewards of another’s property, which has been entrusted to us by the Lord so that we may dispense it well, just as He commands. But if we do not spend the entrusted riches according to the mind **F** of the Lord, and if we abuse them for our own luxury, we shall be accused. For the will of the Lord is to use what is given for the needs of our fellow servants, not for our own pleasures. Furthermore, those who are accused and removed from the stewardship of riches—that is, those who depart from this life—must give an account of their stewardship when they are removed. If we were wise, or even if we were slow to realize what needs to be done, we would make friends for ourselves 

<margin>What are called the riches of unrighteousness.</margin>
out of the riches of unrighteousness. Now, those are called "riches of unrighteousness" which the Lord gave to us to be spent for the use of our brothers and fellow servants, but which we instead keep stored up for ourselves. But let us realize, even if late, where we are being led; for when that day comes, we will not be able to work. For

For we ought to give to the poor first, because they are "debtors" according to that which is said: *The righteous man is merciful and lends all day long* <note>Psalm 37:26</note>. And again: *He who has mercy on the poor lends to God* <note>Proverbs 19:17</note>. It is necessary, therefore, first to give to those good debtors, who return a hundredfold. But because we are found to be stewards **B** of unrighteousness, unrighteously retaining what was set aside for others, we must not remain forever in this faithlessness, but must share with the poor so that we may be received by them into eternal dwellings. Thus, by interpreting the parable in this way, nothing will occur in the narration that is superfluous, or overly curious, or intricate. But He also seems to signify something else when He says: "The children of this world are wiser, etc." This is not poorly connected, nor is it irrelevant. For He calls "children of this world" those who praise everything that is profitable on earth; but "children of light," those who ought to piously share their spiritual riches. This, therefore, is what He is saying: that men placed in charge of human administrations take care and provide in every way so that when they are removed from the office of **C** stewardship, they may have consolation. But the children of light are ordained—that is, those to whom the spiritual stewardship of things is entrusted—yet they do not think about how they may perceive a benefit after this life. Therefore, the children of this world, to whom human stewardships are entrusted, dispense their affairs wisely in their own generation—that is, in this life. But the children of light are those who have received money so that they might dispense it for pious uses. We are found, therefore, to dispense our affairs wisely in human stewardships, so that even if we fall from administration, we have a certain refuge for life. For this reason, we are also called "foolish" rather than wise concerning those things which will benefit us hereafter; specifically, how we might make the poor our friends by sharing the riches of unrighteousness. <note>original: "iniustitię"</note> By this, he means those things given to us so that they might be "weapons of justice," but which are instead held back by us, and therefore belong to unrighteousness. For if riches acquired by just means are considered "unrighteousness" and <term>mammon <note>An Aramaic word for wealth or profit, often personified as a false god of greed.</note></term> whenever they are not well-distributed and given to the poor, how much more so are those gained through injustice! Let us, therefore, make friends for ourselves from these riches, so that when we fail and depart from this life—or to put it another way, when we are faint-hearted and condemned there—they may receive us into eternal dwellings.

<margin>E</margin> Here he further teaches how riches ought to be managed according to God's will. <margin>Christ calls earthly riches "the least thing."</margin> For he who is faithful in "the least thing"—that is, he who has well-distributed the riches entrusted to him in this world—is also faithful in "much"; that is, in the future age, he is truly worthy of riches. He calls earthly riches "the least" because they are truly small, or rather, they are nothing at all since they are transitory. He calls heavenly riches "much," as they are destined to endure forever and always be present. <margin>F</margin> But he who appears unjust in these earthly riches, and claims for himself what was granted for the common use of the brothers, will not be found worthy of that "much," but will be rejected as one who is unjust. <margin>A</margin> ...us; but now, because they are with us, it is clear they are being held and not distributed to the poor. This is to claim for oneself the property of others, and specifically that which belongs to the poor, which is the essence of unrighteousness. Therefore, for the one who manages those riches poorly and unfaithfully—who does not well-distribute the "others' property," that is, the goods and money belonging to the poor—how can they be believed to be "true" riches? Or to put it another way: since we brought nothing into this world and were born naked into this world, who will give us anything of our own? Our true riches are the heavenly and divine ones; there is our <term>citizenship <note>original: "municipatus." A reference to Philippians 3:20, "our citizenship is in heaven."</note></term> because man was created in the image of God. Money and possessions, however, are foreign to us; none of these things are like him. <margin>B</margin> The enjoyment of divine goods and the participation in God are what truly belong to us.

Thus far the Lord has taught us how riches are to be faithfully managed: they are another's, and not our own; for we are stewards in the name of the Lord. Since the management of riches according to God cannot be done rightly unless one is free from affection toward them, he stated this doctrine: "No one can serve God and mammon." This means it is impossible to be addicted to mammon and simultaneously serve God with such an affection. And so, if you wish to faithfully manage riches, do not serve them—that is, do not be held by an affection for them—and then you will truly serve God. Everywhere, the love of money is censured—that is, the emotional attachment to and the pursuit of it.

The rich man also died, and was buried.] These words follow well upon what preceded, for because he had previously taught how we ought to conduct ourselves rightly regarding riches, he fittingly joins this parable, which conveys the same sentiment through the example of the rich man. For this is a parable, and not (as some have thought) a history. For the good things for the righteous and the opposites for sinners were not yet separated; rather, the Lord shaped his discourse to teach the unmerciful what sorts of things would happen <margin>E</margin> to them, and again to teach those who are afflicted how well they will fare in exchange for those things which they endure here. Therefore, he took up the rich man in this place without a name in the parable, as one <margin>Psalm 16 <note>Original: "Psalm. 6"; likely a reference to Psalm 15:4 in the Vulgate, which is Psalm 16 in modern numbering.</note></margin> who is not even worthy to be named by God; just as he says through the prophet: "I will not be mindful of their names through my lips" <note>original: "Non memor ero nominum illorum per labia mea."</note>. But he records the name of the poor man. For the names of the righteous are written in the book of life. For a tradition of the Hebrews relates that a certain Lazarus at that time suffered from extreme poverty and illness, whom the Lord was mindful of in this parable as someone known and recognized. The rich man, therefore, was entirely dissolved in luxury; for he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and besides, he gave himself over to all other delights. For he says "he feasted," and not just once <margin>F</margin> and then not again, but "every day"; and not moderately, but "sumptuously," that is, expensively and prodigally. But Lazarus was poor and gravely ill. For he was "full of sores," he says. Others are sick but lack sores; but this man was afflicted by a heavier evil, and he lay at the vestibule of the rich man. Behold another pain: to see others in delights while he himself was pressed by hunger. For he "desired," he says, "to be filled": not with expensive dishes, but with his crumbs, and even those with which the dogs were filled. Furthermore, he was destitute of all care, and the dogs licked his sores, since there was no one who would drive them away from him. Did Lazarus, then, blaspheme in the midst of such great evils? Did he hurl insults? Did he

<margin>A</margin> cease to endure the luxury of the rich man? Did he condemn the rich man’s inhumanity? Did he reproach the providence of God? None of these; rather, he was strong and of great philosophy <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to spiritual discipline and the patient endurance of suffering.</note>. Hence it is manifest from these things that the angels received him when he died. For if he had been a grumbler and a blasphemer, he would by no means have attained such great honor or been escorted by a company of angels. "The rich man also died, and was buried." For surely even while he lived, his soul was buried, carrying the flesh about like a sepulcher. And therefore when he died, he was not taken up by angels, but was led down into hell <note>original: "infernum"</note>. For he who never knew anything sublime or heavenly is worthy of the lowest place. By saying that he "was buried," <margin>B</margin> the Lord hints in passing that his soul also was allotted to a low and dark place.

And why did he not say "you took" (*accepisti*), but rather "you received back" (*recipisti*)? <margin>*To receive back.*</margin> For we are accustomed to use the word "receive back" regarding those who take what was owed to them. We learn, therefore, that although some are wicked and have reached the peak of malice, they occasionally perform one or two good works; hence, having certain good things for which they are paid in the prosperity of this present life, they are said to "receive back" their reward. Perhaps he too had committed one or two bad deeds, and therefore, by enduring that suffering on earth, he received the payment worthy of those deeds. Whence he now has consolation, but you are tormented. Furthermore, the "gulf" <margin>What the gulf is.</margin> signifies the distance and the difference between the righteous and the sinners. For just as their wills were different, so also their rewards are far apart from each other, each one receiving those things which agree with his life and his will. For as long as the soul is in the body, it is visible through its actions; but after it has departed from the body, it becomes invisible. This, therefore, they have said is "Hell." But they call the "Bosom of Abraham" <margin>Abraham's Bosom; The harbor of the sea.</margin> the containment of the good things which are laid up for the righteous, who enter into the heavenly harbors after the storm of this sea. For even in the sea, we call those places "bosoms" (*sinus*) <note>The Latin "sinus" can mean both a "bosom" and a "bay" or "gulf" of the sea, serving as a metaphor for a safe harbor.</note> which are suitable for harbors and rest.
