Here, the focus shifts to the Rich Man’s request for his five brothers and the deeper symbolic meanings of the parable.</meta>

### CHAPTER 17. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,
### ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE.

For although he himself had not believed the scriptures when he heard them, and had thought that the things said in them were mere fables, he suspected that his brothers were in the same state. He judged them by his own standard: that they would not listen to the scriptures, just as he had not; but if someone were to rise from the dead, then they would believe. Even now, there are people like this who say, "Who has seen the things that are in hell? Who has come from there and reported them to us?" But let them hear Abraham’s response: "If we do not listen to the scriptures, we will not believe even those who come from hell." <margin>John 12.</margin> The Jews proved this clearly; because they did not listen to the scriptures, they did not believe even when the dead had risen. Instead, they even attempted to kill Lazarus <note>Theophylact is referring to the Lazarus whom Jesus raised from the dead in John 12, distinguishing him from the Lazarus in this parable.</note>, and even when many dead arose at the crucifixion of Jesus, the Jews grew more violent and attacked the Apostles. Indeed, if seeing such things would have helped us toward faith, the Lord would have done it often. <margin>We must care for the diligent searching of scripture, not the ghosts of the dead.</margin> Now, nothing is so useful as the diligent searching of the scriptures. For the devil can create false and deceptive visions of the dead to seduce the unwise, sowing doctrines about hell that are worthy of his own malice. But for those who search the scriptures properly, he can deceive them in nothing. For the scriptures are a lamp and a light; when that light shines, the thief is caught and exposed. Therefore, we must believe the scriptures and not concern ourselves with the raising of the dead for proof.

<margin>An allegorical explanation of the parable. 1 Peter 2.</margin> This parable can also be explained through allegory. One might say that the Rich Man signifies the Jewish people. For that people was once "rich," enriched with all knowledge, wisdom, and the words of God, which are more valuable than gold and precious stones. They were "clothed in purple and fine linen," possessing both a kingdom and a priesthood; they were a "royal priesthood" to God. The purple signifies the kingdom, while the fine linen signifies the priesthood. For the Levites were clothed in fine linen priestly garments. He "feasted every day and lived splendidly." For every day they offered a morning and an evening sacrifice, <margin><gloss>perpetual sacrifice</gloss></margin> which they called the *endelechismon* <note>original: <greek>ἐνδελεχισμόν</greek>, a Greek term for the "continual" or "perpetual" daily burnt offering in the Temple.</note>, that is, the perpetual sacrifice. Lazarus, however, represented the Gentile people, who were "poor" in divine grace and wisdom. He "lay at the gate," for the Gentiles were not permitted to enter the house; they were considered a pollution. <margin>Acts 21.</margin> We see this in the Acts of the Apostles, when they cried out against Paul

<column-break/>

for bringing Gentiles into the temple and making that holy place "common" or "unclean." Furthermore, that Gentile people was full of the "sores" of stinking sins, and they fed the "shameless dogs"—the devils—with those sores. For our sins are a pleasure to the demons. They also "desired the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table." They were entirely lacking the "bread which strengthens a man's heart" <margin>Psalm 102 <note>This citation corresponds to Psalm 104:15 in modern numbering: "bread that strengthens man's heart."</note></margin> and were in need of the smallest, thinnest bits of spiritual food, just as the Canaanite woman, being a Gentile, desired to be satisfied by the crumbs. <margin>Matthew 15.</margin> To be brief: the Hebrew people died to God, and their bones became "dead" and no longer moved to perform good works. But Lazarus—the Gentile people—died to sin. And the Jews, who died in their sins, are now "burned in the flame of envy," being jealous (as the Apostle says) that the Gentiles have been accepted into the faith. The Gentile people, who were previously poor and ignoble, now dwell within the "borders" (the bosom) of Abraham, the father of nations. And rightly so! For Abraham himself, while he was still a "gentile" <note>In the sense that Abraham believed God before he was circumcised, thus becoming the father of all who believe, regardless of their origin.</note>, believed God and passed from the worship of idols to the knowledge of God. Therefore, those who share in his transformation and faith rightly rest in his borders, having obtained the same end, the same habitations, and the same reception of good things. Now the Jewish people desire a single "drop" from their ancient legal sprinklings and purifications to cool their tongue, so they might confidently tell us that the Law is still <margin>Matthew 11.</margin> effective and operational—but it is not. <margin>Psalm 39 <note>Psalm 40:6 in modern bibles.</note></margin> For "the Law lasted until John [the Baptist]." And "Sacrifice and offering you did not desire." <margin>Daniel 9.</margin> And Daniel predicted that the "anointing shall be abolished" and the prophets sealed—that is, they would cease and be concluded. Now, you should also explain the parable <margin>A moral explanation of the parable.</margin> in a moral sense. Do not, while you are rich in worldly things, overlook your "hungry mind" which is in a bad state. Do not despise the mind when it is cast down on the ground, even though it was made to tend upward. Do not let it lie outside the gates, but lead it inside; let it not stand outdoors, nor wander, nor lie idle, but let it work. Thus, perform the works of the mind, so that you do not only take delight in the flesh. It is easy to explain the other parts of this parable for the benefit of one's character.

<summary>Theophylact provides both a literal and an allegorical interpretation of the Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus, identifying the Rich Man with the Jewish people and Lazarus with the Gentiles, while emphasizing that the Scriptures are a more reliable guide than supernatural signs.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER 17. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.</header>

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>Matthew 18, Mark 9.</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'D' featuring a portrait of a tonsured figure, possibly a saint or scholar, in profile holding a book.</image-desc>

And he said to the disciples, It is impossible that stumbling blocks <note>original: "offendicula"; refers to things that trip someone up or cause them to lose faith.</note> should not come: but woe to him through whom they come. It would be better for him if a millstone <note>original: "mola asinaria"; literally a millstone turned by a donkey, much larger and heavier than a hand-mill.</note> were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea, rather than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble. Take heed to yourselves. If your brother sins against you, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying, "I repent," forgive him. ] Since the greedy Pharisees were grumbling against the Lord as he spoke about poverty—to whom he also told the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, showing them through it what great punishments they were to suffer for their love of riches—

<margin>The Pharisees are the authors of stumbling blocks.</margin>
he now speaks to the disciples about these same Pharisees, making it clear that they are the authors of stumbling blocks, hindering people from the way of God, and therefore woe is to be inflicted upon them. Let us see, therefore, what he says: *It is impossible that stumbling blocks should not come*, that is, impediments to a good life pleasing to God. For because of the malice of men, it is necessary that many impediments to preaching and truth be found. *But woe to him through whom they come*, that is, to him who does these things, such as the Pharisees, who cause offense and prohibit preaching. Why then do you condemn them, Lord, and call those who cause stumbling blocks "miserable," if they come by necessity? For everything that is necessary is worthy of pardon.

<margin>The necessity of stumbling blocks is not absolute but arises from an evil will.</margin>
But listen: that necessity has its beginning in the will. The Lord means to say this because, seeing the malice of the men who were then present, he saw they were prone to every evil and chose nothing good. Thus, as a consequence of their behavior, it becomes "necessary" for stumbling blocks to come. Therefore, the malice which men pursue is of their own will. The operation of offenses, however, necessarily accompanies that malice, and for this reason the authors of stumbling blocks are to be punished. Come, let us use an example. Seeing someone following a bad diet and being insatiable, one says: "It is necessary for him to fall ill." Is the disease therefore necessary?

<meta>catchword: him</meta>

<page-num>264</page-num>

**A** Yes, insofar as he maintains a bad diet. Therefore, woe to those who hinder preaching, because they have reached such a level of malice that stumbling blocks necessarily occur. And it would be better for a man causing stumbling blocks and offenses that a millstone be hung on his neck and he be thrown into the sea, than that one of the little ones among the faithful be caused to stumble and be subverted. Therefore he fortifies his disciples and says: *Take heed to yourselves.* "Behold," he says, "I tell you beforehand that evils will come. You are without excuse." For it is necessary that they come, but it is not necessary for you to perish, provided you fortify and arm yourselves.

<margin>A comparison.</margin>
For it is necessary for the wolf to come, but if the shepherd remains vigilant, it is not necessary for the sheep to perish; rather, the wolf will go away with his mouth gaping in vain. **B** He said these things, therefore, about those who cause offense—that is, those who hinder and cause harm. Since there are many differences among such people: some are indeed incurable, such as the Pharisees; others, however, are curable, such as the Lord’s own brothers were toward him, for at one point not even they believed in him.

<margin>John 7.</margin>
Because there are many differences in impediments, it is likely that some who share the same faith might behave this way; and therefore he says: *If your brother sins against you, rebuke him* <note>original: "argue eum"; to confront or correct him.</note> alone and in private, and if indeed he listens to you, you have gained him; but if not, take with you one or two, etc., which Matthew explains at length; but Luke passed over what was said by Matthew in silence. Thus, he who listens to the rebuke is worthy of pardon. **C** But he who does not listen, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector <note>original: "ethnicus & publicanus"; in this historical context, those considered outside the religious community.</note>, that is, despised by all and unworthy to be called a brother.

<margin>Chapter 8.</margin>
Afterwards, as if someone were to ask: "So be it, Lord, you have said these things well; but if he has often obtained pardon and harms me again, what should be done to him?" He says: *If he repents, forgive him again.*

<margin>Seven times.</margin>
And again: *If he sins seven times, and turns back, forgive him.* Now, *seven times* <note>original: "septies"</note> in this place is used to mean "many times." Just as when it is said: "The barren woman has given birth to seven." Therefore, as often as he performs penance, so often must he be forgiven. For do not think that the Lord sets a limit on the number of times one may be forgiven; rather, by "seven times" understand "many times," even without number—just as in common speech we say "an army of ten thousand," not meaning exactly ten thousand...

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus' teaching on "stumbling blocks," arguing that while human malice makes such offenses inevitable, individuals remain responsible for their choices. He also outlines the Christian duty of repeated, limitless forgiveness for those who repent.</summary>

<margin>D</margin> and she may not have more husbands, for perhaps she has many; but we wish to say the same thing as if we were saying, "of many men." <note>This likely refers to a symbolic interpretation of the number 'seven' as representing a complete or large number, perhaps referencing the woman with seven husbands mentioned in other Gospel passages.</note> And that he says this is manifest from <margin>Matthew 18.</margin> Matthew. For there, when Peter had said, "Lord, shall I forgive him seven times?" the Lord said, "No, but seventy times seven," and through this he designates an innumerable amount. And the Apostles said to the Lord, "Increase our faith." And the Lord said, "If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you might say to this mulberry tree, <note>original: "sycamino". The Greek and Latin terms often refer to the mulberry tree, which was distinct from the sycamore-fig.</note> 'be uprooted and transplanted into the sea,' and it would obey you." But which of you, having a servant plowing or feeding sheep, will say to him when he has returned from the field, "Come at once and sit down at the table"? And does he not rather say to him, "Prepare what I may eat for supper, and gird yourself and <margin>E</margin> serve me until I have eaten and drunk, and after these things you shall eat and drink"? Does he give thanks to that servant because he did the things that were commanded? I think not. So also you, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, "We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do."] The Apostles certainly believed in the Lord; nevertheless, when they had come to a consciousness of their own weakness, and had heard the Lord speaking to them about certain great things and about the danger of stumbling blocks, they prayed that the power of faith might be increased in them, through which they would be able to perfect these things he describes. For nothing leads so much to the perfecting of that poverty <note>referring to "poverty of spirit" or humility</note> of which he speaks as believing and trusting in the Lord—just as nothing makes one store up treasures so much as <margin>F</margin> failing to believe that he is a great treasurer and that his goodness is an inexhaustible storehouse. Furthermore, so that they might also resist stumbling blocks through faith, they approach him saying, "Increase our faith. Make us more perfect and firmer in faith." Moreover, the Lord, showing them that they ask well and that they ought to hold this mind firmly regarding faith as being greatly effective, says, "If you had faith, you would have transplanted this mulberry tree." Two great things are in this: namely, for something rooted in the earth to be moved to another place, and to be planted in the sea. For what can be planted in water? It is manifest, however, that while he says these things, he is demonstrating the power of faith. Perhaps, however, through allegory someone might say that the mulberry tree is the devil, who to us is the

<margin>A</margin> author and fosterer of the "worm of this age," because of the thoughts which he generates. For the leaves of the mulberry tree feed the worms from which silk is made. <note>Theophylact uses the natural history of the silkworm, which feeds on mulberry leaves, to allegorize how the devil feeds sinful thoughts in the human heart.</note> Faith, therefore, is able to uproot this mulberry tree from the human heart and cast it into the sea, that is, into the abyss of perdition. And because he said these things about faith, he adds another more necessary doctrine. What is this? That one must not be proud of good works. For since faith corrects many things and makes him who possesses it fulfill the commandments—along with the fact that it adorns him with the working of miracles—and because it is likely that a man might fall into pride from these things, he fortifies the Apostles so that they are not extolled for their good works, using a most beautiful example. "For which of you," he says, "having a servant," etc. <margin>B</margin> It is shown through this parable that one ought not to be extolled for any good work, indeed, not even for the fulfillment of all the commandments. For a necessity lies upon the servant to do the commands of his lord, nor ought he to ascribe the good work to himself. Indeed, if he does not work, he is worthy of many lashes; but when he has worked, let him be content that he has escaped the lashes. Therefore, one ought not to seek a reward or honor for this. For it belongs to the generosity of the lord to give, or rather to bestow it upon him. Therefore, he who serves God, even if he performs the commandments, ought not to be puffed up. For he has done nothing great, but woe will be to him unless he does it, <margin>1 Corinthians 9.</margin> as the Apostle says, "Woe to me, unless I preach the gospel." Therefore, if he has attained gifts, he ought not <margin>C</margin> to be proud in them or boast about them. For they are benefits granted to him through the mercy of God, not because the Lord owes him anything; rather, the servant owes it to his lord to do all his commands. But if, even when we have done all the commands, we ought not then to feel ourselves to be anything great, how much do we sin when we do not perform the greatest part of God's commands, and yet we are puffed up? Notice, however, that in the said parable he first placed the one plowing, and added afterward the one feeding sheep. For first one must be a plowman, and then assume pastoral care. For <margin>1 Timothy 3.</margin> he who has plowed his own flesh well, as if it were a kind of earth, will be worthy also to become a shepherd of others. For he who [rules] his own...

# CHAPTER 17. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

...if he does not know how to rule his own house as he ought, how will he take care of the Church? <note>A reference to the requirements for a bishop in 1 Timothy 3:5.</note> Therefore, plow yourself first, then you will feed others. As Jeremiah also says: **"Break up your fallow ground"** <margin>Jeremiah 4.</margin> <note>original: "Novate vobis novalia"</note>; and then he adds: **"Enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge"**: for this is the primary duty of pastors.

**[And it happened while he was going to Jerusalem, and he passed through the middle of Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a certain village, ten lepers met him, who stood far off, and with a loud voice said, "Jesus, Master, have mercy on us." When he saw them, he said to them, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." And it happened that while they were going, they were cleansed. One of them, when he saw that he was cleansed, returned with a loud voice glorifying God, and fell on his face at his feet, giving him thanks, and he was a Samaritan. Jesus answering said, "Were not ten cleansed? But where are the nine? Have none been found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?" And he said to him, "Rise, go your way, your faith has saved you."]**

And from this, anyone can learn that nothing hinders anyone from pleasing God, even if he be of a cursed race, provided he has a good will. For behold, ten lepers met Jesus as he was about to enter a certain city; but they met him outside the city. <margin>Numbers 5.</margin> For it was not permitted for those who were considered "cursed" <note>Leprosy was often viewed as a divine punishment or a state of ritual impurity.</note> to live within the cities. Therefore they stood far off, being ashamed on account of the uncleanness that was visible in them; they did not dare to approach, thinking that they were abominable to him just as they were to others. <margin>Psalm 144.</margin> Therefore they raise their voice and pray. <margin>Leviticus 13.</margin> In their physical location they stand far off, but through prayer they draw near. For the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. And they do not simply pray to him as a man, but as one who is more than a man. For they call him "Master," <margin>Why Christ commanded the lepers to show themselves to the priests.</margin> that is, Lord or Caretaker: which shows they considered him close to God. But he commands that they show themselves to the priests. <margin>For the priests used to examine such people and render a judgment as to whether they were clean or not. The priests had signs by which they investigated incurable leprosy; but...</margin>

---

# AN EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 266

<margin>A</margin> ...and when someone was infected with leprosy and afterwards had obtained health, the priests would examine him, and the gift prescribed in the law would be offered. But in this case, since they were admittedly lepers, what need was there to show themselves to the priests, unless they were surely to be cleansed? For the fact that he commanded them to go to the priests indicated nothing else than that they were about to be made clean; for this reason, the text says they were cleansed while they were going.

But observe this, as we said at the beginning: that although there were ten, nine of them, though they were Israelites, appeared ungrateful; but the Samaritan, though he was of another race, <margin>Samaritans.</margin> returned and sent forth a voice of gratitude. For the Samaritans were descendants of the Assyrians <margin>Assyrians.</margin>: <note>Theophylact reflects the common historical view that Samaritans were descended from colonists brought in by the Assyrian Empire.</note> this is recorded so that no Gentile should despair, and no one should boast merely of having holy parents. This miracle suggests that the common salvation of the entire human race is being accomplished. 

For the ten lepers <margin>What the ten lepers signify</margin> signify the whole race of mankind infected with the "leprosy" of malice, carrying about the foulness of sin, and situated outside the city of the kingdom of heaven because of uncleanness, standing far from God. And this very act of standing far off takes the form of a plea. For to the one who is merciful and willing to do good to all, it is a great occasion for pity to see someone who has no share in his goodness; for this reason he revealed himself, that he might heal those who were in such a wretched state. 

Although he healed all of nature that was infected with leprosy—having been incarnated and having died for all—nevertheless the Jews, although they had been cleansed by the Lord from the uncleanness of the leprosy of sin, were ungrateful. They did not return from the way of their vanity to give glory to him who had made them whole: that is, to believe in him, who, being God, endured the extreme suffering. For this is the glory of God: the flesh and the cross. <note>The "glory of God" is paradoxically found in Christ's humanity and his crucifixion.</note> These men, therefore, did not confess the incarnate and crucified Lord of glory. But the "foreigner"—the people of the nations—recognized the one who had cleansed him, and glorified him by believing that the Lord is so merciful and so powerful that he endured the most humble things for our sake (which is a mark of his mercy); and though he endured them, he received no harm from it (which is a mark of his power).

### CHAPTER 17. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
### COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
**267**
**Ll iij**

**[Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them and said, "The kingdom of God does not come with observation; nor will they say, 'Look here,' or 'Look there.' For behold, the kingdom of God is within you." And he said to his disciples, "The days will come when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, 'Look here,' or 'Look there.' Do not go, nor follow them. For as the lightning flashing from one part under heaven shines to another part under heaven, so will the Son of Man be in his day. But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this nation."]** <margin>D</margin>

In many places in his teaching, the Lord mentions the Kingdom of God. When the Pharisees heard this, they mocked <margin>E</margin> him; and for this reason, they approached him to ask when it would come—mocking him as if he were a madman preaching about something strange and unheard of. None of the teachers or prophets who lived in previous ages had mentioned it. Or perhaps, having in mind that they were soon to kill him, they approached him in mockery and said, as if with irony: "You indeed give speeches about a kingdom, but when will this kingdom of yours arrive? For tomorrow you are to be killed by us, and you will carry a cross and every kind of disgrace."

What then did CHRIST do? He did not answer these foolish people according to their foolish and senseless opinions. Instead, he left them to wander in the mere name of "kingdom" without revealing the reality to them. Indeed, they would not have <margin>F</margin> accepted it if he had explained that his kingdom was not a worldly one, but something far beyond the world. Leaving them, then, as those who were unworthy to hear—since they wanted him to speak about the timing of the kingdom, even though that timing is unknown and cannot be observed—he explained that it does not have a fixed time. Rather, the kingdom is always present to those who desire it.

<margin>The Kingdom of God, and when God is said to reign.</margin> For in every way, the Kingdom of God is to live in the manner of the angels. For God is truly said to reign when nothing worldly moves in our souls, but we live in an entirely different way than the world is accustomed to. We have this life within us—that is, whenever we choose it. For it does not require a long time, nor a long

<column-break/>

journey, but both faith and the divine life following faith are near to us. <margin>A</margin> Even the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in Romans 10:8.</note> said this very thing: **"The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart"**—that is, the word of faith. For to believe, and to walk according to faith as is worthy of one's calling, is within us. And so, the Pharisees mocked the Lord for preaching about the kingdom in this way. But he turned their mockery back on them, showing that they were ignorant of the thing that was within themselves, and which is very easy to grasp for those who wish to. "For now," he says, "since I am in your midst, you can certainly grasp the kingdom of God if you believe in me and wish to live according to my commandments."

But to his disciples he said: **"The days will come,"** etc. This means: "The kingdom of God is also present to you, insofar as I am with you." It is present to you not only because you have believed and <margin>B</margin> followed me, but because you now live in great security and without worry, as I take care of you. "But days will come when I am gone, and you will be handed over to dangers and dragged before kings and governors. Then you will long for that secure life, free from worry, which you lead while I am present—a life like the kingdom of God. And you will often long to have even one of my days—that is, one part of that secure life you lead with me."

Although at the time they were with him, they did not live a life entirely without labor and danger—for they were afflicted as fugitives with a fugitive, and heard insults along with him—yet, if what they bore then were compared <margin>C</margin> with what they were to bear later, that time would seem entirely secure and free from danger. And so the Kingdom of God was "within" the Apostles in this way too: as a kingdom involving very little labor or danger. For after the resurrection, they walked about like captives and those suffering persecution. Furthermore, with these words, he both prepares and strengthens the hearts of the apostles to bear labors, and he foretells things to them so they will not be deceived if people say, "Look here" or "Look there." "Let no one deceive you," he means to say, "by saying that it [the Kingdom] is coming here or there." For my second coming—which will be more glorious and bright—is not confined to a single place. Rather, just as lightning is not hidden but shines visibly from one end of the earth to the other, so also my coming will be brilliant.

<summary>Theophylact explains that the Kingdom of God is an internal, spiritual state of living "like angels" through faith, contrasting the Pharisees' mockery of Jesus with the future hardships the Apostles will face after his departure.</summary>

He also brings the example of Lot’s wife, who, when she turned back, froze into a **pillar of salt** <margin>C</margin> <note>original: "statuam salis"</note>; that is, she did not depart from malice, but remained in her own saltiness <note>Theophylact uses "saltiness" as a metaphor for being "seasoned" in wickedness or stubbornness.</note>, having become entirely evil: and making it famous, as if inscribing on a pillar the evil she suffered; for she remained obstinate in her malice. Certainly (as said above), he who is at the peak of virtue should not descend because of temporal things, being charmed by riches and possessions, and thereby yield to dangers: thus he now speaks of the progress on the path.

### CHAPTER 18. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>While many do not fear God, they yet respect men, and therefore they sin less; but when someone becomes shameless even before men, then the very peak of all malice is seen. Therefore, the Lord later added, "nor respected man," as if saying: He was a judge not fearing God—and what do I say, that he did not fear God? He possessed a greater evidence of malice, because he did not even respect man. Furthermore, this parable teaches us what we often say during our exhortations: that we should not grow weary of prayers. Indeed, as it says elsewhere: If any of you has a friend, and when he comes and knocks at night, he is admitted. <margin>Above, chapter 9.</margin> <note>Theophylact refers to Luke 11:5, though his margin notes "Supra 9," likely referencing a different chapter division or manuscript tradition.</note> For because of his persistence, if for no other reason, he will open the door.

<margin>E</margin>And again: "Which of you, from whom if his son asks for bread," etc. By these examples, diligent and perpetual prayer is prescribed. But some have attempted to explain this parable more curiously <note>original: "curiosius," meaning in a more intricate or allegorical manner</note>. For they say that every soul is a "widow," and that she has dismissed the husband she previously had, the devil; and because of him, she always has an adversary resisting her. She herself approaches God, the "judge of injustice"—that is, the one who condemns injustice—who "neither fears God." For God alone has no other whom He might fear. Nor does He "respect man," for God is no respecter of persons <margin>Galatians 2.</margin>. God takes pity on this widow, who prays with continuous petitions because of her adversary the devil, and He is appeased because of her persistence.

<margin>F</margin>Let him who wishes, and whom these things please, receive this interpretation. For these ideas are proposed so that they might not be unknown. Yet the Lord taught us these things for the reason that it is necessary to pray always; and He indicated by example that even if a judge were iniquitous and full of all malice, he would nevertheless take pity because of our continuous prayers. How much more will God, the leader of all justice, bring about justice quickly? Although He delays and seems not to hear those praying day and night. Therefore, He who taught and showed us that in the time of the end of the age there is need for prayer, so that we may be able to endure in future dangers, adds: "When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?" <margin>Matthew 23.</margin> By this figure of interrogation, He says that the faithful will be found to be rare. For the son of iniquity <note>A common title for the Antichrist</note> will prevail to such an extent that it might be possible that...

<margin>A</margin>...he might seduce even the elect. For He is accustomed to use this figure of interrogation regarding rare things, just as when He says: <margin>Above, chapter 12.</margin> "Who do you think is a faithful and prudent servant?" And in this place, signifying the same thing—that they will be few in number who will keep faith toward God and among themselves—He used this interrogation. Moreover, He rightly connected the discourse on faith to the discourse on prayer, since faith is the foundation and basis of all prayer. For unless a man believes that he is going to receive that which he asks for his own benefit, the prayer he makes is vain. And therefore the Lord, teaching about prayer, also mentions faith, declaring meanwhile that it would then belong to only a few to pray, since faith will be found in few.

<margin>B</margin>Therefore, when the Lord comes in a cloud, He will not find faith upon the earth, except in a few; but He will bring this about then. For against their will, all will confess: The Lord JESUS CHRIST is in the glory of God the Father—if indeed this is to be called faith, and not rather necessity. For there will be no one among the unfaithful who will not believe that He alone is the Savior, whom he previously blasphemed.

<margin>C</margin>But He also spoke this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and despised others: "Two men went up into the temple to pray: one a <term>Pharisee</term> <note>A member of a Jewish sect known for strict adherence to traditional and written law</note>, and the other a <term>publican</term> <note>original: "publicanus," a tax collector for the Roman state, often despised as a traitor or sinner</note>. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.' And the publican, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: 'God be merciful to me a sinner.' I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, more than the other. Because everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted." The Lord does not cease to oppose the vice of pride with many arguments. For it disturbs the human mind more than other vices; therefore, He teaches about this often and at length. Finally, He now cleanses a worse type of it. For there are many shoots of <term>philautia</term> <note>A Greek term for self-love or excessive conceit</note>: a high opinion of oneself, arrogance, and vain...

### CHAPTER 18. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>Pride</margin> Pride is simply the desire for glory, and from this it sprouts. <margin>How ruinous it is.</margin> Pride is more ruinous than all other vices; it is an abomination before God when someone attributes their good works to themselves rather than to God. What else is this but to deny God and to set oneself against Him? Against whom, then, does this vice hold dominion? It opposes a person just as an enemy opposes an enemy. The Lord promises to heal this with a parable. Because they trust in themselves and do not attribute everything to God, but instead look down on others, He speaks these things. He shows that righteousness, although otherwise <margin>Righteousness with pride makes a man weak.</margin> marvelous and bringing a man closest to God, can cast a man down to the lowest place and turn him into a demon when it has admitted pride <note>The Latin text reads "amiserit" (lost), but the context strongly suggests a typo in the original printing for "admiserit" (admitted/let in), as pride ruins righteousness rather than the loss of pride.</note>—for such a man has already made himself equal to God. Thus, the words of the Pharisee from the beginning are similar to the speech of a grateful man: "I give thanks to You," he says, "O God." But how full of arrogance is the rest! <margin>D</margin> For he did not say, "You made me abstain from injustice and robbery," but how did he say it? "I am not." He attributes the good work to himself and his own strength. Yet, how can judging others be the mark of a man who knows that what he has, he has from God? For if he had believed entirely that he possessed another's goods by grace, he would not have despised others, considering that he himself was equally "naked" as far as his own virtue was concerned. For he was clothed freely because of mercy. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, the proud Pharisee, as if ascribing to his own power the things that were mentioned, proceeded so far as to judge others. Moreover, the Lord shows both his pride and the lack of humility through his physical posture. <margin>F</margin> For it is the mark of a humble man to be lowered in his gaze, but this man is recognized as proud in his habit and gesture. Although it is also said of the tax collector that he "stood," see what follows: that he would not even lift his eyes to heaven, which is why his stance was bowed. But the Pharisee’s eyes were lifted to heaven, and his heart was lifted up at the same time. See also the order in the Pharisee's prayer and what it indicates to us: first, he said what he was *not*, and then he enumerated what he *was*. For he said, "I am not like many men." Then he added those things which were marks of virtue, such as fasting twice in the week and giving tithes of everything he possessed. For it is necessary not only

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> to turn away from evil, but also to do good. And first one must stop doing evil, and afterward approach virtue. Just as with a muddy spring: so that pure water may flow, the mud must first be cleared out before you draw the clean water. Consider also this: how he did not seize upon a small word to speak in the singular, but spat these things out in the plural against many, saying: "Because I am not like adulterers," and he added and said: "I fast twice in the *sabbato*" <note>original: "sabbato," which in this context means the week.</note>—that is, twice in the week. <margin>Sabbath. Shabbat. One of the Sabbaths.</margin> For the "Sabbath" is the week, which is named from the completion and the day of rest. For *Shabbat* <note>original: "Sabet," a Latinization of the Hebrew "Shabbat."</note> means "rest." Moreover, he called the week "Sabbaths" in the plural. From this, they also called the first day of the week "one of the Sabbaths," which among us is the Lord's Day. <margin>B</margin> For among the Hebrews, "one" and "first" signify the same thing. There is also another, deeper meaning. For against adultery, he boasted of fasting; for from luxury comes wantonness. Thus, by restraining his body through fasting, he was free from many such passions. The Pharisees used to fast on the second and fifth days of the week. Against robbery and injustice, he put forward the giving of tithes of all that he possessed. "I am so far," he says, "from robbery and injustice that I even spend what is mine." For the giving of tithes seems to some to be commanded simply and once in the Law; but to those who search more deeply, three distinct givings of tithes appear, which you will learn from Deuteronomy if you look closely. <margin>On the giving of tithes. Deuteronomy 12.</margin> And these were the things of the Pharisee. <margin>C</margin> But the tax collector <note>original: "publicanus," a Roman tax official often despised in the New Testament.</note> was different. For he stood far off from the Pharisee—distanced not only in place, but in his gestures, his speech, and the remorse of his heart. For he was afraid to lift his eyes to heaven, judging them unworthy to look upward since they had wanted to look upon earthly goods and enjoy them. And he struck his breast—meaning his heart—because of his bad thoughts and to wake up that which had fallen asleep. And he said nothing else but, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner." And because of all these things, he went down to his house justified rather than the other. For every heart that is proud is unclean before the Lord, and the Lord resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. It is truly wonderful...

<meta>This page continues the commentary by Theophylact of Bulgaria on Luke 18, specifically comparing the self-righteousness of the Pharisee with the defensive self-justification of the biblical figure Job, before moving into the passage where Jesus welcomes the little children and meets the rich young ruler.</meta>

### CHAPTER 18. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> One might ask how the Pharisee is condemned when he spoke only a few words, while Job is crowned with honor even though he spoke many magnificent things about himself. The reason is that the Pharisee, with no one forcing him, stands there babbling such trifles and condemning others for no practical purpose. Job, however, was pressured by his friends who weighed upon him more heavily than the calamity itself, claiming that he suffered because of his sins. He was compelled to enumerate his good works for the sake of God’s glory—specifically, so that men would not fall away from the right path of virtue. For if men had believed that it was Job's sins that caused his suffering, they might have avoided doing good works, or worse, they might have become <margin>E</margin> haters of guests, inhospitable, unmerciful, and unjust. For these were the works of Job. Therefore, lest many people be discouraged by his situation, he recounts his good deeds for their benefit. Job’s reasons were such that we need not even mention that in those words which sound like grandiosity, a perfect humility still shines through. For he says, "Who will grant me to be as I was in the months of old, <margin>Isaiah 43.</margin> when God preserved me?" <note>original: "Quis enim me dabit, inquit, iuxta menses dierum pristinorum quando deus me custodiebat." Reference to Job 29:2.</note> You see that he offers everything to God, and he does not condemn others, but is himself condemned by his friends. The Pharisee, referring everything to himself and not to God, and condemning others without necessity, is rightly assigned condemnation. For "everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled," by God's judgment; "but he who humbles himself" by condemning his own sins "shall be exalted" by God who justifies him. "State your case first," it says, "that <margin>F</margin> you may be justified." <note>original: "Dic igitur tu prior peccata tua, vt iustificeris." A paraphrase of Isaiah 43:26.</note>

<margin>Matthew 19. Mark 10.</margin> And they brought unto Him also infants, that He might touch them. But when His disciples saw it, they rebuked them. But **JESUS**, when He had called them to Him, said, "Suffer the little children to come unto Me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God. Amen I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child shall not <margin>The condition of a child is simple and harmless.</margin> enter therein." This example concerning the children also leads toward humility. For the Lord teaches through them that one must act with total humility and respect everyone. The disciples thought it was beneath such a teacher to have infants offered to Him. But He shows that

<margin>A</margin> humility is to be pursued to such an extent that even the smallest are not to be cast away. And thus He teaches humility by His own action. For He does not send the infants away, but sweetly embraces them. He also teaches through His word that the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who are disposed like children. A child is not puffed up, nor does he despise anyone; <margin>Who are children, and who are not. John 21.</margin> he is innocent, simple, not troublesome in prosperity, nor cast down in times of sorrow. Therefore, he who lives in all humility, simplicity, and innocence is acceptable to God. And he who receives the kingdom of God like a child does so without deceit or "curiosity," <term>curiositas: here meaning a skeptical or meddlesome desire to question divine mysteries rather than accepting them in faith.</term> but faithfully. For the "curious" man, <margin>B</margin> who is always questioning how he may be freed from unbelief, shall not enter the kingdom, because he refused to receive it simply, without meddling, and with humility. Thus all the Apostles, and in short all who believe in **CHRIST**, are called children. For the Lord Himself named the Apostles children, saying, "Children, have you any food?" <note>original: "Numquid opsonii habetis?" Refers to John 21:5, where Jesus addresses the disciples as "pueri" (children/boys).</note> But the wise of the Gentiles, seeking wisdom in a mystery (which is the kingdom of God) and refusing to accept it without rational proof, are deservedly excluded from this kingdom. He did not say, "of these is the kingdom," but "of such," meaning those who voluntarily possess the innocence and humility that children have by nature. Let us therefore receive all those ecclesiastical matters which belong to the kingdom <margin>C</margin> of God faithfully, without meddling, and humbly. For to inquire too curiously would be a mark of pride and vainglorious wisdom.

And a certain ruler asked Him, saying: "Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" And **JESUS** said unto him, "Why callest thou Me good? none is good, save one, that is, God. When **JESUS** heard this, He said unto him, "Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow Me." ### CHAPTER 18. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>A</margin> ...trapping Jesus in his speech. However, this is not likely; rather, he was greedy, for Christ rebuked him precisely because he was such a person. <margin>Mark 10</margin> Indeed, Mark also says that he ran up, knelt, and entreated Jesus, and that Jesus looked upon him and loved him. Therefore, that man was a lover of riches. He approaches Jesus desiring to learn about eternal life, though perhaps even in this he was a seeker of wealth. For nothing is so desirous of life as a man devoted to riches. He suspected, therefore, that Jesus would show him some way by which he could enjoy the possession of his riches forever. But after the Lord said that casting away riches contributes to eternal life—as if rebuking his own questioning and Christ’s response—he went away. Because he held many riches, he sought perpetual life greatly. But when it came to renouncing those riches, what need was there for that eternal life, as it seemed to him? For his life would have had to be spent as a pauper.

Furthermore, he approaches Christ as if to a simple man and a teacher. Therefore, the Lord, demonstrating that it is not right to approach him as a mere human, says: "None is good, except one God." <note>original: "Nullus bonus, nisi vnus Deus."</note> He says, "You called me good; why then did you add 'teacher'? For you seem to hold me as just one among many. If that is so, I am not 'good' in that sense. For no human is properly good, except God. But if you wish to call me good, and speak of me as the Good God, do not approach me as if to a simple man. For if you think me an ordinary human, do not call me good." For God is truly good, the fountain of goodness, and the principle of substantial goodness; we humans, however, even if we are good, are not so in our own right, but are participants in His goodness. We have a shared goodness and we are changeable. 

"You know the commandments: Do not commit adultery, do not kill," and so on. First, the law corrects those things into which we easily fall; then those things which not many people do, nor do they do them often. Adultery is listed because of the <margin>Anger is an evil beast.</margin> natural and internal fire of lust; murder, because anger is an evil beast. Stealing is a lighter matter, and people are more rarely led into false witness. Therefore, those former things are corrected first, because we fall into them easily, even though they are otherwise more serious.

<column-break/>

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
<page-num>273</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> These things—I mean theft and false witness—he places in the second spot as they occur more rarely and are lighter sins. Furthermore, to sin against parents, although it is a great sin, nevertheless happens more rarely. For one does not easily find a person of such bestial character that he would rage against his parents; for such people are few, and it rarely happens, and so he places it later. After the young man said he had kept all these things from his youth, the Lord prescribed <margin>Poverty is the head of virtues.</margin> poverty for him, which is the head of all virtues. 

Observe, then, a law worthy of the Christian life. "All things, whatever you have," He says. For if you leave anything behind, you remain its slave. "And distribute," not to rich relatives, but to the poor. The word "distribute" also carries a certain emphasis: that these goods should be dispersed with discernment, and not by chance. Because it is necessary for a Christian to have other virtues alongside poverty, He therefore says: "And come, follow me." This means: be my disciple in all other things as well, and follow me always—not just today and not tomorrow. 

<margin>B</margin> But although He promised heavenly treasure to the greedy man, that man did not pay attention, for he was a servant of money. Therefore, as soon as he heard this, he went away sad, because he had been told to give up the very possessions for which he desired eternal life—so that he might enjoy those riches forever. Moreover, his sadness proves that he was well-intentioned and yet malicious. <note>Theophylact is noting a complex psychological state: the man truly wanted the goal but hated the cost.</note> None of the Pharisees ever went away sad, but rather exasperated. 

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Praise of Chrysostom.</margin> I am not ignorant of the fact that the great light of the world, Chrysostom, thought that this young man truly desired eternal life and asked about it, but labored under the difficult disease of greed. Nonetheless, he does not lack grace in this matter—that he desired eternal life, even though he was greedy.

Seeing him affected by grief, Jesus said: "How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God. For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God." And those who heard it said: "Then who can be saved?" But He said: "The things that are impossible with men are possible with God." Then Peter said: "Behold, we have left..."

### CHAPTER 18. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...everything, and have followed you. And he said to them, "Truly I say to you, there is no one who has left home, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come, eternal life." <note>original: "Amen dico vobis..."</note> After the rich man heard that riches were to be cast aside, he was struck with sorrow. The Lord says, by a remarkable figure of speech, how difficult it is for those having money to enter into the kingdom of heaven. He did not say that it is impossible for them to enter, but difficult. For it is not impossible for such people to be saved: for it is possible to spend one's money and attain the things above. Yet this is indeed difficult. <margin>Money is stickier than birdlime</margin> <note>Birdlime (viscum) was a sticky adhesive used to trap birds; Theophylact uses it here as a metaphor for how wealth clings to the soul.</note> For money adheres more tenaciously than birdlime, and he who is gripped by such things is pulled away only with difficulty. But not long after, he adds how it is impossible: for he says it is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to be saved. For it is impossible for the eye of a needle to contain a whole camel—whether you understand "camel" as the animal, or as a thick nautical rope. <note>Theophylact references a common linguistic debate in the Greek text between *kamelos* (camel) and *kamilos* (nautical cable or rope).</note> If, therefore, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to be saved, and this is impossible, then it is even more impossible for a rich man to be saved.

What, then, should be said? First, indeed, that it is truly so: it is impossible for him who is "rich" to be saved. Do not tell me that some rich person was saved who gave away his belongings; for he was not saved as a "rich man," but because he became poor, or existing as a steward, he was saved, but not as a rich man. <margin>The rich man and the steward.</margin> For a steward <term>dispensator|A manager or administrator of property that belongs to another</term> is one thing, and a rich man is another. For the rich man is he who reserves riches for himself; but the steward is he to whom they are entrusted for the sake of others. And so here too, if he was saved, he was not saved as a rich man, but (as we said) because he renounced all that he had, or as a steward, he distributed them well. Furthermore, notice this: that it is impossible for a "rich man" to be saved, but for one "having money," it is difficult. It is as if he were saying: he who is possessed and held by money, and serves it, will not be saved; but he who "has" money—that is, he is the master of it, he possesses it and is not possessed by it—will be saved only with difficulty because of human weakness. For it is impossible not to misuse the things we have,

<meta>catchword: have,</meta>

<column-break/>

### AN EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
<page-num>274</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> especially since as long as we have money, the devil strives to trip us up, lest we use the rule of stewardship rightly; it is difficult to escape his snares. And for this reason, poverty is good, and, as it were, superior to temptation. Then those who heard this said, "Who then can be saved?" But he said, "The things that are impossible with men are possible with God." For those who have a human mind that sinks toward lower things and desires earthly things cannot be saved. But as it was said, "it is possible for God"—that is, when someone has God as a counselor, and receives the justifications of God and the mandates of the Master concerning poverty, and invokes His help. For this is possible. For it is ours to <margin>B</margin> will it, but it is God's to perfect it. And put another way: if we transcend that human weakness of the rich and are willing to "make for ourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness," <note>original: "mammona iniquitatis." A reference to Luke 16:9, suggesting the use of worldly wealth for charitable ends.</note> we shall be saved through them and be received into eternal dwellings. For it would indeed be better to leave all things. But if that is too much, at least make the poor your partners, and thus the impossible will become possible. It would indeed be impossible to be saved without leaving all things; nevertheless, it is possible through the mercy of God if we give portions to a fitting use. But here Peter asks: "Behold, we have left all." He asks this not for himself alone, but for the consolation of all the poor. This is so that not only the rich—who left much—might have good hope of attaining much, <margin>C</margin> while the poor might have little hope because they left little, and consequently would receive small rewards. "Everyone," he says, "who for God's sake has despised his resources, even if they are few." For you should not consider the amount, but the fact that these small things were the man's entire livelihood. Just as you expect to be impoverished by giving up many and great things, so he expects it by giving up few and small things. Do not say that he who has little is held by a greater affection for it; this is clear from fathers who, when they have only one child, feel a greater affection toward him than toward many. So also the poor man loves his one house and one field more intensely than you love your many. If not more, then certainly the affection is equal for both, and therefore the reward is the same.

<margin>A</margin> See how he not only made the tax collectors his disciples, but also received Zacchaeus, the chief of the tax collectors, as a captive for salvation. No one doubts that while a tax collector is an abominable thing, a chief <margin>Where tax collectors get their living.</margin> of tax collectors is much more so, being a leader in malice. For tax collectors have no other source for their living than from the tears of the poor. Yet even that chief of tax collectors is not despised; he only shows eagerness, and receives his reward. For he desired to see JESUS. And when he had climbed into the wild fig tree, before he could see, he was first seen by Jesus himself. Thus, in all places, the Lord anticipates us, provided he sees us eager and ready. <margin>B</margin> As soon as JESUS saw him, he hurried him to come down, because he intended to stay in his house. And he was not sluggish. Whence we also ought to be prepared whenever Christ commands anything. So he both descended and received him joyfully, even if many might grumble. Let us see, however, how much benefit he received from the entry of Christ. "Half of my goods," he says, "I give to the poor." Do you see his eagerness? He did not begin to sow sparingly, nor did he give just a few things, but his whole life; and even those things which he possessed justly, he gave so that he might have something to give to those whom he had treated with injustice. For he teaches us that there is no gain if one has money from injustice and shows mercy to others while neglecting <margin>C</margin> those he has wronged. And see how he conducts himself in this. He returns fourfold if he defrauded anyone, so that the loss of the person who was wronged might be repaired. For this is true almsgiving: that not only the simple loss is returned, but even with an increase, according to the law. For the law <margin>Exodus 22</margin> commanded a thief to restore fourfold. However, if we consider it diligently, no money at all was left to him. For he gave half of his goods to the poor. Only half was left, and from these remains, he gave fourfold to those who were wronged by him; and thus, if the life of a chief of tax collectors was built on injustice, and he himself returned fourfold everything he had unjustly taken, consider how he must have been entirely stripped. And from this it is found how much more sublimely...

<header>CHAPTER 19. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA</header>

<margin>D</margin>...had learned what the Law commanded, but now he is instructed by the Gospel; because he loved his neighbor more than himself, promising such things—indeed, doing them. For he did not say, "I will give half," and "I will restore fourfold," but rather, "Behold, I give," and "I restore." For he had heard the admonition of Solomon: <margin>Proverbs 3</margin> "Do not say: Go, and come back, and tomorrow I will give." <note>original: "Ne dicas, rediens redi, & cras dabo"</note> Christ proclaims salvation to him. For He says, "Today you give, and today salvation is yours." By saying "to this house," He signifies Zacchaeus himself, who received salvation. For Zacchaeus is represented by the "house." Indeed, He was not calling an inanimate house a "daughter of Abraham"; but it is manifest that He names the living master of the house a "son of Abraham." Perhaps <margin>E</margin> it is because he had believed and was justified by faith; perhaps also because he was large-hearted in the distribution of riches and a lover of the poor, just as that patriarch <note>Abraham, known for his hospitality</note> was. See, moreover, that He now calls Zacchaeus a son of Abraham when he shows a likeness of character in himself. For He did not say that he *had been* a son of Abraham, but that he *now is*. For previously, when he was a chief of tax collectors and an extortioner, and had nothing in common with Abraham in righteousness, he was not a son. Since some were grumbling that He had stayed with a sinful man, He said, to silence them: "For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost." And this indeed is according to the history. However, it is easy <margin>Moral exposition of the history.</margin> to explain these things otherwise for moral benefit. For every leader of many in malice is "small" in <margin>F</margin> spiritual stature; for the flesh and the spirit are contrary to each other, and for that reason, he cannot see Jesus because of the crowd. For he who is troubled by secular business and affections does not see Jesus working, moving, and walking. For such a person experiences no operation worthy of a Christian. For this is what it means for "JESUS to walk"—that is, for Christ to work something in <margin>Psalm 82</margin> us. But such a man, who has never seen Jesus walking nor felt any operation suitable to Christ, often comes to his conscience through repentance and climbs into a "wild fig tree" <note>original: "caprificum"; the sycamore or wild fig</note>, making foolish and <term>mortifying; killing off or subduing</term> every pleasure and sweetness that is suggested by the fig tree.

<header>COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE</header>
<page-num>277</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> And thus, having become higher than himself and placing "ascents in his heart," <note>A reference to Psalm 84:5</note> he is seen by Jesus. And look: the Lord says to him, "Hurry, come down." That is, you who are ascending through repentance into a more sublime life, come down through humility. Let not a proud sense trip you up; hurry, be humbled. "For if you are humbled, I must stay in your house." For He says, "It is necessary that I remain in the house of the humble." For upon whom shall I look, except the mild and the quiet? <margin>Isaiah 33</margin> Indeed, he who is such a person gives half of his goods to the poor. Our <margin>Our goods are twofold.</margin> goods are twofold: I mean of the body and of the soul. The righteous man grants all corporal things to the truly poor, and to the demons who are destitute of every good. <note>Theophylact is using an allegory here: material goods go to the needy, while the "goods of the soul" are kept away from the "impoverished" demons.</note> But he does not <margin>B</margin> dispense the goods of the soul; this is what we have heard the Lord saying concerning Job: <margin>Job 2</margin> "But do not touch his soul." But if he has defrauded anyone, he restores it fourfold. It is therefore suggested by this that everyone who walks the path of repentance—the path contrary to his former malice—heals all his previous sins through the four virtues; <note>The four cardinal virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note> and thus he receives salvation and is named a son of Abraham, because he himself has gone out from his land and from the kinship of his former malice, and from the house of his father—that is, becoming outside of himself and denying himself. For that "house of his father" was the devil's. Therefore, having been made "outside of himself" and alienated from sin, he attains salvation just like Abraham.
<margin>C</margin> While they were hearing these things, He added a parable, <margin>Matthew 25</margin> because He was near Jerusalem, and because they thought the Kingdom of God was about to appear immediately. He said therefore: "A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and return. And having called ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas <term>minas; a 'mna' was a unit of currency worth about 100 drachmas or several months' wages</term> and said to them: 'Trade until I come.' But his citizens hated him, and sent a delegation after him, saying: 'We do not want this man to reign over us.'"

It seems to me that those men, hearing of the Kingdom of God, suspected it to be a temporal one given by God for the freedom of the Hebrew race; for that reason, they suspected that Jesus, in going up to Jerusalem, was about to take up this kingdom. But the Lord shows them that their folly...

Meanwhile, he also declares this: that as God He knows their thoughts; for this reason He tells this parable and introduces Himself as a "noble man." For although He became man, He nevertheless remained in the height and nobility of the Godhead. But when the mystery of the dispensation <note>The "dispensation" refers to God’s plan for salvation through the life and death of Jesus.</note> in the flesh was completed, He departed to a far country—I mean heaven—so that He might receive a kingdom for Himself; that is, so that as a man He might sit at the right hand of the throne of majesty in His flesh. For in this way God was always of one substance with the Father, but as a man He sat there only when He was taken up, remaining there until His enemies are placed under His feet.

Furthermore, the Lord gave ten minas <note>A "mina" was a Greek unit of currency, roughly equivalent to 100 drachmas; in English Bibles, this is often called the "Parable of the Ten Pounds."</note> to the servants. Those servants are the ones to whom the ministry in the Church has been entrusted; and they are said to be ten because of the perfection of ecclesiastical leadership. For order in the Church possesses a perfect arrangement of those presiding, and there ought to be neither more nor fewer. For example, we see these three things in the Church: purgation, illumination, and perfection. For the three orders have been allotted those three operations. <term>Deacons</term> purge through instruction and teaching; <term>priests</term> <note>original: "presbyteri"</note> illuminate through baptism; <term>bishops and priests</term> <note>original: "episcopi & sacerdotes"</note> establish and perfect the orders—that is, they ordain. You see the orders with their operations, and that there are neither more nor fewer ranks of leaders. He distributed ten minas to them, that is, the gifts given to each person

And it happened that he returned after receiving the kingdom, and he sent to call those servants to whom he had given the money, so that he might know how much each had traded. And the second came, saying: "Lord, your mina has produced five minas." And to this one he said: "You too shall be prefect over five cities." <margin>B</margin> And another came, saying: "Lord, behold your mina, which I have kept laid away in a cloth <note>original: "sudario," literally a face-cloth or napkin.</note>; for I feared you, because you are an austere man: you take up what you did not lay down, and you reap what you did not sow." He said to him: "By your own mouth I will judge you, you wicked servant. You knew that I was an austere man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow; why then did you not put my money in the bank <note>original: "ad mensam," literally "at the table" of the money-changers.</note>, so that when I came, I might have collected it with interest?" And he said to those standing by: "Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has ten minas." And they said to him: "Lord, he has ten minas." For I tell you, that to everyone who has, more will be given; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Since <margin>C</margin> those enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slay them before me.

And having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. Since Christ, that noble man, was to return according to His human nature (for the Lord descended from a royal lineage) and according to His divine nature—this refers to His second coming, when the King will appear with the angels, coming in the glory of the Father, and every knee shall then bow to Him. At that time, He will surely call to account those who received gifts; and they will find that one has indeed profited many and increased the gift tenfold, while another has also profited, but fewer; and another has profited no one, but has lazily passed the time of trading. Therefore, he who increased what he received tenfold is set over ten cities...

...he is protected, that is, he receives manifold rewards; and <margin>D</margin> another in turn receives in proportion to his own work. However, the one who gained nothing is condemned. Let us see also what he says: "Lord, behold your mina <note>A mina was a Greek unit of currency, equivalent to about 100 drachmas or 100 days of wages for a common laborer.</note>, take it; for I had it hidden away in a napkin <note>original: "sudario" — a cloth for wiping sweat, also used as a burial shroud.</note>." The Lord was wrapped in a shroud when He died, and Lazarus’s face was covered with a shroud in the tomb; appropriately, therefore, that lazy man says the gift was hidden in a shroud. For he had made that gift dead and ineffective, not unfolding it <note>The Latin "non evoluens" suggests both failing to unroll the cloth and failing to develop the gift.</note>, nor making a profit. "For I feared you, because you take what you did not lay down." Many people use such pretexts. For, being unwilling to be of use to anyone, they say: "Where God has not sown a good disposition or fitness, let Him not seek a harvest from there." <margin>B</margin> "He did not make me industrious or suited for learning, so why is it required of me that I produce fruit from it?" For this reason, the Lord says: "You, teach, and deposit your money with the money-changers," that is, with all people who are positioned to receive benefit. For every person is ordained as a money-changer by God, so that he may do business in the great workshop of this world. "And I, upon coming, would have demanded it," that is, I would have reclaimed it with interest. Therefore, it is necessary for us to do what is ours to do; the Lord judges the others if they did not wish to receive benefit from it. Therefore, the gift is taken away and given to the good businessman. For although he already has much, for that very reason he ought to receive more. For "to the one who has, it shall be given," that is, to the one who has gained much from the business of doing good, to him even more will be given. For if he made small things grow tenfold, he will be clearly seen by the Lord. <margin>F</margin> But from the negligent and lazy man, who has no zeal to grow or increase what he had received, even that which he has will be taken away, so that the Lord's property—which could be given to another and multiplied—does not sit empty in vain. We explain these things not only regarding speech and teaching, but also regarding moral virtues. For in these also God has given us gifts, <margin>A beautiful exhortation of Theophylact.</margin> such as the gift of fasting to one, the gift of almsgiving to another, the gift of gentleness to another, and the gift of humility to yet another. <margin>D</margin> [Regarding the] prophecy, saying: "Behold, your king comes, sitting upon a donkey." Secondly, he suggests to us figuratively that he was to sit upon a new, untamed, and unclean Gentile people. For at no other time did he ask for a beast of burden to be given to him for a journey. He who had traveled through all of Galilee on foot—how is it that in passing from Bethany to Jerusalem he would ask for a colt to be given to him, when the distance is not so great, as everyone knows? Consequently, as I was saying, these things are mystical. Moreover, the colt was tied and had many masters, but it was untied by <margin>Bethany. Bethphage.</margin> those who were sent. This is the meaning: Bethany <note>original: "Bethania"</note> is interpreted as "the house of obedience." <margin>E</margin> Bethphage <note>original: "Bethphage"</note> indeed means "the house of jaws"; it was certainly a village of priests. For the jaws [of sacrificial animals] were given to the priests, just as it is written in the Law <note>According to Deuteronomy 18:3, the shoulder, jaws, and stomach of a sacrifice were the priests' portion.</note>. Furthermore, the word of doctrine is indicated by the "jaws," which animal jaws produce and grind down <note>Theophylact uses the metaphor of jaws chewing food to represent teachers "breaking down" difficult doctrines for their students.</note>. Therefore, where there is a house of the word, of doctrine, and of obedience toward him, there the Lord's disciples are sent, and they untie the people bound by the chains of sins and by many cares of life; and because they have many masters and gods, they cause them to have one Lord, Jesus Christ, and one God the Father. But where there is no house of obedience, or acceptance of the word of doctrine, there this does not happen, nor is the donkey untied. As for the two being sent, this means that in the leading of the Gentile people to Christ so they may obey him, two orders minister: the prophets and the Apostles. And they lead it from the village <margin>F</margin> so that we may learn that the people were very coarse and unlearned. For the word—whether Mosaic or prophetic—had not yet sat upon them, but they were an untamed colt. Although another Evangelist said it was the children who were shouting: "Hosanna <note>A Hebrew expression of praise meaning "Save us, we pray."</note> to the Son of David," nevertheless they too <margin>Psalm 102</margin> were suggesting a new people. <margin>D</margin> [He thirsted for their salvation] not only before the cross, but even after the cross; it is clear that he thirsted for their conversion from the fact that they were only handed over to the Romans thirty-five years later <note>The Siege of Jerusalem occurred in 70 AD. Theophylact follows a tradition that dates this roughly 35 years after the Crucifixion.</note>. For he delayed their punishment for no other reason than his desire for them to be converted. This is the meaning of: "If you had known the things that now benefit you," which bring peace and rest—namely, faith in me and an end to persecuting me. "But now they are hidden from your eyes," because on account of me, whom you reject, innumerable evils will seize you, and you will suffer this and that because you did not know "the time of your visitation"—that is, of my advent, when I came to visit and save you. Therefore, it was necessary for you to know the things that lead to your peace, so that you might believe in me, and you would certainly have had peace from the Romans and liberation from all malice. For <margin>B</margin> all who believed in Christ were safe from captivity; and so, if everyone had believed, no one would have been captured.

<header>CHAPTER 20. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA</header>

He vindicates the honor of the temple. Moreover, he also shows this: that one should no longer believe God is appeased by animal sacrifices. Therefore, although it was ready at hand what the Lord might answer them (as was said), and he might say that the prophets—or rather, God—commanded these things. Yet, to show them that they are always disobedient to the Holy Spirit, he does not point out that they refused to believe Isaiah, the ancient prophet (of whom they perhaps had no memory), but he shows that they refused to believe even John [the Baptist], an evangelical and by no means carnal man, who had appeared recently. And for this reason, he asks this question worthy of admiration, by which he also confutes them. He shows us as well that if they did not believe such a prophet as John, who was considered greater than himself, when he bore witness of him <note>John the Baptist bore witness to Jesus as the Lamb of God</note>, how would they believe him when he answered by what authority he does these things? It is as if he had said: You want it to be entirely permitted for you to reject and slander my words, just as you rejected the words of John (who was greater in your eyes).

<margin>Isaiah 5; Jeremiah 2</margin>
And he began to tell the people this parable: "A certain man planted a vineyard, and leased it to tenant farmers, and he himself went abroad for a long time. And when it was the right time, he sent a servant to the tenants, so they might give him some of the fruit of the vineyard; but they beat him and sent him away empty-handed. And again he sent yet another servant. They beat this one too, and after treating him with insults, sent him away empty-handed. Again he sent a third. But they, having inflicted wounds, threw him out too. Then the lord of the vineyard said: 'What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps when they see him, they will respect him.' When the tenants saw him, they thought among themselves: 'This is the heir; come, let us kill him, so that the inheritance becomes ours.' And having thrown him outside the vineyard, they killed him. What then will the lord of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants, and give the vineyard to others." This parable is brief indeed, but it teaches us many great things: the immense care God showed toward the Hebrews (who from the beginning were murderers), that there is one God of the Old and New Law, the calling— <note>original: "Vo-"</note>
