<margin>A</margin>
—of the Gentiles, and the casting out of the Jews. This vineyard, then, was the synagogue of the Jews; the cultivators were the scribes and Pharisees who were in charge of the people. Everyone is also a vineyard, and the same person is the farmer; for each of us cultivates himself. Therefore, when the merciful Farmer <note>meaning God</note> had leased this vineyard to the husbandmen, he went abroad; that is, he allowed them to walk according to their own free will. He sent various servants—I mean the prophets—so that he might have even a small profit. For he wished to receive some of the fruit, not all the fruit. For what profit could God gain from us, except the knowledge of himself? Yet that is also our profit, which makes what is ours his.

<margin>B</margin>
But the evil farmers treated those who were sent with insults, and sent them away empty and beaten; that is, they fell into such great ingratitude that they not only turned away from good and gave no fruit, but they even did evil—which is worthy of greater punishment. Therefore, when the prophets had endured such heavy things, the son is sent. "Perhaps they will respect him." He said "perhaps" not as if he were ignorant of the future (knowing they would treat him worse than the prophets), but he says what *ought* to have happened: for they should have respected him. But they so far failed to respect him that they even killed him, which is to their greater accusation. Because after God affirmed that this was good—that respect should perhaps be shown to the son—they reached a plainly opposite decision. This stylistic feature is often found in the Scriptures, as when it is said: "If perhaps they...

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah 26; Ezekiel 2, 3, 12. Scriptural style regarding "if perhaps" and similar phrases.</margin>
...hear." For he does not speak this way because he is ignorant of the future, but so that no one might say that God's foreknowledge is a necessary cause for their disobedience; and for that reason, he uses such a figure of speech. "And having thrown him outside the vineyard, they killed him." "Outside the vineyard" is usually explained as "outside Jerusalem," for Christ suffered outside the city. But since we previously interpreted the vineyard as the *people*, not Jerusalem, what if we say more accurately that the people killed him, but "outside the vineyard" means he was not the author of death by his own hand? Rather, he was handed over to Pilate and the Gentiles. And thus "outside the vineyard"—that is, outside the hands of the people—Christ suffered. For it was not lawful for them to kill...

And the chief priests and scribes sought to lay hands on him in that same hour, yet they feared the people; for they knew that he had spoken this parable against them. Luke indeed (as you hear) says the Lord said that the master of the vineyard would destroy the ungrateful tenants and give the vineyard to others. When the Pharisees heard this, they said, "God forbid!" Matthew, however, tells it differently: namely, that the Lord asked them, "What will the owner of the vineyard do to those farmers?" and the Jews responded and said, "He will bring those wretches to a wretched end and lease the vineyard to other farmers." Are they then contradictory? It is likely that both occurred: that according to Matthew, they themselves passed the sentence, and then they realized where the parable was leading and that it was spoken about them—and then they said what Luke records, namely, "God forbid!" What then does Christ say? He brings forward another testimony from David,

<margin>A</margin>calling himself the "stone," and their teachers the "builders." Just as Ezekiel says: "Those building a wall and smearing it without temper" <note>original: "absque temperatura"—meaning mortar or plaster mixed incorrectly so it does not hold</note>, that is, those who speak only to find favor; they rebuke the sins of the people only on the surface, smearing the sins of the people as if they were a wall. But how did they "reject" that stone? Because they were saying, "He is not from God." Now, he speaks here of
<margin>Two destructions of the Jews.</margin>
two destructions: One of their souls, into which they fell by being scandalized <note>In the biblical sense, "scandalized" means tripped up or led into sin</note>. For everyone who falls upon the stone shall be broken. The other is the destruction of captivity, which that despised stone brought upon them. For on whomever it falls, it will cause him to fly apart. Thus the Jews were broken apart and scattered like
<margin>B</margin>chaff from a single threshing floor into the whole world. Observe, however, that they first fell upon the stone—that is, they were scandalized—and then the stone fell upon them and took vengeance on them. For my sin comes first, and then the just vengeance of God follows. Indeed, the Jews rejected this stone. But that stone was beautiful and chosen, so much so that it was placed as the head of the corner, and it joined the walls together, uniting the Old and New Testaments.
<margin>Isaiah 8</margin>

<margin>C</margin>entered into a conspiracy against him; and had it not been for the fear of the people, they would have laid hands on him. They indeed despised the law which says, "You shall not
<margin>Exodus 23</margin>
kill the innocent and the righteous." But they were afraid, and were restrained by the fear of men from attacking him openly, so they plotted against him secretly.

...does it have an image and inscription? They answered and said, "Caesar's." And he said to them, "Render therefore the things that are Caesar's to Caesar, and the things that are God's to God." And they were not able to rebuke his word before the people; wondering at his answers, they were silent.] The Pharisees prepared a snare which, as it seemed to them, the Lord could hardly escape: but their own foot was caught in it. For see their malice. For if he had said that tribute should be given to Caesar, they would have accused him before the people as one who sought to reduce the nation to slavery—a nation which is the seed of Abraham and subject to no slavery. But if he had forbidden them to give it, they would have dragged him to Caesar as a seditious man. But he escaped their snares like a gazelle, for
<margin>Song of Songs 2</margin>
the Bride <note>The "Bride" here refers to the Church or the soul in the Song of Songs, which calls the Beloved a gazelle or a young stag</note> called him such in the Song of Songs. And he teaches
<margin>Romans 13</margin>
that we should be subject in bodily matters to the one who has power over our bodies, whether that king be a ruler or a tyrant; for this does not hinder us from spiritually pleasing the God of spirits. "Render therefore," he says, "the things that are Caesar's to Caesar, and the things that are God's to God." And notice that he did not say "give" but "render." It is therefore a debt, he says: therefore, pay the debt. Your prince guards you from enemies and makes your life peaceful; you therefore owe him tribute for these things. And in another sense: you have the very coin you hold from him. Therefore, when you return the coin to the king, you in the meantime gain for yourself that through it the necessities of life are provided. Just as, finally, the things that are God's must be rendered to God: he gave you a mind, return it to him by acting according to that mind; he gave you reason, return it to him so that you do not become like the senseless beasts, but do all things as a rational being. And in short, he gave you soul and body; return all things to him and restore his <term>image</term> <note>The "imago Dei" or image of God, which Theophylact argues must be polished and returned to the Creator through virtue</note> to him by walking through faith, hope, and charity. Truly, in another way, the things of Caesar must be rendered to Caesar. For each of us carries either the image of God or the image of the prince of this world. When we have made ourselves like Caesar—having become children of the devil and carrying his image—it is necessary to return that image to him and cast it away, so that he may have what is his and find nothing in us that is properly his own. <margin>D</margin> ...the bodily resurrection. For this reason, because they intended to reject the dogma <note>In this context, "dogma" refers to a fundamental religious teaching or doctrine.</note> of the resurrection, they invented this foolish story <note>The Sadducees had proposed a hypothetical scenario about a woman married to seven brothers in succession, asking whose wife she would be in the afterlife.</note>. Whereupon the Lord immediately shook their foundation and showed that life then will not be physical. As a result, their opinion was immediately dulled, and their weak foundation collapsed. "For you err," He said, "not knowing the scriptures," but rather overturning their meaning. For the children of this world beget and are begotten, they marry and are given in marriage—that is, they take wives. But the children of that world do none of these things, for it is no longer possible for them to die. Consequently, the things that happen in marriage do not happen there; rather, it is an angelic and divine life. For here, because there is death, there is also marriage; and because there is marriage, there is death. But there, with death abolished, what use is there for marriage? <margin>E</margin> <margin>Marriage is an aid to mortal life.</margin> For marriage is an aid to mortal life and a fulfillment of that which is lacking; but there, nothing is lacking, so what need is there for a fulfiller? Thus they are equal to the angels and are children of God. Why? Because they are children of the resurrection. As for what He says, it carries this meaning: He called them children of God because nothing physical is seen in their generation <note>The word "generation" here refers to the way they are brought into being or "born" into the new life of the resurrection.</note>, but all things are divine. For in the resurrection, there is no preceding sexual intercourse, nor seed, nor womb, nor pregnancy; rather, it is God who generates our bodies in ways that He Himself knows. And therefore, because it is God who is at work in the resurrection, those who are born from the resurrection are rightly called children of God. Furthermore, He adds to these reasons the testimony of Scripture. For Moses, He says, told how God spoke to him from the bush, saying: *I am the God of Abraham*, etc. <margin>F</margin> Now, if the patriarchs <note>The patriarchs are the ancient fathers of Israel: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> had utterly vanished and were not living with God in the hope of resurrection, God certainly would not have said, "I am," but "I was." For concerning things that are lost and decayed, we are accustomed to say, "I was the master of this or that thing." But now, because He said, "I am," He shows that He is the God and Lord of the living, and not of those who are entirely decayed—even if they are dead, they live in the hope of rising again. Just as Adam, although he was living, was nevertheless dead; for from the very hour in which he ate, he was said to be dying. Once the Sadducees were silenced, the Pharisees and Scribes approved of Jesus's saying, being their adversaries and rejoicing that they were defeated,

<margin>A</margin> And He said to them, "How do they say that Christ is the son of David? For David himself says in the book of Psalms, <margin>Psalm 109 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 110.</note></margin> *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.* <margin>Matthew 23</margin> David therefore calls Him Lord, so how is He his son?" <margin>Mark 12</margin> Then, while all the people were listening, He said to His disciples, "Beware of the scribes, who want to walk in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces, and the first seats in the synagogues, and the chief places at banquets; who devour the houses of widows, feigning long prayers; these shall receive a greater condemnation."] Being about to approach His Passion <note>The "Passion" refers to the suffering and death of Jesus.</note> very soon, He proclaims His own divinity; and this He does not quite openly, nor boastfully, but modestly. <margin>B</margin> For He questions them and leaves them perplexed, allowing them to reason out the logical conclusion. For if David, He says, calls Him "Lord," how is He merely his son? For He was indeed the son of David according to the flesh, but He was also his God. But they thought Him to be only the son of David, so He overturned their opinion, because they believed Him to be David's son alone. Likewise, He declares that He is not an adversary to God the Father, but has great harmony with Him, since the Father humbles His enemies. And He said these things to the scribes. But because He sent the disciples as the teachers of the world, He rightly warns them not to imitate the arrogance and ambitious mind of the Pharisees; and simply, not to think about how they might please men. <margin>probitas <note>original: "probitas erga simplices" — honesty or uprightness toward the simple/common people.</note></margin> <margin>C</margin> For to strive for greetings in the marketplace is the mark of those who run after flatterers and those who hunt for glory through bad character, or those who take this opportunity to gather riches; indeed, these even devour the houses of widows, being devoted to their bellies and consuming more than is necessary, and their pretext is a seemingly pious one. For they use prayers and the welfare of souls as a cover; they do not teach fasting, but rather drunkenness and gluttony <note>original: "gastrimargiam" — a term for excessive greed of the belly.</note>, and for this reason they will receive a more extensive condemnation: because they not only do evil, but make prayer a pretext; they turn pious honesty and virtue into a cover for sin. It was certainly right to have mercy on widows, but they, entering their houses as if to bless them through long prayers, in the meantime... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing on the next page regarding the exploitation of widows.</note>

He also interprets Jesus's question regarding David's Lord as a modest revelation of His divinity, contrasted with the greed and hypocrisy of the Scribes.</summary>

**R**especting them, he saw the rich people putting their gifts into the treasury. He also saw a certain poor widow putting in two small copper coins. And he said, "Truly I say to you, that this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For all these have put into the
<margin>*Gaza*, which means</margin> offerings of God out of what was abundant for them, but she, out of her poverty, has put in all the livelihood she had." ] They call the treasury the *Gaza* <note>original: "Gazam"; a word of Persian origin meaning a treasure or storehouse</note>. It was a sacred treasury where the pious contributed,
<margin>Priests as merchants.</margin> which they used for the preparation and necessities of sacrifice, and for the ornament of the temple and the nourishment of the poor; although later the priests made a business out of this, distributing the treasury not toward those things for which it had been contributed. Therefore, the Lord praises the widow above all others, because she had given her livelihood out of her poverty. For these two mites <note>small coins of very little value</note>, even if they seemed small, nevertheless were her entire living gathered from begging. For the widow was poor. For the Lord does not return a reward by looking at what is given, but at what remains behind <note>meaning, He measures the sacrifice by what the giver kept for themselves</note>. Therefore,
<margin>E</margin> the rich leave more behind in their houses and offer small and few things; thus, she is rightly more worthy of praise than they. Some have understood that every soul can be represented by the widow; she who has left her former husband—that is, the Old Law—and is not yet joined to the Word of God, now offers an earnest <note>a pledge or down payment</note> worthy of the Word: a thin and small faith, and according to her own measure, possessing pure knowledge, appearing blameless in life and doctrine. For there is a need for works along with faith and a good conscience; if anyone approaches God in this way, they are seen to put in more than all those "rich" in eloquence and those abundant in the virtues of the Gentiles.

Hence, while some were praising the structures of the temple and the things offered to it—I believe he speaks of the sculpted and adorned things, such as the Cherubim and similar items. For perhaps he calls these <gloss>offerings</gloss> <note>original: <gloss>ἀναθήματα</gloss> (anathēmata); objects dedicated to God and displayed in the temple</note>, that is, gifts. The Lord, however, wonders at none of these things, but even predicts their destruction. There will be wars and seditions, for when all charity is taken away, wars and seditions rightly take place. After wars, indeed, come famines and pestilences; pestilence from the air corrupted by the slain, and famine from uncultivated fields.
Some have understood that pestilence and famine would happen not only at the end of the age, but also in the times of the captivity.

<header>CHAPTER 21. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE, COMMENTARY 287</header>

These following things (I speak of the riots, wars, and famine, and the rest) can be understood both as concerning the captivity of Jerusalem and the end of the age <note>original: "consummatione seculi"; refers to the final end of the world</note>.
   "But before all these things, they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you to synagogues and prisons, dragging you before kings and governors for my name's sake; but it will happen to you for a testimony. Therefore, keep it fixed in your hearts not to rehearse your defense beforehand. For I myself will give you a mouth and wisdom <note>This refers to the gift of eloquence and divine insight</note>, which all who oppose you will not be able to contradict or resist. You will be handed over even by parents, and brothers, and relatives, and friends, and they will put some of you to death. And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake, but a hair of your head shall not perish. In your patience, possess your souls."
   "Before all these things"—that is, those things which will happen before the end, or even the captivity. For (as I said) he joins words about the end with words about the captivity. For he says, "They will lay hands on you," my disciples. And before Jerusalem was captured, the apostles suffered persecution from the inhabitants of Jerusalem, God arranging it so that while soldiers were shaking the world and heavily afflicting the Jews, the apostles in the meantime would fill the whole world with their preaching. Therefore, the apostles were led to kings and governors, just as Paul was to Festus, to Agrippa, and to Caesar <margin>Acts 25, 26, 27</margin>, and this happened to them for the glory of testimony. Because they were private and unlearned men, he says, "Let there be no care for this matter," lest they be disturbed when having to give an account before wise men. For you will receive from me eloquence and wisdom, so that even if all your adversaries stood against you as one, they would not be able to resist you—neither by wisdom (that is, the power of logic) nor by eloquence and the certainty of the tongue. For often someone has wisdom in their reason and mind, but he who is not easily disturbed in adversity confuses everything when he must speak to the people. But the apostles, I say, obtained grace in both <margin>Acts 4, Acts 26</margin>. For this reason the priests were astonished at Peter and John because of their immense wisdom, while they grasped 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> them—a wisdom which they previously lacked. Indeed, Festus says to Paul, "Paul, you are mad; much learning is driving you to madness." And when he had shaken off their fear, which they had from a lack of skill, he adds another thing necessary and powerful for shaking souls: "You will be handed over by friends and relatives." He cuts short any surprise regarding this, so that they are not disturbed when it happens suddenly. For this cruelly tortures the soul, just as David says, "For if my enemy had cursed me, I would certainly have borne it; but you, a man of one mind with me," etc. <margin>Psalms 54, 40</margin>. And again, "He who ate my bread with me has lifted up his heel against me." When he had said that some of them were to be hated and killed, he adds the greatest consolation: "A hair of your head shall not perish" <margin>B</margin>. For he says, "You will be saved, and not even the smallest part of you will be destroyed, even if it seems to many to be destroyed; you only need to endure." For through patience you will possess your soul. For the enemy attacks like a foe intending to lead your souls into captivity, and tries to snatch them away through afflictions; but you, give patience in exchange for money <note>Theophylact uses a metaphor of a commercial transaction: paying with endurance to "buy back" or "possess" one's own soul</note>, and you will possess your soul by this compensation, and there will be no loss to you. Notice what he says: "They will kill some of you." You will understand this as a nuanced point, because they will not kill you entirely. Since you consist of two parts—soul and body—they will not put both to death, but will kill one part of you. But you will possess your souls through patience, which is also said elsewhere: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill your soul" <margin>C</margin> <margin>Matthew 10, 24; Mark 13</margin>.
   "But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and those in her midst depart, and those in the countryside not enter her, for these are the days of vengeance, so that all things which are written may be fulfilled <margin>Isaiah 3, 12</margin>. But woe to those who are pregnant and those who nurse in those days. For there will be great distress upon the earth and in this people, and they will fall by the edge of the sword, and be led captive into all nations, and Jerusalem will be trodden down by the nations until the times [of the nations are fulfilled]..."

<summary>Theophylact provides a commentary on Jesus' prophecy of persecution and the fall of Jerusalem, explaining that while the body may be killed, the soul is preserved through divine wisdom and patient endurance. He reconciles the warning of death with the promise that 'not a hair shall perish' by distinguishing between the physical and spiritual self.</summary>

# CHAPTER 21. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...the times of the nations will be fulfilled. And there will be signs in the sun, and moon, and stars, and on the earth distress of nations through despair at the roaring of the sea and the waves, men withering away from fear and expectation of those things which are coming upon the world. "Truly I say to you, that this generation shall not pass away, until all these things happen." He calls a "generation" <note>original: "generationem"; here Theophylact explains that "generation" refers to a category of people—believers—rather than just a specific thirty-year lifespan</note> not those who were then present, but the generation of all the faithful. For Scripture is accustomed to naming a generation in this manner, as in: "This is the generation of those seeking the Lord." Because he spoke of coming disturbances, and wars, and alterations of both the elements and of things, he says "No," so that no one might suspect that perhaps Christianity is destined to be destroyed at some point. For this generation of Christians shall not pass away. Heaven and earth indeed shall be changed, but my words and my Gospel shall not perish, but shall remain. Even if all things are moved, faith in me will not fail. It appears in this place that he prefers the Church over all of creation. For his Church, and the Word, and the Gospel shall by no means perish.

"But take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation <note>original: "crapula"; the physical sickness, headache, or nausea that follows excessive drinking</note> and drunkenness, and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly; for like a snare it will come upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth. Watch therefore at all times, praying that you may be granted to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of Man." You have heard (he says) of the terrors and disturbances; and all these things are great, being symbols of the evils that are going to overtake sinners. But because these are heavy, the great remedy for them is attention and prayer. For to be always prepared and to expect the end will be able to help more than anything else. This, however, will not happen for you unless you are sober, and your hearts are not weighed down by hangover, and drunkenness, and worldly anxiety. Will that day arrive with warning?

## COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

No: but it will arrive unexpectedly and suddenly, in secret: like a snare catching those who are not paying attention. But perhaps someone will examine this phrasing more curiously: "those sitting upon the face of all the earth." For that day will ensnare those who live in leisure and without care; for those are the ones who "sit," and they are the ones who are ensnared. But those who work and are active, and are sober in the performance of good, and are carried toward every good thing, they do not "sit" nor rest upon the earth; rather, they rise up here and say to themselves, "Rise and walk, for you have no rest here," and they seek a better homeland. To these, that day will not be a snare, but a festive day. Therefore, it is necessary to watch and to pray to God, so that we may be able to escape all future things. What things? Perhaps the storms, and famines, and plagues, and other things which will not press upon the elect in the same way; and perhaps also the evils which are perpetually to overtake sinners, which we cannot escape otherwise than by vigilance and prayer. Since, however, it is not enough to flee evil, but there is also a need for some good: after he said "that you may be able to escape all these things to come," he added, "and to stand before the Son of Man," which is the enjoyment of good things. 

<margin>Matt. 18.</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, for a Christian not only to flee hardships, but also to take care that he receives glory. For it is an angelic dignity to stand before the Son of Man and our God. "For the angels truly always see the face of my Father."

"And in the daytime he was teaching in the temple; but at night he went out and stayed on the mount that is called Olivet. And all the people came early in the morning to him in the temple to hear him." The Evangelists hid many things that he taught, especially the three [Synoptic Evangelists]; John himself passed over many things in silence, yet he set forth doctrines more sublime than the other three. Therefore, to those who were gathered in the temple, he discussed many and sublime things, as one may guess. For the Evangelists said little, and did not wish to show everything; and it is indeed manifest from many other places, and from this place we can divine not a little: since the Lord preached for nearly three days, yet they wrote only a few doctrines; if someone were to say that these could be spoken within a single day, he would not be blamed.

# CHAPTER 22. THE WORK OF THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>The Evangelists write a few things out of many.</margin> Therefore, the holy Evangelists have written only a few things for us out of many, offering us a certain taste of sweetness. **D** Christ did not speak in just one way, but offered a discourse suited to each person; for this reason, the crowd would come to him at daybreak. For grace flowed from his lips. By night, however, he would sit upon the mountain <note>The Mount of Olives, where Jesus frequently retreated for prayer.</note>, showing us that at night we ought to speak with God in quietness, but by day we should behave properly and be useful to other people—gathering spiritual strength at night, and distributing what we have gathered during the day. He himself, of course, had no need for prayer or for "conversation" with God. For there was no one else he could turn to, since he himself was God. However, he performed these actions as a model for us: so that, as if at a flowing stream, we might receive a flow of prayer from spiritual veins by night, and by day pour out what we have drawn for those who have need of it. And if anyone had seen the people flocking together so early in the morning to hear him, they would say that the word of David in <margin>Psalm 62.</margin> fit them well: <note>original: "Deus deus meus ad te de luce vigilo. Sitiuit in te anima mea." This is Psalm 63 in modern English Bibles.</note> "O God, my God, for you I watch from the light. My soul has thirsted for you."

# CHAPTER 22. THEOPH[YLACT], ARCHBISHOP OF BULGA[RIA]

...on whose evening the Passover was to be sacrificed. Therefore, <margin>D</margin> the Lord, perhaps on the morning of the fifth day <note>This refers to Thursday, the fifth day of the week in the traditional count leading to the Sabbath.</note>, sends the disciples Peter and John—the former because he was diligent, and the latter because he was beloved. He sends them, moreover, to a house belonging to another. For neither he nor his disciples had a home; otherwise, he would have eaten the Passover in the house of one of his disciples. Do you see his poverty? He sends them to an unknown man to show that he accepted his passion of his own free will. For if he had wished, just as he gave the mind of a man—who did not even know him—the will to receive him, so could he have done whatever he pleased with the Jews. Some, however, say that he did not state the man’s name nor reveal him for this reason, but led them to his house by a certain sign, <margin>B</margin> because of the betrayer <note>Judas Iscariot</note>; so that, the name being unknown, he would not betray the house to the Pharisees, who might have come and seized him before he could finish the supper and deliver his spiritual sacraments. Therefore, later on, Christ says: <note>original: "Desiderio desideraui hoc pascha manducare vobiscum"</note> "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you," which means: I have taken every care to hide from the betrayer, so that we might not suffer the passion before the proper time, before we have delivered the sacraments. Let whoever wishes accept this explanation. And for whose sake does he celebrate the Passover? In all things he shows that, until his very last breath, he was not opposed to the Law. But let us also eat this Passover spiritually. And let us understand the "days of unleavened bread" as every way of life that exists in spiritual light, <margin>F</margin> which possesses none of the oldness of the first disobedience of Adam. If we are in such a way of life, we are to be initiated into the mysteries of Christ. Thus, Peter and John—the active and contemplative [lives], the fervor of zeal and the peacefulness of gentleness—will prepare these sacraments. For it is necessary for the faithful to be both fervent in doing good work and zealous against malice, yet gentle toward those who do evil. For malice is to be held in hatred, but not the person who acts evilly, for whom care must be provided, since he is sick. And this is what it means to act evilly: to be troubled by the evil one and to do wrong. But if we have Peter and John preparing the supper: I mean a good life, which is <margin>John 7.</margin> Peter; and true doctrines, which are John the Theologian <note>In the Eastern tradition, the Apostle John is frequently called "Theologian" because of the profound divine mysteries in his Gospel.</note>:

This water is the grace of the Spirit, as the Evangelist John teaches. The earthenware vessel, however, is the heart, which is easily broken; for he who receives spiritual grace is humble and <margin>James 4 / Job 33.</margin> contrite of heart. For the Lord gives grace to the humble. But he who knows himself to be earth and ashes, and says with Job, "You formed me from the earth," he carries the grace of the Spirit in the vessel of his heart, which is easily moved to sorrow and crushed. And when we have attained this condition, let us go into the house of the mind, whose master of the house will show us a large upper room <margin>B</margin> for the brothers. The upper room is the sublime capacity of such a mind for divine (I say) and spiritual things, in which he dwells, and in which he is kindly received. These things are "spread" or furnished: for there is nothing rough in them, but even <margin>Proverbs 3.</margin> rough things are turned into level plains for such a mind; just as Solomon said: "All things are plain to those who understand, and right to those who find knowledge." He did not say this to sinners, however: because the mind, although it may perform an excellent work, acting according to its own ability, its knowledge is nonetheless "spread out," and yet it holds even lowlier things. But that which is sublime and true knowledge—and above all sublimity—is a state of "unknowing" <note>A reference to apophatic theology, where God is known by moving beyond intellectual concepts.</note> that transcends the mind, when the mind no longer <margin>G</margin> operates, but rather feels and undergoes an operation <margin>C</margin> [from God]. It is necessary for us first to work with our mind, and then we shall feel the operation of the Lord’s grace within us, which will receive us like the prophets and those who experience ecstasy and are deprived of all natural operation. Finally, the "assumption" of the Lord is said in the prophet to happen in this way. Just as Jesus came into this furnished upper room with his disciples and performed the mysteries, so he comes to us, showing both our loss and his own effectiveness; but he does not wait for us to come to him. The disciples of the Word of God are all the words we have spoken. And when the hour had come, he sat down at the table, and the twelve Apostles were with him. And he said to them: <note>original: "Desiderio desideraui hoc pascha comedere vobiscum"</note> "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I say to you, that from now on I will not eat of it again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God." And having taken the cup, he gave thanks, and said: "Take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I say to you, that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine, until the kingdom of God comes." And having taken the bread, when he had given thanks, he broke it, and gave it to them, saying: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me." Likewise also the cup after <margin>E</margin> he had supped, saying: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you."

<margin>How they formerly ate the Passover.</margin> They used to eat the Passover standing up <note>According to the Law in Exodus 12:11, the Israelites were to eat the Passover in haste, standing with staff in hand</note>; how then is the Lord said to recline? They say, therefore, that after he ate the legal Passover, they reclined in the common manner to eat certain other foods. Moreover, he says to the disciples: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer." It is as if he were saying: "This last supper of mine with you is, for that reason, both pleasing and desirable; for I shall not feast with you again." This is similar to those about to set out on a long journey, who share their final conversations most sweetly with their closest companions. Or <margin>F</margin> otherwise: "I have desired to eat this Passover with you" because I am about to deliver great mysteries to you in this supper, namely those which belong to the New Testament. <margin>John 2. Acts 10.</margin> Furthermore, he signifies by these things that he suffers voluntarily. For he was entirely able to withdraw, just as he had at other times, though he knew he was going to suffer. 

However, as to what he says—"I will not drink it until the kingdom of God comes"—certain of the saints have understood this to mean "until I rise again." For after the resurrection, he lived with the disciples, and ate and drank with <margin>As long as the kingdom of death lasted.</margin> them, just as Peter says to Cornelius: "Who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead." That the "kingdom of God" refers to the resurrection is manifest. For the resurrection destroyed death. Death reigned from Adam until Christ; but then, having been destroyed, it 

<column-break/>

<page-num>292</page-num>
## COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

<margin>A</margin> yielded victory and the kingdom to the Lord, just as it <margin>Hosea 13.</margin> was said: "Where is your sting, O death?" and as David said: <margin>Psalm 92.</margin> "The Lord has reigned." Then, interpreting how he has <margin>Isaiah 63.</margin> reigned, he says: "He is clothed with beauty," <margin>Matthew 28.</margin> since his body took on corruption and was beautified by the divinity, as Isaiah says: "This one is beautiful in his robe, with violence and strength." The Lord also, after he rose again, said: "All power has been given to me." Therefore, when the resurrection came—which he called the "kingdom of God" because it destroyed death—he drank again with the disciples, persuading them that he had not risen in appearance only. 

However, some have thought the "kingdom" to be a future state, and that the <margin>B</margin> Lord "drinks" with us in the future through the revelation of mysteries. For in making us joyful, he himself is made glad; and in feeding us, he, the Merciful One, is fed. He considers our drink and nourishment—that is, doctrine—to be his own food. Therefore, in this place, he drinks a certain new potion with the worthy, always revealing to them things that are new and unusual. For this reason, Luke seems to have mentioned the cups. And once indeed he says: "Take and divide it among yourselves," which one might say is a figure of the Old Testament. And again, after he broke and distributed the bread, he himself distributed to the disciples what he also calls the New Testament, saying this is renewed by his own blood. For in the Old [Covenant], the blood was that <margin>C</margin> of brute animals while the Law was in force; but now, since the Word of God has been made man, he has sealed the New Testament for us with his blood. 

By saying, however, "which is given and shed for you," he signifies that his body was given and his blood was shed not for the Apostles alone, but for the whole human race. Therefore, when he says "which is given for you," it means for our human race. For the old Passover was performed for the sake of liberation from Egypt, and the blood of the lamb <margin>Exodus 12.</margin> was for the sake of preserving the firstborn; but the new Passover is for the remission of sins, and for the sanctification of thoughts and their preservation for God. Therefore, let no one err upon hearing "you may eat and drink at my table" here; rather, let them think of it as a metaphor <term>metaphor: a way of describing a spiritual reality using physical terms</term> based on those who are honored by kings. For a created being, it is the role of a handmaid to "stand," even when we speak of sitting and standing in a physical sense.

Therefore, because a "woe" was adjudged to the traitor, while for those who remained in love toward him he predicted such great honor, he speaks so that they might not be puffed up—as if they had done something great by remaining in charity and not betraying him. "Satan," he says, "has asked to sift you" <note>original: "petiuit cribrare"; to sift or shake as with a sieve</note>, that is, to disturb you—not to harm you, but to test you. "But I have prayed." # CHAPTER 22. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

In this place, although Peter was preserved by God, he reached the point of denial because he was abandoned for a short time by a divine dispensation <term>dispensation: a theological term (Latin: dispensatio) referring to God’s specific plan or "economy" in managing human events</term>. Indeed, if it had not been for some small protection from God for the seeds of faith that were hidden within him, what would he not have suffered? For the devil’s goal was to push him into a full betrayal. "For the food of the devil," says the 
<margin>Psalm 36</margin> 
Prophet, "is the chosen." <note>original: "Cibus enim diaboli... electi." While the margin cites Psalm 36, this thought is often associated with Habakkuk 1:16 in the Latin tradition.</note> But thanks be to God, who does not abandon the holy, the righteous, and the good of heart—such as Peter was—who was deeply loving and free from any evil suspicions toward his master.

And he said to them, "When I sent you without a money-bag, or a traveler’s pouch, or sandals, did you lack anything?" And they said, "Nothing." Then he said to them, "But now, let him who has a money-bag take it, and likewise a pouch; and he who does not have one, let him sell his garment and buy a sword. For I tell you, that which is written must still be fulfilled in me: 'And he was counted among the lawless.' For the things concerning me are reaching their end." And they said, "Lord, look, here are two swords." And he said to them, "It is enough." ] In the beginning 
<margin>Matthew 10; Above, Luke 10</margin>
of his preaching, the Lord sent his disciples into the towns and cities even without the necessities of life. He did not give them what they needed, nor did he want them to be anxious; in these trials, it was necessary for them to learn his power. For by taking care of them as if they were weak, he made all necessary things flow to them in abundance, without any effort on their part.

But now he commands the opposite—not that he is contrary to himself, but to show them that up until this time, he had carried them like infants and had not made them 
anxious about anything. Now, however, it is necessary for them to take on the cares of men and provide for themselves. "I, your father," he says, "who have taken care of you until now, am departing. And in this time, be prepared; take care of your own affairs, and do not cast all your care upon me. 
<margin>What is suggested by the bag, the pouch, and the sword</margin> 
For your work will not be so easy or free from labor, but you will be subject to hunger, thirst, and many adversities." These are the things suggested by the bag, the pouch, and the sword.

Therefore, do not be idle: because you will experience hunger and will have need of food, which is signified by the pouch. And be courageous, because you will fall into many adversities; 

<column-break/>

<page-num>295</page-num>
# COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE. 295

this is indicated by the sword. He says these things, however, not so that they should be literally girded with swords, but (as I said) to signify the wars and dangers ahead, and to teach them to be prepared for all things. 
For he did not want later generations to think that the Apostles contributed nothing of their own toward virtue, and that everything was entirely from God. "It will not be so," he says; for I do not wish to use my Apostles like inanimate instruments. Finally, you will find the Apostles—and especially Paul—doing many things correctly through human industry. Read the Acts of the Apostles; though divine help was not absent in those accounts, in the meantime, it was also beneficial to the Apostles so that they would not be puffed up with pride. For if they themselves had taken no care, and everything had been done by God, they might have been inflated with pride as if they had been granted something greater than human strength. Moreover, through the laziness and corruption of human nature, they would have devised nothing on their own, but would have expected everything from the Word <term>the Word: a title for Jesus, the Logos</term>. For this reason, he tells them from this time on to carry pouches—that is, "Be so disposed and take such care as if you are going to suffer hunger." And "Buy a sword"—that is, "Provide for yourselves like those who will fall into many wars and battles." 

Others have explained "Buy a sword" differently. For it signifies that such great plots will soon arise as have never been before, and that men of blood are going to attack them. For because they had previously argued among themselves about who was the greatest, he says, "It is not a time for ambition, but for dangers and slaughter; for I, your master, am being led away to death, and not even to a glorious death."

Nevertheless, this will be fulfilled in me: "He was counted among the lawless." Intending to signal these treacherous plots, he mentions the sword. Yet he did not reveal everything, so that they would not be terrified by fear; nor was he entirely silent, so that they would not be confounded by sudden traps. Rather, he spoke so that afterwards, remembering these things, they might admire him for his foreknowledge and be amazed at how he delivered himself to death for the salvation of men—and therefore, they themselves should not shrink from anything painful so that some might be saved. I believe he spoke these things enigmatically <term>enigmatically: in a puzzling or metaphorical way that requires interpretation</term> for this reason: so that they might gain the benefit later when they remembered and understood. At that time, they were so lacking in understanding that they said, "Lord, look, here are two swords." Because he saw that they did not understand, he said, "It is enough."

The Lord does this when he sees the disciples do not understand what was said; he moves on and allows the outcome of events to explain the meaning of his words, just as when he said: "Destroy this temple" <note>John 2:19</note>.

<margin>A</margin>
He did not take all the disciples, but only three: those who had also been spectators of his glory on the mountain <note>The Transfiguration</note>. Because he was about to pray in a struggle, so that it might not seem like a sign of fear, he takes those who had been witnesses and hearers of his divine glory and heavenly testimony. Thus, when they see him laboring, they might say this belongs to human nature. For so that he might be believed to be a true man, he allowed nature to do what was its own, and he himself, as a man, desires life and prays that the cup might pass. For man is a lover of life. This refutes the heresies that say he was a "phantom" man <note>Referring to Docetism, which taught that Christ's body was an illusion</note>. For since these things happened and they still found ways to talk such nonsense, 
<margin>B</margin>
what would they not have done if these things had not happened? Furthermore, to wish for the cup to pass was human. But immediately, by saying, "Nevertheless, not my will be done but yours," he shows that we too ought to be so disposed—to practice philosophy <term>practice philosophy: here meaning 'to live with spiritual wisdom' or 'to discipline the soul'</term>, to yield to the divine will, and not to obey nature when it opposes itself. "Let not my human will be done, but yours," because your will is not separate from my divine will. For being one Christ having two natures, he also had natural wills or volitions, both divine and human. The human nature therefore wished to live, for that is natural. 

<margin>C</margin>
Then, following the divine will (which wished for all men to be saved and was common to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit), he underwent death; and thus one "willed thing" was made, that is, the saving death. That the prayer came from his human nature—which by permission suffered the common affection by which we love life—and not from his divinity (as the cursed Arians 
<margin>Arians</margin>

# CHAPTER 23. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>Why Herod was glad to see Jesus.</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
...to the prince of Galilee. Now Herod was glad, not so that he might gain anything useful for his soul from the sight of Jesus, but because he had heard about him—that he was wise and performed wonders. He possessed a foolish desire, suffering from the disease of curiosity, wishing to see this famous man and hear what he might say. Do not many people even today suffer from that same disease? For he desired to see some sign performed by Jesus, not so that he might believe, but to delight his eyes; just as in public spectacles we see <term>prestigiators</term> <note>These were traveling entertainers or street performers, similar to magicians or jugglers, who performed sleight-of-hand tricks.</note> appear, who swallow snakes and swords and similar things. For he thought Jesus was much like them. And he questioned him with many words, treating him in a mocking manner and sneering at everything; therefore, Jesus answered him nothing. For he knew when it was time to speak; he did all things <margin>B</margin> with reason, and he received testimony from David that he would "guide his words with discretion." <note>original: "dispesset sermones suos in iudicio." Referring to Psalm 112:5 (Vulgate 111:5).</note> For why should one respond <margin>Psalm 105.</margin> to him who does not ask in order to learn? Likewise, why should pearls be cast before swine? Indeed, as we said above, it is an act of greater mercy to remain silent among such people. For a word spoken to one whom it does not benefit becomes a cause for even greater condemnation if they do not pay attention. He certainly answered Pilate because Pilate was somewhat more prudent than Herod, even if he was not truly wise. For when he asked, "Are you the King of the Jews?" what did the Lord say? "You say so." This response holds a middle ground of sorts. For it can be understood as: "I truly am; you have said what is so," and it can also be understood as: "I am not, but <margin>E</margin> <margin>F</margin> <margin>"You say so" can be understood in two ways.</margin> you are the one saying it." To Herod, however, he answered absolutely nothing, since Herod was a mocker. And truly, over that "evil seed" and "sons of iniquity"—the Jews of that time—mocking and oppressive rulers were set over them. For with a mocking mind and a ridiculous intent, Herod desired to see Jesus and watch for a sign from him. He questioned him with this spirit, and finally proved it by sending him away with contempt and ridicule. And he was not alone in this, but also his whole army; after other insults, they dressed him in a white robe and sent him back to Pilate. Then see how, through everything the devil does, he is hindered. For he stirs up reproaches and insults—

—insults against Christ, and from there the truth is more clearly declared. For by these mockeries, they testify more clearly that the Lord was not seditious or a rebel. For if he had been such a man, they would by no means have mocked him with these jests, especially with the great danger and sedition of the whole nation being stirred up—a nation so suspicious and delighting so much in political upheaval. Now, Pilate and Herod became friends. For Herod, the proof and beginning of this friendship was that Jesus had been sent to him by Pilate, as if Pilate were not claiming any of Herod’s own privileges for himself. Nevertheless, see how the devil gathers together those who disagree, solely to prepare for the death of Christ. For he joins and reconciles enemies into a single conspiracy. Are we not put to shame then, <margin>B</margin> if the devil pacifies enemies to kill Christ, while we, for the sake of our own salvation, do not even keep our friends in their duty? After he was sent back to Pilate (see how the truth shines forth again), Pilate said, "You brought me this man as one subverting the people, and I find nothing in him worthy of death; nor does Herod." You see the testimony—entirely true—of two men, one a governor and the other a king. "Neither I," he says, "nor King Herod have found any cause in him." What will the Jews say to this? The judges themselves testify that the man lacks fault, while you, the accusers, bring no evidence. Whom should we believe? Oh, <margin>3 Esdras 3</margin> how the truth conquers! <note>A reference to 1 Esdras 3:12 and 4:41 from the Apocrypha: "Magna est veritas et praevalet"—Great is truth and it prevails.</note> Jesus remains silent, and his enemies testify <margin>C</margin> for him. The Jews shout, and no one supports their cries. However, Pilate was too soft and not at all constant in the truth. For he feared slander—that he might be accused of having acquitted a rebel. For he had not learned: "Let us not fear their terror, but the Lord <margin>Isaiah 8.</margin> himself shall be our fear." Pilate said, "I will release him after he is punished," that is, corrected through scourging. Now, the Romans were required to release one prisoner to the Jews during the feast day. For they had entered into such a treaty with the Jews, to allow them to live freely according to their own laws and customs. And it was a paternal custom for the Jews to ask for those judged by the prince, just as they once asked Saul for Jonathan. If <margin>1 Samuel 14.</margin> you are ignorant of this history, go to the first book of Kings <note>In the Vulgate, the books of Samuel are called 1 and 2 Kings. The story mentioned is in 1 Samuel 14, where the people rescue Jonathan from Saul's death sentence.</note>.

For he who is crucified is fixed with nails and cannot work. Therefore, a teacher following Christ's example <margin>The duty of a Christian teacher.</margin> ought to be the first to lift the cross himself and fix his own flesh with nails, so that he may shine with the fear of God and be free from passions; only then should he impose it upon his listeners. For through the cross, death has been destroyed and hell has been taken captive. Lamentations bring no consolation to those who suffer by choice. There was also an inscription over him in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters: This is the King of the Jews.] The Devil, wishing to splash the Lord with great infamy, caused the thieves to be crucified with him; but see how he was deprived of even one of them, and how this resulted in the greater glory of the Lord. For no one seeks after the crosses of the others, yet the whole world hangs upon this cross; and here it is clearly shown that the Lord is not a lawbreaker like the thieves, but the Prince of all justice.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>Where Adam's burial is.</margin> They lead him to the place of the Skull <note>original: "locum Cranij," referring to Golgotha or Calvary.</note>, where they say our first parent was buried, so that where the fall occurred through a tree <note>The tree of the knowledge of good and evil in Eden.</note>, there also the resurrection might occur through a tree <note>The wood of the Cross.</note>. Jesus, declaring his extraordinary gentleness, prays for them:
> Father, forgive them,
saying, "for they know not what they do." And indeed their sin would have been forgiven them, had they not remained in their unbelief thereafter. They divided his garments. For what reason? Perhaps many of them were in need of them, or perhaps they did this for greater insult out of sheer wantonness.

<margin>A</margin> For what did they see of value in these clothes? Therefore, laughing and inflicting insult, they did these things. For where even the leaders were mocking, what should we not think of the rest of the common people?
<margin>Matt. 4.</margin>
"He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Christ, the chosen of God." The Devil was speaking through them. For just as on the pinnacle of the temple <note>Refers to the Temptation of Christ in Matthew 4.</note>, so also in this place he speaks; envying our salvation through the cross (which he wished to perish), he moved every engine of his malice. The soldiers offered vinegar, as if serving a king in a certain way so that he might drink. See also another engine of the Devil which is turned against him: he who used characters of three languages to publicize the "rebellion" of Jesus in such a way that it would be hidden from no passer-by,
<margin>B</margin> <margin>What is signified by the trilingual title. Chapter 19.</margin>
as if he had been hung for this reason: that he had made himself a king. This, however—even if it was not done as a symbol from the mind of the writer <note>Referring to Pontius Pilate, who wrote the title.</note>—factually signifies that the most powerful of nations (the Romans), the wisest (the Greeks), and the most religious (the Hebrews), were to be subjected to his kingdom, and they ought to preach him. We shall say more and more sublime things about this in the Gospel of John.

But one of the criminals who were hanging spoke insults against him, saying, "If you are the Christ, save yourself and us." But the other, answering, rebuked him, saying, "Do you not even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive what is due for our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong." And he said to Jesus, "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom." And Jesus said to him,
> Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.
<margin>C</margin>] How is it then that the other Evangelists say the two thieves cast insults at him? It is likely that at first both of them insulted him, but then one of them, becoming more sensible and recognizing the goodness of Jesus from the voice he used for those crucifying him—saying "Father, forgive them"—changed his mind. For he did not say "Lord (I pray) forgive them," but simply thus, and with great power: "Forgive them." This voice is not only full of all mercy, but also carries great authority. From this voice, therefore, as the former blasphemer recognized Jesus as the true king, he refuted the other thief and turned to Jesus.

# CHAPTER 23. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...said, "Remember me in your kingdom." What, therefore, did the Lord say?
> Today you will be with me in paradise.

He spoke as a man upon the cross, but as God he was everywhere; both there and in paradise, filling all things and absent from nowhere. Some, however, ask: how could the Lord say to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise,"
<margin>Hebrews 11</margin> when Paul said that none of the saints have yet received the promise? <note>Referring to Hebrews 11:39, which suggests the Old Testament faithful wait for the final resurrection to receive their full reward.</note> Some say that the Apostle Paul was not asserting this about *all* saints, but only about those whom he had specifically listed. For he listed many others, but did not mention the thief. Listen to what he says: "all these," pointing to those whom his speech enumerated, among whom the thief was not counted. Others have said that the thief has not yet obtained his dwelling in paradise, but because the Lord’s promise is unchangeable and he cannot lie, it was said, "Today you will be with me in paradise" <note>original: "Hodie mecum eris in paradiso"</note> as a certainty. For this is a type of phrasing in the Lord’s words where he speaks of future things
<margin>John 3, John 5</margin> as if they were already happening; as when he says, "He who does not believe is already judged," and so on; or "He who hears my words and believes does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life." Others do not twist the word, but place a punctuation mark after the word "today," so that the sense of the saying is: "Truly I say to you today:" and then adding, "you will be with me in the kingdom." Others, however, who seem to have best grasped the meaning, explain it thus: The good things promised to us are not the entrance into
<margin>Matthew 6, Isaiah 64, 1 Corinthians 1, Genesis 2</margin> paradise, nor the ascent there, but the Kingdom of Heaven. Hence we pray, "Thy kingdom come," not "may that dwelling in paradise come." For it does not seem to me that paradise and the kingdom are the same thing. For the good things of the kingdom "no ear has heard, nor eye seen, nor has it entered into the heart of man." <note>1 Corinthians 2:9, referencing Isaiah 64:4.</note> But the eye of Adam saw paradise, and his ear heard of it. For God said, "Of every tree that is in paradise you may freely eat." For although only one tree was forbidden to them, they truly saw it and heard about it. For Adam rejoiced in the spirit; otherwise, he would not have undertaken such great
<margin>Note on the state after this life.</margin> work in agriculture with joy. And so, what Paul says is not contradictory. The thief, therefore, obtained paradise, but he has not yet attained the kingdom; he will attain it, however, when all those whom Paul

<meta>catchword: Paulus (Paul)</meta>

<margin>A</margin> enumerated also attain it. But now, at this time, he possesses paradise, which is a place of spiritual rest. Many speak of these things, but it must be said that the Kingdom of Heaven and paradise are effectively the same. Therefore, nothing prevents both the Lord and Paul from speaking the truth. For the thief is indeed in paradise—that is, the kingdom—and not he alone, but also all those whom Paul lists. Otherwise, he would not enjoy a perfect participation in those good things. For just as those condemned are not in royal palaces but are held shut in prisons in assigned punishments, so those who are glorified both enter into the kingdoms and now dwell in them; then, when the time for the distribution of royal gifts comes, they shall also obtain those. Thus,
<margin>B</margin> the saints, although they do not yet perfectly enjoy the good things, nevertheless already dwell in bright and fragrant places and beautiful tabernacles, even if they have not yet obtained the full distribution of royal goods. Thus the thief was in paradise, even if he has not yet received everything perfectly, so that he is not made perfect without us. <note>A reference to Hebrews 11:40: "that they without us should not be made perfect."</note> And this I think is the truest explanation of all—not to mention that the grace of the saints in the daily performance of miracles might rightly be called paradise. And all saints,
<margin>Note on the saints.</margin> as many as have been made participants of spiritual gifts and have the "pledge of the Spirit," are in paradise, even if they have not yet been perfected and received the kingdom, just as Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews, even if they have not yet
<margin>Hebrews 2</margin> received the promise. By saying "the promise," he meant
<margin>C</margin> total happiness. But they have not yet received that total happiness, even though they are in the kingdom and paradise. You, however, should marvel at how, like a king bringing back trophies of victory, he leads away the <term>spolia opima</term> <note>original: "spolia opima" — historically, the most honorable spoils of war taken by a Roman general from an opposing commander; here, the thief is the "spoils" won back from the Devil.</note> with him. So too the Lord, because he plundered the strongest vessel of the devil, took him with him and brought him back to man’s first fatherland—I mean paradise. For Christ was in paradise not only as God, but also according to the fact that he had a rational and mental soul. And he was in paradise with his mind, but he descended into hell with his soul. <note>Theology of the "Harrowing of Hell." Theophylact distinguishes between the *nous* (mind/intellect) and the *psyche* (soul).</note> Furthermore, by the fact that he saves the thief—that vessel of malice—he shows what he previously received; for having conquered the enemy, he plundered his spoils.
<margin>Psalm 30</margin> Now it was about the sixth hour, and there was darkness...

<margin>The Lord’s Day.</margin>
"One of the sabbaths" <note>original: "Una sabbatorum"</note> refers to the first of the days of the week—that is, the week of days—which among us is called "the Lord's Day" because of the Lord's resurrection. Therefore, on that day, the women came to the tomb, bringing spices. They came at early dawn, which Matthew calls the "morning of the sabbaths." For "deep twilight" <note>original: "profundum crepusculum"</note> is the same as "very early morning." Moreover, they found the stone rolled away, for an angel had rolled it back. Furthermore, as they entered, two men appeared. In Matthew's account, one sat upon the stone; but here, two men stood within the tomb. For there were various visions. They appeared in flashing garments because of the joy

And they made them remember the things that had been said by Christ: that it "behooved" him—that is, it was necessary—to be delivered into the hands of sinful men, namely the Romans, who were Gentiles and abominable, and to rise on the third day. Indeed, having returned from the sepulcher, when they told these things to the apostles, they seemed to be raving. To such an extent did the miracle of the resurrection seem incredible to men. But Peter was not idle, nor was he slow to grasp the whole matter; he came to the burial place to see only the linens, and then he first received this benefit from his journey to the tomb. "Wondering"—that is, marveling <note>The Latin "subsannans" usually means mocking or deriding, but here the commentator uses it to express a state of being stunned or shaking one's head in disbelief at the impossibility of the event.</note>. # CHAPTER 24. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

<margin>D</margin>...“Today is the third day since these things happened. Moreover, certain women from our group astonished us; they went to the tomb at dawn, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. And some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but they did not see him.”] 

Some say that one of those two disciples was Luke himself; for this reason, the Evangelist hides his own name <note>It was a common tradition that the unnamed companion of Cleopas was the author of the Gospel, St. Luke.</note>. Now, they were speaking to one another about all these things that had happened, not as believers, but as those doubting and stunned by these marvelous events, not immediately giving their assent to such an admirable matter. 

But when Jesus approached, he was with them: now possessing a **spiritual and divine body**, he was not hindered by the distance between places from being present with those he wished. For this reason, because of the physical features in which he then appeared, they were not permitted to recognize him. For as Mark says, *he appeared in another form*, and with different features: for he was no longer ruled by natural laws in his body, but spiritually and beyond nature; hence *their eyes were held*, so that they would not recognize him. 

But why did he appear in another form, and why were their eyes held? Surely so that they might reveal their own uncertain opinion, so that he might uncover the ulcer <note>original: "hulcus"; here used metaphorically for their spiritual wound or secret doubt</note> and they might receive the medicine; so that he might become sweeter to them after a long conversation, and so they might believe more firmly that his body is no longer such as is usually seen by everyone—even though the very same body that suffered has risen—yet he appears to whom he wills. They gain a great advantage from this, for they no longer doubt why he does not move among the common people again, considering that his manner of life after his resurrection is far different and not common: not like that of men, but more divine, as a pattern of the future resurrection, in which we shall live like angels and children of God. For this reason, therefore, their eyes were held, so that they would not recognize him; for he was seen by those to whom he willed to be seen.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>Cleopas, however, objects to his traveling companion, as it seemed. “Are you,” he said, “the only stranger in Jerusalem?”—meaning, “Are you the only one among those living in Jerusalem who is ignorant of what has happened?” Others, however, understand “stranger” this way: “Are you,” he says, “the only traveler, having your home outside the borders of Jerusalem and not participating in the things that happened in the midst of Jerusalem, that you are ignorant of these things?” 

See how small an opinion they had of the Lord. For they truly thought him a prophet, such as Elijah had been, or Joshua son of Nun <note>original: "Iesus Naue"; Nave or Nun is the Hebrew name of Joshua's father.</note>, or Moses—mighty in deed and word. First comes the deed, and then the word. For no word of a teacher is firm unless he first declares himself a doer by teaching. 

<margin>B</margin>Therefore, be mighty first in deed, and then have a care for the word; thus God will also work with you. For first comes the work, and then contemplation and illumination. Unless you purify the mirror with labor and sweat, you will in no way see the desired beauty in the mirror. 

*Blessed are the pure in heart* <margin>Matthew 5</margin>—this happens through works—*for they shall see God*; this is the end of contemplation. It is necessary, however, to be mighty in deed and word before God, and then before all the people. For we ought first to please God, then effort must be given so that we may also live blamelessly among ourselves as much as possible; you should not study how you may please men, but how you may serve God, nor live so as to be a scandal to many. 

<margin>C</margin>But even this must be provided after the former, as the Wise Man says: <margin>Proverbs 20 <note>The quote "Provide good things before God and men" is found in Proverbs 3:4 and later echoed by St. Paul.</note></margin> *Provide good things before God, and then also before men.* And Paul says this very thing. <margin>2 Corinthians 8</margin> “But we were hoping,” they said, “that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel.” 

As if frustrated in their hope, they say, “we were hoping” that he would save others, and behold, he did not even save himself; thus he responded so little to our expectation, and was so powerless. And they were saying almost the same things as the thief on the cross: “He saved others, himself he cannot save.” Therefore he also calls them “foolish” and “slow to believe.” 

Now what is it to “redeem Israel”? <margin>What it means to redeem Israel.</margin> We have said that the common people and the less instructed expected Christ to be a savior and redeemer from the earthly evils that were threatening them...

He emphasizes that spiritual understanding requires "deeds before words" and contrasts the disciples' hope for a political savior with the true nature of Christ.</summary>

# CHAPTER 24. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
308
Qq iiii

<margin>D</margin>
...and from the yoke of Roman servitude; they were hoping that he would rule as an earthly king. For this reason they say: *We were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel*, namely from the Gentile Romans—and yet he did not even escape the unjust sentence passed against him. *And today is the third day, and certain women terrified us,* etc. They say these things as if doubting; it seems to me these men are in a very wavering state of mind, neither completely disbelieving nor rightly believing. For indeed, by saying *we hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel*, they indicate their lack of faith. However, when they say it is the *third day*, they are like men who nearly remember what he told them: *On the third day I will rise again.* And when he says, *they terrified us*, this signifies that their lack of faith is being shaken.

<margin>B</margin>
And if these words are considered altogether, they are human speeches, containing great doubt, and belonging to men perplexed and ignorant of what to do because of the miracle of the resurrection. *But certain of those who were with us,* he says, *went away*—he refers either to Peter alone, or to 
<margin>John 20</margin>
Peter and John. From this it is manifest that what some authors describe at length, others hand down in a summary and pass over quickly. For John included the journey of Peter and John to the tomb with more detail, but this author [Luke], making mention of it in a few words, even omitted their names.

The POWER of the Spirit is perfected in weakness, just as it is written and as we believe—not only in weakness of the body, but also of speech and wisdom, which resides in the tongue. This is manifest from many others, especially from John the great theologian, who was the brother <note>The text calls him "brother of Christ," likely referring to his spiritual intimacy or the tradition of his family relationship to the Virgin Mary.</note> of <margin>B</margin> Christ, by grace. For he was born of a father who was a fisherman and practiced the same craft as his father. For those things which none of the other Evangelists taught us, he himself dared to thunder forth. <margin>D</margin>
He [John] rejoiced when he had read the other things written by the Evangelists, admiring that they told the truth about all things, and judging that they wrote nothing merely to gain the favor of the Apostles. However, those things which they did not state clearly or omitted entirely, he himself began to explain and make clear, adding to his own Gospel, which he wrote while an exile on the island of Patmos thirty-two years after Christ was taken up into the heavens.

<margin>When and where John wrote the gospel.</margin>
John was beloved above all the disciples, especially by the Lord, because he was perfectly mild, of the sweetest manners and a pure heart, being indeed a virgin <note>original: *virgo*, used here to denote lifelong celibacy and spiritual purity</note>. From this, the gift of greater knowledge of God was entrusted to him, and he was delighted by many unknown mysteries. For "Blessed," he said, "are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

<margin>John the virgin. Matthew 5</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
Moreover, he was a relative of the Lord. How so? Listen: Joseph, the spouse of the Mother of God <note>original: *deiparæ*, literally the God-bearer or Theotokos</note>, had seven children from a previous wife—four males and three females: Martha, Esther, and Salome. And that John was truly the son of Salome. Thus the Lord is found to be his uncle, because Joseph was regarded as the father of the Lord, and Salome was the daughter of Joseph, and therefore regarded as the sister of the Lord; and thus John, being her son, was the nephew of the Lord. Perhaps it would not be absurd to reveal the names of both his mother and the Evangelist. For his mother, who was called Salome, is interpreted as "peaceful"; but John means "his grace." Therefore, let every soul know that the peace which is toward men, and which is in the soul free from passions, becomes the mother of divine grace and generates it within us. For it is not likely that a soul which is still disturbed and fights against other men and against itself will obtain divine grace.

<margin>How John was a relative of the Lord.</margin>
<margin>Salome. John.</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
But let us consider something even more wonderful that happened regarding that holy Evangelist. For he appears to have three mothers: the Mother of God, Salome, and Thunder. For he is a "son of thunder" because he was the loudest voice <note>original: *vocalissimus*, meaning most eloquent or resounding in proclaiming the Gospel</note> in the Gospel; of the Mother of God, for He said, "Behold your mother." But let these things said before the exposition suffice; now the unlocking of his words must begin.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>A</margin>

**IN the beginning was the Word.]** Just as I said in the preface, I say again: that while the other Evangelists narrated at length the Lord's lower birth <note>original: *inferiorem natiuitatem*, referring to his human birth and genealogy on earth</note>, his conversation, and his growth, **JOHN** passes over those things as having been sufficiently spoken by his fellow disciples. Instead, he discusses the divinity of Him who became man for us; although if you consider it diligently, neither did those others neglect to speak of the divinity of the Only-begotten, but they made mention of it, though not extensively; nor was this man so intent on the sublimity of the Word that he altogether neglected His dispensation in the flesh <note>original: *dispensationem eius in carne*, referring to the mystery of the Incarnation</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
For there was one Spirit who moved the souls of all. Therefore, he discourses to us concerning the Son. For the Father was known to us from the Old Law, although he is not silent about the Father, but mentions Him while speaking of the Son, showing the eternity of the Only-begotten by saying, *In the beginning was*, that is, *from* the beginning He was. For that which is from the beginning—absolutely no time is found when it was not. And would someone say it is manifest that "in the beginning" is the same as "from the beginning"? From where? From common understanding itself, but especially from that Evangelist. For he says in one of his epistles: *That which was from the beginning, which we have seen.*

<margin>All Evangelists were moved by one Spirit.</margin>
<margin>1 John 1.</margin>
You see, therefore, how that beloved of the Lord interprets himself. "Even so," he says.

<margin>C</margin>
But [an opponent says], I understand *what was in the beginning* in the same way as was said by Moses: *In the beginning God made.* For just as there, *what was in the beginning* is not understood as if the heaven were eternal, so neither in this place is it understood that the Only-begotten is eternal. These are the words of a heretic <note>original: *hæreticus*, a reference to Arian views that Christ was a created being</note>. To this foolish insistence, we say nothing else than this: O sophist of malice, how have you observed what follows? But we shall say these things even against your will. For there indeed Moses says, *In the beginning God made heaven and earth*; but in this place, *In the beginning was the Word.* What connection is there then between the word *made* and the word *was*?
