### CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA | ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 313

<margin>1. Why John said, "In the beginning was the Word," and not rather, "the Son."</margin>
...if it had been written in that place, "In the beginning God made the Son," <note>original: *In principio fecit Deus filium*</note> but now he says, "In the beginning was." From this I understand that the Word was eternal, and not created later, as you [heretics] triflers claim. But why did he not say, "from the beginning was the Son," but rather, "the Word"? Listen: it was because of the weakness of the listeners. Lest, hearing the name of "Son" immediately from the beginning, we might think of a physical birth, he called him "the Word." For you should learn: just as a word is begotten from the mind without <term>passion</term> <note>original: *sine passione*; in theology, this means without physical change, suffering, or biological process</note>, so also here, he was born from the Father without any physical affection. Or otherwise: he called him "the Word" because he announced the Father’s things to us, just as every word announces the wills of the mind. Furthermore, it shows that the Son is co-eternal with the Father. For just as it cannot be said that a mind ever exists without a word, so neither can the Father and God exist without the Son. Moreover, it is said with the article, "the" Word <note>original: *illud verbum*, referencing the Greek *ho logos*</note>. For there are indeed many other words of God, such as prophecies and commands: according to what is said of the angels, "Powerful in virtue, doing his word." But this "Word" is properly a substance, constituting a person.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>ψδος</margin>
<margin>Mark 6.</margin>
**And that Word was with God.** ] And in this place, he more clearly indicates that the Son is co-eternal with the Father. Lest you think that the Father was ever without the Son, he says: "And that Word was with God," that is, with God, within the Father's own boundaries. You must understand "With" <note>original: *apud*</note> as "together with." Just as in another place it is said, "Are not his brothers and sisters with us?" <note>Mark 6:3</note> that is, are they not with us and do they not live among us? So also in this place, understand "with God": that is, he was with God, with God within His boundaries. For it is impossible for God to be without speech and wisdom. Therefore, because the Son exists as the Word and the Wisdom and the Power of the Father, we believe him to be always with the Father and together with the Father. And how, one might ask, is it possible that the Son is not later than the Father? How? Learn from a physical example: the brightness of the sun, is it not from the sun itself? Entirely so. Is it therefore later than the sun, such that the sun could be understood without it? Or how could the sun exist not having its brightness? Therefore, much

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Sabellius, claiming one person, is refuted.</margin>
more so shall this be understood concerning the Father and the Son. For the Son of the Father, since he is the brightness—just as Paul also says <note>Hebrews 1:3</note>—must be believed to shine always with the Father and not to be later than Him. Note here also that Sabellius <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century priest who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons, but merely different "masks" or modes of one God</note> of Libya is refuted by this saying. For he taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit appeared as one person: sometimes as the Father, sometimes as the Son, and occasionally as the Holy Spirit. The son of a lying father <note>meaning the devil</note> trifles with these things, being full of a malignant spirit; but he is clearly rebuked by what is said: "And that Word was with God." For the Evangelist clearly says in this place that the Word is one, and God (that is, the Father) is another. For because the Word was "with" God, it is manifest that two persons are introduced, even if there is one nature in these two. But as to why there is one nature, listen:

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Why Arius and Sabellius are to be confounded.</margin>
**And the Word was God.** ] You see that the Word was also God, and so there was one nature of the Father and the Son, because there is also one divinity. Let both Arius <note>Arius taught that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God</note> and Sabellius, therefore, be confounded. Arius indeed, who says the Son of God is a creature and a thing made, is refuted by this: "In the beginning was that Word," and "the Word was God." But let Sabellius, denying the trinity of persons but asserting a unity of being, be rejected by this: "And that Word was with God." For the great John clearly declares in this place that the Word is one person and the Father is another, even if they are not "one thing and another thing" <note>This refers to a grammatical distinction in Latin/Greek: *alius* (another person) vs. *aliud* (another substance/nature)</note>. For "another" <note>original: *alius*, masculine</note> is said of the person, while "one thing and another" <note>original: *aliud & aliud*, neuter</note> is said of natures. Let us make this clearer by an example: Peter and Paul are "another and another" <note>different persons</note>, for they are two persons, but they are not "one thing and another" <note>different natures</note> in nature, for their nature is one: humanity. So, therefore, it must be taught concerning the Father and the Son. For they are "another and another" <note>two persons</note>, but not "one thing and another," for their nature is one: deity.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>"Another" and "another thing" concerning natures. Paul is called "another."</margin>
**He was in the beginning with God.** ] That God the Word was never separated from God the Father. For because he had said, "The Word was God," lest anyone should be disturbed by a devilish delusion, saying, "Therefore, because the Word is also God, he will at some point rise up against the Father," as the Gentiles fabulate in their myths, and separating himself from Him will become an adversary—therefore he says that although the Word is God, he is nevertheless with God the Father.

Having previously established that the "Word" (Logos) is co-eternal with the Father, he now addresses specific logical traps set by pagan philosophers like Porphyry and the theological errors of the Arians, who viewed the Son as a mere tool of the Father.</meta>

### CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>
Two types of words, neither of which fits the Son of God.
</margin>

...is, and is never separated from Him. It would be no less easy to answer the <margin>D</margin> Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, not equal to the Father.</note>: "Hear, O you deaf, who say that the Son of God is a work and a creation." Understand what kind of name the Evangelist bestowed upon the Son of God. For he called Him "the Word" itself. But you call Him a work and a creation—He who is neither a work nor a creation. For since there are two types of word, one indeed is mental <note>original: *mentale*; refers to the internal thought or the "inner word" of the mind</note>, which we have even when we are saying nothing—understand this as the power of speaking. For in this way, even one sleeping and saying nothing has the power of speech situated within himself, and has not cast away that capacity. There is, therefore, one that is mental and another that is expressive <note>original: *enunciatiuum*; the spoken word</note>, which we bring forth through the lips; this is the power of speaking out, when we bring that which is situated within the mind into action. Since, therefore, there are two types of word, neither of these is suitable for the Son of God. For the Son of God is neither <margin>E</margin> the expressive nor the mental word. For those words are natural, and of the sort found among us humans.

<margin>
The sophism of Porphyry the pagan.
</margin>

But the Word of the Father is above nature, and not subject to those lower artifices of speaking. And thus the sophism of Porphyry the pagan <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who was a famous critic of Christianity.</note> falls. For he, attempting to subvert the Gospel, used such divisions. "If indeed," he said, "the Son of God is a word, he is either expressive or mental. But he is neither this nor that; therefore, he is not the Son." Thus this sophism was solved previously, when we say that mental and expressive words refer to those things which are among us and are natural; but concerning Him who is above nature, there is no such thing. Nevertheless, this must also be said: If the name "Word" were indeed worthy of God, and were spoken of Him properly and substantially, the pagan's doubt would certainly have a place. <margin>F</margin> But no one could find any other proper name worthy of God, nor is the "Word" itself the substantial and proper name of the Only-begotten; rather, it only manifests the Son born of the Father without <term>passion</term> <note>original: *affectione*; in this context, it means without physical change or biological process</note>, just as a word comes from the mind, and shows that the Son is the messenger of the Father's will. And therefore, O wretched man, why do you pick at a name? When He is called Father, and Son, and Spirit, do you slide into material things, and imagine carnal fathers, and sons, and an airy spirit—perhaps a southern one, or a northern one, or another stirring up a storm? But if you wish to know what kind of Word God's is, hear the rest that follows.

### ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

<margin>A</margin>
**All things were made through Him.**] Do not think, he says, of a word which is diffused and dissolved into the air, but of the Maker of all things, both mental and sensible. Here again the Arians rise up and say that just as we say a door is made by an axe as if by an instrument, and the carpenter who moves this tool is another: so also through the Son all things are made—not that He is the Maker, but an instrument, like the axe of God the Father, the Maker, who uses the Son as a tool. And thus (they say) the Son is a creation <note>original: *factura*</note> established by Him, because all things are made through Him, just as an axe is made for the purpose of crafting all artificial things through it. And these are the malicious trifles of Arius. But what shall we say to them?

<margin>B</margin>
Simply and correctly: that if the Father created the Son for this purpose (as he says), as an instrument to have for the completion of creation, the Son would be less worthy than the created things. For just as other things made by an axe (which is an instrument) are more worthy—for the axe is made for their sake, not they for the axe's—so also the creation would be more worthy than the Only-begotten, for (as they say) the Father created Him for its sake, and thus if He were not going to create all things, He would not have produced the Only-begotten. What is more foolish than these words? "Even so," he says, "and how?" He did not say that the Word itself made all things, but he used the preposition "through" <note>original: *per*</note>. How? So that you might not suspect that the Only-begotten is a Son without a source <note>original: *absque principio*</note> and an adversary to God; for that reason he said that the Father made all things through the Word.

<margin>C</margin>
For imagine a certain king who has a son who is also a king, and he is about to build a city, and he grants its construction to him. Just as, therefore, saying that a city was built through the king's son does not call the king's son a slave, but shows that this son has a father and is not alone. So also in this place, the Evangelist, saying that all things were made through the Son, manifested that the Father used Him as a mediator for the creation of things (so to speak)—not as one less than Himself, but of equal power, and as one capable of perfecting such things. Furthermore, I might tell you this: if the preposition "through" <note>original: *per*</note> offends you, and you seek to find in the scripture some discourse that says the Word itself made all things...

### ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

<margin>Psalm 101 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 102:25.</note></margin>
Hear David: *In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.* You see how he did not say "through you the heavens were made and the earth was founded," but rather *you founded* and *they are the works of your hands*, because he says these things about the Only-Begotten Son and not about the Father. Learn this also from the Apostle himself <note>Saint Paul</note>, who uses this 
<margin>Hebrews 1.</margin>

saying in the Epistle to the Hebrews. For he is the one who looked down upon the earth—whether he means this world we inhabit, or our nature which is entangled in the earth, or the flesh according to that saying,
<margin>Genesis 13.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>John 17.</margin>
*You are earth* <note>original: "Terra es"; usually "Dust you are" from Genesis 3:19</note>, which he also took upon himself; and he released us who were bound by the chains of sins, the children of those slain since Adam and Eve, so that he might declare the name of the Lord in Zion. For standing in the temple, he taught about his Father, just as he himself said: *I have manifested your name to men.* To whom, then, do these things apply? To the Father, or to the Son? Entirely to the Son. For he himself announced the name of the Father in Jerusalem while teaching. Therefore, after David said these things, he adds: *And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.* Does he not clearly introduce the Son as the Maker, and not as an instrument? But if the preposition "through" <note>original: "per"</note> seems to suggest a subordinate role to you, what will you say when Paul applies this to the Father? For he says, 
<margin>1 Corinthians 1.</margin>

<margin>Ibid.</margin>
*Paul, an Apostle through the will of God.* But enough of these matters; let us return to where we left off.

### All things were made through Him.
Moses, speaking of the visible creation, revealed nothing to us regarding mental <note>referring to intellectual or spiritual beings like angels</note> things. But the Evangelist, embracing everything in one word, said: *All things were made through Him*, both visible and invisible.

### And without Him was not anything made that was made.
Because he said that he made all things, so that no one might think that he also created the Holy Spirit, he adds that all things were made through him. And what "all things"? Those which were

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
made: just as if he were saying, "If anything exists from the created nature, that was made by the Word; but the Spirit, because he is not of that created nature, was not made by him." Therefore, without the power of the Word nothing was made—that is, nothing that belongs to that created and made nature.

<margin>Spirit-fighters <note>original: "πνευματόμαχοι" (Pneumatomachi)</note></margin>
### In Him was life, and the life was the light of men.
The "Spirit-fighters" <note>A group in the 4th century who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>, who deny that the Spirit is God, read this passage like this: *And without him was not anything made.* Then, having placed a period at that spot, they read as if from a different beginning: *That which was made in him was life.* They interpret the passage according to their own mind, saying that in this place the Evangelist is discussing the Holy Spirit, saying: "That which was made in him—that is, the Holy Spirit—was life." The Macedonians <note>Another name for the Pneumatomachi, followers of Macedonius.</note> say these things,
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Macedonians.</margin>
striving to show that the Holy Spirit is a creature, and to number him among those things which were made. But we do not read it thus; rather, having placed a period after saying *that which was made*, we read a new beginning: *In him was life.* For after he spoke of his office—that all things were made through him—he speaks afterward of his providence: that he not only created, but he himself is the one who preserves the life of all creatures. For *in him was life.* For he did not say, as you might suppose, that this Word is devoid of life, but *in him was life.* I know, however, that a certain one of the saints read the passage this way: *And without him was not anything made; that which was made was in him.* Then, having placed a mark, the following words begin: *Life was.* I think
<margin>C</margin>
also that this reading is not bad, but contains a correct sentiment. For that saint understood it in an orthodox way: that without the Word nothing was made of that which was made in him. For all things, whatsoever were made and created, were made in the Word itself, and without him they were not made. Then there was another beginning: *Life was, and the life was the light of men.* The Evangelist calls the Lord "Life," because he contains the life of all things in himself, and because he was the mediator of spiritual life for all endowed with reason. Moreover, he is "Light"—not some sensible light <note>physical light perceived by the eyes</note>, but spiritual light, which illuminates the soul itself. He did not say, however, that he is the light of the Jews only, but of all men. For all men, according to the mind we have received, are illuminated.

For the reason given to us, by which we are called "rational" <note>original: "rationales"; creatures possessing 'logos'</note>, is a light that leads us to those things which are to be done and those which are not to be done.

> **And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.** ] The light—that is, the Word of God—appears in the darkness—that is, in death and error. For even in death he acted as if he had been conquered, so that he might force death to depart from him, just as he did with those whom death had previously swallowed. And the preaching of the Word shines even in the error of the Gentiles. And the darkness did not comprehend him; for death did not seize him, nor did error. For this light is invincible, I mean God the Word. However, some have thought that the "darkness" meant the flesh and this life. For the Word, having been made flesh, shone in this life and in the flesh. And the darkness—I mean the opposing power <note>the devil or spiritual darkness</note>—tried indeed to persecute the light, but found it invincible and tireless. Moreover, the flesh is called "darkness," yet it does not become so by nature (heaven forbid!), but on account of sin. For the flesh has nothing evil in it at all if it is moved naturally; but if it is moved contrary to nature and serves sin, it becomes and is called "darkness."

> **There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.** ] After we have been told about the existence of the Word of God before the ages, and because the Evangelist is about to speak of the incarnation of the Word, he inserts a discourse concerning the Precursor <note>John the Baptist</note>. And who else but John the Precursor should have a discourse about his birth, who ran before even the birth of the Lord? Therefore, the Evangelist says of the Precursor that he "was a man sent from God"—that is, truly sent by God, for the false prophets were not sent by God. Furthermore, when you hear that he was sent by God, do not think he says anything private or merely human, but that all his words are divine. > **This man came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him.** ] This man, he says, was sent by God to bear witness to the light. Furthermore, lest anyone think that the Only-Begotten had need of this man's testimony for his own glory—as if he were in some part lacking—the Evangelist added that he came to testify of the Son of God, not because the Son has need of his testimony, but so that all might believe in him. But did everyone believe? Not at all. How then does the Evangelist say, "so that all might believe"? How? Insofar as it was within John's power, he testified for this reason: to draw everyone. Although some did not believe, he is not to be blamed for that. For the sun shines for this purpose: to illuminate everyone; but if someone shuts himself up in a dark house and does not enjoy the sunlight, what does that have to do with the sun? So also in this place: John was there so that all might believe; although the opposite happened, he is not the cause.

A saint can be called light, but not *that* light.

> **He was not that light, but came to testify of the light.** ] Since it often happens that the one who testifies is greater than the one to whom he bears witness, the Evangelist—lest you think that John, by testifying for Christ, was greater than him—kills that wicked suspicion by saying: "He was not that light." But someone might say: "Therefore, is neither John nor any of the saints to be called light?" We would certainly be right to call each of the saints a light, but we would by no means call them *the* light <note>referring to the use of the definite article in Greek, 'to phōs'</note>. Hence, if someone says to you, "John is light," agree with them. But if they ask, "Is John *that* light?" say no. For he is not properly light itself, but light by participation, having his brilliance from the true light.

<meta>This page continues Theophylact's commentary on the Prologue of John, specifically addressing the nature of the "True Light" and its relationship to the world, the rejection of early heresies, and the transition into the mystery of the Incarnation.</meta>

### CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
### ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>The heresy of Photinus and Paul of Samosata is overthrown.</margin>
He was the true light even before he was incarnated. And by this, he overthrows the heresy of Photinus and Paul of Samosata <note>Photinus and Paul of Samosata were 3rd and 4th-century bishops who taught that Jesus was a mere man who only began to exist at his birth from Mary.</note>, who teach in their dogmas that the Only-Begotten began only when he was born of Mary, and did not exist before this. Listen also, you Arian <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that the Son of God was a created being, not co-eternal with the Father.</note>, who deny that the Son of God is the true God; hear what the Evangelist says: *He was that true light.* And you also, Manichaean <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that believed the physical world was created by an evil deity.</note>, who say that we are the creatures of an evil craftsman, the devil, listen: because that true light "enlightens every man." If, therefore, that evil craftsman is darkness, he certainly enlightens no one; and thus, am I a creature of the true light? And how, someone might ask, does he enlighten every man, when we see so many shrouded in darkness? As far as he is concerned, he enlightens all. For tell me, I pray: Are not all rational? <margin>E</margin> Does not every nature know what is good? Is it otherwise? Do not all have the power to recognize the Creator from the things he created? And so, the reason <note>original: "ratio"; here meaning the human capacity for logic and moral judgment</note> given to us, and nature instructing us, <margin>Reason and nature are called the natural law.</margin> is what is called the natural law. This is called the light given to us by God. However, because some have not used their reason, they have darkened themselves. Some solve this difficulty in this way: The Lord (they say) enlightens every man coming into the world—that is, those who are in a better state, and who take care that their soul is enlightened, not allowing it to be unadorned and foul.

> **He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.** ]

He was in the world, just as God is present everywhere. Furthermore, because of his providence <margin>F</margin> and sustaining power, by which he preserves all things, he is said to be in the world: although when I say, he says, that he was in the world, it is because the world itself would not have existed unless he had established it. Certainly, he shows him to be the Creator: partly to restrain the madness of the Manichaeans, who <margin>The Manichaean and Arian heresies.</margin> say an evil craftsman produced all things; and to refute Arius, who said the Son of God was a creature; and partly to lead every man to confess the Maker, so that he does not serve the creatures, but adores the Creator. But the world, he says, did not know him: that is, that common crowd which is addicted to worldly affairs. For "the world" signifies both this universe and also—

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
—as it is said in this place—the fact that the world was made through him. However, it also signifies those who "savor" worldly things, just as it says here that "the world did not know him," that is, earthly-minded men. For all the saints and prophets recognized him.

> **He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.** ]

At this point, he most clearly enters into the discourse regarding the Incarnation. And the whole context of the thought is this: The true light was indeed in the world without flesh, and was not recognized. Then, he "came to his own" with flesh. By "his own," understand either the whole world, or the Jews whom he chose as the "portion of his inheritance" and as his own special people. And "his own" did not receive him—either the Jews, or the rest of humanity who were created by him.

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, just as he deplores the madness of men, so he also admires the mercy of the Lord. Those who were "his own," he says, did not all receive him. The Lord compels and drags no one by necessity, but has left it to their will and choice.

> **But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.** ]

Whether they be slaves or free, whether children or old men, whether Barbarians or Greeks, to as many as received him, he gave them the power to become children of God. And who are they? Those who believe in his name; those, namely, who, having accepted the Word, received and declared the <margin>Faith alone does not make one a child of God.</margin> true light through faith. For this reason, he did not say that he *made* them children of God, but that <margin>C</margin> he gave them *power* to become children of God. Why so? Listen: Because it is not enough to be baptized to guard one's purity; but there is also need for much zeal, so that the image of adoption as a son of God, shaped in baptism, may be kept unstained. Therefore, many indeed received the grace of adoption in baptism, but through slothfulness, they did not remain children of God until the end. Perhaps someone might also say that many receive him through the fact that they only believe—such as those called catechumens <note>Students receiving basic religious instruction before being baptized.</note>—but they have not yet become children of God; they have the power, however, when they wish to be baptized, to obtain this grace—I mean the adoption as sons. Someone might also say this: Although in baptism—

<summary>Theophylact explains that Christ is the eternal Light who provides the "natural law" of reason to all, while refuting heresies that deny Christ's divinity or the goodness of creation. He emphasizes that while the Incarnation offers the "power" to become children of God, this grace must be maintained through free will, baptism, and active virtue.</summary>

### CHAPTER 24. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>Galatians 4</margin>
We receive the benefit of adoption now, but we are to receive a perfect adoption in the resurrection, and we hope to receive the most perfect adoption then; just as Paul says, "Because we receive the adoption of sons." <note>original: "Quia adoptionem filiorum accipimus"; Theophylact is referencing Romans 8:23 or Galatians 4:5 regarding the "not yet" aspect of salvation.</note> For this reason, the Evangelist here did not say that "as many as received him, he made them sons of God," but rather "he gave them power to become sons of God," which means he gave them the ability to receive that grace in the future age.

"Who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."] He makes a comparison, in a way, between divine and carnal generation <note>original: "generationis"; referring to the process of being born or brought into existence</note>—and not without reason—bringing to our memory carnal births so that, having recognized the vileness and humility of carnal generation by comparison to divine grace, we might run toward the latter. He says, therefore, "Who were born not of blood," meaning specifically from menstrual blood. For from these, the embryo has its nourishment and growth. Some say, however, that the seed first casts off the nature of blood, and is then transformed into flesh and another arrangement. Because it is probable that some would say the birth of Isaac <margin>Genesis 18.</margin> was almost like the generation of those who believe in CHRIST—for indeed, Isaac was not born of blood, since Sarah’s menstrual cycles had ceased—therefore, because it is possible for some to suspect such things, he adds: "Nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man." For although <margin>1 Samuel 1. Genesis 21.</margin> his birth was not from blood, it was nevertheless from the "will of man." For the man certainly willed to father a boy for himself from Sarah. "Of the will of the flesh," however, is like Samuel from Hannah <note>original: "Anna"; the Latin form of the name Hannah from 1 Samuel.</note>. For one might say Isaac was from the "will of man," but Samuel from the "will of the flesh," that is, of Hannah. For that sterile woman "thirsted" (he says) to possess a son. Perhaps, however, both were from both. But if you wish to learn something else, listen: Carnal intercourse either happens from natural heat—for often a person is of a warmer "complexion" <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of bodily humors determining one's temperament and physical urges.</note> and is therefore more prone to intercourse, and this he calls the "will of the flesh." Or, because of bad habit and lack of restraint in diet, the impulse for copulation becomes more violent, and he calls that the "will of man," because it 

<column-break/>

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, 318

is not from natural constitution, but is the result of a man’s lack of restraint. Perhaps also, because a woman is sometimes found more prone to intercourse, and sometimes a man, by the "will of the flesh" he understood the woman’s [desire], and by the "will of man" he signified the man’s wantonness. But you will understand correctly by "will of the flesh" the concupiscence <note>original: "concupiscentiam"; strong physical desire or lust</note> rising up in the flesh toward intercourse; and by "will of man," the coming together for the union by the one who desires it, which is the beginning of the act. He placed both there because many indeed feel desire, yet are not immediately carried away by it, but command it and do not fall into the act. But those who are conquered are first ignited and stirred by the flesh and titillating concupiscence to want intercourse. Therefore, the Evangelist rightly joined the "will of the flesh" and the "will of man," because in nature, concupiscence precedes intercourse, and in the act of union, both necessarily precede. All these things are said for the sake of those who often ask many things foolishly, since properly speaking, one single thought is declared by all of them: a clearer manifestation of how carnal generation is completed. 

<margin>What is the difference between us and the Israelites while they are called sons of God.</margin>
What more, then, do we who believe in Christ have than the Israelites had under the law? For they too were called "sons of God." There is indeed a great distinction between us and them. For since the law in all things held a "shadow" of things to come <margin>Hebrews 10. Galatians 4.</margin>, it did not give the adoption of the sons of God to the Israelites except as in a figure and a type <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note>. We, however, according to the truth, having received the Spirit of God through baptism, cry out: "Abba, Father." Just as their baptism was in a shadow and a figure, so it also prefigured our adoption; therefore, although they were called "sons," this nevertheless happened to them in a shadow and not in truth; they did not have the same adoption of sons that we have now through baptism.

"And the Word was made flesh."] After he said that we who believe in Christ, if we are willing, are made children of God, he now adds the cause of so great a good. For he says: "Do you wish to learn what secured this adoption as sons for us? It is because the Word was made flesh." But when you hear that "the Word was made flesh," do not imagine that he departed from his own nature and was turned into flesh; for he did not.

Theophylact clarifies that while Old Testament figures were called "sons," only through the Incarnation and Christian baptism do believers receive the "truth" of adoption rather than a mere "shadow."</summary>

### CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>
...He would not have been God if he had been changed or altered; but remaining what he was, he became what he was not. <margin>Apollinarius of Laodicea, a heretic.</margin> Apollinarius of Laodicea <note>A 4th-century bishop whose teachings were declared heretical because he argued that Jesus had a human body but a divine mind, rather than a full human soul.</note> stirred up a heresy from this point. For his dogma was that our Lord and God did not take on a perfect human nature—namely, a body with a rational soul—but only flesh, devoid of a mental and rational soul. "For what need did he have of a soul," he asked, "he who possessed the deity, which governed the body just as our soul directs our body?" He had a pretext, as was thought, from the present saying: *And the Word was made flesh.* <note>original: "Et verbum caro factum est"</note> For, he said, the text did not say, "And he was made man," but rather "flesh." And thus he did not take on a soul which possesses mind and reason, but flesh <margin>E</margin> without mind and reason. But that wretched man was ignorant <margin>Genesis 18.</margin> of the fact that Scripture frequently names the whole by a part; for instance, when it is about to commemorate the whole man, it names him by a part—namely, the soul—as in: "Every soul that is not <margin>Psalm 64.</margin> circumcised shall be put to death." <note>Theophylact is citing the principle of <term>synecdoche</term>, where a part represents the whole.</note> For behold, instead of saying "every man," he says a part, namely "the soul." And again, he names the whole from the <margin>Luke 3.</margin> flesh, as when he said: *And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.* <note>original: "Et videbit omnis caro salutare Dei"</note> For wishing to say "every man," he used the name of "flesh." So also the Evangelist, instead of saying "the Word was made man," said *the Word was made flesh*, naming the whole man, constituted of soul and body, by a part. But perhaps because flesh is more foreign to the divine nature, the Evangelist, wishing to signify the immense mercy of God, mentioned the <margin>F</margin> flesh, so that we might stand in awe of his ineffable kindness, because for the sake of our salvation he assumed that which was foreign to his nature and in every way strange to him—I mean, the flesh. For the soul has a certain kinship with God, but the flesh in no way communicates with him. And therefore I believe the Evangelist used this name: not because the Word was in any way devoid of the assumption of a soul, but for the greater demonstration of the marvelous and astounding sacrament. For if the incarnate Word had not assumed a human soul, our souls would be incurable. For what he did not assume, he did not heal. <note>original: "Nam quod non assumpsit, non sanauit"; this is a central principle of orthodox Christology, famously articulated by Gregory of Nazianzus.</note> And how ridiculous it would be if the soul—which was the first to fall ill (for it was the soul that, when it believed <meta>catchword: the words</meta>

Truly, let Apollinarius be gone! But we, when we hear that *the Word was made flesh*, believe that he was made whole man; since it is the custom of Scripture to name the whole man from a part, whether from the flesh or the soul. <margin>Nestorius</margin> Moreover, Nestorius <note>A 5th-century patriarch of Constantinople who was accused of teaching that Christ was two separate persons, one divine and one human, joined together.</note> is also convicted by this saying. He did not say that he was flesh "apparently," but that he was so in truth and substance, and not a phantom. For it would be absurd and foolish to believe that, since he is and is called the Son of God, he would lie about his incarnation. It is in this manner that a lying phantom always shows itself.

# CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...just as the dweller is the one who lives in it: so also the Word is said to dwell in us, that is, in our nature; and He is of a different nature than our own. Let the <margin>Armenians.</margin> Armenians <note>Theophylact is referring to the non-Chalcedonian Armenian Church, which he characterizes here—from his Byzantine perspective—as holding to a "single nature" (Monophysitism) in Christ.</note> be confounded, who worship only one nature. We learn, therefore, through the phrase, **The Word was made flesh** <margin>D</margin> <note>original: "Verbum caro factum est"</note>, that the Word Himself was made man; and though He is the Son of God, He became the son of a woman, who is properly called the <term>God-bearer</term> <note>original: "Deipara," the Latin equivalent of the Greek "Theotokos."</note>, because she gave birth to God in the flesh. However, through what he says, **He dwelt among us**, we learn that two natures are to be believed in Christ. For even if He is one according to <term>hypostasis</term> <note>The individual "person" or reality of Christ.</note>, that is, according to person, He is nevertheless two according to natures: namely, God and man. Moreover, the divine nature and the human nature were not one, even if they are seen together in the one—I mean, in Christ.

<margin>E</margin>
**And we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.** After he said that He was made flesh, he now adds, *And we beheld His glory*, specifically while He was in the flesh. For since the Israelites were unable to look upon the face of <margin>Exodus 34.</margin> Moses, which had been made radiant from his conversation with God, much more would the apostles have been unable to contain the naked deity of the Only-begotten, unless He had appeared through the flesh. We beheld His glory, however—not such a glory as Moses had, or the glory with which the Cherubim and Seraphim appeared to the prophets—but such a glory as he taught belongs to the Only-begotten of the Father, which is inherent in Him by nature. For the word <margin>The meaning of "As."</margin> "as" <note>original: "velut"</note> here is not a word of similarity, but of confirmation and beyond-doubt determination. Just as when we see a king coming with great glory, we say that he goes forth *as* a king—that is, <margin>F</margin> that he truly is a king—so also in this place you ought to understand *as of the only begotten* to mean that the glory which we beheld was, in truth, the glory of the Son. **Full of grace and truth.** He was indeed full of grace, according to the fact that His speech was gracious; or as I might say, following <margin>Psalm 44.</margin> David: *Grace is poured into your lips.* And the Evangelist says: <margin>Matthew 7.</margin> *All wondered at the words of grace which proceeded from His mouth.* And He bestowed grace upon all the saints, as was fitting for them. Moreover, He was full of truth: because the things which the prophets and Moses himself either said or did were figures in all things. But the things which Christ did and said

were full of truth, since He was grace itself and truth itself, who supplied them to others. But where did they behold it? Some suspect that it was perhaps on Mount Tabor <note>The site of the Transfiguration.</note>. Perhaps this is also true, that not only on the mountain, but also in all things which He said and did, they beheld His glory.
<margin>Matthew 3. Mark 1.</margin>
**John bears witness of Him, and cried out, saying: This was He of whom I said, He who comes after me is preferred before me, for He was before me.** The Evangelist frequently employs the testimony of John, not to make the Lord worthy of faith through the words of a servant, but because the crowds held a great opinion of John; for their sake, he employs John as a witness for Christ, <margin>B</margin> because John was called "great" among them and was believed to be above all others. Moreover, the word "cried out" shows the great confidence and freedom of John. For he did not cry out about Christ in a corner, but with great freedom. But what did he say? *This was He of whom I said.* John, even before he saw Christ, testified about Him; and this was by the singular will of God, so that he might not seem to be testifying honorable things about Christ's person out of personal favor. Therefore he says, *of whom I said*, that is, even before I saw Him. **He who comes after me**, clearly in regards to the time of birth. For the forerunner of Christ was six months older, <margin>Luke 1.</margin> according to his birth in the flesh. **He was before me**, that is, <margin>C</margin> He was more honorable and more glorious than I. Why? Because He was also prior to me according to His divinity. But the foolish <margin>The Arian heresy.</margin> Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> have interpreted this saying poorly. For, wanting to demonstrate that the Son of God was not begotten of the Father but was like one of the other creatures, they say: "Behold, John testifies of Him, *He was before me*, that is, He was before me because He was created by God as one of the creatures." They are refuted, however—having understood the saying badly—by that which follows. For what kind of logic appears if it were said: "This one (namely, Christ) was created 'before me' (that is, earlier than I), *because* He was prior to me"? For it is foolish in every way to say that God created Him earlier than me *because* He was prior to me; rather, it would be more necessary to say the opposite: "Because He is prior to me, therefore He was 'before me'" (that is, was created).

We, however, understand in an orthodox way that He who "was to come after me" according to His birth in the flesh from the Virgin, "was before me"—that is, He was more glorious and more worthy than I, because of the miracles that happened regarding Him at His birth, in His upbringing, and in His wisdom. This is rightly so. For He was prior to me according to His divine birth from the Father, even though He came after me according to His arrival in the flesh.

<margin>B</margin> **And of His fullness we have all received, and grace for grace.** ] These too are the words of the Precursor <note>The "Precursor" refers to John the Baptist.</note>, saying concerning Christ that we and all the prophets have received from His fullness. For He possesses a greater grace than the men who were inspired by the Spirit. For being the fountain of all good, and of all wisdom and prophecy, He overflows; He gives Himself to all who are worthy, and while flowing out, He remains full and is never exhausted. We have received grace—namely, that of the New Testament—in place of the grace of the ancient Law. And because that old testament has become aged, we have received the new in its place. And how, one might ask, did he call the Old Testament "grace"? Because the Jews were adopted as sons and received by grace. For He says, "I chose you not because you were many, but because of your fathers." The fathers also were received by grace, and we, by common confession, have been saved by grace.

<margin>Why the New Testament is called grace, and also why it is called truth.</margin> <margin>F</margin> **Because the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.** ] He interprets for us how we have received a great grace in exchange for a small grace, and he says that the law was indeed "given" through Moses, with God using a man, Moses, as a mediator. But the New Testament is called "grace" because God granted us not only the remission of sins but also the adoption as sons. It is called "truth" because whatever the fathers of old saw or spoke of in figures <note>A "figure" is a symbolic person or event in the Old Testament that points toward a reality in the New Testament.</note>, He clearly proclaims here. Therefore, I say, the New Testament—which is called both grace and truth—was given not through some lowly human mediator, but through the Son of God. And notice how he says of the old: "It was given through Moses." For he was a servant and a subject. But of the New Testament, he did not say it was "gi-

<margin>A</margin> ven," but that it "was made" <note>original: "factum est"</note>: to show that grace and truth were made and brought to fulfillment by our Lord Jesus Christ as a Lord, not as a servant. For the Law was indeed given by God with Moses as a mediator; but grace was *made*—not just given—through Jesus Christ. "To be made" sounds of a certain authority; "to be given" indicates a ministry of service.

<margin>1 John 4.</margin> <margin>B</margin> <margin>Isaiah 6. Genesis 32.</margin> <margin>C</margin> <margin>What "the Father's bosom" signifies.</margin> **No one has ever seen God. But Christ, who is the Son and the Only Begotten, and is in the Father's bosom, not only sees Him but also announces Him to all men. And so, because He is the Son, and sees the Father, and is in His bosom, He rightly gave us grace and truth. But perhaps someone might say here: how do we learn in this place that no one has seen God, when the prophet says, "I saw the Lord"? The prophet indeed saw God, but not His actual substance <note>The "substance" or essence of God is considered invisible and unknowable in Byzantine theology.</note>, but rather a certain likeness and appearance, as much as he was able to grasp. And another saw Him in another figure, and another in yet another. From this, it is clear they did not see the truth itself; for they would not have seen it in different figures if it were simple and without form. Indeed, not even the angels see the substance of God, although they are said to see His face. For this entire expression indicates that God is always appearing to them. Therefore, of all beings, the Son alone sees the Father and declares Him. Furthermore, when you hear of the "Father's bosom," do not suspect anything physical about God. For the Evangelist, wishing to indicate to us that the Son is co-eternal with the Father, and true and inseparable, made mention of this human term.

<meta>This page continues Theophylact’s commentary on the first chapter of the Gospel of John. Having previously discussed the divinity of the Word, the text now moves to the historical testimony of John the Baptist and his interaction with the religious authorities from Jerusalem.</meta>

# CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin>
After witnessing what John testified concerning Christ—namely, that "He was before me," and that we all, including the prophets, have received from His fullness—he adds: *And this is the testimony.* What kind of testimony? That which he said above: "He was before me," and so on. But the things he says thereafter do not belong to Christ; these are the testimonies of John. Furthermore, the Jews had sent the most distinguished men they had to John—namely, priests and Levites, and those from Jerusalem—so that they, being wiser, might persuade John through flattery to confess that he himself was the Christ. Observe, however, how sinister their intention was. They do not immediately ask him, "Are you the Christ?" but rather, "Who are you?" But he, recognizing their malice, does not say who he is, but confesses: *I am not the Christ.* He was looking toward their true aim, and in every way enticing them to believe that the Christ was someone else—one whom they considered lowly, born of a lowly father (namely, a carpenter) and from a despised homeland (namely, Nazareth), from which they believed nothing good could come. Yet they held a great opinion of the Precursor <note>John the Baptist is often called the "Precursor" or "Forerunner" because he prepared the way for Jesus.</note> himself, because he was born of a father who was a chief priest, and he led an "angelic" life, one seemingly free from material needs. Hence we rightly admire God for how He thwarts them through the very means by which they thought they would harm the glory of CHRIST. For they questioned John as a man worthy of trust, intending to use his testimony as a pretext for their unbelief in Christ <margin>E</margin> if he had not confessed that Jesus was the Christ. But it turned out otherwise, and the testimony was turned against them. For when they found that the one they held to be faithful testified such magnificent things about Christ, and did not claim the honor for himself, their plan failed.

<margin>Isaiah 40</margin>
*And they asked him: "What then? Are you Elijah?" and he said, "I am not." "And are you the prophet?" and he replied, "No." They said therefore to him, "Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say of yourself?" He said, "I am the voice of one crying in the desert: Make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said."*] They thought Elijah was going to come, persuaded by an old tradition; hence they asked if he was Elijah, because his life was similar to Elijah's. He denied this, and also the question: "Are you the prophet?" He denied this as well,

# EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.
### PAGE 322

<margin>A</margin>
even though he was a prophet. And how, then, does he deny it? How? Because they did not simply ask him, "Are you a prophet?" but rather, "Are you *the* prophet?" <note>In the original Greek, the use of the definite article "the" indicates a specific, expected figure.</note> making the interrogation with the definite article—that is, "Are you that prophet who was expected," of whom <margin>Deut. 18.</margin> Moses said: *The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you.* Therefore, John did not deny that he was a prophet, but that he was *that* specific prophet who was expected. Because they had heard Moses saying a prophet was to be raised up, they hoped because of certain circumstances that John would be that prophet. Then they pressed him again: "Tell us, who are you?" Then he answered them: *I am the voice of one crying in the desert.* "I am," he says, "the one of whom it is written: 'The voice of one crying in the desert.'" For unless you add "the one of whom it is written," the construction of the speech would seem somewhat absurd. <margin>B</margin> But what is he "crying"? *Make straight the way of the Lord.* "I am a servant," he says, "and I prepare the ways of the Lord in your hearts." Therefore, make those things straight, you who are deceitful and crooked, and make them level, so that the Lord Christ may journey through you. After this, he brings in Isaiah as a witness. For when he had said magnificent things about Christ—that He was the Lord—and had taken up the work of a servant and a herald for himself, he fled to the prophet for confirmation. Perhaps someone might explain "I am the voice of one crying" this way: "I am the voice of Christ crying out," that is, clearly announcing the truth. For all who were under the Law sounded softly and humbly, <margin>C</margin> as those who had not yet reached the time of Gospel truth. And this was surely the "unrefined nature" of the voice in Moses, because the Law was obscure and not manifest. But since CHRIST is the truth itself and announces to us all things that are the Father’s, He is the one "crying out." Therefore John says: "I am the voice of the Word crying out, dwelling in the desert." Then follows another principle: *Make straight the way of the Lord.* John is rightly called a "voice" because he was the precursor of Christ, just as a voice precedes a word. And to speak more clearly: <margin>Voice is an inarticulate breath.</margin> A voice is an inarticulate breath <note>original: "spiritus inarticulatus"</note> that comes out of the chest; but when it is articulated by the tongue, then it becomes a word. First, therefore, is the voice, and then the word. John was first, and then Christ, according to His coming in the flesh.

### CHAPTER I. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

And indeed, the baptism of John was not "articulated" <note>original: *articulatum*; here meaning fully defined or possessing the spiritual power of the Holy Spirit</note>, for <margin>D</margin> it was not done in the spirit; but Christ’s was indeed articulated. For it contained nothing of shadows or figures, but was done in the spirit.

And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees, and they said to him, "Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?" After they could not draw him to their side through flattery, they terrified him with harsher and more threatening words, so that he might say what they wanted, and confess that he was the Christ. "Why then do you baptize?" they asked, saying, "Who gave you this authority?" Moreover, it is shown from this speech that they thought the Christ was one person, and the prophet who was expected was another. For they say, <margin>B</margin> "If you are not the Christ, nor that prophet," understanding Christ as one and that prophet as another, which was a mistaken view. For that prophet is Christ Himself, and our God. All these things they said, as I mentioned, to urge him to confess that he was the Christ. Indeed, if it is permitted to speak more truly, they were questioning him as if envying his glory. Therefore they do not ask if he himself is the Christ, but "Who are you?" as if saying, "Who are you, who attempts such a work, baptizing and purifying those who confess?" For indeed, the Jews do not seem to me to want John to be held as the Christ by the many, but to be questioning him out of malice and envy: "Who are you?" Therefore, the Jews were greatly cursed, and truly a "brood of vipers," who indeed accepted John when he was baptizing, but after they were baptized, they were ungrateful.

<margin>F</margin> John answered them, saying, "I baptize in water; but among you stands one whom you do not know. It is He who is to come after me, who was before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie." See both the gentleness and the truth of the saint. His gentleness, in that he speaks nothing harsh to them, even though they were insolent. His truth, because he was a most free witness of Christ’s glory, nor did he hide the Lord's glory to gain nobility for himself, but he confessed it. "I indeed baptize with an imperfect baptism, for it is in water alone, not having the remission of sins, but preparing for the receiving of the spiritual baptism, which

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> grants the remission of sins. "But among you stands one whom you do not know." For the Lord had mingled himself with the multitude, and it was unknown who he was or from where. Perhaps, however, someone might say that the Lord stood "in the midst" of the Pharisees in another way, but they did not know him: for because they seemed to have learned the Scriptures by heart, in which the Lord was announced, He stood in their midst—that is, in their hearts—but they did not know Him, as if not understanding the Scriptures, even though they held them in their hearts. <margin>1 Tim. 2</margin> Perhaps also, according to how the Lord was the "mediator between God and men" <note>This refers to 1 Timothy 2:5, which describes Christ as the bridge between the human and the divine.</note>, He stood in the midst of the Pharisees, wishing to reconcile them to God, but they did not know Him. He continually places this: "He who is to come after me," showing that <margin>B</margin> neither is his own baptism perfect, but only a precursor to the spiritual baptism. "He was before me"—that is, more worthy and more glorious, to such an extent that I do not dare to count myself even among his lowest servants. For to loosen a sandal is the work of the lowliest service. I know, moreover, that I have read this exposition in the works of a certain saint: the "sandal" is always taken to mean the sinful flesh, subject to corruption; and the "strap" as the bond of sins. Therefore John, in others who came out to him and confessed, was able to loosen the strap of sins. For those constricted by the bonds of their sins came out to him. <margin>Isaiah 53</margin> And through this, because he called them to repentance, he prepared the way for them, so that they might perfectly cast off that strap and the sandal of sin. <margin>C</margin> In Christ, however, finding no strap—that is, no bond of sin—rightly he neither loosened it, nor was he able to loosen it. For how could he loosen what he did not find? For "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth" <note>Isaiah 53:9</note>. The "sandal," however, is the coming of the Lord to us; and the "strap" is the manner of His incarnation, by which the Word of God was united and, in a certain way, bound together; certainly, it is impossible to untie this knot. For who could untie how God was bound to a body?

These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing. Why does he say these things happened in Bethany? To show the freedom of the great herald...

### CHAPTER OF THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

<margin>Bethabara.</margin> ...truth, that he preached these things concerning Christ not in a house, nor in a corner, but around the Jordan in the midst of a great multitude. It should be known, however, that the more corrected manuscripts say "in Bethabara." For Bethany is not across the Jordan, but near Jerusalem. <note>Theophylact is correcting a common geographical confusion in early manuscripts between Bethany (near Jerusalem) and Bethabara (the site of the baptism).</note>

->The next day John sees JESUS<-
coming to him, and says, Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world.] The Lord frequently came to his precursor <note>The "precursor" or forerunner is John the Baptist.</note>; why? Either simply because, as one among many, he himself was to be baptized by John, or so that some would not think that he was baptized as one liable to sins, just like the others. For this reason he came again, giving John the opportunity to correct this opinion; and therefore the Baptist says: <margin>B</margin> Behold the lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. For he who is so pure that he is able to take away and abolish the sins of others clearly did not receive the baptism of confession in the same way as the others. Furthermore, examine this saying diligently: "Behold the lamb of God." For this speech is addressed to those desiring and seeking to see that lamb who was foretold by Isaiah. <margin>Isaiah 15. <note>Likely a reference to the "Suffering Servant" in Isaiah, though the chapter number differs in modern Bibles.</note></margin> "Behold," he says, "the lamb you seek is here." For it is probable that many, having been taught by the prophetic book of Isaiah, had sought after who that lamb might be. Therefore, John points him out. He did not simply say "a lamb," but "the lamb." For there are indeed many lambs, just as there are many "christs" <note>original: *christi*; here used in the sense of "anointed ones," like kings or priests</note>, but he is the true lamb, who was prefigured by Moses and foretold by Isaiah. Furthermore, CHRIST is called the lamb of God <margin>F</margin> <margin>Why Christ is called the lamb of God.</margin> either because God accepted the death of Christ for our salvation, or because God delivered him over to death for us, just as we are accustomed to say, "this is his sacrifice"—meaning, he offered this sacrifice. Thus, the Lord is called the lamb of God because God the Father, out of his love toward us, gave him unto death. Note that he did not say, "who *took* away sin" <note>past tense</note>, but "who *takes away*" <note>present tense</note> our sins. For he daily takes away our sins: the sins of some through baptism, and of others through repentance. And while the lambs that were sacrificed under the Old Law abolished no one's sin at all, this one takes away and abolishes the sin of the whole world from our midst. Why, then, did he not say "sins,"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> but "sin"? Perhaps because by saying "sin" in the singular, he spoke of it as a whole. For just as we are accustomed to say, "Man has fallen away"—meaning all of humanity has fallen from God—so in this place, by saying "sin," he signified all sins. Or perhaps, because man was disobedient to God and fell into various passions, the "sin of the world" was that disobedience, which the Lord removed from our midst <margin>Philippians 2.</margin> by becoming obedient even unto death, healing the contrary with its opposite. <note>Theophylact uses a medical metaphor here: Christ's obedience "heals" the disease of human disobedience.</note>

This is he of whom I said: After me comes a man who was before me, because he was prior to me.] Previously indeed, to those who had come from the Pharisees, John said: "In the midst of you stands one whom you do not know, because he was before me." Now <margin>B</margin> he points to him with his finger and reveals him to those who are ignorant, saying: "This is he of whom I testified to the Pharisees, that he was before me"—meaning, more worthy and more distinguished than I. Why? Because he was prior to me. Listen, Arius! <note>Arius was a 4th-century priest who taught that Jesus was a created being, not eternally God.</note> He did not say he was "created" or "made" prior to me, but that he *was* <note>original: *erat*; emphasizing eternal existence</note>. Listen also, you sect of Paul of Samosata <note>Paul of Samosata taught that Jesus was a mere man who became divine at his baptism.</note>, who say the Lord did not begin to be until he was born of Mary: he was prior to the precursor <unclear>confuting</unclear> according to his substance, which he had before the ages. For if, as you talk nonsense, the Lord had taken the beginning of his substance from Mary, <margin>Luke 1; Luke 3; 1 Corinthians 2.</margin> how could he have been prior to the precursor? For the precursor clearly preceded the Lord by six months according to his birth in the flesh. Moreover, the Lord is called "Man" <margin>C</margin> perhaps because of his perfect age, since he was thirty years old when he was baptized. Or perhaps because he is the "Man" (the husband) of every soul and the bridegroom of the Church. "For I have betrothed you," says Paul, "to one man, that I might present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." Therefore, the precursor says: "I am indeed the groomsman and the messenger; but after me comes the Man. For I indeed draw souls to faith in Christ, but he is the Man who will join them to himself."

And I did not know him; but so that he might be revealed to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water. And John gave testimony, saying: I saw the Spirit descending from heaven in the likeness of a dove, and it remained upon him. And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize with water...

### CHAPTER 1. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>
[...he said to me, "Upon whom you see the Spirit descend and remain upon him, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." And I saw, and I have testified, that Christ is the **Son of God**.] Since the precursor <note>The "precursor" is John the Baptist, who "ran before" Christ to prepare the way.</note> was a relative of the Lord—for the angel said to the Virgin, <margin>Luke 1</margin> "Behold, your relative Elizabeth has conceived"—John repeatedly says, "And I did not know him," so that no one would suspect that the precursor was showing favoritism to the Lord because of their kinship, or that he was bearing witness for the sake of family grace. He removes this suspicion, saying instead: "I have come to baptize so that he may be manifested to Israel." In other words, "I have come so that all may be led to faith in him and he may be shown to the peoples." For this is why I baptize: when I baptize, the people run together, and when they are gathered, Christ is made manifest to them, who is preached by me and shown present to those present. For if they did not flow together for the sake of baptism, how would the Lord be shown by John? For John did not walk about from door to door to point Christ out by hand and show him to each individual. <margin>E</margin> Therefore, for this reason he says: "I have come to baptize with water so that he might be manifested by me to the peoples as they gather for baptism." 

<margin>Fictional miracles of Christ’s childhood.</margin>
In this place we learn that the miracles of Christ’s childhood are fictional and lies, composed by those who wished to mock the mystery. For if they had been true, how could the Lord, who performed them, have remained unknown? For it is by no means likely that someone performing such miracles would not have been famous. But it is not so. For he performed no signs before he was baptized, nor was he known. <margin>F</margin> Instead, "He who sent me to baptize told me, 'Upon whom you see the Spirit descend, that is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'" John (as I said), in order to make his testimony concerning Christ unsuspicious, refers the testimony back to God the Father. "For I indeed," he says, "did not know him, but the Father revealed him to me at the baptism." 

<margin>Objection. Matthew 3.</margin>
Furthermore, someone might ask: "If John did not know him, how does Matthew say that he forbade him, saying, 'I ought to be baptized by you'?" <note>original: "Ego debeo a te baptizari"</note> It must be said, therefore, that it should be understood in this way: "I had not known him for a long time," or "before the baptism I had not known him." For at the time of the baptism...

<column-break/>

#### EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN
<page-num>325</page-num>

<margin>A</margin>
...he knew him. Or it must be said another way: that he indeed knew that he was the Christ, but that he was the one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit, he only learned when he saw the Spirit descending. I say, therefore, that "I did not know him" means he did not know he was the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit; yet he knew him to be greater than many others, and therefore, according to Matthew, he recognized him as entirely superior. But after the Holy Spirit descended, he recognized him more clearly and preached him to others. 

Now, the Spirit appeared to all who were present, and not to John alone. Why then, someone might ask, did they not believe? Because their foolish hearts were darkened; for even when they saw him performing miracles, they did not believe. <margin>B</margin> Some, however, say that not everyone saw it, but only those who were more pious. For although the Spirit descended in a physical form, it is likely that it did not appear to everyone, but only to the worthy. Indeed, <margin>Daniel 10; Ezekiel 1, 9, 10, 21.</margin> even the prophets saw many things in a perceptible form, just as Daniel and Ezekiel did, which nevertheless no one else saw. 

"And I saw and have testified that this is the Son of God." And where did John testify that this is the Son of God? For nowhere is it written; indeed, he calls him the "Lamb," but nowhere the "Son of God." From this, it is likely to guess that many other things were omitted. For not everything was written down. 

"The next day John stood again, and two of his disciples; and looking at Jesus as he walked, he says, 'Behold <margin>C</margin> the Lamb of God.' And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus."] Because of the sluggishness of the listeners, John is compelled to say the same things, so that by frequent testimony he might achieve something; and he was not mistaken. For he immediately offered two disciples to Christ. For since he was truly a friend of the bridegroom, <note>original: "pronubus" - a term for the person who attends the bride or groom and facilitates the marriage.</note> he did everything to lead human nature to the bridegroom. 

<margin>The Marriage and its Custom.</margin>
Therefore Christ remains silent, like a bridegroom, while the wedding attendant <note>The "pronubus," referring here to John the Baptist.</note> speaks everything. And truly the Lord came to the multitude like a bridegroom. For in a marriage, it is not the bride who goes to the bridegroom, but the bridegroom who goes to her, even if he is a king’s son. Therefore the Lord, intending to marry our nature, descended to it on earth, and once the wedding was performed, he himself took her into his house.

...of the father. And so, when John had gazed upon Jesus—that is, when he had shown even with his physical eyes the joy he felt in Christ and the miracle— <margin>D</margin> he said: "See, that is the lamb." But the disciples, soothed by his frequent testimonies, followed Jesus; they did not do this because they despised John, but rather because they were obeying him, as he was testifying to better things concerning Christ.

When Jesus turned around and saw them following him, he said to them: "What do you seek?" They said to him: "Rabbi" (which, if translated, means "Teacher"), "where are you staying?" He said to them: "Come and see." They went, therefore, and saw where he was staying, and they remained with him on <margin>Matthew 4</margin> <margin>E</margin> that day. While Matthew, after recounting the baptism, immediately leads him up into the mountain to be tempted, the present Evangelist <note>The "Evangelist" refers to John, the author of the Gospel.</note> leaves aside the things said by Matthew and reports what happened after the descent from the mountain. Therefore, after he was on the mountain and was tempted, there follows the gathering of the disciples and their approach to Christ. I believe this discourse demonstrates <margin>Who should be appointed a teacher.</margin> that no one should be appointed a <term>doctor</term> <note>In this context, "doctor" is used in the traditional sense of a "Doctor of the Church" or an authoritative teacher of the faith.</note> unless he has first ascended to the summit of virtues (for this is what the "mountain" signifies) and has overcome every temptation, bringing back a triumph over the tempter. Thus, the disciples follow first, and then they ask him where he stays. For it was not appropriate to speak in public with many people present, but rather to talk privately, as if concerning certain necessary matters. <margin>F</margin> Indeed, they are not even the ones to ask first, but CHRIST himself leads them to the questioning. For he says to them: "What do you seek?" He does not ask as if he were ignorant—for how could he be ignorant, he who knew the hearts of men?—but so that through the question he might provoke them to say what they wanted. It is likely that they were blushing and felt deep reverence for him, to whom John had given testimony as being more than just a man. I would wish you to admire their good affection toward Christ. For they not only followed him, but they also greet him as "Rabbi," that is, teacher, even though they had heard nothing yet from his own lips. Desiring therefore to learn something from him in private, they ask where he stays. For in quietness, things are both spoken and heard more conveniently. The Lord, however, does not give them the location of the house, but says: "Come,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and see." He does this both to entice them more toward following him, and to test their desire to see if they are burdened by the journey. For if they had approached with a cold or half-hearted mind, they would by no means have followed him all the way to the house. But how is it that Christ says elsewhere that the Son of Man <margin>Objection</margin> <margin>Luke 9</margin> has "nowhere to lay his head," while in this place he seems to have a house? These two points are not in disagreement. For when he says he has nowhere to lay his head, he does not mean that he has no lodging at all, but that he has nothing of his own. If, therefore, he lived in a house, he did not inhabit his own, but another's. <margin>B</margin> Not in vain does the Evangelist assign the time, noting that it was the "tenth hour" <note>The "tenth hour" in the Roman/Jewish system was roughly 4:00 PM, near the end of the day.</note>, but he does so to teach both teachers and disciples that they should defer their duties for no reason of time. The teacher should not make an <margin>Fitting time.</margin> excuse and say it is evening; and the disciple should know that every time is the right time for doctrine, nor should the hearing of it be put off until tomorrow. From this we learn that the disciples had stomachs that were minimally burdened, but were accustomed to fasts; for the time that others spend on the rest of the body—being heavy with food and unable to focus on serious work—they spent on doctrine. Thus were the disciples of John distinguished by their fasts. But look, I pray you, how Christ turns himself toward those following him and shows them his face. For unless you have followed Jesus through good action, you will not reach the contemplation of the face of the Lord, <margin>C</margin> nor will you go to his dwelling—that is, you will not arrive at the illumination of divine knowledge. For he dwells, it says, "in unapproachable light." <margin>1 Timothy 6</margin> <note>The original margin notes "1 Tim 7," but 1 Timothy only has six chapters; the quote "unapproachable light" is from 1 Timothy 6:16.</note> Therefore, unless one has purified himself and followed after purification, how will he be enlightened by knowledge?

Now Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard from John and followed him. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him: "We have found the Messiah" (which is, if you interpret it, Christ). And he led him to Jesus. Jesus, having looked at him, said: "You are Simon, son of Jonah; you shall be called Cephas" (which may be interpreted as Peter). He gives us the name of Andrew, but not of the other disciple. Some say that other person was John, the one who wrote these things. Not—

### CHAPTER 1. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

Some say that [the other disciple] was not one of the more noble ones. Besides, there would have been no benefit in knowing his name. But he mentions Andrew because he was more distinguished, and because he brought his own brother. Observe, I pray, how much he loved his brother and how he did not hide the good from him, but shared the treasure with him and released a cry of joy, saying: "We have found him." And it is likely that they had desired this for a long time and had meditated on seeking him. Nor does he simply say "Messiah," but "the Messiah"—with the article—meaning the one who is properly the Christ. For there was only one who was expected by them, although there were many "christs" <note>The word "christ" (christos) in Greek means "anointed one." In the Old Testament, many kings and priests were "christs" or anointed ones, but Andrew refers to *The* Christ, the promised Savior.</note> who were also called sons of God.

<margin>B</margin>
Moreover, he led him to Jesus, not because he [Peter] was of such flighty character as to be moved by every word, but because he had received the words his brother spoke about Christ with a fervent and good spirit. For it is likely that Andrew said more to him and clearly announced Christ to him, as one who had been taught certain more secret things during the time he stayed with Christ. But if someone persists in arguing that Peter was easily led, let him learn this: it is not written that he immediately believed Andrew, but that Andrew led him to Jesus. This indicates a more solid mind, not one tossed about by any wind. For he did not simply accept Andrew’s word, but wanted to see Christ himself; so that if he found him worthy of faith, he would follow, and if not, he would withdraw. Thus, being led to Jesus was a sign of a studious mind, not a frivolous one. What, therefore, does [Jesus] do? For since prophecies are not the least of signs—indeed, they persuade men the most—he predicts things concerning Peter: "You," he says, "are Simon son of Jonah; <margin>Prophecies.</margin> then, regarding what shall be, "You shall be called <term>Cephas</term>." <note>Cephas is the Aramaic word for "Rock," which translates to "Petros" in Greek and "Peter" in English.</note> For when that which is present is spoken of, that which is future also becomes credible. However, he did not say "I will call you Peter," but "you shall be called." For he did not want to indicate his own authority from the beginning, because they did not yet have firm faith in him.

<margin>Mark 3</margin>
But why does he give this man the name Peter, while he calls the sons of Zebedee "Sons of Thunder"? <note>original: "Boanerges"</note> It is so that...
