### AN EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN
<page-num>327</page-num>

A ...he might show that he is the same one who long ago gave names; <margin>Genesis 17</margin> and just as he does now, so also then he changed the name of "Abraam" to "Abraham," and "Sarai" to "Sarah." You should know that "Simon" is interpreted as "obedience," while "Jonah" means "dove." Therefore, obedience is the daughter of the gentleness signified by the dove; and he who possesses obedience is himself made into a "Peter" <note>the Rock</note>, advancing through obedience so that he may be strengthened in what is good.

<margin>B</margin>
The next day, Jesus wanted to go out into Galilee. And he found Philip, and Jesus said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law and the prophets: Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth." Andrew, having heard the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist</note>, and Peter, having heard Andrew, followed Jesus. But Philip seems to have heard no one, and yet immediately followed the Lord when he said "Follow me." Why is it, then, that he believed so instantly? It seems, first, that the voice of the Lord touched his soul with a certain "sting of love." For the voice of the Savior was not spoken simply, but immediately caused those who were worthy to burn inwardly with love for him; just as Cleopas said: <margin>Why the disciples called by Christ followed immediately. Luke 24</margin> "Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road?" Furthermore, because Philip had a concerned heart and meditated much on the writings of Moses, and was always expecting the Christ, he believed as soon as he saw him. For this reason he also says, "We have found JESUS," which shows <margin>C</margin> that he had always been seeking him. Perhaps, however, he had also learned about Christ from Peter and Andrew. Indeed, it is likely that they, being from the same homeland, had spoken to him and told him about CHRIST; this is what the Evangelist seems to hint at when he says: "Now Philip was from the city of Andrew and Peter." That city was small—it would be more correctly called a village—which makes Christ’s power more worthy of wonder: that from those who brought forth no "fruit" <note>referring to the humble, uneducated nature of the village</note>, he chose his chief disciples. Therefore, Philip does not keep this good thing to himself, but shares it with Nathanael; and because Nathanael was learned in the law, Philip sends him to the law and the prophets, because...

**And Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come from Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see." Those words of his were not born of unbelief, but of a diligent mind well-versed in the Law, which knew that <term>Christ</term><note>Theophylact emphasizes that Nathanael’s skepticism was actually a sign of his deep study of messianic prophecies.</note> would come not from Nazareth, but from Bethlehem. What then of Nathanael? Does he become less cautious because of these praises? Not at all; he presses on more clearly and evidently, wishing to learn something further. Therefore he asks, "How do you know me?" But Christ, by telling him things that no

### CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin>
...that the Lord saw Nathanael and enlightened his understanding, even though he was still under the Law. You should also know this, if these things please you, that the Lord saw Nathanael while he was still "under the Law"—meaning he was within the Law and searching its depths. For if he had not searched the depths of the Law, the Lord would never have seen him.

You should also know this: that the name "Galilee" is interpreted as "rolling" or "flowing" <note>original: "devolubilis". Theophylact uses this etymology to symbolize the ever-changing, unstable nature of the physical world.</note>. Therefore, the Lord went out into the "rolling" region of this world, or even into human nature itself. We also are "under the fig tree," which signifies the sweetness of sin, though it also contains no small amount of bitterness because of the repentance and judgments that follow. 

Just as the Merciful One sees and chooses those who confess Him as the Son of God and the King of His Israel—that is, the one who "sees God" <note>A traditional etymology of the name "Israel."</note>. <margin>B</margin> And if we apply our zeal, He will deem us worthy of even greater sights, and we shall see angels "ascending" to the height of the knowledge of God, yet "descending" again, because they are unable to grasp His unknowable substance. Or to put it another way: a person "ascends" when engaged in discourses on the divinity of the Only-begotten, but "descends" when they take joy in discussing the Incarnation and His descent into the lower regions.

### CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>Ornamental historiated drop cap 'E' featuring a scene with several figures standing before a classical architectural facade with a central archway.</image-desc>
**And on the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. And both Jesus and His disciples were called to the marriage. And when the wine failed, <margin>F</margin> the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine." Jesus said to her, "Woman, what is that to me and to you? My hour has not yet come."** 

They call the Lord to the wedding, not because they had seen miracles or any other great thing, but simply because He was known to them as an acquaintance. The Evangelist indicates this by saying, "The mother of Jesus was there, and his brothers." Therefore, just as they invited her and the brothers, they invited Jesus as well. He attended and did not reject the invitation, because He did not look for a prestigious house, but rather for our benefit and advantage. For He who did not disdain to become a servant much less disdained to come to a wedding. 

The mother encourages Him <header>COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 329</header>
<page-num>329</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> to perform a great miracle, having a high opinion of His power over her, both because of His miraculous conception and His birth. For she "kept all these things in her heart," and from them <margin>Luke 2</margin> she considered that her son was capable of something beyond human power. 

Nor was His mother moved to ask God to perform a miracle because of anything she had seen Him do previously. For while He was a child, He performed no miracles; if He had, He would have been known to everyone. However, His mother had heard the testimonies of John the Baptist regarding Him, and she already saw disciples following Him; from all these clues she inferred the power of her Son. 

Yet He rebukes her, and not without reason. He says, in effect: if wine is lacking, it is those who are in need who should approach and ask, not you, the mother. <margin>B</margin> For when a person is urged by their own family, it can cause a scandal to those watching; but when those who actually have the need ask for themselves, the request is free from suspicion.

Furthermore, in saying "My hour has not yet come," He does not mean that He is subject to the necessity of time or that He observes "lucky hours" (for how could we say this of the Maker of times and ages?), but rather that He performs all things at the most fitting moment. Because He was still unknown and hidden from many, and did not yet have all His disciples, and because those at the wedding did not yet recognize Him (otherwise they would have come and asked for wine themselves), He said, "My hour has not yet come"—meaning the opportune time is not yet here.

<margin>C</margin> But at this point the madness of Arius <note>Arius was a 4th-century priest who argued that Christ was a created being. Theophylact is refuting the Arian idea that Christ was "subject to time" like a normal human.</note> still presses on, attempting to show that the Lord is subject to hours and times. Learn then, O accursed one, that if He were subject to hours and times, how could He have performed the miracle immediately afterward? According to your argument, He should have been a slave to the "hour," and since the hour had "not yet come," He should have been unable to act. But He performed the miracle anyway; therefore, He does not serve the hours. 

Observe, I pray, how He does not resist His mother until the very end, nor in all things. Once He had briefly corrected her, He then fulfills her request to show her honor, and thereby gives us a model of the reverence we should show toward our parents.

**His mother said to the servants, "Whatever he says to you, do it." Now there were set there six stone water-jars...**

<margin>D</margin> ...according to the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three measures <note>original: "metretas", a Greek unit of liquid measure roughly equal to 9 gallons.</note>. Jesus said to them, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them to the very brim. And he said to them, "Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast," and they took it. <margin>]</margin> The mother [of Jesus] says to the servants, "Whatever he tells you, do it." This was so that as the need became greater, and as the others also approached and asked Him to show himself, He would not appear to rush or hasten into the performing of miracles for the sake of ostentation and vainglory. There were stone jars there for the purification of the Jews. For the Jews would wash themselves almost every hour, and then eat; for example, if they had touched a leper, or a corpse, or had been <margin>E</margin> with a woman, they would wash as if they were unclean. 
<margin>Palestine is waterless</margin> And since Palestine is a waterless region, and springs are not found everywhere, they always kept the jars filled with water so they would not have to run to the rivers, lest perhaps they become "unclean" [on the way]. It was not for nothing, therefore, that it said, "according to the purification of the Jews." It was to prevent certain unbelievers from suspecting that some remains of the vintage had stayed in the jars, and that when water was poured in, it produced a very thin wine; this detail shows that they were never containers for wine. Now, could He not have created wine out of nothing even without the jar being filled with water? He certainly could have, but often the sheer magnitude of a miracle makes it harder for people to believe. In the meantime, this allowed the servants who had poured the water into the jars to become witnesses of the miracle. <margin>F</margin> Furthermore, let us say that He is the very one who, in the vine, converts the liquid of water into wine. He commands the servants to present it to the master of the feast to taste. This was not without reason, but to prevent some from suspecting that it was a gathering of drunkards whose taste was corrupted, and who in their intoxication mistook water for wine. <margin>An exhortation from Theophylact and a moral exposition</margin> Therefore, so that such a suspicion would have no ground, He commands it to be given to the master of the feast, who was sober. For those to whom such a ministry is entrusted are more sober, so that by their command everything there is done in an orderly and composed manner. Otherwise, let us pray that these things may be fulfilled in us even now: namely, that a wedding may take place—that is, the 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> joining of God with our soul, as long as we are in Cana of Galilee—a place (I say) of this lower and "rolling" world <note>original: "devolubilis". Theophylact allegorically connects the name Galilee with the idea of a world that is unstable and constantly changing.</note>, which turns and causes other things to turn. That wedding cannot happen without the presence of Christ, His mother, and His disciples. For unless one believes in Christ, who was born of the Virgin Mary and spoke through the Apostles, how shall he be joined to God? Let us therefore understand what the Lord works through miracles in such weddings, and in such a joining of God to the soul. He converts water into wine and fills our six stone water jars. By "water," you should understand our dissolution and softness in our path and doctrine. By the "six jars," <margin>B</margin> understand the five senses through which we stumble in our actions, and the sixth jar, the "rational force," through which we are endangered in our doctrines. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ—the Word (I say) of the Gospel—converts anything in our senses that is watery and weak into wine that is flavorful and gladdens life and speech, whether in practical virtue or contemplative life. Thus our jars are filled with this good drink: the senses, so that we do not stumble in our active power; and the reason, so that we do not fall into wicked dogmas. Observe, however, that the "stone jars" stood there "because of the purification of the Jews." For "Judah" is said to mean "confession" <note>A traditional etymology; here it refers to the spiritual purification that comes through confessing one's sins.</note>; and he who repents is purified through the five senses by which he previously sinned. <margin>C</margin> The eye had looked wickedly, but the eye again pours out tears in confession and thus serves the purification. The ear heard the words of a harlot, but again it inclines itself to the words of the mouth of God; and so it is with the other senses. So also the rational virtue sins in dogmas, but again it cleanses the former malice when it returns to pious dogmas. Furthermore, they are "stone" jars either because we were formed from the earth, or because such wine must have solid containers and never be leaky. Paul was a "stone jar" in his rational power, even when he was a persecutor. <margin>Galat. 1.</margin> For he was a "zealot for the ancestral traditions" above all his contemporaries—and also when he was preaching. For he possessed such power of the word that he was believed by the Lycaonians to be Mercury, <margin>Acts 14</margin> as the "leader of the word."

But after the master of the feast <term>architriclinus</term> <note>original: "architriclinus", the official in charge of the banquet and seating arrangements</note> had tasted the water turned into wine, and did not know where it had come from—though the servants who had drawn the water knew—he called the bridegroom and said to him: "Every man puts out the good wine first, and when they have drunk freely, then that which is inferior. For if he had questioned the servants, they surely would have revealed the miracle, but no one would have believed them. For this was the beginning of his signs, and no one yet held such an high opinion of Christ; thus, if the servants had told the story, no one would have believed the miracle yet. Therefore, after other signs were shown, it became more credible, and gradually the servants, by telling this to everyone, were held as faithful witnesses. For this reason, the Lord arranged it so that the servants were not questioned, but the bridegroom was. Furthermore, He did not simply make wine, but the very best. For those things which are made through the miracles of Christ are much better than those produced by nature. And that the water was made into wine, the servants who drew the water were witnesses; but that it was indeed the best, the master of the feast testified. Surely all these things, as time went on, were proclaimed and made more credible to those who heard them. You can also understand the wine to be the word of the Gospel, while the water represents everything that came before the Gospel. They were more liquid and tasteless, not reaching toward that perfection.

# CHAPTER 2. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>How many years the temple of Solomon was under construction</margin>
...that they would do it, he affirms it will certainly come to pass. Let the Arians <note>Followers of Arius who argued that Jesus was a created being, not fully God.</note> hear how he speaks as the Lord and the destroyer of death: "I will raise." For he does not say, "the Father will raise," but "I will raise," using his own power and needing nothing from outside himself. However, the Jews, thinking he was speaking of the physical temple, mocked him. Since it was built in forty-six years, how (they ask) do you say you will raise it in three days? 

It should be known, however, that when the temple was first built by Solomon, all things were perfectly finished in twenty years. Later, after the captivity, when the Hebrews received the power to rebuild it, they began building under King Cyrus. But hindered by those who envied them, they prolonged the construction until the reign of King Artaxerxes <note>A reference to the long delay in rebuilding the Second Temple described in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah.</note>. Under him, having obtained an abundance of resources, they were scarcely able to finish the work with all their effort. Whence it is said that the Jews, while building, held a sword in one hand and a builder’s tool in the other, so much did they fear the neighboring Idumeans <note>The Edomites.</note>—though not the Persians, from whom (as I said) they received all their funding. And so they say that the construction after the captivity was done in forty-six years, because the Jews were prohibited and hindered from the time of Cyrus until Artaxerxes. 

And it is no wonder that the Jews did not recognize the miracle, since not even the disciples understood it. For two great obstacles stood in the way: first, that the resurrection was in itself so difficult to grasp—indeed, unknown to all—and second, that God inhabited his body. For after the resurrection, the disciples understood and believed the scripture. Which scripture? All of it that speaks of the resurrection; but most clearly that which says, "You will not abandon 

<margin>Psalm 15 <note>In modern Bibles, Psalm 16:10.</note></margin>
<margin>Isaiah 53</margin>
<margin>According to the Translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX).</note></margin>

...you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from and where it goes. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit. The Lord, leading Nicodemus away from a physical birth, says: *That which is born of flesh is flesh, and that which is born of Spirit is spirit*—that is, the person who is born through baptism is spiritual. For by "spirit," you should understand "spiritual." The Divine Spirit does not become baptized; rather, when a person receives the adoption of sons in the Spirit, along with grace and honor, they deserve to be called spiritual. Seeing that Nicodemus is still troubled, He says: *Do not marvel*, and then tries to teach him using a sensible example. *The Spirit* (He says) *blows where it wills.* From the wind (He says), learn greater things. For the wind—which in this passage He calls "spirit" <note>original: "spiritum." In both Latin and Greek, the same word signifies both "breath/wind" and "spirit," a wordplay lost in English translation.</note>—blows where it wills, and you hear its sound, yet you are ignorant of where it is carried. For it cannot be grasped or held back. By its natural power, it is carried toward some uncertain place. Furthermore, when He says "where it wills," it is not because the wind has a will of its own, but (as I said) the power implanted in it by nature is being shown. Therefore, if you are ignorant of how and where the wind blows—which is a "spirit" subject to the senses—how can you inquire so inquisitively into regeneration from the Divine Spirit? If this [physical] spirit cannot be grasped, much less will the grace of the Holy
<margin>
Macedonius.
Eunomius.
</margin>
Spirit be subject to the laws of nature. Let Macedonius <note>A 4th-century bishop who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit, claiming it was a created being.</note>, the opponent of the Spirit, be confounded, and Eunomius <note>A radical Arian who argued that the nature of God was entirely comprehensible to the human mind.</note> who preceded him. For the former makes the Spirit a servant, even though he hears in this place that *the wind blows where it wills*; therefore, the Holy Spirit has a much freer motion and will work where He wills and how He wills. Eunomius, however, sinning in that very same way, both called the Spirit a creature and reached such a level of stubbornness as to claim he knew God just as God knows Himself. Let him hear, therefore, that he knows neither the Spirit's impulse nor its end. How then will this impostor know the substance of God?

<summary>Theophylact uses the metaphor of the wind to explain the mystery of spiritual rebirth to a confused Nicodemus, while simultaneously rebuking early Christian heretics who tried to rationalize or diminish the Holy Spirit. He argues that if Nicodemus, a master of Israel, cannot understand the "earthly" miracle of baptismal rebirth, he will never grasp the "heavenly" mystery of the Son’s eternal divine origin.</summary>

<margin>Apollinarius</margin>

For this is what <term>Apollinarius</term> <note>Apollinarius of Laodicea (c. 310–390 AD) taught that Christ had a human body but a divine mind, a view later declared heretical because it undermined Christ’s full humanity.</note> taught: that Christ had a body from heaven, and passed through the Virgin as if through a pipe or channel. 

<margin>One hypostasis in Christ</margin>

Truly, because there is one <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hypostasis." A technical theological term referring to the distinct personhood of Christ, in whom divine and human natures are united.</note>—that is, one person, Christ, constituted from two natures—therefore all things that belong to the man are spoken of the Word, and again, those things which belong to the Word are attributed to the man. Thus, in this passage also, the "Son of Man" is said to descend from heaven because there is one person and one hypostasis. 

<margin>E</margin>

Furthermore, lest when you hear "he who descended," you think he is no longer in heaven, he says: *He who is in heaven.* Do not suspect that I am not there simply because I descended; for I am present here bodily, and I sit there with the Father as God.

->And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but have eternal life.<-

<margin>Numbers 21</margin>

He also teaches that, just as the Jews escaped death by looking at the image of the bronze serpent, much more shall we escape the death of the soul by looking toward the Crucified One and believing. See now, I pray, the figure, and compare it with the truth. There, the likeness of the serpent had the form of a beast, but it had no venom. In the same way here, the Lord is a man, but free from the venom of sin; he came in the likeness of sinful flesh—that is, in the likeness of flesh subject to sin—

<margin>A</margin>

though his flesh was not in the least "flesh of sin." And in that former time, those who looked escaped the death of the body; but now, those who look escape the death of the soul. Then, a suspended object healed the bites of a serpent; now, Christ cures the wounds of the spiritual dragon. When you hear "lifted up," understand it to mean "to be suspended." For he was suspended on high so that he might sanctify the air, he who had already sanctified the earth by walking upon it. 

<margin>The Cross: The Glory of Christ</margin>

But understand also what it means to be glorified. For in truth, the cross was the glory of Christ. For through this, by which he seemed to be condemned, he condemned the prince of this world. To speak more clearly: Adam died justly, for he had sinned; the Lord died unjustly, for he had not sinned. Therefore, until the crucifixion of the Lord, death justly prevailed over men. But because Christ was found without sin, what right did the devil have to kill him? And thus, because he died unjustly, he conquered the one by whom he was killed; and so he liberated Adam from the death which was justly inflicted upon him as one who had sinned. 

And another way: there were two things that held lordship over the human race: pleasure and 

<margin>B</margin>

sorrow. But the Lord was found unconquered by those two. For the devil had 

<margin>Matthew 4</margin>

taken him up the mountain, tempting him through pleasure; and when he found that Christ could not be conquered by this path, he later employed a greater engine—namely, sorrow—so that at least through that he might overcome him. 

<margin>C</margin>

For this reason, he stirred up all the disciples against him so that they might deny him; 

<margin>Matthew 4</margin>

the soldiers so they might mock him; the passersby so they might blaspheme; 

<margin>Matthew 26, 27</margin>

and in short, the Jews so they might crucify him—and even so, he found him unconquered. 

<margin>Luke 23</margin>

For the pain of the cross could not cause him to hate those who were crucifying him; rather, he loved them and prayed for them, saying: *Father, do not hold this sin against them.* You see how he conquered through the very thing by which he seemed to be conquered. So, therefore, his exaltation and glory was the cross.

Wondrous is the love of God toward the world—and so great that he did not give a prophet or an angel, but his Son.

### CHAPTER 3. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...his Son, and him the only-begotten. Indeed, if he had given an angel <margin>D</margin>, it would have been no small thing, since an angel is his faithful minister and servant, while we were enemies and apostates. But now, having given his Son, how much more excellent is the love he has shown? Likewise, if he had many sons and gave one, even that would have been great; but now he has given his only-begotten. Therefore, his goodness is worthily to be praised.

<margin>Arians</margin>

The <term>Arians</term> <note>Followers of Arius (4th century) who argued that Jesus was a created being and not of the same substance as God the Father.</note> say that he is called "only-begotten" because he alone was made and created by God, and all other things were made through him. To them we simply respond: If he had been called "only-begotten" without being called "Son," your shameless fiction might have some logic. But now, since he is called not only "only-begotten" but also "Son," <margin>B</margin> he does not allow it to be understood that way, but signifies that he alone was born from the Father.

Observe, I pray, how just as he said above that the Son of Man descended from heaven—even though the <margin>alternately</margin> flesh did not descend from heaven, but because of the one person and one <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hypostasis." A term for the individual person of Christ in whom divine and human natures are united.</note> he attributed the things of God to the man—so also in this place <margin>divine</margin> he attributes the things of man to the Word of God. For he says: "God gave his Son unto death," even though <margin>in Christ, both divine and human</margin> God remained impassible <note>original: "impassibilis." The theological doctrine that God’s divine nature cannot suffer pain or change.</note>. Yet because he was one and the same through the hypostasis—both the Word of God and the man who suffered for us—he is said to be the Son, and to have been "given" insofar as he truly suffered, not in his own nature [as God], but in his flesh.

What profit is there in the Son being given? Oh, it is great and beyond the human mind! So that everyone who believes in him may gain two things: one, that he does not <margin>F</margin> perish; the other, that he has life, and indeed eternal life.

<margin>Old Law. Gospel. Exodus 29, Deuteronomy 5:17, 32. Romans 3.</margin>

For the Old Law promised that those who pleased God would be filled with a length of days; but the Gospel bestows not a temporary life, but an eternal and indissoluble one. Because there are two advents of Christ—the one that has happened and the one that is to come—he says of the first advent that the Son was not sent to condemn the world. (For if he had come for this purpose, all would surely have been condemned, for all have sinned, as Paul also says.) Rather, he first came for this: to save the world, and this was his intention. However, by "accident" <note>In this context, a philosophical term meaning a secondary result that was not the primary goal.</note> he judges those who did not believe. For the Mo-

<column-break/>

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN
<page-num>337</page-num>

<margin>A</margin> -saic Law preceded him to rebuke sin and condemn transgressors. For it forgives no one, but as soon as it finds someone sinning in any respect, it inflicts punishment. Therefore, the first advent was not made for the sake of judgment, except accidentally judging those who did not believe, who are already judged. But the second advent will be to judge all, and to render to each according to his works.

He who believes in the Son is not judged; but he who does not believe is already judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. And this is the condemnation: that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness more than light. For their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his <margin>B</margin> works be exposed. But he who works the truth comes to the light, so that his deeds may be made manifest, because they were done through God.

What does "he who believes in the Son is not judged" mean? If he leads an unclean life, is he not judged? Most certainly he is, for such people are not truly "faithful," as Paul says: "They profess that they know God, but in works they deny him." Nevertheless, <margin>Immunity of life [virtuous living], not truly faithful, Titus 1. Unbelief is condemnation. Genesis 3, Psalm 1, John 12.</margin> in this place he says that because of the act of believing itself, he is not judged. However, he will pay heavy penalties for his evil works; but he will not be punished for the unbelief which he does not have, for he has believed once and for all. But he who has not believed is already judged.

How? First, because <margin>C</margin> unbelief itself is a condemnation. To be outside the light is itself the greatest punishment. Furthermore, although he has not yet been handed over to Gehenna [hell] here, he has gathered the causes of future punishment here. Just as a murderer, even if not yet condemned by a judge's sentence, is nonetheless condemned by the very nature of the deed. And Adam, on the day he ate from the tree, died; and although he still lived, he was dead by sentence and by the nature of the deed. Therefore, every unbeliever is condemned, and departing from here, he is soon to be handed over to punishment, not to be brought into judgment; according to that saying: "The impious shall not rise in judgment." For the impious are considered unworthy of giving an account, just like the devil. Therefore, they shall not rise into judgment, but into condemnation. Thus, in the Gospel, the Lord says that the prince of this world is already judged, not only because he did not believe...

<summary>Theophylact explains that Christ’s first coming was intended for salvation rather than judgment, though unbelief results in an immediate spiritual condemnation. He also refutes Arian claims by emphasizing Christ’s status as the true Son born of the Father.</summary>

### CHAPTER 3. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
### COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN
->338<-

<margin>How far parables should be adopted.</margin>
...but even made Judas a traitor, and was the author of destruction for others. Although the Lord in (D) parables introduces those who are to be punished—as if they were people from whom a reckoning is taken—do not be surprised. First, for this very reason, because the things said are parables, it is not necessary to take everything said in parables as <term>canons</term> <note>Strict rules or legal standards.</note> and laws. For on that day, each person, having a conscience as an unerring judgment, will have no need of another to rebuke them, but each will refute themselves and depart. Next, the Lord does not introduce the unbelieving as if they deserve to give an account; rather, he introduces the believers who were unmerciful. We, however, are speaking of the impious and unbelieving. For an impious and unfaithful person is one thing, and an unmerciful sinner is another. *This is the judgment, because light came into the world.* He shows in this place that the unbelievers are deprived of every excuse. For this is the condemnation (he says), because light came to them, and even so they did not approach it. For they did not sin in this alone, that they themselves did not seek the light, but this is the worst part: that the light came to them, and they did not receive it; therefore they were condemned. For if the light had not come, people could have pretended they were ignorant of what was good; but because God the Word truly came and gave his Word to illuminate them, yet they did not receive it, they are henceforth without any excuse. To prevent anyone from saying, "No one prefers darkness to light," he sets down the cause why people have clung to darkness. For (he says) <margin>What Christianity requires.</margin> (E) their works were evil. Because Christianity requires not only correct doctrines but also an honest life, and they themselves wished to be involved in the mud of sin, therefore the wicked do not want to come to the light of Christianity and subject themselves to my laws. Furthermore, he who "does the truth" and strives and aspires to a life that pleases God, he approaches Christianity as if to the light, so that he may profit more in what is good, and his works may appear to have been done according to God. Whoever is such, with right faith, also establishes an honest life and shines before all people; in him God is glorified. And thus, for the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>Non-Jewish peoples, often used here to refer to those outside the Christian faith.</note>, the cause of their unbelief was the uncleanness of their life. But perhaps someone will say: "What then? Are there not also wicked Christians and honest Gentiles

<column-break/>

(A) of life?" I myself confess there are wicked Christians; but I would not assert that good Gentiles are found. Certain ones may indeed be found who are naturally gentle and good, but not by virtue. For no one will be found good through practice and meditation; and even if some have been held as good, they nevertheless did everything for vain glory. But he who is good for the sake of glory and not for the sake of the good itself will, if he finds the opportunity, indulge in evil desires. For if among us, with the threat of <term>Gehenna</term> <note>A term for hell or the place of spiritual punishment.</note> and every other effort of life and the examples of innumerable saints, people are barely preserved in virtue, in what way will the trifles of the Gentiles keep them in the good? It would even be a great thing if they did not make them even worse. After this, Jesus and his disciples came into the (B) land of Judea, and there he stayed with them and baptized. John was also baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there, and they came and were baptized. For John had not yet been cast into prison.] Jesus was in Jerusalem until the feast of Passover, and after that had passed, he went out into the land of Judea and stayed near the Jordan, where many were gathering. He did not seek out crowded places for the sake of vain glory or display, but he desired to communicate his goodness to more people and to be of service; since for that reason he had also gone up to the feast, as one who would benefit many by his teaching and miracles. <margin>Why Christ himself did not baptize.</margin> Hearing, however, that he baptized, do not think that he (C) baptized by himself, but through his disciples: for this work of the disciples the Evangelist refers to the Master; since that same Spirit-led Evangelist said that Jesus did not baptize, but his disciples did. But you ask, "Why did he not baptize himself?" Learn. Above, John said, "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit." But the Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because the time was not yet. Therefore, if he had baptized, he would have baptized either without the Spirit—and what then would he have offered over John? Or he would have given the Spirit before the time; but that is unworthy of God, who does all things in their proper time. What, then, was the time for giving the Spirit? The time after the <term>Assumption</term> <note>Here referring to the Ascension of Christ into heaven.</note>. Accordingly, the disciples of Jesus baptized so that they might lead more people to the Savior’s teaching. Wherefore also to these...

### CHAPTER 3. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
### AN EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

->338<-

While others were baptizing, John also continued to baptize and did not cease, thereby achieving two good things. One, certainly, was that he could lead those coming to him toward Christ by speaking of Him. The other was that he took care lest his disciples be provoked into greater jealousy and contention; for if he had stopped baptizing, what might his disciples not have done, since they were already pursuing Christ with great envy? For if he so often persuaded them to go to Him, into how much greater envy would he have driven them if he had ceased his own baptizing? For this reason, Christ also began to preach most especially when John was imprisoned, on account of the envy of the Baptist’s disciples.

<margin>Theophylact’s opinion on the death of John</margin>
The opinion of some, however, is that John’s death was permitted to be hastened so that all the people, being prepared, might pass over to Christ, and that opinions might no longer be divided between Christ and John. Therefore, Christ's disciples were baptizing with a baptism that held nothing more than the baptism of John: for both were imperfect and did not yet possess the Spirit, and both had the same purpose—that those being baptized might be led to Christ.

<margin>E</margin>
*Now a question arose among John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, behold, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him." John answered and said, "A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven."*

<margin>F</margin>
A dispute was stirred up by a certain Jew with John’s disciples as they were contending over baptism. For the Jew preferred the baptism of Christ’s disciples, while John’s disciples preferred the baptism of their own master. Because they had a question about purification—that is, about baptism—they went to their master and began to flatter him, saying: "Rabbi, he who was with you, who was in the order of your disciples, has now departed from you and is baptizing; the one to whom you gave testimony—that is, the one you baptized and whom you made famous—now dares to do the same things as you. But even more, no one comes to you now, but everyone goes to him." "Everyone," they said, "is going to him," in order to show contempt for John. But John, wishing to terrify them and show them that they are fighting...

<column-break/>

->339<-

...against God by trying to restrain Christ and take away from His glory, says: "A man cannot take anything for himself," etc. For unless it had been granted from above (he says), the one you envy would never have grown in this way. Thus, you are in two sins: for you are both contrary to the divine counsel and you are attempting the impossible. In the meantime, he also consoles them calmly, because it is not a man who overcomes them, but God. "Indeed," he says, "we also held what we held from above, not from ourselves. So if the things Christ does are more excellent, one should not wonder, for God wills it."

*You yourselves are witnesses that I said, "I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him." He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. This joy of mine, therefore, is fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease.* "You yourselves know," he says, "that I gave testimony to him, that he is greater than I. Therefore, if you pay any attention to my testimony, learn that he is to be preferred over me." And this is my joy: that everyone approaches him. Indeed, if the bride—that is, the people—had not approached the bridegroom, I, the groomsman <note>original: "pronubus"</note>, would surely have grieved; but now that this is happening, I rejoice greatly. For I see Christ the Bridegroom speaking to the bride—the people, that is—and teaching them. Moreover, he did not simply say, "He who stands."

<margin>G</margin>
For he shows that his own works have reached their end, and that he now stands as one no longer working; he must now stand still and only listen to Christ teaching and addressing the bride. "For my work," he says, "is perfected, and I have handed over the people." It is necessary, therefore, for my glory to be diminished, and for his to be increased. How then is the glory of the Forerunner diminished? It is entirely like the Morning Star <note>original: "Lucifer"</note> being hidden by the sun: and it seems to many that the light has been extinguished, but in truth it is not extinguished, but is merely hidden by a greater light. In the same way, the Forerunner, like the Morning Star hidden by the spiritual Sun, is said to be diminished. But Christ "grows" insofar as he gradually manifests himself through signs and miracles—not according to progress in virtues (God forbid, for that would be the delirium of Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century archbishop whose teachings were condemned because they were interpreted as suggesting Christ was a man who "became" God or that his humanity and divinity were separate persons.</note>), but according to the showing and manifestation of his deity. For gradually...

### CHAPTER 3. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...he declared that he was God, and not all at once. Therefore, he says, "my joy is fulfilled" in the bride. For I see that my work, which is granted to me as the <term>groomsman<note>original: "pronubus"; the friend of the bridegroom who assisted in wedding arrangements</note></term>, has progressed. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, the Lord is the bridegroom of every soul; the bridal chamber where the union takes place is the place of baptism—that is, the Church. He gives the bride a <term>pledge<note>original: "arrabonem"; a down-payment or earnest money</note></term>, which is the remission of sins through the communion of the Holy Spirit; but he will give more perfect things in the future, when he will lead those who are worthy into better and more sublime things. Note, however, that there is no other bridegroom but Christ alone. <margin>Nestorius?<note>A reference to the Nestorian heresy regarding the nature of Christ</note></margin> All those who teach are merely groomsmen, just as the Precursor [John the Baptist] was. <margin>Christ is the only bridegroom; Teachers are groomsmen.</margin> There is no other giver of good things than the Lord alone. All others are mediators and ministers of the good things which are given by the Lord.

<margin>E</margin>
**He who comes from above is above all; he who is from the earth is earthly and speaks of the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies, and no one accepts his testimony. He who accepts his testimony has certified that God is truthful. For he whom God sent speaks the words of God. For God does not give the Spirit by measure.** <margin>Romans 3:1, John 5.</margin> The Precursor compares himself to CHRIST and says that He indeed comes from above from the Father, is more excellent than all, and preserves his Father’s excellence. "But I, who am from the earth, speak earthly things—vile and humble things if they are compared with the doctrine of Christ." Although the things done by the Precursor <margin>F</margin> were divine, yet when compared with those of Christ, they appeared very humble. "He speaks," he says, "what he has seen and heard"; that is, he clearly knows what he heard from the Father and what he saw, and those things he speaks and testifies. And his testimony is received by no one among those who do not pay attention to the truth. But he who receives the testimony—that is, his doctrine—has "certified": that is, he has shown and established that God is true. For he who believes him who was sent by God believes God, and consequently certifies and demonstrates that he has believed something true. <margin>Truth, the basis of faith.</margin> Conversely, he who does not believe him who was sent by God shows that he [God] is a liar; for this reason he does not believe him, as if he were a liar. And so, he who believes Christ shows that God is truthful, because he believed the one by whom he was sent.

<column-break/>

<page-num>340</page-num>
### AN EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

<margin>A</margin> For it is manifest that he believed him as one who is truthful. And rightly so. For all the rest of us have received the working of the Spirit by measure, but to Christ himself he did not give one or two virtues by measure, but he possesses the entire Spirit <term>substantially<note>original: "substantialiter"; meaning the Spirit is part of his very essence or being, not just a gift</note></term>. Therefore, God also gave the Spirit to the prophets—that is, the working of the Spirit—and he gave it by measure. But to Christ, he did not give it by measure, nor did he "give" it in a general sense at all: for Christ possesses the Spirit substantially. However, when you hear that Christ speaks those things which he heard from the Father, do not think that he needs to learn knowledge from him; rather, because whatever the Son knows, he knows naturally from the Father as one who is <term>consubstantial<note>original: "consubstantialis"; of the same essence or "stuff" as the Father</note></term> with him, for this reason he is said to hear from the Father what he knows. <margin>B</margin> Just as if you were to see a son similar to his father in all things, you would say he has everything from the father—that is, he is like no one but the father. Hearing, therefore, that he was "sent," understand him to be sent from the Father alone, like a ray of light. Do we not usually say that the sun "emits" rays—that is, sends them to the earth? And we never say a ray is of another substance or later than the sun itself. So also, consider the Son to be sent from the spiritual sun (namely, the Father) into this world as a radiation, a ray, or a light—however you wish to call him, so long as it is fitting. It would not be untimely in this place <margin>C</margin> to say how the Son possesses the Spirit and how he is called the "Spirit of the Son." <margin>Galatians 4, Romans 8. Theophylact, with the ancient Greeks, denies that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. Now, however, we all confess it.<note>This marginal note was likely added by a later Catholic editor to "correct" Theophylact's Eastern Orthodox view</note></margin> For the Apostle also says: *He sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying out, Abba, Father.* And again: *If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his.* Certainly, the Latins, explaining these things poorly and understanding them incorrectly, say that the Spirit also "proceeds" from the Son. But we first say this to them: that it is one thing to be *from* someone, and another to be *of* someone. Thus, the Spirit is indeed the "Spirit of the Son" without doubt, as is approved by all Scripture; but that he is *from* the Son, no Scripture testifies, lest we introduce two principles of the Spirit: the Father and the Son. "Indeed," they say, "for he breathed on the disciples and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.'" Oh, what foolishness! If he gave the Spirit to the disciples then, when he breathed on them, how did he later say to them, "You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, not many days from now"? Or how...

# CHAPTER 3. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 341

<margin>Who proceeds from the Father and the Son. <note>original: "patre filioque"; this margin note reflects the Latin "Filioque" doctrine, though the main text provides a more nuanced Eastern perspective.</note> John 20. Acts 1. Isaiah 11.</margin>
...do we believe the descent of the Spirit occurred at Pentecost? <margin>D</margin> If indeed he gave it on the evening of the day of the resurrection: for then he breathed upon them. But this would be quite ridiculous. For it is manifest that he did not then give them the [fullness of the] Holy Spirit, but one gift of the Holy Spirit, namely, the remission of sin: for he immediately adds, "Whose sins you remit." But the Son possesses the Spirit substantially, as being <term>consubstantial<note>original: "consubstantiale"; sharing the same essence or being</note></term> with himself, not as one from whom he receives an operation, as the prophets did. Moreover, he says the Spirit is of the Son according to truth, power, and wisdom. For the Holy Spirit is described by Isaiah as the Spirit of truth, of strength, and of wisdom. And in another sense, because the Spirit is given to men through the Son, for that reason he is called the Spirit of the Son. Believe, therefore, that the Spirit indeed proceeds from the Father, but is given to the creature through the Son; and let this be for you the <term>canon<note>original: "canon"; a rule or standard of measurement for doctrine</note></term> of orthodox doctrine. <margin>B</margin>

**The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.**] After he had spoken sublime things concerning Christ, now he speaks humble things again, tempering his speech for his listeners so that it might be grasped. Therefore, he says, "The Father loves the Son," as if speaking of some admirable man. "And he has given all things into the hand of the Son" according to his humanity. But if it is also according to his divinity: what of this? The Father gave all things to the Son by reason of nature, but not of grace; since he also has his very being from the Father, he is rightly said to have all things from the Father. Therefore, the Son possesses all things, both those in heaven and <margin>F</margin> those on earth. For he rules over all, even if some are unwilling. But later, in the second coming, when every knee shall bow to him, he will receive the perfect lordship of all: when malice shall no longer have power, but remaining ineffective, it will reveal the nature of the good which was <margin>Acts 17.</margin> implanted in all things from the beginning, and which contains all things. "He who believes in the Son has eternal life" in him; I speak of that Christ who is truly life. For in him we live <margin>Colossians 3.</margin> and move. "But he who is unbelieving will not see life." For how shall he who has voluntarily withdrawn from life possess that life which is CHRIST? Just as Paul says, "When Christ, our life, is manifested, then we also,"

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
who have died to malice and become immovable, shall be manifested in glory. "But the wrath of God remains upon him." He did not say that it "awaits" him, but "remains" upon him, showing that it shall never depart from him. So that you may not believe death to be merely temporal, he says that it remains upon the one who has been unbelieving, and the punishment shall be perpetual. Through all these words, the Baptist introduces and compels all listeners to the faith of Christ. For he did not say these things in vain, but he instructs his own disciples and all others not to envy Christ, but to listen to Him as God.

**When therefore the Lord knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—though Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples—he left the land of Judea and went again into Galilee. And it was necessary for him to pass through Samaria.**] The merciful Lord, having once been incarnated for our sake, does all things for our salvation. Finally, even now when he had heard that the Pharisees had heard of his glory, and knowing they would be stirred up to envy against him, he withdraws into Galilee. Teaching us two things: One, indeed, that we should spare our enemies and in every way try not to give them occasion for scandal or envy. The other, that we should not cast ourselves into temptation foolishly <margin>C</margin> and uselessly, but withdraw for a time until the madness subsides. Although he was powerful enough to restrain those envying him, even if they pressed upon him with a certain force, he nevertheless did not do this, lest he should seem to have a <term>phantastic body<note>original: "phantasticum corpus"; an illusory body that only appears to be physical</note></term>. ...to overcome them, so that they cannot say that having <margin>D</margin> abandoned them, he surrendered to the nations <note>Gentiles</note> whom they detested. But when they drove him away, then he went to the Gentiles, and even then not by primary purpose, but in passing.

**He came, therefore, into a city of Samaria, which is called Sychar, near the plot of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Now Jacob's well was there.**] It is worth explaining where the Samaritans originated and how they obtained that name. For the mountain was called *Somoron* <note>original: "Somoren"; the Latinized version of the Hebrew "Shomeron," meaning "Watchtower," the hill of Samaria.</note> <margin>Isaiah 7</margin> after the one who possessed it; as Isaiah also says, *And the head of Somoron is Ephraim*. Those who lived near that mountain were not first called Samaritans, but were called Israelites. But when <margin>E</margin> they had offended God, they were handed over at various times to the Assyrians. At last, the Assyrian king, when they were contemplating rebellion, came upon them, took them captive, and did not permit them to return to their own region again, suspecting they would rebel once more. Instead, he transported them to the lands of the Babylonians and Medes. He gave Samaria as a colony to peoples gathered from various places. Furthermore, when these things had happened, God, wishing to show the barbarians that he had made the Jews serve them not because of His own weakness but because of their sins, sent lions among those who lived in Samaria—the foreigners—who were destroying them all. When the King heard this, he sent for some of the Jewish elders and asked what should be done so that the lions would no longer destroy those foreigners in Samaria. <margin>F</margin> They explained that the God of Israel protected that place and would not allow those to live there who were ignorant of His <term>ordinances<note>original: "legitima"; the specific religious laws and customs of the Mosaic Law.</note></term>. Therefore, if the foreigners there were to be cared for, he should send Jewish priests to hand down God's laws to them, and thus they might appease God. The king complied and sent a certain priest to hand over the law of God to the foreigners in Samaria. But they did not receive all the books, only the five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy <note>The Samaritan Pentateuch.</note>. Nor did they depart perfectly from their impiety; though in later times they refrained from the worship of idols and worshipped God. Therefore, the Jews returning from cap-

<column-break/>

-tivity were jealous of them, since they were Assyrian <margin>A</margin> by race, and they called them Samaritans after the mountain. They, however, named Abraham and Jacob as their ancestors; <margin>Abraham was a Chaldean</margin> since Abraham had been a Chaldean, and the well of Jacob which he had there was considered their own. <margin>John 8. Matthew 10.</margin> But the Jews detested these people along with the other nations. Hence, when insulting the Lord, they said, "You are a Samaritan." And he himself said to his disciples, "Do not enter into a city of the Samaritans." Why then does the Evangelist discuss the place of Jacob and the well so diligently? First, indeed, so that when you hear the woman saying, *Our father Jacob gave us that well*, you may <margin>B</margin> not wonder. For that place was <term>Shechem<note>original: "Sycima"</note></term> <margin>Genesis 34</margin>, where the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, committed that heavy slaughter because the prince of the Shechemites had violated their sister Dinah. Moreover, we learn this from the Evangelist telling us those things about the well and the place: that they were also rejected of old because of their sins, and when they had offended God, the nations possessed their places. The things which the patriarchs had possessed because of their faith in God, those people lost because of their impiety; and so it is nothing new if now the Gentiles are brought into the kingdom of heaven instead of the Jews. <margin>Jacob's estate was Shechem.</margin> The estate that Jacob gave to Joseph was called Shechem. <margin>C</margin> Since the sons of Jacob had destroyed the Shechemites and desolated the city, the father gave it as an inheritance to his son Joseph because it was desolated.

**Jesus therefore, being wearied from his journey, sat thus by the well. It was about the sixth hour <note>Roughly noon, the hottest part of the day.</note>. A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink." For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.**] By the Evangelist describing the Lord as weary from his journey, <margin>When the Lord was a stranger to pride.</margin> he shows us that the Lord was a stranger to pride and the abundance of things. For he did not use beasts of burden for the journey, but went on foot, instructing us also that we do not have need of many things. Furthermore, he says that he walked vigorously and not sluggishly. From this we also learn that we should do the work of God with constancy and diligence. The fact that he "sat thus" signifies simply, and as if by chance...

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 343

<margin>D</margin> ...He was sitting, and not upon a throne, but simply—that is to say, upon the ground—refreshing his body and resting himself by the fountain <note>the well</note>. Then he introduces another reason why he sat by the fountain: it was the midday hour. For the hour (he says) was about the sixth <note>roughly 12:00 PM</note>; and because of the heat of that hour, he had need of cooling and rest. Or, to put it another way, he says this so that no one might criticize the Lord: how is it that, after he had commanded his disciples not to enter the way of the Gentiles, he himself came to the Samaritans? Therefore, the text says he was sitting in that place because of fatigue, and that his conversation with the woman had a reasonable cause: namely, thirst. For since he was thirsty, he consequently, after the human manner, required a drink. <margin>E</margin> While he was seeking this, a woman arrived with a soul eager to learn. What, then, was to be done? Should he have driven away a woman so studious, who was speaking with him and thirsting to hear about the things she doubted? This would not have been in keeping with divine mercy. But look, I pray, and see from this how far the Lord was from pride. For he was left alone on the road when the disciples had gone into the city to buy food. They had so little concern for their bellies that, at the time when almost everyone else is sleeping, they were buying food—and bread only—so that we too might learn to make little of a variety of foods. Look, I beseech you, also at the diligence of the Evangelist <note>John</note>; for he did not say affirmatively "it was the sixth hour," but so as not to fall short of the truth, he said "nearly the sixth," making his speech cautious.

<margin>F</margin> **The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman?" For the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans. But see how circum-

For if care was to be taken, it was the Lord’s responsibility, not hers; for she did not say that the Samaritans have no custom with the Jews, but that *the Jews* have no custom with the Samaritans. Nevertheless, she does not remain silent even then, but thinking the Lord is doing something forbidden, she corrects what was being done contrary to the law. Christ, however, does not reveal himself until the virtue of the woman is demonstrated. After the woman's virtue was indicated—and how circumspect and diligent she was—then finally he begins to speak with her about sublime matters. The woman says to him, "Sir." Do you see how, immediately ceasing from her lowly thoughts, she attributes great honor to him by calling him "Lord" <note>or "Sir"</note>? For she had not yet reached the depth of Christ's words. For he speaks in one way, while <margin>C</margin> she understands his words about water in another.

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,

...she wonders at the variety of the givers. For she says, "If you <margin>D</margin> are going to give such water, you are altogether greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this water." The fact that he himself drank from it is a praise of the water’s goodness, for that spring pleased the patriarch so much. And that he drank, and his children, and his cattle, is a sign of the abundance of the waters. For the water is not only sweet—and so sweet that even Jacob drank from it—but also generous; and so generous that it sufficed for the multitude of the patriarch Jacob’s cattle. But when the woman said, "Are you greater than our father?" the Lord indeed does not say clearly, "I am certainly greater," so that he might not seem <margin>E</margin> arrogant, having not yet displayed any specimen of his power. However, he prepares for this through what he says: for he says, "He who drinks of this water will thirst again; but he who drinks of my water will not thirst forever." And so, if you marvel at Jacob, who gave such water, you ought to admire much more the one who offers far better water. For the water that I give becomes a fountain of water, and day by day it is multiplied more and more. For the saints do not keep the little they receive from God just as it is until the end, but they receive the seeds <margin>Matthew 25</margin> and beginnings of good through grace. But they themselves expend it and make it grow, which the Lord signifies through the parable of the talents and through the innkeeper <note>original: "hospitem", referring to the host in the parable of the Good Samaritan who is told he will be repaid for extra care</note>. For he who had received two talents gained another two, but by his own effort; and to the innkeeper who had received the man wounded by thieves, the Lord promises: "whatever you spend beyond this of your own, I will give back to you." Therefore, in this place also it is inferred: <margin>F</margin> I indeed give water to the thirsty; but that which I give does not only remain, but is even multiplied and becomes a fountain. The Lord gave Paul a small amount of water—Ananias’s instructions—but Paul showed that small fountain of <margin>Acts 9</margin> Ananias’s teachings to be a great spring, so that the flowing streams of that fountain reached from Jerusalem all the way to Illyricum <note>A Roman province in the Balkans</note>. And how is the woman affected by these things? She still carries herself humbly indeed, for she thinks the discussion is about physical water, yet she truly points to something. For at first she was doubting, saying, "From where do you have living water?" but now she accepts the speech without drawing back, saying, "Give me the water."

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,
### ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 345

He reveals another, greater doctrine <note>original: "dogma"</note>, something he had not revealed to either Nicodemus or Nathanael. For he says, "The hour is coming when God will be worshiped neither in Jerusalem nor in this place." For you, he says, try to show that the affairs of the Samaritans are more worthy than those of the Jews; but I tell you that neither these nor those possess that dignity, but another state of things altogether will be more worthy than them. Nevertheless, even so, I affirm that the Jews are worthier than you Samaritans. For you, he says, "worship what you do not know; but we Jews worship what we know." Furthermore, he counts himself among the Jews because he is speaking according to the woman’s opinion. For she suspected that he was a Jewish prophet, and for that reason he says, "we worship."
<margin>E</margin>
But how did the Samaritans not know what they worshiped? They thought that God was confined to a specific place. Therefore, as was said above, when they were being devoured by lions and sent word to the King of the Assyrians that they were not being accepted by "the God of the place," they remained there for a long time, worshiping idols as well as the true God himself. The Jews, however, were free from this error and knew that there is one God of all, even if not all of them lived up to it. "For salvation is from the Jews." This gives us a double meaning. For it means either that good things have come to the world from the Jews—for the knowledge of God, the despising of idols, and all other sound doctrines had their beginning there—and even the worship practiced among you Samaritans, though it was not correct, took its origin from the Jews.
<margin>F</margin>
Alternatively, he calls his own advent "salvation," which was from the Jews. Moreover, the Lord himself can be called "salvation," because he was from the Jews according to the flesh.

"But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father seeks such as these to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth."] Although we Jews, as far as the manner of worship is concerned, have more than you Samaritans, nevertheless the affairs of the Jews are also now coming to an end. For the change will not only be in the locations, but the very mode of worship will be altered; these things are at the doors, and "now is the hour." For these things will not be deferred for a long time like the things spoken of by the prophets.

<column-break/>

He calls "true worshipers" those who live according to his law, who do not confine God to a specific place (like the Samaritans) or worship with a physical ritual (like the Jews), but worship in "spirit and truth"—that is, through the soul and through purity of mind. For because God is spirit—that is, incorporeal—it is necessary to worship him incorporeally, namely in the soul; for this is what "in spirit" signifies. Indeed, the soul is an incorporeal spirit.
<margin>The soul also <note>Latin: "Aia qp", abbreviation for "Anima quoque"</note></margin>
But since many seem to worship in the soul but do not have correct knowledge (such as heretics), he added "and in truth." For it is necessary to worship God with the mind and also to hold a sound opinion of him. Perhaps someone might say that two parts of our philosophy are suggested here: I mean "practice" <note>original: "praxis"</note> and "contemplation" <note>original: "contemplatio"</note>, represented by these two terms.
<margin>Romans 8. Galatians 5.</margin>
For when he says "in spirit," practice is taught. For "whoever is led by the spirit of God mortifies the works of the body," according to the divine Apostle; and again, "The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh." And so, practice is suggested by the phrase "in spirit." By the phrase "in truth," however, he suggests the contemplative life.
<margin>1 Corinthians 5.</margin>
Furthermore, Paul also says this: "Let us feast," he says, "on the unleavened bread of sincerity"—that is, purity of life, which belongs to practice—"and of truth," which belongs to contemplation. For contemplation is occupied with the truth of the word’s doctrine.
<margin>C</margin>
Or alternatively: since it was peculiar to the Samaritans to confine God to a place and say that one must worship "in this place," whereas among the Jews all things were done in "figure and shadow," worshiping "in spirit" is opposed to the worship of the Samaritans, so that this saying has the following meaning:
<margin>1 Corinthians 10.</margin>
You Samaritans offer a certain localized worship to God, but true worshipers will not offer localized worship. For they will worship "in spirit"—that is, with the mind and soul. But neither will they worship like the Jews, in "type and shadow,"
<margin>2 Corinthians 3.</margin>
but "in truth," because the end of Jewish customs and observations is coming. Perhaps the Jewish law, understood according to the letter, was a figure and a shadow. What is called "in spirit" is opposed to the "letter." For the law of the letter is not observed by us, but the law of the spirit. For the letter...

...for "the letter kills, but the spirit gives life" <note>original: "littera quidem occidit, spiritus autem vivificat" — a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, a key verse for medieval interpreters who looked for spiritual meanings beyond the literal text</note>. And what is said to be "in truth" is contrasted with shadows and figures. Therefore, he says, "the hour is coming, indeed it is now," referring to the time of my physical arrival, when true worshipers will worship neither in one place like the Samaritans, but in every place according to the spirit, offering their worship in an incorporeal <note>non-physical</note> manner. As Paul says, "I serve in my spirit" <margin>Romans 1.</margin>. Since he is spirit, he seeks spiritual ones; and since he is truth, he seeks true ones.

[The woman says to him, "I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called CHRIST; when he comes, he will tell us everything." JESUS says to her, "I am he, who speaks to you." And immediately his disciples came and wondered that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said, "What are you looking for?" or "Why are you speaking with her?"]

How did the woman know the Messiah was coming, who is called CHRIST? From the Mosaic scriptures. For we said above that the Samaritans received the five books of Moses. Therefore, because they had received the books of Moses, they knew from them the prophecies about Christ, and that he is the Son of God. For when it is said, "Let us make man," <margin>Genesis 1. Genesis 17, 18. Genesis 48. Deuteronomy 18.</margin> it is clear that these words were spoken by the Father to the Son. The Son also spoke to Abraham in the tent, and Jacob, predicting him, said: "The prince shall not fail from Judah until he comes for whom it is reserved" <note>original: "donec veniat cui repositum est" — This is a Latin translation of Genesis 49:10, often interpreted as referring to the coming of the Messiah/Shiloh</note>. And Moses himself also says, "The Lord will raise up a prophet for you from your brothers like me; you shall listen to him." And many other things predict the coming of Christ. Therefore the woman says, "I know that the Messiah is coming." But now the Lord reveals himself to her, as the logic of the conversation requires. Indeed, if he had said from the very beginning, "I am Christ," he would not have persuaded the woman, and he would have seemed like some troublesome and arrogant person; but now, leading her to this point bit by bit, until the expectation of Christ is mentioned, he reveals himself to her. For this reason, he did not reveal himself to the Jews, who were constantly asking, "Tell us if you are the CHRIST"; but to the woman he says it. To those [Jews]...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...he says nothing, because they were not asking for the sake of learning, but with a mind for slandering. But to her, because she was eager, he clearly reveals himself. For it is manifest from what follows that she asked with a simple mind and thought, and a desire to learn. For as soon as she heard, not only did she herself believe, but she also led others to faith, and she always appears both faithful and diligently inquiring. When the conversation and teaching with the woman was finished, the disciples arrived at the opportune time, and they marveled at his humility—that although he was so glorious and celebrated among everyone, he did not disdain to have a conversation with such a poor Samaritan woman with such modesty. However, although they marveled, they did not dare to ask what he was saying to her; <margin>B</margin> they were so well-disciplined, preserving their reverence toward their teacher. Even if they elsewhere appeared to speak boldly—like JOHN, who would recline upon his breast <margin>John 13. Matthew 18. Matthew 20.</margin> or when they approached and said, "Who is the greatest?" or when the sons of Zebedee begged that one might sit at his right hand and the other at his left—in those cases they were inquiring about things pertaining to themselves and what seemed necessary to them then. But in this place, because it did not matter so much to them to ask, nor was it entirely necessary, they did not use such boldness, since they did not have an opportune time.

[Therefore the woman left her water jar and went into the city and says to those men: "Come, see a man who told me everything I have done; is this not the CHRIST?" So they went out from the city and were coming to him.]

<margin>C</margin> The heart of the woman was so set on fire by the Lord's words that she even left her water jar behind. Thus, she immediately preferred the fountain of Christ over the water of Jacob; she became an "Apostle," ordained by the faith that had occupied her heart, and she teaches and draws the whole city. "Come," she says, "see him who told me everything I have done." Truly, since her soul was set on fire by divine fire, she looks back at none of those things that are on earth: not to confusion, not to shame, nor to anything else. See, therefore, even this: although she could have said it differently—"Come, see a Prophet prophesying"—she did not do so.

### CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA. 347

<margin>D</margin> She disregards her own glory and looks only to this: that she might preach the truth. She does not say affirmatively, "This is the Christ," but rather, "Could this be the Christ?" wishing them to add their own judgment and make the word easier to believe. For if she had affirmed that he was the Christ, perhaps some would have rejected her opinion and not believed such a widespread rumor. However, some have understood the "five husbands" of the Samaritan woman to be the five books of Moses <note>The Pentateuch: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy</note>, which were the only ones the Samaritans accepted. "The one you have now," he says—that is, the word you are now receiving from me—"is not your husband." For you have not yet been joined, says JESUS, to my doctrine.

<margin>B</margin> Someone might say that the Samaritan woman represents a type of human nature. For our nature once dwelt on a mountain—meaning a mind full of divine grace. For before Adam sinned, he was adorned with all divine gifts. He was even a prophet. Whence, having been awakened from sleep, he predicted the formation of the woman and the relationship of a man toward her; he said, "This is now bone of my bones... and for this reason a man shall leave his father and mother" <note>Genesis 2:23-24</note>. Therefore, our nature was then on the high mountain of the mind. But when it stumbled, it was led away captive; and the devil led its holy seed away to Babylon—by which I mean every more divine thought—that is, into the confusion of this world. And there he made barbaric thoughts dwell in their place—that is, <margin>F</margin> "lions," which devoured the thoughts that once dwelt in us, until they were persuaded to receive the divine words, though even then not entirely. For once malice has begun to dwell in the mountain of our mind, it may receive the books of Moses, yet it does not embrace the good entirely but remains under a curse. Therefore, making a journey—that is, crossing many paths and employing various methods for our salvation: sometimes with threats of evils, sometimes with afflictions, sometimes with benefits, and sometimes with promises of good things—He seeks to win back our life. And he was indeed weary from attempting to correct us in such ways without success; however, he found another mode of ruling which pleased him, whence...

To this nature of ours, five "husbands" were joined—namely the various laws given to it by God: the law in paradise; the law in the <margin>Gen. 9</margin> time of Noah; the law given to Abraham; <margin>Gen. 17</margin> <note>The text reads "Gene. 7," likely a printer's error for Genesis 17, where circumcision is commanded</note> the law given to Moses; and the law given through the Prophets. For Noah after the flood received a certain precept, and Abraham circumcision; and so nature, joined to these five laws, also received a sixth, which it did not have as a husband, for it was not yet joining the law of the New Testament to itself.

And again, "They played the harlot after every piece of wood," namely because of the carvings and wooden idols it worshipped. For nature had reached such a point of madness that it even sacrificed to beautiful trees because of their beauty—namely to <margin>C</margin> Cypresses and Plane trees and similar things. 

When, therefore, men loved that sixth adulterer and fell into idolatry, then the Lord, coming, freed us from it. Therefore he says, "the one you have now."
