# CHAPTER 4. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.
## COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 348
XX iiij

<margin>D</margin> ...delight: from which the mind itself drinks, as do its thoughts (which are called its "children") and its "cattle"—the irrational parts of the soul, such as anger and desire. For tears become a refreshment to the mind, its thoughts, and all the rest.

[Meanwhile the disciples were asking him, saying: "Teacher, eat." But he said to them: "I have food to eat that you do not know about." Therefore the disciples said to one another: "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" JESUS says to them: "My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to finish his work."] <margin>E</margin> The disciples were asking the Lord—that is, they were entreating him to eat—not out of a rash spirit, but out of great love for their teacher. For they saw him exhausted from the journey and the burning heat. But the Lord, knowing that almost the entire city of Samaria was about to be called to him and that the Samaritans would believe in him, said: "I have food to eat." By this, he meant the salvation of humanity, which he longed for with a desire greater than any of us feel for physical food. "But this food which I have to eat, you, my disciples, do not know." For while you are still unrefined <note>Original: "Crassi," literally "thick" or "dense," referring to their lack of spiritual insight at this stage</note> and cannot yet understand the things I say obscurely, you do not realize that I call the salvation of people "food." Or to put it another way: "You do not know this food," meaning you are unaware that the Samaritans are about to believe in me <margin>F</margin> and be saved. What then did the disciples do? They were still wondering if someone had brought him something to eat. However, because of their deep reverence for him, they did not dare to ask him directly. Furthermore, even though they did not ask, he reveals the meaning of his obscure statement and says: "My food is to do the will of him who sent me." For the will of God is the salvation of humanity, "and I will finish his work." The prophets and the Law were by no means able to finish the work of God. They were imperfect, insofar as they contained only figures and shadows of things to come; but the Lord finished the work of God—meaning our salvation and renewal. Perhaps you can also understand "the work of God" as humanity itself, whom the only Son of God—having taken on our offended nature but remaining subject to no sins—perfected; that is,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> he declared humanity perfect and complete in every good work through a divine life in the flesh, and he conquered the world even to the end. The Law of God is also his work, according to Deuteronomy 9 <margin>Deuteronomy 9</margin>, because it was written by the finger of God; this Law the Lord perfected. For "Christ is the end of the law" <margin>Romans 10</margin>, because he brought an end to all things that were done under the Law and transferred it from physical worship to spiritual worship. Furthermore, the Lord often speaks obscurely to make his listeners more attentive and to rouse them to ask and learn what was being said unclearly. By calling the salvation of men "food," he teaches the disciples that since they have been ordained as teachers of the world, they should value physical food less <margin>B</margin> and direct all their desire toward saving souls. Observe, however, that the Lord himself used to accept food offered by others. For the disciples say: "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" <margin>Psalm 135</margin> He did not do this because he needed the service of others—for how could he who "gives food to all flesh" <note>A reference to Psalm 136:25, which is numbered as 135 in the Latin Vulgate</note> require human help? Rather, he did it so that those who provided for him might receive a reward, and so that the disciples might become accustomed to feeding others <margin>Those who teach should be fed by those who learn.</margin>. And further, he sets an example for all people, so that we should not be ashamed of poverty nor think it a burden if we are fed by others—especially those of us who teach. Indeed, it is very necessary to have others as providers of food, so that we, not being distracted by such cares, may be free for the ministry of the word. For this reason, he commanded the disciples to be <margin>C</margin> supported by those they taught.

[Do you not say: "There are still four months, and then the harvest will come"? Behold, I say to you: lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for the harvest. And he who reaps receives a reward and gathers fruit for eternal life, so that both he who sows and he who reaps may rejoice together. For in this the saying is true: "One sows and another reaps." I sent you to reap what you did not labor for. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.]

He begins now to reveal more clearly to the disciples what he had previously spoken obscurely. For you indeed, he says, "say"—that is, you think—that the physical harvest is four months away; but I tell you that a spiritual harvest is already here.

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus' statement that His "food" is to do the Father's will, identifying this "food" as the salvation of the Samaritans and all humanity. He contrasts the temporary nature of the Mosaic Law with the perfection brought by Christ and provides a justification for why spiritual teachers are supported by their students.</summary>

<margin>D</margin> He said these things because of the Samaritans, who were already coming toward him. Therefore, "Lift up your eyes," whether spiritual or physical, and look upon the multitude of Samaritans, and see their souls eager and ready for faith; they are like regions turned white that have need <margin>A beautiful comparison.</margin> of reapers. For just as the ears of grain, when they have turned white, are ready for the harvest, so too are these souls prepared for salvation. And the reaper receives a reward and gathers fruit into eternal life, so that both the sower and the reaper may rejoice together. This has the following meaning: the Prophets sowed, but they did not reap; yet they were not deprived of joy for that reason. For although they do not reap alongside us—which is something that does not happen in a physical harvest—it is not so in spiritual matters. In a physical harvest, if it happens that one sows and another reaps, there is sadness for the one who does not reap. But in spiritual things, it is different. The Prophets preached beforehand and softened the minds of men; therefore, they rejoice with you who capture these men for salvation. "I sent you to reap what you did not labor for." The Lord says this so that the disciples, when sent out to preach, might not be troubled as if they were being sent to a difficult task. For the burdensome work had been undertaken by the Prophets; you, however, are to reap in a field already prepared. But he speaks a true word, a proverb commonly tossed about: "One is the sower, and another is the reaper." Note how all these things indicate his authority and lordship: "I sent you to reap." Let the <margin>Marcionites. Manichaeans. Proverb. Arians.</margin> cursed Marcionites <note>Followers of Marcion, an early heretic who rejected the Old Testament and its God, claiming the New Testament God was different.</note> and Manichaeans <note>Followers of Mani, who believed in a dualistic struggle between light and dark and often rejected the physical world and the Old Testament.</note> and those like them hear this, for they alienate the Old Testament from the New; indeed, they are <margin>F</margin> refuted in this very place. For if the Old Testament had been alien, how could the Apostles have reaped what was sown by the Prophets? Since the Apostles reaped the things in the Old Testament, it is not alien to the New Testament; rather, both are one. Let the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being and not of the same substance as God the Father.</note> also hear how he sends the disciples as one who is Lord and possesses power. He sends them, however, to reap from the earthly regions, and to cut away those who were fixed to earthly things—both Gentiles and Jews—and to lead them into the threshing floor—I mean the Church—in which they are trodden upon by the oxen (that is, the teachers) and lie under them to be threshed. When they have cast aside all the chaff, and the fuel for the fire, and whatever is

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> of the flesh, they may be stored as pure grain in the heavenly granary and then become food for God, who rejoices in their salvation. In this way Paul reaped, cutting us away from the earth and teaching us that "our citizenship is in heaven." <margin>A witty jest about the elderly.</margin> Someone once wittily joked about this saying regarding the elderly: that they seem to be "regions white for the harvest" because of their grey hair, signaling the harvest of death.

<margin>B</margin> Now from that city, many of the Samaritans believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified that "he told me everything I ever did." Therefore, when the Samaritans had come to him, they asked him to stay with them; and he stayed there two days, and many more believed because of his own word. And they said to the woman: "We no longer believe because of your speech; for we ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Savior of the world, the Christ." Because of the woman's word, many Samaritans believed, wisely judging among themselves that the woman would not have publicized her own life just to please another, unless the one she was preaching about was truly someone great and above many. Therefore, demonstrating their faith through their deeds, they earnestly begged him to stay with them. For "to stay" means to have a permanent dwelling among them. Truly, he does not comply in this, but stays for only two days; yet from this, many more believed because of his teaching. Although the Evangelist does not recount the wonderful words of his teaching in detail, he shows by the outcome that we should understand the power of that divine teaching. <margin>C</margin> For the Evangelists pass over many other things because they write not for show, but to declare the truth. Thus, since the Lord was among the Samaritans, it is likely that he taught certain more divine things; for this reason, they believe without having seen a sign and beg him to stay. The Jews, however, though they enjoyed very many words and signs, still persecuted him. Truly, "a man’s enemies are those of his own household." <margin>Matthew 7. Matthew 10.</margin> See also how quickly the multitude surpasses the woman by whom they had been taught; for they do not call him "Prophet" nor "Savior of Israel," but "of the world." They use the article <note>The "definite article" (the) in Greek is used here to emphasize that Jesus is *the* unique Savior, not just one among many.</note>: "This is *the* Savior," the one who properly and truly saved all. For many have come to save—the Law, the Prophets, and the Angel—but this is the one true Savior.

<summary>Theophylact explains the metaphor of the harvest, arguing that the Apostles reap the spiritual fruits sown by the Old Testament Prophets, which refutes heretical claims that the two Testaments are disconnected. He also contrasts the Samaritans' ready faith, based on Christ's words, with the Jews' persistent rejection despite miracles.</summary>

In short, he healed the fever of the boy, but the unbelief of the father. You should know, however, that a "sign" is one thing, and a "wonder" is another. For a <margin>The difference between a wonder and a sign.</margin> **wonder** <note>original: "prodigium"</note> occurs beyond the course of nature, such as opening the eyes of a man born blind or raising the dead. But a **sign** <note>original: "signum"</note> is that which is not beyond nature, such as healing a sick person. May the Lord perform this miracle even now. Every human being is a kind of **nobleman** <note>original: "regius", referring to the "official" or "royal man" in the Gospel text</note>, not only <term>because</term> he is related to the King of all things through his soul, but also <term>because</term> he himself has received a royal dignity above all other creatures. Often, however, a person is found having a "mind" which is like a son, suffering terribly from the fire of illicit pleasures and lusts. If, therefore, he approaches Jesus and <margin>B</margin> asks him to "come down"—that is, to have mercy and forgive his sins—before he dies entirely from the disease of pleasures. For if God did not have mercy on us, but observed our iniquities and took vengeance according to them, who could endure it? This means: do not be motionless regarding the good, but "go," and show an unceasing movement toward what is right. For then your son—your mind—shall live. But if you rest and do not walk, your mind will surely die, for <term>the reason that</term> you have not moved yourself toward the good.

### CHAPTER 5. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

<margin>That pool signifies baptism</margin>
<margin>Concerning the water of baptism.</margin>
...might approach and perform a miracle. Indeed, <margin>D</margin> divine wisdom seemed to prepare a way from afar for the Jews to have faith in Christ by preordaining the miracle of the pool. For since baptism was going to give great power and a most magnificent gift—inasmuch as it purifies sin and gives life to souls—God prefigures baptism in the affairs of the Jews. He gives them also water that might purify filth; not that it was actual "filth," but it was regarded as such, as when they had touched a corpse, or a leper, or something of that kind. He also grants a miracle to this pool so that he might lead them toward the acceptance of baptism. For an angel would descend at the opportune time and stir the water, and would instill a healing power within it. <margin>E</margin> For such a thing is never found in the nature of water itself—that it should heal by its own power—otherwise this would happen perpetually. Instead, the whole matter depended on the angel; whatever effectiveness there was came from him. So it is also with us: the water of baptism is simply water, but when the grace of the Holy Spirit has approached it because of the invocation of God, it dissolves the diseases of souls. If anyone were blind—their soul's eyes being blinded so that they could not distinguish good from evil—or if anyone were lame, not moving toward doing good or progressing toward better things, or if one were "withered" and in a state of utterly desperate disease, sharing in no good thing, they would be cured by that water. At that time, infirmity hindered some from being healed, but now in baptism there is no obstacle. For it is not the case that once one person is healed, the others are left uncured; rather, if the entire world were to flow together toward it, grace would not be diminished. <margin>F</margin>

**Now there was a certain man there who had been held by a disease for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there, and knew that he had already been held by the disease for a long time, he said to him: "Do you wish to be made whole?" The sick man answered him: "Lord, I have no man to put me into the pool when the water is stirred; but while I am coming, another descends before me."** ] The constancy of the <term>paralytic</term> <note>original: "paralytici", a person suffering from loss of movement</note> is stupendous. He had suffered for thirty-eight years, and every year he sat there waiting to be freed from his disease. Even though he was hindered by more powerful people who got there first, he still did not give up, nor did he despair; therefore...

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> ...the Lord also questions him, wishing to show us the man’s fortitude. For he does not ask as if he needed to be told something. This would not only be superfluous, but it would be strange to look at a sick man and ask if he wants to be healed. The question was asked, therefore, so that the man’s patience might be shown to us. What then does he do? He answers with great gentleness: "Yes," he says, "Lord, I certainly wish it, but I have no man who can carry me into the water." He answered with nothing blasphemous; he did not rebuke Christ as if he were asking a foolish question, nor did he curse the day of his birth, as we often do out of faint-heartedness—and that even when we fall into much lighter illnesses. Instead, he gives a gentle and calm <margin>B</margin> answer, even though he did not know who it was that was questioning him. Did he think this was the only help coming to him—perhaps that this man might carry him into the water—and for that reason he spoke kindly to Christ? Christ, however, did not say "I will heal you" when he asked "Do you wish it?", so that he would not seem to be seeking his own glory.

**Jesus says to him: "Rise, take up your mat and walk." And immediately that man was made whole, and he took up his mat and walked. Now it was the Sabbath on that day. The Jews therefore said to him who had been healed: "It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your mat."** ] He commands the <term>bed</term> <note>original: "grabbatum", a poor man's pallet or cot</note> to be carried because he wanted the miracle to be made more believable; <margin>C</margin> for unless the man's limbs had been firmly strengthened, he could not have carried the bed. He did not, however, demand faith from him before he healed him, as he did with certain others, because that sick man had not yet seen him performing signs. Indeed, the Lord was not accustomed to demand faith from those people before he performed miracles in their sight; but after they had seen the miracles, he did demand faith. Note, however, that as soon as the man heard the command, he believed. For he did not murmur to himself and say: "You command me to rise, I who have been like this for thirty-eight years and have never attained health, and now I should rise so suddenly?" He thought no such thing, but believed and rose. He heals on the Sabbath, teaching man to understand the observance of the Sabbath differently, and not [to think] that the Sabbath consists only of bodily leisure, but [of abstaining] from evil...

### CHAPTER 5. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 358

And so you yourselves are witnesses that John was truthful; although I myself, being who I am, have no need of human testimony, nor does the Lord need the testimony of a servant. But because you thought him more worthy of faith and paid more attention to him than to me—indeed, you went to him, yet you do not believe me even when I perform miracles—for this reason I bring back to your memory the testimony of John. I accept even things unworthy of my divinity so that you might be saved. 
<margin>Why John is a burning lamp.</margin>
He calls John a **burning lamp**, because he has his formation from the earth and was not light by his own nature, but from the grace of the Spirit, and only for a time. But when the "Day of the Lord" appeared—that is, his teaching—the lamp was hidden. <note>Theophylact uses the metaphor of a lamp versus the sun to distinguish between John’s derivative, temporary light and Jesus’s eternal, essential light.</note> However, you accepted what was said by him only for an hour, and you exulted in him, but then, forgetting the things he said about me, you remained in your former unbelief. For if you had once firmly believed him, he would have led you to faith in me as soon as possible.

<margin>F</margin>
*But I have a testimony greater than that of JOHN. For the works which the Father gave me to accomplish—the very works that I do—bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself testified of me; you have never heard his voice, nor seen his form, and you do not have his word remaining in you, because you do not believe him whom he sent.* JOHN indeed testified of me; nevertheless, because it is likely there would be some who might say, "And what is it to us if JOHN wanted to do you a favor and therefore testified to some rather flattering things?", he says: *You sent to JOHN and questioned him,* 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
regarding him as truthful in all things. Nevertheless, I have another testimony greater than John. 
<margin>John 5.</margin>
For the works which the Father gave me—that is, which the Father ordained for me to finish—these bear witness of me. He calls these "works" his miracles, such as the healing of the paralytic and so on. <note>This refers to the healing of the man at the pool of Bethesda earlier in Chapter 5.</note> However, because they were rebuking him for doing these things on the Sabbath, saying, "This man is not from God because he does not keep the Sabbath," he showed them that he does the things decreed by the Father, and that he is more truly from God because he performs the works joined to him by God. For he says: *The works which the Father gave me to accomplish.* Since, therefore, the Father gave those to me, you are adversaries of God when you 
<margin>B</margin>
oppose those works. *And the Father who sent me has himself testified of me.* Where, however, did the Father testify of him? Some say 
<margin>Matthew 17.</margin>
it was at the baptism, when he said: *This is my beloved Son.* <note>The "Voice from Heaven" at Jesus's baptism and later at the Transfiguration (recorded in Matthew 17) is a primary example of the Father's testimony.</note> But I think he means rather that God testified of him throughout all of Scripture, both through the Law and through the Prophets. But, he says, *you have neither heard his voice* (the Father’s, I mean) *nor seen his form.* Therefore, he is unknown to you in every way. Therefore, you do not have his word remaining in you—that is, you do not know the Scriptures which testify of me—even though you seem to know and boast in the oracles of God which were entrusted to you. From this it is manifest that you do not know the Scriptures, because you do not believe in him whom he sent. Therefore, just as you have not heard the voice of God—for God 
<margin>C</margin>
does not have a physical voice—nor seen his form 
<margin>God lacks form and figure.</margin>
(for he lacks shape and figure), so you do not have his word (I mean the Scriptures which testify of me) within you.

*Search the scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life. And it is they that testify of me; yet you do not want to come to me that you may have life. I do not receive glory from men, but I know you, that you do not have the love of God in you.* He had said to them: "The Word of God—that is, the Scriptures that testify of me—are not in you." How then could they have the Word of God? He says: *Search the scriptures,* for in them you think you have life. But see how he does not say...

He argues that the Jewish leaders' rejection of Jesus proves they do not truly understand the Law or the Prophets.</summary>

### CHAPTER 5. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 359

<margin>D</margin>
...[If you search the scriptures], you think you have life, but you only seem to, showing that they perceive no true fruit if they expect to be saved by reading alone without faith being added. *For these indeed bear witness of me, but you do not want to come to me, so that you may have life.* From this we learn that they were evil by choice. For he did not say, "you are not able to come," but *you do not want to come.* 
<margin>The Manichaeans, who deny free will, are refuted</margin>
Let the Manichaeans <note>A dualist sect that believed human nature was inherently evil and denied free will.</note> hear this: that evil consists not in nature, but in the will. After he reminded them of the testimony of John, and of the Father, and of his own works—which he did only for the sake of their salvation—many might have suspected that he said these things out of a love for glory. Therefore he says:
<margin>g</margin>
> *I do not receive glory from men,*
that is, I have no need of it, nor do I have such a nature that requires human glory. But you persecute me, [claiming] that you do this because of the love of God, but it is not so. For I know that you do not have the love of God in you, even if you boast greatly that you persecute me for God's sake. Rightly, therefore, are the Jews said not to have the love of God, because they persecute Love itself: the Son of God. Hence they are also rightly said not to have the word of God dwelling in themselves. For they rejected both the Word and GOD.
> *I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive.*
How can you believe, you who receive glory from one another, and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?
<margin>F</margin>
Do not think that I am going to accuse you before the Father; there is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope. For if you had believed Moses, you would certainly have believed me, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? I indeed (he says) have come in my Father's name. For everywhere he celebrates the Father, and says he was sent by him, and can do nothing of himself, and speaks many humble things, wishing to remove every reason for lack of gratitude. But another will come, namely the Antichrist, who is going to show himself as if he alone were God. Therefore, me indeed, who came in the name of the Father, that

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
is, I say I was sent by the Father, you do not receive; but him you will receive. Furthermore, this will happen to you because he will promise you the glory of life which you seek, desiring to receive mutual glory and spitting out the true glory which is from God alone. I, however, promise you nothing magnificent [in this world], but you see much difficulty in the things spoken by me, and for that reason (he says) 
<margin>A truly spoken word. The origin of infidelity, but not the only one.</margin>
you do not believe me. For you expect to have nothing from me that is pleasant in this life. And in another way: you do not believe me, you who receive glory from one another. For the leaders and teachers themselves, wishing alone to be held in high regard among the common people, will not receive me, lest their glory be diminished. But the people, seeking
<margin>B</margin>
favors from the leaders, do not want to come to me, so that they might not lose, on my account, the honor they have from the leaders. Since they were boasting much about Moses, he says: he himself will accuse you, for he wrote about me. But where did he write about him? Indeed, this saying,
> *The Lord shall raise up a prophet for you,* <note>original: "Prophetam suscitabit vobis dominus." A reference to Deuteronomy 18:15.</note>
was about CHRIST; and many other things, both in words and in signs and 
<margin>Deut. 18. Exod. 3.</margin>
symbols, such as the miracle of the bush. For the fire represents the deity; but the thorny bush <note>original: "rubus autem spinosus."</note> represents sinful nature, which the fire of the deity took up and kept unconsumed, shining with light; it communicated its rays to it, but did not take its imperfections into itself. Moses also said this, which contributed greatly to faith in Christ; for he says:
<margin>C</margin>
> *If a prophet arises performing signs, and making you turn away from God, do not believe him,*
which is how the Antichrist will be.
> *But if a prophet arises performing signs, and leading to God and the Father, and not making you turn away, believe him.*
Therefore CHRIST came in the name of the Father, and while performing signs, he did not command them to turn away from the worship of God; he was the one predicted by Moses. Therefore, if you do not believe the writings of Moses, how will you believe my words? He (Christ) says: Moses wrote, and those books are always before your eyes, even if you should forget them, you can easily bring them back to memory. Nevertheless, you do not believe the written things; so how will you believe my words which are not written? Why then do you say these things, O Lord?

...since you knew that they would not believe? Although I know, he says, that they do not believe, I speak anyway, so that they may not afterwards have a pretext for saying, "If he had spoken, we would have believed." And in another sense: Those who were there at that time, being ungrateful, did not believe; but for those who were to believe later, it was not likely, nor just, that the benefit of Christ’s words be taken away.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Matthew 14, Mark 6, Luke 9</margin> <note>The OCR says Luke 19, but this is a likely typo in the original print for Luke 9, which contains the parallel account.</note>
<margin>D</margin> After these things, Jesus went over the sea of Galilee, which is that of Tiberias, and a great multitude followed him, because they saw his signs which he performed on those who were infirm. But JESUS went up into a mountain, and there he sat with his disciples. Now <margin>E</margin> the Passover, a feast day of the Jews, was near. ] After the Lord spoke to the Jews with harsher words by which they were kindled to envy and became annoyed, he now soothes them by withdrawing, and goes across the sea of Tiberias. Moreover, he calls the lake a "sea." <note>original: "Mare autem dicit stagnum."</note> For divine scripture calls any large gatherings of waters "seas." And in another sense: He moves from place to place, testing the zeal of the multitude. For the lazier ones stayed in their own places, but the more studious followed him. Nevertheless, see that even those following did not follow for the sake of the teaching, but for the benefit of bodily miracles. For this reason it says, "because they saw the signs he performed on those who were infirm." But they become better and more eager for wisdom. For they were astonished, it says, at his teaching, because <margin>F</margin> he taught them as one having authority. He ascended the mountain for the sake of the miracle to come. For he was not arrogant, nor desirous of vain glory, so as to perform miracles in the middle of cities; but fleeing the vain glory of men, he sought solitude, teaching us also. Furthermore, wishing to communicate certain mysteries to the disciples, he ascended the mountain—a thing he was always accustomed to do—because there is a need to be freed from all tumult and to seek a place pure from all noise if one wishes to speak of such things. For the feast day of the Jews, it says, was near,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> yet he did not go up <note>to Jerusalem</note>, but went up into Galilee; for he was no longer subject to legal precepts, such that he had to fulfill the feast days of the Law. And in another sense: with Jewish malice pursuing him, he takes the opportunity to gradually abolish the Law, showing to those paying attention that the figure <note>the symbolic representation</note> had ceased once the Truth <note>Christ</note> had arrived. Observe, however, that it was a "feast of the Jews," but it was not a "feast day of Christ."

<margin>B</margin> When Jesus then had lifted up his eyes, and saw that a great multitude was coming to him, he says to Philip, "Where shall we buy bread, that these may eat?" But this he said to test him: for he himself knew what he was going to do. Philip answered him, "Two hundred denarii <note>A denarius was a standard silver coin representing a day's wage for a laborer; two hundred denarii was a significant sum.</note> worth of bread is not sufficient for them, that each one may take even a little." One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, says to him, "There is one lad here, who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are these among so many?" ] Why did it say, "when he had lifted up his eyes"? So that we may learn that <margin>Christ was not accustomed to wander with his eyes.</margin> Christ was not accustomed to wander here and there with his eyes, but was composed and attentive, not wandering about, as one teaching the disciples more divine things. Finally, he sees the disciples, and asks about the multitude, how it should be fed. Now, he asks no one else but Philip. For he [Philip] was in need of greater instruction, he who later said: <margin>John 14.</margin> "Show us the Father, and it is enough for us." For this reason, he instructs him beforehand, and <margin>C</margin> leads him through a question, so that he might always be mindful of the miracle. For if the miracle had simply been performed, it would not have seemed like such a miracle to him; but now, before it happened, he compels him to confess the scarcity of bread, so that he might more clearly learn the magnitude of the miracle to come, and not cast out from memory those things which he had confessed. Therefore he says, "Where shall we buy so that these may eat?" But he says these things to test Philip, wishing to make known what faith he had. Nor did he ask as one ignorant of Philip's opinion, but he wished to show it to others as well. For the Lord himself knew what he was going to do. Therefore as he tested Philip, and whether he had faith, he found him still thinking like a [mere] man; moreover, he found Andrew also like this, although sensing something more sublime than Philip:

# CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
## ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

<sig>Z 2</sig>

<margin>D</margin> For while the former <note>referring to Philip</note> was saying that two hundred denarii worth of bread would not suffice, the latter <note>Andrew</note> pointed out five barley loaves and two <margin>2 Kings 6</margin> <note>The Latin text cites 4 Kings, which in the Vulgate corresponds to 2 Kings in modern Bibles. The reference is to the miracle of Elisha feeding one hundred men with twenty loaves.</note> fishes. For he was perhaps thinking of the miracles of the prophets, such as the sign of the bread given by Elisha when Samaria had come to the extreme of poverty. Nevertheless, Andrew is also found wanting, thinking nothing worthy of the Lord; for he says, *But what are these among so many?* For he supposed that while the Lord was indeed going to multiply the loaves, the multiplication would be greater if there were more to begin with—judging everything according to human limitation. For the Lord could have made loaves even out of nothing to suffice for the crowd; yet, lest it should seem that the creation was not from his own wisdom, he used the created thing itself as the material for his <margin>E</margin> miracles, and having received the five loaves, as if they were a certain raw material, <margin>The remarkable wickedness and impiety of the Manichaeans</margin> he performed that most famous miracle. Let the Manichaeans <note>A dualist sect that believed the physical world was created by an evil deity.</note> be put to shame, who say that bread and all created things were made by an evil God; for that reason, if anyone offers them bread, they do not receive it from his hands, but command it to be thrown far away. Standing there and cursing the one who gave it, they say: "May he who sowed you be scattered, and may he who kneaded you be kneaded in flesh and family." <note>original: "Qui seminauit te dispergatur: & qui pinsuit te, pinsatur carne, & familia." This refers to a Manichaean ritual curse intended to distance themselves from the "sin" of harvesting or preparing food.</note> Therefore, let them be put to shame, seeing that Christ, the Son of the good God, multiplied the loaves. For if the creature were evil, the blessed God would certainly not have multiplied it—to say nothing of the fact that he himself ate the bread. Furthermore, if anyone should ask whether this is the same miracle of the loaves as the one <margin>Matt. 14.</margin> described in Matthew, we say it is certainly the same. Although in that account the disciples approach him, <margin>F</margin> advising that the crowd be dismissed, while in this place Jesus himself asks where they may be fed, there is no need to wonder. For it is probable that both happened: that the disciples first advised the Lord about dismissing the crowds, and then Philip was questioned by the Lord as to how they might be fed.
  Jesus then said, *Make the men sit down.* Now there was much grass in that place. So the men sat down, in number about five thousand. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to the disciples, and the disciples to those sitting down. Likewise also of the 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> fishes, as much as they wanted. And when they were filled, he said to his disciples, *Gather up the fragments that remain.* They gathered them up, therefore, and filled twelve baskets with the fragments of the five barley loaves which remained to those who had eaten. ] He ordered them to sit down as if at a prepared table. The disciples, although they were skeptical before, nevertheless swiftly made the men sit down. Now there was grass, because it was spring. For it says the Passover was near, which was celebrated in the first month of spring. Furthermore, only the men are numbered by the Evangelist, following the custom of the Law. For even Moses numbered the people from twenty years old and upward, making <margin>Num. 26, 32</margin> no mention of the women; by which we are taught that all <margin>Why only men are numbered in Scripture</margin> <margin>B</margin> that is manly and youthful is deemed worthy to be numbered by God. And having taken the loaves, he gives thanks, showing that thanks must be given to God before food. Moreover, because there was a crowd, he gives thanks in the presence of the crowd so that he might persuade all that he has come according to the will of God, that he is not an adversary to God, but refers all things to the Father. For when he performs a miracle in private, he does no such thing, even if he performs a greater one; but when he works a miracle before many, then he looks toward God. He shows, moreover, that he heals not out of weakness, but because of the "dispensation" <note>The divine plan or "economy" of salvation.</note> we mentioned, acting by a certain authority and as Lord. Some say, moreover, that he gave thanks for this reason: so that he might remain <margin>C</margin> unknown to the prince of this world <note>The devil</note> until the time of his passion; thus the demon would not recognize him as God, but would be deceived and "baited," and so be finished by the cross. Furthermore, the Lord permits so many fragments to remain not for the sake of ostentation, but lest it be believed that the men were satisfied by a mere phantom <note>A refutation of Docetism, the belief that Christ's body or actions were only an illusion.</note>. Let it be apparent to all that they were truly satisfied, since there were so many remains; and for this reason he ordered the fragments to be gathered, so that seeing them, they might be more mindful of the miracle performed. One ought not only to wonder that there were remains, but also that there were neither more nor fewer than twelve baskets of leftovers—equal to the number of the disciples—so that they might all carry them, and not even Judas himself <note>would be without evidence of the miracle.</note>

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

Let it be demonstrated to him that God is the master, from whom he should take his final lesson; otherwise, this very thing might turn into his condemnation because of his malice. For he <note>Judas, or perhaps the unbelieving listener</note> was the one who, despite the great things Christ had done—of which he himself even carried the baskets—later betrayed Him. It was not without cause that He commanded the apostles to carry the baskets, but so that they would be mindful of the miracle, as they were the future teachers of the entire world. For the multitude indeed was not going to perceive any great utility; they were prone to forget the miracle immediately. But the disciples were to gain no common profit from it. Let us also learn from this miracle not to be fainthearted in narrow straits and poverty, nor to be timid in hospitality and sharing; but let us believe that even if we have only one loaf, He will multiply it, who made so much left over from only five loaves.

By way of allegory, however, He went out from <margin>Jeremiah 12</margin> Jerusalem, according to what was said in the prophecy: *I have forsaken my house, I have left my inheritance* <note>Jeremiah 12:7</note>. Then indeed He goes into "Galilee of the nations" <note>Matthew 4:15</note>, looking upon the Gentiles, and a great crowd follows Him. He goes up into a mountain—that is, the cross, so that He might draw all people to Himself—or into heaven, to the honor and great glory of God. For as He ascended into the heavens and began to be glorified by us as God, and not as a mere man, He is said to have ascended the mountain. For the high opinion of Him is a mountain.

But to us, who receive through our five senses, He gives <margin>1 Corinthians 4 <note>The text likely refers to 1 Corinthians 14:19, where Paul speaks of "five words" of understanding.</note></margin> five rational loaves, because they are five in number; for He gives to each sense a suitable "bread," that is, a word. Just as Paul says, *I would rather speak five words in the church*, which are suitable for the edification of the five senses. We cannot, however, grasp the five entire words of the mysteries; there are things we cannot grasp and eat because we are worldly <note>original: "carnales," or fleshly</note>. The <margin>Psalm 97 <note>In the Vulgate/Septuagint numbering, Psalm 91:13 (Modern Psalm 92:12): "The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree."</note></margin> apostles carry these in their five baskets for the sake of satisfied souls. The baskets are made solely from palm leaves, and it is written that *the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree.*

Those men, therefore, when they had seen the sign that Jesus had performed, said: "Truly this is that Prophet who is to come into the world."

### COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.
<page-num>363</page-num>

[Jesus therefore, when He knew that they were about to come and seize Him to make Him king, withdrew again to the mountain by Himself.] See the gluttony of the common people: though He had performed innumerable miracles, and even more wonderful ones, they did not marvel; but behold, because of the food, they say: "This is that prophet." No longer do they argue with Him about the violation of the Sabbath, no longer do they defend the Law; but they so revere Him because of the loaves that they not only proclaim Him a Prophet, but even deem Him worthy of the kingdom. But He flees, teaching us to despise worldly honors. He ascends the mountain by Himself, taking none of the disciples with Him, so that He might test their devotion, to see if they would endure His absence.

<margin>B</margin>
[But when evening came, His disciples went down to the sea, and having boarded a ship, they were crossing the sea toward the town of Capernaum. And it was already dark, and Jesus had not come to them. But the sea was swelling because a great wind was blowing. When they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty furlongs, they see JESUS walking on the sea and drawing near to the ship, and they were afraid. But He says to them, "It is I; do not be afraid." Then they were willing to take Him into the ship, and immediately the ship reached the land to which they were going.] The Lord indeed ascended the mountain alone so that (as we have said) He might test the devotion of the disciples. But they waited until evening for Him to come, and when He did not appear, they did not endure it, but, kindled with the desire of seeking Him, they <margin>C</margin> boarded a ship. The Evangelist did not reveal the time by chance or accident, but through this, he declared their vehement love, seeing as the evening had almost kept them back.

On the other hand, He was testing them with a trial of their skill <note>original: "priscitati," perhaps referring to their old trade as fishermen</note>, so that when tranquility was restored by a miracle, they might rejoice all the more, and the memory of Him might sit indelibly in their hearts. He was there, therefore, as the storm raged, and by His word, He took away their fear and brought peace to the sea, performing a double act of mercy by calming the disturbance of both their souls and the sea. Furthermore, He did not board the ship immediately, wishing to manifest the miracle. For see three miracles: one, that He walked upon the sea; second, that He restrained the waves...

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> 
...the third [miracle], that he immediately caused the ship to be at the land where they were going, although it was a great distance from the land when the Lord stood by it. Therefore, the Jews indeed crossed the Red Sea with Moses as their leader. But he did all things as a servant and was proclaimed as such; but this man [Christ] did so with all power. And in the former case, as the wind blew, the water gave way so that it provided a passage as if on dry land; however, in this place a greater miracle occurs. For while the sea remained in its own nature, it bore the Lord upon its surface, so that the prophetic word might be fulfilled: *He who walks upon the sea as upon a pavement.* <note>original: "Qui ambulat super mare vt super pauimentum." This is an allusion to Job 9:8 or a variant translation of the Psalms.</note>

<margin>Psalm 65 according to another translation.</margin> 
Moreover, many of us are even now in spiritual darkness and are in danger of sinking in the spiritual sea; but let us receive Christ, and we shall be saved from all dangers. And although sometimes certain things stir up a tumult for us—either devils or men testing us, and striving to shake us through terrors—let us nevertheless hear Christ crying out, <margin>Jerome</margin> *do not fear, it is I.* Now, what He says has this meaning: Terrifying things indeed pass away, therefore do not fear those things which pass away; for I am, that is, I am always remaining, and I am like that God who is <note>A reference to the Divine Name "I AM" revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14, signifying eternal existence.</note>. Therefore, because terrifying things are temporary and do not truly exist, but I am—that is, I remain and never pass away, and I truly exist—do not lose your faith in me because of temporary things.

<margin>An Exhortation.</margin>
Observe, I pray, how Christ does not appear immediately at the beginning of the danger, but in the heat of it, and He dissolves the fear. For He allows us to be in the midst of dangers so that when we have struggled in tribulation and have been hard-pressed, we may become more proven; and so that when we have moved all our own strength and wisdom and found it weak, we may flee to Him alone, who is able to save from the unexpected. For when the human mind has become exhausted, then divine salvation suddenly comes to aid, and it prepares us to flee to Him alone who can save, so that we do not ascribe salvation to ourselves.

<margin>What it means to receive Christ into the ship.</margin> 
If we also wish to receive Christ into our ship—that is, to give Christ a dwelling place in our heart—we will immediately be found in the land to which we are going. And what is that land? Surely the land of the heavenly promise, the land of the meek, and of those who live in peace having been liberated from malice.

### EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

<margin>A</margin> 
The next day, the crowd that stood across the sea saw that there was no other small boat there except that one into which his disciples had entered, and that Jesus had not entered into the small boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. However, other small boats arrived from Tiberias near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks. When the crowd therefore saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves also climbed into the small boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus. And when they had found him across the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?" Jesus answered them and said, "Amen, amen, I say to you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and <margin>B</margin> were filled." 

Jesus indeed went on foot over the sea into the region across the sea. The crowds, however, on the following day, when they had sought Him and seen that only one ship had been present in which the disciples had entered, and not Jesus Himself, they pondered this miracle among themselves and suspected that He had crossed the sea on foot. For if another ship had also been present, it would have been likely for them to think that He did not sail with the disciples but entered another to cross the sea. But now, since there was only one, which received the disciples alone and not the Lord, the miracle is manifest. Therefore the crowds understood these things: and later they found other ships that had crossed over, they boarded them, and crossed to <margin>C</margin> Capernaum. 

There, however, having found the Lord, they do not supplicate Him or ask to learn how He crossed, nor do they ask about this sign, but they say lazily: "How did you come here?" For those who were seeking to seize Him and make Him king, having found Him, deliberate on no such thing; but having cast aside the miracle, they seek rather to enjoy the table as they did before. For this reason, the Lord reproaches them: "For you seek me," He says, "because you ate of the loaves, and for that reason you are held by a desire for me, so that I might prepare a table for you again." Observe, however, that although He refutes them, He does not use a harsh rebuke. For He did not say, "O slaves of the belly and gluttons," but wishing to correct them with gentleness, He argues with them, again through this which He reveals...

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> ...the secrets of their hearts, wishing to lead them to a greater faith. That their correction was intended as a rebuke is manifest from what follows. For he delivers to them a most useful teaching and says:

<margin>The food which perishes.</margin>
> **Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for on him God the Father has set his seal.**

"You indeed," he says, "seek me because of the loaves, because you desire that food. It is necessary, however, that you should not be entirely devoted to the belly, but rather take the greatest spiritual care, and not expend all your anxiety upon bodily food." For he called that "the food that perishes." Now, because many people desire to live in idleness—especially the **Messalians** <note>original: "Masseliani"; a 4th-century ascetic sect, also known as Euchites, who were accused of rejecting manual labor in favor of perpetual prayer.</note>, 
<margin>Messalian heretics devoted to idleness. Ecclesiasticus 33.</margin>
who have used this saying to defend their own laziness—it is worthwhile to clarify this statement. For our Lord Jesus Christ did not say this because he wished to remove bodily labor from them and force them into idleness. Indeed, idleness has taught every kind of malice; and if it must be said clearly, the very desire to live idly is "the food that perishes." Thus, it is necessary for one who follows Christ to work, so that he may have something to share with others; for this carries a reward and the promise of the future kingdom. 

"And how then," they ask, "does the Lord say that one must not work for the food that perishes, rejecting constant preoccupation with food and leading us significantly toward spiritual things?" Certainly, the Lord says this to exclude excessive bodily preoccupation. This is also manifest from what he says to Martha: 
<margin>Luke 10. Matthew 6.</margin>
*Martha, you are anxious and troubled, but one thing is necessary; Mary has chosen the better part.* And again: *Do not be anxious for tomorrow.* These are the things cited by those who wish to be fed through laziness. But what do we say? The word spoken to Martha was not about work and labor, or about idleness, but about the observation of time: that the time for listening should not be consumed by the preoccupations of preparing food. He persuades her, therefore, not to waste the time of teaching in vain because of a preoccupation with the things of the belly. As for his saying "do not be anxious," he does not reject labor by this word either. For **worry** is one thing and **labor** is another.

He wants us to work each day, saying, *Do not be anxious about tomorrow*—as if he were saying: "Do not be anxious about how you might rest tomorrow by working today; but rather, preparing your food daily through daily labor, do not be anxious for the morrow." 

By "the food that endures," he means the mystical reception of the body of the Lord, which the Son of Man gives to us, having become man for us. "Whom the Father has sealed" <note>original: "consignauit/obfignauit"; meaning to authenticate or set a mark of ownership and identity upon.</note>—that is, he showed and confirmed that this is his Son. Christ himself showed this through miracles; but because he is speaking with the Jews, 
<margin>B</margin> and so they would not be troubled, he refers back to the Father, saying that he was "sealed" by Him. This means he was demonstrated and confirmed by testimonies, because the Son is the image of the Father, and his seal and character <note>original: "character"; here meaning the exact representation or "imprint" of God's essence, as in Hebrews 1:3.</note>. Understand that he was "sealed" by him just as an image is a seal. Thus, what he says holds this meaning: "This one, who appeared as the Son of Man, the Father has sealed"—that is, he begot his own seal and image, who would have in himself everything that the Father himself had, and a natural identity with him.

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> ...it would benefit the stomach; and that this is true is manifest from what follows.
**Our fathers ate manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat. Jesus said to them, Amen, amen I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you that bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. They said therefore to Him, Lord, always give us this bread.**
<margin>E</margin> It was not in vain that we said those who serve their bellies were seeking a sign, specifically a sign involving bread. Behold, they even mention manna, and not any other miracle—neither those in Egypt nor at the Red Sea. For wishing to incite Him to perform such a sign by which they might be carnally fed, they remember the manna on account of their immoderate gluttony. What, then, does the immense wisdom of God, our Lord JESUS CHRIST, answer them? "It was not Moses who gave you the bread"—that is, Moses did not give you the *true* bread; for those things were types <note>original: "typi" — in biblical interpretation, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows something in the New Testament.</note> of the things that are happening now. For Moses held the figure of the true God, the leader of the spiritual Israelites; but that bread is a figure of me, who descended from heaven, and I truly feed, and I truly exist. Furthermore, He calls Himself the true bread, not because the manna was false, but because that was a figure and a shadow, not the truth itself. For properly speaking, the manna is the only-begotten Son of God made man, the Word, and a hearing that causes one to be amazed. For "manna" is interpreted as "What is this?" <note>Theophylact is referencing the Hebrew *Man hu* (Exodus 16:15), which the Israelites exclaimed when they first saw the substance.</note> For the Jews, seeing that which had rained down in abundance before each man's tent, <margin>F</margin> <margin>Exodus 16.</margin> and being struck by the unusual and foreign sight, asked one another: "What is this?" Therefore, the Lord, the Son of God made man, is Himself the manna which strikes everyone with awe, so that they say, "What is this?" How is He the Son of God and the Son of Man? How is there one person from two different natures? What is this mystery? This bread, therefore, being life according to its nature—as the Son of the living Father—does what is proper to itself: for it gives life to all things. Therefore, just as bread from the earth sustains the weak nature of the flesh, not allowing it to decay, so also CHRIST, through the operation of the Spirit, gives life to the soul,

<margin>A</margin> and also preserves the body itself in incorruption. For through Christ, the resurrection of human nature from <margin>Resurrection of human nature from the dead granted through Christ</margin> the dead and the incorruption of bodies has been granted. But the Jews, still devoted to their bellies and entirely earthly, understand these sayings as referring to physical bread and say, "Give us this bread always." Thus, speaking foolishly, they were rebuked; and they say "always," meaning not for one or two days. They said this, however, out of greed. So that there might be no need to spend much on food, they say: "Always give us this easily obtained bread."
<margin>B</margin> **But JESUS said, I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst. Whence He says: "I am the bread of life." He did not say the bread of nourishment, but of life. For when all things were deadened, CHRIST—who is the bread—gave us life through Himself, because we believe the leaven of the human <margin>C</margin> mixture <note>original: "conspersionis" — refers to the "kneaded dough" of human nature assumed by Christ in the Incarnation.</note> was baked by the fire of the deity. But He is the bread of life, not of this usual life, but of a transformed life that does not fail in death. Moreover, he who believes in that bread shall not hunger, nor suffer famine by hearing the word of God, nor shall he thirst with a spiritual thirst, because he has the water of baptism and the sanctification of the Spirit. For he who is not baptized suffers thirst and great dryness, being devoid of the holy cooling water. But the baptized person has the Spirit, by whom he is always refreshed. Showing that faith in Christ is not <margin>Faith is a distinguished gift of God</margin> some common thing but a gift of God given by the Father to those who are worthy and upright of heart, He says: "All that the Father gives me shall come to me," that is, those whom the Father gives me shall believe in me...

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 366

<margin>D</margin> [Thirdly.] But you Jews, since you are unworthy, are not given to me by the Father; for that reason you neither come to me, nor do you have a righteous heart, so that God the Father, who loves you, might lead you to faith in me. But I will not cast out the one who comes to me, that is, I will not let him perish, but I will save him, and I will refresh him with great care. For I descended from heaven, not to do anything else besides the will of the Father. Furthermore, He says these things so they may learn that He is not an adversary to the Father’s will. Because they called Him an adversary of God, He turns the accusation back upon them, though not explicitly, and says: "You are the adversaries of God, you who do not receive me, I who do the will of the Father." Where is Nestorius in this place, who says that Christ was deified <note>original: "deificatus" — the process of being made divine.</note> after the resurrection? <margin>Nestorius?</margin> Do you not hear, miserable man, that He descended from heaven? Now, He who descended from heaven was certainly not a bare man. For a bare man <note>original: "nudus homo" — referring to a person who is merely human without a divine nature.</note> does not descend; rather, if a man ascends into heaven, God grants him this on account of virtue. The descent of the Lord alone precedes the ascent. He Himself, therefore, both descended from heaven as God, since He deigned to be incarnated, and ascended into heaven with His flesh, as a man specifically, to where He was previously as God. Therefore, Christ was not a bare man afterwards deified, as Nestorius raved, but God before the ages, incarnated in these latest times.

<margin>E</margin> "And this is the will of the Father who sent me: that I should lose nothing of all that He has given me, but that I should raise it up on the last day." And this is the will <margin>F</margin> of Him who sent me: "that everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him may have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."] Here He repeatedly places the phrase "The Father gave to me," so that He might prick their hearts, and they might recognize that they are unworthy of God's gift. For if the Father gives faith in Christ as something great and worthy, but they themselves do not possess it, it is manifest that they have fallen away from the gift of God. Therefore, I (He says) will not lose those whom the Father gives me—that is, those who believe in me—but I will raise them up; that <margin>A double resurrection.</margin> is, in the resurrection, I will deem them worthy of clarity. For there is a double resurrection: one is common and general, by which all, even sinners, rise; the other is that by which only the righteous are taken up to meet the Lord in the air,

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> and first meet the Lord with great confidence. This resurrection Paul names <term>exanastasis</term><gloss>exanastasis</gloss>, <gloss>exanastasis</gloss>—that is, an "out-resurrection" <note>original: "ἐξανάστασιν" — a specific Greek term suggesting a "rising up out of" the rest of the dead, often interpreted as the special resurrection of the righteous.</note>—on account of the elevation from the earth. For sinners indeed rise from their graves onto the earth, but from the earth they will not rise into the air. For they will remain below like those who are condemned. But the righteous both rise and rise up, being caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. Sinners, however, only rise. Furthermore, the Lord, interpreting what "everything the Father gave me" means, says the same idea in other words: "that everyone who sees the Son and believes may have eternal life." For He says nothing else than what He said above. For this <margin>B</margin> phrase, "everything the Father gave me," is the same as "he who sees the Son and believes." And this which He says, "I will not lose," is the same as saying "he has eternal life." He frequently makes mention of the resurrection to persuade men not to limit God's providence only to those things that are seen, but to know that there is also another state in which they will undoubtedly enjoy the rewards of virtue. Although retribution is not currently clear in this life, it is for that reason not yet connected with the course of virtue.

The Jews therefore murmured about Him, because He had said, "I am that bread which descended from heaven." And they said, "Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? <margin>C</margin> How then does He say, 'I descended from heaven'?" JESUS therefore answered and said to them, "Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day."] The Jews therefore murmured when the Lord said, "I am the bread." For up to this point, they thought He was speaking of physical bread, and they bore Him mildly, hoping that He was going to give this bread to gratify their bellies. But now, because He revealed to them that He was not speaking of physical bread but spiritual, they murmur in contempt of it. For how could they understand spiritual food, and life, and resurrection? Thus they were scandalized in Him, seeing His mother, but hearing Him say, "I descended from heaven." Therefore, not understanding that He Himself was God, [they murmured].

<margin>Take care: Free Will.</margin> Now, He says this not to take away the freedom of the will—heaven forbid—but to show that he who is to believe has great need of cooperation from God. And in another sense, the Father draws those who have a readiness of will. But those who do not make themselves suitable, He does not draw to faith.

<margin>Comparison of a magnet.</margin> For just as a magnet does not draw everything, but only iron, so also God approaches everyone, but He draws those who are more suitable and who display a familiarity toward Him. Therefore, the Father indeed draws and leads people to the Son. The Son, however, raises them up and gives them life, granting life and breath <note>original: "spirationem" — a technical term referring to the proceeding of the Holy Spirit, often compared to the breath of life.</note> in good things, which is to say, the Holy Spirit. For everyone who lives also has breath.

Observe, moreover, the authority of the Son: "I," He says, "will raise him up." He did not say, "my Father will raise him up," but "I." For He does not speak in humble terms through all things, but sometimes He reveals the heights of His divinity.

But now, with the Only-begotten having become incarnate, knowledge comes from the Father Himself in the Holy Spirit, so that the prophetic saying is fulfilled: "In your light" (that is, the Father’s light), "which is the Spirit, we shall see the light" (which is the Son).

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>The bread in the sacred mysteries is not only a figure, but the flesh of the Lord.</margin>
...rection <note>original: "rectionis" — the conclusion of "resurrectionis" (resurrection) from the previous page</note>. Clearly, in this place, He speaks to us about the mystical <term>communion</term> <note>original: "communione" — the act of sharing in the Eucharist</note> of His body. For the bread (He says) which I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. Furthermore, indicating His own power—that He is to be crucified not as a servant or one lesser than the Father, but voluntarily—He says, "I will give my flesh for the life of the world." For although He is said to have been handed over by the Father, He is nevertheless said to have handed Himself over: and the former is so that we may learn of His harmony with the Father, while the latter is so that we may not be ignorant of the Son's free will. Take note, however, that the bread which is eaten by us in the mysteries is not only a figure or a certain representation of the Lord's flesh, but the very flesh of the Lord itself. For He did not say, "The bread which I will give is a figure of my flesh," but rather, "it is my flesh."

<margin>E</margin>
For that bread is transformed by secret words through a mystical blessing and the coming of the Holy Spirit into the flesh of the Lord. And let it not disturb anyone that the bread must be believed to be flesh. For even when the Lord was walking in the flesh and receiving nourishment from bread, that bread which was eaten was changed into His body and became like His holy flesh, contributing to its growth and sustenance according to human custom. Therefore, even now the bread is changed into the flesh of the Lord. And why (one might ask) does it not appear to us as flesh, but as bread? So that we do not shrink away in horror from eating it. For if it had indeed appeared as flesh, we would have been unpleasantly affected toward the communion. But now, with the Lord condescending to our weakness, the mystical food appears to us as the kind of thing we are otherwise accustomed to. For the life of the world, however, He gave His flesh unto death; for by dying, He destroyed death.

<margin>F</margin>
Understand also by "the life of the world" the resurrection. For the death of the Lord brought about a general resurrection for the entire human race. Perhaps He also named "life" in terms of sanctification and blessedness. For although not all have received sanctification and life in the spirit, nevertheless the Lord gave Himself for the world, and as far as it depended on Him, the world was saved and nature sanctified, because it received the power to conquer sin through one man, our Lord Jesus Christ, just as through one sin, Adam had fallen.

### ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

The Jews therefore argued among themselves, saying, "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink." When the Jews heard about the eating of that flesh, they disbelieved. Therefore they also spoke a word of unbelief: "How?" For when thoughts of unbelief enter the soul, the word "how" enters at the same time. Therefore,

<margin>B</margin>
wanting to show that this is not impossible, but even very necessary—and that life cannot be had in any other way except by eating my flesh, etc.—He said this. In the same way, Nicodemus also said out of unbelief, "How can a man enter into his mother’s womb?" Therefore, when we hear, "unless you eat the flesh of the Son, you will not have life," we ought to retain an undoubting faith in receiving the divine mysteries, and not ask "in what way." For the <term>natural man</term> <note>original: "animalis homo" — referring to 1 Corinthians 2:14, describing a person relying on human intellect rather than spiritual insight</note>, that is, one who follows human and natural thoughts, is not capable of those things which are supernatural and spiritual. And so he does not understand the spiritual eating of the Lord's flesh:

<margin>The natural man. 1 Corinthians 2</margin>

<margin>C</margin>
those who are not partakers of this will not be partakers of eternal life, because they have not received Jesus, who is eternal life. For it is not the flesh of a mere man that is eaten, but that of God, and it is able to deify <note>original: "deificare" — to make divine or unite with God's nature</note>, as it is mixed with the deity. This is also true food, because it does not last for a short time, nor is it corrupted like perishable food, but it becomes a support for eternal life. Likewise, the drinking of the Lord’s blood is truly drink, because it does not satisfy thirst for a time, but preserves one always without thirst, nor does it allow the drinker to be in want: just as He said to the Samaritan woman, "He who drinks of the water that I shall give will not thirst." For whoever receives the grace of the Holy Spirit through the taking of the divine mysteries will suffer neither spiritual hunger nor thirst, as the unbelieving do.

He argues that eternal life requires participation in these mysteries, which cannot be understood by human logic alone but must be accepted through faith.</summary>

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>The flesh of the Lord is life-giving.</margin>
**D** "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. Just as the living Father sent me, so I also live because of the Father. And whoever eats me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven: not as your fathers ate manna and died; whoever eats this bread will live forever." [In this passage we learn of the sacrament of communion. For whoever eats and drinks the flesh and blood of the Lord remains in the Lord himself, and the Lord in him. For a new mingling <note>original: "contemperatio"; a term used by Greek fathers like Theophylact to describe the union of the believer with Christ</note> takes place, beyond all human reason, so that God is in us and we are in God. You do not hear a terrifying report: we do not eat a "naked" God, for he cannot be touched and is incorporeal, and can be apprehended neither by eyes nor <margin>E</margin> hands. <margin>Flesh by its own nature is of no benefit.</margin> On the other hand, the flesh of a mere human being could be of no benefit; but because God has united flesh to himself according to an inexpressible mingling, the flesh is life-giving—not because it has passed over into the nature of God (heaven forbid!), but in the likeness of **glowing iron**, which remains iron and yet displays the operation of fire. Thus, therefore, the flesh of the Lord, while remaining flesh, is life-giving, as it is the flesh of God. Therefore, just as I (he says) live because of the Father—that is, just as I was born from the Father, who is life—so also he who eats me lives because of me, while he is in a certain way mixed with me and "trans-elemented" <note>original: "transelementatur"; a Greek theological term (metastoicheiosis) suggesting a fundamental change in the elements of the person</note> into me, who can give life. But when you hear "I live," do not think that he lives by a participation in life—otherwise God would be called a "living creature" <note>original: "animal"; here meaning a being that merely possesses an "anima" or soul like a creature</note>—but he is not; for neither is <margin>F</margin> God named a living creature, nor will any created thing be called "Life." Moreover, he frequently and repeatedly brings up the phrase: <margin>What the Manna signified.</margin> "Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness," so that he might persuade the people. For if it was possible for people to be fed for forty years without harvest or sowing, and for their lives to be preserved, much more will the Lord now preserve our spiritual life with a better bread: his own flesh, which was formed from a Virgin without the seed of man. Everywhere, however, he mentions life, and frequently adds this name because nothing is so sweet to men as that thing. Therefore, you also are able to eat and drink the flesh and blood of the Lord, not only according to the mystical communion, but also in another certain way. For indeed, <margin>A</margin> someone eats the flesh when he walks by way of **practice** <note>original: "practicen"; refers to the "active life" of moral struggle and labor</note>. For flesh is active, just as practice is laborious. But he drinks the blood like wine, by which the heart of the **contemplative** is gladdened. For contemplation is free from labor—indeed, it is the rest from labors—and is likened to a drink, because drinking requires less labor than eating.
"These things he said in the synagogue, teaching in Capernaum. Many of his disciples, therefore, having heard these things, said, 'This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?' But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were murmuring about this, said to them, 'Does this offend you? What then <margin>B</margin> if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?'"] Why did he teach in the synagogue? Partly because he wished to "hunt" the multitude, and partly because he was showing that he was not contrary to the Law, which was read in the synagogues. But why did he bring forth such speeches in public, even though he knew no one would receive benefit from them, but many would even be more offended? For even his disciples, having heard these things, said, "This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?" Therefore, what profit came from these words? Truly, the most and greatest profit. For since they were constantly mindful of physical food, he showed them that all those things were figures from the shadow, but the things now introduced by him are the truth; <margin>C</margin> for the sake of this he says these things, and reminds them of spiritual food, so that he might make them emerge a little from sensory things, and despise figures and shadows, and run toward the truth. But since they could understand nothing above the senses, they do not become better, but rather recoil, and say, "This is a hard saying"—that is, harsh and unable to be received. For who, being carnal, could receive spiritual food, and the bread that comes down from heaven, and the flesh which is eaten? But when you hear that his "disciples" depart, do not understand those who are truly disciples, but those who followed in the order of disciples and seemed to bear the figure of disciples while they were being taught by him. For indeed, even among the disciples there were some who, compared to the rest...

### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> Compared to the general crowd, these were called his disciples. For they remained with him for a longer time than the multitudes. However, when compared to the other true disciples, they were of no account, because they believed in him only for a time, and with a certain (so to speak) "cold heat" <note>original: "frigido quodam calore"; a rhetorical paradox describing a lukewarm or superficial faith</note>. Observe, however, their foolishness. For they ought to have asked and learned the things of which they were ignorant; instead, they recoiled, and interpreted nothing spiritually, but took everything exactly as it appeared. Because they had heard the word "flesh," they thought he was forcing them to become devourers of flesh and blood. But because we understand these things spiritually, we are not eaters of flesh—on the contrary, we are sanctified through such food. Wishing to show them that, as God, nothing in their hearts was hidden from him, <margin>E</margin> he says, "Does this offend you? What then if you should see me—who seem to you to be the son of man—ascending into heaven, where I was before as God?" For he himself ascended as a man to where he was previously as God. He said this to lead them away from their opinion, for they thought he was the son of Joseph. For whoever believes that he was in heaven before will certainly believe that he is not the son of Joseph, but the Son of God, and will have faith in the things spoken by him. Now, when you hear that the Son of Man was in heaven before, do not think that his body descended from heaven, as <margin>Marcellus and Apollinarius, heresiarchs.</margin> the leaders of heresy, Marcellus and Apollinarius, raved <note>Marcellus of Ancyra and Apollinaris of Laodicea were early Christian thinkers whose views on the nature of Christ were later condemned as heretical; Apollinaris specifically was accused of teaching that Christ had a "heavenly body."</note>; rather, because the Son of Man and God the Word were one and the same person, he is said, as we have stated, to ascend as man to where <margin>F</margin> he was before as God.

<margin>A</margin> it," that is, they are spiritual and they are life, having nothing carnal about them and bringing eternal life.
