Rather, consider that the Father does good to those, and gives the gift of faith to those, in whom choice and will cooperate <note>Theophylact emphasizes "synergism," the idea that divine grace and human free will work together.</note>. For he who is not aided by his own will, even if he is "assumed" by God, perceives no benefit. To give an example: God gives to all, but some both receive it well and use what is given, and by guarding it, they manifest God's gift. Others receive it, but waste the things given, so that they seem to have received nothing. Therefore, when the Evangelist says, "unless it has been <margin>C</margin> granted to someone by the Father," he cannot come to the Son, he means this: he comes to the Son to whom the Father is going to give [the gift]—that is, the one by whom the gift given by God has been guarded. Therefore, many disciples went "backwards," that is, they separated themselves from the Master; and they moved forward not by progressing, but by going "backwards" into unbelief. For truly, whoever divides himself from Christ goes backward; but he who, according to Paul, "clings to the Lord," always stretches himself toward the things that are ahead. <margin>1 Corinthians 6.</margin> <note>Specifically 1 Cor 6:17: "But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him."</note> But he himself, showing that he lacks nothing—neither their service nor the care they bestowed on him—says to them: "Do you also want to go away?" ### CHAPTER 6. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.

<margin>D</margin> ...the twelve, why were they not dismissed along with the others? Partly because he maintained a dignity appropriate to a teacher; partly because in this way they could be more effectively drawn to him. For if he had indeed praised them, they might have suffered some human weakness and become more arrogant, thinking they were doing him a favor by staying with him. But by demonstrating to them that he needed no one’s company, he was better able to hold them together, so that they might realize they were receiving a benefit rather than granting one; and that they were receiving more than they were giving. And <margin>Free Will.</margin> consider how prudently he spoke. For he did not say, "Go away"—for that would have been the word of someone pushing them away—but he asked, "Do you also wish to go away?" By which word he made them free agents, whether they would follow or not, and he demonstrated that he did not want them to accompany him merely out of reverence for him, but so they might know it was a benefit <margin>B</margin> to follow him.

Simon Peter therefore answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe and have known that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus answered them, "Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" Now he was speaking of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot. For this man was going to betray him, though he was one of the twelve. Peter, being a lover of his brothers, answers for the whole choir <note>The "choir" (Latin: *chorus*) refers to the unified group of the twelve apostles.</note>. For he did not say, "Lord, to whom shall I go?" and "I have known and I have believed," but, "to whom shall we go?" etc. Moreover, he says the Lord has the words of eternal life <margin>E</margin> because he had heard him saying, "He who believes in me, I will raise him up, and he shall have eternal life." For they had already accepted the resurrection and the entire doctrine; and unlike the others who heard, they had not been offended by the words, but rather by their own negligence in paying attention, their laziness, and their lack of prudence. For these twelve heard the same things, yet they were not offended, but remained. What then does Christ do? Does he praise Peter, as he does in another place? Not at all, so that he might not seem to flatter him, and so that he might remain humble. But what did he say to Peter? "I indeed chose you twelve. Nevertheless, not even all of you are worthy of that choice, but one of you is a devil." This, however, is to be understood in two ways: either that he even now slanders all my deeds...

# 371
### COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.
A ...and receives none of them; or, because he is going to slander me. For in actual fact, Judas appeared as such, slandering the Lord among the Jews and bringing his mysteries to them. Just as David says of himself, "He went <margin>Psalm 40 <note>original: "Psal. 40"; in modern Bibles, this corresponds to Psalm 41:6.</note></margin> outside and spoke of the same thing." Now, the Lord says these things to Peter to correct him: for because Peter had said, "we have known and we have believed," the Lord implies, "Do not think you have known me fully." Observe, moreover, how the Lord says these things beforehand, rebuffing and restraining the malice of the traitor; knowing indeed that it would be of no profit to him, yet nevertheless doing what was his own part, he neither exposed him fully nor permitted him to be entirely hidden.

<margin>B</margin> The former was done so that he would not become more shameless and contentious; the latter so that he would not commit the crime with a sense of license, thinking it was a secret. From this we also learn that God is not accustomed to make people better through coercion or a kind of force, nor does his <term>election: God’s act of choosing individuals for a specific role or for salvation</term> compel our will to become good when it is evil. Rather, the choice is made by God, who exhorts us toward the good and imparts his goodness to us, but it rests in our own mind and will to be saved and to walk worthily of that choice, or the opposite. Marvel, then, that the devil is so hostile that he was able to snatch away even one of the twelve, who were raising the dead, performing miracles, and enjoying the spiritual and life-giving <margin>C</margin> doctrine of the Lord. And where then is the hope of salvation for us, who of our own accord enslave ourselves to malice from our youth? Therefore, the Evangelist also said, as if marveling, "Though he was one of the twelve." For although, he says, he was from that holy choir, yet by his own evil will he was found unworthy. Thus man is a creature changeable by his very nature. Let the Mani- <margin>Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were a religious group who believed people were born with a fixed nature (either good or evil) that could not be changed.</note></margin> chaeans therefore be gone. For we are not evil by nature; otherwise, malice would work all things in us. But in this case, Judas was not always evil, but was also at one time of a holy will. Therefore, evil things are both born and they grow.

<summary>Theophylact explains that Jesus offered the Apostles the freedom to leave to emphasize that following Him is a privilege, not a favor to God. He also refutes the idea of predetermined evil, using Judas as an example of how free will, rather than nature, leads to spiritual fall.</summary>

<margin>D</margin>

Therefore, he now withdraws, confirming that he was truly human and refuting all those who say that he was incarnate only in appearance, as the <margin>Manichæans.</margin> Manichæans, Marcion, Basilides, and their like claim <note>These groups were early Christian heretics who often denied the physical reality of Christ's human body.</note>. For then they gave thanks to the Lord, all the fruits having been gathered. ### A

<margin>D</margin> For that the work of five months flowed in the interval is manifest from this. When he performed the miracle of the loaves, it was Passover <term>Pascha: The Jewish festival of Passover, occurring in spring.</term>, which was held among them in the first month, which the Romans call March: now, however, the Scenopegia <term>Scenopegia: The Feast of Tabernacles or Booths (Sukkot), held in the autumn.</term> occurs in the month of September. Why then did the Evangelist <note>The Evangelist refers here to John the Apostle.</note> do this? Because there was no need to enumerate everything. And otherwise: the Evangelists strove to speak of those things through which some rebuke or controversy among the Jews followed. Moreover, it is worthy to admire their truthfulness, how they do not blush to say those things which seemed to bring a certain ignominy upon the teacher. Hence the Evangelist, passing over many miracles and words of the Lord, narrates the unbelief of his brothers and the things they reproached him with. But from where did that unbelief come? <margin>B</margin> From will and envy. For relatives are always accustomed to envy. Nevertheless, take note that those who were affected by such great unbelief in him before he was crucified, were the very ones who, when they saw him glorious and performing miracles, after the cross and the apparent ignobility, bore witness as Apostles, and became preachers and bishops. Hence they saw without contradiction that he had risen. For they would not have exposed themselves for him unless they had certain and solid arguments regarding his resurrection.

[ Jesus therefore says to them, **J E S V S**, "My time is not yet here, but your time is always ready. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me, because <margin>F</margin> I bear witness of it, that its works are evil. You go up to this feast day. I am not yet going up to this feast, because my time is not yet fulfilled."] His brothers indeed, envying the Lord, accuse him of fear and arrogance. But what does he say to them? Does he speak harshly? Not at all, but mildly. For he did not say, "Who are you to give me such advice and teach me so?" But what does he say? "My time is not yet here," that is, the time of the cross and death. "But your time is always ready." You, he says, even if you always meet with the Jews, they would not kill you who follow the same things as they do: Me, however, they will kill immediately

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> if they see me coming to the feast. Or this is to be understood another way. For he who makes the mourners blessed in this world also speaks similar things now, which can pertain to all the saints. <margin>Note.</margin> For it is not, he says, a time of festivity, when I see all malice flourishing in the fullness of the Jews: for it is a time of grief and lamentation when the truth is resisted and the divine will is not kept. Therefore, for these reasons, it is not a time of festivity for me; but for you indeed, as those who conspire with the Jews and are addicted to the world. It is no wonder if you keep the feast with those who are <margin>Response.</margin> like you, and indeed the world cannot hate you—that is, those who savor worldly things, as (as has been <margin>B</margin> said) they are like their own. Me, however, it hates, because I rebuke its works. For a freer rebuke gives birth to hatred. He sends the brothers, therefore, to the festival, showing that he does not force them to stay there if they do not wish. But take note how he gives two responses to the two charges they were bringing against him—namely fear and vainglory. To "fear," by saying: "I rebuke the works of the world," that is, of those who savor the world. I would not have rebuked them if I were fearful as you think. To "vainglory," by not compelling them to stay with him. For if he had been subject to the charge of vainglory, he would by no means have dismissed them from himself: because great pomp is dear to the hearts of the arrogant. Therefore, because they <margin>C</margin> reproached him with these two things, he rightly resisted those two, showing their grave suspicion. "For my time is not yet fulfilled" signifies that it is not yet the time of death and the cross: for it is necessary for me still to live in the flesh, that I may perform more signs and set forth more doctrines, and so that I may instruct more crowds in the faith and strengthen my disciples, both through more signs and through doctrines. Not yet, he says, does the time of death press upon me that I should expose myself to those who are insane against me, and for that reason I do not go up to the feast.

[ When he had said these things to them, he remained in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he also went up to the feast, not openly, but as if in secret. ]

->CH. 7. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.<-
->ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 374<-

<margin>D</margin>
Why then, after telling his brothers, "I am not going up to the feast," did he go up? He did not say simply, "I am not going," but "not now," <note>original: "nunc," often translated in this context as "not yet" or "not at this time."</note> which is to say, "not with you." For at the beginning he refused to go up because the Jews were burning with fury. But after this, when the feast was already being celebrated, he went up at a time when it was likely that their madness had been mitigated. And there is another reason: he did not act contrary to what he said. For he did not go up to observe the feast, but to teach; and he did not go with the gaiety with which people are accustomed to celebrate holidays, but secretly. Moreover, he hid himself to confirm that he was truly a man. For if he had appeared openly, they would surely have raged against him, desiring to kill him, and he would not have allowed them to do this, because the time for his passion <term>Passion: The suffering and death of Jesus.</term> had not yet arrived. But if he had escaped suffering while in their midst by supernatural means, it could have been held that he was not truly incarnate <term>Incarnate: God becoming human in the form of Jesus.</term>, but only appeared to be so. Therefore, he fled and withdrew as a man, doing what was natural for a human to do.

<margin>E</margin>
The Jews therefore sought him during the feast and said, "Where is he?" and there was much murmuring among the crowds concerning him. For some said, "He is a good man." But others said, "No, he is leading the crowd astray." Yet no one spoke openly about him for fear of the Jewish leaders.
Out of great hatred, the Jews did not even utter his name. For they did not say, "Where is Jesus?" but "Where is that man?" Thus they opposed even his brief name. Consider, moreover, how greedy they were for slaughter, since they <margin>F</margin> did not even spare him during the time of the festival, but wished to hunt him down through it; and for that reason, they sought him. They showed so little reverence for the holy day, and such were their works. There was much murmuring about him among the crowds because there were various opinions concerning him: the leaders saying, "He leads the crowds astray," while many others said, "He is a good man." Those who called him good were from the common crowd. That this is true is manifest from what the Evangelist <note>The "Evangelist" refers to the author of the Gospel, John.</note> says: that no one dared to speak freely for fear of the Jews. It is clear that for a long time they had not dared to speak openly about him, and they remained silent out of fear of the Jewish leaders. But as for those who were saying, "He leads the crowd astray," 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
the conjecture is that these were the leaders who were slandering him. For if they had been from the crowd, they would have said, "He leads *us* astray"; but now, when they say, "He leads the *crowd* astray," it shows they were not of the crowd, but were from the leaders who said such things. Notice how the leaders everywhere are corrupt, while the subjects are uncorrupted. Nevertheless, because they lacked a more manly spirit, they remained as yet imperfect and dared nothing freely.

Now when the feast was already half over, Jesus went up into the temple and began to teach. And the Jews marveled, saying, "How does this man know letters, since he has never studied?" Jesus answered them and said, "My doctrine is <margin>B</margin> not mine, but his who sent me." Why did he go up when the feast was half over? To soothe their spirits, and furthermore, so that they might listen with greater attention to the things said by him, lest the noise of the feast should block their ears. For at the beginning of the feast, it is likely they were occupied with the festivities. Therefore, when he suddenly appeared to them, everyone simply listened: some calling him good, others an impostor. Some listened to perceive some benefit and to marvel; others, however, to attack and seize him as a deceiver. Furthermore, the Evangelist did not say *what* he taught; but he showed that he said certain wonderful things by which he restrained them and <margin>C</margin> changed their minds into a state of wonder, through the fact that he says: "They marveled how he knew letters, having never studied." Nevertheless, although they marveled, even so their minds were not freed from malice. For they did not admire the doctrine, nor did they receive the things being said; rather, they marveled at how he knew <margin>Comparison of the envious</margin> letters—that is, they were stunned, which is what usually happens to envious people. It is as if some poor neighbor suddenly comes forth in more splendid clothing, and the envious neighbor sees him and says: "How is he dressed in such expensive clothes, who a moment ago was most poor? Where did he get that garment?" He says these things not because he truly admires the object, but because he burns with envy, using such speech. For he is essentially saying, "He stole that garment." Thus, therefore,

->CH. 7. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA.<-

And the Jews said: "How does this man know his letters?" <note>original: "Quomodo hic scit literas?" This refers to the Jews' surprise that Jesus possessed deep scriptural knowledge without having undergone formal rabbinic training.</note> Surely he gets this from Beelzebub. <term>Beelzebub: A name derived from a Philistine god, used in the New Testament to refer to the prince of demons.</term> However, they ought to have gathered from this that his knowledge was not merely human. But because they were unwilling to admit this, he answered them by teaching that his doctrine is from God and the Father. "Nothing is mine," he said, "nor do I speak from myself as if I were an adversary to God; but whatever these words may be, they are the Father’s words and mine."

<margin>Who does the will of God</margin> "If anyone wills to do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be from God, or whether I speak from myself. He who speaks of himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him, he is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him." He had said, "My doctrine is not mine"—meaning it is not contrary to God—but rather belongs to my Father. If anyone does the will of God—that is, if he embraces virtue, and is not a slave to envy, nor blinded by a vain hatred against me—he will know the power of my words, <margin>E</margin> whether I speak the things that are the Father’s or some alien and unworthy things. Moreover, the one who searches the scriptures and the prophets also does the will of God. Therefore, such a person will be able to know of the Lord's doctrine, that it is from God. For the prophets do not portray the Lord as an adversary to God or as one speaking from himself, but as one saying and doing everything that is consistent with God.

Furthermore, he provides another reason, saying: "He who speaks from himself"—that is, he who wishes to establish his own personal doctrine—does this for no other reason than to gain some empty glory from it. "But if I," he says, "do not want the fruit of my own glory but seek the glory of him who <margin>F</margin> sent me, for what reason would I want to teach other things?" Therefore, I am true, and there is no injustice in me; that is, I do not snatch away the glory due to another, for that would be an injustice. Thus, my doctrine embraces both truth and justice within itself. For it is not out of arrogance that it contains lies or injustice. <margin>Who is arrogant.</margin> Truly, the arrogant man both lies—because he says more about himself than he deserves—and acts unjustly, because he snatches a glory that is foreign and not suited to him. But the Lord, because he sought the things of the Father and said nothing at all arrogantly about himself, is both true and just. We have often said, and now we say again:

<column-break/>

->ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 375<-

<margin>A</margin> that when the Lord is seen to say certain humble things, one must not think he says them because he is lesser in nature than the Father. Rather, it is so that he is not considered an adversary to God, and because of the weakness of his listeners, and because he is clothed in flesh, teaching us to be modest and not to say anything grand about ourselves. However, when he speaks of sublime things and of his divine glory, we ought to believe those great things as if spoken by one equal to the Father, because of the greatness of his nature.

"Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law? Why do you seek to kill me?" The crowd answered and said, "You have a demon; who seeks to kill you?" <margin>B</margin> These words might seem disconnected from what preceded them, but to one who considers them carefully, they appear very consistent. For when they accused him of breaking the Sabbath and <margin>Exodus 20. Deuteronomy 5.</margin> transgressing the law, he pressed them on this point, showing them that they were the greater transgressors of the law. "For the law indeed says," he argues, "'Thou shalt not kill,' yet you seek to kill me; and so you are the ones breaking the law, not I." Therefore, while you ignore your own condemnation, you slander me as if I were transgressing the law because I healed a man on the Sabbath. He said "none of you keeps the law" because all those he was speaking with were seeking to kill him. See how he speaks to them with a gentle voice, while they speak insultingly and boldly, saying, "You have a demon"— <margin>C</margin> because they thought they could terrify him and that his soul would be tormented by their insults. Furthermore, he says Moses gave the law, even though he himself was the Lord of Moses and the giver of the law, because of the weakness of the Jews and because they were senseless. For how could they have endured him saying, "Moses did not give you the law, but I did, I who am the Lord of Moses and of the law"?

Jesus answered and said to them, "I have done one work, and you all marvel. <margin>Refer to Chapter 5.</margin> Therefore Moses gave you circumcision—not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers—and yet <margin>Leviticus 12</margin> on the Sabbath you circumcise a man. If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses should not be broken..."

### CHAPTER 7. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 376

[Are you indignant with me because I made a whole man healthy on the Sabbath? Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.] Through a certain logical argument <note>original: "Syllogismo." Theophylact is highlighting the structured logic Jesus uses to expose his critics' inconsistency.</note>, he shows that they labor in hatred toward him without cause. He says: "I did one work on the Sabbath"—referring to the healing of the paralytic—"and you all marvel because of it," which is to say, you are troubled and in an uproar. Yet Moses, that great lawgiver, "broke" the Sabbath by commanding that every soul be circumcised on the eighth day. For it often happens that the eighth day, on which a boy must be circumcised, falls on the Sabbath. Thus, the Sabbath rest was set aside by Moses himself for the sake of circumcision, and nothing prohibited a man from being circumcised on the Sabbath day. 
<margin>E</margin> But even if it were the Sabbath or the eighth day, the law concerning Sabbath rest is set aside so that the law of circumcision is not broken. If these things were so, why are you incensed and angry with me because I made an entire man healthy on the Sabbath? Although circumcision was not originally from Moses but from the patriarchs <note>This refers to the practice starting with Abraham, predating the Mosaic Law.</note>, nevertheless, it even sets aside the law of the Sabbath given by Moses. If circumcision, which inflicts a wound and pain, is not prohibited on the Sabbath, then I—who have set a man free from pain and made him healthy—am rebuked? Do not judge according to outward appearance, but judge justly and without partiality. You do not place Moses under reproach for breaking the Sabbath for circumcision; therefore, you should not judge me as one who does not observe the Sabbath,
<margin>F</margin> especially since I am doing good to a man. It is manifest that you are showing favoritism if you condemn me because of my humility, while you do not condemn Moses because of his high standing.

> [Then some of those from Jerusalem said: "Is this not he whom they seek to kill? And yet, look, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Have the rulers truly known that this is indeed the **CHRIST**? But we know where this man is from. When the **CHRIST** comes, however, no one knows where he is from."]

He did not add "some of the Jerusalemites" simply or without cause, but to show that although the greatest miracles happened among them, they remained the most wretched of all. For how are they not wretched when, having seen the great sign of his divinity,

<column-break/>

they still possess a corrupted judgment? Indeed, they would have had a great sign, had they wished to see it, in the fact that he walked freely in their midst and suffered nothing from them, even while they were unwilling and raging against him. But they did not wish to recognize his power through this sign. Instead, they doubt, saying: "Have the rulers perhaps recognized that this is truly the **CHRIST**?" Yet they do not remain even in this opinion, but conclude that no one will know from where Christ is to come. "We know where this man is from; therefore, he is not the Christ." Furthermore, see their malice, and how they contradict themselves. For their own leaders, when questioned by Herod, said <margin>B</margin> <margin>Matthew 2</margin> that the Christ was to be born in Bethlehem of Judea. Yet here they say that no one knows where the **CHRIST** is from. Do you see the contradiction in their words? And again, elsewhere they say: "We <margin>John 9</margin> know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from." Yet in this place they say: "We know where this man is from." Have you seen the speeches of those who are out of their minds—"we know" and "we do not know"? What is equal to this conflict of words? For they aimed at one thing: that they should not believe. Thus, when it suited their purpose, they said "We know"; but when it did not, they denied it. This variety of opinions arose from malice. But if one asks where they were moved to say this, they claim that when Christ comes, no one will know where he is from. For unless <margin>C</margin> they had some testimony from the scriptures, or a solid tradition, the scribes would not have spoken so clearly to Herod, stating plainly that he would be born in Bethlehem of Judea; and again they say that Christ comes from the city of Bethlehem. What then should be said? From the scriptures they said both: that he would be born in Bethlehem, and that he would be of the city of David. For they had the prophet Micah as a witness, just as Matthew says: "And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the princes of <margin>Micah 5</margin> Judah, for out of you shall come a leader." And again, from the same passage they cite the same Micah: "Because his coming forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity," which declares his origin to be unknown. For no man knows how he has his "coming forth" from the beginning and from the days of eternity—that is, his divine birth. For men are in time, but he is in the days of eternity.

...and from the beginning. But how can those who are under the constraints of time know that which is eternal? For Isaiah also says: *Who shall declare his generation?* <note>original: "Generationem eius quis enarrabit?" This refers to Isaiah 53:8, a verse often used by early Christian commentators to argue for the mysterious and divine origin of Jesus which transcends human explanation.</note>
<margin>Isaiah 53.</margin> <margin>D</margin> Therefore, they were persuaded by these words that "No one knows where Christ is from." For they did not understand that the Lord Jesus was of a twofold nature. <note>Theophylact is explaining the "Hypostatic Union," the doctrine that Jesus is simultaneously fully human and fully divine.</note> According to his birth in the flesh, he was from the Virgin, and it was known where he was from—namely, that he was born in Bethlehem. But according to his incorporeal birth, by which he was ineffably <note>Beyond the power of words to describe.</note> born of the Father before the ages, the account of his birth is beyond all speech. Therefore, those people of Jerusalem admit they know where his birth in the flesh is from; but as for that birth which is before the ages—according to which no one knows where Christ is from—they do not acknowledge it. 
<margin>E</margin> Thus, because they did not understand him to be of two natures, and while one was indeed known, the other was not, they say that he is not the Christ.

*Jesus therefore cried out in the temple, teaching and saying: "You both know me, and you know where I am from; and I have not come of myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know. But I know him, because I am from him and he has sent me."*] Since they said "We know where this man is from" for no other reason than to show he was of the earth and the son of a carpenter, he therefore leads them back to heaven, saying: "You both know me, and you know where I am from," namely, that I am from heaven. That is to say: although you remain silent because of your malice, you nevertheless know where I am from and that I have been sent by him 
<margin>F</margin> who is true. Because he is true, I also am certainly truthful and not a liar; for he who is true would not wish to send a deceiver and a liar. But this one who sent me, you indeed do not know; rather, you are ignorant of him, since you do not declare your knowledge through your works. For (as 
<margin>Titus 1.</margin> <note>The text cites Titus 3, but the quote "They profess to know God, but by their works they deny him" is from Titus 1:16.</note> Paul says) there is an ignorance even within knowledge: "They profess to know God," he says, "but by their works they deny him." And you Jews indeed do not know my Father because of your evil works 
<margin>Two natures in Christ.</margin> and your very wicked mind. But I know him, nor do an evil mind or works which displease him hinder me from knowing him. For I am from him—that is, out of him, not from another substance or a stranger to him—and he has sent me. See also in this place, that two natures are revealed by Christ.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> *They sought therefore to seize him, and no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come. But many of the crowd believed in him and said: "When Christ comes, will he perform more signs than these which this man has performed?"*] Showing that they were invisibly restrained, and that he suffered of his own will and not from weakness, the Evangelist says: *They sought to seize him, but no one laid hands on him.* As for the statement that *his hour had not yet come*, he said this not because he was subject to time, but because he did all things at the opportune time and the fitting hour. For when he judged it to be the right season to suffer, then he also permitted himself to be given to the crucifiers. For he 
<margin>B</margin> does and governs all things at opportune and appropriate times: just as it was fitting for the Law to be given at a suitable time, so similarly for the prophets and the Gospel. Thus, the mention of the "hour" shows the evident prudence and wisdom of the Savior. But many believed in him, saying: "Will Christ do more signs than this man has done?" This was said concerning the wine in Cana of Galilee, the king's son, the paralytic, the loaves, and in short, all the other signs which even the Evangelists did not mention because of their great number. 
<margin>The nature of the faith of those who believed suddenly after seeing signs.</margin> Nevertheless, when you hear that many believed, you should know that their faith was not exact <note>Meaning "not fully formed" or "theologically imprecise."</note>, but of the kind 
<margin>C</margin> likely to be found among the common crowd, which continually changes its opinion.

*The Pharisees heard the crowd murmuring these things about him. And the Pharisees and the chief priests sent officers to seize him. Jesus therefore said to them: "Yet a little while I am with you, and I go to him who sent me. You will seek me and will not find me. And where I am, you cannot come." The Jews therefore said among themselves: "Where is this man going that we will not find him? Is he going to the dispersion of the Gentiles to teach the Gentiles? What is this word that he said: 'You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come'?"*] Because the crowd was murmuring, it is clear that they had a more favorable disposition toward him.

...thing, and a certain diminished faith toward the Lord. **D** For the crowd wished to be separated from the rulers; perceiving this, the rulers sent officers to seize Jesus, for the sole reason that he was believed to be the Christ. They sent them, but did not come themselves, fearing the crowd might riot; therefore they sent servants, withdrawing themselves so that no danger would arise, while exposing those servants to the fury of the people. In every way, they followed their own interests. But the Lord speaks words full of humility: *I am with you for a little time longer; why do you pant to kill me? Why do you persecute me? Wait for a little time, and I will not hinder you if you wish to hold me.* Furthermore, when he says, *I am with you*, **E** the meaning is this: Even if you persecute me, even if you drive me away, I am still with you—that is, I care for you and speak those things which lead to your salvation—and *I go to him who sent me.* For it is clear that those who treat the one who was sent with dishonor, strike at the one who sent him. 

<margin>What is signified by "I go."</margin>
By saying *I go*, he signified his voluntary death. Moreover, showing that his death is not like the common death of all, he says: *Where I go, you cannot come.* For if it were a common death, he would not have said, *you cannot come.* For we all go toward a common death. Therefore, wishing to show what I was saying—that his death is not like common death—he says, *Where I go, you cannot come.* And by saying, *You will seek me, and you will not find me*, he indicates that he would become desirable to them. When 
<margin>Luke 24</margin>
did they seek him? Luke says that many women mourned over him. It is likely that this happened to many others as well; and when the city was being captured, they were mindful of him and his miracles, and they sought his presence. Furthermore, he said all these things wishing to win them over and soothe them. For when their servants came, wishing to seize him, he showed that he knew the cause of their coming and that they wished to kill him. Therefore, he predicts his death to them, saying that it is a short time until he goes to the Father. But to predict one’s death

<column-break/>

**A** is a great thing, and not human. For this reason, David also says in Psalm 38 <note>Psalm 39 in modern Bibles. original: "Psal. 38"</note>: *Lord, make me know my end.* But the Jews were saying, *Is he going to the dispersion of the Gentiles?* See how it happened to them, and how they were broken by the things he said; this is clear from their question: *Is he going to the dispersion of the Gentiles?* For if this were the case, they would surely have said, "He wants to leave; this is what we prayed for, this will be pleasing to us." But now, no such thing was said, but as if grieving lest they be deprived of him, they ask where he is going. This is also clear because they say, *he is going to the Gentiles and will teach them*; for they did not say he would "seduce" them, but "teach" them. **B** They called the Gentiles "The Dispersion," <note>The "Dispersion" or *Diaspora* refers to groups living outside their traditional homeland.</note> as they were scattered in every place. For the Jews of old did not mix with anyone, but were gathered in one place in Palestine; they used to reproach the Gentiles with the very thing that was later turned against themselves. For the Hebrews themselves became the "Dispersion."

*On the last day, the great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the Scripture says: rivers of living water shall flow from his belly."* They called the first day of the feast and this seventh, the last day, "great"; because the Law, in naming the seventh day of the feast, called it holy. Therefore, following that, the Evangelist <note>The author of the Gospel, John.</note> calls the last day "great." It was fitting that he spoke with the crowds on the last day, as if giving provisions for the journey <term>viatica</term> <note>Latin: "viatica" – traditionally, provisions or money for a journey; here used metaphorically for spiritual strength.</note> to those about to return home. For with those who were intent on pleasures during the middle days, 
<margin>2 Chronicles 6</margin>
**C** it was untimely to speak; for they would not have listened. But Jesus cried out, partly so that he might be better heard, and partly to manifest his freedom in speaking, and that he looked down on no one. But what does he say? *He who believes in me, as the Scripture says.* For in this place, one must make a pause. <note>Theophylact is suggesting a specific way to punctuate the Greek text to clarify the meaning.</note> Then another beginning must be made: *rivers shall flow from his belly.* For because many believed because of signs, he shows that one should not 
<margin>Where right faith comes from</margin>
believe because of signs, but because of the Scripture. For right faith is from the Scriptures. For this reason he says, *He who believes in me as the Scripture says*—that is, just as the Scripture testifies of me—that I am the Son of God, that I am the Creator, and that I am the Lord of the universe.

# CHAPTER 7. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,

<margin>D</margin>
For many think they believe, but not as the Scripture says, and thus they have followed their own sects, as do all heretics. But he said that "rivers shall flow from the belly" of the one who is truly 
<margin>“Belly” is a Hebrew metaphor for the heart.</margin>
faithful. He calls the heart the "belly" by a Hebrew metaphor <note>original: "tropo Hebraico"</note>, just as David also says: *And your law is in the middle of my belly* <note>Psalm 40:8 in modern Bibles; Psalm 39 in the Latin Vulgate</note>, which is to say, of my heart. 
<margin>Psalm 39</margin>
Moreover, he spoke of "rivers" flowing, rather than a single river of living water, to suggest the generous grace and abundance of the Spirit. For such is the Spirit: into whatever soul it enters and resides, it makes that soul gush forth more abundantly than any spring. And one may learn how rivers flow from the belly of a believer "according to the Scripture" if one considers the tongue of Peter, the drive of Paul, and the wisdom of Stephen. Nothing escaped them when they spoke,
<margin>B</margin>
but all followed them, as if swept away by the force of rushing rivers.

*But this he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive. For the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.*] Interpreting what these "rivers of living water" are, the Evangelist says: *But this he said concerning the Spirit.* For he says the Holy Spirit was not yet given. But at this point someone might ask: How can the Evangelist say that the Holy Spirit had not yet been given? Did not the prophets speak by the Spirit, and the apostles too? How did they perform healings? We say, therefore, that the prophets undoubtedly spoke by the Spirit, but this gift had been contracted; it had withdrawn from the earth. And although it operated by God’s power in the times of the prophets, at that time—because of the unworthiness of the people, and while Christ was walking in the flesh—prophecy was not familiar, nor did grace look upon their holy things and temple. Because the operation of the Spirit was not then present but was yet to be given, he says for this reason that "the Holy Spirit was not yet"—meaning it was not active among the Jews, nor appearing through miraculous works. The apostles, meanwhile, were performing miracles not by the Spirit, but by the power of the Lord. 
<margin>Matthew 10, Luke 10</margin>
For listen to what the Gospel says: *Because he was about to send them, he gave them power*, but not the Holy Spirit. And so, whatever miracles they performed, they did not by the Spirit, but by the power and name of the Lord. For

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
when he had risen from the tomb, he then said to them: *Receive the 
<margin>John 20, Acts 1</margin>
Holy Spirit.* And at Pentecost the Holy Spirit came upon them. To put it another way: the power of the Spirit was indeed in the prophets and in the Apostles before the Cross, but not in such a way as after the Ascension—namely, more largely and more copiously, so that it deserved to be compared to "rivers." Thus the Evangelist rightly said that the Holy Spirit was "not yet," meaning it had not yet been poured out as abundantly as it was later. For even before the Cross it existed, but was not so bountiful; for Jesus was not yet "glorified," with the Evangelist using the name "glory" for the Cross in this passage. For through the Cross he cast down the tyrant and took up his reign. Therefore, as the Cross was not yet established, nor sin abolished, nor our nature made victorious over the world in Christ and 
<margin>B</margin>
reconciled to God, it is rightly said that the abundant gift of the Spirit had not been given. For it was necessary for us first to become friends of God, which was accomplished through the Cross. Furthermore, the gift of God must be received just like a worldly one: first one looks to see who is a friend of the King, and then they receive the gifts. Thanks be to God, who has bestowed such a great benefit upon us, more than even to the prophets. For the prophets indeed possessed the grace of the Spirit, but they did not abound toward others as the apostles did, who were filled with countless gifts.

*Therefore many from the crowd, when they had heard this speech, said: "This is truly the Prophet." Others said: "This is the 
<margin>Matthew 5, Matthew 2</margin>
Christ." But some said: "Does the Christ come from Galilee? Does not the Scripture say that from the seed of David, 
<margin>C</margin>
and from the town of Bethlehem where David was, the Christ shall come?" So a dissension arose in the crowd because of him.*] Appressed by his freedom of speech, some of the crowd—not the rulers (for the rulers always resisted out of envy)—confess that this is the Prophet who was expected. But others, who were from the unlearned and unobservant crowd, said: "He is the Christ," not understanding that he was one and the same, and not two different people, the Christ and that Prophet. Others, more ungrateful, said: "The Christ does not come from Galilee, but from Bethlehem, and from the seed of David." They said this with a malicious mind, and not like Nathanael, who spoke as one learned in the law and a student, saying: *Can anything good come 
<margin>John 1</margin>
from Nazareth?* <note>Nathanael’s question was a sincere inquiry based on scripture, whereas the crowd uses it as an excuse to reject Jesus.</note> For this reason, the Lord also praises him...

...him, as one not deceitful, but rather saying this out of zeal for the law. But these others say this deceitfully, because Christ does not come from Galilee. For they seem to know indeed that Jesus is from Bethlehem. For although he was brought up in Galilee, out of envy they were unwilling to admit his birth from Bethlehem, but called him a "Galilean." But even if they were truly ignorant that he was from Bethlehem and from the seed of David, how could they have remained in doubt? Did Mary not clearly trace her lineage from David? From this it is clear that they were speaking deceitfully. But a dissension arose in the crowd, not among the rulers. For the rulers were of one opinion: that he should not be accepted as the Christ.

<margin>B</margin> *But some of them wanted to seize him, but no one laid hands on him. Then the officers came to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to them, "Why have you not brought him?" The officers answered, "Never has a man spoken as this man speaks."* ] Those who were not of such great malice were adversaries of Christ's glory in words alone; but those who were more impudent even wanted to lay hands on him. They were bound invisibly, however, by a divine power that restrained them, and yet they were not even corrected by this miracle. Indeed, David spoke of such people: *They were divided, and were not pricked in heart* <note>original: "Discissi sunt, & non sunt compuncti." A reference to the Latin Vulgate version of Psalm 34:16 (Psalm 35:15 in modern Bibles), describing people who attack without conscience.</note>. As for the officers <note>The Latin "ministri" refers to the temple guards or servants sent by the Sanhedrin.</note> sent to bring him, let us see how they responded to the Pharisees, for they did so very wisely. For the Pharisees, who seemed to be wiser, readers of the scriptures, and witnesses to miracles, were raging against Jesus and questioning the guards as if they were dealing with a thief: "Why have you not brought him?" But those guards, even without seeing signs, were persuaded by his teaching alone. Thus they were fit for the good. The fact that they were captured not by miracles but by his words—which is a much greater thing—is clear from their answer. For they did not say, "Never has a man performed such a miracle," but rather, "so spoke." Thus they were prepared and eager to receive the word of salvation. One must admire not only their wisdom but also their freedom of speech. For they did not fear the anger of the Pharisees, nor did they say what was pleasing to the rulers just because they were sent as servants; instead, they bore witness to the truth.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> All the ministers of rulers ought to imitate these men, and not obey in those things which are contrary to God—just as Saul was not obeyed when he commanded the bystanders to kill the priests against the law <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 22, where Saul's servants refused to kill the priests of Nob.</note>.

*Then the Pharisees answered them, "Are you also led astray? Has any of the rulers believed in him, or of the Pharisees? But this crowd that does not know the law are cursed." Nicodemus said to them (the one who had come to him by night, who was one of their number), "Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?"* ] For what reason do the Pharisees speak to the officers not in anger but mildly, saying calmly, "Are you also led astray?" <margin>John 3</margin> Because they feared that those men would be entirely pulled away and follow CHRIST, they spoke to them more gently and flatteringly: "Are you, who are among the wiser of our people and always cling to us who are learned in the law, also led astray?" But they also attempt to persuade them with a very foolish argument. For they say, "Has any of the rulers believed in him?" Yet whose fault is this? Christ’s, or the fault of those who did not believe? For all those who did not believe are the ones truly cursed. They say the crowd is cursed because it believed, yet they themselves are worthy of countless curses, being unbelievers and the authors of unbelief in others. For what reason did the Evangelist note regarding Nicodemus <margin>C</margin> that he had come to Jesus by night and that he was one of them, except to show the Pharisees to be liars? For since they had said that none of the rulers believed in him, he shows that they were lying in this too. For behold, Nicodemus, though he was a ruler and one of them, believed in CHRIST. How does Nicodemus speak with them? "Does our law," he says, "judge a man unless it first hears?" He shows from this, therefore, that they neither knew the law nor did what the law required, even though they boasted much of the law. For the law commands that no one be killed uncondemned; but these men rush to the slaughter of one who has not been heard. Thus they are clearly transgressors of the law. By saying, therefore, "and knows what he does," he shows that one must hear a case not superficially, but perfectly and diligently.

He highlights Nicodemus as a silent refutation of the Pharisees' claim that no ruler believed in Jesus.</summary>

> They answered and said to him, "Are you also a Galilean? Search and see that a prophet has not arisen from Galilee."

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>A significant fragment has been omitted here concerning that woman caught in adultery.</margin> <note>original: "Omissū est hic fragmen tū nō par uulū, de muliere illa in adulterio dephēsa." Theophylact follows the tradition of many early Greek manuscripts that do not include the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11).</note>
> Therefore Jesus spoke to them again, saying, "I am the light of the world; he who follows me does not walk in darkness, but has the light of life." ]

Since Nicodemus very <margin>E</margin> prudently rebuked the Pharisees—as they were committing injustices—they became perplexed and responded quite rudely, even ferociously, saying: "Are you also from Galilee?" For what logical connection does this have to the things spoken by Nicodemus? He said that it is not right to condemn Jesus without an examination and a trial, but rather according to the law; they had even sent officers to seize him and had done everything, as he was saying. And yet these men say, "Are you also from Galilee?" Do you see their foolishness? Do you see how there is no logical sequence in their words? Then, treating him with ignominy as if he were unlearned, they say: "Search and see that a prophet has not arisen from Galilee." This is to say: "Go, learn, because until this time you have not learned that a prophet has not arisen from Galilee." Moreover, they say these things by ascribing ignorance to him. 

But what did Nicodemus say, O Pharisees? Did he say that Jesus was a prophet? He said that it is not lawful to kill a man without a trial. <margin>F</margin> How then do you respond in this way to him who said such things? But Christ—because they were frequently throwing Galilee in his face and doubting him as if he were merely one of the prophets—shows them that he is not just one of those prophets by saying: "I am the light of the world." Properly "light," not a prophetic light which has a partial and small splendor, but the true light which is not circumscribed by the borders of Galilee or Palestine. Instead, I am the light of the world and the Lord of all men, and concerning me the Prophet said: <margin>Isaiah 42</margin> "Behold, I have set you as a light for the nations." <note>original: "Ecce posui te in lucem gentium."</note> 

Moreover, you may also use this present saying against Nestorius: <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century bishop whose teachings were condemned for appearing to divide Christ into two separate persons, one human and one divine.</note> for he did not say, "in me is the light of the world," but "I am the light of the world." For he himself who

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> appeared was both man and the Son of God, and the light of the world—not as Nestorius raves, that the Son of God merely dwells in a pure man; far be it. For he was the one Son (as has been said) of Mary and of God. "But he who follows me," he says, "does not walk in darkness," that is, he will not remain in error, but will be liberated from error and darkness. Meanwhile, he both praises Nicodemus and the officers who had spoken so freely, implying that they were in the light. However, the Pharisees are also censured for being in error and darkness, and for secretly plotting deceptions.

Therefore the Pharisees said to him, "You testify about yourself; your testimony is not true." Jesus answered and said to them, "Even if I testify about myself, <margin>B</margin> my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going; but you do not know where I come from and where I am going." ] Because he had said, "I am the light of the world," they accuse him as if he were testifying about himself. Oh, what foolishness! He himself draws the scriptures this way and that to testify, and they argue against him as if he were testifying only of himself. Therefore, he even responds to their malice: "Suppose I do testify of myself, although I do not actually do this alone, but I have three witnesses: my Father, my works, and the scriptures, as was said above. Nevertheless, let us grant that I testify of myself; therefore, even if I were to testify to myself, my testimony would be true because I know that I am the Son of God, and not a mere man, but one coming from above as <margin>C</margin> God." 

How then will my testimony be a lie, since I am God? And for that reason, I am worthy of being believed. For God is altogether the most suitable witness for himself. But also, as one wishing to go to the true God, how would I lie, being about to depart to the One who is not a liar?

> "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. And yet if I do judge, my judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me." ]

I indeed (he says), since I am God and have come from the highest things, whereas you only look at that which appears; and because I am in the flesh, you suspect me to be a despised fleshly being and not God, nor to have come from God. You judge "according to the flesh," that is, dangerously.

**Column 1:**

<margin>A</margin> For just as one who lives in the flesh is said to live wickedly, so also he who judges according to the flesh is said to judge unjustly. Then, as if someone had asked: "If we Jews judge unjustly, why do you not punish us? Why do you not condemn us?" he says: *I did not come for this purpose, to judge: for I judge no one now.* And yet *if I judge, my judgment is true.* For you would indeed have been condemned if I had wished to judge; but because now is not the time, I shall defer your condemnation until my second coming, just as in another place he says: *Because I did not come to judge the world, but to save it.* <margin>B</margin> <margin>John 12. John 5.</margin> But as to the fact that he himself is the judge of all, listen to the mouth that knows not how to lie: *The Father has given all judgment to the Son.* And so, when you hear "I judge no one," understand this as being said not regarding his future coming, but regarding the present. By saying, however, *I am not alone, but my Father is with me,* he shows that "not I alone condemn you, but also the Father." For I do not judge in one way and the Father in another; but as I judge, so does he, and as he judges, so do I.

Furthermore, it is written in the law that *the testimony of two men is true. I am he who bears witness of myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness of me.* ] Let the Arians and Eunomians <note>Followers of Arius and Eunomius, fourth-century theologians who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being and not of the same essence as God the Father.</note> speak to this point—those who say the Son is not <term>consubstantial</term> <note>Of the same substance or essence; the Greek term is 'homoousios'.</note> with the Father. If he were not of the same substance, how would he have dared to say: "I am of the same authority as the Father, and equally worthy of being believed"? For just as when two men testify about the same matter and their testimony is true, it is manifest that each has the same fitness for testifying; so also in this place he declares his own testimony to be nothing less than the testimony of the Father. For listen to what is consequently said with great authority: *I am he who bears witness of myself, and the Father bears witness of me.* Do you see the equal authority, and how he makes himself equally fit for testimony as the Father? He would not have dared to say this if he were inferior to the Father in dignity, and not equal to him and consubstantial. For if he had wished to show subjection or some kind of lessening, he would not have <margin>Deut. 17. 19. 2 Cor. 13. Heb. 10.</margin>

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

<margin>A</margin> counted himself alongside the Father, nor placed his own testimony with the Father’s. Instead, if he were a servant—as the heretics blasphemously claim—he would have looked to one of his fellow servants and made him a co-witness, such as John [the Baptist] or the prophets. In short, if he had desired such testimony, he would have found it; but now, wishing to show himself consubstantial with the Father, he counts himself with the Father. Do not wonder, however, if in another place he brings forward John, Moses, and the prophets as witnesses of himself. For he does this according to the understanding of his listeners; since they preferred John and Moses to him, for their sake he draws into testimony those who were considered great and noble among them. And so, because they held a high opinion of God the Father—for whom else did they glorify as God?—he now brings forward the Father himself as a witness in all things. And because he aligns himself with such a witness, who can neither be deceived nor lie, it is most manifest that he has the same authority and power as the Father. Let those be put to shame who call him a servant and in every way inferior to the Father.

<margin>John 8.</margin>
> They said therefore to him, "Where is your father?" Jesus answered, "You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would also know my Father." These words Jesus spoke in the treasury, teaching in the temple. And no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come. ]

Because they questioned him about his father as a way of testing him, and not for the sake of learning, he does not <margin>F</margin> deign to give them a direct answer, but says: *You know neither me nor my Father.* <margin>G</margin> That is: "You cannot know the Father without me." And so, if you think you worship God, but do not believe that he is my Father—I who am the true Son—it will profit you nothing. Nor do you know how to recognize him as you ought; for if you recognized me, you would also honor me. But now, because you do not know me, nor honor me, you do not know or honor him either, even if you think you do. As for the fact that you do not know me, there is no other cause but yourselves. Do you hear this, you who impiously subject the Son to the Father? If he were not consubstantial with the Father, how could he have said: *If you knew me, you would also know my Father?* For if (as you say) the Son is a creature, how does he who knows a creature also know God? For he who knows the substance of an angel does not thereby know the substance [of God]...

# CHAPTER 8. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA,

**Column 1:**

<margin>D</margin> ...the essence of God. <note>original: "tiam Dei", likely "essentiam Dei"</note> For since he who knows the Son also knows the Father, it follows that the Father is of the same substance as the Son. He also says: "Does he who knows the creature <note>Refers to the created world</note> also know God?" Not at all. For many—indeed all—see and know the creature, but no one has seen or known God. Jesus spoke these things in the **treasury** <term>gazophylacium: the area of the Temple where the collection boxes for offerings were kept</term> in the middle of the temple, and he spoke so freely. Nevertheless, those who sought to kill him and had him in their hands did not dare to seize him. Nor even then did they understand. This was truly a work of divine power: that he should remain unhurt and untouched in the middle of his enemies, especially since they had been seeking him and laying snares for him before **Passover** <term>pascha: the major Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus; here it signals the proximity of the Crucifixion</term>. Therefore, him whom they sought when he was absent, and against whom they raged, they are unable to hold even when they have him in their very nets; yet they did not recognize his power even then. Because **his hour had not yet come**, that is, the suitable time for death in which he was to hand himself over was not yet pressing. For they could not have done anything against him unless it had been the opportune time which he had chosen for himself. For his being crucified was not a result of powerlessness, but of permission. For he permitted it when he willed. Though they had long desired to kill him, they were held back by the invisible chains of his power.

<margin>E</margin> For he permitted himself to remain longer in this life according to the flesh, so that he might be the author of greater benefit to men by demonstrating signs, sermons, and doctrines. Some, however, understand the phrase "Where is your father?" as being said by the Jews to the Lord as an insult and a reproach.

<margin>F</margin> For they said these things as if he were born of fornication, and as if he did not know his own father. Or otherwise, they regarded his father **Joseph** as a common man, and so they say, "Where is that father of yours?"—as if saying, "Your father is obscure and ignoble; why do you boast of him so much?"

Jesus therefore said to them again: *I go, and you shall seek me, and you shall die in your sin. Where I go, you cannot come.* The Jews therefore said: "Will he kill himself, because he says, 'Where I go, you cannot come'?" and he said to them: *You are from below, I* <meta>catchword: I</meta>

**ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.**

**Column 2:**

<margin>A</margin> *am from above. You are of this world, I am not of this world. I said to you that you will die in your sins. For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.* ] For this reason, he frequently says to them, "I go and you will seek me," so that he might thus shake and terrify their souls. And see how they immediately fell into worries; perplexed in mind, they said, "Will he kill himself?" Although they desired to be freed from him and wished him removed from their midst—even plotting to kill him—yet they imagined something so significant about this statement that they were left perplexed. Furthermore, he often said "I go" to show that he foreknew his own death, and that the cross was not a work of their power, but of his own will.

<margin>B</margin> For I go (he says), you do not lead me; I go of my own accord. By saying, however, "You cannot come where I go," he shows that he himself is to rise again in glory and take his seat at the right hand of the Father, while they are to die in their sins. What then do they say to these things? "Will he kill himself?" But the Lord, removing this suspicion of theirs, shows that to kill oneself does not lack condemnation. "You are from below," he says, "and being unable to think anything divine, you think in such a way. But as for me, since I am not of this world—that is, I **savor** <note>original: "sapio", meaning to taste, understand, or set one's mind upon</note> nothing mundane or earthly—I shall never arrive at such madness as to kill myself." For this is diabolical, and not divine.

taking this opportunity and following all the **Manichaeans** <note>Followers of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that often viewed the physical world as evil and Christ's body as not truly physical.</note>, says: "Do you see that the body of the Lord was not of this world, but from above and from heaven, just as Saint Paul also says, that the **second man is the Lord from heaven**?"

What then must be said? One must ask him how he understands what is said by the Lord to the apostles: *You are not of the world.* Did they also have a heavenly body and not one of this creation? Or did the Lord say this because they do not "savor" the things of this world? It is manifest that he said it because they did not savor the things of this world. So also it is to be understood here: "I am not of this world," that is, "I am not one of you, who savor mundane things." Just as Paul...

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus' discourse in the Temple treasury, refuting the Jews' insults regarding his parentage and clarifying that his impending death is a voluntary act of divine power rather than a result of human strength or suicide. He also provides a theological defense against Apollinarian and Manichaean interpretations of Christ's nature, arguing that being "not of this world" refers to spiritual orientation rather than physical composition.</summary>

[...Paul] to certain people saying, "You are not in the flesh" <note>Romans 8:9</note>: he does not mean they are incorporeal, but testifies how they are devoted to virtues and free from carnal affections. What else does the Lord say to them? "If you do not believe in me," he says, "you will die in your sins." For since he came for this purpose, to take away the sins of the world, we can receive the remission of sins in no other way than through **baptism** <term>baptismum: the Christian rite of initiation involving water, signifying spiritual cleansing and rebirth</term>. 

<margin>It is impossible to baptize an unfaithful person.</margin>
It is impossible for one who has not believed to be baptized. Therefore, it is entirely necessary for the unbeliever to die in his sin afterward. For he has not "put off the old man" <note>A reference to Colossians 3:9, meaning the unregenerate human nature</note> because he was not baptized. 

<margin>John 3.</margin>
For this reason, in another place the Lord says, "He who does not believe is already judged" <note>John 3:18</note>, not only because he did not believe, but also because he dies while still holding his previous sins.

<margin>E</margin>
They said to him, "Who are you?" And Jesus said to them, "The beginning, which I also speak to you." <note>original: "In primis, quod & loquor vobis." In the Latin Vulgate tradition, this was often interpreted as Jesus calling himself "The Beginning" (Principium), though modern translations often read it as "What I have told you from the beginning."</note> "I have many things to speak and to judge concerning you, but he who sent me is true, and the things I have heard from him, these I speak in the world." They did not know that he was speaking to them about the Father. After so much time, after the offense of so many miracles, they ask him, "Who are you?" They were so foolish and mocking. But the Lord said, "The beginning, which I also speak to you." "You," he says, "are unworthy to hear my words and learn who I am. For you say these things as a test, and you hear nothing of what I speak. But I could even rebuke you—and not only rebuke, but also punish." For he hints at these two things when he says, "I could speak many things to you, and judge." 

<margin>F</margin>
By "speak," understand a rebuke; by "judge," understand condemnation. "And he who sent me," he says, "did not send me for this, that I might judge and rebuke. For God did not send his Son to judge the world, but that he might save the world." <note>John 3:17</note> Therefore, because my Father sent me to save, and he is true, I rightly judge no one now, but only speak those things which I heard from my Father, namely those which pertain to salvation, not to rebuke. He said these things so they would not think he was unable to punish them; he shows that he does not punish them not because he is powerless, but because he is unwilling: since he came not to punish, but to save.

<margin>A While he was saying these things,</margin>
they were so foolish that they did not recognize (it says) that he was speaking of his Father to them, even though so many things had been said to them about the Father; indeed, their foolish hearts were truly darkened. Some, however, understand it this way: "He who sent me is true." "I could," he says, "judge you even now, but I reserve it for the future age. You do not believe, and you do not suspect a time of retribution. <margin>B</margin>
Jesus therefore said, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am [he], and I do nothing of myself; but as the Father taught me, I speak these things. And he who sent me is with me. The Father has not left me alone, because I always do those things that are pleasing to him." After he performed many signs for them and did not win them over, he now speaks to them about the **Cross** <term>crux: the instrument of execution; Jesus refers to his crucifixion as being "lifted up"</term>. "For you," he says, "will think then that you will be beyond all worry and fear, and liberated from me, when you have crucified me; but I say that then you will know that I am he—that is, the Christ, the Son of God—who carries and leads all things, and I am not contrary to the Father, nor do I do or speak from myself: for I do not have a private will separate from the Father's will." 

How were they to know him on the 

<margin>C Cross? From the signs that occurred then: and from the resurrection and captivity:</margin>
for all these things were able to declare his strength. Therefore, you will know both: my strength, when you crucify me, and my harmony with the Father. For the Father would not have avenged me by giving your city over to the Romans <note>A reference to the Roman Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, interpreted by early theologians as divine punishment for the Crucifixion</note>, or by signs performed in the heavens, unless I were his Son, and of the same knowledge, and not his adversary. Then, therefore, you will know that the things I teach and speak are entirely divine and the words of God, coming from him, and not mine, but his who sent me. Then, lest they think that being "sent" implies an inferior status, he says, "My Father is with me." For although he sent me as a man, yet I am not separated from him, but he is with me, as God with God. And again, bringing his speech down to humbler terms, he says, "And he has not [left me alone...]"

# CHAPTER 8. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>D</margin> [The Father] has sent me alone, because I do the things that are pleasing to him. <note>The Latin text here reads "misit me solum," though the standard Gospel text is "non reliquit me solum" (he has not left me alone). Theophylact is commenting on Christ's unity with the Father.</note> However, he speaks such humble words for the sake of the Jews. For because they were saying that he is not from God because he does not keep the Sabbath, he says: "I do those things which are well-pleasing to him," and thus, although I break the Sabbath, this is pleasing to him. 

By these humble words, he did not harm his own glory at all, but he brought benefit to his listeners; indeed, through these words he even established his own glory. For those hearing him refer everything to the Father were further drawn to him and believed in him. And so, humble things rather exalted him. You see the works of blessed **humility**. And that these things are so, hear what follows.

<margin>E</margin> As he spoke these things, many believed in him. Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him: "If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."

<margin>Christ often speaks humbly of himself for the sake of his listeners.</margin>

As I was saying, the Evangelist signifies that more listeners came to him through these humble words. For "as he spoke these things," he says, "many believed." These humble words, which seemed beneath his glory, were the cause. Therefore, whenever you hear him speak something small or humble about himself, do not be disturbed. He speaks such things for the sake of the listeners, who are not strong enough to grasp anything more sublime, but would immediately become fierce <note>Theophylact suggests the audience would have reacted with violent hostility if Jesus had revealed his full divine nature too abruptly.</note>. What would have happened if they could not even reach the depth of the theological mystery, when the height of his glory is unattainable even to Christians who acknowledge his power and are saved by him?

<margin>F</margin> When you hear that "many believed," understand it thus: that they believed in a common or superficial way, and not as they ought, but as if they were soothed and charmed by the humility of his words. For it is clear that they were not all truly faithful. For he said to those Jews who had believed: "If you remain in my word." This signifies that they believed superficially and, for that reason, were not going to remain in the faith. By this rebuke, he also indicates that he knows their hearts and that he is God. Because those who were previously thought to be his disciples also drew back, he says to those who have now believed: "Those others indeed drew back, but if you remain in the word and the faith..."

<margin>A</margin> ...you will know the truth, which is me. For I am the truth. It is as if he says: "Right now you do not know the truth." For all the things that you believe you hold in the Law are not the truth, but a **shadow and type** <term>shadow and type: a theological concept where Old Testament laws and rituals were seen as mere symbols or "foreshadows" of the reality found in Christ</term>. "But if you acknowledge me, who am the truth, the truth will set you free"—that is, I will set you free from sins. 

For he who believes in him who takes away the sin of the world is entirely set free from sins. Therefore, just as he said to those who do not believe, "You will die in your sins," so to those who remain in the faith, he promises freedom from sins. For the legal sprinklings and sacrifices do not free one from sins. For they were a figure. But the spiritual and true sacrifice through faith and knowledge frees us, so that we are no longer slaves, but are made **sons of God**.
