### CHAPTER 8. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
### AN EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 388

"Which of you convicts me of sin? If I tell you the truth, why do you not believe me? He who is of God hears the words of God; for this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God. Therefore the Jews answered and said to him, 'Do we not say well that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?' Jesus answered, 'I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father; you have treated me with dishonor. But I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges.'"

Because they were calling themselves sons of God, he says: "If you are sons of God, you surely ought to hate a sinner. If, therefore, you can convict me—whom you hate—of sinning, it is manifest that you pursue me with hatred justly. But if no one can convict me, it is manifest that you hold me in hatred because of the truth." <margin>B</margin> But what truth? Entirely because he had said he was the Son of God, which is most true. Since, however, he who is from God hears the words of God, so also you, if you were sons of God, would not turn away from hearing me, nor would you seek the death of him who comes from the highest as the Son of God, and who speaks those things which are of God. 

Therefore, the Lord spoke so mildly with them; yet they proceed to insults. "Do we not say well," they say, "that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?" They called him a Samaritan because he was destroying Jewish custom, namely the Sabbath. For the Samaritans did not <margin>Luke 11.</margin> strictly follow Jewish law. Moreover, they call him "demon-possessed," perhaps in the same way they said he cast out demons by the prince of demons. For they were always slandering him, saying he cast out demons by Beelzebub <note>A Philistine deity, whose name was used by Jewish leaders as a derogatory term for the prince of demons.</note> when he performed miracles. Or perhaps, because he revealed their thoughts, they thought he had a demon, believing the secrets of the heart were revealed to him by demons. <margin>Not all the Evangelists wrote that they called him a Samaritan.</margin> But when did they call him a Samaritan? For nowhere do the Evangelists say this. It is clear, then, that the Evangelists passed over many things and did not write everything, as we have noted in another place. Therefore, they bring forth such things for his dishonor; but he himself patiently takes the injuries upon himself. For while they were calling themselves sons of God, he vehemently

<column-break/>

### AN EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

<margin>A</margin> rebuked them, defending the truth. But when they treat him with injury, he does not take revenge, teaching us also to defend those things which are against God, but to bear mildly those things which are against ourselves. Just as he himself said mildly: "I," he says, "do not have a demon, but I honor my Father." But how did he honor the Father? By rebuking them and not allowing those who were murderers and liars to be called children of the Savior and of the truth. 

"You, therefore," he says, "because I honor my Father—whom you treat with injury when you falsely claim he is your father—for this reason you treat me with dishonor. But although I do not avenge myself, but endure it when I am treated with injury, <margin>B</margin> do not think this injury will go unpunished. For there is a Father who avenges me, because I am treated with injury for the reason that I avenge him, and I do not tolerate you who claim to be his sons. There is, therefore, one who seeks my glory, and who can also judge and condemn those who treat me with injury. For often someone seeks to take revenge but cannot judge himself. Therefore the Father both seeks the Son's glory and is able to judge; for this reason he said: 'There is one who seeks and judges.'"

"Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he shall not see death forever. Therefore the Jews said: 'Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham is dead, and the prophets, and you say: If anyone keeps my word, he shall not taste death forever.'"

O, what mercy! They treat him with injury, yet he, entrusting the question of his own glory and the defense of the Father, turns to admonition and teaching, doing good to those who pursue him with injury. In this way we also ought to avenge <margin>How one must take vengeance on enemies.</margin> ourselves on enemies. ### CHAPTER 8. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA
### AN EXPOSITION ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 389

...against me? He is so far from being held by death that he confers true life even more to others. <margin>D</margin> For those who believe, although they die naturally, yet they live in God. But what do the Jews say to this? They think he is possessed by a demon, because he says such strange things, as if he were out of his mind: "Have not Abraham and the prophets, who perceived the words of God with their ears, died? And yet you say those who listen to your words will not die?" Certainly now, they say, we have realized through many and abundant arguments that you say these things because you are driven by demons.

<margin>E</margin>
**"Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets are dead. Whom do you make yourself out to be? Jesus answered, 'If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say that he is your God, and yet you have not known him; but I know him. And if I say that I do not know him, I shall be a liar like you; but I know him and keep his word.'"** ] Those foolish men, since they did not understand of what "death" the Lord was speaking—a death that would not harm those believing in him—spoke most stupid and ignorant words to him. For look at how they respond: *Are you greater than our father Abraham?* Indeed, they ought to have said: *Are you greater than God?* Did those who heard the word of God die, while those who hear yours do not? But they did not say it that way. And what do they say? They wish to show him to be even lesser than Abraham. But the Lord himself does not reveal to them yet which "death" he meant; <margin>F</margin> however, a little later he persuades them that he is indeed better than Abraham. As for their question, *Whom do you make yourself out to be?*, they say this insultingly. "You, who are of no importance, the son of a carpenter, from Galilee—whom do you make yourself out to be? Not your works, nor the truth, nor the scriptures, but *you*—whom do you make yourself out to be? For you are seizing glory for yourself." But the Lord replies: *If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing,* just as you suppose. But now there is another who glorifies me: my Father. For the Father always glorifies him, through the prophecies written about him, through the testimonies from the heavens, and through innumerable and immense miracles. "And this Father," he says, "you claim is your God." But 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
you neither recognize him as my Father, nor as your God. For if you recognized him as Father, you would certainly treat his Son with honor. But since you do not honor the Son, it is manifest that you do not know him as my Father. Nor do you <margin>Exodus 20. Deuteronomy 5.</margin> know him as God; otherwise you would fear his words as the words of God. As it is, you despise him to such an extent that although he commanded "you shall not kill," you plot my death—and this when you cannot convict me of any sin. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that you are ignorant of him in every way. But I truly know him, having all knowledge of him by my very nature. For such as I am, such also is the Father. Therefore, because I know myself, he also knows me. *And if I say that I do not know him, I shall be a liar like you.* For you indeed lie by arrogantly saying that you know him; but if I were to say I do not know him when I truly do, I would be denying the truth. What evidence, then, do you bring that you know him? "Because," he says, "I keep his word," <note>original: "sermonem eius servo"</note> calling the commandments his "word." For I am not his adversary, nor do I speak arrogantly against God, nor do I break his commandments. But you, because you are transgressors of his words, and are gripped by evil desires, and thirst for slaughter, and do many other things forbidden by the law, clearly declare that you do not know him. For if you had known him, you would surely keep his word—that is, his commandments. Some, however, understand the phrase *I keep his word* in this way: <margin>C</margin> "I know him because I have within myself the 'word' of his essence <term>essence (Latin: *essentia*); the fundamental nature of what God is</term> diminished in nothing." That is to say, I possess the same definition and nature as the Father, a "word" <term>word (Latin: *sermo*); here used to mean the expression of one's internal substance</term> in no way inferior to his. For the nature is the same, and the word of substance is the same for the Father and the Son, and thus I know the Father: for I preserve the word of his substance in nothing less. Moreover, this is a common figure of speech in Scripture, where the word "and" is used to mean "for." For example, when it is said: *Give us help from trouble, and vain is the help of man.* <margin>Psalm 59.</margin> In this place, the conjunction "and" is placed instead of "for," so that the sentence has this meaning: *Give us help, for the help of man is vain.* So also in this place: *I know him, and I keep his word*—the conjunction "and" stands for "for."

For he indeed sufficiently taught them, both concerning himself and concerning the Father, and showed them true nobility and freedom, which is free from sins, and that the only foul slavery is that of sin; and in short, he left nothing undone of those things that were necessary, yet they stone him. Therefore he leaves them, because they would no longer receive correction. Note, however, that those stoning him were those of whom the Evangelist said that they "believed in him." For thus their faith was not true faith, but a certain temporary and cold affection for those things which were being said by Christ.

# CHAPTER IX.

<margin>D</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E featuring a scholar or saintly figure in clerical robes seated at a desk with an open book on a lectern, surrounded by ornate floral and foliage patterns.</image-desc>**And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man who was blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, saying, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"** ] The Lord indeed went out from the temple so that the fury of the Jews might be calmed; yet he turned to the healing of the blind man, attempting even through this sign to break their hardness and refusal to be persuaded, even though it would ultimately not benefit them. Furthermore, he showed them that it was not without cause, nor arrogantly, that he had said: "Before Abraham was, I am." For behold, he performs a miracle such as no one had ever done before.

<margin>B</margin>For even if someone had opened the eyes of a blind person, they had never done so for one blind from birth. It is manifest, therefore, that he is God and was before Abraham—he who did this, which has not been done since the beginning of the world. Moreover, he came to the blind man by deliberate effort; the man did not come to him. Consequently, when the disciples saw him looking so intently at the blind man, they asked: "Who sinned? This man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" Indeed, the question seems rather cold <note>The author uses "cold" (frigidior) to mean illogical or lacking sense in this context.</note>. For how could he have sinned before he was born? For the apostles had not accepted the Gentile nonsense <note>The "Gentile nonsense" refers to the Platonic or Pythagorean idea of the transmigration of souls, where a soul might be punished in a new body for sins committed in a previous life.</note> that a soul, living in another world before the body, might sin and then receive a certain punishment upon descending into a body. For being fishermen, they had never heard such a thing, because these were the doctrines of philosophers.

<margin>F</margin><margin>John 5.</margin>The question seems foolish, therefore, but only to one who does not pay close attention. Learn, then, what the apostles were thinking: when Christ said to the paralytic, "Behold, you are made whole; sin no more, lest a worse thing happen to you," and they then saw this blind man, they were in doubt and said something like this: "Suppose that man was a paralytic because of his sins—but what would you say of this one? Did he himself sin? But you cannot say this, for he has been blind from birth. Was it his parents? But a son is not punished for his father." Therefore, they do not so much ask a question as voice their doubt. But the Lord, resolving their doubt, says: "Neither has this man sinned (for how could he have sinned before he was born?) nor his parents." He does not say this as if he were acquitting 

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>them of all sins. For he did not simply say that the parents had not sinned, but added, "that he should be born blind." For his parents had indeed sinned, but the blindness did not come to him from that. For it is not just that children who do not act unjustly should be afflicted for the sins of their parents; and God teaches this through Ezekiel, saying: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the <margin>Ezekiel 18.</margin>children’s teeth are set on edge." <note>This is a famous biblical proverb. Theophylact is arguing against the idea of inherited guilt leading to physical disability.</note> He also placed this law before Moses: "A father shall not die for his son." But someone might say: "How is it written <margin>Exodus 20.</margin> that he returns the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation?" It must be said, therefore, first that this sentence is not general, nor spoken against everyone, but only against those who went out of Egypt. Furthermore, one must pay attention to the meaning. For he did not say this because children are punished for the sins of their fathers, but that the sins of the fathers—that is, the punishments—are to be inflicted also on their children *insofar as they have committed similar offenses.* For lest those <margin>When the children of sinners have been followers of their parents' sins, they bear the full punishments.</margin> who went out of Egypt think that because their parents sinned more heavily, they themselves would not be punished with the same penalties, he says: "It shall not be so; but the sins of the fathers—that is, the punishments—shall also reach you, because you have not become better, but have committed the same and worse sins." Moreover, when you often see children die, and that because of the parents' punishment, know that God takes away their life out of mercy, so that those who survive do not become worse than their parents, living to the harm of their own souls and many others. However, the abyss of divine judgments keeps these things within itself. Let us proceed to the following.

<margin>C</margin>**Jesus answered, "Neither has this man sinned, nor his parents; but that the works of God might be made manifest in him. I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. Night comes when no man can work. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world."** ] Behold, here is another doubt. For someone will ask: "How was this said? Was a man deprived of light and treated with such injury just so the works of God might be manifested? Could they not be manifested otherwise? With what injustice was he treated?" He was deprived of light, the objector says. But what kind of loss is it to be deprived of physical light and yet have the eyes of the soul illuminated? And so the blindness turned into a good for him, since through the healing he came to know the true Sun of Justice.

<summary>Theophylact interprets the healing of the man born blind, explaining that his disability was not a result of pre-natal sin or inherited guilt, but an opportunity for God's power to be revealed. He refutes the idea of reincarnation and addresses the theological difficulty of children suffering for their parents' sins.</summary>

### CHAPTER 9. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 392

<margin>

Therefore, the man born blind was not treated with injustice but actually received a benefit. Furthermore, you should know this, whoever you are who searches the Divine Scriptures: "so that" and "in order that" <note>original: ἵνα & ὅπως</note>—which in our language mean "that"—are often used in Scripture not to indicate the *cause*, but to designate the *result*. It is just as David said: *...that you may be justified in your words.* <note>Psalm 51:4 (50:6 in the Latin Vulgate numbering). Theophylact is arguing that David did not sin for the purpose of making God look just, but that God’s justice was the result revealed after the sin.</note> For David did not sin so that God might be justified, but because, as a consequence of David's sinful acts, it happened that God was justified. For when God had given him so much, though he was not worthy to receive it, and he himself had nonetheless transgressed the command of God, committing murder and adultery, and had abused his kingship in contempt of God—what else resulted from that crime but that God, who was judging and contending with David, should be entirely justified and appear victorious while the king was condemned? Because he rejected the One from whom he had received his kingdom, even while he was king. For if he had been a private citizen, he could not easily have committed those two evils at once. Do you see how here, "that you may be justified," speaks not of the cause, but of the result? There are countless other examples in the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> as well. For the knowledge of God is manifest among the Gentiles, *so that they might be without excuse*—though God did not give knowledge to the Gentiles for the purpose of them sinning without excuse. For He gave it so they would *not* sin; yet because they did sin, the knowledge they had resulted in them being without excuse. And again: *The Law entered so that condemnation might abound.* Although it was given to suppress sin, because those who received the Law did not wish to restrain it, the Law became for them an abundance of sin; for it was imputed more heavily to them since they sinned despite having the Law. Thus, in this place as well, *so that the works of God might appear in him* designates the result, not the cause. <margin>A Comparison.</margin> For from the fact that the blind man was healed, it is understood that God is glorified. For just as an architect often works on a house in parts, leaving one part unfinished so that if someone does not believe he is the one who built it, he can demonstrate by finishing the incomplete part that he is indeed the creator of the whole structure; so too our God, Jesus, by healing the blinded members and restoring them to their proper nature, shows that He is the one who created the other members as well. In saying, however, *that the glory of God might be manifested,* He speaks of Himself, not the Father. For the Father's glory was already manifest, but it was necessary to manifest His own glory—that He Himself was the one who had made man from the beginning. And clearly it was no small glory to

<column-break/>

manifest that He, who now appeared as a man, was the same God who created humanity. But that He says this about Himself, listen to what follows. For He added: *I must work the works of Him who sent me.* "I must," He says, "manifest myself and do works that can show I do the same things as the Father." Observe how He did not say, "I must work *similar* works to those the Father does," but *those very works* which the Father does. For He says, "I must work *those* works"—the very works that He who sent me performs. "But I must work these things as long as it is day," that is, as long as this present life lasts, so that men may be able to believe in me. For "the night is coming in which no one can work," which means to believe. For He calls "faith" a work. Therefore, in the future age, no one can believe. For the present life is "day" because we are able to work now as if in the light. Although Paul calls this life "night," because in it a person is ignorant of who works virtue or who works sin, and because, compared to the future light, it shines less brightly upon the righteous. "Night," however, refers to the future age because no one will be able to work there—though Paul calls that same age "day" because then the righteous shine as if in light, and the deeds of each person are made manifest. Therefore, in the future age, there will be no "faith" [as a choice], but both the willing and the unwilling will obey. "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world," because through my teaching and the display of miracles, I illuminate souls; thus it is necessary for me to enlighten the souls of many by healing this blind man and illuminating the pupils of his eyes. For since I am the Light, it is necessary for me to enlighten both physically and spiritually.
<margin>Ephesians 6. Faith will not exist in the future age.</margin>
When He had said this, He spat on the ground and made clay from the saliva, and smeared the clay over the eyes of the blind man, and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam" (which, if interpreted, means *Sent*). So he went and washed, and came back seeing. In saying these things, Jesus was not content with words alone, but added an action. For He spat on the ground and made clay and anointed the eyes of the blind man, showing through the clay that He is the same one who formed Adam out of the clay. For to say, "I am the one who formed Adam," would have seemed too arrogant to the listeners, but when shown through an action, it did not offend so much. Therefore, He forms eyes for him out of clay in the manner of a craftsman, by which Adam also was formed. Yet He did not merely form the eyes, nor only open them, but He also granted the ability to see, which is a sign that He also breathed a soul into Adam.

<summary>Theophylact explains that the man's blindness was a means for God's glory to be revealed as a result, not a punishment, comparing Jesus to an architect who finishes a building to prove his authorship. He interprets the use of clay in the healing as a symbolic link to Jesus's role as the Creator who formed Adam from the earth.</summary>

<margin>D</margin>
For when the eye does not perform its function, even if the organ itself exists, it does not see. Furthermore, He anoints the eyes with spit because He was about to send him to Siloam <note>A pool in Jerusalem; the name means "Sent."</note>, so that the miracle would not be credited to the waters of the spring. Instead, let us learn that by the power proceeding from His mouth, He Himself formed and opened the man's eyes; for this reason, He spat on the ground and made mud from His mouth. Next, so that you do not think the miracle belonged to the earth itself, He commands that all the mud be washed away. Some, however, say that the mud was not washed away, but was actually formed into an eye.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Why Christ sends the blind man to Siloam.</margin>
Moreover, He commands him to go to Siloam, partly so that we might learn of the blind man's faith and how obedient he was. He did not think to himself, "Since mud and spit have been applied to my eyes, why do I need Siloam to wash?" Instead, he obeyed the one giving the command. Furthermore, it was to confound the ingratitude of the Jews; for it was likely that many had seen him with the mud smeared over his eyes and had observed him closely, so they could not later say, "This is he," or "This is not he." Thirdly, by sending him to Siloam, He showed that He was not opposed to the Old Law. For this reason, the Evangelist also provides the interpretation of "Siloam," so that you may learn that Christ healed him there, and that Siloam is a figure <note>A symbolic representation or "type."</note> of CHRIST. For just as the spiritual rock is Christ, so also the spiritual Siloam is Christ. And just as that stream of Siloam appeared suddenly and with a more powerful, terrifying flow, so also the coming of the Lord—hidden and unknown even to the angels—washed away all sin by His power.

<margin>F</margin>
Therefore the neighbors, and those who had seen him before when he was a beggar, said, "Is this not the one who used to sit and beg?" Others said, "This is he." Others again said, "He looks like him." But he said, "I am he." They said to him, therefore, "How were your eyes opened?" He answered and said: "That man who is called JESUS made mud, and anointed my eyes, and said to me, 'Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.' So when I went and washed, I received my sight." Struck by the wonderful miracle, the neighbors were incredulous, even though his journey to Siloam with mud-anointed eyes was intended to ensure many would see him and not later deny it as if they did not know where he came from; nevertheless, they are still unbelieving. Now, the Evangelist did not note without reason that he was a beg-

### ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

<margin>A</margin>
-gar, but rather to show the ineffable mercy of the Lord, which stoops down even to the weak, such that He would care for even a beggar with the greatest diligence. And from this we ourselves might learn not to despise the lowly. The blind man, neither blushing at his former blindness nor fearing the people, confesses: "I am he," thus preaching of his benefactor. He says, "A certain man, who is called Jesus." He calls the Lord a "man" because he had not yet recognized anything great about Him; he confesses as much as he knew at that time. But how did he know that it was Jesus? From the conversation with the disciples. For because certain disciples had questioned Jesus about him, He spoke many things to them, namely: *I must work the works of Him who sent me...* <note>John 9:4</note> and that *I am the light of the world.* <note>John 9:5</note>

<margin>B</margin>
No one else taught such things except Jesus alone. And He used those words frequently. From this, the blind man recognized that it was Jesus. For he recognized the one making the mud and anointing his eyes through the sense of touch. He did not recognize Him by the spitting in the same way, for he did not know it happened since He had not yet moved toward him or applied it. Thus He was truly a man.
They said to him therefore, "Where is he?" He said, "I do not know." And they lead the man who had been blind to the Pharisees. Now it was the Sabbath when JESUS made the mud and opened his eyes. Therefore the Pharisees also questioned him again how he had received his sight. But he said to them, "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see."

<margin>C</margin>
Some of the Pharisees therefore said, "This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath." Others however said, "How can a man who is a sinner perform such signs?" And there was a dissension among them. Since the Lord, when healing and performing miracles, was accustomed to withdraw (because He was far from all ostentation), the blind man, when questioned, says, "I do not know." He was speaking entirely truthfully in this as well. But they lead him to the Pharisees so that he might be questioned more diligently and exactly. Furthermore, the Evangelist pointed out that it was the Sabbath to show their malice—that they seized an occasion against CHRIST and argued against Him because of the violation of the Sabbath, and thus they tried to overshadow the miracle. ...had opened his eyes, slandering the Lord in every way because He had worked on the Sabbath, forcing the blind man to recall that He made mud—on the Sabbath, of course. He, however, as if speaking to those who had already heard the story, mentions neither the name of Jesus nor what the Lord had said to him, but only: "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see." For it was likely that he had heard the Pharisees—from those who were bringing him to them—perhaps accusing Jesus and saying, "Look at what things Jesus does on the Sabbath." It is worth seeing the freedom of the blind man in speaking, as he addresses the Pharisees without fear. For they were indeed trying to force him, so that, struck with fear, <margin>E</margin> he might deny the healing. But he cries out more clearly, "I see." Therefore, some of the Pharisees—not all, but the more impudent ones—were saying: "This man is not from God." But others said: "How can a man who is a sinner do such things?" Do you see how many are softened by signs <note>miracles</note>? Behold, even these were Pharisees and rulers, yet they are appeased by the sign and take up a defense. And there was a division among them. This division first arose among the crowd: for some said one thing, and others another. But now it also arises among the rulers. And many of the Pharisees were divided from them and became patrons of the miracle. Nevertheless, although they were divided, they pressed forward for Christ rather half-heartedly, doubting and being double-minded rather than firm. <margin>F</margin> Hear indeed what they say: "How can a man who is a sinner do such things?" Do you see how gently they press the point? But observe also the malice of those who bring the accusations. They do not care that He does not keep the Sabbath; they cry out from top to bottom not about the benefit [of the healing], but announcing the violation of the day. Note also this: how the rulers are slower toward the good than the crowd. For the crowd was already divided in their opinions, and not all were speaking harshly because of Christ. The rulers, however, came later to this <margin>Matt. 10.</margin> praiseworthy dissension. For it is even good to disagree, just as the Lord says: "I have come to send a sword upon the earth," <note>original Latin: "Gladium veni mittere super terram"</note> by which opinions are divided toward everything good and pious.

<margin>A</margin>
They said to the blind man again: "What do you say of Him, who opened your eyes?" He said: "He is a prophet." Therefore the Jews did not believe concerning him that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of him who had received his sight and questioned them, saying: "Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?" Those who were questioning the blind man, asking "What do you say of Him?" were clearly perhaps from the well-disposed group. For after they had said, "How can a sinner do such signs?" they brought him in as a witness so that they would not seem to be patronizing the one who had received the benefit in vain. In this way, through the one who had felt the power, they might refute the slanderers. See indeed how <margin>B</margin> kindly they question him. For they did not say, "What do you say of Him who made mud because He did not keep the Sabbath?" but they remember the miracle: "Because He opened your eyes." It is as if they were sharpening the one who was cured so that he might say things worthy of CHRIST. For they bring it back to his memory: "Because He opened your eyes, He followed you with a benefit," they say, "and thus you ought to proclaim Him." Therefore the blind man then confesses what he could: that He is not a sinner, but from <margin>The Jews, who break the Sabbath with their whole hand, rebuke Christ.</margin> God. "For He is a prophet," he says. This was despite others saying that He was not from God because He did not keep the Sabbath. Even though Christ seemed to break the Sabbath with one finger because He had anointed the mud, they themselves, breaking the Sabbath with their whole hand by slaughtering animals for use on the Sabbath, <margin>C</margin> seemed to be pious. Therefore, the harsh and unpersuadable ones call his parents, wanting to make them entangled and thus deny the son's blindness. For because they could not obstruct his grateful mouth, they made his parents hesitant, standing them in the middle and questioning them with much fury—indeed, with much malice. For they did not say, "Is this your son, who was formerly blind?" but "whom you say," as if saying, "whom you made out to be blind," everywhere sowing that speech, pretending and lying. But O wicked Pharisees! Would a father lie like that against his own son? They press them in two narrow places and force them to deny their son by saying, "whom you said," and "how then does he now see?"

<margin>D</margin>For you see that they recount this sign <note>original: "signum," referring to the miracle</note>, which he saw afterward, in such a way as if they were claiming that people had lied about him being blind previously. For either what he himself now says is a lie, or the fact that he was blind is a lie; but the latter is the truth, for he clearly sees now. Therefore, according to them, it must be a lie that you preached he was blind before.

But his parents answered them and said, "We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind; but how he now sees, we do not know; or who opened his eyes, we do not know. He is of age, ask him; he will speak for himself." His parents said these things because they feared the Jews. For the Jews had already conspired that if anyone should confess Him to be the Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, <margin>B</margin>"He is of age, ask him." The Pharisees had presented three questions to the parents of the blind man: whether he was their son, whether he was born blind, and how he had received his sight. They indeed admit the first two—that he was their son and that he had been blind—but they claim ignorance of the manner of the healing. This was done entirely so that the confession of the truth might become stronger; thus, he who had actually felt the benefit and was more worthy of belief might testify to those things, just as his parents say, "he is of age." Is he a fool or stupid, that he would not understand how he was healed? His parents said these things because they feared the Pharisees, the text says; thus they were still untrained <note>in faith</note> and more ignoble than their son. For the son remained an unshaken witness of the truth, and so the eyes of his mind were also enlightened.

Therefore they called again the man who had been blind, and said to him, "Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner." He therefore answered and said, "Whether he is a sinner, I do not know; one thing I know, that whereas I was blind, now I see." They said to him again, "What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?" He answered them, "I have told you already, and you did not listen; why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?" <column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>insisted that their son should be questioned, these troublesome men do exactly that. They bring him forward not to ask questions, but so that material might be supplied for slandering the healer. For "Give glory to God" <note>original: "Da gloriam Deo"</note> means this: "Confess that Jesus worked nothing in you." For they think it is to the glory of God to attest to nothing good regarding Jesus. "For we know," they say, "that he is a sinner." Why then did you not convict him when he called out to you, saying, "Which of you convicts me of sin?" <margin>John 8</margin> But the blind man said, "Whether he is a sinner, I do not know." That is to say: "I am not examining this now, nor am I affirming it; but this I know clearly, that he performed a miracle upon me. Let the matter itself now be considered on its own merits, and let it pass judgment on itself." Then, because they were frequently questioning him—"What did he do to you?"—on account of the anointing with mud which was done on the Sabbath, they were laying snares for the Savior. The man perceived that they were prepared not for learning, but for catching him in his interrogation, and he answered them more sharply: "I no longer deem you worthy of my speech. For how many times have I told you, and you did not pay attention?" <margin>On John 5</margin> Then he adds what tortured them most: "Do you also want to become his disciples?" He declares, in effect, that he himself indeed wishes to be His disciple. Furthermore, he says these things while calmly attacking them, which was surely the mark of a free and intrepid soul that did not care for their madness. To his reproach they replied, "Be you his disciple; we are disciples of Moses." They appear to be liars even in this; for if they had been disciples of Moses, they would have been disciples of Christ as well, just as He said to them: "If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me." They did not say, "we have heard," but "we know that God spoke to Moses." However much they might have heard from their parents, they claimed to have exact knowledge regarding things they had only received through hearing. Yet the one whom they had seen with their eyes performing miracles, and whom they had heard speaking heavenly things, they called an impostor. You see the foolishness that arises from malice.

### CHAPTER 9. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN. 396

<margin>Whom God hears, and whom He does not.</margin>
...who opened the eyes of the man born blind. "Unless this man were from God, he could not do anything." <note>original: "Nisi esset hic a deo, nō potuisset facere quicquam."</note> He says: You, O Jews, have rejected him who healed me as if you do not know where he is from; but I say that he is all the more wonderful for this reason, because he is not one of the noble men among us, nor endowed with honor, yet he can do such things. And so it is manifest from every side that he is of a certain greater power and does not need human help. Furthermore, because some of them had previously said, "How can a man who is a sinner perform such signs?" he now adopts their own judgment, bringing their own words back to their memory. "For we all know," they say, "that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does His will, He hears him." Consider in this place how he not only declares the Lord free from sins, but also shows that He greatly pleases God and does all things that pertain to Him by saying: "but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does His will." Moreover, because he knew they wanted to overshadow the miracle, he proclaims its benefit: "For unless this man had been from God, he would not have performed such a miracle, the likes of which has not been seen since the world began." For perhaps the eyes of the blind have been opened before, but those were not blind from birth, but by some other accident; however, this thing which has now happened is rare. It is manifest, therefore, that he who performed such a miracle is greater than men. 
<margin>What it means that God does not hear sinners. Wisdom 1.</margin>
But some ask a cold and sophisticated question: how could he say that God does not hear sinners, when He hears those praying that their sins might be forgiven? For He is merciful. What then does it mean (they ask) when it says in this place, "He does not hear sinners"? One ought not even respond to such things, yet it must be answered: When it says God does not hear sinners, it means that God does not grant to sinners the performance of signs <note>original: "signorum operationem," referring to miracles</note>. For the Spirit does not dwell in a body subject to sins. Therefore, He hears those seeking the remission of sins truly and from the heart, not as "sinners," but as "penitents." For as soon as they seek forgiveness, they are transferred from the rank of sinners into the rank of penitents. It is likely, therefore, said that God does not hear sinners. For He does not 

<column-break/>

<margin>Faith and works are required in the worship of God. 1 Timothy 1.</margin>
<margin>Works and faith mutually give life to one another. James 2.</margin>
give the grace of signs to sinners. For how would He hear those whom He hates, even if they should sometimes ask for something, attributing to Him those things which do not suit Him? And although He hears those seeking forgiveness, He hears them not as sinners, but as penitents. Consider, however, how he said "if anyone is a worshiper of God," and immediately added, "and does His will." For many are indeed worshipers of God, but they do not do the will of God. It is necessary for both to be present: the worship of God and the fulfillment of the divine will—that is, faith and works; or (as Paul names it) faith and a good conscience; or to put it more briefly, contemplation and action <note>original: "theoriam & praxin," the Greek-derived terms for the visionary and active life</note>. For then faith truly lives, when it has works pleasing to God, from which a good conscience is born, just as from evil works a bad conscience is born; and again, works then live when they have faith. But separated from each other they are dead, just as when there is faith without works, it is dead, and works without faith are dead. See how the truth grants to a beggar of no importance the freedom of speech <note>original: "libertatem dicendi," or parrhesia</note> to rebuke those who are great and honored among the Jews. Such is the great power of truth, just as a lie brings a lack of freedom and a humbled speech follows it.

They answered and said to him, "You were born entirely in sins, and do you teach us?" And they cast him out. Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and when he had found him, he said to him, "Do you believe in the Son of God?" He answered and said, "Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?" And Jesus said to him, "You have both seen him, and it is he who speaks with you." And he said, "Lord, I believe," and he worshiped him. As long as they hoped the man would speak according to their wishes, they called him and questioned him often. But when they recognized from his answers that he did not favor their views but favored the truth, they despised him as one born in sins, quite foolishly throwing his blindness in his face and thinking it a curse, as if he had been condemned before birth to be born blind—which was devoid of reason. They cast him out of the temple as a witness <note>original: "confessorem," a confessor or one who testifies</note> to the truth and a son of lies. But see the gain! He was cast out of the temple, and immediately he found the Lord of the temple. He was despised as a beggar...

### CHAPTER 9. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

...by their rejection for Christ’s sake, and he was honored by the recognition of the Son of God. For it says that Jesus found him, coming to him as if by deliberate effort for this purpose: to console him, much like an <term>agnothetes</term> <note>original: "agnothetes"; a Greek term for the judge or president who presided over athletic games and awarded prizes.</note> consoles an athlete who has labored greatly, and to receive him as one who has earned the crown. And what does He say? "Do you believe in the Son of God?" Why does He ask "Do you believe?" after such a great dispute with the Jews and after so many words? He does this not out of ignorance, but wanting to make Himself known to the blind man. For when Jesus was healing him, the man had not yet seen Him clearly—how could he have, when he was being dragged here and there by those worst of dogs, the Jews? For this reason, Jesus now asks him, so that when the man asks who the Son of God might be, Jesus may consequently reveal Himself. Furthermore, He indicates to him that He highly values his faith, saying in a way: "This people treats you with contempt, but I have no care for them. I take account of the faith of a single man." But he replied, "Who is he, Lord, the Son of God?" He spoke these words with a soul full of longing. But the Lord said, "You have both seen him, and he who speaks with you is he." He did not say, "I am the one who healed you, who told you to go and wash," but at first He spoke humbly and somewhat obscurely. "You have seen him," He said; then more clearly, "And he who speaks with you is he." The Lord seems to say "You have seen him" with deliberate intent to bring back to the man's memory his healing, and that he had received the power of sight from Him. And the man believed immediately, and showed the work of a fervent and true faith by adoring Him, confirming by word and deed that he glorifies Christ as God. For the law cautioned that adoration <note>In this context, "adoratio" refers to the worship due to God alone.</note> must be paid to God alone.

<margin>Deuteronomy 6</margin>
¶ Understand, moreover, that this miracle was also fulfilled spiritually. For every human being was blind from birth—that is, from the time one is under the process of generation, to which corruption is entirely joined, and by which we are condemned and judged to mortality while we grow from that birth which is subject to passions. For from that time a certain thick mist, and perhaps a "tunic of skin" <note>original: "pellicea fortassis tunica"; a reference to the "garments of skin" in Genesis 3:21, which many Church Fathers interpreted as the mortal, physical nature of fallen humanity.</note> (as the sacred scriptures say), was poured over the eyes of our mind. Or even, the people of the Gentiles are blind. For they were also blind from birth, because they were blinded and deified those things which are created and corruptible, according to how their foolish hearts were darkened.

### EXPLANATION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

<margin>A</margin>
Such were the Persian Magi, who spent their lives on horoscopes and the prediction of future events. Jesus, therefore, saw this blind man—whether he represents every human being simply, or the Gentile people. For because he could not see the Creator, the Creator Himself visited us through the "bowels of mercy," rising from on high. How did He see him? By "passing by"—that is, not remaining in heaven, but proceeding through the words of His self-emptying <note>Referring to the "kenosis" or the humility of the Incarnation.</note>, looking down from the heavens according to the prophecy, and seeing all the sons of men. And in another sense, "passing by," He saw the Gentile people—that is, not coming to them first. For He came to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel. Then, as if in passing on the way, He made His visitation to that people who sat entirely in the darkness of all ignorance.

<margin>Luke 1</margin>
<margin>Psalm 13, 53</margin>
<margin>Matthew 15</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
How does He heal the blindness? When He had spat on the ground and made clay. For just as a drop descends to the earth, into the Holy Virgin, the eyes of this spiritual eye are anointed from the spit and the clay of the earth—that is, by the one Christ, who is from divinity (symbolized by the drop and the spit) and humanity (symbolized by the earth, from which the Lord’s body came). Is the end of healing, then, simply in believing? Not at all; but it is also necessary to go away to Siloam, the fountain of baptism, and be baptized in Christ. For as many of us as have been baptized spiritually have been baptized into Christ. Truly, when someone has been baptized, then he will also be subject to temptations. For he will be led before kings for the sake of Christ, who healed him.

<margin>Galatians 3</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Matthew 24</margin>
<margin>John 16</margin>
It is necessary, therefore, to conduct oneself firmly, and to stand constantly in confession, and not to deny Him out of fear; but even, if necessary, to become excommunicated. According to that saying: "You will be hated by all because of my name," and "they will put you out of the synagogues." They even cast out the one who confesses, for men hate the truth and persecute others for the sake of those things which they hold sacred and venerable—I mean riches and glory. For Jesus will find such people. And then, all the more, when one has been marked with disgrace by enemies, he will be honored by Christ with recognition and a more certain faith. For then he will all the more adore Christ, who appears as a man, yet is also the Son of God. For there is not one who is the Son of God and another who is the son of Mary. For this is the impiety of Nestorius <note>Nestorius was a 5th-century bishop whose teachings were condemned for appearing to divide Christ into two distinct persons (divine and human) rather than one person with two natures.</note>. Rather, there is but one Son of God.

### CHAPTER 10. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

...and of man. For see how the Lord, when the blind man says, "Who is the Son of God, that I may believe in him?" answers, "It is he," and "He who speaks with you is he." Who, then, was the one speaking? It was certainly he who was born of Mary and yet is the Son of God; they are not two different persons. Therefore, the holy 
<margin>Why Mary is called the Mother of God.</margin> 
Mary is properly called the <term>Mother of God</term> <note>original: "Θεοτόκος" (Theotokos); literally the "God-bearer," a title affirming that Jesus is one person who is both fully God and fully man.</note>, because she gave birth to the Son of God made flesh—one who exists indivisibly, a single person of dual nature, who is Jesus Christ.

[And Jesus said, "For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see; and those who see may become blind." And some of the Pharisees who were with him heard these things and said to him, "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now you say, 'We see,' therefore your sin remains."] After the Lord saw that the Pharisees were more offended by the miracle than they were helped by it, he declared them worthy of greater condemnation. As it happened, he says, "For judgment I have come," meaning for greater condemnation and punishment, so that those who do not see (the spiritually humble) may see, and those who see (the Pharisees) may become blind in the eyes of their souls. For behold, that man did not see from birth, and now he sees in both soul and body; but those who seem to see are blinded in their minds. For in this place, he speaks of two kinds of sight and two kinds of blindness. The Pharisees, however, always focused on physical things, thought he was speaking of physical blindness; they were only ashamed of this bodily blindness. But the Lord, wishing to show them that it would be better for them to be physically blind than to be unbelieving, said: "If you were blind, you would have no sin." For if you were blinded by a necessity of nature, pardon would be given to you while you struggled with unbelief. But now, because you claim to see, and have even clearly become spectators of this miracle worked on the blind man, yet you still persist in unbelief, you are not worthy of pardon. For your sin remains indelible. And you will be punished more severely because you are not drawn to faith by the miracles you see. Perhaps one might also understand it this way: "If you were blind," meaning, you ask about physical blindness, but I am speaking of the blindness of the soul. If you were

<column-break/>

blind—that is, ignorant of the Scriptures—you would not have such sin, because you would be sinning through ignorance. But now you say that you see, and you set yourselves up as wise men and experts in the law, and thus you are condemned by your own claims. You have a greater sin because you sin knowingly.

<margin>B</margin> ["Amen, amen, I say to you: he who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, the same is a thief and a robber. And what does he do? He sets forth the signs of the true shepherd and of the destructive wolf, and thus shows himself to be on the side of the good, taking testimony from his own works. First, he sets forth the signs of the destroyer. That man, 
<margin>C</margin> 
he says, does not enter through the door—that is, through the Scriptures. For he does not use the Scriptures or the prophets as witnesses. Indeed, the Scriptures are the "door" through which we are led to God. They do not allow the wolves to enter; they bar the heretics so that we may be secure, and they provide an explanation for all things we wish to know. Therefore, he who does not enter the sheepfold through the Scriptures is a thief, and is caught out by them. Instead, he "climbs up another way," meaning he prepares for himself another, unusual path, just as the corrupt do. Such a one will be the Antichrist. For his testimonies will not be from the Scriptures. Furthermore, he notes the scribes. ### CHAPTER 10. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.

Signs of a thief,

It belongs to a thief to leap over the fence and to do all things with danger. Have you seen the signs of a thief? See also what the signs of a shepherd are. For the shepherd enters through the scriptures, and the gatekeeper opens for him. By the "gatekeeper," he understands either Moses, to whom the divine oracles were entrusted. Moses opens to the 
<margin>John 5</margin>
Lord, speaking entirely about him, just as the Lord himself says: "If you believed Moses, you would surely believe me." Or, the Holy Spirit is the gatekeeper. For because the scriptures are understood and opened in the Holy Spirit, they reveal Christ to us; rightly then is the Holy Spirit the gatekeeper, in whom—as the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge—the scriptures are opened, through which the Lord enters into our care, and through which the shepherd is revealed. The sheep hear the voice of that shepherd. For because they <note>The Pharisees and critics of Jesus.</note> often called him a deceiver, and confirmed this out of their unbelief, saying, "Has any of the rulers believed in him?" Christ shows that he should not be considered harmful just because they do not believe, but rather that they themselves are to be cast out from the kind of the sheep. "For if I indeed," he says, "enter through the door, it is manifest that I am truly the shepherd. But you who have not followed, appear not to be sheep." From where does he lead out his own sheep? Either from the midst of the unbelievers, just as he led the blind man from the midst of the Jews, who both heard him and recognized him. And he also goes before the sheep, although it is otherwise with physical sheep; for shepherds usually walk behind them. But in this passage, he shows that he leads everyone to the truth: because he sends his disciples like sheep into the midst of wolves, 
<margin>Acts 5</margin>
and so the pastoral care of Christ is quite unique. But they will not follow a stranger, for they recognize the voice of strangers. Again, in this place, he notes <term>Theudas and Judas</term> <note>These were historical figures who led failed revolts in Judea; Theophylact uses them as examples of "thieves" who led people to ruin rather than truth.</note>, whom the sheep did not follow. For they stole away a certain few, and these dispersed after their deaths. But after Christ, both living and dead, the whole world especially followed. He also notes the <term>Antichrist</term>, for although he will seduce for a short time, he will not have those who follow his perdition. For that they do not follow him is made manifest by this: because after the death of those who seduce, there will be no one to attend to or follow them. The "door" is indeed the Scripture. The Lord leads the sheep out to pasture through this door. And what is the food? Either future delights, or the seat into which the Lord leads us.

<column-break/>

A Although in another place he calls himself the "door," it is not to be wondered at. For when he wishes to demonstrate his care toward us, he calls himself a shepherd; but when he wishes to show that he is the one who leads to the Father, then he calls himself a door; for he himself, according to one sense or another, is both sheep and shepherd. Moreover, if the words of the divine scriptures are the door, and the Lord himself is said to be the "Word," he is rightly called the door as well.

[Jesus spoke this <term>parable</term> <note>original: "parœmiam"; a proverb or enigmatic saying.</note> to them, but they did not understand what things he was speaking to them. Therefore Jesus said to them again, "Truly, truly I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not hear them."] Jesus spoke this parable, that is, a comparison, to them, speaking to them obscurely so that he might make them more attentive. Therefore, after he taught this, he now resolves the obscurity, saying: "I am the door." As for his saying that "all who came" <note>This refers to those who came without divine commission, not the holy prophets of the Old Testament.</note>, he is not speaking of the prophets, as the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>An ancient religious group that believed the physical world was evil and therefore rejected the Old Testament and its prophets.</note> rave. For they, wishing to show that the Old Testament is not from God and that the prophets were not sent by God, use this saying: "All who came before me are thieves and robbers." He is not, therefore, saying this about the prophets, but about other seditious people. That he says it of these is manifest. "For the sheep," he says, "did not hear them." For the sheep did not hear those seditious ones, but they did hear the prophets and believed through them. And otherwise, he said "they did not hear them" as a way of praising the sheep. For he is never seen to praise those who are disobedient to the prophets; on the contrary, he vehemently accuses and pursues them. Moreover, carefully note the word itself: "Whoever *came*," he says, not "whoever was *sent*." For the prophets indeed arrived having been sent; but the false prophets, 
<margin>Jeremiah 23</margin> <note>The text says Jeremiah 2. 27, but the quote is from Jeremiah 23:21.</note>
such as those seditious ones mentioned, came without being sent by anyone, just as the Lord said: "They were running, and I did not send them."

But the shepherd, such as the Lord is, knows His own sheep because He takes care of them, and in turn He is known by those whom He deems worthy of a visitation, and because of the familiarity of those who recognize their caretaker. See, however, that He is the first to know us, and then we [know] Him.

He emphasizes that Christ's care leads to both internal spiritual life and the external "pascua" or abundant rewards of the kingdom of heaven.</summary>

Yielding to it <note>This refers to Christ’s submission to the Father’s will or the natural order of his sacrifice.</note>, he says: "I myself have the power of my own death, as the lord of death." Therefore he says, "I have the power to lay down my life." Although each one of you has the power to lay down your own life—for it is possible for anyone who wishes to kill themselves—the Lord does not speak in this way. Rather, he means that against his will, no one is able to do this, which is not the case among men. For we are killed by others even against our will. But the Lord never suffered involuntarily, because he was not subject to death except insofar as he willed it. He also possesses something greater: that he may take up his life again. "This commandment," he says, "was received from the Father," that he should die for the world. "I am so far from being an adversary to God," he says, "that even this very act of dying was commanded to me by the Father." Furthermore, he first says something sublime: "I have the power to take up my life." For by this he shows himself to be the Lord of death and the leader of life. Then, by adding a humble word, he connects both so wonderfully that he is not considered inferior or a servant of the Father, nor an adversary to him, but of the same power and will.

And this was also beneficial to many of the listeners, because even as he spoke, a dissension arose. For while some, to whom these words seemed more obscure, thought he was driven by a demon and spoke things he did not understand; others, who understood these things even moderately, said, "These are not the words of one driven by a demon." Moreover, because they could not refute the others with words—for even those who were well-disposed did not fully grasp what was being said by the Lord, nor had they been persuaded by those words—they attempted to defend Christ by his works, saying that these are not the words of a demoniac. <margin>John 8</margin>

# CHAPTER 9. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA, ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN, COMMENTARY 405

<margin>The Law, that is, all scripture</margin>
...do you stone me? But they say: "Because of blasphemy we stone you, because you make yourself the Son of God." Yet he does not deny this, nor does he say, "I do not make myself God," or "I am not equal to the Father." Instead, he confirms their understanding and asserts that he is God based on what is written in the Law. By "Law," he refers here to the Book of David <note>original: "librum Dauid"; referring to the Psalms.</note>, as he simply calls all Scripture "the Law." The meaning of what he says is this: If those who received deification <term>deification: the process by which a human is made 'god-like' through God's grace</term> by grace are called "gods," and no one accuses them, how can I be justly rebuked by you? For I am God by nature, whom the Father has sanctified—that is, set apart—to be slain
<margin>What "holy" is called.</margin>
for the world. For that which is set apart for God is called "holy" <note>original: "Sanctum". Theophylact is explaining the Greek/Latin root of holiness as being "set apart" or "consecrated" for a specific divine purpose.</note>. It is clear, then, that the Father sanctifies and sets me apart for the salvation of the world; therefore, I am not equal to those other "gods," but am the true God. For it is truly the work of God to save, and not the work of a man who has merely been deified by grace. If, therefore, I am the one to whom the word of God was made—for I am the Word of God, and I dwelt in them and granted them to be adopted as sons—if they are therefore sons of God, I am much more beyond all blame in calling myself God, I who am God by nature and grant this status to others. Let the Arians
<margin>Arians and Nestorians are refuted</margin>
and Nestorians be confounded <note>The Arians claimed Jesus was a created being; the Nestorians were seen as dividing Christ's personhood. Theophylact defends the orthodox view of Christ's unified nature and eternal divinity.</note>. For Christ is the Son of God and God in substance and nature, and not a creature; he gives divinity to those he reaches, for he is the Word of God, but he himself is not deified by grace. For he clearly separates himself from those who are deified by grace because of what is said there; he shows that he is the very author of their deification, for he is the Word of God and dwells within them. This is what he signifies by saying "to whom the word of God was made," which means, those in whom he dwelt. How then do I blaspheme by saying I am the Son of God? For although I carry flesh and am from the seed of David, you are ignorant of the sacrament <note>original: "sacramentum"; here used in the sense of a "divine mystery" or "hidden plan."</note>, and that the fleshly nature of men could not have received familiarity with God in any other way than through the flesh, as if he had become familiar through a veil.

->If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if<-
->I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe the works, so that<-
->you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in him.<-

<column-break/>

Do you wish (he says) to know my equality with the Father? You cannot know it from my substance <term>substance: the essential nature or "being" of God, which remains invisible and incomprehensible</term>, for it is impossible to know the substance of God; but you can take judgment from the equality and identity of my works, an identity according to power. From these works you have the testimony of my divinity, and you shall know and believe that I am nothing other than what the Father is. For I have the same substance while remaining the Son and yet distinct. Similarly, the Father remains the Father, distinct in his personhood <term>hypostasi: the Greek term for an individual 'person' within the Trinity</term>, and is nothing other than the Father according to substance and nature. Although we differ by our persons, the persons are not separated; rather, they are in one another, Father and Son, without confusion. For just as among us
a father is separate from a son, even though they are one in nature, so it is in the divine persons, yet they are in one another without confusion. Because of this, we are called "three men" insofar as we exist separately and are not properly one being. But in the divine Trinity, there is one God and not three gods, because of the "mutual indwelling" <term>circumincessionem: also known as perichoresis, the theological concept that the three persons of the Trinity exist within one another</term> of the persons—and, one might add, because of their identical will.

They sought again to seize him, but he escaped from their hand and went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing, and he stayed there. And many came to him and said: "John indeed performed no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there. ] They sought to seize the Lord because they could not bear him offering such sublime testimony about himself; they could not endure his "higher theology." But he departed from there, yielding to their fury and allowing their sickness to be softened by his absence. He withdrew against their will, showing (as we have often said) that he would not have been held even on the cross unless he had surrendered himself voluntarily. Where did he go? Across the Jordan, where John baptized. He did not go there without reason, but to bring to mind the many things done and said there by John concerning him. The Evangelist adds that his stay there won over many people, saying, "And many came to him." And remembering the place, they said, "John indeed performed no sign..."

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus's defense against charges of blasphemy by distinguishing between humans "deified by grace" and Christ "God by nature," while also clarifying the relationship between the persons of the Trinity.</summary>

->CHAPTER 11. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA<-

none. Furthermore, what he says is this: If we believed him <note>Referring to John the Baptist</note> who never performed a sign, how much more should we believe him who worked so many and such great signs? Moreover, because John indeed bore witness concerning Christ but performed no sign, and for this reason perhaps might not have deserved as much faith, he added, saying: *But all things whatsoever John said of this man were true.* They do not affirm him <note>Jesus</note> based on him <note>John</note> anymore, but rather affirm him as faithful based on the things that Christ did. Therefore, he says, *many believed in him there.* By saying "there," he indicates that the place itself was wonderfully beneficial. Indeed, for this reason the Lord led the people out into solitary places, free from the company of wicked men, so that he might benefit them more; just as he is seen to have done in the Old Law. For having led them out of Egypt into the wilderness, he baptized and formed a people for himself by giving them the Law. Notice also the withdrawal of Christ, which happens spiritually. For he withdraws from Jerusalem—that is, the Jewish people—into a place having springs, namely the Church from the Gentiles, in which are the springs of baptism.

<margin>Baptism is signified by the crossing of the Jordan.</margin>
From which many approached him, crossing the Jordan, which is to say, baptism: for the crossing of the Jordan signifies the passage of baptism. For in no other way does one approach Jesus and truly become faithful, unless he passes through the baptism which is signified by the Jordan.

### CHAPTER XI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, in a pastoral landscape with hills and a building in the distance.</image-desc>
*Now a certain man was sick named Lazarus, of Bethany, from the village of Mary and Martha her sister. It was that Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment, and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was sick. Therefore his sisters sent to him, saying: "Lord, behold, he whom you love is sick."*] John alone mentions this history of Lazarus. He mentions it, however, to instruct us so that no one should take it hard if good men and those who are friends of God are gripped by disease, because even Lazarus, though he was a friend of Christ, fell ill. Nor should it be ignored that this was not that Mary who had anointed the Lord

with ointment, the prostitute <note>original: "meretrix"; a reference to the woman in Luke 7, whom many traditions conflated with Mary of Bethany.</note> who appears in Luke or Matthew, but another who was not a prostitute, but respectable, religious, and dutiful. For she diligently served Christ when he was received, as John testifies, and even has the testimony of having "chosen the better part." These sisters were so famous and admirable that even Lazarus himself was made better known 

<margin>Matthew 8. Luke 7. John 4.</margin>
through them. For he says, *Lazarus of Bethany was from the village of Mary and Martha.* But why did they send messengers to summon Jesus, and not come themselves, like the Centurion and the Royal Official? Because they trusted Christ greatly; and because they were women, it was not fitting for them to leave the home so easily; and because they were occupied with mourning and caring for their brother. That they did not do this out of contempt is manifest from what follows. For they exhibit great honor, piety, and constancy of prayer. In saying, *Behold, he whom you love is sick,* they wished to move the Lord to mercy, because they were mindful of the name of friendship. This word of the women also declares a certain faith. For they knew the Lord had such great power that they wondered how a man loved by him could suffer from infirmity. For it seems to hold a sort of wonder: *Behold, he whom you love is sick.*

*Jesus hearing this, said: "This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified by it." Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus.*

<margin>C</margin>
*When he heard therefore that he was sick, he remained in the same place for two days.*] Since he was going to remain there for two days, he said for that reason: *This sickness is not unto death,* even though it was unto death. But as I was saying, wishing to console the messengers so they would not grieve too much, he says: *This sickness is not unto death.* And in another sense, if you consider it well, the sickness was not unto death because those who have lived a long time die <note>meaning a permanent death</note>, but this was temporary and lasted four days. For because he rose after four days, looking at the end of the matter, we say the sickness was not unto death but for the glory of God: he adds, *that the son of God may be glorified,* for the glory of God—I mean the Father—is in nothing greater

# CHAPTER 10. THEOPHYLACT, ARCHBISHOP OF BULGARIA

<margin>The Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being and not of the same substance as God the Father.</note></margin>
<margin>The word "that" [ut] does not indicate the cause, but the outcome, as we have often said. For Lazarus did not fall ill specifically so that God might be glorified; rather, the illness happened for another reason, but the Lord used it for the glory of God.</margin>
<margin>Frequently</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
¶ For the Son is God, just as the Father is, properly and truly. For where there is one glory, there is also one substance. Therefore, the **Arians** are also confounded by this passage. You should not think the word "that" <note>original: *ut*</note> indicates the cause, but rather the outcome, as we have often said. For Lazarus did not fall ill *for the purpose* of God being glorified; rather, the infirmity came upon him for some other reason, but the Lord turned it to the glory of God. Moreover, he remained for two days until Lazarus expired and was buried, so that no one could say it was merely a heavy sleep or a trance, and that he had not truly died. For this reason, he waits so long that the body might even begin to decay, and his sister would say that he already smelled.

<margin>B</margin>
Then after this, he says to the disciples, "Let us go into Judea again." The disciples say to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?" Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because the light is in him." ] In no other place does he predict where he is about to go, but here alone he seems to announce it beforehand because the disciples were greatly afraid to go into Judea. Therefore, he predicts it so they are not disturbed by a sudden departure if they were being led into a region they feared. Because they were afraid both for him and even more for themselves—for they did not yet have perfect knowledge of Christ—they say, "The Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?" But he encourages them and says: "Just as he who sees the light does not stumble, but he who walks in the night stumbles; so too, he who does good and walks in enlightened works will experience nothing painful. But he who does evil will suffer. And so there is no need to be fearful. For we have done nothing worthy of death." Or even another way: "If he who sees the light does not stumble, much more so he who is with me—unless he falls away from me—does not stumble. And thus, since you are with me, who am the Light, you fear in vain." Others, however, understand the "day" to mean the time before the **Passion** <note>The suffering and death of Jesus.</note>, and the "night" to mean the time of the Passion itself. "You therefore," he says, "as long as it is day—that is, as long as the time of the Passion is not yet at hand—will not stumble. For you will not suffer persecution from the Jews, nor will any other heavy thing

<margin>A</margin>
befall you. But when the night comes—meaning my Passion—then certainly you will be humbled, retreating into a small house for fear of the Jews. From that time on, you will have afflictions and tribulations, and many obstacles and adversities, because I, who am the Light, will no longer dwell with you in the flesh; you will have a night of afflictions."

<margin>B</margin>
He says these things, and after this, he says to them, "Lazarus our friend sleeps, but I go that I may awaken him from sleep." His disciples therefore said, "Lord, if he sleeps, he will be well." But Jesus had spoken of his death; however, they thought he was speaking of the rest of sleep. Then Jesus said to them plainly: "Lazarus is dead, and I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, so that you may believe; but let us go to him." Therefore Thomas, who is called **Didymus** <note>Greek for "the Twin."</note>, said to the disciples, "Let us go also, that we may die with him." ] Since they had dreaded going into Judea, the Lord says to them, "Although the Jews were seeking to stone me—and they did this because I rebuked them by speaking to them—now I do not go to speak to them, but to visit a friend, and so there is no need to tremble. For I am not going for the same reasons as before, such that I should dread danger from the Jews, but I will awaken a friend from sleep."

<margin>C</margin>
But they, wishing to hinder him from the journey, said, "It is enough if he sleeps; he will be well." Therefore, there is no need for us to go, for it is not necessary. Even though he added, "our friend," to show the necessity of the journey there, they argued it was not necessary since he had been made "well" by sleeping. Indeed, not only is your arrival unnecessary, but even harmful to our friend. For if sleep is for his health (as we think), and you are going to wake him, you will be working against his health. Therefore, there is no need for you to go and wake him, for this would be harmful to him. So, when he saw they were still hesitant, he then said plainly: "He is dead." For what reason did he not say it plainly at first, but spoke hiddenly, calling death "sleep"? For many reasons. One, indeed, because he was far from boastfulness; for he did not wish, for the sake of showing off...

<summary>Theophylact explains Jesus's metaphor of the "twelve hours of the day" as a way to reassure his fearful disciples before returning to Judea. He also discusses why Jesus referred to Lazarus's death as "sleep"—to demonstrate humility and to ensure the miracle's timing proved Lazarus was truly dead.</summary>
